sets.title: Early surgery versus watchful management
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Early elective surgery versus watchful management for an asymptomatic arterial lesion.

Objective. To compare overall survival with early elective surgery and with watchful management in adults with an asymptomatic, slowly enlarging arterial lesion ("lesion type V").

Design. Randomised, open-label trial with blinded adjudication of the cause of death; median follow-up 5 years.

Setting and participants. 600 adults aged 55 to 80 years at 24 hospitals; 300 assigned to each group.

Interventions. Elective open repair within 6 weeks of randomisation, or surveillance imaging every 6 months with surgery if the lesion became symptomatic or reached a prespecified size.

Main outcome. Death from any cause.

Results.

OutcomeEarly surgery (n = 300)Watchful management (n = 300)
Death within 3 months of randomisation6.0%1.0%
Alive at 5 years (Kaplan-Meier estimate)70%58%
Hazard ratio for death over the whole follow-up (Cox model)0.95 (95% CI, 0.75–1.20)
Test of the proportional hazards assumptionP < .01 (assumption violated)

The Kaplan-Meier curves are shown in the figure; they crossed at about 18 months.

Conclusions. Early surgery increased short-term mortality and was associated with higher survival at 5 years.

sets.title: Oral drug K for acute pyelonephritis (non-inferiority trial)
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Objective. To determine whether a 7-day course of a new oral antibiotic, drug K, is non-inferior to the standard regimen of 1 day of intravenous antibiotic followed by 6 days of an oral antibiotic for acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis in women.

Design and setting. Open-label, randomized non-inferiority trial in 24 emergency departments; outcome assessors were blinded to group.

Participants. 1,200 nonpregnant women aged 18 to 65 years with acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis, randomized 1:1 (600 per group).

Main outcome. Clinical cure 14 days after the end of treatment. The prespecified non-inferiority margin was −10 percentage points for the difference in cure rates (drug K minus standard).

Results. In the drug K group, 31 women stopped treatment early or were switched to another antibiotic; in the standard group, 26.

AnalysisDrug K cureStandard cureDifference (95% CI), percentage points
Intention-to-treat528/600 (88.0%)540/600 (90.0%)−2.0 (−5.5 to 1.5)
Per-protocol500/560 (89.3%)512/565 (90.6%)−1.3 (−4.8 to 2.2)

Conclusions. Oral drug K met the prespecified criterion for non-inferiority in both analyses.

sets.title: Drug V for postoperative delirium (meta-analysis)
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Objective. To assess whether perioperative drug V prevents delirium in adults aged 65 years or older having surgery for hip fracture.

Data sources and selection. Systematic search of three bibliographic databases and two trial registries, without language restriction; randomized trials comparing drug V with placebo were included. Two reviewers independently selected trials, extracted data and rated risk of bias.

Results. Six trials (1,973 patients) were included. Two large trials were rated at low risk of bias; four small trials were rated at high risk of bias, mainly because of unclear allocation concealment and unblinded delirium assessment.

Conclusions. Drug V was associated with less postoperative delirium overall; the estimate was smaller and not statistically significant when restricted to trials at low risk of bias.

sets.title: A point-of-care assay for appendicitis in children
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Accuracy of a point-of-care blood assay (assay L) for acute appendicitis in children.

Objective. To measure the diagnostic accuracy of assay L in children with acute abdominal pain.

Design and setting. Prospective diagnostic accuracy study in two pediatric emergency departments. Assay L was measured at arrival; clinicians were blinded to the result.

Participants. 600 consecutive children aged 4 to 17 years with abdominal pain of less than 72 hours in whom the treating physician considered appendicitis.

Reference standard. Histopathology for children who had surgery; telephone follow-up at 6 weeks for the others.

Results. 150 children (25%) had appendicitis. The area under the ROC curve was 0.86 (95% CI, 0.82–0.90). Results at the lower of two prespecified cut-offs:

Assay L at cut-off ≥ 20 unitsAppendicitisNo appendicitis
Positive138135
Negative12315
Cut-offSensitivitySpecificity
≥ 20 units92%70%
≥ 40 units70%94%

Conclusions. Assay L discriminates well between children with and without appendicitis; the choice of cut-off depends on its intended use.

sets.title: A sleep medicine and hip fracture in older adults
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Use of drug V, a fictional prescription sleep medicine, and hip fracture in older adults: a case-control study.

Objective. To estimate the association between recent drug V use and hip fracture.

Design and setting. Case-control study nested in the records of 60 primary care practices. In the source population, the annual risk of hip fracture is about 1%.

Participants. 400 adults aged 65 years or older admitted with a first hip fracture (cases) and 800 adults without hip fracture matched by age, sex and practice (controls).

Exposure. A pharmacy record of drug V dispensing in the 90 days before the index date.

Results. Drug V had been dispensed to 80 cases (20%) and 80 controls (10%).

AnalysisOdds ratio (95% CI)
Crude2.25 (1.61–3.15)
Adjusted for frailty index, prior falls, body mass index, benzodiazepine use and dementia1.60 (1.10–2.30)
Adjusted, low daily dose1.20 (0.80–1.90)
Adjusted, high daily dose2.40 (1.40–4.10)

Conclusions. Recent drug V use was associated with hip fracture after adjustment, with a stronger association at higher doses.

Drug T to prevent gout flares
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A randomized trial of a new oral anti-inflammatory agent for gout.

Objective. To determine whether drug T, a fictional once-daily oral agent, prevents gout flares in adults with recurrent gout.

Design and setting. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled superiority trial at 40 outpatient rheumatology and primary care sites; allocation by central computer.

Participants. 1,200 adults with at least two gout flares in the previous year who were taking stable urate-lowering therapy.

Intervention. Drug T or matching placebo once daily for 12 months (600 per group).

Main outcome. At least one patient-reported, physician-confirmed gout flare during 12 months. Primary analysis by intention to treat.

Results.
OutcomeDrug T (n = 600)Placebo (n = 600)
≥1 flare in 12 months90 (15.0%)150 (25.0%)
Stopped study drug early96 (16.0%)30 (5.0%)
Relative risk of a flare, 0.60 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.76; P < .001). Diarrhoea was the most common reason for stopping drug T. In a per-protocol analysis restricted to participants who kept taking study drug, the relative risk was 0.48.

Conclusions. Drug T reduced the proportion of patients with gout flares over 12 months.

sets.title: Drug M and bone density
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A randomized trial of a new injectable agent in women with low bone mass.

Objective. To assess the effect of drug M, a fictional monthly subcutaneous injection, on bone mineral density (BMD).

Design. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 55 sites; follow-up 24 months.

Participants. 1,800 postmenopausal women aged 55 to 75 years with osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score −1.0 to −2.4) and no previous fragility fracture.

Intervention. Drug M or placebo monthly for 24 months (900 per group); all participants received calcium and vitamin D.

Main outcomes. Primary: percentage change in lumbar spine BMD at 24 months. Secondary: new clinical fractures.

Results. Lumbar spine BMD rose by 5.1% with drug M and 0.4% with placebo (difference, 4.7 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.1 to 5.3; P < .001). New clinical fractures occurred in 26 women (2.9%) given drug M and 28 women (3.1%) given placebo (relative risk, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.55 to 1.57). Injection-site reactions occurred in 7% versus 2%.

Conclusions. Drug M substantially increased BMD and should be considered for fracture prevention in postmenopausal women with osteopenia.

sets.title: Drug V and heart failure in diabetes
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A large outcome trial of a new oral agent in type 2 diabetes, with subgroup analyses.

Objective. To determine whether drug V, a fictional once-daily oral agent, reduces hospitalization for heart failure in adults with type 2 diabetes.

Design. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 300 sites in 20 countries; median follow-up 3 years.

Participants. 12,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor.

Intervention. Drug V or placebo (6,000 per group) added to usual care.

Main outcome. First hospitalization for heart failure.

Results. The primary outcome occurred in 240 participants (4.0%) given drug V and 294 (4.9%) given placebo (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.97). The investigators then examined 12 subgroups that had not been prespecified:
SubgroupHazard ratio (95% CI)P for interaction
Women0.62 (0.47 to 0.82).01
Men0.98 (0.79 to 1.21)
Age <65 years0.84 (0.66 to 1.07).78
Age ≥65 years0.80 (0.63 to 1.02)
The other subgroup comparisons showed no interaction.

Conclusions. Drug V reduces heart-failure hospitalization in women but not in men.

sets.title: Supplement Z and hip fracture
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A prospective cohort study of a dietary supplement and fracture risk in older adults.

Objective. To examine whether regular use of supplement Z, a fictional plant-based supplement, is associated with hip fracture.

Design and setting. Prospective cohort study using a community health survey linked to hospital records; follow-up 8 years.

Participants. 24,000 adults aged 60 years or older; 4,000 reported regular use of supplement Z at baseline. Compared with non-users, users were more likely to have a college education (58% vs 31%), exercise at least three times a week (64% vs 35%) and never have smoked (71% vs 52%), and less likely to report a fall in the previous year (12% vs 21%).

Main outcome. Hospitalization for hip fracture.

Results. Hip fracture incidence was 4.1 per 1,000 person-years in users and 6.0 per 1,000 person-years in non-users (crude hazard ratio, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.57 to 0.82). After adjustment for age, sex, education, income, smoking, physical activity and previous falls, the hazard ratio was 0.97 (95% CI, 0.82 to 1.15).

Conclusions. Users of supplement Z had fewer hip fractures than non-users.

sets.title: Drug S for chronic insomnia
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A randomized trial of a new hypnotic in adults with chronic insomnia.

Objective. To assess the efficacy and safety of drug S, a fictional nightly oral hypnotic, in chronic insomnia disorder.

Design and setting. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 30 sleep clinics; 12 weeks of treatment after a 2-week single-blind placebo run-in.

Participants. Adults aged 18 to 64 years with chronic insomnia disorder. Exclusions: age 65 years or older, untreated sleep apnoea, psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders and use of other sedating drugs. Of 930 people who entered the run-in, 290 (31%) were excluded before randomization because their sleep improved on placebo or they took fewer than 80% of doses; 640 were randomized.

Main outcomes. Primary: change in diary-recorded total sleep time. Secondary: change in a 0-to-28-point insomnia severity scale, for which the investigators prespecified a minimal clinically important between-group difference of 4 points.

Results. Total sleep time increased by 38 minutes with drug S and 22 minutes with placebo (difference, 16 minutes; 95% CI, 9 to 23; P < .001). Insomnia severity scores fell by 5.6 and 4.2 points (difference, −1.4 points; 95% CI, −2.2 to −0.6; P < .001). Next-morning dizziness occurred in 9% versus 3%. No falls were reported.

Conclusions. Drug S is effective and well tolerated in chronic insomnia.

sets.title: Kidney cancer screening programme
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A regional report on a screening programme using a fictional blood test.

Objective. To describe outcomes after a health region introduced annual screening for kidney cancer with KX, a fictional serum marker.

Design. Observational comparison of the 10 years before and after introduction of screening (2012 to 2022), with a neighbouring region that did not screen.

Population. Adults aged 55 to 75 years; 62% of eligible residents had at least one KX test.

Results.
MeasureScreening region, before → afterNeighbouring region, before → after
New kidney cancers per 100,000 per year14 → 2713 → 14
5-year survival after diagnosis62% → 84%61% → 63%
Kidney cancer deaths per 100,000 per year4.1 → 4.04.2 → 4.1
In the screening period, most screen-detected tumours were smaller than 3 cm. Five-year survival was 91% for screen-detected cancers and 58% for interval cancers (those diagnosed after symptoms appeared between annual tests).

Conclusions. KX screening improved survival from kidney cancer and should be expanded.

sets.title: Drug L in peripheral artery disease
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A randomized trial of an added antithrombotic agent with a composite primary end point.

Objective. To determine whether drug L, a fictional oral antithrombotic agent, added to aspirin reduces cardiovascular and limb events in symptomatic peripheral artery disease.

Design. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; median follow-up 3 years.

Participants. 8,000 adults with symptomatic peripheral artery disease (4,000 per group).

Main outcomes. Primary (efficacy): first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke or urgent limb revascularization. Primary (safety): major bleeding.

Results.
Outcome (first event)Drug L + aspirinPlacebo + aspirin
Primary composite400 (10.0%)500 (12.5%)
Cardiovascular death124 (3.1%)128 (3.2%)
Myocardial infarction80 (2.0%)84 (2.1%)
Ischaemic stroke60 (1.5%)56 (1.4%)
Urgent limb revascularization136 (3.4%)232 (5.8%)
Major bleeding112 (2.8%)64 (1.6%)
Hazard ratio for the primary composite, 0.79 (95% CI, 0.69 to 0.90).

Conclusions. Drug L reduced major cardiovascular and limb events by 21%.

sets.title: Drug E for vomiting in childhood gastroenteritis
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A randomized emergency department trial of a single antiemetic dose in children.

Objective. To determine whether a single dose of drug E, a fictional oral antiemetic, reduces the need for intravenous fluids in children with gastroenteritis.

Design and setting. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 6 paediatric emergency departments.

Participants. 500 children aged 1 to 10 years with acute gastroenteritis, at least one episode of vomiting in the previous 4 hours and mild to moderate dehydration. Children with severe dehydration, chronic illness or previous abdominal surgery were excluded.

Intervention. A single oral dose of drug E or placebo (250 per group), followed by oral rehydration.

Main outcomes. Primary: intravenous fluids given within 72 hours. Seven secondary outcomes, including hospitalization and return visit to the emergency department within 72 hours.

Results. Intravenous fluids were given to 20 children (8.0%) in the drug E group and 35 (14.0%) in the placebo group (P = .03). Return visits occurred in 15 (6.0%) and 28 (11.2%) children (P = .04). The other six secondary outcomes did not differ significantly.

Conclusions. A single dose of drug E reduces intravenous fluid use and return visits in children with gastroenteritis.

sets.title: Herbal product W and liver injury
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A case-control study of an over-the-counter herbal product and acute liver injury.

Objective. To examine whether use of product W, a fictional herbal weight-loss tea, is associated with acute liver injury.

Design and setting. Case-control study at 5 hospital liver units.

Participants. Cases: 240 adults with acute liver injury after viral, alcohol-related, autoimmune, biliary and other drug causes had been excluded. Controls: 960 outpatients matched for age, sex and hospital.

Exposure. Use of product W in the 90 days before symptom onset (cases) or interview date (controls), by structured interview.

Results. Product W had been used by 43 cases (17.9%) and 38 controls (4.0%) (odds ratio, 5.3; 95% CI, 3.3 to 8.4). The odds ratio was 3.1 for up to one serving a day and 8.4 for more than one serving a day. Among 12 exposed cases with repeat testing after stopping product W, aminotransferase levels returned to normal in 11 within 3 months.

Conclusions. Product W use is strongly associated with acute liver injury.

sets.title: A septic shock trial stopped early
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Intravenous kelvastan, an investigational drug, added to standard care in septic shock.

Objective. To determine whether kelvastan reduces 28-day all-cause mortality in adults with septic shock.

Design. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 41 intensive care units. A planned sample of 2,400 participants; two interim analyses after one third and two thirds of participants completed 28 days, reviewed by an independent data and safety monitoring board using prespecified group sequential boundaries that were very strict at early looks.

Participants. Adults within 12 hours of meeting criteria for septic shock. Most were enrolled with consent from a legally authorized representative.

Intervention. Kelvastan or matching placebo infusion for 5 days, plus usual care.

Main outcome. Death from any cause by day 28. Survivors entered a planned 1-year follow-up of function and quality of life.

Results. At the second interim analysis, 1,500 participants had 28-day outcomes, and the efficacy boundary was crossed. On the board's recommendation, enrolment was stopped.

OutcomeKelvastan (n = 750)Placebo (n = 750)
Death by day 28165 (22.0%)225 (30.0%)
Serious adverse events96 (12.8%)90 (12.0%)

Relative risk of death 0.73 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.87).

Conclusions. The authors conclude that kelvastan reduces 28-day mortality in septic shock. The drug is not yet approved by the FDA.

Interpreter type and discharge comprehension
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Objective. To compare discharge comprehension among emergency department patients with limited English proficiency by the type of interpretation used.

Design and setting. Prospective cohort study at two urban emergency departments. The type of interpretation was whatever was used in routine care; investigators did not assign it.

Participants. 500 adults with limited English proficiency who were discharged home. Interpretation at discharge was by a professional interpreter (in person, telephone or video) for 300 patients and ad hoc (a family member or untrained bilingual staff member) for 200 patients. Ad hoc interpretation was more common on night shifts and in the busiest hours.

Main outcomes. Primary: correct explanation of the diagnosis and medication instructions (teach-back) during a telephone call 48 hours after discharge, scored by an assessor unaware of the interpretation type, using a professional interpreter. Secondary: return emergency visit within 14 days.

Results.

OutcomeProfessional (n = 300)Ad hoc (n = 200)
Correct teach-back240 (80%)110 (55%)
Return visit within 14 days24 (8%)24 (12%)

After adjustment for age, language and triage level, the odds ratio for correct teach-back with professional interpretation was 2.9 (95% CI, 1.9–4.4). The difference in return visits was not statistically significant (P = .14).

Conclusions. Professional interpretation at discharge was associated with better comprehension.

sets.title: Clinician teach-back training and anticoagulant knowledge
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). Objective. To test whether training primary care clinicians in teach-back improves patients' understanding of a new oral anticoagulant.

Design and setting. Cluster-randomized trial in 12 primary care practices; 6 practices were randomized to a 2-hour teach-back training for all clinicians and 6 to usual care.

Participants. 640 adults starting a once-daily oral anticoagulant (drug K) for atrial fibrillation or venous thromboembolism.

Intervention. After explaining the new medication, trained clinicians asked patients to describe in their own words how and when they would take it and what to do about a missed dose or bleeding, then re-explained anything missed.

Main outcomes. Correct answers on a 5-item knowledge check at 2 weeks; any self-reported dosing error by 3 months.

Results. Knowledge check fully correct: 78% intervention vs 60% control. Any dosing error: 9% vs 15%. Analyses accounted for clustering by practice. Mean visit length was 1.5 minutes longer in intervention practices.

Conclusions. Teach-back training improved anticoagulant knowledge and reduced dosing errors at a small cost in visit time.

Design and setting. Cross-sectional anonymous survey of residents in all specialties at 14 US teaching hospitals during one month.

Participants. 1,200 residents completed the survey (response rate 61%).

Measures. Burnout was defined by high scores on a validated burnout inventory. Residents reported whether they had made a major medical error in the previous 3 months.

Results.

sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A health system's quality office reports the following analysis.

Objective. To examine malpractice claims before and after a communication-and-resolution program.

Design. Retrospective comparison of two consecutive 4-year periods. No comparison hospitals were studied.

Setting. Four acute care hospitals in one fictional regional health system in the United States.

Intervention. Beginning in the second period, clinicians were trained and required to disclose adverse events promptly and to apologize; each event was investigated; and when care was judged unreasonable, the system offered compensation before any claim was filed.

Main outcomes. New malpractice claims per patient-day; months from claim to resolution.

Home telemonitoring after heart failure admission: a cost-utility analysis
sets.introHtml:
Study summary (fictional). A cost-utility analysis of a home telemonitoring programme for heart failure, built on patient-level data from a randomised trial.

Objective. To estimate the costs and health effects of Program R (daily home weight and symptom transmission with nurse follow-up) compared with usual care.

Design and setting. Health-system perspective; 5-year horizon; costs and effects discounted at 3% a year; 6 community hospitals.

Participants. 1,240 adults discharged after a heart failure admission, randomly assigned to Program R or usual care.

Main outcome measures. Total health-system costs per patient; quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) per patient.

Results.

GroupStrategyMean cost per patientMean QALYs per patient
All participantsUsual care$18,4003.10

In one-way sensitivity analyses for all participants, the incremental ratio ranged from $22,000 to $48,000 per QALY.

items.stemHtml: A prospective cohort study enrols 1,000 adults with normal blood pressure. Over 5 years, 600 participants complete the full 5 years of follow-up, and 400 withdraw after an average of 2.5 years. A total of 60 participants develop hypertension during the study. Which of the following is the incidence rate of hypertension, per 1,000 person-years?
items.explanationHtml:
An incidence rate uses person-time at risk as its denominator. The completers contribute 600 × 5 = 3,000 person-years and those who withdrew contribute 400 × 2.5 = 1,000 person-years, for 4,000 person-years in total. Incidence rate = 60 ÷ 4,000 = 0.015 per person-year = 15 per 1,000 person-years. (Strictly, people who developed hypertension stop contributing at-risk time at diagnosis; the stem's simplified figures ignore this.)

Person-time lets each participant contribute exactly the time they were observed, which is why rates are preferred when follow-up is uneven. Exam stems signal this with withdrawals, late entry or different follow-up lengths.

Takeaway: incidence rate = new cases ÷ total person-time actually observed at risk.

whyNot.A: 12 assumes all 1,000 people were followed for 5 years (5,000 person-years), crediting the withdrawals with time nobody observed.
whyNot.C: 20 counts only the 3,000 person-years from completers and ignores the time contributed by those who withdrew.
whyNot.D: 24 applies the 2.5-year follow-up of the withdrawals to every participant (2,500 person-years).
whyNot.E: 60 per 1,000 is the proportion of participants who became cases (60 of 1,000), a cumulative incidence, not a rate per person-year.

items.objective: Calculate an incidence rate using person-time when follow-up is incomplete.

items.stemHtml: In a stable population, a chronic skin disorder has an incidence of 4 new cases per 1,000 people per year. Once it develops, the disorder lasts an average of 5 years before it resolves. Incidence and duration have not changed for many years. Which of the following is the best estimate of the prevalence of the disorder, per 1,000 people?
items.explanationHtml:
In a steady state with a fairly uncommon condition, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration: 4 per 1,000 per year × 5 years = 20 per 1,000 (2%).

The relationship explains why chronic conditions with long duration have a prevalence many times their annual incidence, and why therapies that change duration change prevalence without changing incidence.

Takeaway: P ≈ I × D in a steady state; multiply, don't divide or add.

whyNot.A: 0.8 divides incidence by duration instead of multiplying.
whyNot.B: 1.25 divides duration by incidence, which has no epidemiologic meaning.
whyNot.C: 4 is the annual incidence; it ignores that each case remains prevalent for about 5 years.
whyNot.D: 9 adds the incidence and the duration, combining numbers with different units.

items.objective: Estimate prevalence from incidence and average disease duration.

items.stemHtml: A national household survey asks 20,000 adults whether they have had wheezing or whistling in the chest at any time during the past 12 months. A total of 2,400 answer yes. The investigators report that 12% of adults were affected. Which of the following measures does this figure represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Cumulative incidence

options.label: B
options.html: Incidence rate

options.label: C
options.html: Lifetime prevalence

options.label: D
options.html: Period prevalence

options.label: E
options.html: Point prevalence

items.explanationHtml:
The survey counts anyone who had the symptom at any time during a defined interval (the past 12 months), whether it began before or during that interval. That is period prevalence: existing plus new cases during the period ÷ the population.

Cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence. Point prevalence uses a single moment ("do you have wheezing now?"); lifetime prevalence uses "ever". Incidence requires following people who were free of the condition and counting new onsets.

Takeaway: "at any time during the past X" → period prevalence.

whyNot.A: Cumulative incidence counts only new cases among people known to be free of the condition at the start; the survey did not exclude people who already wheezed.
whyNot.B: An incidence rate needs new cases over person-time of follow-up, which a single survey does not collect.
whyNot.C: Lifetime prevalence would ask whether the person had ever wheezed, not within the past 12 months.
whyNot.E: Point prevalence would ask about wheezing at the moment of the survey, not over a year.

items.objective: Distinguish point, period and lifetime prevalence from the wording of a survey question.

items.stemHtml: In one year, a town with a population of 50,000 records 450 deaths from all causes. During the same year, 400 residents are diagnosed with an acute infectious disease, and 20 of them die of it. Which of the following is the case-fatality rate of the infectious disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Case-fatality = deaths from the disease ÷ people who have the disease = 20 ÷ 400 = 5.0%. It measures how lethal the disease is for those who get it.

The other options are the other common measures built from the same numbers: the cause-specific mortality rate (20 ÷ 50,000 = 0.04%), the incidence (400 ÷ 50,000 = 0.8%), the crude mortality rate (450 ÷ 50,000 = 0.9%) and the proportionate mortality (20 ÷ 450 ≈ 4.4%).

Takeaway: case-fatality has cases in the denominator; mortality has the whole population in the denominator.

whyNot.A: 0.04% is the cause-specific mortality rate (deaths from the disease ÷ the whole population).
whyNot.B: 0.8% is the incidence (new cases ÷ population), which says nothing about lethality.
whyNot.C: 0.9% is the crude all-cause mortality rate of the town.
whyNot.D: 4.4% is the proportionate mortality: deaths from this disease as a share of all deaths.

items.objective: Distinguish case-fatality, cause-specific mortality, crude mortality and proportionate mortality.

items.stemHtml: Investigators study 2,000 workers at a quarry. Applying national age- and sex-specific death rates for chronic lung disease to the workers' age and sex structure predicts 30 deaths from chronic lung disease over the study period. The workers actually have 45 such deaths. Which of the following is the standardised mortality ratio for chronic lung disease in these workers?
items.explanationHtml:
Indirect standardisation compares observed deaths with the number expected if the study group had the reference population's age-specific rates. SMR = observed ÷ expected = 45 ÷ 30 = 1.5: the workers had 50% more deaths from chronic lung disease than expected for their age and sex structure.

Indirect standardisation suits small groups such as occupational cohorts, whose own age-specific rates would be unstable. An SMR above 1 means excess deaths; below 1, fewer than expected.

Takeaway: SMR = observed ÷ expected deaths.

whyNot.A: 0.33 is the excess (15) divided by the observed deaths, not a standardised ratio.
whyNot.B: 0.50 is the excess divided by the expected deaths, which is the SMR minus 1, not the SMR.
whyNot.C: 0.67 inverts the ratio (expected ÷ observed).
whyNot.E: 15 is the absolute number of excess deaths, not a ratio.

items.objective: Calculate and interpret a standardised mortality ratio.

items.stemHtml:
A state health officer compares two counties before deciding where to place a new cardiovascular prevention programme. County R has many retirement communities; County U is home to a large university. The table shows mortality from cardiovascular disease last year.

Measure (per 100,000 per year)County RCounty U
Crude cardiovascular death rate410150
Age-adjusted cardiovascular death rate (US standard population)165172

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by these data?

options.label: A
options.html: County R has a higher cardiovascular risk at every age

options.label: B
options.html: County U has markedly worse cardiovascular risk than County R

options.label: C
options.html: The difference in crude rates is mainly due to differences in age structure

options.label: D
options.html: The age-adjusted rates are invalid because they disagree with the crude rates

options.label: E
options.html: Cardiovascular deaths are underreported in County U

items.explanationHtml:
Crude rates reflect both age-specific risk and the age structure of the population. Once both counties are put on the same standard population, their rates are almost identical (165 vs 172 per 100,000). The large crude gap therefore comes mainly from County R's older population.

Age-adjusted rates are the right basis for comparing underlying risk between places with different age structures; crude rates and counts remain the right basis for planning how many patients each county must serve.

Takeaway: when crude rates differ but age-adjusted rates do not, age structure explains the difference.

whyNot.A: Age-adjusted rates are nearly equal, which argues against a higher risk at every age in County R.
whyNot.B: County U's age-adjusted rate is only slightly higher (172 vs 165); these figures do not show markedly worse risk.
whyNot.D: Crude and adjusted rates are expected to differ when age structures differ; that is the purpose of adjustment.
whyNot.E: Nothing in the data suggests underreporting; County U's low crude rate is explained by its young population.

items.objective: Interpret crude versus age-adjusted rates when comparing populations.

items.stemHtml: A county health department investigates pertussis among households. There are 12 households, each with one index case, and 60 other household members. Of these 60 people, 8 had laboratory-confirmed pertussis within the past year and are considered immune. Over the next 4 weeks, 13 of the household members develop pertussis. Which of the following is the secondary attack rate, to the nearest whole percent?
items.explanationHtml:
The secondary attack rate counts new cases among susceptible contacts. Susceptible contacts = 60 − 8 immune = 52. Secondary attack rate = 13 ÷ 52 = 25%. Index cases are excluded from both numerator and denominator.

The measure is used to judge how readily an infection spreads within households, schools or wards, and to compare the effect of prophylaxis or vaccination among contacts.

Takeaway: secondary attack rate = new cases among contacts ÷ susceptible contacts.

whyNot.A: 18% (13 ÷ 72) wrongly adds the 12 index cases to the denominator and leaves the immune contacts in it.
whyNot.B: 22% (13 ÷ 60) keeps the 8 immune contacts in the denominator, although they could not become cases.
whyNot.D: 35% (25 ÷ 72) mixes index and secondary cases and uses every household member as the denominator, which is an overall attack rate, not a secondary one.
whyNot.E: 48% (25 ÷ 52) wrongly adds the 12 index cases to the numerator.

items.objective: Calculate a secondary attack rate using only susceptible contacts.

items.stemHtml: A health system's planning committee is told that a newly approved one-time therapy permanently cures a chronic, non-infectious autoimmune liver disease that previously required lifelong treatment. The therapy does not change who develops the disease. The committee asks how the burden of the disease in its population will change over the next 3 years if the therapy is widely used. Which of the following is the most likely change?

options.label: A
options.html: Incidence decreases; prevalence decreases

options.label: B
options.html: Incidence decreases; prevalence is unchanged

options.label: C
options.html: Incidence is unchanged; prevalence decreases

options.label: D
options.html: Incidence is unchanged; prevalence increases

options.label: E
options.html: Incidence increases; prevalence increases

items.explanationHtml:
Incidence counts new cases; a cure does not prevent anyone from developing the disease, so incidence is unchanged. Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration, and a cure shortens duration, so prevalence falls.

For planning, a falling prevalence means fewer people needing long-term specialist follow-up and maintenance drugs, although each new patient still needs diagnosis and the curative treatment.

Takeaway: cures and deaths shorten duration and lower prevalence; only prevention lowers incidence.

whyNot.A: Incidence would fall only if the therapy prevented the disease; it treats people who already have it.
whyNot.B: This reverses the effect: the therapy changes duration (and so prevalence), not the occurrence of new cases.
whyNot.D: Prevalence rises when survival is prolonged without cure; a cure removes people from the pool of existing cases.
whyNot.E: Nothing about the therapy creates new cases; a rise in incidence would require more exposure or more detection.

items.objective: Predict how a curative treatment changes incidence and prevalence.

items.stemHtml:
A state epidemiologist is preparing a report on stroke mortality in Town A. To allow comparison with other towns, she will apply Town A's age-specific rates to the state's standard population.

Age groupTown A stroke death rate (per 1,000 per year)Town A populationStandard population
Under 65 years26,00070,000
65 years and older204,00030,000

Which of the following is Town A's age-adjusted stroke death rate, per 1,000 per year?
items.explanationHtml:
Direct standardisation applies the town's age-specific rates to the standard population. Expected deaths = 70,000 × 2/1,000 + 30,000 × 20/1,000 = 140 + 600 = 740 deaths among 100,000 people = 7.4 per 1,000.

Town A's crude rate is higher (9.2 per 1,000) because 40% of its population is 65 or older, compared with 30% in the standard population. Reporting the adjusted rate removes that difference so the town can be compared fairly with others standardised to the same population.

Takeaway: direct adjustment = Σ (study age-specific rate × standard population in that age group) ÷ total standard population.

whyNot.B: 9.2 is Town A's crude rate, weighted by its own older age structure (60% and 40%), not the standard population.
whyNot.C: 11.0 is the simple average of the two age-specific rates, which ignores the size of each age group.
whyNot.D: 14.6 swaps the standard weights, giving 70% weight to the older group instead of 30%.
whyNot.E: 22.0 adds the two age-specific rates, which double-counts the population.

items.objective: Calculate a directly age-adjusted rate.

items.stemHtml: An infection-prevention nurse reports central line-associated bloodstream infections for a medical intensive care unit. In one quarter, 150 patients had a central venous catheter, the unit recorded a total of 2,400 central line-days, and 6 infections occurred. Which of the following is the infection rate, per 1,000 central line-days?
items.explanationHtml:
Device-associated infections are expressed as an incidence density: infections ÷ device-days × 1,000. Here 6 ÷ 2,400 × 1,000 = 2.5 per 1,000 central line-days.

Using device-days rather than patients makes units comparable when catheters stay in for different lengths of time; a unit whose patients keep lines for weeks will otherwise look worse simply because exposure is longer.

Takeaway: hospital-acquired infection rates use device-days or patient-days as person-time.

whyNot.B: 4.0 is the percentage of patients infected (6 ÷ 150), a cumulative incidence per patient, not per 1,000 line-days.
whyNot.C: 6.0 treats the raw count as if it occurred over exactly 1,000 line-days.
whyNot.D: 25 results from a decimal-place error (6 ÷ 240 × 1,000).
whyNot.E: 40 is the number of infections per 1,000 patients (6 ÷ 150 × 1,000), which ignores how long the lines were in place.

items.objective: Express a hospital-acquired infection rate per 1,000 device-days.

items.stemHtml: A primary care network lowers the threshold it uses to diagnose a chronic metabolic disorder, after a professional society revises its diagnostic criteria. The network's electronic records are used to track the disorder. True biologic risk in the population is unchanged. Which of the following changes in the network's recorded data is most likely during the following year?

options.label: A
options.html: Recorded incidence and recorded prevalence both decrease

options.label: B
options.html: Recorded incidence and recorded prevalence both increase

options.label: C
options.html: Recorded incidence increases and recorded prevalence is unchanged

options.label: D
options.html: Recorded incidence is unchanged and recorded prevalence increases

options.label: E
options.html: Recorded incidence and recorded prevalence are both unchanged

items.explanationHtml:
Broader diagnostic criteria label people as having the disorder who would not have qualified before. Newly labelled people appear as new (incident) cases, and because the condition is chronic they then join the pool of existing (prevalent) cases. Both recorded incidence and recorded prevalence rise, although nobody's biology changed.

This is a common explanation for apparent epidemics of chronic disease after guideline changes or new tests. Before concluding that a condition is becoming more common, check for changes in definitions, testing and reporting.

Takeaway: a looser case definition raises both recorded incidence and prevalence.

whyNot.A: A stricter, not looser, definition would lower both measures.
whyNot.C: Newly diagnosed people with a chronic condition remain cases, so prevalence rises along with incidence.
whyNot.D: People newly meeting the criteria are counted as new diagnoses, so recorded incidence also rises.
whyNot.E: True risk is unchanged, but recorded measures depend on the case definition, which did change.

items.objective: Recognise that changes in diagnostic criteria alter recorded incidence and prevalence.

items.stemHtml: A region's vital statistics for one year record 25,000 live births and 120 fetal deaths at 20 weeks' gestation or later. Among infants born that year, 100 die before 28 days of age and a further 50 die between 28 days and 1 year of age. Which of the following is the infant mortality rate, per 1,000 live births?
items.explanationHtml:
Infant mortality rate = deaths before age 1 year ÷ live births × 1,000 = (100 + 50) ÷ 25,000 × 1,000 = 6.0 per 1,000 live births. Fetal deaths are not infant deaths and are not part of this measure.

The infant rate is the sum of the neonatal rate (deaths under 28 days: 100 ÷ 25,000 = 4.0) and the postneonatal rate (deaths from 28 days to under 1 year: 50 ÷ 25,000 = 2.0). Measures that include fetal deaths add them to the denominator.

Takeaway: infant mortality = deaths under 1 year per 1,000 live births = neonatal + postneonatal.

whyNot.A: 2.0 is the postneonatal mortality rate (deaths from 28 days to under 1 year).
whyNot.B: 4.0 is the neonatal mortality rate (deaths in the first 27 days).
whyNot.C: 4.8 is the fetal death rate (120 ÷ 25,120 × 1,000), which concerns stillbirths, not infants.
whyNot.E: 10.7 combines fetal and infant deaths over live births plus fetal deaths; this is not the infant mortality rate.

items.objective: Calculate the infant mortality rate and distinguish it from neonatal, postneonatal and fetal measures.

items.stemHtml: A ministry of health wants to report its maternal mortality ratio using the standard international definition. Officials have the number of deaths of women during pregnancy or within 42 days after its end from causes related to or aggravated by the pregnancy. Which of the following should be used as the denominator?

options.label: A
options.html: All deliveries, including stillbirths

options.label: B
options.html: All pregnancies, including miscarriages and induced abortions

options.label: C
options.html: Live births in the same period

options.label: D
options.html: The total female population

options.label: E
options.html: Women aged 15 to 49 years

items.explanationHtml:
The maternal mortality ratio is maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. Live births are used because they are counted reliably by vital registration, whereas all pregnancies are not (early miscarriages and many abortions go unrecorded). Because live births are a proxy for, rather than the true, population at risk, the measure is called a ratio.

A maternal mortality rate per women of reproductive age also exists, but it mixes the risk per pregnancy with how often women become pregnant, so it is not the standard figure for obstetric risk.

Takeaway: maternal mortality ratio = maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.

whyNot.A: Deliveries including stillbirths are not the standard denominator and are less consistently registered than live births.
whyNot.B: All pregnancies would be conceptually closer to the population at risk, but they cannot be counted reliably, so they are not used.
whyNot.D: The whole female population includes girls and older women who cannot be at risk of a pregnancy-related death.
whyNot.E: Women aged 15 to 49 years is the denominator of the less specific maternal mortality rate, not the ratio.

items.objective: Identify the denominator of the maternal mortality ratio.

items.stemHtml: A county health department calculates years of potential life lost (YPLL) before age 75 for one month. Five deaths were recorded, at ages 5, 25, 40, 60 and 80 years. Which of the following is the total YPLL for the month?
items.explanationHtml:
Each death before the cut-off contributes (75 − age at death); deaths at or after 75 contribute nothing. YPLL = (75 − 5) + (75 − 25) + (75 − 40) + (75 − 60) + 0 = 70 + 50 + 35 + 15 = 170.

YPLL gives more weight to deaths at young ages, so injuries, overdoses, suicide and perinatal conditions rank higher by YPLL than by death counts. It is used to set priorities for preventing premature death.

Takeaway: a death after the cut-off age adds zero YPLL, never a negative number.

whyNot.A: 130 uses a cut-off of 65 years instead of the stated 75.
whyNot.B: 165 subtracts 5 years for the death at age 80, as if a death after the cut-off could have negative YPLL.
whyNot.D: 175 adds 5 years for the death at age 80, counting the years lived beyond the cut-off.
whyNot.E: 210 is the sum of the ages at death, not years of life lost.

items.objective: Calculate years of potential life lost with a fixed cut-off age.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman lives alone. She bathes, dresses, uses the toilet, moves from bed to chair and feeds herself without help. Her son has noticed that over the past 6 months she has missed bill payments, run out of groceries and taken her blood pressure tablets twice on some days and not at all on others. Which of the following domains of functional status is impaired?

options.label: A
options.html: Basic activities of daily living

options.label: B
options.html: Continence

options.label: C
options.html: Instrumental activities of daily living

options.label: D
options.html: Mobility

options.label: E
options.html: Self-care

items.explanationHtml:
Paying bills, shopping and managing medications are instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), the more complex tasks needed to live independently in the community. Her basic ADLs (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, feeding) are intact.

IADLs are usually lost before basic ADLs, and new IADL impairment in an older adult is a common early sign of cognitive impairment that deserves evaluation.

Takeaway: money, medications, shopping, cooking, transport and the telephone are IADLs.

whyNot.A: Her basic ADLs, which include bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring and feeding, are all performed independently.
whyNot.B: Continence is a basic ADL, and nothing in the history suggests incontinence.
whyNot.D: She transfers and moves about her home independently, so mobility is not the impaired domain.
whyNot.E: Self-care tasks such as bathing, dressing and feeding are intact; her problems are with complex household tasks.

items.objective: Distinguish basic from instrumental activities of daily living.

items.stemHtml: A country's most recent period life table shows a life expectancy at birth of 78 years. The same table shows that people who have reached age 65 have a life expectancy of a further 20 years, to age 85. Which of the following best explains why 65 + 20 exceeds the life expectancy at birth?

options.label: A
options.html: Death rates are expected to fall over the next 65 years

options.label: B
options.html: Life expectancy at birth excludes deaths in the first year of life

options.label: C
options.html: People who reach 65 have already survived the deaths that occur at younger ages

options.label: D
options.html: The life table at older ages is based on a healthier sample of volunteers

options.label: E
options.html: Women make up a larger share of the population at older ages

items.explanationHtml:
Life expectancy at a given age is conditional on having survived to that age. Life expectancy at birth averages over everyone born, including those who die in infancy, youth and middle age; by age 65, those deaths have already happened, so the survivors' expected age at death is higher.

Period life expectancy is calculated from current age-specific death rates held constant. It is not a forecast and does not build in future improvement.

Takeaway: remaining life expectancy at older ages is conditional on survival, so age + remaining life expectancy rises with age.

whyNot.A: A period life table holds current death rates fixed; it does not assume future improvements in mortality.
whyNot.B: Infant deaths are included in life expectancy at birth; they are one reason it is lower than 65 + 20.
whyNot.D: A national life table uses death registrations and population counts for everyone, not a volunteer sample.
whyNot.E: A higher share of women at older ages affects the overall figure for both sexes combined, but it does not explain why the gap appears in each sex separately as well.

items.objective: Explain why life expectancy at older ages implies a higher expected age at death than life expectancy at birth.

items.stemHtml: A longitudinal study of 8,000 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older asks each participant to rate their own health in general on a single five-point item (excellent, very good, good, fair or poor). Participants also have a physical examination, blood tests and a record review for chronic diseases. Over 10 years of follow-up, which of the following findings about the single question is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: It predicts death only in participants with depression

options.label: B
options.html: It predicts death, but not after adjusting for diagnosed chronic diseases

options.label: C
options.html: It predicts death independently of diagnosed diseases and examination findings

options.label: D
options.html: It predicts hospital use, but not death

options.label: E
options.html: It does not predict any later health outcome

items.explanationHtml:
Self-rated health is one of the best-studied single measures of health status. In many cohorts, people who rate their health as fair or poor have higher mortality and more future disability than those who rate it as excellent, and the association persists after adjustment for diagnosed diseases, examination findings and laboratory results.

The question captures information that clinical measures miss: symptoms, early functional decline, undiagnosed disease, mood and the person's own sense of reserve.

Takeaway: self-rated health is a valid, independent predictor of mortality and decline.

whyNot.A: The association is seen across the population, not only in people with depression, although mood contributes.
whyNot.B: Adjusting for diagnosed disease weakens the association only partly; self-rated health remains an independent predictor.
whyNot.D: Self-rated health predicts mortality as well as health service use.
whyNot.E: Self-rated health has consistently predicted mortality, disability and service use in longitudinal studies.

items.objective: Recognise self-rated health as an independent predictor of mortality.

items.stemHtml:
A county health director reviews infant deaths for two consecutive years. Births were similar in both years.

Measure (per 1,000 live births)Year 1Year 2
Neonatal mortality (under 28 days)3.83.7
Postneonatal mortality (28 days to under 1 year)1.93.6
Infant mortality5.77.3

A review of death records finds that most of the additional deaths were sudden and unexpected and occurred during sleep. Which of the following interventions most directly addresses this change?

options.label: A
options.html: Antenatal corticosteroid programme for threatened preterm labour

options.label: B
options.html: Community campaign on safe infant sleep practices

options.label: C
options.html: Expansion of the county's neonatal intensive care beds

options.label: D
options.html: Expansion of prenatal screening for congenital anomalies

options.label: E
options.html: Universal newborn screening for inherited metabolic disorders

items.explanationHtml:
The rise in infant mortality is entirely in the postneonatal component, and most of the extra deaths were sudden unexpected infant deaths during sleep. Safe-sleep education (placing infants on their backs, on a firm, flat surface of their own, without soft bedding, pillows or bed-sharing) directly targets these deaths.

Neonatal deaths are driven mainly by prematurity, low birthweight, congenital anomalies and complications of delivery; postneonatal deaths are more often due to sudden unexpected infant death, infections and injuries. Splitting infant mortality into its components points to the right fix.

Takeaway: a rise in postneonatal mortality with sleep-related deaths calls for safe-sleep interventions, not neonatal intensive care.

whyNot.A: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce deaths from prematurity, which are mainly neonatal; neonatal mortality did not change.
whyNot.C: Neonatal intensive care addresses neonatal deaths, which were stable; the new deaths occurred after 28 days and at home during sleep.
whyNot.D: Congenital anomalies cause mainly neonatal deaths and were not identified as the cause of the increase.
whyNot.E: Newborn screening is valuable, but inherited metabolic disorders do not explain a rise in sudden sleep-related deaths.

items.objective: Use the neonatal and postneonatal components of infant mortality to choose an intervention.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old man is seen in clinic 2 weeks after discharge from a hospitalisation for heart failure. He lives alone in his own apartment. He bathes, dresses, uses the toilet and walks with a cane independently. His daughter, who lives 10 minutes away, reports that he has been confused about which of his seven medications to take and has missed several doses of furosemide. His Mini-Cog screen suggests mild cognitive impairment. He wants to stay in his apartment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Advise him to move to a skilled nursing facility

options.label: B
options.html: Arrange medication support such as pharmacy blister packs and home health nursing visits

options.label: C
options.html: Discontinue furosemide to simplify his regimen

options.label: D
options.html: Report his situation to adult protective services

options.label: E
options.html: Tell his daughter to take over all of his medical decisions

items.explanationHtml:
He has impaired instrumental activities of daily living (medication management) with intact basic ADLs. The appropriate response matches support to the specific deficit: simplify the regimen where possible, use pharmacy-filled blister packs or a pill organiser, involve his daughter as he agrees, and arrange home health nursing for medication supervision and heart failure monitoring. His cognitive impairment also warrants a fuller evaluation.

Functional assessment tells clinicians what help a patient needs to remain safely at home; it respects his wish to stay independent while reducing the risk of readmission.

Takeaway: IADL loss with intact basic ADLs calls for targeted support at home, not institutional care.

whyNot.A: Skilled nursing care is for people who need daily skilled or hands-on care; his basic ADLs are intact and he wants to stay home.
whyNot.C: Furosemide treats his heart failure; stopping it to simplify the regimen would risk decompensation rather than solve the adherence problem.
whyNot.D: There is no evidence of abuse, neglect or exploitation; difficulty with medications alone is not a reason for a protective services report.
whyNot.E: Mild cognitive impairment does not remove his capacity to make his own decisions; his daughter can help with his agreement but should not replace him.

items.objective: Match support to impaired instrumental activities of daily living in an older adult.

items.stemHtml:
A county board of health wants to focus its next prevention campaign on the cause responsible for the most premature mortality, measured as years of potential life lost before age 75. The table shows last year's deaths before age 75 by cause and the mean age at death among those deaths.

CauseDeaths before age 75Mean age at death (years)
Cancer15063
Heart disease12066
Motor vehicle crashes3533
Suicide3042
Unintentional drug overdose6036

Which cause accounts for the most years of potential life lost before age 75?

options.label: A
options.html: Cancer

options.label: B
options.html: Heart disease

options.label: C
options.html: Motor vehicle crashes

options.label: D
options.html: Suicide

options.label: E
options.html: Unintentional drug overdose

items.explanationHtml:
For deaths before the cut-off, YPLL = number of deaths × (75 − mean age at death). Cancer: 150 × 12 = 1,800. Heart disease: 120 × 9 = 1,080. Motor vehicle crashes: 35 × 42 = 1,470. Suicide: 30 × 33 = 990. Unintentional overdose: 60 × 39 = 2,340, the largest.

Overdose causes far fewer deaths than cancer, but they occur about 27 years earlier on average. Ranking by YPLL directs prevention toward causes that kill young people; ranking by deaths favours diseases of older age.

Takeaway: YPLL rewards preventing early deaths; a cause with fewer deaths can rank first.

whyNot.A: Cancer causes the most deaths (150), but at a mean age of 63 it accounts for 1,800 YPLL, less than overdose.
whyNot.B: Heart disease deaths occur late (mean age 66), giving only 1,080 YPLL.
whyNot.C: Motor vehicle deaths occur young, but there are only 35 of them, giving 1,470 YPLL.
whyNot.D: Suicide gives 30 × 33 = 990 YPLL, the smallest total in the table.

items.objective: Rank causes of death by years of potential life lost to set prevention priorities.

items.stemHtml: A rheumatology practice starts a group exercise and self-management programme for patients with knee osteoarthritis. The practice wants one outcome measure that shows whether the programme improves how patients manage their daily lives. Which of the following is the most appropriate primary outcome?

options.label: A
options.html: Change in erythrocyte sedimentation rate from baseline to 6 months

options.label: B
options.html: Change in radiographic joint-space width on standing knee films

options.label: C
options.html: Change in a validated patient-reported pain and function score

options.label: D
options.html: Number of clinic visits per patient during the programme year

options.label: E
options.html: Proportion of patients prescribed an opioid for knee pain

items.explanationHtml:
The question is about how patients function and feel day to day, so the outcome should come from the patient: a validated patient-reported outcome measure of pain and physical function. Such instruments are reliable, responsive to change and meaningful to patients.

Laboratory and imaging measures are surrogates that correlate poorly with symptoms in osteoarthritis, and utilisation measures reflect many factors besides health status.

Takeaway: to measure how a treatment changes daily life, use a validated patient-reported function or quality-of-life measure.

whyNot.A: Osteoarthritis is not a systemic inflammatory disease, and the ESR does not reflect pain or function.
whyNot.B: Joint-space width changes slowly and correlates poorly with symptoms and function.
whyNot.D: Visit counts reflect scheduling and access as much as health; they do not measure function.
whyNot.E: Opioid prescribing is a process measure influenced by prescriber habits and does not capture function directly.

items.objective: Choose a patient-reported functional outcome to measure health status.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man comes for an annual visit. He has well-controlled hypertension. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and examination and routine laboratory results are normal. On the intake questionnaire, he rates his overall health as "poor", although last year he rated it "very good". Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Everything we checked today looks fine, so there's no need to worry."

options.label: B
options.html: "I see you rated your health as poor this year. What has changed for you?"

options.label: C
options.html: "I'd like to order a full-body CT scan to be thorough."

options.label: D
options.html: "Poor self-ratings are common at your age and usually don't mean anything."

options.label: E
options.html: "Let's repeat the questionnaire next year and compare."

items.explanationHtml:
A fall in self-rated health is meaningful: it independently predicts mortality and functional decline, even when examination findings are normal. The best first step is to explore it with an open question. The answer often reveals depression, pain, a new symptom, functional loss, bereavement or financial strain that a targeted evaluation can address.

Exploring before acting is both good communication and good medicine; it guides any further testing rather than replacing it with blanket reassurance or blanket testing.

Takeaway: a patient's poor rating of their own health is a finding to explore, not dismiss.

whyNot.A: Premature reassurance ignores a valid warning sign and closes the conversation before the cause is known.
whyNot.C: Untargeted whole-body imaging has no evidence of benefit and exposes him to radiation and incidental findings.
whyNot.D: Poor self-rated health is not a normal part of ageing, and his rating fell sharply from last year.
whyNot.E: Waiting a year delays recognition of a potentially treatable problem behind the change.

items.objective: Respond to a decline in self-rated health by exploring its cause.

items.stemHtml:
A rural county with about 1,000 live births per year recorded 3 infant deaths last year and 6 this year. A local newspaper reports that the county's infant mortality rate has doubled. The county medical officer is asked to respond at a public meeting.

YearLive birthsInfant deathsInfant mortality (per 1,000 live births)
Last year1,01033.0
This year99066.1

Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Infant care in the county has deteriorated and needs urgent reorganisation

options.label: B
options.html: The change may be due to chance; several years of data should be combined and each death reviewed

options.label: C
options.html: The county's prenatal care programme should be ended because it has failed

options.label: D
options.html: The increase proves a new environmental hazard in the county

options.label: E
options.html: The rate cannot be calculated because the number of deaths is too small

items.explanationHtml:
With so few events, rates are unstable: a difference between 3 and 6 deaths is well within the range expected from random variation (counts of rare events vary roughly by their square root). The sound response is to combine several years (or neighbouring counties) to get a stable rate, compare it with state figures and review each death individually for preventable causes.

Overreacting to a single year's small-number change wastes resources and can damage effective programmes; ignoring it entirely would miss a real problem. Case review answers the question that the rate alone cannot.

Takeaway: rates based on a handful of events need pooling over time and case review before conclusions are drawn.

whyNot.A: One year's change of three deaths is not enough evidence of deterioration to justify reorganising services.
whyNot.C: There is no evidence linking the deaths to the prenatal care programme, and small-number variation is the likelier explanation.
whyNot.D: A doubling based on three extra deaths does not prove any cause, environmental or otherwise.
whyNot.E: The rate can be calculated; it is simply imprecise, which is why pooling and review are needed.

items.objective: Interpret vital statistics rates based on small numbers.

items.stemHtml:
Overall survival in a randomized trial of two regimens (A and B) for an advanced cancer is displayed as Kaplan-Meier curves in the figure.

What is the median overall survival in the regimen B group?

options.label: A
options.html: 7 months

options.label: B
options.html: 12 months

options.label: C
options.html: 18 months

options.label: D
options.html: 24 months

options.label: E
options.html: 30 months

items.explanationHtml:
The median survival is the earliest time at which the survival curve falls to 0.5 or below. Reading across from 0.5 on the vertical axis, the dashed regimen B curve first drops below 0.5 at 12 months (from 0.65 to 0.45). The solid regimen A curve does so at 24 months.

On the exam, draw a horizontal line at 0.5 and drop a vertical line from the point where each curve first meets or crosses it.

Takeaway: median survival is read at 0.5 on the y-axis, at the first point the curve reaches or falls below it.

whyNot.A: At 7 months regimen B drops from 0.80 to 0.65; more than half are still alive.
whyNot.C: By 18 months regimen B is already well below 0.5; 18 months is not where it first crossed.
whyNot.D: 24 months is the median for regimen A (solid curve), not regimen B.
whyNot.E: At 30 months only about a quarter of regimen B patients are alive; the curve crossed 0.5 much earlier.

items.objective: Read median survival from a Kaplan-Meier curve.

items.stemHtml:
The figure plots Kaplan-Meier survival curves for adults with advanced cancer randomly assigned to regimen A or regimen B.

Reading from the regimen A curve, approximately what percentage of these patients were still alive 12 months after randomization?
items.explanationHtml:
Go up from 12 months on the horizontal axis to the solid regimen A curve, then across to the vertical axis. The curve stepped down to 0.80 at 9 months and does not step down again until 15 months, so survival at 12 months is about 80%.

Flat segments of a Kaplan-Meier curve are periods with no events; the estimate at any time inside a flat segment equals the value after the last step.

Takeaway: survival at time t is read straight up from t to the curve and across to the y-axis.

whyNot.A: 45% is regimen B's survival at 12 months, read from the dashed curve.
whyNot.B: 65% is regimen B's value between 7 and 12 months, not regimen A's.
whyNot.C: 70% is regimen A's survival after its step at 15 months, later than 12 months.
whyNot.E: 90% is regimen A's survival between 4 and 9 months, before the step at 9 months.

items.objective: Read survival at a specified time from a Kaplan-Meier curve.

items.stemHtml:
A cancer trial reports survival with regimens A and B using the Kaplan-Meier curves shown in the figure.

Both curves carry small vertical tick marks. Which of the following do these tick marks represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Deaths that occurred at those times

options.label: B
options.html: Interim analyses of the accumulating data

options.label: C
options.html: Nonfatal events such as hospital admissions

options.label: D
options.html: The limits of the 95% confidence interval at those times

options.label: E
options.html: Participants whose follow-up ended without the event at those times

items.explanationHtml:
Tick marks on a Kaplan-Meier curve show censored observations: participants who left observation while still alive (the study ended, they withdrew or were lost to follow-up). The curve does not step down at a tick; censored people are simply removed from the number at risk from then on.

Deaths are shown as the downward steps. Censoring is not death, and treating censored participants as deaths would underestimate survival.

Takeaway: steps are events; ticks are censored participants.

whyNot.A: Deaths appear as the downward steps in the curve; the curve stays flat at a tick mark.
whyNot.B: Interim analyses are not marked on the curve; they are reported in the methods or results text.
whyNot.C: The curve tracks only the outcome being analysed (death), and other events are not drawn on it.
whyNot.D: Confidence limits, when shown, are drawn as separate bands or lines around the curve, not as ticks.

items.objective: Recognise censoring marks on a Kaplan-Meier curve.

items.stemHtml: In a cohort study of time to death in adults with advanced heart failure, participants who became too unwell to attend study visits stopped follow-up and were censored at their last visit. No further information was collected about them. Which of the following is the most likely effect on the Kaplan-Meier survival estimate?

options.label: A
options.html: It overestimates survival

options.label: B
options.html: It underestimates survival

options.label: C
options.html: It is unbiased because censored participants are removed from the number at risk

options.label: D
options.html: It is unbiased because censoring affects only the width of the confidence interval

options.label: E
options.html: It cannot be calculated when censoring occurs

items.explanationHtml:
The Kaplan-Meier method assumes non-informative censoring: people censored at a given time have the same future risk as those who remain under follow-up. Here the opposite is true. The sickest participants, who were most likely to die soon, left observation; those remaining at risk are healthier than the original cohort, so the curve stays too high and survival is overestimated.

The exam signal is a reason for drop-out that is linked to prognosis (too ill to attend, moved to hospice). Remedies include active tracing of vital status through registries and sensitivity analyses.

Takeaway: informative censoring of sicker patients biases Kaplan-Meier survival upward.

whyNot.B: Underestimation happens when censored people are wrongly counted as deaths, or when healthier people preferentially drop out; here the sicker ones left.
whyNot.C: Removing censored people from the risk set is unbiased only if their prognosis matches those who remain, which it does not here.
whyNot.D: Informative censoring biases the point estimate itself, not only its precision.
whyNot.E: Handling censoring is the reason the Kaplan-Meier method exists; the estimate can be calculated, but here it is biased.

items.objective: Explain how informative censoring biases a Kaplan-Meier estimate.

items.stemHtml: Investigators randomly assign 400 adults with a newly diagnosed lymphoma to one of two regimens and follow them for up to 5 years. Many participants are censored because they enrolled late in the study. The investigators want to test whether the entire survival experience differs between the two groups. Which of the following statistical methods is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Chi-square test comparing the proportions alive at 2 years

options.label: B
options.html: Correlation coefficient between regimen and survival time

options.label: C
options.html: Log-rank test

options.label: D
options.html: Paired t test of survival times

options.label: E
options.html: Two-sample t test comparing mean survival times

items.explanationHtml:
The log-rank test compares two or more survival curves over the whole follow-up period. At each event time it compares the observed number of deaths in each group with the number expected if survival were the same, and it uses the information from censored participants correctly.

Methods that ignore censoring or that look at one arbitrary time point lose information or give biased answers. The log-rank test gives a P value; the size of the effect is usually expressed as a hazard ratio from a Cox model.

Takeaway: comparing Kaplan-Meier curves → log-rank test.

whyNot.A: A chi-square test at one time point discards the timing of events and the information from people censored before 2 years.
whyNot.B: A correlation coefficient describes linear association between two continuous variables and cannot handle censoring or a binary treatment variable properly.
whyNot.D: A paired t test compares two measurements in the same individuals, but each participant here has only one survival time.
whyNot.E: Mean survival cannot be calculated validly when many survival times are censored, because their true values are unknown.

items.objective: Choose the log-rank test to compare survival curves.

items.stemHtml: A randomised trial of a new drug in adults with pulmonary fibrosis reports a hazard ratio for death of 0.60 (95% CI, 0.45–0.80) for drug versus placebo over 4 years of follow-up. The proportional hazards assumption was met. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: At the end of the trial, 60% fewer patients in the drug group had died

options.label: B
options.html: Each patient in the drug group had a 0.60 probability of dying during the trial

options.label: C
options.html: Median survival was 40% longer in the drug group

options.label: D
options.html: Throughout follow-up, patients still alive in the drug group had about a 40% lower rate of death

options.label: E
options.html: The result is not statistically significant because the interval is wide

items.explanationHtml:
A hazard ratio compares the instantaneous event rates among people still at risk. An HR of 0.60 means that, at any time during follow-up, the death rate in the drug group was about 40% lower than in the placebo group. Because the assumption of proportional hazards was met, this ratio applies across the whole follow-up period. The 95% CI (0.45–0.80) excludes 1.0, so the result is statistically significant.

An HR is not a ratio of cumulative proportions, not a probability and not a statement about median survival; translating it into absolute benefit needs the event rates.

Takeaway: HR 0.60 = 40% lower hazard (instantaneous rate) at any point in time, not 40% fewer deaths overall.

whyNot.A: The HR compares rates over time, not the proportions who died by the end; and 0.60 would mean 40% lower, not 60% lower.
whyNot.B: A hazard ratio is a ratio of rates between groups, not the probability of death for an individual.
whyNot.C: A lower hazard does not translate into a fixed percentage increase in median survival; that depends on the shape of the curves.
whyNot.E: The interval 0.45–0.80 does not include 1.0, so the result is statistically significant.

items.objective: Interpret a hazard ratio and its confidence interval.

items.stemHtml: A reader notes that the overall hazard ratio for death is 0.95 with a confidence interval that includes 1.0, yet 5-year survival differs by 12 percentage points. Which of the following best explains why the overall hazard ratio should be interpreted with caution in this trial?

options.label: A
options.html: The confidence interval for the hazard ratio excludes 1.0, so the result is significant

options.label: B
options.html: Censoring was more common in the surgery group than in the watchful group

options.label: C
options.html: Kaplan-Meier curves are not valid for comparing groups in randomised trials

options.label: D
options.html: Survival at 5 years was the same in both groups despite the early deaths

options.label: E
options.html: Surgery's effect on the death rate changes over time, so one ratio averages early harm and later benefit

items.explanationHtml:
A Cox hazard ratio is a single average ratio that assumes the relative effect is constant over time (proportional hazards). Here that assumption is violated: the curves cross at about 18 months, with more early deaths after surgery and fewer later. Averaging an early harm with a later benefit produces a ratio near 1.0 that describes neither period.

When curves cross, report time-specific results (early mortality, survival at 5 years) or analyses that allow the hazard ratio to change over time.

Takeaway: crossing survival curves mean non-proportional hazards; a single hazard ratio is then misleading.

whyNot.A: The interval 0.75–1.20 includes 1.0; the problem is not significance but what the ratio represents.
whyNot.B: The summary gives no evidence of different censoring between groups, and censoring would not explain crossing curves.
whyNot.C: Kaplan-Meier estimation is standard in randomised trials; it is the single hazard ratio that is problematic here.
whyNot.D: Survival at 5 years differed (70% vs 58%), which is part of why the near-null hazard ratio is misleading.

items.objective: Recognise non-proportional hazards when survival curves cross.

items.stemHtml: Based on the 5-year survival estimates, how many patients need to undergo early surgery rather than watchful management for one additional patient to be alive at 5 years?
items.explanationHtml:
Absolute difference in 5-year survival = 70% − 58% = 12 percentage points = 0.12. NNT = 1 ÷ 0.12 = 8.3, rounded up to 9, because a fraction of a patient cannot be treated and rounding down would overstate the benefit.

At the population level, for every 100 patients offered early surgery, about 12 more would be alive at 5 years, at the cost of about 5 extra deaths in the first 3 months (6% vs 1%, NNH = 20). Presenting both numbers lets patients and policy makers weigh the trade-off.

Takeaway: NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk difference, rounded up, for a stated time frame.

whyNot.A: 4 is 1 divided by the relative reduction in 5-year mortality (12 ÷ 42 ≈ 29%), which uses a relative instead of an absolute difference.
whyNot.B: 8 rounds 8.3 down; NNT is always rounded up to the next whole patient.
whyNot.D: 12 is the absolute difference expressed in percentage points, not its reciprocal.
whyNot.E: 17 is the reciprocal of the 6% early surgical mortality, which ignores the comparison group and the later benefit.

items.objective: Calculate a number needed to treat from survival proportions.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man who meets the trial's entry criteria asks what the study means for him. Which of the following statements best reflects the trial's findings?

options.label: A
options.html: "About 6 in 100 people die in the first 3 months with watchful management."

options.label: B
options.html: "Surgery doubles the chance of being alive at 5 years."

options.label: C
options.html: "Surgery is safer than watchful management at every point after the operation."

options.label: D
options.html: "Surgery has a higher risk of death in the first 3 months, but more people are alive at 5 years."

options.label: E
options.html: "Surgery made no difference to survival, because the hazard ratio was close to 1."

items.explanationHtml:
The trial shows a time-dependent trade-off: mortality in the first 3 months was 6% with surgery and 1% with watchful management, but at 5 years 70% of the surgery group and 58% of the watchful group were alive. A statement that names both the early risk and the later benefit, in absolute terms, is accurate and lets the patient weigh them according to his own values.

Shared decision-making is especially important when one option front-loads risk; some patients will prioritise avoiding the early risk, others the long-term gain.

Takeaway: when curves cross, counsel with time-specific absolute risks, not one summary ratio.

whyNot.A: The 6% early mortality occurred after surgery; watchful management had 1% mortality in the first 3 months.
whyNot.B: 5-year survival rose from 58% to 70%, a relative increase of about 21%, not a doubling.
whyNot.C: Surgery carried a higher risk of death in the first months; the curves cross only at about 18 months.
whyNot.E: The near-null hazard ratio averages an early harm and a later benefit and does not mean surgery has no effect.

items.objective: Counsel a patient about a treatment with early harm and later survival benefit.
