items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman with newly diagnosed metastatic pancreatic cancer has read that, for the chemotherapy regimen she will receive, "median overall survival was 11 months". She asks whether that means she has 11 months to live. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Yes, 11 months is the most likely amount of time you have left to live."

options.label: B
options.html: "Most people on this treatment die within 11 months of starting it."

options.label: C
options.html: "Half the people in that study were alive at 11 months, and some lived much longer."

options.label: D
options.html: "Those statistics don't apply to you, so it's best not to read them at all."

options.label: E
options.html: "You should ask your oncologist; I can't discuss survival figures with you."

items.explanationHtml:
Median survival is the time by which half of the study population had died: half lived longer, and survival distributions in cancer often have a long right tail. The response should explain the figure accurately, then acknowledge that it cannot predict what will happen to her as an individual, leaving room for her questions and hopes.

Accurate, honest explanation of prognosis supports informed decisions and advance care planning; false precision and false reassurance both undermine trust.

Takeaway: median survival = the time by which half had died; it is not an individual prediction.

whyNot.A: The median is not the most likely survival time for an individual; individual outcomes vary widely around it.
whyNot.B: By definition, half of the patients, not most, had died by the median survival time.
whyNot.D: Dismissing the data avoids her question and withholds information she is entitled to understand.
whyNot.E: Any physician caring for her can explain what a median means; deflecting the question is unnecessary.

items.objective: Explain median survival to a patient accurately.

items.stemHtml:
An oncologist reviews her clinic registry of 50 patients treated for a rare sarcoma, to give patients an estimate of survival. All deaths and censored observations are shown below.

MonthPatients at riskDeathsCensored before the next death time
35055
84046
14306—

Using the Kaplan-Meier method, which of the following is the estimated probability of surviving beyond 14 months, to the nearest whole percent?
items.explanationHtml:
Kaplan-Meier survival is the product of the conditional survival at each death time: (45/50) × (36/40) × (24/30) = 0.90 × 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.648 ≈ 65%. Censored patients leave the risk set but are never counted as deaths.

The method uses all available follow-up: a patient censored at 10 months contributes to the estimate up to that point. Simple proportions either treat censored patients as deaths (too pessimistic) or as survivors to the end (too optimistic).

Takeaway: S(t) = Π (1 − deaths ÷ at risk) at each event time up to t.

whyNot.A: 48% (24 ÷ 50) treats every censored patient as if they had died.
whyNot.B: 60% subtracts the interval death proportions (10% + 10% + 20%) instead of multiplying the conditional survival probabilities.
whyNot.D: 70% (35 ÷ 50) subtracts the 15 deaths from 50 and treats the 11 censored patients as survivors to 14 months.
whyNot.E: 80% is the conditional survival at month 14 alone, ignoring the earlier deaths.

items.objective: Calculate a Kaplan-Meier survival estimate from a table with censoring.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with relapsed leukaemia shows his physician a published Kaplan-Meier curve for a new cellular therapy. The curve falls steeply in the first year and then stays flat at 0.30 from 3 to 5 years. The numbers at risk printed below the curve are 120 at baseline, 14 at 3 years, 6 at 4 years and 2 at 5 years. He asks whether this means that 30% of people are cured. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: About 30% of patients are cured by the therapy

options.label: B
options.html: Long-term survival is unlikely because the curve fell steeply in the first year

options.label: C
options.html: The flat tail is based on very few patients, so long-term survival estimates are imprecise and cannot establish cure

options.label: D
options.html: The flat segment shows that the therapy stops working after 3 years

options.label: E
options.html: Patients censored in the tail must have died

items.explanationHtml:
The plateau rests on 14, then 6, then 2 patients at risk; a single death among them would drop the curve sharply. The tail therefore has very wide uncertainty. A flat segment means no deaths were observed among the few people still being followed, not that the remaining patients are cured. Cure requires long follow-up of an adequate number of patients.

Before interpreting any part of a survival curve, look at the numbers at risk under it.

Takeaway: late plateaus with few patients at risk are imprecise; they cannot prove cure.

whyNot.A: A plateau supported by 2 to 14 patients cannot establish a 30% cure rate; the estimate could change markedly with one event.
whyNot.B: Early events do not make later survival impossible; the curve does show some patients surviving, though imprecisely estimated.
whyNot.D: A flat segment means no observed deaths; it says nothing about the therapy stopping working.
whyNot.E: Censored patients left observation alive; assuming they died would misread the curve.

items.objective: Interpret the tail of a Kaplan-Meier curve using the numbers at risk.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman had surgery and adjuvant therapy for colon cancer 3 years ago and has no evidence of disease. At diagnosis, she was told that for her stage, 3-year overall survival is 60% and 5-year overall survival is 48%, based on a large registry. She asks what her chance is now of being alive 2 years from today. Which of the following is the best estimate?
items.explanationHtml:
Having survived 3 years, she is in the group that has escaped the deaths of the first 3 years. Her conditional survival to 5 years is S(5) ÷ S(3) = 0.48 ÷ 0.60 = 0.80, or 80%.

Conditional survival usually improves the longer a patient survives, and it is the relevant figure for counselling survivors. Quoting the 5-year estimate from diagnosis would understate her prospects.

Takeaway: chance of surviving from time a to time b, given survival to a, = S(b) ÷ S(a).

whyNot.A: 12% is the absolute difference between the two survival figures, a fraction of the original cohort, not her conditional probability.
whyNot.B: 48% is 5-year survival from diagnosis; it includes deaths in the first 3 years, which she has already survived.
whyNot.C: 60% is 3-year survival from diagnosis, a probability she has already realised.
whyNot.E: 88% (1 − 0.12) subtracts the absolute difference from 1 instead of dividing the two survival probabilities.

items.objective: Calculate conditional survival for a patient who has survived part of the follow-up.

items.stemHtml: A district health office estimates the burden of a chronic liver disease for one year. The disease caused 20 deaths, each at an age at which the standard remaining life expectancy is 30 years. During the year, 400 people lived with the disease for the whole year; its disability weight is 0.25. Which of the following is the number of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) due to the disease that year?
items.explanationHtml:
DALYs = years of life lost (YLL) + years lived with disability (YLD). YLL = 20 deaths × 30 years = 600. YLD = 400 people × 0.25 × 1 year = 100. DALYs = 700.

One DALY is one year of healthy life lost. The disability weight runs from 0 (full health) to 1 (equivalent to death), so a year lived with a condition of weight 0.25 counts as a quarter of a healthy year lost.

Takeaway: DALY = YLL + YLD, with YLD = cases × disability weight × duration.

whyNot.A: 100 is the YLD alone; it leaves out the 600 years of life lost to death.
whyNot.B: 500 subtracts the YLD from the YLL instead of adding them.
whyNot.C: 600 is the YLL alone; it ignores the disability borne by people living with the disease.
whyNot.E: 1,000 adds 400 full years for the people living with the disease, ignoring the disability weight.

items.objective: Calculate DALYs from years of life lost and years lived with disability.

items.stemHtml: A decision analysis compares two treatments for an advanced lung disease. With treatment X, patients are expected to live 4 years with a health utility of 0.75. With treatment Y, patients are expected to live 5 years with a health utility of 0.50. How many quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) does treatment X provide compared with treatment Y?
items.explanationHtml:
QALYs = years lived × utility. Treatment X: 4 × 0.75 = 3.0 QALYs. Treatment Y: 5 × 0.50 = 2.5 QALYs. X provides 0.5 more QALYs than Y, although Y gives a year more of life.

QALYs combine length and quality of life so that a treatment that extends life in poor health can be compared with one that gives fewer but better years. Utilities run from 0 (death) to 1 (full health).

Takeaway: QALY = years × utility; more years does not always mean more QALYs.

whyNot.A: −1.0 compares life-years only (4 − 5) and ignores quality of life.
whyNot.B: 0.25 is the difference in utilities, not in QALYs; it ignores how long each state lasts.
whyNot.D: 2.50 is the QALYs from treatment Y alone, not the difference.
whyNot.E: 3.00 is the QALYs from treatment X alone, not the difference.

items.objective: Calculate and compare QALYs for two treatments.

items.stemHtml:
A cost-utility analysis compares a new treatment with standard treatment for a chronic inflammatory disease over a lifetime horizon.

StrategyTotal cost per patientQALYs per patient
Standard treatment$30,0004.0
New treatment$90,0005.5

Which of the following is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of the new treatment compared with standard treatment, per QALY gained?
items.explanationHtml:
ICER = (difference in cost) ÷ (difference in QALYs) = ($90,000 − $30,000) ÷ (5.5 − 4.0) = $60,000 ÷ 1.5 = $40,000 per QALY gained.

Decision makers compare the ICER with what they are willing to pay for a QALY. Average ratios (a strategy's total cost divided by its total QALYs) do not answer the question of what the extra money buys.

Takeaway: ICER = Δcost ÷ ΔQALY.

whyNot.A: $7,500 is the average cost per QALY of standard treatment ($30,000 ÷ 4.0), not an incremental ratio.
whyNot.B: $16,364 is the average cost per QALY of the new treatment ($90,000 ÷ 5.5), not an incremental ratio.
whyNot.C: $20,000 divides the cost of standard treatment, rather than the extra cost, by the QALY gain.
whyNot.E: $60,000 is the incremental cost alone, without dividing by the 1.5 QALYs gained.

items.objective: Calculate an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio.

items.stemHtml: In a 10-year cohort study of factory workers, the cumulative incidence of bladder cancer is 30 per 1,000 among workers exposed to an industrial dye and 6 per 1,000 among unexposed workers. Assuming the association is causal, which of the following is the percentage of bladder cancer among exposed workers that is attributable to the dye?
items.explanationHtml:
Attributable risk percent in the exposed = (Iexposed − Iunexposed) ÷ Iexposed = (30 − 6) ÷ 30 = 80%. Equivalently, (RR − 1) ÷ RR = (5 − 1) ÷ 5 = 80%.

It answers the question, "Of the cases in exposed people, what share would not have occurred without the exposure?" It is relevant to an exposed individual or group, whereas the population attributable fraction also depends on how common the exposure is.

Takeaway: AR% = (RR − 1) ÷ RR.

whyNot.A: 2.4% is the absolute attributable risk (24 per 1,000) expressed as a percentage, not the attributable fraction.
whyNot.B: 20% (6 ÷ 30) is the share of exposed workers' risk that is not due to the dye, the reciprocal of the relative risk.
whyNot.D: 400% is the excess relative risk (RR − 1) expressed as a percentage, not an attributable fraction.
whyNot.E: 500% is the relative risk of 5 expressed as a percentage.

items.objective: Calculate attributable risk percent in the exposed.

items.stemHtml: In a population, 40% of adults are exposed to a dietary risk factor. The relative risk of a chronic disease among exposed compared with unexposed people is 3.0. Assuming the association is causal and unconfounded, which of the following is the closest estimate of the percentage of all cases in the population that would be prevented if the exposure were eliminated?
items.explanationHtml:
The population attributable fraction (PAR%) = Pe(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + Pe(RR − 1)] = 0.4 × 2 ÷ (1 + 0.8) = 0.8 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 44%.

The PAR% depends on both the strength of the association and the prevalence of the exposure. The attributable fraction among the exposed is higher (67%), but because 60% of the population is unexposed and still develops some disease, the share of all cases that are preventable is lower.

Takeaway: PAR% = Pe(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + Pe(RR − 1)].

whyNot.A: 27% multiplies the attributable fraction in the exposed by the proportion of the population exposed; that shortcut needs the proportion of cases who are exposed, not of the population.
whyNot.B: 33% is the reciprocal of the relative risk (1 ÷ 3), which has no direct meaning as a population fraction.
whyNot.C: 40% is the prevalence of exposure, not the share of cases caused by it.
whyNot.E: 67% is the attributable fraction among the exposed, (RR − 1) ÷ RR, not in the whole population.

items.objective: Calculate the population attributable fraction from exposure prevalence and relative risk.

items.stemHtml: A city health department learns that a chemical in household water pipes is associated with a higher incidence of a childhood neurologic disorder. Before funding pipe replacement, officials want to know how many cases of the disorder in the whole city would be prevented if the exposure were removed. Which of the following measures best answers this question?

options.label: A
options.html: Attributable risk in the exposed

options.label: B
options.html: Number needed to treat

options.label: C
options.html: Odds ratio

options.label: D
options.html: Population attributable risk

options.label: E
options.html: Relative risk

items.explanationHtml:
The population attributable risk (Ipopulation − Iunexposed), and its proportional form the population attributable fraction, estimate how much of the disease in the whole population is due to the exposure. Multiplying it by the population gives the number of cases that would be prevented by removing the exposure, assuming causality.

It combines the strength of the association with how common the exposure is, which is why it guides public health priorities. Relative measures describe strength alone.

Takeaway: "how many cases in the community would be prevented?" → population attributable risk.

whyNot.A: Attributable risk in the exposed describes the excess risk for exposed children only; it ignores how many children are exposed.
whyNot.B: Number needed to treat describes how many people must receive an intervention to prevent one event in a trial; it does not estimate the city-wide burden from an exposure.
whyNot.C: The odds ratio measures the strength of association, usually from a case-control study; it does not give a count of preventable cases.
whyNot.E: Relative risk measures strength of association but not the population burden, which also depends on exposure prevalence.

items.objective: Choose the population attributable risk to estimate the public health impact of an exposure.

items.stemHtml:
A health plan evaluates three strategies for preventing fractures in older women. Costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) are per patient over a lifetime horizon.

StrategyCostQALYs
Usual care$2,00010.00
Strategy A$4,00010.10
Strategy B$6,00010.05

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by these data?

options.label: A
options.html: Strategy A is dominated by strategy B

options.label: B
options.html: Strategy B is dominated by strategy A

options.label: C
options.html: Strategy B is preferred because it is the most expensive

options.label: D
options.html: Usual care dominates both strategies

options.label: E
options.html: The strategies cannot be compared without a willingness-to-pay threshold

items.explanationHtml:
Strategy B costs more than strategy A ($6,000 vs $4,000) and yields fewer QALYs (10.05 vs 10.10). It is therefore dominated by A and is excluded without calculating a ratio. Strategy A's incremental cost-effectiveness ratio versus usual care is $2,000 ÷ 0.10 QALY = $20,000 per QALY gained; whether that is acceptable depends on the plan's willingness to pay.

The standard approach is to order strategies by cost, remove any that are dominated, and then calculate incremental ratios between the remaining neighbours.

Takeaway: a strategy that costs more and gives fewer QALYs than an alternative is dominated and is dropped.

whyNot.A: Strategy A is cheaper and more effective than B, so A dominates B, not the other way round.
whyNot.C: Cost alone does not indicate value; B is both costlier and less effective than A.
whyNot.D: Usual care is cheaper but less effective than both strategies, so it does not dominate either.
whyNot.E: Dominance can be identified without any threshold; a threshold is needed only to judge A's ratio versus usual care.

items.objective: Identify a dominated strategy in a cost-effectiveness table.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man is considering long-term treatment with a drug to reduce his risk of a recurrent venous thromboembolism. In the drug's main trial, major bleeding occurred in 3% of patients who received the drug for 1 year and 1% of patients who received placebo. He asks how likely the drug is to cause a serious bleed. How many patients would need to take the drug for 1 year for one additional major bleed to occur?
items.explanationHtml:
Absolute risk increase = 3% − 1% = 2% = 0.02. Number needed to harm (NNH) = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 patients treated for 1 year for one additional major bleed.

Absolute measures, framed with a time period, are the clearest way to discuss harms with patients and should be presented alongside the number needed to treat for the benefit so that the patient can weigh them.

Takeaway: NNH = 1 ÷ (risk with treatment − risk without), for a stated duration.

whyNot.A: 3 is the relative risk of bleeding (3% ÷ 1%), not a number of patients.
whyNot.B: 25 is 1 ÷ 0.04, which adds the two bleeding risks instead of subtracting them.
whyNot.C: 33 is 1 ÷ 0.03, which uses the bleeding risk on the drug without subtracting the placebo risk.
whyNot.E: 100 is 1 ÷ 0.01, the reciprocal of the placebo group's bleeding risk.

items.objective: Calculate a number needed to harm to counsel a patient.

items.stemHtml:
A county health department can fund one programme to reduce the incidence of a chronic disease. Two causal exposures are under consideration; the programme would eliminate one of them.

ExposurePrevalence in adultsRelative risk of the disease
Exposure X (occupational)1%10.0
Exposure Y (dietary)40%2.0

Assuming both exposures act independently and the associations are causal, which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Both programmes would prevent the same proportion of cases

options.label: B
options.html: Eliminating exposure X would prevent more cases because its relative risk is higher

options.label: C
options.html: Eliminating exposure Y would prevent more cases because it is much more common

options.label: D
options.html: Neither programme should be funded until the relative risks are equal

options.label: E
options.html: The number of cases prevented cannot be estimated without odds ratios

items.explanationHtml:
The share of all cases preventable by removing an exposure is the population attributable fraction: Pe(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + Pe(RR − 1)]. Exposure X: 0.01 × 9 ÷ 1.09 ≈ 8%. Exposure Y: 0.40 × 1 ÷ 1.40 ≈ 29%. Eliminating Y would prevent more than three times as many cases, although its relative risk is much smaller.

Strength of association matters to an exposed individual; the population burden depends on how many people are exposed. Public health priorities follow the population attributable fraction.

Takeaway: a common exposure with a modest RR can cause more cases than a rare exposure with a large RR.

whyNot.A: The attributable fractions differ substantially (about 8% vs 29%).
whyNot.B: Exposure X has the larger RR but affects only 1% of adults, so it accounts for only about 8% of cases.
whyNot.D: The relative risks do not need to be equal; the attributable fractions can be compared directly.
whyNot.E: Relative risks and exposure prevalence are sufficient to estimate the attributable fraction; odds ratios are not needed.

items.objective: Use population attributable fractions to choose between public health programmes.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who smokes asks how much smoking adds to his yearly risk of a particular cancer. In a large cohort study, the incidence of this cancer was 2.0 per 1,000 per year among smokers and 0.4 per 1,000 per year among never-smokers. Assuming the association is causal, how many additional cases per 1,000 smokers per year are due to smoking?
items.explanationHtml:
The absolute excess risk (attributable risk, risk difference) = 2.0 − 0.4 = 1.6 per 1,000 per year. In plain words: among 1,000 smokers like him, about 1 to 2 extra cases each year are due to smoking.

Patients understand absolute numbers better than relative ones. Here the relative risk is 5, and 80% of smokers' risk is attributable to smoking; giving both the absolute and the relative picture conveys that the risk is real while keeping it in proportion.

Takeaway: attributable risk = incidence in exposed − incidence in unexposed.

whyNot.A: 0.4 per 1,000 is the background incidence in never-smokers, not the excess due to smoking.
whyNot.C: 2.0 per 1,000 is the total incidence in smokers, which includes the background risk.
whyNot.D: 2.4 adds the two incidences instead of subtracting them.
whyNot.E: 5.0 is the relative risk (2.0 ÷ 0.4), which has no units and is not a number of cases.

items.objective: Calculate and explain absolute attributable risk to a patient.

items.stemHtml: A national health ministry compares two rankings of conditions: one by the number of deaths and one by disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Which of the following conditions is most likely to rank much higher by DALYs than by deaths?

options.label: A
options.html: Acute myocardial infarction

options.label: B
options.html: Major depressive disorder

options.label: C
options.html: Pancreatic cancer

options.label: D
options.html: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm

options.label: E
options.html: Septic shock

items.explanationHtml:
DALYs add years lived with disability (YLD) to years of life lost (YLL). Conditions that are common, start in early adulthood, last for years and impair function but rarely cause death directly accumulate large YLD. Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of DALYs worldwide despite causing few deaths directly (deaths by suicide are coded separately).

Ranking by DALYs brings mental disorders, musculoskeletal pain, hearing and vision loss into priority setting; ranking by deaths leaves them out.

Takeaway: disabling, rarely fatal, long-lasting conditions rise in the rankings when DALYs are used.

whyNot.A: Myocardial infarction causes many deaths; most of its burden is years of life lost, so it ranks high by both measures.
whyNot.C: Pancreatic cancer is rapidly fatal, so survivors live with it only briefly and its burden is almost all years of life lost.
whyNot.D: A ruptured aneurysm causes sudden death or recovery; it adds little disability time.
whyNot.E: Septic shock causes many deaths with relatively short illness, so its DALYs come mainly from mortality.

items.objective: Recognise which conditions contribute disproportionately to DALYs through disability.

items.stemHtml:
The figure shows population pyramids for three countries (Populations 1, 2 and 3).

Which of the following best describes the demographic situation of Population 2?

options.label: A
options.html: Fertility below replacement for some decades, with an ageing population

options.label: B
options.html: High birth and death rates with rapid growth

options.label: C
options.html: Low birth and death rates that have been stable for many decades

options.label: D
options.html: Recent high child mortality from an epidemic

options.label: E
options.html: Recent large in-migration of working-age men

items.explanationHtml:
Population 2 is a constrictive pyramid: its youngest bands are narrower than the middle-aged bands, and a large share of the population is 60 or older. This shape results from birth rates that have been below replacement for a generation or more, combined with low death rates and long life expectancy. The population is ageing and may begin to shrink.

Population 1 is expansive (high fertility, steep taper from high mortality), and Population 3 is near-stationary (nearly equal bands until older ages).

Takeaway: a base narrower than the middle = constrictive = low fertility and an ageing population.

whyNot.B: High birth and death rates give a broad base and a steep taper, the shape of Population 1.
whyNot.C: Long-stable low birth and death rates give nearly equal bands until older ages, the shape of Population 3.
whyNot.D: An epidemic killing children would leave a notch in specific young bands, not a narrow base with a large older population.
whyNot.E: Male labour migration would create a male-only bulge in working ages; Population 2's bars are similar for both sexes.

items.objective: Interpret a constrictive population pyramid.

items.stemHtml:
The figure shows population pyramids for three countries (Populations 1, 2 and 3).

Compared with Population 3, Population 1 most likely has which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: A higher crude birth rate

options.label: B
options.html: A higher life expectancy at birth

options.label: C
options.html: A higher old-age dependency ratio

options.label: D
options.html: A higher proportion of deaths from chronic noncommunicable disease

options.label: E
options.html: A lower infant mortality rate

items.explanationHtml:
Population 1 has a very broad base (28% of the population is under 10) that narrows steeply with age: an expansive pyramid. Its large youngest cohorts reflect a high birth rate, and the steep taper reflects high mortality at every age.

Expansive populations are typically in the early stages of the demographic and epidemiologic transitions, with high youth dependency, lower life expectancy and a larger share of deaths from infections, malnutrition and maternal and perinatal causes.

Takeaway: a wide base means many recent births; a steep taper means high mortality.

whyNot.B: The steep taper indicates high mortality at all ages, which goes with a lower, not higher, life expectancy.
whyNot.C: Population 1 has very few people over 65, so its old-age dependency ratio is low; its youth ratio is high.
whyNot.D: Populations early in the epidemiologic transition have a larger share of deaths from infectious, maternal and perinatal causes.
whyNot.E: Expansive populations with high mortality typically have higher, not lower, infant mortality.

items.objective: Relate an expansive pyramid to birth rate and other demographic indicators.

items.stemHtml: A small country has 30,000 residents aged 0 to 14 years, 60,000 aged 15 to 64 years and 10,000 aged 65 years and older. Which of the following is the total dependency ratio, per 100 people of working age?
items.explanationHtml:
Total dependency ratio = (people aged 0–14 + people aged 65+) ÷ people aged 15–64 × 100 = (30,000 + 10,000) ÷ 60,000 × 100 = 66.7 dependants per 100 people of working age.

It splits into a youth ratio (30,000 ÷ 60,000 × 100 = 50) and an old-age ratio (10,000 ÷ 60,000 × 100 ≈ 16.7). Expansive populations have high youth ratios; ageing populations have rising old-age ratios.

Takeaway: the denominator of a dependency ratio is the working-age population (15–64), not the total.

whyNot.A: 16.7 is the old-age dependency ratio alone; it leaves out children.
whyNot.B: 40 divides dependants by the total population (40,000 ÷ 100,000) instead of by the working-age population.
whyNot.C: 50 is the youth dependency ratio alone; it leaves out people aged 65 and older.
whyNot.E: 150 inverts the ratio (working-age ÷ dependants).

items.objective: Calculate a total dependency ratio.

items.stemHtml: Over 25 years, a low-income country introduces childhood vaccination, safe drinking water and improved sanitation. Mortality among children younger than 5 years falls by half. Average fertility does not change during this period, and there is little migration. Which of the following changes in the population is most likely during these 25 years?

options.label: A
options.html: A falling crude birth rate with a stable population size

options.label: B
options.html: A higher old-age dependency ratio than youth dependency ratio

options.label: C
options.html: A rectangular population pyramid

options.label: D
options.html: Rapid population growth with a widening base of the pyramid

options.label: E
options.html: Shrinking population size with a narrowing base of the pyramid

items.explanationHtml:
The country is in stage 2 of the demographic transition: death rates (especially in childhood) fall while birth rates remain high. More children survive to join each age band, so the population grows rapidly and the base of the pyramid widens. As those children reach reproductive age, growth gains further momentum.

Only when fertility falls (stage 3, with education of women, urbanisation and access to contraception) does growth slow and the pyramid begin to narrow at the base.

Takeaway: falling mortality with unchanged high fertility = rapid growth and an expanding young population.

whyNot.A: The stem states that fertility did not change, so the crude birth rate is not falling and the population is not stable.
whyNot.B: Gains in child survival add mainly to the young population; the old-age ratio stays small for decades.
whyNot.C: A rectangular pyramid requires sustained low fertility and low mortality, typical of stage 4.
whyNot.E: Shrinkage and a narrowing base follow fertility below replacement, not falling child mortality with high fertility.

items.objective: Apply the demographic transition to predict population change.

items.stemHtml: Over the next 30 years, the number of people aged 80 years and older in a country is projected to double, while the rest of the population stays about the same size. Age-specific incidence of dementia and survival after a diagnosis of dementia are expected to remain unchanged. Which of the following changes in dementia prevalence is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Age-specific prevalence and crude prevalence both increase

options.label: B
options.html: Age-specific prevalence and crude prevalence both remain unchanged

options.label: C
options.html: Age-specific prevalence increases and crude prevalence remains unchanged

options.label: D
options.html: Age-specific prevalence remains unchanged and crude prevalence increases

options.label: E
options.html: Age-specific prevalence remains unchanged and crude prevalence decreases

items.explanationHtml:
If incidence and duration within each age group are unchanged, the age-specific prevalence is unchanged. But a larger share of the population will be in the oldest age groups, where dementia is most common, so the crude prevalence (and the number of people with dementia) rises. Age-adjusted prevalence would stay the same.

This distinction matters for planning: services must be sized to the crude numbers, while judgments about whether risk is changing should use age-specific or age-adjusted rates.

Takeaway: population ageing alone raises crude prevalence of age-related disease without changing age-specific rates.

whyNot.A: Age-specific prevalence would rise only if incidence or survival within each age group changed, which the stem rules out.
whyNot.B: The crude figure averages over the age structure, and the age structure is shifting toward the oldest groups.
whyNot.C: This reverses the effect: the age structure changes the crude figure, not the age-specific ones.
whyNot.E: More people in high-prevalence age groups raises the crude prevalence; it cannot lower it.

items.objective: Predict the effect of population ageing on crude versus age-specific prevalence.

items.stemHtml: The population pyramid of a small, oil-producing country shows an unusually large number of men aged 20 to 44 years, about three times the number of women of the same ages. The bands for children and for adults older than 60 years are similar in size for males and females. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A
options.html: A baby boom about 30 years earlier

options.label: B
options.html: Higher maternal mortality among young women

options.label: C
options.html: Labour in-migration of working-age men

options.label: D
options.html: Recent war deaths among young adults

options.label: E
options.html: Sex-selective abortion

items.explanationHtml:
A large excess of men of working age only, with balanced sex ratios among children and older adults, is the signature of labour in-migration: men arrive as adults for temporary work, often without families, and leave before old age.

Irregular bulges and notches in a pyramid usually trace migration or historical events. Asking which ages and which sex are affected identifies the cause.

Takeaway: a working-age, one-sex bulge points to labour migration.

whyNot.A: A baby boom would enlarge the cohort in both sexes, not create a threefold male excess.
whyNot.B: Maternal mortality would reduce the number of young women only slightly and could not produce a threefold imbalance.
whyNot.D: War deaths create a deficit (notch), usually of young men, not an excess of them.
whyNot.E: Sex-selective abortion skews the sex ratio at birth and in the youngest bands, which here are balanced.

items.objective: Interpret a sex-specific bulge in a population pyramid as migration.

items.stemHtml:
The figure shows population pyramids for three countries (Populations 1, 2 and 3).

A regional health authority serves Population 2 and is preparing its 10-year capital plan. Which of the following is the most appropriate priority?

options.label: A
options.html: Expand adolescent sexual health clinics

options.label: B
options.html: Expand chronic disease, dementia and long-term care services

options.label: C
options.html: Expand neonatal intensive care capacity

options.label: D
options.html: Expand obstetric delivery units

options.label: E
options.html: Expand school-based immunisation programmes

items.explanationHtml:
Population 2 is constrictive: its narrow base reflects few recent births, and a large share of its people are in their 50s and older, with more women than men at the oldest ages. Over the next decade the large middle-aged cohorts will move into older age, so demand for chronic disease management, dementia care, rehabilitation and long-term care will grow.

Matching services to the population structure is a core use of the pyramid. Child and maternal services remain necessary but will not be the growth area.

Takeaway: a constrictive pyramid predicts rising demand for services for older adults.

whyNot.A: The adolescent bands are among the smallest in Population 2, so demand for adolescent services will not grow.
whyNot.C: Few births are occurring, so neonatal intensive care demand is unlikely to grow.
whyNot.D: Births are low and the cohort of women entering reproductive age is small, so delivery units are not the priority.
whyNot.E: School-age cohorts are small and shrinking; immunisation programmes need maintaining, not expanding.

items.objective: Use a population pyramid to set health service priorities.

items.stemHtml: A rural county's population aged 65 years and older is projected to grow by 40% over the next decade. Its primary care network wants to start one preventive programme for community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older who are at increased risk of falls. Which of the following programmes is best supported by current evidence?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual hip radiographs to identify early osteoarthritis

options.label: B
options.html: Advice to limit walking outdoors to avoid falls

options.label: C
options.html: Routine use of hip protectors at home

options.label: D
options.html: Vitamin D supplementation for all older adults without vitamin D deficiency

options.label: E
options.html: Supervised exercise focusing on gait, balance and strength

items.explanationHtml:
Exercise interventions that train gait, balance and functional strength reduce falls in community-dwelling older adults at increased risk, and the USPSTF recommends them (grade B). With a rapidly ageing population, a scalable group exercise programme is an efficient preventive investment.

The USPSTF recommends against vitamin D supplementation to prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults who are not deficient, because trials showed no benefit.

Takeaway: for an ageing community, exercise-based falls prevention is the evidence-based primary prevention programme.

whyNot.A: Radiographic screening does not prevent falls and would expose people to cost and radiation without benefit.
whyNot.B: Restricting activity worsens deconditioning and increases, rather than lowers, the risk of falls.
whyNot.C: Hip protectors have not been shown to reduce fractures convincingly in community-dwelling adults, and adherence is poor.
whyNot.D: Trials show vitamin D supplementation does not prevent falls in older adults without deficiency, and the USPSTF recommends against it for that purpose.

items.objective: Choose an evidence-based preventive programme for an ageing population.

items.stemHtml: A community health centre opens in a neighbourhood where many refugee families have recently resettled. A local population count shows that 45% of residents are younger than 15 years, many women are aged 18 to 35 years and fewer than 3% of residents are 65 or older. Which of the following services should the centre prioritise?

options.label: A
options.html: Bone density screening for postmenopausal women

options.label: B
options.html: Cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction

options.label: C
options.html: Memory assessment clinic for cognitive decline

options.label: D
options.html: Prenatal care, well-child visits and catch-up immunisation

options.label: E
options.html: Palliative care consultation for serious illness

items.explanationHtml:
The neighbourhood has an expansive age structure: many children and many women of reproductive age, very few older adults. The greatest needs are prenatal care, well-child care and catch-up immunisation (many resettled children have incomplete or undocumented vaccination), along with family planning and nutrition.

Matching services to the population pyramid is the first step in planning a new practice; services for older adults will be needed by few residents.

Takeaway: a young, expansive population needs maternal, child and immunisation services first.

whyNot.A: Bone density screening is aimed mainly at older women, who make up a very small share of this community.
whyNot.B: Cardiac rehabilitation serves adults after cardiac events, which are uncommon in a young population.
whyNot.C: Memory clinics serve older adults, fewer than 3% of residents.
whyNot.E: Palliative care is needed by some residents, but it is not the main service need of a predominantly young community.

items.objective: Choose services that match an expansive population structure.

items.stemHtml:
A state cancer registry reports colorectal cancer incidence for two periods. Diagnostic and screening practices were similar in both periods.

Measure (per 100,000 per year)Period 1Period 2 (15 years later)
Crude incidence5263
Age-adjusted incidence (US standard population)4140
Residents aged 65 years and older13%19%

A legislator asks whether an environmental investigation should be started. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "The rise reflects an ageing population, not higher risk; we should plan for more patients."

options.label: B
options.html: "The rise shows a new environmental cause, and an investigation should start immediately."

options.label: C
options.html: "The registry data are unreliable because the crude and adjusted rates disagree."

options.label: D
options.html: "The rise is explained by more screening, so screening should be reduced."

options.label: E
options.html: "Colorectal cancer risk has fallen, so fewer oncology services will be needed."

items.explanationHtml:
The crude incidence rose by about 21%, but the age-adjusted incidence is essentially unchanged (41 vs 40). Meanwhile, the share of residents aged 65 and older rose from 13% to 19%. The increase in cases is explained by population ageing, not by an increase in risk at any given age, so there is no signal for an environmental investigation.

The practical implication is the opposite of complacency: more patients will need diagnosis and treatment, so oncology, endoscopy and surgical capacity must grow with the older population.

Takeaway: rising crude but flat age-adjusted incidence = ageing population; plan capacity, do not chase a cluster.

whyNot.B: An environmental cause would be expected to raise age-specific (and so age-adjusted) incidence, which is flat.
whyNot.C: Crude and adjusted rates are expected to diverge when the age structure changes; that is not a sign of unreliability.
whyNot.D: The stem states that screening practices were similar; and the age-adjusted rate did not rise.
whyNot.E: Age-adjusted risk is stable, and the absolute number of cases is rising, so more, not fewer, services will be needed.

items.objective: Interpret rising crude but stable age-adjusted incidence in an ageing population.

items.stemHtml: A primary care practice opens in a small city whose population pyramid shows a large bulge of residents aged 18 to 24 years because of a new university campus. The practice reviews which preventive services will be needed most often by its new patients. Which of the following services is most likely to be in highest demand?

options.label: A
options.html: Abdominal aortic aneurysm screening by ultrasonography

options.label: B
options.html: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea screening for sexually active women

options.label: C
options.html: Colorectal cancer screening by colonoscopy or stool test

options.label: D
options.html: Lung cancer screening with low-dose CT of the chest

options.label: E
options.html: Osteoporosis screening with bone density testing

items.explanationHtml:
A university town adds many young adults. The USPSTF recommends screening all sexually active women aged 24 years or younger for chlamydia and gonorrhoea (and older women at increased risk), so this service will be frequent. Contraception, HPV vaccination catch-up, mental health and alcohol and injury prevention are other common needs of this age group.

The other screening services all apply to older age groups and would be uncommon in this practice's population.

Takeaway: a young-adult bulge in the pyramid predicts demand for sexual and reproductive health services.

whyNot.A: Aortic aneurysm screening is recommended once for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked, not for young adults.
whyNot.C: Colorectal cancer screening begins at age 45 for average-risk adults.
whyNot.D: Lung cancer screening is for adults aged 50 to 80 years with a substantial smoking history.
whyNot.E: Osteoporosis screening is recommended for women aged 65 and older and younger postmenopausal women at increased risk.

items.objective: Match preventive services to a young-adult population structure.

items.stemHtml:
A health system plans memory-care services for its catchment area. Current dementia prevalence by age and the population projected in 20 years are shown. Age-specific prevalence is expected to stay the same.

Age groupDementia prevalencePopulation nowPopulation in 20 years
65–74 years3%10,00012,000
75–84 years10%6,0009,000
85 years and older30%2,0004,000

Which of the following is the projected number of people aged 65 and older with dementia in 20 years?
items.explanationHtml:
Apply each age-specific prevalence to the projected population: 12,000 × 0.03 + 9,000 × 0.10 + 4,000 × 0.30 = 360 + 900 + 1,200 = 2,460 people, compared with 300 + 600 + 600 = 1,500 now, a 64% increase.

The number of cases rises much faster than the 65+ population (which grows by about 39%) because the oldest group, with the highest prevalence, doubles. Projections must be built age group by age group.

Takeaway: project caseload by applying age-specific rates to the projected age structure.

whyNot.A: 1,500 is the current number of cases; it ignores the projected growth and ageing of the population.
whyNot.B: 2,083 scales today's cases by the growth of the whole 65+ population (25,000 ÷ 18,000), ignoring the shift toward the oldest group.
whyNot.C: 2,100 projects growth only in the 85+ group and leaves the younger groups at their current size.
whyNot.E: 3,000 simply doubles current cases, as if every age group doubled.

items.objective: Project future disease burden from age-specific rates and a changing age structure.

items.stemHtml:
A county health department investigates an outbreak of a febrile rash illness in a primary school community. The figure shows the epidemic curve of cases by day of symptom onset.

Which of the following modes of spread is most consistent with this epidemic curve?

options.label: A
options.html: Continuous exposure to a contaminated water supply

options.label: B
options.html: Intermittent contamination of a food product

options.label: C
options.html: Single exposure to a contaminated meal

options.label: D
options.html: Transmission by a vector with a seasonal peak

options.label: E
options.html: Person-to-person transmission

items.explanationHtml:
The curve shows a single early case, followed by successive waves at intervals of about 12 days, each wave larger and broader than the one before. That is a propagated pattern: each generation of cases infects the next, and the spacing between waves corresponds to the serial interval of the infection.

Common-source outbreaks look different: a point source gives one sharp peak within one incubation period; a continuous source gives a rise and plateau; an intermittent source gives irregular peaks with no regular spacing or systematic growth.

Takeaway: regularly spaced, growing waves on an epidemic curve = person-to-person (propagated) spread.

whyNot.A: A continuous source produces a rise followed by a plateau of cases, not distinct waves separated by quiet days.
whyNot.B: Intermittent contamination produces irregular peaks tied to contamination episodes, not regularly spaced waves that grow with each generation.
whyNot.C: A single shared meal produces one peak within about one incubation period, not four waves over 6 weeks.
whyNot.D: Vector-borne outbreaks follow vector abundance and do not show waves spaced at one serial interval in a school community.

items.objective: Recognise a propagated outbreak from the shape of an epidemic curve.

items.stemHtml: Forty-two of 110 guests at a wedding reception develop sudden nausea, vomiting and abdominal cramps. The meal was served at 7 PM and included cream-filled pastries that had been left at room temperature during the afternoon. Symptom onset ranged from 9 PM to 1 AM, with a sharp peak at 11 PM. No one has fever, and most are better within 24 hours. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Clostridium perfringens

options.label: B
options.html: Listeria monocytogenes

options.label: C
options.html: Norovirus

options.label: D
options.html: Salmonella enterica

options.label: E
options.html: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin

items.explanationHtml:
The epidemic curve is a single sharp peak (a point-source outbreak) with a very short incubation period: 2 to 6 hours, median about 4 hours after the meal. Such a short incubation means the toxin was already formed in the food. Staphylococcus aureus, introduced by a food handler and allowed to multiply in a moist, protein-rich food kept warm, produces a heat-stable enterotoxin that causes abrupt vomiting without fever and resolves within a day.

Estimating the incubation period from the time of exposure to the peak of a point-source curve is a standard outbreak-investigation step and narrows the list of agents.

Takeaway: vomiting a few hours after a shared meal, no fever, recovery within a day → preformed toxin such as S. aureus enterotoxin.

whyNot.A: C. perfringens produces toxin in the gut after an incubation of about 6 to 24 hours, and its illness is mainly diarrhoea and cramps rather than abrupt vomiting.
whyNot.B: Listeria has an incubation period of days to weeks and causes fever, sepsis or meningitis in vulnerable people, not same-evening vomiting.
whyNot.C: Norovirus usually has an incubation period of about 12 to 48 hours, longer than the 2 to 6 hours seen here.
whyNot.D: Salmonella usually causes fever and diarrhoea after an incubation of roughly 6 to 72 hours, most often 12 to 36 hours.

items.objective: Use the incubation period from a point-source epidemic curve to infer the agent.

items.stemHtml: After several cases of a drug-resistant bacterial infection are reported, staff of a state health department telephone the infection-prevention office of every acute care hospital in the state each week and ask whether any new cases have been identified. Which of the following types of surveillance is this?

options.label: A
options.html: Active surveillance

options.label: B
options.html: Passive surveillance

options.label: C
options.html: Sentinel surveillance

options.label: D
options.html: Serologic surveillance

options.label: E
options.html: Syndromic surveillance

items.explanationHtml:
In active surveillance, the health department reaches out on a regular schedule to providers or laboratories to look for cases, rather than waiting for reports. It is more complete and timely than passive surveillance but needs more staff, so it is used during outbreaks and for priority conditions.

In passive surveillance, clinicians and laboratories report notifiable conditions on their own initiative; it is cheaper but underreports.

Takeaway: the health department actively soliciting reports = active surveillance.

whyNot.B: Passive surveillance relies on providers to send reports themselves; here the department is calling them.
whyNot.C: Sentinel surveillance uses a selected subset of sites, whereas every hospital in the state is being contacted.
whyNot.D: Serologic surveillance measures antibodies in population samples to estimate past infection, which is not what is described.
whyNot.E: Syndromic surveillance analyses pre-diagnostic data such as emergency department complaints, not confirmed cases solicited by telephone.

items.objective: Distinguish active from passive, sentinel and syndromic surveillance.

items.stemHtml: For the past 10 years, a county has recorded 2 to 4 cases of shigellosis each month, with no seasonal pattern. In March of this year, 19 laboratory-confirmed cases are reported, and reporting practices have not changed. Which of the following terms best describes the occurrence of shigellosis in the county in March?

options.label: A
options.html: Endemic

options.label: B
options.html: Epidemic

options.label: C
options.html: Hyperendemic

options.label: D
options.html: Pandemic

options.label: E
options.html: Sporadic

items.explanationHtml:
An epidemic (outbreak) is the occurrence of cases clearly in excess of what is normally expected in a given area and time. Nineteen cases against a long-standing baseline of 2 to 4 per month, with unchanged reporting, qualifies.

The county's usual level of 2 to 4 cases a month is the disease's endemic level. Confirming that an apparent increase exceeds the baseline, and is not an artefact of reporting or testing, is the first step in an outbreak investigation.

Takeaway: endemic = the usual level; epidemic = clearly above the usual level.

whyNot.A: Endemic describes the county's usual level of 2 to 4 cases a month, not the March excess.
whyNot.C: Hyperendemic describes a persistently high usual level, not a sudden rise above a low baseline.
whyNot.D: A pandemic spreads across several countries or continents; this is a single county.
whyNot.E: Sporadic cases occur irregularly and infrequently, not as a sharp cluster several times the baseline.

items.objective: Define an epidemic relative to the endemic baseline.

items.stemHtml: Investigators suspect that a restaurant is the source of an outbreak of diarrhoeal illness. Their draft case definition is: "onset of diarrhoea between June 3 and June 14 in a person who ate at Restaurant Q during that period". Which of the following is the most important flaw in this case definition?

options.label: A
options.html: It does not require laboratory confirmation of every case

options.label: B
options.html: It does not specify the age of cases

options.label: C
options.html: It is restricted to a defined time period

options.label: D
options.html: It uses clinical criteria rather than a specific organism

options.label: E
options.html: It includes the suspected exposure, so the restaurant's role cannot be tested

items.explanationHtml:
A case definition should combine clinical criteria with restrictions by person, place and time, but it must not include the exposure being investigated. If only people who ate at Restaurant Q can be cases, every case is exposed by definition, and the analytic study cannot compare exposure among cases and non-cases.

Early case definitions are often broad and clinical (without laboratory confirmation) to find cases; later they are tiered into confirmed, probable and possible.

Takeaway: never build the hypothesised exposure into the case definition.

whyNot.A: Requiring laboratory confirmation is not essential, especially early; confirmed and probable tiers can be used.
whyNot.B: Age restrictions are optional and only used if the outbreak affects a specific group; their absence is not the main flaw.
whyNot.C: Restricting by time is a required element of a case definition, not a flaw.
whyNot.D: Clinical criteria are appropriate in an early case definition; the organism may not yet be known.

items.objective: Recognise that a case definition must not include the exposure under study.

items.stemHtml: Over 4 weeks, 38 people across a large metropolitan area develop culture-confirmed infection with the same strain of Salmonella. They live in different neighbourhoods and did not attend any common event. The health department suspects a widely distributed food product but has no list of the people who ate it. Which of the following study designs is most appropriate to test this hypothesis?

options.label: A
options.html: Case-control study

options.label: B
options.html: Cross-sectional survey

options.label: C
options.html: Ecological study

options.label: D
options.html: Randomised controlled trial

options.label: E
options.html: Retrospective cohort study

items.explanationHtml:
When the population at risk cannot be enumerated (no guest list or roster), the efficient analytic design is a case-control study: compare the food histories of the cases with those of suitably matched controls from the same community and calculate odds ratios for each suspected food.

A retrospective cohort study is preferred when the exposed group is a well-defined, closed population, such as all guests at a banquet, so that attack rates can be calculated directly.

Takeaway: closed group → retrospective cohort; dispersed community cases → case-control.

whyNot.B: A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and disease at one time in a sample and is inefficient for 38 cases scattered across a city.
whyNot.C: An ecological study compares groups, not individuals, and cannot link individual cases to the food they ate.
whyNot.D: Randomly assigning people to eat a suspected contaminated food would be unethical and is never done in outbreaks.
whyNot.E: A cohort study needs a defined list of exposed and unexposed people, which the department does not have.

items.objective: Choose a case-control design for a community-wide outbreak without a defined cohort.

items.stemHtml:
Forty of 100 people who attended a church picnic develop vomiting and diarrhoea within 2 days. The county health department interviews all 100 attendees about what they ate.

FoodAte the foodDid not eat the food
IllTotalIllTotal
Chicken30601040
Green salad20502050
Ice cream25401560
Lemonade3890210
Potato salad3645455

Which food is the most likely vehicle of the outbreak?

options.label: A
options.html: Chicken

options.label: B
options.html: Green salad

options.label: C
options.html: Ice cream

options.label: D
options.html: Lemonade

options.label: E
options.html: Potato salad

items.explanationHtml:
Compare the attack rate in those who ate each food with the attack rate in those who did not. Potato salad: 36/45 = 80% vs 4/55 ≈ 7%, a ratio of about 11, and it accounts for 36 of the 40 cases. The other foods have ratios between 1 and 2.5: chicken 50% vs 25% (2.0), green salad 40% vs 40% (1.0), ice cream 63% vs 25% (2.5), lemonade 42% vs 20% (2.1).

Lemonade was drunk by the most ill people (38), but it was also drunk by 90% of attendees, so its attack rate barely differs from that of the 10 who did not drink it. The few ill people who did not eat potato salad may have been misclassified in interviews or infected secondarily.

Takeaway: the vehicle has a high attack rate in eaters, a low one in non-eaters and explains most cases.

whyNot.A: Chicken's attack rate among eaters (50%) is only twice that among non-eaters (25%), and 10 ill people did not eat it.
whyNot.B: Green salad has identical attack rates (40%) in eaters and non-eaters, showing no association.
whyNot.C: Ice cream has a modest ratio (about 2.5), probably because many people ate it together with potato salad.
whyNot.D: Lemonade has the most ill drinkers only because almost everyone drank it; its attack rate ratio is about 2.

items.objective: Identify the vehicle of a food-borne outbreak from food-specific attack rates.

items.stemHtml: Over 3 weeks, emergency departments in a town of 40,000 people see 130 patients with watery diarrhoea; Cryptosporidium is identified in stool samples from 22 of them. The epidemic curve rose over the first 4 days and has stayed at a plateau of 5 to 8 new cases per day since then. A rapid interview study shows that almost all patients drink unfiltered tap water from the municipal supply, which recently had a treatment-plant malfunction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the health department?

options.label: A
options.html: Close all schools and childcare centres in the town

options.label: B
options.html: Issue a boil-water advisory together with the water utility

options.label: C
options.html: Recommend empiric antibiotic treatment for all residents with diarrhoea

options.label: D
options.html: Wait for a completed case-control study before taking any action

options.label: E
options.html: Wait for the curve to begin declining before acting

items.explanationHtml:
The plateau pattern indicates a continuous common-source outbreak, and the epidemiologic and environmental evidence points to the municipal water supply. Control measures should start as soon as a likely source is identified: here, a boil-water advisory issued with the water utility while the plant is repaired and the water is tested. Cryptosporidium oocysts resist chlorine, so filtration failure lets them through; boiling kills them.

Outbreak investigation and control run in parallel. Waiting for definitive proof while exposure continues allows more people to become ill.

Takeaway: once a likely continuing source is identified, act to stop exposure while the investigation continues.

whyNot.A: Person-to-person spread in childcare settings can follow, but closing schools does nothing about the continuing water exposure that drives this plateau.
whyNot.C: Cryptosporidiosis is not treated with antibiotics, and mass treatment would not remove the source.
whyNot.D: An analytic study can continue, but delaying control measures while people keep drinking the water causes avoidable cases.
whyNot.E: With a continuous source, the curve will not decline until exposure stops; waiting simply prolongs the outbreak.

items.objective: Implement control measures promptly in a continuous common-source outbreak.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man who works as a cook in a restaurant has jaundice, fatigue and dark urine. Serum IgM antibody to hepatitis A virus is positive. He asks the physician not to tell anyone because he is afraid of losing his job. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Agree not to report the case, to protect his confidentiality

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the hospital ethics committee whether reporting is permitted

options.label: C
options.html: Contact his employer directly to arrange his exclusion from work

options.label: D
options.html: Report the case only if he gives written consent

options.label: E
options.html: Report the case to the local health department and explain to him why it is required

items.explanationHtml:
Acute hepatitis A is a notifiable disease, and a food handler with the infection is a public health priority because the health department may need to exclude him from food handling temporarily and offer post-exposure prophylaxis to restaurant patrons and contacts. Physicians are legally required to report notifiable diseases, and the HIPAA Privacy Rule permits disclosure to public health authorities without the patient's authorisation.

The physician should report the case and tell him so honestly, explain that the health department keeps the report confidential and works with employers in a way that protects both the public and the worker, and address his fears about employment.

Takeaway: reportable diseases are reported regardless of the patient's wishes; tell the patient, and explain why.

whyNot.A: Confidentiality yields to a legal reporting duty that protects others; agreeing not to report would break the law and risk further cases.
whyNot.B: The reporting duty is clear; an ethics consultation would only delay a time-sensitive public health action.
whyNot.C: The physician reports to the health department, which decides on exclusion and contacts; telling the employer directly is an unnecessary disclosure.
whyNot.D: Public health reporting does not require patient consent, so conditioning the report on consent is wrong.

items.objective: Report a notifiable disease to public health without patient consent while explaining why.

items.stemHtml: The county syndromic surveillance system, which analyses emergency department chief complaints, flags a doubling of visits for "vomiting" in one ZIP code over 2 days compared with the usual level. No clinician has reported a cluster, and no laboratory reports of enteric pathogens have increased. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the county epidemiologist?

options.label: A
options.html: Close all restaurants in the ZIP code until the cause is known

options.label: B
options.html: Ignore the signal because no laboratory reports have increased

options.label: C
options.html: Issue a public alert advising residents to avoid tap water

options.label: D
options.html: Review the flagged visits and contact the emergency departments to verify the signal

options.label: E
options.html: Start mass stool testing of all residents in the ZIP code

items.explanationHtml:
Syndromic systems give early warning but produce many false alarms from changes in triage coding, software, a single large family or random variation. The first step is to verify the signal: review the individual visits, look for common features (age, address, onset dates, a shared event), check for any coding changes and talk to the emergency department clinicians. If a genuine cluster emerges, a full investigation follows.

This mirrors the first steps of any outbreak investigation: confirm that the excess is real and verify the diagnosis before deploying control measures.

Takeaway: a syndromic surveillance alarm is verified before action is taken.

whyNot.A: Closing restaurants on an unverified, unexplained signal would cause harm without any evidence of a food source.
whyNot.B: Laboratory reports lag behind clinical visits, which is the reason syndromic surveillance exists; the signal should be checked, not ignored.
whyNot.C: There is no evidence implicating the water, and an unwarranted public alert causes alarm and loses public trust.
whyNot.E: Mass testing is costly and premature before the signal has been verified and a case definition exists.

items.objective: Verify a syndromic surveillance signal before acting.

items.stemHtml: Two days after a county fair, several attendees are admitted with bloody diarrhoea, and Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli is isolated from two of them. The health department begins case finding among the 3,000 fair attendees. Which of the following case definitions is most appropriate at this stage of the investigation?

options.label: A
options.html: Any fair attendee with diarrhoea beginning within 10 days after the fair

options.label: B
options.html: Any fair attendee with haemolytic uraemic syndrome

options.label: C
options.html: Any fair attendee with stool culture positive for the outbreak strain with a matching genetic fingerprint

options.label: D
options.html: Any person in the state with bloody diarrhoea during the year

options.label: E
options.html: Any fair attendee who visited the petting zoo and had bloody diarrhoea

items.explanationHtml:
Early in an investigation the case definition should be sensitive, so that as many potential cases as possible are found: clinical criteria (diarrhoea) restricted by person (fair attendees), place (the fair) and time (a window covering the incubation period). Cases can later be classified as confirmed, probable or possible, and a stricter definition used for the analytic study.

The definition must not include a suspected exposure, and it should not be so broad that it includes unrelated illness from the general population.

Takeaway: broad and sensitive to find cases early; specific (laboratory-confirmed) for analysis.

whyNot.B: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome affects only a minority of infected people, so this definition would miss most cases.
whyNot.C: Requiring a matching genetic fingerprint is highly specific but would miss the many cases without stool cultures; it suits a confirmed-case tier, later.
whyNot.D: Including everyone in the state for a whole year captures mostly unrelated illness, swamping the outbreak.
whyNot.E: Building the petting zoo into the definition includes a suspected exposure, so its role could no longer be tested.

items.objective: Choose a sensitive case definition early in an outbreak investigation.

items.stemHtml: A hospital laboratory replaces stool culture with a multiplex PCR gastrointestinal panel in January. Over the next 3 months, reported Campylobacter infections from the hospital rise from an average of 4 per month to 11 per month. The cases are spread across the hospital's large catchment area, have no common exposures and include patients of all ages. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.label: A
options.html: A common-source food-borne outbreak

options.label: B
options.html: A nosocomial outbreak on one ward

options.label: C
options.html: A propagated person-to-person outbreak

options.label: D
options.html: Contamination of the PCR reagents in one batch

options.label: E
options.html: Increased detection due to the more sensitive test

items.explanationHtml:
The rise began exactly when a more sensitive test was introduced, and the cases have no clustering in time, place or exposure. The most likely explanation is an artefactual increase from improved detection: culture-independent PCR panels find infections that culture missed. Confirming that an outbreak truly exists, by comparing with the baseline obtained with the same methods and excluding changes in testing or reporting, is an early step of any investigation.

Public health laboratories still ask for isolates (reflex culture) from PCR-positive specimens so that strains can be typed and true clusters recognised.

Takeaway: a rise that starts with a new, more sensitive test and lacks clustering is usually a detection artefact.

whyNot.A: A common-source outbreak would show clustering in time and a shared exposure, which these cases lack.
whyNot.B: A ward outbreak would involve inpatients on one unit, not community patients across a large catchment area.
whyNot.C: Person-to-person spread would show linked cases and waves on an epidemic curve, not scattered, unrelated cases.
whyNot.D: Reagent contamination would cause a burst of positives in one batch over a short period and positives without matching illness, not a steady 3-month rise in symptomatic patients.

items.objective: Recognise an artefactual increase in reported cases after a change in testing.

items.stemHtml: A respiratory virus has a basic reproduction number (R0) of 4 in a particular population. A vaccine prevents infection in 95% of vaccinated people. Assuming random mixing and no natural immunity, which of the following is the minimum proportion of the population that must be vaccinated to prevent sustained transmission, to the nearest whole percent?
items.explanationHtml:
The herd immunity threshold is the proportion that must be immune: 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/4 = 0.75. Because only 95% of vaccinated people become immune, the vaccination coverage needed is 0.75 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 0.789, or 79%.

When the immune proportion exceeds the threshold, the effective reproduction number falls below 1 and chains of transmission die out. Less effective vaccines or more transmissible pathogens push the required coverage higher, sometimes above what is achievable.

Takeaway: coverage needed = (1 − 1/R0) ÷ vaccine effectiveness.

whyNot.A: 25% is 1/R<sub>0</sub>, the susceptible fraction that can be tolerated, not the immune fraction required.
whyNot.B: 71% multiplies the threshold by the vaccine effectiveness instead of dividing by it, giving too low a target.
whyNot.C: 75% is the proportion that must be immune; it ignores that 5% of vaccinated people remain susceptible.
whyNot.E: 95% is the vaccine effectiveness, not the required coverage.

items.objective: Calculate the vaccination coverage needed for herd immunity, accounting for vaccine effectiveness.

items.stemHtml: During an epidemic of a new viral infection in a city, an increasing proportion of residents become immune through infection and vaccination. Contact patterns, the virus and the duration of infectiousness do not change. Which of the following quantities decreases as a result?

options.label: A
options.html: Basic reproduction number (R<sub>0</sub>)

options.label: B
options.html: Effective reproduction number (R<sub>t</sub>)

options.label: C
options.html: Incubation period

options.label: D
options.html: Serial interval

options.label: E
options.html: Herd immunity threshold

items.explanationHtml:
The effective reproduction number is the average number of secondary cases per case at a given time, given current immunity and control measures. It is approximately R0 × the proportion still susceptible, so it falls as immunity accumulates. When it drops below 1, the epidemic declines.

R0 is defined in a fully susceptible population and depends on the pathogen, contact rates and duration of infectiousness, none of which changed here. The herd immunity threshold (1 − 1/R0) is fixed by R0.

Takeaway: immunity lowers Rt, not R0.

whyNot.A: R<sub>0</sub> describes spread in a fully susceptible population and does not change as people become immune.
whyNot.C: The incubation period is a property of the infection in each host and is unaffected by population immunity.
whyNot.D: The serial interval depends on the timing of infectiousness and symptom onset, which are unchanged.
whyNot.E: The herd immunity threshold is 1 − 1/R<sub>0</sub>; since R<sub>0</sub> is unchanged, so is the threshold.

items.objective: Distinguish the effective from the basic reproduction number.

items.stemHtml: Studies of a new respiratory virus find that infected people become infectious about 3 days after infection and develop symptoms about 5 days after infection. Which of the following is the most important implication for control of the virus?

options.label: A
options.html: Isolating people only after symptoms begin will not prevent all transmission

options.label: B
options.html: Quarantine of exposed contacts is unnecessary

options.label: C
options.html: The infection cannot be spread by people without symptoms

options.label: D
options.html: The serial interval must be longer than the incubation period

options.label: E
options.html: Transmission occurs only after symptom onset

items.explanationHtml:
The latent period (infection to infectiousness, about 3 days) is shorter than the incubation period (infection to symptoms, about 5 days). People are therefore infectious for about 2 days before they feel ill, and presymptomatic transmission occurs. Isolating people once symptoms appear misses this window, so quarantine of exposed contacts, testing and other measures are needed.

When the latent period is longer than the incubation period (as in many infections where people are most infectious after symptom onset), symptom-based isolation is much more effective.

Takeaway: latent period shorter than incubation period → presymptomatic spread → symptom-based isolation is not enough.

whyNot.B: Because exposed people can transmit before symptoms, quarantine of contacts is more, not less, important.
whyNot.C: People are infectious from day 3 but not symptomatic until day 5, so presymptomatic spread is expected.
whyNot.D: With presymptomatic transmission, the serial interval can be shorter than the incubation period, not necessarily longer.
whyNot.E: Infectiousness begins about 2 days before symptoms, so transmission is not confined to the symptomatic period.

items.objective: Relate latent and incubation periods to presymptomatic transmission.

items.stemHtml: A multistate outbreak of hepatitis A is traced to a single brand of imported frozen berries. Cases have no contact with one another and live in 14 states. Which of the following modes of transmission best describes this outbreak?

options.label: A
options.html: Airborne

options.label: B
options.html: Direct contact

options.label: C
options.html: Droplet

options.label: D
options.html: Vector-borne

options.label: E
options.html: Vehicle-borne

items.explanationHtml:
An inanimate substance (here a contaminated food) that carries the agent to many people is a vehicle. Vehicle-borne transmission is a form of indirect transmission and the classic cause of common-source outbreaks, including food- and waterborne outbreaks and outbreaks from contaminated blood products or medication vials.

Hepatitis A is shed in stool and spreads by the faecal-oral route, either from person to person or through contaminated food and water; frozen produce can carry the virus for long periods.

Takeaway: food, water, blood products and shared vials are vehicles.

whyNot.A: Airborne transmission involves small particles suspended in air; hepatitis A is transmitted by the faecal-oral route.
whyNot.B: Direct contact requires physical contact between people, and these cases had no contact with one another.
whyNot.C: Droplet transmission involves large respiratory droplets over a short distance, not a distributed food product.
whyNot.D: Vector-borne transmission requires a living carrier such as an insect, not a food product.

items.objective: Classify a food-borne common-source outbreak as vehicle-borne transmission.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman who works as a food handler had typhoid fever 14 months ago, which was treated. She has felt well since then. Stool cultures obtained during a public health investigation of two typhoid cases among her customers grow Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Which of the following best describes her status?

options.label: A
options.html: Chronic carrier

options.label: B
options.html: Convalescent carrier

options.label: C
options.html: Incubatory carrier

options.label: D
options.html: Index case of a propagated epidemic

options.label: E
options.html: Reinfected case

items.explanationHtml:
She is well but continues to shed S. Typhi more than a year after her illness, making her a chronic carrier. Chronic typhoid carriage is often associated with persistent infection of the gallbladder, especially when gallstones are present. Carriers are important reservoirs because they look healthy and can contaminate food for long periods.

Carriers are classified by timing: incubatory (shedding before illness), convalescent (shedding during recovery, usually for weeks to months) and chronic (shedding for about a year or longer). Some carriers never have symptoms at all.

Takeaway: healthy and still shedding a year after illness = chronic carrier.

whyNot.B: Convalescent carriage lasts weeks to a few months after recovery; 14 months later she meets the definition of a chronic carrier.
whyNot.C: An incubatory carrier sheds the organism before developing illness; she was ill more than a year ago.
whyNot.D: Typhoid spread from a food handler to customers is a common-vehicle pattern, and she has no current illness to make her an index case of a propagated epidemic.
whyNot.E: She has no new illness, and persistent shedding since her infection is much more likely than a new infection.

items.objective: Classify carrier states by timing relative to illness.

items.stemHtml: A hospital infection-prevention team reviews which patients require placement in an airborne infection isolation room. Which of the following infections requires airborne precautions?

options.label: A
options.html: Clostridioides difficile colitis

options.label: B
options.html: Influenza

options.label: C
options.html: Meningococcal meningitis

options.label: D
options.html: Pertussis

options.label: E
options.html: Measles

items.explanationHtml:
Measles virus spreads by small airborne particles that remain suspended and infectious in a room for up to about 2 hours after the patient has left. Airborne precautions (a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room and a fit-tested N95 or higher respirator for staff) are required, as for pulmonary tuberculosis and varicella.

Most respiratory pathogens spread by large droplets over short distances and need droplet precautions; organisms on skin and surfaces need contact precautions.

Takeaway: airborne precautions are for measles, varicella (and disseminated zoster) and pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis.

whyNot.A: C. difficile spreads by spores on hands and surfaces, which requires contact precautions and soap-and-water hand washing.
whyNot.B: Influenza is managed with droplet precautions in routine care.
