whyNot.C: Meningococcal disease requires droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy.
whyNot.D: Pertussis spreads by respiratory droplets and requires droplet precautions.

items.objective: Identify infections that require airborne precautions.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man is admitted from the emergency department with 2 months of productive cough, night sweats and an 8-kg weight loss. He recently moved from a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis. Chest radiograph shows a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe. Sputum samples have been collected for acid-fast bacilli smear and nucleic acid amplification testing. Which of the following is the most appropriate infection-control measure while results are pending?

options.label: A
options.html: Contact precautions with gown and gloves in a shared room

options.label: B
options.html: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask for staff

options.label: C
options.html: Standard precautions until a smear is positive

options.label: D
options.html: Discharge home with instructions to wear a mask

options.label: E
options.html: Placement in an airborne infection isolation room with N95 respirators for staff

items.explanationHtml:
Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis calls for airborne precautions immediately, on suspicion: a single negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room, a fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirator for anyone entering and a surgical mask for the patient when he must leave the room. Precautions continue until tuberculosis is excluded or he is no longer considered infectious on effective treatment.

Waiting for confirmation before starting precautions exposes staff and other patients during the most infectious period.

Takeaway: cavitary upper-lobe disease with tuberculosis risk factors → airborne isolation now, not after results.

whyNot.A: Tuberculosis is airborne; gowns and gloves do not prevent inhalation, and a shared room exposes another patient.
whyNot.B: Surgical masks do not protect the wearer from airborne particles; staff need fitted respirators.
whyNot.C: Precautions are started on clinical suspicion; waiting for a smear exposes others, and a negative smear does not exclude infectiousness.
whyNot.D: He needs inpatient evaluation; and if he were managed at home, that would need health department coordination, not simply a mask.

items.objective: Start airborne isolation on suspicion of pulmonary tuberculosis.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman in a medical ward develops profuse watery diarrhoea on day 6 of intravenous antibiotics for pneumonia. A stool test confirms Clostridioides difficile infection. Which of the following infection-control measures is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room

options.label: B
options.html: Contact precautions with gown and gloves, and hand washing with soap and water

options.label: C
options.html: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask

options.label: D
options.html: Standard precautions with alcohol-based hand rub only

options.label: E
options.html: No special measures because the infection resulted from her antibiotics

items.explanationHtml:
C. difficile spreads by spores on hands, equipment and surfaces. Contact precautions (single room or cohorting, gown and gloves on entry, dedicated equipment) are required, and staff should wash hands with soap and water, because alcohol-based rubs do not kill spores. Rooms are cleaned with a sporicidal agent.

Although the infection followed antibiotic use, the organism is transmissible to other patients, many of whom are also on antibiotics.

Takeaway: C. difficile → contact precautions plus soap-and-water hand hygiene and sporicidal cleaning.

whyNot.A: C. difficile is not spread through the air; airborne isolation uses scarce rooms and does not address spores on hands and surfaces.
whyNot.C: Surgical masks protect against respiratory droplets, which are not how C. difficile spreads.
whyNot.D: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores, so reliance on alcohol rub alone allows spread.
whyNot.E: The spores can spread to other patients regardless of how her infection arose; transmission-based precautions are needed.

items.objective: Choose contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene for C. difficile infection.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is brought to clinic because 2 days ago he sat for an hour in an urgent care waiting room next to a child who was later diagnosed with measles. He has received no vaccines because his parents had concerns about vaccine safety; they now want to protect him. He is healthy and takes no medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give intravenous ribavirin

options.label: B
options.html: Give MMR vaccine today

options.label: C
options.html: Give vitamin A and observe for symptoms

options.label: D
options.html: Observe and give MMR only if no rash appears after 3 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Reassure the parents that a brief exposure carries little risk

items.explanationHtml:
For a susceptible person aged 12 months or older, MMR vaccine given within 72 hours of exposure can prevent measles or reduce its severity, and it also begins his routine protection. He is at day 2, so vaccination today is the appropriate post-exposure measure. Immune globulin is reserved for people who cannot receive the vaccine (such as young infants, pregnant women without immunity and severely immunocompromised people) or who present between 3 and 6 days after exposure.

The exposure is also reported to the health department, which manages contact follow-up and advises on exclusion from childcare.

Takeaway: susceptible, exposed to measles, within 72 hours, no contraindication → MMR now.

whyNot.A: Ribavirin is not a recommended post-exposure prophylaxis for measles.
whyNot.C: Vitamin A is given to children who have measles to reduce complications; it does not prevent infection after exposure.
whyNot.D: Waiting 3 weeks wastes the 72-hour window in which vaccine can prevent disease.
whyNot.E: Measles is highly transmissible, and an hour in the same room is a significant exposure for an unvaccinated child.

items.objective: Give MMR as post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours of a measles exposure.

items.stemHtml: A state health department reports that the estimated effective reproduction number (Rt) for a respiratory infection fell from 2.4 to 0.8 over the 6 weeks after a vaccination campaign and other measures. A hospital administrator asks what this means for the coming weeks. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Each case is now infecting fewer than one other person on average, so case numbers should decline gradually

options.label: B
options.html: New cases will stop immediately

options.label: C
options.html: The basic reproduction number of the infection has fallen below 1

options.label: D
options.html: The epidemic is still growing but more slowly

options.label: E
options.html: Herd immunity has been reached permanently, so all measures can be stopped

items.explanationHtml:
An effective reproduction number below 1 means that, on average, each case currently infects fewer than one other person. Case numbers should therefore shrink generation by generation, but they do not fall to zero at once: cases continue for several serial intervals as transmission chains die out.

R0 has not changed; the fall in Rt reflects immunity and control measures. If measures are relaxed while many people remain susceptible, Rt can rise above 1 again.

Takeaway: Rt < 1 = a shrinking epidemic, not an ended one.

whyNot.B: With R<sub>t</sub> of 0.8, cases decline over several generations rather than stopping immediately.
whyNot.C: R<sub>0</sub> is defined in a fully susceptible population and is not altered by immunity or measures; R<sub>t</sub> is what fell.
whyNot.D: An epidemic grows only while R<sub>t</sub> exceeds 1; at 0.8 it is shrinking.
whyNot.E: R<sub>t</sub> below 1 depends partly on current measures; stopping them could push it back above 1.

items.objective: Interpret a change in the effective reproduction number for planning.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 38 weeks' gestation is found on prenatal screening to be positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. She delivers a healthy term boy by vaginal delivery. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the newborn?

options.label: A
options.html: Avoid breastfeeding and give vaccine at 2 months

options.label: B
options.html: Give hepatitis B immune globulin alone at birth

options.label: C
options.html: Give the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine at the 2-month visit

options.label: D
options.html: Test the newborn for HBsAg at 1 week before giving any prophylaxis

options.label: E
options.html: Give hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth

items.explanationHtml:
Infants born to mothers positive for hepatitis B surface antigen should receive both hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth, at different injection sites, then complete the vaccine series and have post-vaccination testing for HBsAg and antibody after the series. This combination prevents most perinatal transmission.

Breastfeeding is not contraindicated for infants who receive this prophylaxis. Universal prenatal screening exists so that this time-critical intervention is not missed.

Takeaway: HBsAg-positive mother → vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth.

whyNot.A: Breastfeeding does not add meaningful risk after prophylaxis, and delaying the vaccine to 2 months misses the critical window.
whyNot.B: Immune globulin gives only temporary passive protection; the vaccine is needed at the same time for lasting immunity.
whyNot.C: Delaying the first vaccine dose to 2 months leaves the infant unprotected during the period of highest risk.
whyNot.D: Prophylaxis must be given within 12 hours; testing first would delay it beyond the effective window.

items.objective: Prevent vertical transmission of hepatitis B with newborn vaccine and immune globulin.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old university student is admitted with meningococcal meningitis confirmed by cerebrospinal fluid culture. She shares a dormitory room with one roommate and attended a 300-student lecture 2 days ago. The roommate is well. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure for the roommate?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis given as soon as possible

options.label: B
options.html: Droplet precautions for 10 days

options.label: C
options.html: No action unless symptoms develop

options.label: D
options.html: Meningococcal vaccination alone

options.label: E
options.html: Throat culture, with treatment only if positive

items.explanationHtml:
Close contacts of a person with invasive meningococcal disease (household members, roommates, and people directly exposed to oral secretions) are at much higher risk and should receive chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of identification of the index case. Options include rifampin for 2 days, a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone or a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin; local ciprofloxacin resistance can change the choice, and the health department advises on it.

Classmates in a large lecture are not close contacts and do not need prophylaxis. Vaccination may be added in an outbreak, but it does not act quickly enough to replace chemoprophylaxis.

Takeaway: meningococcal disease → prompt chemoprophylaxis for close contacts only.

whyNot.B: Droplet precautions apply to the patient in hospital, not to a well contact; the roommate needs prophylaxis.
whyNot.C: Waiting for symptoms risks fulminant disease; close contacts are given prophylaxis while well.
whyNot.D: Vaccine-induced protection takes days to develop and does not cover every serogroup; it does not replace chemoprophylaxis.
whyNot.E: Throat cultures are unreliable for identifying carriage and delay prophylaxis; all close contacts are treated.

items.objective: Give chemoprophylaxis to close contacts of meningococcal disease.

items.stemHtml: A city council adopts zoning rules that create protected walking and cycling routes to schools, limit new fast-food outlets within 500 metres of schools and fund playgrounds in low-income neighbourhoods. The stated goal is to keep children from developing obesity, high blood pressure and other cardiovascular risk factors in the first place. Which of the following levels of prevention does this policy represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Primordial prevention

options.label: B
options.html: Primary prevention

options.label: C
options.html: Secondary prevention

options.label: D
options.html: Tertiary prevention

options.label: E
options.html: Quaternary prevention

items.explanationHtml:
Primordial prevention acts on the social, economic and environmental conditions that allow risk factors to emerge in a population. Shaping the built environment so that children are less likely to become obese or hypertensive is the classic example.

Primary prevention, by contrast, prevents disease in people who may already have risk factors (treating hypertension to prevent a first stroke, vaccination). The distinction is whether the target is the risk factor's emergence or the disease's onset.

Takeaway: preventing risk factors from arising, through policy and environment, is primordial prevention.

whyNot.B: Primary prevention prevents disease onset, often by modifying existing risk factors; this policy aims to stop the risk factors from appearing at all.
whyNot.C: Secondary prevention detects disease early in people without symptoms, for example by screening.
whyNot.D: Tertiary prevention reduces complications and disability in established disease.
whyNot.E: Quaternary prevention protects people from unnecessary medical intervention.

items.objective: Recognise primordial prevention.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 35-year-old man has had three normal ECGs, a normal exercise test and a normal echocardiogram over the past year for brief, sharp chest twinges that occur at rest. He now asks for coronary angiography. His physician explains that further testing is more likely to cause harm than benefit, offers regular follow-up and discusses ways to manage his anxiety. Which of the following levels of prevention does the physician's approach represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Primordial prevention

options.label: B
options.html: Primary prevention

options.label: C
options.html: Secondary prevention

options.label: D
options.html: Tertiary prevention

options.label: E
options.html: Quaternary prevention

items.explanationHtml:
Quaternary prevention protects patients from overmedicalisation: unnecessary tests, procedures and treatments, and the harms of the cascades they start. Declining invasive testing with no reasonable indication, while staying engaged with the patient's concern, is the textbook example.

The other levels are defined by the stage of disease; quaternary prevention applies at any stage and is aimed at harm from health care itself.

Takeaway: avoiding harm from unnecessary care is quaternary prevention.

whyNot.A: Primordial prevention addresses conditions that create risk factors in populations, not testing decisions for an individual.
whyNot.B: Primary prevention prevents disease from starting, for example with vaccination or treatment of risk factors.
whyNot.C: Secondary prevention is early detection of disease; the physician is deliberately avoiding further detection testing that is not indicated.
whyNot.D: Tertiary prevention reduces complications of established disease, which he does not have.

items.objective: Recognise quaternary prevention.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with no symptoms has a stool-based colorectal cancer screening test that is positive. Colonoscopy finds a 12-mm adenomatous polyp, which is removed completely. Which of the following levels of prevention is represented by the screening programme that found the polyp?

options.label: A
options.html: Primordial prevention

options.label: B
options.html: Primary prevention

options.label: C
options.html: Secondary prevention

options.label: D
options.html: Tertiary prevention

options.label: E
options.html: Quaternary prevention

items.explanationHtml:
Screening asymptomatic people to detect disease, or a precursor lesion, at an early stage when treatment improves the outcome is secondary prevention. Removing an adenoma before it becomes invasive cancer is the point of colorectal screening.

Screening only counts as prevention if there is a detectable preclinical phase and early treatment is more effective than treatment after symptoms appear; both are true for colorectal adenomas and early cancers.

Takeaway: screening of people without symptoms = secondary prevention.

whyNot.A: Primordial prevention acts on the conditions that create risk factors, such as diet policy, not on testing individuals.
whyNot.B: Primary prevention stops disease before any biologic change; screening finds changes that have already begun.
whyNot.D: Tertiary prevention applies after clinical disease, for example rehabilitation after colectomy for symptomatic cancer.
whyNot.E: Quaternary prevention avoids unnecessary care; this was a recommended screening test.

items.objective: Classify screening as secondary prevention.

items.stemHtml: A community health centre reviews its preventive services. Which of the following is an example of tertiary prevention?

options.label: A
options.html: A supervised cardiac rehabilitation programme after myocardial infarction

options.label: B
options.html: Blood pressure measurement at every adult visit

options.label: C
options.html: A school-based policy restricting sugar-sweetened drinks

options.label: D
options.html: Tetanus-diphtheria booster vaccination for adults

options.label: E
options.html: Mammography every 2 years for women aged 40 to 74

items.explanationHtml:
Tertiary prevention limits complications, disability and recurrence once clinical disease is established. Cardiac rehabilitation after a myocardial infarction improves function and reduces readmission and cardiovascular death.

Classify by stage on the natural history: no disease → primary (or primordial if it targets the conditions that create risk factors); asymptomatic disease → secondary; established clinical disease → tertiary.

Takeaway: rehabilitation after an established event is tertiary prevention.

whyNot.B: Routine blood pressure measurement detects hypertension in asymptomatic people, which is screening (secondary prevention).
whyNot.C: A drinks policy aims to prevent risk factors such as obesity from arising, which is primordial prevention.
whyNot.D: Vaccination prevents infection in susceptible people, which is primary prevention.
whyNot.E: Mammography detects breast cancer in women without symptoms, which is secondary prevention.

items.objective: Identify tertiary prevention among preventive services.

items.stemHtml: In a town, adults with severe hypertension have the highest individual risk of stroke but make up only 10% of the population. Most strokes occur in the much larger group of adults whose blood pressure is only mildly elevated or in the high-normal range. A population-wide reduction in salt in processed food would lower average blood pressure slightly in everyone. Which of the following principles explains why this population strategy may prevent more strokes than treating only those with severe hypertension?

options.label: A
options.html: Prevention paradox

options.label: B
options.html: Berkson bias

options.label: C
options.html: Ecological fallacy

options.label: D
options.html: Lead-time bias

options.label: E
options.html: Simpson's paradox

items.explanationHtml:
The prevention paradox describes the finding that a large number of people at small or moderate risk may give rise to more cases than the small number at high risk. A measure that shifts the whole risk distribution therefore prevents many cases in total, although it offers little benefit to each individual who takes part.

High-risk and population strategies complement each other: treating the high-risk group helps those individuals greatly, while population measures reach where most cases actually arise.

Takeaway: most cases come from the many at moderate risk, so small population-wide shifts can prevent the most disease.

whyNot.B: Berkson bias is a selection bias in hospital-based case-control studies, unrelated to prevention strategy.
whyNot.C: The ecological fallacy is wrongly inferring individual-level associations from group-level data.
whyNot.D: Lead-time bias is the apparent survival gain from earlier diagnosis by screening.
whyNot.E: Simpson's paradox is the reversal of an association when data are combined across groups, a form of confounding.

items.objective: Explain the prevention paradox behind population strategies.

items.stemHtml: A public health committee considers screening programmes for four conditions. Which of the following characteristics of a condition most strongly favours population screening?

options.label: A
options.html: A detectable preclinical phase lasting years, during which treatment improves outcomes

options.label: B
options.html: A disease that is usually fatal within weeks of becoming detectable

options.label: C
options.html: A low prevalence with no effective treatment at any stage

options.label: D
options.html: Rapid progression from biologic onset to symptoms

options.label: E
options.html: Symptoms that appear at the same time as the disease becomes detectable

items.explanationHtml:
Screening works only if a disease can be found during a detectable preclinical phase, the interval between when a test can detect it and when symptoms would appear. That phase must be long enough for periodic testing to catch it, and treatment in the phase must be more effective than treatment after symptoms.

Other requirements include an important health problem, an acceptable and accurate test, and facilities for diagnosis and treatment. Benefit must be shown by lower disease-specific mortality, not by longer survival after diagnosis.

Takeaway: a long detectable preclinical phase plus effective early treatment is what makes screening worthwhile.

whyNot.B: If disease is fatal soon after it becomes detectable, there is no window in which early treatment can change the outcome.
whyNot.C: Without effective treatment, earlier detection only lengthens the time a person knows they are ill.
whyNot.D: Rapid progression gives a very short preclinical phase that periodic screening would usually miss.
whyNot.E: If detectability coincides with symptoms, there is no preclinical phase to screen for.

items.objective: Identify the disease characteristics that make screening worthwhile.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. She is healthy, has never smoked and takes no medications. Her cervical, breast and colorectal cancer screening are up to date. She received all routine childhood vaccines and an influenza vaccine this season. She has not received any vaccine against herpes zoster. The physician wants to offer an evidence-based primary prevention measure today. Which of the following is the most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Coronary artery calcium scan

options.label: B
options.html: Low-dose CT of the chest

options.label: C
options.html: Serum CA-125 measurement

options.label: D
options.html: Whole-body MRI

options.label: E
options.html: Recombinant zoster vaccine series

items.explanationHtml:
Primary prevention prevents disease from starting in people who do not have it. Adults aged 50 and older are recommended to receive the two-dose recombinant zoster vaccine to prevent shingles and postherpetic neuralgia, regardless of whether they recall having chickenpox.

The remaining options are tests to detect disease (secondary prevention), and none of them is indicated for this average-risk woman.

Takeaway: vaccines due for age are the clearest primary prevention measures at a health maintenance visit.

whyNot.A: Coronary calcium scoring is a detection test, not primary prevention, and it is not routinely recommended for asymptomatic low-risk adults.
whyNot.B: Low-dose CT screening for lung cancer is for adults aged 50 to 80 with a substantial smoking history; she has never smoked.
whyNot.C: CA-125 screening for ovarian cancer is not recommended for average-risk women because it has not reduced mortality and causes harm.
whyNot.D: Whole-body MRI has no evidence of benefit in asymptomatic adults and leads to incidental findings and further testing.

items.objective: Choose an age-appropriate primary prevention measure.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old warehouse worker has had low back pain for 5 days after lifting boxes. He has no fever, weight loss, history of cancer, trauma, bowel or bladder symptoms, or leg weakness. Examination shows paraspinal tenderness and a normal neurologic examination. He asks for an MRI "to see what's wrong". Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "An MRI now is unlikely to change your care; let's talk about what will help you recover."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'll order the MRI today so that we can be completely sure."

options.label: C
options.html: "I'll refer you to a spine surgeon, who can decide on imaging."

options.label: D
options.html: "Let's get plain radiographs of your lower back instead of an MRI."

options.label: E
options.html: "There's nothing seriously wrong, so you don't need any treatment at all."

items.explanationHtml:
Acute low back pain without red flags usually improves within weeks, and early imaging does not improve outcomes; it often shows degenerative findings that are common in people without pain and can lead to unnecessary procedures. Explaining this while addressing his concern and offering an active plan (staying active, heat, analgesia such as an NSAID if suitable, when to return) is quaternary prevention combined with good communication.

Declining a test is not the same as dismissing the patient; the response should engage with what worries him and set clear safety-net advice.

Takeaway: no red flags in acute back pain → no imaging; explain why and offer a plan.

whyNot.B: Ordering the MRI to satisfy the request exposes him to incidental findings and cascades without improving his recovery.
whyNot.C: Surgical referral is not indicated for acute back pain without neurologic deficits or red flags.
whyNot.D: Plain radiographs are equally unhelpful without red flags and add radiation exposure.
whyNot.E: Dismissing his pain without a plan is unhelpful; he still needs advice and symptom management.

items.objective: Practise quaternary prevention by declining unnecessary imaging with an explanation.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman with no symptoms asks to be screened for ovarian cancer with a CA-125 test and transvaginal ultrasonography because a friend recently died of the disease. She has no family history of ovarian or breast cancer and no known genetic mutation. Pelvic examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'll order both tests today; with ovarian cancer it's better to be safe than sorry."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'm sorry about your friend. In women at average risk, these tests don't save lives and can cause harm; what worries you most?"

options.label: C
options.html: "Ovarian cancer is rare at your age, so there's really no reason to be concerned."

options.label: D
options.html: "Before any screening, we should test you for BRCA mutations to check your risk."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll order the CA-125 blood test alone, because it is less invasive than ultrasound."

items.explanationHtml:
For asymptomatic women at average risk, screening for ovarian cancer with CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasonography has not reduced ovarian cancer mortality in large trials and leads to false-positive results and unnecessary surgery with complications; the USPSTF recommends against it. The best response acknowledges her loss, explains the evidence honestly and explores her concerns, including symptoms that should prompt evaluation and her family history.

Applying screening principles to an individual request means neither ordering a harmful test nor dismissing the fear behind it.

Takeaway: do not screen average-risk women for ovarian cancer; explain why with empathy.

whyNot.A: Ordering both tests exposes her to false positives and surgical harms without a mortality benefit.
whyNot.C: Dismissing her concern ignores the grief and worry that prompted the request.
whyNot.D: Genetic testing is offered to women with a personal or family history suggesting increased risk, which she does not have.
whyNot.E: CA-125 alone is also not recommended for screening and has the same problems of false positives and no mortality benefit.

items.objective: Decline non-recommended screening while addressing the patient's concern.

items.stemHtml:
A county health department has funding for one programme to reduce strokes over the next decade. Its data show the following distribution of adults and strokes by blood pressure category.

Blood pressure categoryShare of adultsShare of all strokes
Normal50%15%
Elevated or stage 1 hypertension40%55%
Stage 2 hypertension10%30%

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by these data?

options.label: A
options.html: A programme confined to people with normal blood pressure would prevent the most strokes

options.label: B
options.html: A programme confined to stage 2 hypertension can prevent at most about 30% of strokes, so a population-wide measure could reach more

options.label: C
options.html: Blood pressure is not related to stroke risk in this county

options.label: D
options.html: People with stage 2 hypertension have a lower individual risk of stroke than others

options.label: E
options.html: Stroke prevention should wait until all adults have stage 2 hypertension treated

items.explanationHtml:
People with stage 2 hypertension have the highest individual risk (10% of adults, 30% of strokes), but 70% of strokes occur in the 90% of adults with lower pressures. Even a perfect programme for the highest-risk group could prevent at most about 30% of strokes. A measure that lowers blood pressure slightly across the whole population (such as reducing sodium in processed food) acts on the groups where most strokes occur.

This is the prevention paradox. In practice, high-risk treatment and population-wide measures are complementary.

Takeaway: when most cases arise in the large moderate-risk group, population strategies can prevent more events than high-risk strategies alone.

whyNot.A: People with normal blood pressure account for only 15% of strokes; a programme confined to them would prevent few events.
whyNot.C: The share of strokes rises steeply relative to population share as blood pressure rises, showing a strong relationship.
whyNot.D: Stage 2 hypertension carries the highest individual risk: 30% of strokes from 10% of adults.
whyNot.E: Waiting for complete high-risk treatment ignores the 70% of strokes arising outside that group.

items.objective: Apply the prevention paradox to choose between high-risk and population strategies.

items.stemHtml: A state introduced a screening programme for a slowly progressive cancer 10 years ago. A report shows that 5-year survival after diagnosis rose from 55% to 78%, and the number of cancers diagnosed each year rose by 40%. Over the same period, the age-adjusted death rate from the cancer has not changed. A legislator cites the survival figures as proof that the programme saves lives. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The programme has reduced mortality from the cancer

options.label: B
options.html: The programme should be expanded because more cancers are being found

options.label: C
options.html: The rise in diagnoses proves that the cancer is becoming more common

options.label: D
options.html: The stable death rate proves that the screening test is inaccurate

options.label: E
options.html: The improved survival may reflect lead time and overdiagnosis, because the death rate has not changed

items.explanationHtml:
Survival measured from diagnosis is inflated by screening even when nobody lives longer: lead time starts the survival clock earlier, length-time bias preferentially detects slow-growing tumours, and overdiagnosis adds cancers that would never have caused harm (consistent with the 40% rise in diagnoses). The decisive measure, the age-adjusted death rate in the population, is unchanged, so there is no evidence that the programme prevents deaths.

Screening programmes should be judged by disease-specific mortality in the whole screened population, ideally in randomised trials.

Takeaway: rising survival and incidence with flat mortality after screening = lead time and overdiagnosis, not proof of benefit.

whyNot.A: The age-adjusted death rate did not fall, so the data do not show reduced mortality.
whyNot.B: Finding more cancers is expected with screening and with overdiagnosis; it is not itself a benefit.
whyNot.C: A rise in diagnoses after screening begins usually reflects detection of existing and indolent disease, not a true rise in occurrence.
whyNot.D: An accurate test can still fail to reduce deaths if detected cancers would not have been fatal or early treatment does not change the outcome.

items.objective: Recognise lead-time bias and overdiagnosis when evaluating a screening programme.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man wakes at night to find a bat flying in his bedroom. He is not aware of being bitten, and examination shows no wounds. The bat escaped through a window before it could be caught. He has never received rabies vaccine and has no immune compromise. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give rabies immune globulin and begin rabies vaccine

options.label: B
options.html: Give rabies vaccine only if symptoms develop

options.label: C
options.html: Observe him for 10 days

options.label: D
options.html: Reassure him because there is no visible bite

options.label: E
options.html: Start empiric antiviral therapy

items.explanationHtml:
Bat bites can be tiny and go unnoticed. When a bat is found in the room of a person who was asleep and the bat cannot be tested, rabies post-exposure prophylaxis is recommended: human rabies immune globulin (infiltrated at any wound site, with the rest given intramuscularly) and a series of rabies vaccine doses for a person who has never been vaccinated.

Post-exposure prophylaxis is still primary prevention: it acts during the incubation period, after exposure but before disease. Once symptoms of rabies appear, the disease is almost always fatal, so there is no later point of intervention.

Takeaway: a bat in the room of a sleeping person, bat unavailable for testing → rabies immune globulin plus vaccine.

whyNot.B: Clinical rabies is nearly always fatal, so waiting for symptoms abandons the only effective point of intervention.
whyNot.C: A 10-day observation applies to a healthy dog, cat or ferret that bit someone, not to the person after a bat exposure.
whyNot.D: Bat bites may leave no visible mark; the absence of a wound does not exclude exposure.
whyNot.E: No antiviral therapy prevents rabies after exposure; immune globulin and vaccine are the effective measures.

items.objective: Choose post-exposure prophylaxis as the point of intervention after a possible rabies exposure.

items.stemHtml: A dermatologist writes up a 47-year-old man who developed widespread blistering of the palms and soles 10 days after starting a newly approved oral drug for psoriasis. She describes his history, examination, skin biopsy findings, the drug's withdrawal and his recovery over 6 weeks. No other patients are included. Which of the following best describes this publication?

options.label: A
options.html: Case report

options.label: B
options.html: Case series

options.label: C
options.html: Case-control study

options.label: D
options.html: Cross-sectional study

options.label: E
options.html: Retrospective cohort study

items.explanationHtml:
A detailed description of one patient is a case report. It is the smallest unit of descriptive research: no comparison group, no denominator and no test of a hypothesis.

Case reports earn their place by flagging something new: an unexpected adverse reaction to a recently marketed drug, an unusual presentation or a new disease. They generate hypotheses that analytical studies then test.

Takeaway: one patient described in detail = case report; several similar patients = case series.

whyNot.B: A case series describes several patients with the same exposure or condition; this paper describes a single patient.
whyNot.C: A case-control study compares people with the outcome with people without it; there is no comparison group here.
whyNot.D: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome in a defined sample at one time; a single clinical narrative is not a sample.
whyNot.E: A retrospective cohort study follows exposed and unexposed groups through past records; one patient is not a cohort.

items.objective: Identify a case report and distinguish it from a case series and from analytical designs.

items.stemHtml: Over 8 months, physicians at an urban clinic see 9 previously healthy men aged 22 to 35 years with an unusual fungal pneumonia. All 9 had attended the same indoor climbing gym. The physicians publish a description of the 9 patients, their symptoms, imaging, treatment and outcomes. Which of the following is the most important reason this report cannot show that the gym caused the illness?

options.label: A
options.html: Patients were likely to recall their gym use inaccurately

options.label: B
options.html: Too many patients were lost to follow-up

options.label: C
options.html: There is no group of people without the pneumonia for comparison

options.label: D
options.html: Earlier diagnosis made survival appear longer

options.label: E
options.html: Group-level data were applied to individual patients

items.explanationHtml:
A report of several patients who share a condition is a case series. It can show that the patients have something in common, but without a comparison group it cannot show that the shared feature is more common in people with the disease than in people without it. Many young men in that city may also climb at that gym.

The series is still valuable: it raises a specific hypothesis (an environmental fungal source at the gym) that a case-control study or an environmental investigation can test.

Takeaway: descriptive studies generate hypotheses; without a comparison group they cannot test them.

whyNot.A: Recall bias needs a comparison of recall between groups; the larger problem is that there is no comparison group at all.
whyNot.B: Loss to follow-up is a problem of cohort studies and trials; this report does not follow a defined group over time.
whyNot.D: Lead-time bias concerns screening and survival; the report makes no survival comparison.
whyNot.E: The ecological fallacy needs group-level data; this report describes individual patients.

items.objective: Explain why a case series cannot establish causation.

items.stemHtml: A neurologist describes 24 patients who developed a new peripheral neuropathy while taking an investigational antiviral drug. Eighteen of the 24 patients had symptoms that began in the feet, and 15 improved after the drug was stopped. The report includes no information about patients who took the drug without developing neuropathy. Which of the following can be calculated from this report?

options.label: A
options.html: The incidence of neuropathy among patients taking the drug

options.label: B
options.html: The relative risk of neuropathy with the drug

options.label: C
options.html: The odds ratio for drug exposure in neuropathy

options.label: D
options.html: The attributable risk of neuropathy due to the drug

options.label: E
options.html: The proportion of affected patients whose symptoms began in the feet

items.explanationHtml:
A case series has a numerator but no population denominator. Within the series you can describe the cases: 18/24 = 75% had symptoms that began in the feet and 15/24 = 62.5% improved after withdrawal. These proportions describe the clinical picture of the cases.

Every measure of risk or association (incidence, relative risk, odds ratio, attributable risk) needs either the number of people at risk or a comparison group, and the report has neither.

Takeaway: from a case series you can describe the cases (proportions, timing, outcomes) but not estimate risk.

whyNot.A: Incidence needs the number of people at risk (all users of the drug) as the denominator, which the report does not give.
whyNot.B: A relative risk needs incidence in both exposed and unexposed groups; neither is available.
whyNot.C: An odds ratio needs exposure information in a comparison group without neuropathy.
whyNot.D: Attributable risk is a difference in incidence between exposed and unexposed people; neither incidence is known.

items.objective: Recognise which measures can and cannot be derived from a case series.

items.stemHtml: A pathologist notices that 5 of the 7 cases of a rare liver tumour diagnosed at her hospital in the past 3 years occurred in men who worked at the same plastics factory. She publishes a short report describing the 7 patients and their work histories. Which of the following is the most appropriate use of this report?

options.label: A
options.html: Establishing that factory exposure causes the tumour

options.label: B
options.html: Generating a hypothesis to be tested in an analytical study

options.label: C
options.html: Estimating the incidence of the tumour among factory workers

options.label: D
options.html: Calculating the relative risk of the tumour among workers

options.label: E
options.html: Showing a dose-response relationship with years of exposure

items.explanationHtml:
A cluster of a rare disease in people who share an exposure is a classic signal. Its proper use is to generate a hypothesis (a factory chemical causes this tumour), which is then tested with an analytical design. Because the tumour is rare, a case-control study comparing the occupational histories of cases and suitable controls would be the efficient next step.

Historically, several occupational and drug hazards were first noticed exactly this way, by an observant clinician describing a handful of unusual cases.

Takeaway: case reports and series raise hypotheses; analytical studies test them.

whyNot.A: Causation needs a comparison group and ideally consistent findings from several analytical studies; a case series cannot establish it.
whyNot.C: The number of workers at risk is not known, so incidence cannot be estimated.
whyNot.D: A relative risk needs incidence in exposed and unexposed workers; the report has neither.
whyNot.E: Dose-response needs exposure measured across people with and without the tumour; seven cases cannot show it.

items.objective: State the main scientific role of a case series.

items.stemHtml: Investigators obtain, for each of 30 countries, the national average daily salt intake from food-supply data and the age-standardised stroke death rate from government statistics. They report that countries with higher average salt intake have higher stroke death rates. No information is collected on any individual person. Which of the following best describes this study design?

options.label: A
options.html: Cross-sectional study

options.label: B
options.html: Case series

options.label: C
options.html: Case-control study

options.label: D
options.html: Ecological study

options.label: E
options.html: Prospective cohort study

items.explanationHtml:
When the unit of analysis is a group (a country, county or school) and both exposure and outcome are group summaries, the study is ecological. Ecological studies are cheap, use routine data and are good at generating hypotheses about population-level factors.

The contrast with a cross-sectional study is the unit: a cross-sectional survey records each person's salt intake and stroke history at one time point. An ecological study cannot say whether the individuals who ate more salt were the ones who had strokes (the ecological fallacy).

Takeaway: group-level exposure and group-level outcome = ecological; individual-level data at one time = cross-sectional.

whyNot.A: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome in individual people at one time; here only country-level averages are used.
whyNot.B: A case series describes individual patients with a condition; this study uses population summaries.
whyNot.C: A case-control study selects individuals by outcome status and compares their past exposure; no individuals are selected here.
whyNot.E: A cohort study follows individuals from exposure to outcome; no individuals are followed.

items.objective: Distinguish an ecological study from a cross-sectional study by the unit of analysis.

items.stemHtml: In the 18 months after approval of a new oral drug for type 2 diabetes, the manufacturer receives 40 voluntary reports of acute pancreatitis in people taking it. A drug-safety analyst wants to estimate the incidence of pancreatitis among people taking the drug. Which of the following additional pieces of information is most essential for that estimate?

options.label: A
options.html: The number of pancreatitis cases among people not taking the drug

options.label: B
options.html: The age and sex distribution of the 40 reported patients

options.label: C
options.html: The number of people who took the drug and for how long

options.label: D
options.html: The daily dose taken by each reported patient

options.label: E
options.html: The time from starting the drug to symptom onset

items.explanationHtml:
Incidence = new cases ÷ people at risk (or person-time at risk). Spontaneous adverse-event reports supply only a numerator, and an incomplete one, because most events are never reported. To estimate incidence, the analyst needs the number of people exposed and the duration of their exposure, for example from prescription or claims databases.

This is the core limit of passive reporting systems: they detect signals but cannot by themselves measure risk.

Takeaway: case reports supply a numerator; incidence also needs the exposed population and their time at risk.

whyNot.A: Cases in non-users help compare risk, but the incidence among users still needs the number of users and their time at risk.
whyNot.B: Describing the cases does not supply the denominator that incidence requires.
whyNot.D: Dose information describes the cases but does not supply the population at risk.
whyNot.E: Time to onset describes the reported cases; it is not the denominator needed for incidence.

items.objective: Explain why spontaneous adverse-event reports cannot measure incidence without a denominator.

items.stemHtml:
A case-control study examines whether past occupational exposure to aromatic amine dyes is associated with bladder cancer. The results are shown.

Bladder cancer (cases)No bladder cancer (controls)
Exposed to dyes6050
Not exposed140450
Total200500

Which of the following is the odds ratio for bladder cancer associated with dye exposure, rounded to one decimal place?
items.explanationHtml:
Odds ratio = (a × d)/(b × c) = (60 × 450)/(140 × 50) = 27,000/7,000 ≈ 3.86, which rounds to 3.9. Equivalently, the odds of exposure in cases (60/140 = 0.43) divided by the odds of exposure in controls (50/450 = 0.11).

In a case-control study the investigator chooses how many cases and controls to enrol, so the proportion of exposed people who become cases is meaningless and a relative risk cannot be calculated. The odds ratio approximates the relative risk only when the disease is rare (as bladder cancer is).

Takeaway: case-control → odds ratio = ad/bc; the rare-disease assumption lets it stand in for the relative risk.

whyNot.A: 0.26 is the inverse of the odds ratio, (140 × 50)/(60 × 450): the cells are placed upside down.
whyNot.B: 0.43 is the odds of exposure among cases alone (60/140), not the ratio of the two odds.
whyNot.C: 1.2 divides exposed cases by exposed controls (60/50), ignoring the unexposed row.
whyNot.D: 3.0 treats the columns as if they were risks (60/200 ÷ 50/500); risks cannot be calculated in a case-control study because the investigator fixed the number of cases and controls.

items.objective: Calculate an odds ratio from a case-control 2 × 2 table.

items.stemHtml: In 2024, investigators use employment records from a shipyard to identify 3,000 workers who were employed between 1975 and 1985 and classify each as having worked with or without asbestos-containing insulation. They then use a national death registry to compare deaths from mesothelioma through 2023 between the two groups. Which of the following best describes this study design?

options.label: A
options.html: Prospective cohort study

options.label: B
options.html: Retrospective cohort study

options.label: C
options.html: Case-control study

options.label: D
options.html: Cross-sectional study

options.label: E
options.html: Ecological study

items.explanationHtml:
Selecting people by exposure and comparing the incidence of an outcome makes a study a cohort. When exposure and outcomes are reconstructed from existing records, so that everything has already occurred when the study begins, it is a retrospective (historical) cohort. The logic still runs forward in time, from exposure to outcome, and a relative risk can be calculated.

The giveaway on exams is the selection step: by exposure = cohort (whatever the calendar), by disease = case-control.

Takeaway: selected by exposure from past records and followed forward on paper = retrospective cohort.

whyNot.A: In a prospective cohort, outcomes occur after the study begins; here all exposures and outcomes had already happened by 2024.
whyNot.C: Participants were selected by exposure status, not by whether they had mesothelioma.
whyNot.D: Exposure was measured at an earlier time and outcomes were followed over decades, not measured at one point.
whyNot.E: Exposure was classified for individual workers, not as a group average.

items.objective: Recognise a retrospective (historical) cohort study.

items.stemHtml: In 2010, 20,000 women enrol in a study and provide blood samples that are frozen. By 2025, 150 have developed ovarian cancer. To save costs, investigators measure a hormone in the stored samples of these 150 women and of 600 women from the same study who were free of ovarian cancer at the time each case was diagnosed, matched on age and date of enrolment. Which of the following best describes this design?

options.label: A
options.html: Prospective cohort study

options.label: B
options.html: Case-crossover study

options.label: C
options.html: Nested case-control study

options.label: D
options.html: Cross-sectional study

options.label: E
options.html: Randomized controlled trial

items.explanationHtml:
A nested case-control study draws cases and controls from within an established cohort. Because the blood was collected before disease developed, the exposure measurement cannot be influenced by the disease or by recall, which is the main weakness of ordinary case-control studies. Because only 750 samples are assayed rather than 20,000, it is efficient.

Controls are usually chosen from cohort members still at risk when each case occurs (risk-set sampling), which lets the odds ratio estimate the rate ratio.

Takeaway: cases and controls sampled from inside a cohort with stored baseline data = nested case-control.

whyNot.A: Only a sample of the cohort is analysed, selected by outcome status, rather than analysing the whole cohort by exposure.
whyNot.B: A case-crossover study compares each case with himself or herself at different times; here cases are compared with other women.
whyNot.D: Exposure was measured years before the outcome, not at the same time.
whyNot.E: No intervention was assigned to anyone.

items.objective: Recognise a nested case-control study and its advantages.

items.stemHtml: Investigators want to know whether episodes of heavy physical exertion can trigger acute aortic dissection. They interview 180 patients with dissection about whether they performed heavy exertion in the 1 hour before symptom onset and in the same 1-hour period on the previous day. Each patient's exertion before the event is compared with his or her own exertion at the earlier time. Which of the following best describes this design?

options.label: A
options.html: Crossover trial

options.label: B
options.html: Matched case-control study with community controls

options.label: C
options.html: Prospective cohort study

options.label: D
options.html: Case-crossover study

options.label: E
options.html: Ecological study

items.explanationHtml:
In a case-crossover study only cases are enrolled, and each serves as his or her own control: exposure in a hazard period just before the event is compared with exposure in one or more earlier control periods. Fixed characteristics (sex, genetics, chronic disease) are controlled automatically.

The design suits brief, intermittent exposures with immediate, short-lived effects on an acute event (exertion, heavy meals, anger, air-pollution spikes and myocardial infarction or dissection). It does not suit chronic exposures.

Takeaway: cases only, each compared with themselves at an earlier time, for an acute trigger = case-crossover.

whyNot.A: In a crossover trial the investigator assigns each participant to treatments in sequence; here exposure was not assigned.
whyNot.B: The comparison is within the same patients at another time, not with separate control people.
whyNot.C: Participants were selected after the outcome had occurred, not followed from exposure.
whyNot.E: Exposure and outcome are recorded for individuals, not for groups.

items.objective: Recognise a case-crossover design and the exposures it suits.

items.stemHtml: An analysis of 50 counties finds that counties with a higher proportion of households owning a dog have a lower average adult body mass index. A local newspaper reports that "people who own dogs weigh less." Which of the following is the main error in the newspaper's conclusion?

options.label: A
options.html: Recall bias

options.label: B
options.html: Berkson bias

options.label: C
options.html: Lead-time bias

options.label: D
options.html: Hawthorne effect

options.label: E
options.html: Ecological fallacy

items.explanationHtml:
The data link dog ownership and body mass index only at the county level. Concluding that the individual dog owners are the people with lower weight is the ecological fallacy. Counties with many dog owners may differ in income, age structure, housing or parks, and within each county the dog owners may weigh the same as everyone else.

Ecological associations are useful hypotheses; testing them needs individual-level data (a cross-sectional survey or a cohort).

Takeaway: a group-level association does not show the same association in individuals.

whyNot.A: Recall bias arises when groups remember past exposures differently; no one was asked to recall anything here.
whyNot.B: Berkson bias comes from selecting hospital-based subjects; this analysis uses population summaries of counties.
whyNot.C: Lead-time bias concerns survival measured from an earlier diagnosis after screening.
whyNot.D: The Hawthorne effect is a change in behaviour because people know they are observed; no one was observed.

items.objective: Identify the ecological fallacy.

items.stemHtml:
A cross-sectional survey of 1,000 adults in one city records whether each participant lives within 200 m of a major highway and whether he or she currently has physician-diagnosed asthma.

AsthmaNo asthmaTotal
Lives near highway45255300
Lives farther away56644700

Which of the following is the prevalence odds ratio for asthma associated with living near the highway, rounded to one decimal place?
items.explanationHtml:
Prevalence odds ratio = (a × d)/(b × c) = (45 × 644)/(255 × 56) = 28,980/14,280 ≈ 2.03, which rounds to 2.0.

A cross-sectional study measures prevalence (existing cases at one time), not incidence. Its natural measures are the prevalence ratio (here 45/300 = 15% versus 56/700 = 8%, ratio 1.875) and the prevalence odds ratio. When the outcome is common, the odds ratio is further from 1 than the prevalence ratio. Because exposure and outcome are measured together, the survey cannot show which came first.

Takeaway: cross-sectional data give prevalence and the prevalence (odds) ratio, not incidence or relative risk.

whyNot.A: 0.5 is the inverse of the prevalence odds ratio: the cells were placed the wrong way up.
whyNot.B: 0.8 compares the numbers of asthma cases (45/56) without using the people who do not have asthma.
whyNot.C: 1.9 is the prevalence ratio (15% ÷ 8%), a different measure from the prevalence odds ratio that was asked for.
whyNot.E: 2.2 mixes measures: the odds of asthma near the highway (45/255) divided by the prevalence farther away (56/700).

items.objective: Calculate a prevalence odds ratio from a cross-sectional survey and distinguish it from the prevalence ratio.

items.stemHtml: In a trial of a new short-acting drug for chronic stable angina, each of 40 participants takes the drug for 3 weeks and placebo for 3 weeks, in an order chosen at random. Between the two periods, all participants take no study medication for 2 weeks. Which of the following is the main purpose of the 2-week interval?

options.label: A
options.html: To keep participants unaware of which treatment they are taking

options.label: B
options.html: To reduce the number of participants lost to follow-up

options.label: C
options.html: To prevent effects of the first period from carrying over into the second

options.label: D
options.html: To conceal the allocation sequence from the recruiting staff

options.label: E
options.html: To make the results applicable to a wider population

items.explanationHtml:
This is a crossover trial: each participant receives both treatments in random order and acts as his or her own control, which removes between-person variability and needs fewer participants. The gap is a washout period, long enough for the first treatment's effects to disappear so that they do not contaminate the second period (carryover effect).

Crossover designs suit stable chronic conditions and treatments with quick, reversible effects. They do not suit curative treatments or outcomes such as death.

Takeaway: washout = protection against carryover in a crossover trial.

whyNot.A: Blinding is achieved with identical-looking drug and placebo, not by a gap between periods.
whyNot.B: A treatment-free gap does not keep participants in the trial; if anything it lengthens it.
whyNot.D: Allocation concealment concerns the moment of assignment, before treatment starts.
whyNot.E: Generalizability depends on who is enrolled and the setting, not on the interval between periods.

items.objective: Explain the purpose of a washout period in a crossover trial.

items.stemHtml: A trial randomly assigns 8,000 older adults to one of four groups: drug M plus supplement N, drug M plus a placebo supplement, a placebo drug plus supplement N, or both placebos. The investigators analyse the effect of drug M and the effect of supplement N on the incidence of hip fracture. Which of the following best describes this trial design?

options.label: A
options.html: Crossover trial

options.label: B
options.html: Cluster randomized trial

options.label: C
options.html: Community trial

options.label: D
options.html: Factorial trial

options.label: E
options.html: Non-inferiority trial

items.explanationHtml:
In a 2 × 2 factorial trial participants are randomized to two interventions at once, giving four groups. Each intervention is evaluated by comparing everyone who received it with everyone who did not (half the trial each time), so two questions are answered for roughly the price of one, provided the two interventions do not interact.

The trial can also test for interaction (whether M works differently with or without N), but it is usually underpowered for that.

Takeaway: randomizing to two interventions at once in four groups = factorial design.

whyNot.A: In a crossover trial each participant receives each treatment in sequence; here each participant stays in one group.
whyNot.B: Individuals, not groups such as clinics or villages, were randomized.
whyNot.C: A community trial assigns whole communities to an intervention; here individuals were assigned.
whyNot.E: A non-inferiority trial tests whether a new treatment is not unacceptably worse than an active comparator; this trial tests two interventions against placebo.

items.objective: Recognise a factorial trial design.

items.stemHtml: A health department plans to evaluate a classroom hand-washing program for preventing absence due to gastrointestinal illness. Rather than randomly assigning individual children, it randomly assigns 40 elementary schools either to receive the program in every classroom or to continue usual practice. Which of the following is the main reason to randomize schools rather than individual children?

options.label: A
options.html: Children in the same classroom would otherwise share the program, contaminating the comparison

options.label: B
options.html: Randomizing schools gives greater statistical power than randomizing children

options.label: C
options.html: Randomizing schools allows the children to be blinded to their group

options.label: D
options.html: Randomizing schools removes the need for parental permission

options.label: E
options.html: Randomizing schools prevents confounding by the children's ages

items.explanationHtml:
In a cluster randomized trial the unit of randomization is a group (school, ward, clinic, village). It is chosen when the intervention is delivered to the whole group or when individuals in the same group would share it, so that individual randomization would cause contamination of the control children and bias the result toward no effect.

The price is statistical: children in one school are more alike than children in different schools, so a cluster trial needs more participants (the design effect), and the analysis must account for clustering.

Takeaway: randomize groups when the intervention acts on groups or would spill over between individuals.

whyNot.B: Randomizing clusters usually lowers power, because children in the same school resemble each other.
whyNot.C: Children in program schools will still know they are washing their hands; blinding is not achieved.
whyNot.D: Cluster randomization changes how consent is handled but does not remove ethical review or the need to inform families.
whyNot.E: Simple randomization of individuals would balance age just as well.

items.objective: Explain why a cluster randomized design is chosen.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial compares knee arthroscopy with a structured physiotherapy program for degenerative knee pain. Participants and treating clinicians obviously know which treatment each participant received. The primary outcome is a physical-function score recorded by an examiner at 12 months. Which of the following design features best protects the outcome measurement from bias?

options.label: A
options.html: Concealment of the allocation sequence from the recruiting surgeons

options.label: B
options.html: Outcome assessors who do not know each participant's treatment group

options.label: C
options.html: Analysis of all participants in the group to which they were randomized

options.label: D
options.html: Stratified randomization by baseline pain severity

options.label: E
options.html: A run-in period before randomization

items.explanationHtml:
When participants and clinicians cannot be blinded (surgery versus physiotherapy), the trial can still blind the people who measure the outcome. A blinded assessor scoring function cannot be swayed by expectations about which treatment should work, which protects against measurement (observer) bias.

Blinding terms are used loosely; say who is blinded. "Single-blind" usually means participants, "double-blind" participants and investigators, and "triple-blind" adds the outcome assessors or data analysts.

Takeaway: when treatment cannot be hidden, blind the outcome assessors.

whyNot.A: Allocation concealment prevents selection bias at enrolment; it does not stop an examiner who knows the treatment from scoring differently.
whyNot.C: Intention-to-treat analysis preserves randomization but does not protect a subjective measurement.
whyNot.D: Stratification balances a prognostic factor; it does not affect how outcomes are recorded.
whyNot.E: A run-in period selects adherent participants; it does not affect outcome measurement.

items.objective: Identify blinded outcome assessment as protection against measurement bias.

items.stemHtml: A new monoclonal antibody that has shown activity in animal models is given for the first time to humans. Twenty-four healthy volunteers receive single doses that are increased step by step across small groups, with close monitoring of adverse effects and blood concentrations. Which phase of clinical drug development does this study represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Phase 1

options.label: B
options.html: Preclinical testing

options.label: C
options.html: Phase 2

options.label: D
options.html: Phase 3

options.label: E
options.html: Phase 4

items.explanationHtml:
Phase 1 studies are the first human studies: small numbers (often healthy volunteers, or patients when the drug is too toxic for volunteers, as in oncology), dose escalation, and the goals of safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics.

PhaseWhoMain question
1Tens; often healthy volunteersIs it safe? What dose? How is it handled?
2Up to a few hundred patientsDoes it seem to work? Which dose?
3Hundreds to thousands of patientsDoes it work better than or as well as the comparator?
4Everyone prescribed it after approvalRare and long-term harms in real use

Takeaway: first in humans, small, dose escalation, safety and pharmacokinetics = phase 1.

whyNot.B: Preclinical work is done in the laboratory and in animals, before any human receives the drug.
whyNot.C: Phase 2 studies give the drug to patients with the target disease to look for efficacy and refine the dose.
whyNot.D: Phase 3 trials are large comparative trials in patients that confirm efficacy and safety before approval.
whyNot.E: Phase 4 studies follow a drug after approval to detect rare or long-term adverse effects.

items.objective: Identify a phase 1 clinical study from its design.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial compares a new inhaled asthma controller with the standard controller. The outcome is the number of symptom-free days per month, where more days is better. The investigators prespecified that equivalence would be shown if the entire 95% confidence interval for the difference (new minus standard) lay between −5 and +5 days, and non-inferiority if the lower limit lay above −5 days. The observed difference is +3 days (95% CI, −1 to +7 days). Which of the following conclusions is supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The new controller is superior to the standard controller

options.label: B
options.html: The new controller is equivalent to the standard controller

options.label: C
options.html: The new controller is non-inferior, but equivalence is not shown

options.label: D
options.html: The new controller is inferior to the standard controller

options.label: E
options.html: The trial is inconclusive for non-inferiority

items.explanationHtml:
Compare the confidence interval (−1 to +7) with each prespecified boundary:

  • Non-inferiority: lower limit −1 > −5 → shown.
  • Equivalence: needs −5 < whole interval < +5; the upper limit +7 exceeds +5 → not shown (the new drug could be meaningfully better).
  • Superiority: needs the lower limit above 0; −1 is below 0 → not shown.

Non-inferiority asks a one-sided question (is the new treatment not unacceptably worse?), equivalence a two-sided one (is it neither meaningfully worse nor meaningfully better?). The margins must be set before the trial, from clinical judgement and the comparator's known effect.

Takeaway: place the whole confidence interval against each margin; non-inferiority looks only at the lower limit.

whyNot.A: The interval includes 0, so a difference of no effect is compatible with the data and superiority is not shown.
whyNot.B: The upper limit (+7) lies outside +5, so the interval is not wholly inside the equivalence margins.
whyNot.D: The whole interval lies above −5 days, so an unacceptable loss of benefit is excluded.
whyNot.E: The lower limit (−1) is above the −5 margin, so non-inferiority is shown.

items.objective: Interpret a confidence interval against prespecified non-inferiority, equivalence and superiority boundaries.

items.stemHtml: Two review articles summarize treatments for chronic plantar fasciitis. The first is written by an expert who discusses the studies she considers most important. The second describes the databases searched, the search terms and dates, the criteria used to include or exclude studies, how two reviewers independently extracted data, and how the risk of bias of each study was rated. Which of the following best describes the second article?

options.label: A
options.html: Narrative review

options.label: B
options.html: Meta-analysis of individual patient data

options.label: C
options.html: Case series

options.label: D
options.html: Clinical practice guideline

options.label: E
options.html: Systematic review

items.explanationHtml:
A systematic review answers a focused question with an explicit, reproducible method: a prespecified protocol, a comprehensive search of several sources, stated inclusion criteria, duplicate independent screening and data extraction, and a formal appraisal of each study's risk of bias. A narrative review relies on the author's selection and is more open to bias.

A meta-analysis is the optional statistical step of pooling the results of the included studies; a systematic review can be done without one if the studies are too different to combine.

Takeaway: explicit search + criteria + appraisal = systematic review; statistical pooling = meta-analysis.

whyNot.A: A narrative review, like the first article, selects and summarizes studies without an explicit, reproducible method.
whyNot.B: Pooling individual patient data is a specific statistical method; the description does not mention any statistical pooling.
whyNot.C: A case series describes patients, not published studies.
whyNot.D: A guideline makes recommendations for care; it may use a systematic review but is not defined by search and selection methods.

items.objective: Distinguish a systematic review from a narrative review.

items.stemHtml:
Five placebo-controlled randomized trials tested agent L for prevention of recurrent symptomatic kidney stones, and their results were pooled in the meta-analysis summarized in the forest plot.

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the forest plot?

options.label: A
options.html: Agent L has no effect, because every individual trial's interval includes 1

options.label: B
options.html: Agent L reduces recurrence, although no single trial showed a statistically significant effect

options.label: C
options.html: The trials are too inconsistent to be pooled

options.label: D
options.html: Study E provides the strongest evidence, because its effect is largest

options.label: E
options.html: Agent L doubles the risk of recurrence

items.explanationHtml:
Each trial's horizontal line crosses the vertical line of no effect (RR = 1), so no trial on its own was statistically significant. The pooled estimate, the diamond, is RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.88): its whole width lies to the left of 1, so the combined evidence shows about a one-third relative reduction in recurrence.

This is the main purpose of meta-analysis: pooling several small, consistent trials gives the precision that none had alone. The low heterogeneity (I² = 0%) and similar point estimates make pooling reasonable.

Takeaway: judge the overall result by the diamond: if it does not touch 1, the pooled effect is statistically significant.

whyNot.A: Each trial was too small on its own, but the pooled diamond (0.51 to 0.88) lies entirely below 1, which is the result the analysis was designed to produce.
whyNot.C: The estimates are similar, the intervals overlap widely and I² is 0%, so there is no sign of important heterogeneity.
whyNot.D: Study E has the widest interval and the smallest square, so it carries the least weight despite its large point estimate.
whyNot.E: Values below 1 favour treatment; a pooled risk ratio of 0.67 is a reduction, not an increase.

items.objective: Interpret the pooled diamond of a forest plot.

items.stemHtml:
The forest plot shows a meta-analysis of agent L versus placebo that pools five trials with kidney stone recurrence as the outcome.

Which trial contributed the most weight to the pooled estimate?

options.label: A
options.html: Study A

options.label: B
options.html: Study B

options.label: C
options.html: Study C

options.label: D
options.html: Study D

options.label: E
options.html: Study E

items.explanationHtml:
In inverse-variance meta-analysis, each trial is weighted by the inverse of the variance of its estimate. More events and more participants mean a narrower confidence interval and a larger weight. On the plot, weight is shown by the size of the square and is mirrored by the narrowness of the interval. Study B has the largest square and the narrowest interval (0.46 to 1.11), carrying about 38% of the weight.

A dramatic point estimate from a small trial (Study E) contributes little.

Takeaway: biggest square and narrowest line = most weight; the size of the effect does not matter.

whyNot.A: Study A's interval (0.36 to 1.32) is wider than Study B's, so it carries less weight.
whyNot.C: Study C has the widest interval of the five, so it is the least precise and carries little weight.
whyNot.D: Study D is the second most precise trial, but its interval is wider than Study B's.
whyNot.E: Study E shows the largest effect, but the weight depends on precision, not on the size of the effect.

items.objective: Identify the most heavily weighted study on a forest plot.

items.stemHtml: A meta-analysis of 18 trials of an herbal extract for knee osteoarthritis pain reports a pooled benefit. A funnel plot of the trials shows that the large trials lie close to the pooled estimate, while the small trials lie only on the side showing benefit; there are no small trials showing no effect or harm. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Small trials with unfavourable results were less likely to be published

options.label: B
options.html: Random error is greater in large trials than in small trials

options.label: C
options.html: The meta-analysis used a random-effects model

options.label: D
options.html: The trials differed in their definitions of pain

options.label: E
options.html: The large trials were at high risk of bias

items.explanationHtml:
A funnel plot graphs each study's effect against its precision. Without bias, small imprecise studies scatter widely but symmetrically around the pooled effect, making an inverted funnel. A missing corner, with small studies present only on the favourable side, is the typical sign of publication bias (or other small-study effects): small "negative" studies tend to go unpublished, so the meta-analysis overestimates the benefit.

Asymmetry is suggestive rather than proof; small trials can also be of lower quality or enrol different patients. Searching trial registries and unpublished data helps.

Takeaway: asymmetric funnel with missing small null studies → suspect publication bias.

whyNot.B: Random error is smaller in large trials, which is why they sit near the top and centre of a funnel plot.
whyNot.C: The choice of model affects the pooled estimate and its interval, not where individual trials fall on the plot.
whyNot.D: Differences in outcome definition would scatter results in both directions rather than remove one corner of the funnel.
whyNot.E: Bias in the large trials would move the top of the funnel; it would not explain missing small negative trials.

items.objective: Interpret funnel plot asymmetry as a sign of publication bias.

items.stemHtml: A meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials of a weight-loss drug reports a pooled mean weight reduction of 4.1 kg compared with placebo. The individual trial results range from a reduction of 0.5 kg to 9.0 kg, and the I² statistic is 78%. Which of the following is the best interpretation of the I² value?

options.label: A
options.html: The pooled estimate has a 78% probability of being correct

options.label: B
options.html: 78% of participants lost weight with the drug

options.label: C
options.html: The trials are similar enough that differences between them are due to chance

options.label: D
options.html: Most of the variation between trial results reflects real differences between trials rather than chance

options.label: E
options.html: There is a 78% chance of publication bias

items.explanationHtml:
I² estimates the percentage of the total variation across study estimates that is due to true differences between studies (heterogeneity) rather than sampling error. Roughly, values near 25% are low, 50% moderate and 75% or more high. An I² of 78% means the trials disagree more than chance explains, perhaps because of different doses, durations or populations.

High heterogeneity should prompt the reviewers to look for its sources (subgroup analysis, meta-regression), to use a random-effects model if pooling at all, and to interpret a single pooled number cautiously.

Takeaway: I² = share of between-study variation that is real rather than chance; high I² → explain before you pool.

whyNot.A: I² describes the spread between studies, not the probability that the pooled estimate is correct.
whyNot.B: I² summarizes variation between trials, not the proportion of participants who responded.
whyNot.C: An I² of 78% means substantial heterogeneity, the opposite of results that differ only by chance.
whyNot.E: Publication bias is judged from funnel plots and searches for unpublished trials, not from I².

items.objective: Interpret the I² statistic in a meta-analysis.

items.stemHtml: A meta-analysis of 9 trials finds moderate heterogeneity between trial results. The investigators report the pooled estimate from both a fixed-effect model and a random-effects model. Compared with the fixed-effect result, which of the following is the random-effects result most likely to show?

options.label: A
options.html: A narrower confidence interval around the pooled estimate

options.label: B
options.html: Elimination of the heterogeneity between trials

options.label: C
options.html: Correction for publication bias

options.label: D
