options.html: Greater relative weight for the largest trials

options.label: E
options.html: A wider confidence interval around the pooled estimate

items.explanationHtml:
A fixed-effect model assumes all trials estimate one true effect and that differences are chance alone. A random-effects model assumes the true effects vary between trials around an average and adds a between-study variance term to every trial's variance. Consequently its pooled estimate has a wider confidence interval when heterogeneity is present, and its weights are more even, so small trials gain relative influence.

When heterogeneity is zero, the two models give the same answer.

Takeaway: random effects = allows true effects to differ = wider interval, more even weights.

whyNot.A: Allowing for between-study variation adds uncertainty, so the interval widens rather than narrows.
whyNot.B: No model removes heterogeneity; the random-effects model only allows for it in the pooled estimate.
whyNot.C: Neither model corrects for missing studies; random effects can even give more relative weight to small, possibly biased trials.
whyNot.D: Random-effects weighting gives relatively more weight to small trials than fixed-effect weighting does.

items.objective: Compare fixed-effect and random-effects pooled estimates.

items.stemHtml: To estimate the prevalence of hypertension among adults in a state, investigators divide the state's adult population into four regions and then draw a separate simple random sample within each region, sized in proportion to the region's population. Which of the following sampling methods is being used?

options.label: A
options.html: Simple random sampling

options.label: B
options.html: Stratified random sampling

options.label: C
options.html: Cluster sampling

options.label: D
options.html: Systematic sampling

options.label: E
options.html: Convenience sampling

items.explanationHtml:
In stratified sampling the population is first divided into non-overlapping subgroups (strata) and a random sample is drawn from every stratum. It guarantees that each subgroup is represented and improves precision when the strata differ in the outcome.

Contrast cluster sampling, in which only some groups are chosen at random and people within those groups are studied; it is cheaper in the field but less precise.

Takeaway: sample within every subgroup = stratified; sample some whole groups = cluster.

whyNot.A: In simple random sampling every person is drawn from one list with equal probability, without first dividing the population into groups.
whyNot.C: In cluster sampling whole groups are selected at random and everyone (or a sample) within the chosen groups is studied; here every region is sampled.
whyNot.D: Systematic sampling takes every kth person from a list after a random start.
whyNot.E: Convenience sampling takes whoever is easily available; this design uses random selection.

items.objective: Recognise stratified random sampling.

items.stemHtml: A survey on vaping among adults aged 18 to 64 years selects telephone numbers at random from a directory of landline numbers. Of those reached, 70% agree to take part. Most young adults in the region use only mobile phones. Which of the following is the main threat to the representativeness of this survey?

options.label: A
options.html: The response rate is too low for valid conclusions

options.label: B
options.html: Telephone interviews make recall bias inevitable

options.label: C
options.html: The sampling frame does not match the target population

options.label: D
options.html: Random selection of numbers introduces confounding

options.label: E
options.html: The sample size cannot be calculated for a survey

items.explanationHtml:
The sampling frame is the list from which the sample is actually drawn. If it omits part of the target population, those people have no chance of selection (undercoverage), and random sampling from the frame cannot repair the gap. Here, young adults who use only mobile phones, probably the group with most vaping, are excluded, so the survey will tend to underestimate prevalence.

Non-response is a separate problem: people who were selected but did not take part.

Takeaway: random sampling from the wrong list still gives a biased sample; check the frame against the target population.

whyNot.A: A 70% response rate is acceptable; the larger problem is that many young adults could never be selected.
whyNot.B: Recall bias can occur in any interview, but it does not explain who was excluded from selection.
whyNot.D: Random selection does not cause confounding; confounding concerns the relation between exposures and outcomes.
whyNot.E: Sample sizes for prevalence surveys are routinely calculated from the expected prevalence and desired precision.

items.objective: Identify a mismatch between the sampling frame and the target population.

items.stemHtml: In a randomized trial of a new wound dressing, the allocation for each participant is printed on a card inside a sealed envelope. Recruiting nurses discover that the cards can be read by holding the envelopes up to a bright light, and some nurses start enrolling patients with severe wounds only when the next envelope shows the new dressing. Which of the following trial safeguards has failed?

options.label: A
options.html: Allocation concealment

options.label: B
options.html: Blinding of participants

options.label: C
options.html: Blinding of outcome assessors

options.label: D
options.html: Intention-to-treat analysis

options.label: E
options.html: Stratified randomization

items.explanationHtml:
Allocation concealment keeps the next assignment hidden from the people enrolling participants until the participant is irreversibly entered in the trial. When it fails, recruiters can choose which patients get which treatment, reintroducing selection bias and destroying the benefit of randomization. Central telephone or web-based randomization, or opaque sequentially numbered envelopes, protect it.

Concealment is different from blinding: concealment protects the sequence before assignment and is always possible; blinding hides the treatment after assignment and is not always possible.

Takeaway: foreseeable assignments = failed allocation concealment = selection bias.

whyNot.B: Participants' knowledge of their dressing would affect reported outcomes, but the problem here arises before assignment, at enrolment.
whyNot.C: Assessor blinding protects measurement after treatment, not the choice of whom to enrol.
whyNot.D: Intention-to-treat analysis protects against bias from post-randomization changes, not from manipulated enrolment.
whyNot.E: Stratification balances known factors by design; it would not stop staff from steering patients toward an assignment they can foresee.

items.objective: Distinguish allocation concealment from blinding.

items.stemHtml: A small trial plans to enrol 60 participants over 2 years at one hospital. Participants are randomized in blocks of 4, so that within each consecutive group of 4 participants, 2 receive the drug and 2 receive placebo, in random order. Which of the following is the main advantage of this method?

options.label: A
options.html: Recruiting staff can never predict the next assignment

options.label: B
options.html: Known prognostic factors are guaranteed to be balanced

options.label: C
options.html: Participants do not know which treatment they receive

options.label: D
options.html: The two groups stay close to equal in size throughout enrolment

options.label: E
options.html: Fewer participants are needed for the same power

items.explanationHtml:
With simple randomization, a small trial can end up unbalanced (for example, 36 versus 24) or with groups enrolled at different times. Block randomization forces equal numbers within each block, so group sizes never differ by more than half a block and the groups are spread evenly over calendar time.

Its weakness is predictability; using random, varying block sizes that recruiters do not know keeps allocation concealed. Combining blocks within strata (stratified block randomization) also balances key prognostic factors.

Takeaway: blocks balance numbers; strata balance factors; concealment prevents prediction.

whyNot.A: With a fixed, known block size the last assignment in each block can be predicted, which is why block sizes are often varied and kept secret.
whyNot.B: Blocking balances group sizes; balancing a prognostic factor needs stratification by that factor.
whyNot.C: Blinding is a separate safeguard achieved with matching placebo.
whyNot.E: Power depends on sample size and effect size; blocking does not reduce the sample size needed.

items.objective: State the purpose and weakness of block randomization.

items.stemHtml: A case-control study investigates whether obesity increases the risk of myocardial infarction. For each patient with myocardial infarction, the investigators select a control of the same age and sex who also has the same diabetes status, because diabetes is strongly associated with myocardial infarction. Obesity is known to cause diabetes. How will matching on diabetes status most likely affect the odds ratio for obesity?

options.label: A
options.html: It will bias the odds ratio toward 1

options.label: B
options.html: It will bias the odds ratio away from 1

options.label: C
options.html: It will correctly remove confounding by diabetes

options.label: D
options.html: It will introduce recall bias about body weight

options.label: E
options.html: It will have no effect because cases and controls are matched on age

items.explanationHtml:
Matching controls confounding by making cases and controls alike on a factor. It is appropriate only for confounders: factors associated with the exposure and the outcome that are not on the causal pathway. Diabetes is partly caused by obesity and lies between obesity and infarction. Matching on it forces controls to resemble cases in obesity too, so part of the real effect is matched away: overmatching, which biases the odds ratio toward 1 and wastes efficiency.

Also remember that a factor used for matching can no longer be studied as a risk factor in that study.

Takeaway: never match on a consequence of the exposure; overmatching hides real associations.

whyNot.B: Matching on a consequence of the exposure makes cases and controls more alike in exposure, which moves the estimate toward, not away from, 1.
whyNot.C: Diabetes is on the causal pathway from obesity to infarction, so it is not a confounder and should not be matched on.
whyNot.D: Matching determines who is selected as a control; it does not change how participants remember their weight.
whyNot.E: Age matching is reasonable, but the additional matching on diabetes still affects the obesity comparison.

items.objective: Recognise overmatching and its effect on the odds ratio.

items.stemHtml: Investigators plan a case-control study of cigarette smoking and bladder cancer. Cases are all patients newly diagnosed with bladder cancer at the hospitals serving a defined county. They are considering several sources of controls. Which of the following control groups is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Patients admitted to the same hospitals' pulmonary wards

options.label: B
options.html: Volunteers who answer an advertisement for a health study

options.label: C
options.html: Patients with other cancers of the urinary tract

options.label: D
options.html: Medical staff working at the same hospitals

options.label: E
options.html: Randomly selected county residents without bladder cancer, of similar age and sex

items.explanationHtml:
Controls should come from the same source population that produced the cases and should have the same chance of exposure as anyone in that population; in other words, they are people who would have become cases at these hospitals had they developed bladder cancer. Population-based controls drawn at random from the county best fit this when cases are all new cases in a defined area.

Hospital controls are convenient but risky: patients admitted with conditions that are themselves related to the exposure (here, smoking-related lung disease) distort the exposure frequency among controls.

Takeaway: pick controls from the population that gave rise to the cases, not from groups whose condition is linked to the exposure.

whyNot.A: Many lung diseases are caused by smoking, so these controls would smoke more than the source population and bias the odds ratio toward 1.
whyNot.B: Volunteers tend to be healthier and to smoke less than the population, so their exposure is not representative.
whyNot.C: Smoking is linked to other urinary tract cancers as well, so these controls would share the exposure under study.
whyNot.D: Hospital staff differ from the county population in occupation, education and smoking habits.

items.objective: Choose an appropriate control group for a case-control study.

items.stemHtml: In a randomized trial of a lipid-lowering drug versus placebo, 15% of participants assigned to the drug stop taking it within 6 months, and 5% of those assigned to placebo start taking a lipid-lowering drug prescribed by their own physicians. In the primary analysis, every participant's outcome is counted in the group to which he or she was originally assigned. Which of the following best describes this analysis?

options.label: A
options.html: Per-protocol analysis

options.label: B
options.html: Intention-to-treat analysis

options.label: C
options.html: As-treated analysis

options.label: D
options.html: Last observation carried forward

options.label: E
options.html: Subgroup analysis

items.explanationHtml:
Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis keeps every randomized participant in the group to which he or she was assigned, whether or not they took the treatment, stopped early or crossed over. It answers the question "what happens when this treatment is offered?" and preserves the balance created by randomization.

AnalysisWho is included, and where
Intention-to-treatEveryone, as randomized
Per-protocolOnly those who followed the protocol
As-treatedEveryone, regrouped by treatment actually received

Takeaway: analysed as randomized, whatever happened afterward = intention-to-treat.

whyNot.A: A per-protocol analysis would exclude participants who stopped the drug or crossed over.
whyNot.C: An as-treated analysis would regroup participants by the treatment they actually took.
whyNot.D: Last observation carried forward is a method for filling in missing values, not a way of assigning participants to groups.
whyNot.E: A subgroup analysis examines a subset of participants, such as women or older adults, rather than all participants as randomized.

items.objective: Define intention-to-treat analysis.

items.stemHtml: In a trial of an antihypertensive drug, participants who stop taking the drug are older and sicker than those who keep taking it. A statistician insists that the primary analysis include all participants in the groups to which they were randomized. Which of the following is the main reason for this approach?

options.label: A
options.html: It gives the largest possible estimate of the drug's effect

options.label: B
options.html: It measures the drug's biological effect in participants who take it

options.label: C
options.html: It keeps the groups comparable in both known and unknown prognostic factors

options.label: D
options.html: It removes the need to follow participants who stop the drug

options.label: E
options.html: It corrects for differences in blood pressure measurement between sites

items.explanationHtml:
Randomization makes the groups comparable at baseline in measured and unmeasured factors. Adherence happens after randomization and is itself linked to prognosis (sicker people stop). Dropping or regrouping non-adherent participants rebuilds groups on a post-randomization characteristic and reintroduces confounding. Intention-to-treat analysis keeps the randomized groups intact, so the comparison stays unbiased.

The price is dilution: non-adherence and crossover make the groups more alike, so ITT usually underestimates the effect of actually taking the drug.

Takeaway: ITT protects randomization; its estimate is conservative in a superiority trial.

whyNot.A: Intention-to-treat estimates are usually smaller (more conservative) than per-protocol estimates when adherence is incomplete.
whyNot.B: That question is addressed, with risk of bias, by per-protocol analysis; intention-to-treat measures the effect of assigning the drug.
whyNot.D: Intention-to-treat requires outcomes for everyone, including those who stop treatment.
whyNot.E: Measurement differences are handled by standardised methods and blinding, not by the choice of analysis population.

items.objective: Explain why intention-to-treat analysis preserves the benefits of randomization.

items.stemHtml:
A randomized trial assigns 1,000 adults with coronary disease to a new drug or placebo (500 each) and counts major cardiovascular events over 2 years. Outcomes were obtained for every participant.

Assigned groupTook assigned treatmentEventsDid not (or crossed over)Events
Drug (n = 500)40020100 never took the drug15
Placebo (n = 500)4504550 took the drug outside the trial2

Which of the following is the absolute risk reduction with the drug by intention-to-treat analysis, in percentage points?
items.explanationHtml:
Intention-to-treat keeps everyone in the assigned group:

  • Drug group risk = (20 + 15)/500 = 35/500 = 7.0%.
  • Placebo group risk = (45 + 2)/500 = 47/500 = 9.4%.
  • Absolute risk reduction = 9.4 − 7.0 = 2.4 percentage points (NNT ≈ 42).

For comparison, per-protocol = 45/450 − 20/400 = 10.0% − 5.0% = 5.0 points; as-treated = 60/550 − 22/450 = 10.9% − 4.9% = 6.0 points. The adherent-only analyses look better partly because people who keep taking a drug differ from those who stop.

Takeaway: for ITT, add up events by assigned group regardless of what was taken.

whyNot.B: 4.4 compares only the adherent drug group (5.0%) with the whole placebo group (9.4%), mixing two analysis populations.
whyNot.C: 5.0 is the per-protocol result (10.0% − 5.0%), which drops the non-adherent and crossover participants.
whyNot.D: 6.0 is the as-treated result, regrouping everyone by the treatment actually taken (10.9% − 4.9%).
whyNot.E: 25.5% is the intention-to-treat relative risk reduction (2.4/9.4), not the absolute reduction.

items.objective: Calculate intention-to-treat, per-protocol and as-treated risk differences from the same trial.

items.stemHtml: Before randomization in a trial of a once-daily heart-failure drug, all 3,200 eligible patients take the active drug for 4 weeks. The 700 who miss more than 20% of doses or have adverse effects during this period are excluded, and the remaining 2,500 are randomized to the drug or placebo. Which of the following is the main disadvantage of this design feature?

options.label: A
options.html: It destroys the comparability created by randomization

options.label: B
options.html: It makes blinding of participants impossible

options.label: C
options.html: It lowers the trial's statistical power

options.label: D
options.html: It causes recall bias in reporting symptoms

options.label: E
options.html: The results may overstate the benefit and understate the harm in routine practice

items.explanationHtml:
A run-in period before randomization screens out people who will not adhere or who cannot tolerate the treatment. It improves adherence and power within the trial without harming internal validity, because the exclusion happens before random assignment.

The cost is external validity: the randomized patients are the adherent, tolerant subset, so the trial may overestimate benefit and underestimate adverse effects compared with unselected patients in practice. A report should state how many people were excluded during the run-in (here 700 of 3,200, about 22%).

Takeaway: run-in = better adherence and power, worse generalizability.

whyNot.A: The exclusions happen before randomization, so the randomized groups remain comparable with each other.
whyNot.B: Participants can still be blinded after randomization with matching placebo.
whyNot.C: Excluding poor adherers improves adherence in the randomized groups and so tends to increase power.
whyNot.D: Recall bias is a problem of retrospective reporting of exposures, not of a pre-randomization treatment period.

items.objective: State the advantages and disadvantages of a run-in period.

items.stemHtml: In a 12-month randomized trial of a new antidepressant versus placebo, 32% of participants in the drug group and 9% of those in the placebo group withdraw, most of them because of nausea and sedation in the drug group. The authors analyse only participants who completed the trial and report a large benefit from the drug. Which type of bias is of greatest concern in this analysis?

options.label: A
options.html: Recall bias

options.label: B
options.html: Lead-time bias

options.label: C
options.html: Ecological fallacy

options.label: D
options.html: Attrition bias

options.label: E
options.html: Berkson bias

items.explanationHtml:
Attrition bias arises when participants leave a study in ways that differ between groups and are related to the outcome. Here many more drug-group participants withdrew, mainly because of adverse effects, and those who remained are the ones who tolerated (and perhaps responded to) the drug. Analysing completers only compares a selected drug group with a nearly complete placebo group and is likely to exaggerate benefit.

Protection comes from minimising losses, collecting outcomes even after people stop treatment, an intention-to-treat analysis with a principled method for missing data, and sensitivity analyses.

Takeaway: unequal, outcome-related dropout = attrition bias; completer analyses hide it.

whyNot.A: Recall bias concerns how participants remember past exposures; outcomes here are measured prospectively.
whyNot.B: Lead-time bias concerns survival measured from an earlier diagnosis made by screening.
whyNot.C: The ecological fallacy needs group-level data applied to individuals; this trial measures individuals.
whyNot.E: Berkson bias arises from hospital-based selection in case-control studies, not from withdrawals after randomization.

items.objective: Recognise attrition bias from differential loss to follow-up.

items.stemHtml: A 12-month randomized trial of a new drug for Alzheimer disease measures cognition every 3 months on a scale in which scores decline as the disease progresses. Many participants in the drug group withdraw at 3 months because of adverse effects, whereas withdrawals in the placebo group are fewer and later. Missing values are filled in with each participant's last observed score. How is this method most likely to affect the estimated benefit of the drug?

options.label: A
options.html: It will overestimate the benefit of the drug

options.label: B
options.html: It will underestimate the benefit of the drug

options.label: C
options.html: It will not bias the estimate because all randomized participants are analysed

options.label: D
options.html: It will widen the confidence interval but leave the estimate unbiased

options.label: E
options.html: It will remove the effect of the adverse events on the results

items.explanationHtml:
Last observation carried forward (LOCF) assumes a participant's outcome would have stayed exactly where it was when he or she left. In a progressive disease that assumption is optimistic. Because drug-group participants dropped out earlier, their frozen scores reflect less decline than they would have had, and the drug looks better than it is. LOCF also treats invented values as real, so intervals are falsely narrow.

Better approaches include collecting outcomes after people stop treatment, multiple imputation (filling each gap several times from a model of the observed data and combining the results, which carries the uncertainty), mixed models, and sensitivity analyses under different assumptions.

Takeaway: LOCF is biased whenever outcomes change after dropout; in a declining disease it flatters the arm with earlier dropouts.

whyNot.B: Freezing scores early in a declining disease makes the early drug-group dropouts look better than they would have been, which favours the drug.
whyNot.C: Including everyone is good practice, but the imputed values themselves can be biased.
whyNot.D: Single imputation tends to make intervals too narrow, because filled-in values are treated as if they were observed.
whyNot.E: Carrying values forward does not account for why participants left, so the adverse events still shape the results.

items.objective: Predict the direction of bias from last observation carried forward.

items.stemHtml: To understand how new parents decide whether to vaccinate their infants, researchers invite 8 parents at a time to a 90-minute discussion led by a trained moderator who uses open-ended questions and encourages participants to respond to one another. Sessions are recorded and transcribed. Which of the following methods is being used?

options.label: A
options.html: Structured questionnaire survey

options.label: B
options.html: In-depth individual interview

options.label: C
options.html: Focus group

options.label: D
options.html: Participant observation

options.label: E
options.html: Case series

items.explanationHtml:
A focus group is a moderated discussion among a small group (often 6 to 10) who share some characteristic. The interaction itself is data: participants build on, question and contrast each other's views, which can bring out shared norms and the language people use.

Focus groups are less suitable for sensitive or stigmatised topics and can be dominated by a few voices, where individual in-depth interviews work better.

Takeaway: moderated group discussion with interaction as data = focus group.

whyNot.A: A survey uses fixed questions and response options answered individually, not a moderated group discussion.
whyNot.B: An in-depth interview involves one participant at a time, so participants cannot respond to each other.
whyNot.D: Participant observation means the researcher takes part in or watches everyday activities in their natural setting.
whyNot.E: A case series describes patients with a condition, usually from clinical records.

items.objective: Recognise a focus group.

items.stemHtml: A qualitative study explores why patients with type 2 diabetes stop taking a prescribed medication. Researchers interview patients and analyse transcripts as they go. After the 17th interview they find that the last several interviews have produced no new themes, and they stop recruiting. Which of the following concepts guided their decision?

options.label: A
options.html: Triangulation

options.label: B
options.html: Reflexivity

options.label: C
options.html: Statistical power

options.label: D
options.html: Member checking

options.label: E
options.html: Data saturation

items.explanationHtml:
Qualitative studies do not set their sample size by a power calculation. They continue collecting data until further interviews add no new themes or insights relevant to the question, a point called saturation. Analysis therefore runs alongside data collection, not after it.

Samples are small (often 10 to 40 interviews), chosen for information richness rather than statistical representativeness.

Takeaway: stop when new data stop producing new themes = saturation.

whyNot.A: Triangulation compares several sources, methods or researchers to check findings; it is not a reason to stop recruiting.
whyNot.B: Reflexivity is the researchers' scrutiny of how their own position shapes the study.
whyNot.C: Power is the probability of detecting a true effect in hypothesis testing, which qualitative studies do not perform.
whyNot.D: Member checking returns findings to participants to confirm interpretations.

items.objective: Define data saturation in qualitative research.

items.stemHtml: A research team wants to interview people who sell sex about their experiences of health care. Because there is no list of this population, the team interviews 5 people known to an outreach worker and asks each to invite others in their network, who are then asked to invite others in turn. Which of the following sampling methods is being used?

options.label: A
options.html: Snowball sampling

options.label: B
options.html: Simple random sampling

options.label: C
options.html: Stratified random sampling

options.label: D
options.html: Cluster sampling

options.label: E
options.html: Systematic sampling

items.explanationHtml:
In snowball (chain-referral) sampling participants recruit further participants from their own networks. It reaches hidden or hard-to-reach populations for whom no sampling frame exists and for whom trust matters. Its weaknesses are that people with large networks are over-represented and isolated people are missed.

Snowball sampling is a kind of non-probability sampling, as is purposive sampling, in which researchers deliberately choose people who can inform the question.

Takeaway: participants recruit participants = snowball sampling, for hidden populations.

whyNot.B: Random sampling needs a list of the whole population to draw from, which does not exist here.
whyNot.C: Stratified sampling needs a list divided into subgroups, from which random samples are drawn.
whyNot.D: Cluster sampling selects predefined groups at random; here participants recruit one another.
whyNot.E: Systematic sampling picks every kth person from a list after a random start.

items.objective: Recognise snowball sampling and when it is used.

items.stemHtml: A study of how hospital teams handle handoffs between shifts collects data from interviews with nurses and physicians, direct observation of 40 handoffs, and review of written handoff notes. The researchers compare the findings from each source to see whether they agree. Which of the following qualitative techniques does this comparison represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Saturation

options.label: B
options.html: Triangulation

options.label: C
options.html: Snowball sampling

options.label: D
options.html: Reflexivity

options.label: E
options.html: Audit trail

items.explanationHtml:
Triangulation uses more than one data source, method, investigator or theory to look at the same question. Agreement across sources strengthens the credibility of the findings; disagreement is also informative (people may describe ideal handoffs in interviews that differ from what observers see).

TechniquePurpose
TriangulationCross-check findings across sources or methods
Member checkingConfirm interpretations with participants
ReflexivityAcknowledge the researcher's influence
Audit trailMake analytic decisions traceable

Takeaway: several sources or methods compared on one question = triangulation.

whyNot.A: Saturation is the point at which new data yield no new themes; it does not involve comparing sources.
whyNot.C: Snowball sampling is a way of recruiting participants through their networks.
whyNot.D: Reflexivity is the researchers' examination of their own influence on the study.
whyNot.E: An audit trail documents decisions so others can follow the analysis; it does not compare data sources.

items.objective: Recognise triangulation in a qualitative study.

items.stemHtml: A researcher who previously worked as an intensive care nurse conducts interviews with families of patients who died in an intensive care unit. Throughout the study she writes memos about how her own experiences and beliefs about end-of-life care might shape the questions she asks and the way she interprets what families say, and she reports this in the methods section. Which of the following best describes this practice?

options.label: A
options.html: Member checking

options.label: B
options.html: Data saturation

options.label: C
options.html: Transferability

options.label: D
options.html: Reflexivity

options.label: E
options.html: Purposive sampling

items.explanationHtml:
In qualitative research the researcher is part of the instrument. Reflexivity is the continuous, explicit examination of how the researcher's background, assumptions and relationship to participants shape data collection and interpretation. Reporting it lets readers judge the findings in that light.

Reflexivity does not remove the researcher's influence (that is impossible); it makes the influence visible.

Takeaway: researcher openly examines her own influence = reflexivity.

whyNot.A: Member checking involves returning interpretations to participants, not the researcher's reflection on herself.
whyNot.B: Saturation concerns when to stop collecting data.
whyNot.C: Transferability concerns whether findings can apply to other settings.
whyNot.E: Purposive sampling is the deliberate selection of informative participants.

items.objective: Define reflexivity in qualitative research.

items.stemHtml: A qualitative study of how rural patients experience telehealth visits includes a detailed description of the region, the clinics, the internet access available, the participants' ages and occupations and the way visits were scheduled. The authors state that this description is intended to help readers in other places decide whether the findings are likely to apply to their own patients. This part of the report most directly addresses which quality criterion?

options.label: A
options.html: Credibility

options.label: B
options.html: Transferability

options.label: C
options.html: Dependability

options.label: D
options.html: Confirmability

options.label: E
options.html: Saturation

items.explanationHtml:
Qualitative research judges rigour by criteria that parallel quantitative ones:

Qualitative criterionRough quantitative parallelTypical strategy
CredibilityInternal validityTriangulation, member checking
TransferabilityExternal validityThick description of context
DependabilityReliabilityAudit trail
ConfirmabilityObjectivityReflexivity, audit trail

Transferability is not claimed by the authors; they provide thick description so that readers can judge whether their own setting is similar enough.

Takeaway: detailed context so readers can judge applicability elsewhere = transferability.

whyNot.A: Credibility concerns whether the findings truly represent participants' experiences, supported by triangulation or member checking.
whyNot.C: Dependability concerns whether the research process is consistent and documented, for example by an audit trail.
whyNot.D: Confirmability concerns whether findings are grounded in the data rather than in the researcher's preferences.
whyNot.E: Saturation is the point at which new data stop producing new themes.

items.objective: Match qualitative rigour strategies to quality criteria.

items.stemHtml: Over 2 months, an internist sees three patients who develop severe, previously undescribed hair loss within 3 weeks of starting a newly marketed oral anticoagulant. In each patient, hair growth resumes after the drug is switched to another anticoagulant. No such reaction is listed in the drug's prescribing information. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the internist?

options.label: A
options.html: Report the three cases to the FDA's adverse event reporting program

options.label: B
options.html: Wait until a cohort study confirms the association before reporting

options.label: C
options.html: Stop prescribing all oral anticoagulants to her patients

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the three patients to re-start the drug to confirm the reaction

options.label: E
options.html: Publish the cases in a journal instead of reporting them

items.explanationHtml:
Unexpected reactions to newly marketed drugs are often first noticed by clinicians in a few patients. These observations are case reports, and the system that collects them (in the United States, the FDA's voluntary reporting program for health professionals and the public) depends on clinicians submitting suspected reactions even when causation is uncertain. Pooled reports can generate a signal that triggers analytical studies, label changes or other regulatory action.

A report does not need proof of causation; a plausible temporal link and improvement on withdrawal (dechallenge) are good reasons to report.

Takeaway: suspect a new adverse drug reaction → report it; case reports are how post-marketing signals start.

whyNot.B: Spontaneous reporting exists to detect signals early; waiting for an analytical study defeats its purpose.
whyNot.C: Three cases with one drug do not justify withholding an entire drug class that prevents strokes and clots.
whyNot.D: Deliberate rechallenge exposes patients to harm without clinical need; the reaction already resolved on withdrawal.
whyNot.E: Publication can be valuable, but it is not a substitute for reporting the suspected reaction to the regulator.

items.objective: Act on a suspected new adverse drug reaction by reporting it.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with episodic migraine brings a printout of a published case report describing a woman whose migraines stopped after she began taking a herbal supplement. She asks whether she should start the supplement. Her migraines occur 3 to 4 times per month. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "This was published in a journal, so the supplement should work for you too."

options.label: B
options.html: "One case can't show the supplement caused the change. Let's look at what trials show."

options.label: C
options.html: "Case reports are worthless, so you should just ignore this one."

options.label: D
options.html: "Supplements are natural, so there is no harm in trying it for a while."

options.label: E
options.html: "I can't discuss treatments that are not prescription drugs, I'm afraid."

items.explanationHtml:
The best response is honest about what a case report can show and then moves to evidence-based options. A single patient's improvement after a supplement has many possible explanations: natural fluctuation of migraine, regression to the mean (people try something new when attacks are at their worst), other changes in her life, and placebo response. Only controlled trials can separate these from a real effect.

The response also respects her interest and keeps the conversation open, which is more likely to lead to an effective preventive plan.

Takeaway: a case report suggests, it does not prove; redirect to controlled evidence without dismissing the patient.

whyNot.A: Publication of a single case does not show efficacy; migraine frequency fluctuates and placebo responses are common.
whyNot.C: Dismissing the report is inaccurate (case reports are useful for raising hypotheses) and does not engage with her question.
whyNot.D: Natural products can interact with drugs and cause harm, and this response skips any discussion of evidence.
whyNot.E: Refusing to discuss the supplement abandons her question and misses the chance to discuss effective options.

items.objective: Explain to a patient the limits of a case report while respecting her question.

items.stemHtml: A pulmonologist reads a case series of 25 patients who developed myocarditis after receiving a new injectable monoclonal antibody for severe asthma. In 20 of the 25 patients, chest pain began within 7 days of the first dose, and all had elevated troponin concentrations. The report does not state how many patients received the drug. She has several patients starting the drug next month. Which of the following is the most appropriate use of this report in her practice?

options.label: A
options.html: Tell patients that about 1 in 25 who receive the drug will develop myocarditis

options.label: B
options.html: Stop the drug in all patients currently taking it without complications

options.label: C
options.html: Tell patients starting the drug to seek care for chest pain in the first week

options.label: D
options.html: Conclude that the drug does not cause myocarditis because there is no control group

options.label: E
options.html: Measure troponin weekly for a year in every patient taking the drug

items.explanationHtml:
A case series cannot estimate how often a reaction happens, because it has no denominator, and it cannot prove causation, because it has no comparison group. What it does well is describe the clinical picture: who was affected, when, and how the reaction presented. Here most cases began within a week of the first dose, which is directly useful for counselling patients on what symptoms to watch for and when.

The signal should also prompt the clinician to report any cases she sees and to look for analytical studies as they appear.

Takeaway: use a case series to recognise a reaction early; do not quote a risk from it.

whyNot.A: The 25 are cases only; with no count of people treated, the risk of myocarditis cannot be estimated.
whyNot.B: A case series cannot quantify risk, and stopping an effective drug in patients doing well may cause harm.
whyNot.D: The lack of a control group means causation is unproven, not disproven; the signal still matters.
whyNot.E: The series points to the first week after the first dose; indefinite weekly testing is not supported by it.

items.objective: Apply the descriptive findings of a case series to patient counselling without overinterpreting risk.

items.stemHtml: A dermatologist wants to know how many of the 900 adults with psoriasis currently followed in her group practice have clinically significant depressive symptoms, to decide whether to add routine depression screening to visits. Which of the following study designs is most appropriate for this question?

options.label: A
options.html: Case-control study of patients with and without depression

options.label: B
options.html: Randomized trial of depression screening versus no screening

options.label: C
options.html: Prospective cohort study following patients for new depression

options.label: D
options.html: Cross-sectional survey of the practice's patients with psoriasis

options.label: E
options.html: Ecological study comparing practices with different psoriasis rates

items.explanationHtml:
The question is about prevalence: how many patients have the condition at one point in time. A cross-sectional survey, ideally of all 900 patients or of a random sample, using a validated depression questionnaire, answers it directly and quickly.

Choose the design from the question: prevalence → cross-sectional; incidence and risk → cohort; rare outcome and its causes → case-control; effect of an intervention → randomized trial.

Takeaway: "how many have it now?" is a prevalence question for a cross-sectional survey.

whyNot.A: A case-control study compares exposure between people with and without an outcome; it cannot give the proportion of her patients who are depressed.
whyNot.B: A trial could test whether screening improves outcomes, but the question asked is how common depressive symptoms are now.
whyNot.C: A cohort measures incidence of new cases over time; she wants current prevalence.
whyNot.E: Group-level comparisons cannot tell her how many of her own patients are affected.

items.objective: Match a prevalence question to a cross-sectional design.

items.stemHtml: An oncologist reads a report from a single cancer centre describing 6 patients with a rare sarcoma whose tumours shrank by more than half after treatment with an off-label drug. In the methods, the authors note that 40 patients with this sarcoma received the drug at the centre during the same period and that the report describes "illustrative cases with a response." Which of the following conclusions about this report is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.html: The drug has a response rate of 100% in patients with this sarcoma

options.label: B
options.html: The drug is superior to standard treatment for this sarcoma

options.label: C
options.html: The report proves that the drug causes shrinkage of this tumour

options.label: D
options.html: The report should be ignored because the sarcoma is rare

options.label: E
options.html: It cannot show how often the drug works, as non-responders are not described

items.explanationHtml:
The authors chose cases by their outcome (responders), so the report can only describe what responses looked like. At best it shows that responses occur: 6 of 40 treated patients, 15%, is the most that can be said about responders at this centre, and even that ignores how many tumours would have shrunk with other care. Selective reporting is a major weakness of case series, along with the lack of a comparison group.

The appropriate next step is a prospective study, such as a single-arm phase 2 trial with a predefined response criterion that includes every treated patient.

Takeaway: a case series chosen by outcome tells you what can happen, not how often.

whyNot.A: Only responders were reported; selecting cases by outcome makes the apparent response rate meaningless.
whyNot.B: No comparison with standard treatment was made, so superiority cannot be judged.
whyNot.C: A selected case series without a control group cannot establish causation.
whyNot.D: Reports on rare tumours are especially useful for raising hypotheses; the problem is the selection of cases, not the rarity.

items.objective: Recognise selective reporting in a case series.

items.stemHtml: A surgical resident cares for a 52-year-old man who develops a previously unreported complication after a common abdominal procedure. The attending surgeon suggests they write up the case for a journal. The published report would include the patient's age, a clinical photograph and the date and location of his surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate step before submitting the report?

options.label: A
options.html: Obtain the patient's written consent for publication of his information

options.label: B
options.html: Remove the patient's name and submit without contacting him

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the hospital's legal department to consent on the patient's behalf

options.label: D
options.html: Register the case report in a public clinical trial registry

options.label: E
options.html: Wait until a second similar patient is found

items.explanationHtml:
A case report describes one identifiable person. Journals generally require the patient's written informed consent for publication, especially when photographs or other potentially identifying details are included, and the patient should be told what will be published. Under HIPAA, publishing identifiable health information in a journal is not a treatment, payment or operations use, so it generally needs the patient's written authorization unless the information has been properly de-identified.

Even with consent, authors should include only the details needed and remove the rest.

Takeaway: before publishing a case report, get the patient's written consent and minimise identifying details.

whyNot.B: Removing the name alone leaves identifying details (photograph, date, location), and consent should be sought.
whyNot.C: A capable adult patient decides about publication of his own information; no one else can consent for him.
whyNot.D: Trial registration applies to prospective clinical trials, not to a single-patient case report.
whyNot.E: A single unusual case can be published; waiting does not address the patient's privacy or consent.

items.objective: Identify consent requirements before publishing a case report.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with mild depression has read that countries where people eat the most fish have the lowest rates of depression. He asks whether eating fish twice a week would protect him. He is taking an SSRI and feels somewhat better. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Yes. The study shows that eating fish lowers your risk of depression."

options.label: B
options.html: "Country data can't show that the people who eat fish are the ones who are less depressed."

options.label: C
options.html: "You can stop your antidepressant if you eat fish regularly."

options.label: D
options.html: "That kind of study is never useful in medicine, so ignore it."

options.label: E
options.html: "Fish raises serotonin levels, so the effect must be real for you."

items.explanationHtml:
Comparing national fish consumption with national depression rates is an ecological study. Countries differ in diet, income, sunlight, culture and how depression is diagnosed, and within each country the individuals who eat fish may be no less depressed than others. Inferring individual benefit from such data is the ecological fallacy.

The best response explains this honestly and briefly, and can go on to say that a healthy diet is reasonable but is not a replacement for his current treatment.

Takeaway: population correlations generate hypotheses; they do not tell an individual what will happen to him.

whyNot.A: Country-level data cannot show an effect on individuals; this commits the ecological fallacy.
whyNot.C: Stopping effective treatment on the strength of a population correlation risks relapse.
whyNot.D: Ecological studies are useful for generating hypotheses; dismissing them is inaccurate and unhelpful.
whyNot.E: A plausible mechanism does not turn a group-level correlation into evidence of individual benefit.

items.objective: Explain the ecological fallacy to a patient.

items.stemHtml: A state health department notices an apparent increase in a rare congenital heart defect that affects about 1 in 10,000 live births. Officials want to examine several possible maternal exposures during early pregnancy, including medications, occupational solvents and infections, as quickly as possible. Which of the following study designs is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Prospective cohort study of pregnant women

options.label: B
options.html: Randomized controlled trial

options.label: C
options.html: Case-control study

options.label: D
options.html: Cross-sectional survey of newborns

options.label: E
options.html: Ecological study of counties

items.explanationHtml:
For a rare outcome with several candidate exposures, the efficient design is a case-control study: identify affected infants (for example, from a birth-defects registry) and comparable unaffected infants from the same population, then compare their mothers' early-pregnancy exposures. It is fast and inexpensive and can examine many exposures at once.

Its weaknesses are recall bias (mothers of affected infants may search their memories harder) and the difficulty of choosing appropriate controls; using records made before the birth helps.

Takeaway: rare disease, many possible causes → case-control.

whyNot.A: Following pregnant women would need hundreds of thousands of pregnancies to observe enough cases of a 1-in-10,000 defect.
whyNot.B: Randomly assigning pregnant women to potentially harmful exposures would be unethical and impractical.
whyNot.D: A survey of newborns would find very few cases and could not efficiently compare earlier exposures.
whyNot.E: County-level comparisons cannot link a mother's own exposures to her infant's defect.

items.objective: Choose a case-control design for a rare outcome with several possible exposures.

items.stemHtml: An occupational health physician is concerned about workers at a single factory who handle a new industrial solvent. About 2,000 workers are exposed. The physician wants to know whether exposure increases the risk of several outcomes, including chronic kidney disease, liver injury and peripheral neuropathy. Which of the following study designs is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Case-control study of patients with chronic kidney disease

options.label: B
options.html: Randomized trial assigning workers to solvent exposure

options.label: C
options.html: Case series of exposed workers who became ill

options.label: D
options.html: Cohort study comparing exposed workers with similar unexposed workers

options.label: E
options.html: Ecological study of solvent sales by region

items.explanationHtml:
For a rare exposure concentrated in a defined group, a cohort study is efficient: identify the exposed workers and a comparable unexposed group (for example, workers in other departments or a similar factory), then compare the incidence of each outcome. A cohort can examine multiple outcomes of one exposure and gives incidence and relative risks. If good exposure records exist, a retrospective cohort is faster.

QuestionUsual design
Rare outcome, many exposuresCase-control
Rare exposure, many outcomesCohort
Current prevalenceCross-sectional
Acute trigger of an eventCase-crossover

Takeaway: rare exposure, several outcomes → cohort.

whyNot.A: A case-control study starts from one outcome; it would find very few exposed people because the exposure is rare in the general population.
whyNot.B: Deliberately assigning a suspected toxin to workers would be unethical.
whyNot.C: A case series has no comparison group and cannot show whether exposure raises risk.
whyNot.E: Regional data cannot show whether individual exposed workers develop disease.

items.objective: Choose a cohort design for a rare exposure with several possible outcomes.

items.stemHtml:
A prospective cohort study enrols 2,000 pregnant women at 12 weeks' gestation, records whether each works regular night shifts, and follows them to delivery.

Preterm birthTerm birthTotal
Night-shift work48352400
No night-shift work1201,4801,600

A 29-year-old pregnant nurse who works night shifts asks how her risk compares with that of women who do not. Which of the following is the relative risk of preterm birth associated with night-shift work in this study, rounded to one decimal place?
items.explanationHtml:
Risk in exposed women = 48/400 = 12.0%. Risk in unexposed women = 120/1,600 = 7.5%. Relative risk = 12.0/7.5 = 1.6.

The absolute difference is 4.5 percentage points, which is often more meaningful when counselling a patient: in this study about 12 in 100 women working night shifts and about 7 or 8 in 100 of those who did not had a preterm birth. Because this is an observational cohort, the association may reflect confounding (for example, by socioeconomic factors) rather than an effect of night work itself.

Takeaway: cohort → incidence in each group → relative risk = risk exposed ÷ risk unexposed.

whyNot.A: 0.4 divides the number of preterm births in the two groups (48/120) and ignores the group sizes.
whyNot.B: 0.6 is the inverse of the relative risk: the unexposed risk was divided by the exposed risk.
whyNot.C: 1.4 divides the exposed risk (12%) by the overall risk in the whole cohort (8.4%) instead of by the unexposed risk.
whyNot.E: 1.7 is the odds ratio (48 × 1,480)/(352 × 120); a cohort study can give the relative risk directly.

items.objective: Calculate and explain a relative risk from a cohort study.

items.stemHtml: Investigators plan a case-control study of whether an over-the-counter decongestant taken in the first trimester is associated with a particular birth defect. Mothers of affected infants and mothers of unaffected infants will be interviewed about medication use 6 to 12 months after delivery. A reviewer worries that mothers of affected infants will recall and report medication use more completely. Which of the following changes would best reduce this problem?

options.label: A
options.html: Measure exposure from pharmacy and prenatal records made during pregnancy

options.label: B
options.html: Double the number of cases and controls

options.label: C
options.html: Match controls to cases on maternal age

options.label: D
options.html: Lengthen the interview with more detailed medication questions

options.label: E
options.html: Restrict both groups to first-time mothers

items.explanationHtml:
Recall bias is a differential error in reported exposure: mothers of affected infants have often thought hard about what might have caused the defect, so they report exposures more completely than control mothers. It typically exaggerates the odds ratio.

The strongest fix is to use exposure information recorded before the outcome was known, such as prescription, pharmacy or prenatal records, or to nest the study in a pregnancy cohort that collected exposure data prospectively. For over-the-counter products, records are less complete, which is itself worth noting.

Takeaway: fight recall bias with exposure data recorded before the outcome was known.

whyNot.B: A larger sample improves precision but does not remove a systematic difference in recall.
whyNot.C: Matching on age controls confounding by age; it does not equalise recall.
whyNot.D: Longer interviews are applied to both groups but cannot correct the greater motivation of case mothers to remember.
whyNot.E: Restriction may control confounding by parity but does not address differential recall.

items.objective: Choose a design change that reduces recall bias in a case-control study.

items.stemHtml: A pediatric resident designs a prospective cohort study to examine whether the number of hours that 12-year-olds spend on social media each day predicts depressive symptoms 2 years later. Baseline sleep duration and household income will also be recorded and adjusted for. In this study, which of the following is the dependent variable?

options.label: A
options.html: Daily hours of social media use

options.label: B
options.html: Household income

options.label: C
options.html: Baseline sleep duration

options.label: D
options.html: Age of the participants at enrolment

options.label: E
options.html: Depressive symptoms at 2 years

items.explanationHtml:
The dependent variable is the outcome, the thing that is measured to see whether it depends on something else: here, depressive symptoms at 2 years. The independent variable is the exposure or predictor (social media use). Variables such as income and sleep are covariates, included to control confounding.

In a trial, the independent variable is the assigned intervention; in an observational study it is the measured exposure.

Takeaway: outcome = dependent variable; exposure or intervention = independent variable.

whyNot.A: Social media use is the exposure that the researchers suspect causes the outcome, which makes it the independent variable.
whyNot.B: Income is a covariate (potential confounder) included in the analysis, not the outcome.
whyNot.C: Sleep is another covariate recorded at baseline; it is not the outcome being predicted.
whyNot.D: Age is fixed at 12 by the inclusion criteria and is not the outcome.

items.objective: Identify dependent and independent variables in a study.

items.stemHtml: A health system's pharmacy committee must decide whether to add a new once-weekly oral drug for type 2 diabetes to its formulary. It wants to know how well the drug works in the system's usual primary care patients, many of whom are older, have several chronic diseases and do not always take medications as prescribed. Which of the following trial designs would best answer the committee's question?

options.label: A
options.html: An explanatory trial in specialist centres that excludes patients with other diseases

options.label: B
options.html: A crossover trial of 30 adherent volunteers with a washout period

options.label: C
options.html: A phase 1 dose-escalation study in healthy volunteers

options.label: D
options.html: A per-protocol analysis of a trial restricted to fully adherent participants

options.label: E
options.html: A pragmatic trial in routine clinics with broad eligibility and usual follow-up

items.explanationHtml:
Explanatory trials ask whether a treatment can work (efficacy) under ideal conditions: narrow eligibility, expert centres, close monitoring. Pragmatic trials ask whether it does work (effectiveness) in everyday care: broad eligibility, usual clinicians, flexible delivery, patient-important outcomes and intention-to-treat analysis. Most trials sit somewhere between the two.

A health system deciding about routine use needs the pragmatic answer, because its patients are older, have more comorbidity and adhere less than the participants of a typical explanatory trial.

Takeaway: "does it work in our usual patients?" → pragmatic trial.

whyNot.A: Strict selection and close supervision show whether the drug can work under ideal conditions, not how it performs in this population.
whyNot.B: A small, highly selected crossover trial answers a narrow efficacy question and suits short-acting drugs, not formulary decisions.
whyNot.C: Phase 1 studies address safety and pharmacokinetics in a handful of people, not effectiveness in practice.
whyNot.D: Restricting to adherent participants overstates the effect expected when the drug is prescribed to typical patients.

items.objective: Distinguish pragmatic from explanatory trials and match them to decisions.

items.stemHtml: A company plans a phase 3 trial of a new oral anticoagulant for preventing stroke in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and a high stroke risk. Several anticoagulants are already proven to reduce strokes in this population. The research ethics board is reviewing the choice of comparator. Which of the following is the most appropriate comparator for this trial?

options.label: A
options.html: An established anticoagulant at its approved dose

options.label: B
options.html: Placebo

options.label: C
options.html: No treatment, with open-label observation

options.label: D
options.html: Historical controls from an earlier trial

options.label: E
options.html: A lower dose of the new drug as the only comparison

items.explanationHtml:
When a proven effective treatment exists and withholding it risks serious or irreversible harm, the new drug should be compared with that active control, not placebo. The trial can be designed to show superiority or, more commonly, non-inferiority (that the new drug is not unacceptably worse, perhaps with other advantages such as fewer bleeds or no monitoring).

Placebo controls are appropriate when no proven treatment exists, or when withholding treatment for a short time carries only minor, reversible risk and participants are protected, for example add-on designs in which everyone also receives standard care.

Takeaway: proven treatment + serious harm from withholding it → active control.

whyNot.B: Giving placebo to high-risk patients when effective treatment exists exposes them to preventable disabling strokes.
whyNot.C: Withholding proven therapy is just as harmful as placebo and also loses blinding.
whyNot.D: Historical controls differ in era, care and patient selection, making the comparison unreliable.
whyNot.E: Comparing two doses of an unproven drug leaves both groups without a proven treatment.

items.objective: Select an active comparator when effective therapy exists.

items.stemHtml: A clinical research group wants to use a crossover design, in which each participant receives both treatments in random order with a washout between them, to reduce the number of participants needed. For which of the following research questions is a crossover design most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Does a 7-day antibiotic course cure community-acquired pneumonia?

options.label: B
options.html: Does a short-acting hypnotic shorten sleep latency in chronic insomnia?

options.label: C
options.html: Does a vaccine prevent a first episode of shingles?

options.label: D
options.html: Does early surgery for appendicitis reduce complications?

options.label: E
options.html: Does a drug given after myocardial infarction reduce 2-year mortality?

items.explanationHtml:
A crossover trial works only when the condition is chronic and stable, the treatment effect is rapid in onset and reversible after a washout, and the outcome can be measured repeatedly in the same person. Chronic insomnia treated with a short-acting hypnotic fits all three.

Curative treatments, vaccines, surgery, acute illnesses, and irreversible outcomes such as death make crossover impossible, because the first period changes the participant permanently.

Takeaway: crossover suits stable chronic conditions, reversible treatments and repeatable outcomes.

whyNot.A: Pneumonia is cured or not after the first period, so there is no comparable condition left for the second treatment.
whyNot.C: Vaccination has lasting effects and the outcome is a one-time event, so there can be no washout or second period.
whyNot.D: Surgery is irreversible and appendicitis is an acute, one-time condition.
whyNot.E: Death cannot be followed by a second period, and long-term outcomes cannot be compared within one person.

items.objective: Identify research questions suited to a crossover design.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer that has progressed after two lines of chemotherapy is offered enrolment in a phase 1 trial of a new drug at an academic cancer centre. He says, "I'm signing up because this drug is going to cure me." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "That's the right attitude. Staying positive will help the drug work."

options.label: B
options.html: "You should not enrol in this trial if you are hoping for any benefit."

options.label: C
options.html: "This trial mainly aims to find a safe dose and may not help your cancer. What are you hoping for?"

options.label: D
options.html: "Phase 1 trials only test drugs that have already been shown to work."

options.label: E
options.html: "Don't worry about the details. The research team will decide what is best."

items.explanationHtml:
Believing that a research study is designed to benefit you personally is the therapeutic misconception. In a phase 1 oncology trial the primary goals are safety, tolerability and dose finding; some participants benefit, but the chance is uncertain and usually small. For consent to be informed, the patient must understand the purpose, the risks, the uncertain benefit and the alternatives (including palliative care).

The best response corrects the misunderstanding gently and honestly and opens a conversation about his goals rather than deciding for him.

Takeaway: correct the therapeutic misconception: early-phase trials test safety and dose, not cure.

whyNot.A: This reinforces a misunderstanding of the trial's purpose, so his consent would not be adequately informed.
whyNot.B: Hoping for benefit is understandable and does not disqualify him; the task is to correct the misunderstanding, not to exclude him.
whyNot.D: This is false: phase 1 trials are the first studies in humans, before efficacy is known.
whyNot.E: This is paternalistic and leaves his misconception about the trial in place.

items.objective: Address the therapeutic misconception when discussing a phase 1 trial.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, which of the following conclusions about drug K is best supported by the intention-to-treat result?

options.label: A
options.html: It is superior to the standard regimen

options.label: B
options.html: It is inferior to the standard regimen

options.label: C
options.html: It is equivalent to the standard regimen in all outcomes

options.label: D
options.html: It is non-inferior to the standard regimen

options.label: E
options.html: The trial is inconclusive because the difference is not statistically significant

items.explanationHtml:
In a non-inferiority trial, look at the confidence interval for the difference (new minus standard) and compare its lower limit with the prespecified margin. Here the lower limit is −5.5 percentage points, above the −10 margin, so the data exclude a loss of cure as large as the margin: drug K is non-inferior. The interval also includes 0, so it is not shown to be better.

The margin represents the largest loss of effect that clinicians would accept in exchange for the new treatment's advantages (here, avoiding intravenous therapy).

Takeaway: non-inferiority = lower confidence limit above the margin; superiority needs the interval to exclude 0 on the favourable side.

whyNot.A: The interval includes 0 and its point estimate favours the standard regimen, so superiority is not shown.
whyNot.B: An inferiority conclusion would need the interval to lie below the margin; the whole interval lies above −10.
whyNot.C: Equivalence needs a two-sided margin specified in advance, and only clinical cure was tested; neither was part of this design.
whyNot.E: In a non-inferiority trial, a nonsignificant difference is expected; the question is whether the lower limit clears the margin, which it does.

items.objective: Interpret a non-inferiority trial result against its margin.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, which of the following is the main reason the investigators also reported a per-protocol analysis?

options.label: A
options.html: Per-protocol analysis preserves the balance created by randomization better than intention-to-treat analysis

options.label: B
options.html: Nonadherence and switching can make the groups look alike, which in this trial design can hide a real difference

options.label: C
options.html: Per-protocol analysis is required because the trial was open-label

options.label: D
options.html: Per-protocol analysis gives a larger sample and therefore more power

options.label: E
options.html: Per-protocol analysis removes the need for a non-inferiority margin

items.explanationHtml:
In a superiority trial, the dilution caused by nonadherence and crossover biases intention-to-treat results toward no difference, which makes it harder to claim superiority, a conservative error. In a non-inferiority trial, a bias toward no difference makes it easier to claim non-inferiority, an anticonservative error. A sloppy trial could look non-inferior simply because both groups were treated poorly.

For that reason non-inferiority trials usually report both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses and are most convincing when both clear the margin, as they do here (lower limits −5.5 and −4.8 versus −10).

Takeaway: in non-inferiority trials, ITT is not automatically conservative; check that per-protocol agrees.

whyNot.A: The reverse is true: per-protocol analysis excludes participants after randomization and can unbalance the groups.
whyNot.C: Open-label design threatens measurement, which is handled here by blinded assessors; it does not determine the analysis population.
whyNot.D: Per-protocol analysis includes fewer participants (560 and 565 rather than 600 each).
whyNot.E: The same margin is applied to both analyses; neither removes it.

items.objective: Explain why non-inferiority trials report both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.

items.stemHtml: Suppose that, in this trial, the intention-to-treat difference in cure had instead been −5.5 percentage points with a 95% confidence interval of −12.0 to 1.0. Which of the following conclusions would then be best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Non-inferiority is not shown, and inferiority is not shown either

options.label: B
options.html: Drug K is non-inferior, because the interval includes 0

options.label: C
options.html: Drug K is inferior, because the lower limit is beyond the margin

options.label: D
options.html: Drug K is superior, because its point estimate is close to 0

options.label: E
options.html: Drug K is equivalent, because the difference is not statistically significant

items.explanationHtml:
With an interval of −12.0 to 1.0, the data are compatible both with no difference (0 lies inside the interval) and with a loss of cure larger than the acceptable margin (−12.0 lies beyond −10). The trial therefore fails to show non-inferiority but also does not show inferiority: it is inconclusive, usually because it was too small or had more variability than planned.

Where the 95% CI lies (margin −10)Conclusion
Entirely above −10Non-inferior
Entirely above 0Non-inferior and superior
Crosses −10, includes 0Inconclusive
Entirely below 0, crossing −10Inferior, possibly by less than the margin

Takeaway: "not significantly different" is not the same as "non-inferior"; check the lower limit against the margin.

whyNot.B: Including 0 shows the difference is not statistically significant; non-inferiority needs the lower limit above −10, and −12.0 is below it.
whyNot.C: To show inferiority the whole interval would need to lie below 0 (or below the margin); this interval reaches +1.0.
whyNot.D: A point estimate of −5.5 favours the standard regimen, and the interval includes 0.
whyNot.E: A nonsignificant difference is not evidence of equivalence; the interval is too wide to exclude a large loss of cure.

items.objective: Recognise an inconclusive non-inferiority result.

items.stemHtml: A hospital's hip-fracture service has a baseline postoperative delirium rate of 20% in patients aged 65 years or older. If the pooled risk ratio from the meta-analysis were applied to this service, approximately how many patients would need to receive drug V to prevent one case of delirium?
items.explanationHtml:
Relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25. Applied to a baseline risk of 20%: risk with drug V = 0.20 × 0.75 = 0.15. Absolute risk reduction = 0.20 − 0.15 = 0.05. NNT = 1/0.05 = 20.

Relative effects from a meta-analysis are often fairly constant across populations, whereas absolute effects depend on the baseline risk. Applying the pooled relative risk to the local baseline risk is the standard way to estimate the absolute benefit for your own patients. In this case, the low-risk-of-bias estimate (0.85) would give a smaller benefit, so 20 may be optimistic.

Takeaway: NNT = 1/(baseline risk × relative risk reduction).

whyNot.A: 4 is 1 divided by the relative risk reduction (0.25); the number needed to treat uses the absolute reduction.
whyNot.B: 5 is 1 divided by the baseline risk (0.20), ignoring the size of the drug's effect.
whyNot.C: 7 is 1 divided by the expected risk with treatment (0.15), which is not a measure of benefit.
whyNot.E: 25 corresponds to an absolute reduction of 4 percentage points, which would follow from a risk ratio of 0.80, not 0.75.

items.objective: Convert a pooled relative risk into a number needed to treat for a local baseline risk.

items.stemHtml: What does the reported I² value of 0% most accurately indicate about these trials?

options.label: A
options.html: The pooled estimate is certainly the true effect of drug V

options.label: B
options.html: None of the patients in the trials developed delirium

options.label: C
options.html: Trial results vary no more than chance predicts, which does not exclude shared bias

options.label: D
options.html: A random-effects model would give a very different pooled estimate

options.label: E
options.html: Publication bias can be excluded from this meta-analysis

items.explanationHtml:
An I² of 0% means the variation between trial estimates is no greater than expected from sampling error alone: there is no detectable statistical heterogeneity. With only six trials, I² is itself imprecise, and low heterogeneity says nothing about risk of bias. Here the small high-risk trials all point the same way, so they are consistent with each other while possibly sharing a bias (unblinded delirium assessment can inflate effects).

Takeaway: low I² = consistent results, not valid results.

whyNot.A: I² describes consistency between trials, not correctness; consistent trials can share the same bias.
whyNot.B: I² is a statistic about variation between trial results, not about event rates.
whyNot.D: With no heterogeneity, fixed-effect and random-effects models give essentially the same estimate.
whyNot.E: Heterogeneity statistics do not detect missing trials; that needs funnel plots and searches of registries and unpublished data.

items.objective: Interpret a low I² value and its limits.

items.stemHtml: Which conclusion about drug V is most consistent with the results of this meta-analysis?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug V reduces delirium by 25%, and the restricted analysis can be ignored because it includes fewer patients

options.label: B
options.html: Drug V has been shown to have no effect on delirium

options.label: C
options.html: The six trials are too different from each other to be combined

options.label: D
options.html: The meta-analysis is invalid because it did not include observational studies

options.label: E
options.html: The overall benefit depends partly on trials at high risk of bias, so the evidence for drug V is weaker than the pooled estimate suggests

items.explanationHtml:
A sensitivity analysis restricted to trials at low risk of bias tests whether the result depends on weaker studies. Here the larger, well-conducted trials suggest a smaller effect (RR 0.85, interval crossing 1) than the small trials at high risk of bias (each about 0.55 to 0.62). A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it pools; when the overall result is driven by trials with methodological problems, confidence in it should be reduced.

The honest summary is that drug V may reduce delirium modestly, but the best evidence is uncertain, and a large, well-conducted trial would help.

Takeaway: if the result shrinks when weak trials are removed, trust the pooled estimate less.

whyNot.A: The restricted analysis includes the two largest, best-conducted trials (1,520 of 1,973 patients), so it should not be dismissed.
whyNot.B: A nonsignificant result from two trials (0.67 to 1.08) is compatible with both no effect and a modest benefit.
whyNot.C: I² is 0%, so there is no statistical evidence that the trials are too heterogeneous to pool.
whyNot.D: Meta-analyses of interventions properly restrict to randomized trials; including observational studies would add confounding.

items.objective: Interpret a risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis in a meta-analysis.

items.stemHtml: A primary care physician reads a meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials of supplement R for preventing upper respiratory infections in adults. The pooled risk ratio is 0.70. The funnel plot is shown. A patient asks whether she should start taking the supplement. Which of the following conclusions about the meta-analysis is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The plot shows that the supplement's benefit is the same in large and small trials

options.label: B
options.html: Small trials without benefit may be missing, so the pooled effect probably overstates the true benefit

options.label: C
options.html: The asymmetry shows that the large trials were at high risk of bias

options.label: D
options.html: The pattern proves that the trials were fraudulent

options.label: E
options.html: The funnel plot shows that the supplement is harmful

items.explanationHtml:
The funnel plot is asymmetric: the precise trials at the top lie close to the pooled estimate, and the small trials lie only on the side of large benefit, with an empty lower-right region where small trials showing little or no benefit would be expected. This pattern suggests publication bias or other small-study effects (small trials are often less rigorous), and it means the pooled risk ratio probably overstates the benefit. The largest trials suggest a smaller effect, with risk ratios of about 0.8 to 0.9.

For the patient, the physician can explain that the evidence for supplement R is weaker than the headline result suggests.

Takeaway: an empty corner in the funnel → suspect missing small unfavourable studies and an inflated pooled effect.
