whyNot.A: The small trials show much larger effects than the precise trials near the top, which is the opposite of a consistent effect.
whyNot.C: The large, precise trials lie near the pooled line; the problem lies in the small trials.
whyNot.D: Asymmetry suggests publication bias or other small-study effects; it does not establish fraud.
whyNot.E: None of the trials lies to the right of the no-effect line, and the pooled estimate is below 1.

items.objective: Interpret an asymmetric funnel plot when applying a meta-analysis.

items.stemHtml: A family physician wants the most reliable evidence on whether a drug reduces fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Several types of studies are available. Assuming each is well conducted, which of the following provides the strongest evidence for this therapy question?

options.label: A
options.html: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials

options.label: B
options.html: A single large randomized controlled trial

options.label: C
options.html: A prospective cohort study of women who chose to take the drug

options.label: D
options.html: A case-control study of women with and without fractures

options.label: E
options.html: The opinion of a national expert panel

items.explanationHtml:
For questions about the effect of a therapy, the usual hierarchy of evidence, from strongest to weakest, is: systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized trials → individual randomized trials → cohort studies → case-control studies → case series and case reports → expert opinion. Randomization removes confounding; systematic review adds completeness and precision.

The hierarchy is a starting point, not a rule. A poorly done meta-analysis of biased trials can be less reliable than one large, rigorous trial, and some questions (rare harms, prognosis) are best answered by observational designs.

Takeaway: for therapy, a well-done systematic review of randomized trials sits at the top.

whyNot.B: A single trial is strong evidence, but a well-done synthesis of all relevant trials is stronger and more precise.
whyNot.C: Women who choose a drug differ from those who do not, so confounding remains despite adjustment.
whyNot.D: Case-control studies are more prone to selection and recall bias than trials for a therapy question.
whyNot.E: Expert opinion without systematic appraisal of evidence ranks lowest in the hierarchy.

items.objective: Rank study designs by strength of evidence for a therapy question.

items.stemHtml: A meta-analysis pools 22 cohort studies, with more than 1 million participants in total, and finds that regular use of a multivitamin is associated with a 15% lower risk of death (pooled relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.89). A 63-year-old man asks whether this proves that starting a multivitamin will help him live longer. Which of the following is the most accurate conclusion?

options.label: A
options.html: The large number of participants proves that multivitamins prevent death

options.label: B
options.html: The narrow confidence interval shows that confounding has been excluded

options.label: C
options.html: The result should be ignored because meta-analyses can only include randomized trials

options.label: D
options.html: Pooling observational studies increases precision but does not remove the confounding in each study

options.label: E
options.html: The result proves multivitamins are harmful in the people who stopped taking them

items.explanationHtml:
People who take multivitamins regularly tend to differ from non-users: they smoke less, exercise more and see physicians more often (the healthy-user effect). Each cohort study carries that confounding, and pooling 22 such studies produces a very precise estimate of a possibly biased association. Statistical precision is not validity.

When randomized trials of a similar question exist, they are a better guide to whether starting a treatment changes outcomes.

Takeaway: a meta-analysis inherits the biases of its studies; pooling cohorts gives precision, not causation.

whyNot.A: Size narrows the confidence interval but cannot correct systematic error such as confounding by healthy behaviour.
whyNot.B: A narrow interval reflects random error only; confounding is a bias that is not shown in the interval.
whyNot.C: Observational studies can be meta-analysed; the problem is interpreting the pooled result as causal.
whyNot.E: The analysis did not study stopping, and its result points to lower, not higher, risk among users.

items.objective: Explain why a meta-analysis of observational studies does not remove confounding.

items.stemHtml: A district health officer in a rural region needs to estimate measles vaccination coverage among children aged 12 to 23 months. There is no list of all children in the district, but there is an up-to-date list of its 400 villages with their populations. Travel between villages is slow and expensive. Which of the following sampling approaches is most practical for this survey?

options.label: A
options.html: Draw a simple random sample of children from a district-wide list

options.label: B
options.html: Survey children brought to the district hospital's clinic

options.label: C
options.html: Randomly select villages, then survey eligible children in the selected villages

options.label: D
options.html: Survey every eligible child in the district

options.label: E
options.html: Ask village leaders to report the coverage in their village

items.explanationHtml:
In cluster sampling, groups (here villages) are selected at random, often with probability proportional to their size, and individuals are sampled within the chosen groups. It needs a list of clusters, not of individuals, and concentrates fieldwork in fewer places, which makes it the standard approach for household vaccination-coverage surveys.

The trade-off is precision: children in the same village resemble each other, so a cluster sample needs more children than a simple random sample for the same precision (the design effect), and the analysis must account for clustering.

Takeaway: no list of individuals, a list of groups and high travel cost → cluster sampling.

whyNot.A: A simple random sample needs a list of all eligible children, which does not exist, and would scatter visits across many villages.
whyNot.B: A clinic sample over-represents families who use health services and are therefore more likely to be vaccinated.
whyNot.D: A full census would be accurate but far too slow and costly for this purpose.
whyNot.E: Reported estimates from leaders are unverified and prone to error and to overstating coverage.

items.objective: Choose cluster sampling for a field survey.

items.stemHtml: An 82-year-old woman with heart failure and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 25 mL/min/1.73 m² asks whether she should start a new drug that reduced hospitalisations by 30% in a large randomized trial. The trial enrolled patients aged 40 to 75 years and excluded those with an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about applying the trial's results to her?

options.label: A
options.html: The benefit and harms are uncertain for her, because patients like her were excluded

options.label: B
options.html: The trial results apply fully to her because it was randomized

options.label: C
options.html: The drug is proven to be harmful for patients with her kidney function

options.label: D
options.html: She should receive double the trial's dose to compensate for her age

options.label: E
options.html: The trial is invalid because it excluded older patients

items.explanationHtml:
A well-conducted randomized trial has high internal validity, but its external validity (generalizability) extends only to patients reasonably similar to those enrolled. Inclusion and exclusion criteria define that population. This patient is older than any participant and has kidney function below the exclusion threshold, so the trial does not tell us her balance of benefit and harm; harms, in particular, may be greater.

The physician should share that uncertainty, look for other evidence (subgroups, other trials, prescribing information on dosing in kidney disease) and decide together with her.

Takeaway: check the eligibility criteria before applying a trial to the patient in front of you.

whyNot.B: Randomization protects internal validity, not applicability to patients outside the eligibility criteria.
whyNot.C: Exclusion means the trial provides no evidence about her group, not evidence of harm.
whyNot.D: Nothing in the trial supports a higher dose; reduced kidney function may increase drug exposure.
whyNot.E: Exclusions limit generalizability but do not make the trial's results invalid for the patients it studied.

items.objective: Judge whether a trial's results apply to a patient outside its eligibility criteria.

items.stemHtml: A sports medicine clinic estimates the prevalence of low vitamin D concentrations among adults in its city by testing 300 volunteers who respond to a poster displayed in local gyms and running stores. Of the volunteers, 8% have low concentrations. A city health official wants to use this figure for planning. Which of the following is the main limitation of the estimate?

options.label: A
options.html: The sample size is too small to estimate any prevalence

options.label: B
options.html: Vitamin D concentrations cannot be measured accurately

options.label: C
options.html: The study should have been a randomized trial

options.label: D
options.html: The volunteers are unlikely to be representative of the city's adults

options.label: E
options.html: Confounding by age makes the prevalence meaningless

items.explanationHtml:
A convenience (volunteer) sample recruited at gyms and running stores over-represents active people who spend time outdoors and may take supplements, so the estimate is probably too low for the general adult population. This is selection bias: the way people entered the sample is related to the outcome. A larger convenience sample would give a more precise but equally biased estimate.

A representative estimate needs probability sampling from a frame that covers the target population.

Takeaway: convenience samples answer "what is true of these volunteers?", not "what is true of the population?".

whyNot.A: Three hundred people can give a reasonably precise prevalence if they are representative; the problem is who they are.
whyNot.B: Laboratory measurement is not the main issue here.
whyNot.C: A prevalence question needs a representative survey, not a trial.
whyNot.E: Confounding distorts associations between exposures and outcomes; this is a single prevalence estimate whose problem is selection.

items.objective: Recognise selection bias in a convenience sample.

items.stemHtml: Investigators plan a randomized trial of a new treatment for acute severe alcohol-associated hepatitis in 120 patients at 6 hospitals. Disease severity at enrolment strongly predicts 90-day mortality, and with only 120 patients they worry that chance might put more severely ill patients in one group. Which of the following approaches best ensures that severity is balanced between the groups?

options.label: A
options.html: Use simple randomization and a larger significance level

options.label: B
options.html: Randomize separately within strata of severity, using blocks within each stratum

options.label: C
options.html: Alternate assignment by order of admission

options.label: D
options.html: Allow physicians to choose treatment for the sickest patients

options.label: E
options.html: Randomize hospitals rather than individual patients

items.explanationHtml:
In small trials, simple randomization can by chance create groups that differ in an important prognostic factor. Stratified randomization addresses this: patients are first classified by the factor (for example, severity above or below a prespecified score threshold, and often by hospital), and a separate randomization list, usually with permuted blocks, is used within each stratum. This forces balance on that factor.

Only a few strata are practical, and the stratification factors should be included in the analysis. Randomization still balances unmeasured factors on average.

Takeaway: to guarantee balance on a strong prognostic factor in a small trial, stratify the randomization.

whyNot.A: Changing the significance level affects hypothesis testing, not the balance of severity between groups.
whyNot.C: Alternation is not random, is predictable and invites selection bias.
whyNot.D: Physician choice reintroduces confounding by indication and destroys randomization.
whyNot.E: Cluster randomization of 6 hospitals would make imbalance in severity more likely, not less.

items.objective: Choose stratified randomization to balance an important prognostic factor.

items.stemHtml: In an emergency department trial of two strategies for sepsis fluid management, patients arriving on odd-numbered days receive strategy 1 and those arriving on even-numbered days receive strategy 2. An audit shows that enrolling physicians more often enrolled the sickest patients on strategy-1 days, and baseline lactate concentrations differ between groups. Which of the following changes would best prevent this problem in a new trial?

options.label: A
options.html: Blind the patients to their assigned fluid strategy

options.label: B
options.html: Analyse the results by intention-to-treat only

options.label: C
options.html: Enrol more patients so that differences average out

options.label: D
options.html: Adjust the analysis for baseline lactate only

options.label: E
options.html: Assign by a concealed central random sequence after enrolment

items.explanationHtml:
Day-of-the-week or odd/even allocation is quasi-random and completely predictable. When clinicians know the next assignment, they can choose whom to enrol, and the groups differ systematically: selection bias. The fix is a truly random sequence with allocation concealment: the patient is registered first, and only then is the assignment revealed, typically through a central web or telephone system.

Statistical adjustment cannot correct for the unmeasured judgements that physicians used when selecting patients.

Takeaway: predictable allocation = selection bias; use a concealed random sequence revealed only after enrolment.

whyNot.A: Patient blinding would not stop physicians from choosing whom to enrol based on a predictable schedule.
whyNot.B: Intention-to-treat analysis cannot repair groups that were unbalanced at the moment of enrolment.
whyNot.C: Systematic selection is not reduced by larger numbers; it is reproduced in every period.
whyNot.D: Adjustment can address the measured imbalance but not the unmeasured factors physicians used when selecting patients.

items.objective: Fix predictable allocation with concealed randomization.

items.stemHtml: A primary care clinic enrols 150 patients whose office systolic blood pressure was 170 mm Hg or higher at a single routine visit into a new nurse-led coaching program. Three months later the mean systolic pressure in the group has fallen from 178 mm Hg to 158 mm Hg. The clinic director wants to expand the program to other clinics. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The program lowers systolic blood pressure by 20 mm Hg

options.label: B
options.html: The program has no effect because the study was not randomized

options.label: C
options.html: Part of the fall may reflect regression to the mean, so a concurrent control group is needed

options.label: D
options.html: The fall is explained by recall bias

options.label: E
options.html: The program works only in patients with systolic pressure above 170 mm Hg

items.explanationHtml:
Patients were selected because of one extreme measurement. On repeat measurement, extreme values tend to move toward the patient's usual level whatever is done: regression to the mean. Other changes in the same period (medication adjustments, attention, seasonal variation) could also lower the pressure. Without a concurrent control group, the program's own effect cannot be separated from these.

A fair test would randomize similar patients to coaching or usual care, ideally after confirming high blood pressure on repeated measurements.

Takeaway: before-after changes in people selected for extreme values need a control group to be interpreted.

whyNot.A: Without a comparison group, the 20 mm Hg fall cannot be attributed to the program.
whyNot.B: Lack of randomization means the effect is unknown, not that it is absent.
whyNot.D: Blood pressure was measured, not recalled, so recall bias does not apply.
whyNot.E: No other patients were studied, so the study cannot compare effects between groups.

items.objective: Explain why an uncontrolled before-after study cannot show an intervention's effect.

items.stemHtml: A physician reads a randomized trial of a new drug to prevent recurrent gout flares. One in five participants assigned to the drug stopped taking it early. By intention-to-treat analysis, flares were reduced by 15% relative to placebo; by per-protocol analysis, the reduction was 25%. The physician wants to estimate the benefit that her clinic's patients as a whole can expect if she starts prescribing the drug. Which of the following estimates is most appropriate for this purpose?

options.label: A
options.html: The per-protocol estimate

options.label: B
options.html: The average of the two estimates

options.label: C
options.html: The intention-to-treat estimate

options.label: D
options.html: Neither estimate, because one in five stopped the drug

options.label: E
options.html: Whichever estimate has the smaller P value

items.explanationHtml:
The intention-to-treat result estimates what happens when the drug is offered to patients, including those who stop it, which is exactly what the clinic will do. It also preserves randomization. The per-protocol estimate applies to patients who take the drug as directed, but it is vulnerable to bias, because people who adhere differ from those who do not.

For an individual patient who is likely to adhere and tolerate the drug, the benefit may be closer to the per-protocol estimate, which is a useful point to discuss when counselling, but the policy-level estimate is ITT.

Takeaway: "what if we prescribe it?" → intention-to-treat.

whyNot.A: Per-protocol analysis includes only adherent participants and so overstates the benefit of prescribing to a whole group that will include non-adherent patients.
whyNot.B: Averaging the two has no statistical meaning and does not correspond to any population.
whyNot.D: Some nonadherence is expected in practice; intention-to-treat incorporates it rather than making the trial useless.
whyNot.E: The choice of estimate depends on the question asked, not on which result is more significant.

items.objective: Choose the intention-to-treat estimate to predict the effect of prescribing.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial compares a structured exercise-counselling program with usual care for adults with prediabetes. During the trial, many usual-care participants learn about the program from friends in the intervention group and begin exercising regularly on their own. Results are analysed by intention-to-treat. Which of the following is the most likely effect of this on the trial's result?

options.label: A
options.html: The estimated benefit of the program will be larger than its true effect

options.label: B
options.html: There will be no effect, because intention-to-treat analysis corrects for it

options.label: C
options.html: The groups will no longer be comparable at baseline

options.label: D
options.html: The estimated benefit of the program will be smaller than its true effect

options.label: E
options.html: The trial will show that the program is harmful

items.explanationHtml:
Contamination occurs when control participants receive some of the intervention (and crossover when participants switch arms). Both make the groups more similar, so an intention-to-treat comparison is biased toward the null: the program's true effect is underestimated, and a real benefit may be missed. Cluster randomization (for example, by clinic or community) is a common way to prevent it in behavioural trials.

In a superiority trial this bias is conservative; in a non-inferiority trial, it would favour a false claim of non-inferiority.

Takeaway: contamination of controls → smaller apparent effect (bias toward null).

whyNot.A: Exercise among controls improves their outcomes, narrowing rather than widening the difference between groups.
whyNot.B: Intention-to-treat keeps the groups as randomized but cannot remove the effect of controls receiving the intervention.
whyNot.C: Contamination happens after randomization; baseline comparability is not affected.
whyNot.E: Contamination makes the groups more alike; it does not make the intervention appear harmful.

items.objective: Predict the effect of contamination on an intention-to-treat estimate.

items.stemHtml:
A physician reviews a 6-month randomized trial of a new drug for chronic low back pain. The trial flow is summarized below.

DrugPlacebo
Randomized250250
Withdrew because of adverse effects5510
Withdrew because of lack of benefit1040
Completed 6 months185200
Mean pain reduction among completers (0–10 scale)3.11.9

The authors analysed completers only. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The drug reduces pain by 1.2 points in all patients who start it

options.label: B
options.html: Withdrawals differ between groups in number and reason, so the completer analysis may be biased

options.label: C
options.html: The withdrawals do not matter because the numbers completing are similar

options.label: D
options.html: The drug is better tolerated than placebo

options.label: E
options.html: The placebo group's withdrawals show that placebo is harmful

items.explanationHtml:
Overall completion looks similar (185/250 = 74% versus 200/250 = 80%), but the reasons for leaving differ: drug-group participants left mainly because of adverse effects, placebo-group participants mainly because of lack of benefit. Placebo participants who had no relief were removed from the placebo average, while drug participants who could not tolerate the drug were removed from the drug average. The completers are no longer randomized groups, so the comparison is open to attrition bias in either direction.

A better report would collect outcomes for everyone, analyse by intention-to-treat with a principled method for missing data, and show sensitivity analyses.

Takeaway: look at how many left each arm and why; differential, outcome-related dropout undermines completer analyses.

whyNot.A: The 1.2-point difference applies only to completers, a selected group; it is not an estimate for everyone who starts the drug.
whyNot.C: The totals are similar, but the reasons differ sharply, so the completing groups are not comparable.
whyNot.D: Adverse-effect withdrawals were much more common with the drug (55 versus 10).
whyNot.E: Placebo withdrawals were mostly for lack of benefit, which is expected when a treatment is inactive.

items.objective: Interpret differential withdrawal in a trial flow table.

items.stemHtml: In a randomized trial of a smoking-cessation drug, 18% of participants have missing outcome data at 12 months. Participants with missing data were younger and had more cigarettes per day at baseline, and these characteristics were recorded for everyone. The statistician proposes multiple imputation instead of analysing only participants with complete data. Which of the following is the main advantage of multiple imputation in this situation?

options.label: A
options.html: It fills gaps several times from observed data, carrying the uncertainty forward

options.label: B
options.html: It recovers the true value of every single missing outcome

options.label: C
options.html: It removes all bias, whatever the reason the data are missing

options.label: D
options.html: It allows the trial to exclude participants who stopped the drug

options.label: E
options.html: It replaces each missing value with the participant's baseline value

items.explanationHtml:
Multiple imputation builds a model of the outcome from the observed variables (age, smoking intensity, treatment group and so on), fills in each missing value several times with plausible draws from that model, analyses each completed dataset and combines the results. Because the imputed values vary between datasets, the final confidence interval reflects the extra uncertainty from the missing data.

It reduces bias when missingness depends on recorded characteristics ("missing at random"). It cannot fix missingness that depends on the unobserved outcome; for smoking-cessation trials, a common sensitivity analysis counts missing participants as still smoking.

Takeaway: multiple imputation = repeated, model-based filling in that keeps uncertainty honest; it is better than single imputation or complete-case analysis.

whyNot.B: Imputed values are predictions, not recovered data; the true outcomes remain unknown.
whyNot.C: If missingness depends on the unobserved outcome itself, imputation from observed data can still be biased.
whyNot.D: Imputation is used to keep participants in the analysis, not to exclude them.
whyNot.E: Carrying the baseline value forward is a single-imputation method, not multiple imputation.

items.objective: Describe the advantage of multiple imputation for missing trial data.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial assigns 4,000 adults with stable coronary disease to a new anti-inflammatory drug or placebo. By intention-to-treat, 5-year mortality is 9.8% with the drug and 10.0% with placebo. In a secondary analysis, participants who took at least 80% of their assigned pills had lower mortality than those who did not, in both the drug group and the placebo group, by similar amounts. A news article reports that "patients who took the drug faithfully lived longer." Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The drug reduces mortality in adherent patients and should be prescribed with adherence support

options.label: B
options.html: Placebo reduces mortality in adherent patients

options.label: C
options.html: The drug has not been shown to reduce mortality; good adherers have better outcomes for other reasons

options.label: D
options.html: The intention-to-treat result is biased because nonadherence dilutes a real effect

options.label: E
options.html: The trial should be reanalysed as-treated to find the true effect

items.explanationHtml:
The key clue is that adherence predicts survival in the placebo group too. People who take their pills faithfully tend to have healthier lifestyles, better access to care and fewer competing illnesses: the healthy-adherer effect. Comparing adherers with non-adherers, or using an as-treated analysis, is therefore an observational comparison inside a trial and is confounded.

The intention-to-treat comparison (9.8% versus 10.0%) preserves randomization and shows no meaningful benefit. The appropriate comparison for adherers would be adherent drug takers versus adherent placebo takers, and here they did similarly.

Takeaway: if adherence improves outcomes on placebo, adherence is a marker of prognosis; trust the randomized comparison.

whyNot.A: Adherent placebo takers did just as well, so the lower mortality reflects the type of person who adheres, not the drug.
whyNot.B: Placebo pills have no plausible effect on survival; adherence marks healthier behaviour and better prognosis.
whyNot.D: With no benefit among adherent patients relative to adherent placebo takers, there is no masked effect to dilute.
whyNot.E: An as-treated analysis groups people by adherence and would mix in the same healthy-adherer bias.

items.objective: Recognise the healthy-adherer effect and the limits of as-treated analyses.

items.stemHtml: A hospital's quality committee notes that 6% of patients admitted for alcohol withdrawal leave against medical advice, a rate higher than at similar hospitals. Members agree that they do not understand why patients are leaving and want to design an intervention. Which of the following study approaches is most appropriate as a first step?

options.label: A
options.html: A randomized trial of a new discharge policy

options.label: B
options.html: A case-control study of the risk of leaving with a new medication

options.label: C
options.html: A cross-sectional survey of the hospital's average length of stay

options.label: D
options.html: A meta-analysis of trials of discharge policies at other hospitals

options.label: E
options.html: In-depth interviews with patients who left and with ward staff

items.explanationHtml:
When the question is why or how something happens and the relevant factors are not yet known, a qualitative approach fits best. In-depth interviews with patients who left (and staff who cared for them) can reveal reasons the committee had not thought of, such as untreated withdrawal symptoms, stigma, family or work obligations, or ward rules, and so guide the design of an intervention.

A quantitative study (survey, trial) can then measure how common these reasons are or test whether an intervention works.

Takeaway: unknown reasons or experiences → start with qualitative methods; known variables to measure or test → quantitative.

whyNot.A: Testing an intervention before understanding the problem risks evaluating the wrong solution.
whyNot.B: Without knowing patients' reasons, the committee has no basis for choosing which exposure to study.
whyNot.C: Length of stay does not explain why patients leave early.
whyNot.D: Pooled trials of policies elsewhere cannot reveal the local reasons that the committee needs to understand.

items.objective: Choose a qualitative method for an exploratory quality-improvement question.

items.stemHtml: A team wants to understand how women who have experienced intimate partner violence decide whether to disclose it to their physicians. Participants will be recruited through a community advocacy organization. The team is choosing between focus groups and individual interviews. Which of the following is the most appropriate data-collection method?

options.label: A
options.html: Focus groups of 8 to 10 women from the same neighbourhood

options.label: B
options.html: Individual in-depth interviews in a private, safe setting

options.label: C
options.html: A structured questionnaire with yes or no responses

options.label: D
options.html: Review of medical records for documented abuse

options.label: E
options.html: Observation of clinic visits by a researcher

items.explanationHtml:
Individual in-depth interviews suit sensitive, stigmatised or personal topics and questions about individual decision-making. They allow privacy, follow-up questions and a pace set by the participant. Safety planning (where and when the interview happens, and what to do if the participant is in danger) is essential in research on intimate partner violence.

Focus groups are better for exploring shared views, norms and language on less sensitive topics, where interaction between participants is useful.

Takeaway: sensitive personal topic → individual interviews; shared views on a less sensitive topic → focus groups.

whyNot.A: Group discussion of a sensitive and potentially dangerous topic risks privacy breaches and may discourage disclosure.
whyNot.C: Closed questions cannot capture how women reason about disclosure, which is the aim of the study.
whyNot.D: Records capture only what was disclosed and documented, not the decision process.
whyNot.E: Observing visits would not reveal women's private reasoning and could endanger participants.

items.objective: Choose individual interviews over focus groups for a sensitive topic.

items.stemHtml: A county health department surveys 2,400 adults and finds that only 31% of eligible adults have had colorectal cancer screening. To understand the reasons behind the low rate, it then conducts interviews with 25 survey respondents who were eligible but unscreened, chosen to vary in age, insurance status and language. The findings from both parts are combined to design an outreach program. Which of the following best describes this overall study design?

options.label: A
options.html: Cross-sectional study only

options.label: B
options.html: Qualitative study only

options.label: C
options.html: Case-control study

options.label: D
options.html: Mixed-methods study

options.label: E
options.html: Community trial

items.explanationHtml:
A mixed-methods study deliberately combines quantitative and qualitative components and integrates their findings. Here a survey measures how common a problem is, and interviews explain why (a sequential design in which the quantitative phase is followed by a qualitative one that helps explain it). The reverse sequence, interviews first to develop a survey, is also common.

Choosing interviewees to vary in key characteristics is purposive (maximum-variation) sampling.

Takeaway: numbers to measure the problem plus interviews to explain it, integrated = mixed methods.

whyNot.A: The survey part is cross-sectional, but the study also includes and integrates a qualitative interview phase.
whyNot.B: The study also includes a quantitative survey of 2,400 adults.
whyNot.C: There is no comparison of people with and without an outcome to assess past exposures.
whyNot.E: No intervention was assigned to communities; the program is still being designed.

items.objective: Recognise a mixed-methods design.

items.stemHtml: A team plans interviews to learn how patients with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes and their families experience the first month after diagnosis. They want to capture as wide a range of experiences as possible, including families who speak different languages, live in rural areas, or had an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis at diagnosis. Which of the following sampling approaches is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Simple random sampling from the clinic register

options.label: B
options.html: Consecutive sampling of the next 20 families seen

options.label: C
options.html: Purposive sampling chosen to include each of these characteristics

options.label: D
options.html: Systematic sampling of every fifth family on the register

options.label: E
options.html: Recruiting only families who volunteer through a newsletter

items.explanationHtml:
Qualitative studies aim for information-rich cases rather than statistical representativeness. Purposive sampling means deliberately selecting participants who can illuminate the question; its maximum-variation form seeks a wide range of characteristics so that common themes, and important differences, emerge. Sampling continues until saturation.

Probability sampling methods suit surveys that estimate how common something is, not interviews that explore experiences.

Takeaway: deliberately pick participants to cover the experiences you need = purposive sampling.

whyNot.A: Random sampling of a small number could easily miss the less common groups the team specifically wants to hear from.
whyNot.B: Consecutive families may all be similar and may not include the experiences the team is looking for.
whyNot.D: Systematic sampling is a probability method aimed at representativeness, not at deliberately covering a range of experiences.
whyNot.E: Volunteers through one channel tend to be more engaged and may omit families the team most needs to include.

items.objective: Choose purposive sampling for a qualitative interview study.

items.stemHtml: Researchers conduct interviews with 20 patients about their experience of returning home after a stroke and develop five themes. Before finalising their report, they want to strengthen confidence that the themes accurately reflect participants' experiences. Which of the following steps is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Recruit 200 more participants to achieve statistical significance

options.label: B
options.html: Calculate P values for the frequency of each theme

options.label: C
options.html: Randomize participants to two interviewers and compare results

options.label: D
options.html: Replace the interviews with a validated questionnaire

options.label: E
options.html: Share a summary of the themes with participants and ask whether it reflects their experience

items.explanationHtml:
Member checking (respondent validation) returns findings or interpretations to participants to see whether they recognise them as accurate. Together with triangulation, peer debriefing and searching for cases that contradict the themes, it supports the credibility of qualitative findings.

Quantitative tools such as P values, power and randomization answer different questions and are not measures of rigour in qualitative analysis.

Takeaway: check your interpretations with the people you interviewed = member checking → credibility.

whyNot.A: Qualitative findings are not tested for statistical significance, and adding many interviews does not check interpretations.
whyNot.B: Counting themes and computing P values does not address whether the themes are accurate interpretations.
whyNot.C: Randomization serves causal comparisons; it is not a method for checking qualitative interpretations.
whyNot.D: Switching to a questionnaire would lose the depth the study aimed for and does not check the existing themes.

items.objective: Use member checking to strengthen the credibility of qualitative findings.

items.stemHtml: A physician reads a qualitative study based on interviews with 18 patients at one urban clinic about why they declined influenza vaccination. The main themes were distrust of pharmaceutical companies, fear of side effects, and believing they were not at risk. Distrust was mentioned by 12 of the 18 participants. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by this study?

options.label: A
options.html: Two-thirds of patients who decline influenza vaccine distrust pharmaceutical companies

options.label: B
options.html: Distrust causes patients to decline vaccination

options.label: C
options.html: The findings apply equally to all clinics in the country

options.label: D
options.html: The study is invalid because it did not include a control group

options.label: E
options.html: These are reasons some patients decline the vaccine, but the study cannot show how common each reason is

items.explanationHtml:
Qualitative studies tell us what concerns exist, how people think about them and why they act as they do. They do not estimate how many people hold each view, because participants are chosen purposively and in small numbers; counts such as 12 of 18 describe the sample, not a population. Whether the themes apply elsewhere is a matter of transferability, judged from the description of the setting and participants.

A physician can use the themes to anticipate patients' concerns and plan conversations, and a survey could then measure their prevalence.

Takeaway: qualitative results show the range of reasons, not their frequency.

whyNot.A: With a small purposive sample, 12 of 18 is not an estimate of prevalence in any population.
whyNot.B: Qualitative studies describe meanings and reasons; they do not test causal effects.
whyNot.C: Transferability depends on how similar other settings are; it cannot be assumed.
whyNot.D: Qualitative studies are not designed to compare groups; their rigour is judged by other criteria.

items.objective: Draw appropriate conclusions from a qualitative study.

items.stemHtml:
A prospective cohort study follows 2,000 adults without gout for 6 years. At baseline, 800 report drinking at least one sugar-sweetened beverage every day and 1,200 report drinking them rarely or never. The results are shown.

Incident goutNo goutTotal
Daily sugar-sweetened beverages48752800
Rarely or never361,1641,200

Which of the following is the relative risk of gout associated with daily sugar-sweetened beverage intake?
items.explanationHtml:
Risk in the exposed = 48 ÷ 800 = 0.06. Risk in the unexposed = 36 ÷ 1,200 = 0.03. Relative risk = 0.06 ÷ 0.03 = 2.0: daily drinkers had twice the 6-year risk of gout.

A cohort starts from exposure and counts new cases, so incidence can be calculated in each group and compared as a ratio. Always divide each row's cases by that row's total, not by the column or the grand total.

The odds ratio (2.06) is close to the relative risk here because gout was uncommon (3–6%); the two measures diverge as an outcome becomes common.

Takeaway: RR = [a ÷ (a + b)] ÷ [c ÷ (c + d)], calculated row by row from a cohort table.

whyNot.A: 0.03 is the risk difference (0.06 − 0.03), an absolute measure, not a ratio.
whyNot.B: 0.50 is the ratio inverted (unexposed risk ÷ exposed risk).
whyNot.C: 1.33 divides the raw case counts (48 ÷ 36) and ignores the different group sizes.
whyNot.E: 2.06 is the odds ratio (48 × 1,164) ÷ (752 × 36); a cohort study reports risks directly, so the relative risk is the measure asked for.

items.objective: Calculate a relative risk from a cohort 2×2 table.

items.stemHtml: A cohort study of 9,000 adults examines daily coffee intake and the 10-year risk of a first kidney stone. Compared with no coffee, drinking 2 or more cups daily has a relative risk of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.64–1.05). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this result?

options.label: A
options.html: Coffee intake lowered the risk of kidney stones by 18%

options.label: B
options.html: Coffee intake raised the risk of kidney stones by 5%

options.label: C
options.html: The study shows that coffee has no effect on kidney stone risk

options.label: D
options.html: The P value for the association is less than 0.05

options.label: E
options.html: The association is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level

items.explanationHtml:
A relative risk below 1 suggests lower risk in the exposed group, but the 95% confidence interval (0.64–1.05) contains 1.0, the value of no association. The result is therefore not statistically significant at α = 0.05.

The interval is compatible with anything from a 36% lower risk (0.64) to a 5% higher risk (1.05). A non-significant result is not proof of no effect; the study may simply lack precision.

On the exam, check the interval before reading the point estimate: for ratio measures (RR, OR, HR) the null value is 1; for differences it is 0.

Takeaway: a ratio whose 95% CI crosses 1 is not statistically significant, and absence of significance is not evidence of absence.

whyNot.A: A causal 18% reduction is not established: the interval includes 1.0 and the design is observational.
whyNot.B: 1.05 is only the upper bound of the interval, not the estimate of effect.
whyNot.C: Failing to reject the null is not proof of no effect; the interval still allows up to a 36% reduction.
whyNot.D: A 95% confidence interval that contains 1.0 corresponds to a two-sided P value above 0.05.

items.objective: Interpret a relative risk whose 95% confidence interval includes 1.

items.stemHtml:
Investigators enrol 90 adults with acute Achilles tendon rupture and 180 adults of similar age seen in the same clinics for ankle sprain. Each participant is asked about medicines taken in the previous 30 days.

Tendon ruptureAnkle sprain
Fluoroquinolone in prior 30 days189
No fluoroquinolone72171
Total90180

Which of the following is the odds ratio for tendon rupture associated with recent fluoroquinolone use?
items.explanationHtml:
In a case-control study the odds ratio is the cross-product: OR = (a × d) ÷ (b × c) = (18 × 171) ÷ (9 × 72) = 3,078 ÷ 648 = 4.75.

Equivalently, odds of exposure among cases = 18 ÷ 72 = 0.25; among controls = 9 ÷ 171 ≈ 0.053; 0.25 ÷ 0.053 ≈ 4.75. The odds of exposure ratio equals the odds of disease ratio, which is why the OR can be read as an association with the outcome.

Because the investigator chose how many cases and controls to enrol, the proportion with the outcome is set by design; risks and relative risks cannot be calculated directly.

Takeaway: case-control design → odds ratio = ad ÷ bc, with the outcome in the columns.

whyNot.A: 0.21 is the reciprocal of the correct odds ratio (controls' odds over cases').
whyNot.B: 0.84 multiplies the wrong diagonal: (18 × 72) ÷ (9 × 171).
whyNot.C: 2.00 divides the exposed counts (18 ÷ 9) without accounting for unexposed participants.
whyNot.D: 4.00 is the ratio of exposure proportions (20% ÷ 5%), which treats the case-control columns as if they were risks.

items.objective: Calculate an odds ratio from a case-control 2×2 table.

items.stemHtml: A cohort study of 1,500 adults admitted with community-acquired pneumonia examines prior inhaled corticosteroid use and 30-day readmission. Readmission occurs in 30% of patients without inhaled corticosteroid use. Logistic regression gives an odds ratio for readmission of 2.5 with inhaled corticosteroid use. Which of the following best describes the relative risk of readmission in this study?

options.label: A
options.html: Less than 1.0

options.label: B
options.html: Equal to 1.0

options.label: C
options.html: Greater than 1.0 but less than 2.5

options.label: D
options.html: Approximately equal to 2.5

options.label: E
options.html: Greater than 2.5

items.explanationHtml:
The odds ratio approximates the relative risk only when the outcome is rare (roughly under 10%). With a 30% baseline risk, the OR exaggerates the association: it lies farther from 1 than the RR.

Working: baseline odds = 0.30 ÷ 0.70 ≈ 0.43. Exposed odds = 0.43 × 2.5 ≈ 1.07, so exposed risk = 1.07 ÷ 2.07 ≈ 0.52. RR ≈ 0.52 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 1.7, between 1 and 2.5.

On the exam, an OR quoted for a common outcome (readmission, symptom resolution, any adverse event) should not be described as "times as likely".

Takeaway: for a common outcome, the RR lies between 1 and the OR.

whyNot.A: An odds ratio above 1 always corresponds to a relative risk above 1 in the same data.
whyNot.B: A relative risk of 1 would require an odds ratio of 1.
whyNot.D: The OR approximates the RR only when the outcome is rare; a 30% baseline risk is not rare.
whyNot.E: When the outcome is common, the OR lies farther from 1 than the RR, so the RR is smaller, not larger.

items.objective: Explain why the odds ratio overstates the relative risk when the outcome is common.

items.stemHtml: In a randomized trial of adults with advanced heart failure, a new drug is compared with placebo over a median follow-up of 2 years. A Cox proportional hazards model gives a hazard ratio for death of 0.70 (95% CI, 0.58–0.85) for the drug. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: At any time during follow-up, the death rate with the drug was about 30% lower

options.label: B
options.html: 30% of patients taking the drug died during the study

options.label: C
options.html: Patients taking the drug lived 30% longer on average

options.label: D
options.html: The drug reduced the absolute risk of death by 30 percentage points

options.label: E
options.html: The drug prevented death in 70% of the patients who took it

items.explanationHtml:
A hazard ratio is the ratio of the instantaneous event rates (hazards) in two groups. Under the proportional hazards assumption this ratio is constant over follow-up, so HR 0.70 means that at any time point, patients on the drug died at about 70% of the rate of those on placebo, a 30% lower hazard.

The 95% CI (0.58–0.85) excludes 1, so the reduction is statistically significant. Hazard ratios come from time-to-event (survival) analysis, which uses each patient's follow-up time and handles censoring.

Takeaway: HR = ratio of event rates over time; 1 − HR is the relative reduction in the hazard, not an absolute or survival-time difference.

whyNot.B: A hazard ratio compares event rates between groups; it says nothing about the proportion who died.
whyNot.C: A hazard ratio is a ratio of instantaneous event rates, not of survival times.
whyNot.D: A ratio cannot be read as an absolute difference; that needs the event proportions in each group.
whyNot.E: 0.70 is the ratio of hazards, not a proportion of patients helped.

items.objective: Interpret a hazard ratio from a time-to-event analysis.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year cohort study of factory workers finds that the incidence of new-onset asthma is 40 per 1,000 among workers exposed to an isocyanate spray and 10 per 1,000 among unexposed workers. Assuming the association is causal, which of the following is the attributable risk percent among exposed workers?
items.explanationHtml:
Attributable risk (risk difference) = 40 − 10 = 30 per 1,000. Attributable risk percent = (risk exposed − risk unexposed) ÷ risk exposed = 30 ÷ 40 = 75%.

Equivalently, ARP = (RR − 1) ÷ RR = (4 − 1) ÷ 4 = 0.75. It estimates the proportion of cases among exposed workers that would not have occurred without the exposure, which assumes a causal link.

Takeaway: ARP = (RR − 1) ÷ RR; the denominator is the risk in the exposed.

whyNot.A: 3% is the attributable (excess) risk itself, 30 per 1,000, not the fraction of exposed cases due to exposure.
whyNot.B: 25% is the unexposed risk divided by the exposed risk, the share of exposed cases that would have occurred anyway.
whyNot.C: 30 is the excess risk per 1,000 read as a percentage, a unit error.
whyNot.E: 300% is (RR − 1) × 100, the percent increase in risk, not the attributable fraction.

items.objective: Calculate attributable risk percent among the exposed.

items.stemHtml: In a city, 20% of adults have an exposure that triples the risk of a particular disease (relative risk = 3.0). Assuming the association is causal and there is no confounding, approximately what proportion of all cases of the disease in the city would be prevented if the exposure were eliminated?
items.explanationHtml:
The population attributable fraction (PAF) depends on both the strength of the association and how common the exposure is: PAF = p(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + p(RR − 1)].

Here p = 0.20 and RR = 3: 0.20 × 2 = 0.40; 0.40 ÷ 1.40 ≈ 0.286, about 29%.

The attributable risk percent among the exposed is larger (67%) because it ignores the unexposed majority, whose cases the exposure did not cause. Public health planners use PAF to decide which exposures account for the most disease in a population.

Takeaway: PAF = p(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + p(RR − 1)]; a common moderate risk factor can matter more to a population than a rare strong one.

whyNot.A: 20% is the prevalence of the exposure, not the share of cases it causes.
whyNot.C: 40% is p × (RR − 1) without dividing by 1 + p × (RR − 1).
whyNot.D: 67% is the attributable risk percent among exposed people only, (RR − 1) ÷ RR, not the population fraction.
whyNot.E: 200% is RR − 1 expressed as a percentage, the relative excess risk.

items.objective: Calculate a population attributable fraction from exposure prevalence and relative risk.

items.stemHtml: A cohort study of nursing home residents counts new pressure injuries. Residents enter and leave the cohort at different times. Among residents using a standard mattress, 30 injuries occur during 6,000 resident-years; among those using a pressure-redistributing mattress, 20 injuries occur during 10,000 resident-years. Which of the following is the incidence rate ratio for the standard mattress compared with the pressure-redistributing mattress?
items.explanationHtml:
When follow-up varies, divide events by person-time. Standard: 30 ÷ 6,000 = 5.0 per 1,000 resident-years. Pressure-redistributing: 20 ÷ 10,000 = 2.0 per 1,000 resident-years.

Rate ratio = 5.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.5. Rate difference = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 per 1,000 resident-years, the excess rate attributable to the standard mattress if causal.

Takeaway: with unequal follow-up, compare incidence rates (events per person-time), not counts or simple proportions.

whyNot.A: 0.4 is the rate ratio inverted (pressure-redistributing ÷ standard).
whyNot.B: 1.5 compares the counts (30 ÷ 20) and ignores the different person-time in each group.
whyNot.D: 3.0 per 1,000 resident-years is the rate difference (5.0 − 2.0), not the ratio.
whyNot.E: 5.0 per 1,000 resident-years is the rate in the standard-mattress group alone.

items.objective: Calculate an incidence rate ratio using person-time.

items.stemHtml: A survey of 2,400 high school students in one week measures daily recreational screen time and checks visual acuity on the same day. Myopia is present in 30% of students with more than 4 hours of daily screen time and in 15% of the other students. Which of the following measures of association, with its value, is most appropriate for these data?

options.label: A
options.html: Hazard ratio of 2.0

options.label: B
options.html: Incidence rate difference of 15 per 100 person-years

options.label: C
options.html: Odds ratio of 2.0

options.label: D
options.html: Relative risk of incident myopia of 2.0

options.label: E
options.html: Prevalence ratio of 2.0

items.explanationHtml:
This is a cross-sectional study: exposure and outcome are measured at one time, so the outcome is prevalent disease. The natural ratio is the prevalence ratio = 30% ÷ 15% = 2.0.

A prevalence odds ratio could also be reported (≈ 2.4), but it is not 2.0, and with a common outcome it overstates the prevalence ratio. Incidence-based measures (RR, rate ratio, HR) need longitudinal follow-up.

Takeaway: cross-sectional design → prevalence ratio (or prevalence odds ratio); it cannot show which came first.

whyNot.A: No time-to-event data were collected, so a hazard ratio cannot be estimated.
whyNot.B: A single-time survey measures existing (prevalent) cases, not new cases over person-time.
whyNot.D: Incident (new-onset) risk requires following people free of myopia over time.

items.objective: Match the prevalence ratio to a cross-sectional design.

items.stemHtml: Investigators follow all adults who start dialysis in a region over 8 years. Patients enter at different dates and leave at transplantation, death or the end of the study, so follow-up ranges from 2 weeks to 8 years. The investigators compare the number of bloodstream infections per patient-year between patients dialysed through a catheter and those dialysed through a fistula. Which of the following measures of association is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Correlation coefficient

options.label: B
options.html: Cumulative incidence ratio

options.label: C
options.html: Odds ratio

options.label: D
options.html: Prevalence ratio

options.label: E
options.html: Incidence rate ratio

items.explanationHtml:
With an open (dynamic) cohort and unequal follow-up, the right denominator is person-time. Each group's incidence rate is events ÷ patient-years, and the ratio of the two rates is the incidence rate ratio (incidence density ratio).

Choosing the measure from the design is a frequent exam task: cohort with fixed follow-up or RCT → RR (cumulative incidence ratio); variable follow-up → rate ratio, or a hazard ratio from survival analysis; case-control → OR; cross-sectional → prevalence ratio or prevalence OR.

Takeaway: events counted over unequal follow-up call for rates per person-time and an incidence rate ratio.

whyNot.A: A correlation coefficient describes a linear relation between two continuous variables, not a comparison of event rates in two groups.
whyNot.B: A cumulative incidence ratio needs everyone followed for the same fixed period; here follow-up varies widely.
whyNot.C: An odds ratio fits case-control or cross-sectional data and wastes the person-time information collected here.
whyNot.D: Prevalence ratios compare existing cases at one time point; this study counts new events over follow-up.

items.objective: Choose the incidence rate ratio for a dynamic cohort with variable follow-up.

items.stemHtml: In a study of adults evaluated for a suspected condition, a physical examination finding is present in 60% of those who have the condition and in 12% of those who do not, as confirmed by a reference standard. Which of the following is the positive likelihood ratio for this finding?
items.explanationHtml:
A likelihood ratio compares how often a result occurs in people with versus without the condition. LR+ = P(finding | condition) ÷ P(finding | no condition) = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity) = 0.60 ÷ 0.12 = 5.0.

The LR is a measure of association between a test result and disease status. Unlike predictive values, it does not depend on prevalence, so it can be applied to any patient's pre-test odds.

Takeaway: LR+ = sens ÷ (1 − spec); here, the finding is five times as frequent in people with the condition.

whyNot.A: 0.20 divides the wrong way (12% ÷ 60%).
whyNot.B: 0.45 is the negative likelihood ratio, (1 − 0.60) ÷ (1 − 0.12).
whyNot.C: 0.48 is the difference in proportions (0.60 − 0.12), not a ratio.
whyNot.E: 11.0 is the diagnostic odds ratio, (0.60 ÷ 0.40) ÷ (0.12 ÷ 0.88).

items.objective: Calculate a positive likelihood ratio from the frequency of a finding in diseased and non-diseased people.

items.stemHtml:
The figure shows the length of hospital stay for 124 patients admitted to a medical ward. Three summary values of the distribution are marked by vertical lines P, Q and R.

Which of the following correctly identifies the three lines?

options.label: A
options.html: P = mean, Q = median, R = mode

options.label: B
options.html: P = median, Q = mode, R = mean

options.label: C
options.html: P = mode, Q = mean, R = median

options.label: D
options.html: P = mode, Q = median, R = mean

options.label: E
options.html: P = mean, Q = mode, R = median

items.explanationHtml:
Length of stay is positively (right) skewed: most patients stay a few days, and a few stay much longer. The mode is the peak (tallest bar, P); the median is the middle value (Q); the mean is pulled toward the long tail (R). Order: mode < median < mean.

In these data the mode is 3 days, the median 4 days and the mean about 5.1 days. In a negatively skewed distribution the order reverses: mean < median < mode.

Takeaway: the mean follows the tail; in right skew, mode < median < mean.

whyNot.A: The mean is pulled toward the long right tail, so it cannot be the leftmost line.
whyNot.B: The mode sits at the tallest bar, which is P, not Q.
whyNot.C: In a right-skewed distribution the mean lies beyond the median, not before it.
whyNot.E: The mean is the summary most affected by the long stays and lies farthest to the right.

items.objective: Identify the mode, median and mean on a right-skewed histogram.

items.stemHtml: A random sample of 64 adults from a community has a mean systolic blood pressure of 120 mm Hg with a standard deviation of 16 mm Hg. Which of the following is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean systolic blood pressure of the community?

options.label: E
options.html: 88.6 to 151.4 mm Hg

items.explanationHtml:
The standard error of the mean (SEM) = SD ÷ √n = 16 ÷ √64 = 16 ÷ 8 = 2 mm Hg. The 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SEM = 120 ± 3.9 = 116.1 to 123.9 mm Hg.

The SD describes variability among individuals and does not shrink as the sample grows; the SEM describes uncertainty in the estimated mean and falls with √n. Quadrupling the sample size halves the SEM.

Takeaway: 95% CI for a mean ≈ mean ± 1.96 × SD ÷ √n.

whyNot.A: This uses 16 ÷ 64 as the standard error, dividing by n instead of √n.
whyNot.B: This is ±1 standard error, which gives only about a 68% interval.
whyNot.D: This is ±1 SD, which describes the spread of individual values, not the precision of the mean.
whyNot.E: This is ±1.96 SD, the range containing about 95% of individual values, not a confidence interval for the mean.

items.objective: Calculate a 95% confidence interval for a mean using the standard error.

items.stemHtml: In a study of knee osteoarthritis, participants rate their morning stiffness as none, mild, moderate or severe. Which of the following best describes the scale of measurement for this variable?

options.label: A
options.html: Dichotomous

options.label: B
options.html: Nominal

options.label: C
options.html: Ordinal

options.label: D
options.html: Interval

options.label: E
options.html: Ratio

items.explanationHtml:
The categories have a natural order but unknown, unequal distances between them, which defines an ordinal scale. Ordinal outcomes are summarised with medians and compared with rank-based (nonparametric) tests or ordinal regression rather than t-tests on the labels.

Hierarchy of scales: nominal (named categories, e.g. blood group) → ordinal (ranked) → interval (equal steps, arbitrary zero, e.g. temperature in °C) → ratio (equal steps and a true zero, e.g. creatinine).

Takeaway: ranked categories with uneven spacing are ordinal.

whyNot.A: A dichotomous variable has only two categories; this one has four.
whyNot.B: Nominal categories have no inherent order, but none, mild, moderate and severe are ranked.
whyNot.D: Interval data have equal spacing between values; the step from mild to moderate is not necessarily equal to the step from moderate to severe.
whyNot.E: Ratio data have equal intervals and a true zero, like weight; ranked severity labels have neither.

items.objective: Classify a ranked categorical variable as ordinal.

items.stemHtml: Study 1 reports a Pearson correlation of −0.80 between daily step count and fasting insulin. Study 2 reports a Pearson correlation of +0.40 between waist circumference and fasting insulin. Which of the following is the most accurate comparison?

options.label: A
options.html: Study 1 shows a stronger linear association than study 2

options.label: B
options.html: Study 2 shows a stronger association because its coefficient is positive

options.label: C
options.html: Both studies show associations of equal strength

options.label: D
options.html: Study 1 shows that steps cause lower insulin levels

options.label: E
options.html: Study 1 shows a steeper regression slope than study 2

items.explanationHtml:
The Pearson coefficient r ranges from −1 to +1. Its absolute value gives the strength of the linear association and its sign gives the direction. |−0.80| > |+0.40|, so study 1 shows the stronger linear association (an inverse one).

r is unitless and is not the slope: two variables can be perfectly correlated with a shallow or a steep slope. Neither study can show causation.

Takeaway: strength = |r|; direction = sign; r ≠ slope ≠ causation.

whyNot.B: The sign gives only direction; strength depends on the absolute value.
whyNot.C: The absolute values differ (0.80 vs 0.40).
whyNot.D: A correlation coefficient cannot establish causation.
whyNot.E: r does not give the slope; slope depends on the units and spread of each variable.

items.objective: Compare the strength of two correlations using the absolute value of r.

items.stemHtml: In a sample of 300 adults, the Pearson correlation coefficient between body mass index and systolic blood pressure is 0.60. Approximately what proportion of the variation in systolic blood pressure is explained by its linear relationship with body mass index?
items.explanationHtml:
The coefficient of determination r² = 0.60² = 0.36: 36% of the variance in systolic pressure is accounted for by its linear relationship with BMI, and 64% is due to other factors.

In simple linear regression, r² equals the model R². Even a moderately strong correlation leaves most of the variation unexplained.

Takeaway: variance explained = r².

whyNot.A: 6% treats r = 0.60 as if it were a percentage divided by 10.
whyNot.C: 40% is 1 − r, which has no interpretation.
whyNot.D: 60% is r itself; the variance explained is r squared.
whyNot.E: 64% is 1 − r², the proportion of variation not explained.

items.objective: Calculate the proportion of variance explained from r.

items.stemHtml: The figure shows average nightly sleep duration and a cardiometabolic risk score for 60 adults in a survey. Which of the following is closest to the Pearson correlation coefficient for these two variables?
items.explanationHtml:
The points form a clear U shape: risk is lowest around 7 hours and higher with both short and long sleep. Pearson r measures only linear association; the downward half and the upward half cancel, giving r close to 0 (about −0.01 for these data).

An r near 0 means no linear relation, not no relation. Always look at the scatter plot; a curved pattern needs a different model (e.g. a quadratic term), and a monotonic but non-linear pattern suits Spearman correlation.

Takeaway: a strong curved relation can have r ≈ 0.

whyNot.A: A coefficient near −0.9 needs points falling steadily along a downward line.
whyNot.B: A moderate negative r needs a general downward trend; here scores fall and then rise again.
whyNot.D: A moderate positive r needs a general upward trend across the whole range.
whyNot.E: A strong positive r needs points close to a rising straight line.

items.objective: Recognise that Pearson r misses a strong non-linear relationship.

items.stemHtml: Researchers want to know whether ABO blood group (O, A, B or AB) is associated with having had a venous thromboembolism (yes or no) among 1,200 adults. Which of the following statistical tests is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Analysis of variance

options.label: B
options.html: Chi-square test

options.label: C
options.html: Paired t-test

options.label: D
options.html: Pearson correlation

options.label: E
options.html: Two-sample t-test

items.explanationHtml:
Both variables are categorical (blood group: 4 nominal categories; thromboembolism: yes/no). The chi-square test compares observed counts in the 4 × 2 table with those expected if the variables were independent. With small expected counts (< 5 in a cell), Fisher's exact test is used instead.

Quick rule: categorical vs categorical → chi-square; continuous outcome, 2 groups → t-test; 3 or more groups → ANOVA; two continuous variables → correlation or regression.

Takeaway: two categorical variables → chi-square.

whyNot.A: ANOVA compares means of a continuous variable across groups; neither variable here is continuous.
whyNot.C: A paired t-test compares two related means, such as before and after measurements in the same people.
whyNot.D: Pearson correlation needs two continuous variables.
whyNot.E: A two-sample t-test compares the means of a continuous outcome between two groups.

items.objective: Choose the chi-square test for two categorical variables.

items.stemHtml: A study of 45 adults with chronic low back pain records each participant's pain on a 0–10 rating scale and their functional limitation grade (1 = none to 5 = complete). Several participants have extreme values and neither variable is normally distributed. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to measure the association between the two variables?

options.label: A
options.html: Chi-square test

options.label: B
options.html: Kappa statistic

options.label: C
options.html: Paired t-test

options.label: D
options.html: Pearson correlation

options.label: E
options.html: Spearman rank correlation

items.explanationHtml:
Spearman's rank correlation (ρ) converts each variable to ranks and then correlates the ranks. It measures a monotonic association, suits ordinal data and is robust to outliers and skewed distributions.

Pearson r is appropriate for two continuous, roughly normally distributed variables with a linear relation. Like r, ρ runs from −1 to +1.

Takeaway: ordinal or skewed data with outliers → Spearman rank correlation.

whyNot.A: Collapsing ranked data into categories for chi-square ignores their order and loses information.
whyNot.B: Kappa measures agreement between raters classifying the same thing, not association between two different variables.
whyNot.C: A paired t-test compares two measurements of the same quantity, not the association between two different variables.
whyNot.D: Pearson r assumes interval data and is distorted by outliers and non-normal distributions.

items.objective: Choose Spearman rank correlation for ordinal or non-normal data.

items.stemHtml: In a sample of adults, linear regression of systolic blood pressure (mm Hg) on daily sodium intake (g) gives the equation: systolic pressure = 112 + 2.4 × sodium intake. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of the value 2.4?

options.label: A
options.html: Each additional gram of daily sodium is associated with a 2.4 mm Hg higher systolic pressure

options.label: B
options.html: 72% of the variation in blood pressure is explained by sodium intake

options.label: C
options.html: Blood pressure is 2.4 times higher in people with high sodium intake

options.label: D
options.html: The correlation between sodium intake and blood pressure is 2.4

options.label: E
options.html: Systolic pressure is 2.4 mm Hg in a person with no sodium intake

items.explanationHtml:
In y = a + b x, b (the slope) is the average change in y for a one-unit increase in x: here 2.4 mm Hg per additional gram of sodium per day. The intercept (112 mm Hg) is the predicted value when x = 0, which may lie outside the observed data.

The slope has the units of y per unit of x and depends on scale; the correlation coefficient is unitless. A significant slope shows association, not causation.

Takeaway: slope = change in outcome per one-unit change in predictor; intercept = value at x = 0.

whyNot.B: Variance explained is R², which is not given by the slope.
whyNot.C: The slope is an additive change per unit, not a multiplicative ratio.
whyNot.D: A correlation coefficient cannot exceed 1; 2.4 is a slope in mm Hg per gram.
whyNot.E: The predicted value at zero intake is the intercept, 112 mm Hg.

items.objective: Interpret the slope and intercept of a linear regression equation.

items.stemHtml: A public health department is deciding whether to start a population screening programme for a disease. Which of the following features of the disease most strongly supports screening?

options.label: A
options.html: It is rare and usually detected at autopsy

options.label: B
options.html: It has a detectable preclinical phase and earlier treatment improves outcome

options.label: C
options.html: It progresses rapidly from onset to symptoms over a few days

options.label: D
options.html: It is detected only by an invasive test with frequent complications

options.label: E
options.html: It has no effective treatment at any stage

items.explanationHtml:
Screening helps only if the disease is an important burden, has a detectable preclinical phase long enough to find it, and earlier treatment improves outcomes compared with treatment at symptom onset. The test must be acceptable, safe, affordable and accurate, and the system must be able to follow up positive results.

Without effective early treatment, screening only moves the date of diagnosis earlier (lead time) without extending life.

Takeaway: screen when a common, serious disease can be found before symptoms and early treatment changes the outcome.

whyNot.A: A rare condition yields few true positives and many false positives, and finding it at autopsy offers no benefit.
whyNot.C: A very short preclinical phase leaves little window for a screening test to find it early.
whyNot.D: A screening test must be safe and acceptable to healthy people.
whyNot.E: Early detection without effective treatment adds anxiety and cost without improving outcomes.

items.objective: Identify the disease features that justify a screening programme.

items.stemHtml: A clinic tests a new automated scale by weighing a 10.0-kg reference weight five times. The readings are 12.1, 12.0, 12.1, 12.0 and 12.1 kg. Which of the following best describes this scale?

options.label: A
options.html: High reliability and high validity

options.label: B
options.html: Low reliability and high validity

options.label: C
options.html: Low reliability and low validity

options.label: D
options.html: Random error without systematic error

options.label: E
options.html: High reliability and low validity

items.explanationHtml:
Reliability (precision, reproducibility) is how closely repeated measurements agree; validity (accuracy) is how close measurements are to the true value. These readings cluster tightly (reliable) but are about 2 kg too high (systematic error, not valid).

Random error reduces reliability; systematic error (bias) reduces validity. A measurement can be reliable without being valid, but an unreliable one cannot be consistently valid.

Takeaway: tight but off-target = reliable, not valid.

whyNot.A: The readings are consistent but all about 2 kg away from the true value, so validity is poor.
whyNot.B: The readings vary by only 0.1 kg, so reliability is high, not low.
whyNot.C: Repeat readings agree closely, so reliability is high.
whyNot.D: The consistent 2-kg offset is systematic error; random error here is small.

items.objective: Distinguish reliability (precision) from validity (accuracy).

items.stemHtml: Two radiologists independently classify 200 chest radiographs as showing or not showing pneumonia. They agree on 90% of the films. Given how often each radiologist calls a film positive, the agreement expected by chance alone is 80%. Which of the following is the kappa statistic for their agreement?
items.explanationHtml:
Kappa measures agreement beyond chance: κ = (observed − expected) ÷ (1 − expected) = (0.90 − 0.80) ÷ (1 − 0.80) = 0.10 ÷ 0.20 = 0.50.

κ = 1 is perfect agreement; κ = 0 is no better than chance; negative values mean less than chance. High raw agreement can hide modest kappa when one category is common, because much agreement then happens by chance. Kappa describes inter-rater reliability, not accuracy against a reference standard.

Takeaway: κ = (po − pe) ÷ (1 − pe).

whyNot.A: 0.10 is observed minus expected agreement without dividing by the maximum agreement possible beyond chance (1 − 0.80).
whyNot.C: 0.80 is the agreement expected by chance, not kappa.
whyNot.D: 0.90 is the raw observed agreement, which kappa corrects for chance.
whyNot.E: 1.13 is observed ÷ expected agreement; kappa cannot exceed 1.

items.objective: Calculate and interpret the kappa statistic for inter-rater reliability.

items.stemHtml: Two tests for a disease are available. Test A has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. Test B has a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90%. Their errors are independent of each other given disease status. A clinic adopts a strategy in which a patient is called positive only if both tests are positive. Which of the following are the sensitivity and specificity of this strategy?

options.label: A
options.html: Sensitivity 72%, specificity 98%

options.label: B
options.html: Sensitivity 80%, specificity 80%

options.label: C
options.html: Sensitivity 85%, specificity 85%

options.label: D
options.html: Sensitivity 90%, specificity 90%

options.label: E
options.html: Sensitivity 98%, specificity 72%

items.explanationHtml:
Requiring both tests to be positive is serial (series) testing. A diseased person must be detected by both: sensitivity = 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.72. A healthy person is called positive only if both are falsely positive: 0.20 × 0.10 = 0.02, so specificity = 1 − 0.02 = 0.98.

Parallel testing (positive if either test is positive) does the reverse: sensitivity = 1 − (0.10 × 0.20) = 0.98, specificity = 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72. Serial testing is used to confirm (rule in), parallel testing to avoid missing disease (rule out).

Takeaway: serial testing raises specificity and lowers sensitivity; parallel testing does the opposite.

whyNot.B: These are the lower values of each test, which is not how combined testing works.
whyNot.C: Averaging the two tests does not describe any combined strategy.
whyNot.D: Requiring two positives cannot keep the better sensitivity of either test; sensitivity must fall.
whyNot.E: These values apply to parallel testing, in which either positive test counts as positive.

items.objective: Calculate combined sensitivity and specificity for serial testing.

items.stemHtml: After a region introduces an imaging-based screening programme for a slowly growing cancer, the recorded incidence of early-stage cancer doubles within 5 years. Over the following 15 years, the incidence of advanced-stage cancer and the death rate from this cancer stay unchanged. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Confounding by age

options.label: B
options.html: Lead-time bias

options.label: C
options.html: Recall bias

options.label: D
options.html: Selection bias

options.label: E
options.html: Overdiagnosis

items.explanationHtml:
When screening finds many more early cancers but advanced-stage incidence and mortality do not fall, many of the extra cancers would never have caused symptoms or death: overdiagnosis. Those patients receive treatment that cannot help them.

Lead-time bias (earlier diagnosis lengthens apparent survival without delaying death) and length-time bias (screening preferentially finds slow-growing tumours) distort survival comparisons. Population mortality is the outcome they cannot fake. Bias is covered in more depth with study interpretation.

Takeaway: rising early-stage incidence with flat late-stage incidence and mortality signals overdiagnosis.

whyNot.A: Age-standardised rates would not explain a rise in early cases with no change in deaths.
whyNot.B: Lead-time bias inflates survival measured from diagnosis; it does not create extra early-stage cases.
whyNot.C: Recall bias concerns inaccurate reporting of past exposures by study participants.
whyNot.D: Selection bias affects who enters a study; this is population-wide incidence and mortality data.

items.objective: Recognise overdiagnosis from incidence and mortality trends after screening.

items.stemHtml:
A new urine dipstick for urinary tract infection is compared with urine culture, the reference standard, in 400 women with urinary symptoms.

Culture positiveCulture negative
Dipstick positive8430
Dipstick negative16270

Which of the following is closest to the negative predictive value of the dipstick in this population?
items.explanationHtml:
NPV is the probability of no disease given a negative test, read along the negative-test row: true negatives ÷ all negatives = 270 ÷ (270 + 16) = 270 ÷ 286 ≈ 94%.

Sensitivity and specificity are read down the columns (by true disease status); predictive values are read across the rows (by test result). Predictive values depend on the prevalence, here 100 of 400 = 25%.

Takeaway: NPV = d ÷ (c + d), across the negative-test row.

whyNot.A: 74% is the positive predictive value, 84 ÷ 114.
whyNot.B: 84% is the sensitivity, 84 ÷ 100.
whyNot.C: 89% is the overall accuracy, (84 + 270) ÷ 400.
whyNot.D: 90% is the specificity, 270 ÷ 300.

items.objective: Calculate negative predictive value from a 2×2 table.

items.stemHtml: A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is drawn for a serum marker at many cut-off values. Sensitivity is plotted on the vertical axis. Which of the following is plotted on the horizontal axis?

options.label: A
options.html: Specificity

options.label: B
options.html: 1 − specificity

options.label: C
options.html: 1 − sensitivity

options.label: D
options.html: Positive predictive value

options.label: E
options.html: Prevalence

items.explanationHtml:
