An ROC curve plots the true-positive rate (sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (1 − specificity) for every possible cut-off. Each point is one cut-off; a stricter cut-off moves toward the lower left and a looser one toward the upper right.

The upper-left corner (0, 1) is a perfect test; the diagonal from (0, 0) to (1, 1) is a test no better than chance.

Takeaway: ROC: y = sensitivity, x = 1 − specificity.

whyNot.A: Plotting specificity itself would reverse the curve; the standard axis is the false-positive rate.
whyNot.C: 1 − sensitivity is the false-negative rate, which is already implied by the vertical axis.
whyNot.D: Predictive values depend on prevalence and are not used to build the ROC curve.
whyNot.E: Prevalence is not a property of the test cut-off and does not appear on the ROC plot.

items.objective: Identify the axes of an ROC curve.

items.stemHtml: A study reports that a new blood test for sepsis has an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.80 against a reference standard. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this value?

options.label: A
options.html: A random patient with sepsis has a more abnormal value than a random patient without sepsis 80% of the time

options.label: B
options.html: 80% of patients with a positive result at the chosen cut-off have sepsis

options.label: C
options.html: At the best cut-off, the test has a sensitivity and a specificity of 80% each

options.label: D
options.html: The test correctly classifies 80% of all patients tested, with or without sepsis

options.label: E
options.html: The test fails to detect 20% of the patients who have sepsis at any cut-off

items.explanationHtml:
The AUC has a probability meaning: if one person with the disease and one without are chosen at random, the AUC is the probability that the diseased person has the more abnormal test value. 0.5 = no discrimination (a coin toss); 1.0 = perfect separation.

The AUC is a summary of discrimination across all cut-offs. It does not tell you sensitivity, specificity or predictive values at the cut-off actually used, which still has to be chosen for the clinical purpose.

Takeaway: AUC = probability that a random case outranks a random non-case.

whyNot.B: That describes a positive predictive value, which depends on prevalence and the cut-off chosen.
whyNot.C: The AUC summarises all cut-offs; it does not give the values at any single one.
whyNot.D: Accuracy at a cut-off is a different quantity and depends on prevalence.
whyNot.E: The false-negative rate depends on the cut-off chosen, not on the AUC.

items.objective: Interpret the area under an ROC curve.

items.stemHtml: The figure shows the ROC curve for a new serum marker for a disease, with five candidate cut-offs numbered 1 to 5. Missing a case and falsely labelling a healthy person are judged equally harmful. Which of the following cut-offs gives the largest sum of sensitivity and specificity?

options.label: A
options.html: Point 1

options.label: B
options.html: Point 2

options.label: C
options.html: Point 3

options.label: D
options.html: Point 4

options.label: E
options.html: Point 5

items.explanationHtml:
Sensitivity + specificity is largest where the curve is farthest above the diagonal, the point with the largest Youden index (J = sensitivity + specificity − 1). Here point 3 (sensitivity ≈ 0.77, 1 − specificity ≈ 0.22) gives J ≈ 0.55, compared with ≈ 0.46 at points 2 and 4.

Geometrically, this is usually the point nearest the upper-left corner. When the two errors are not equally harmful, the cut-off moves: toward the upper right (higher sensitivity) to avoid missing serious, treatable disease, or toward the lower left (higher specificity) to avoid harmful treatment of false positives.

Takeaway: with equal error costs, choose the ROC point farthest from the diagonal (maximum Youden index).

whyNot.A: Point 1 has high specificity but sensitivity below 0.3, so the sum is low.
whyNot.B: Point 2 has higher specificity but much lower sensitivity than point 3; its sum is about 1.46, below point 3's 1.55.
whyNot.D: Point 4 gains a little sensitivity but gives up much more specificity than point 3.
whyNot.E: Point 5 has near-perfect sensitivity but a false-positive rate of about 75%.

items.objective: Choose the ROC cut-off that maximises sensitivity plus specificity.

items.stemHtml: Investigators evaluate a serum protein as a marker of a liver disease, calling values above a threshold positive. The ROC curve lies below the diagonal line across its full length, with an area under the curve of 0.30. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.label: A
options.html: The marker has no ability to separate patients with and without the disease

options.label: B
options.html: The marker discriminates in the opposite direction, with low values indicating disease

options.label: C
options.html: The marker would perform better in a population with a higher prevalence

options.label: D
options.html: The marker misclassifies 70% of the patients tested

options.label: E
options.html: The marker is perfectly specific but has low sensitivity

items.explanationHtml:
A curve below the diagonal means that, at every cut-off, patients without the disease are more likely than those with it to test positive. The marker carries information but in the opposite direction: disease is associated with lower values. Reversing the rule (calling low values positive) mirrors the curve and gives an AUC of 1 − 0.30 = 0.70.

Only an AUC of exactly 0.5 (the diagonal) indicates no discrimination.

Takeaway: AUC < 0.5 means the positivity rule is backwards; flip it to get 1 − AUC.

whyNot.A: An AUC of 0.5 means no discrimination; 0.30 is well away from 0.5.
whyNot.C: ROC curves and AUC do not depend on prevalence.
whyNot.D: AUC is not the proportion misclassified at any cut-off.
whyNot.E: A curve below the diagonal has sensitivity lower than the false-positive rate at every cut-off.

items.objective: Interpret an ROC curve that lies below the diagonal.

items.stemHtml: A serum test is validated in a population in which 5% of patients have the disease, producing an ROC curve with an area of 0.84. The same test is then applied, with the same spectrum of disease severity, in a referral population in which 30% have the disease. Which of the following best describes the expected ROC curve in the referral population?

options.label: A
options.html: The area under the curve rises because more patients have the disease

options.label: B
options.html: The area under the curve falls because there are fewer healthy patients

options.label: C
options.html: The curve moves toward the diagonal

options.label: D
options.html: The curve moves toward the upper-left corner

options.label: E
options.html: The curve is essentially unchanged

items.explanationHtml:
Each point on an ROC curve is a (1 − specificity, sensitivity) pair. Sensitivity is computed only among diseased people and specificity only among non-diseased people, so neither depends on prevalence. With the same spectrum of disease, the curve and its AUC stay essentially the same.

What does change with prevalence is the predictive value: at the same cut-off, PPV rises and NPV falls when prevalence rises. A different spectrum (e.g. sicker cases in referral centres) can change sensitivity and specificity, which is a separate issue.

Takeaway: prevalence changes predictive values, not the ROC curve.

whyNot.A: Sensitivity and specificity, the coordinates of the curve, do not change with prevalence.
whyNot.B: The number of healthy patients changes the predictive values, not the curve.
whyNot.C: Moving toward the diagonal would mean worse discrimination, which prevalence does not cause.
whyNot.D: Better discrimination would need a better test or a different spectrum of patients.

items.objective: Explain why the ROC curve does not depend on prevalence.

items.stemHtml: A fictional serum marker for sepsis is reported as positive at values of 2.0 ng/mL or higher. The laboratory lowers the positive cut-off to 1.0 ng/mL. Which of the following describes how the operating point moves along the marker's ROC curve?

options.label: A
options.html: Down and to the left, with lower sensitivity and higher specificity

options.label: B
options.html: Up and to the right, with higher sensitivity and lower specificity

options.label: C
options.html: Straight up, with higher sensitivity and unchanged specificity

options.label: D
options.html: To a new curve with a larger area

options.label: E
options.html: Toward the diagonal, with lower sensitivity and lower specificity

items.explanationHtml:
With a lower threshold, more people test positive: more diseased people are detected (sensitivity ↑) but more healthy people are also called positive (false-positive rate ↑, specificity ↓). On the ROC plot, the operating point moves up and to the right along the same curve.

Changing the cut-off trades sensitivity against specificity; only a better marker shifts the whole curve toward the upper-left corner.

Takeaway: lower threshold → up and right on the ROC curve.

whyNot.A: Moving down and left is what raising the cut-off does.
whyNot.C: On a fixed curve, more true positives come with more false positives for an imperfect test.
whyNot.D: Changing the cut-off moves along the same curve; the AUC is a property of the marker.
whyNot.E: Lowering the threshold cannot reduce sensitivity, because every previous positive stays positive.

items.objective: Predict how lowering a cut-off moves the operating point on an ROC curve.

items.stemHtml: A patient starts two unrelated medicines. Drug 1 causes a rash in 10% of patients and drug 2 causes a rash in 5% of patients, and the two risks are independent. Assuming no interaction, what is the probability that the patient develops a rash from both drugs?
items.explanationHtml:
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.10 × 0.05 = 0.005 = 0.5%.

Contrast: P(at least one) = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − (0.90 × 0.95) = 0.145. Adding probabilities (0.15) is valid only for mutually exclusive events and otherwise double-counts the overlap.

Takeaway: "both" for independent events → multiply.

whyNot.B: 5% is the risk from drug 2 alone.
whyNot.C: 7.5% averages the two risks, which has no probability meaning.
whyNot.D: 14.5% is the probability of a rash from at least one drug, 1 − (0.90 × 0.95).
whyNot.E: 15% adds the probabilities, which applies to mutually exclusive events, not to both events occurring.

items.objective: Apply the multiplication rule to independent events.

items.stemHtml: A healthy adult undergoes three independent screening tests. Each test has a 5% probability of a false-positive result in a person without disease. What is the probability that this person has one or more false-positive results?
items.explanationHtml:
Use the complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − 0.95³ = 1 − 0.857 = 0.143, about 14%.

The more independent tests a healthy person has, the more likely at least one abnormal result is: with 20 such tests, 1 − 0.9520 ≈ 64%.

Takeaway: "at least one" → 1 − P(none).

whyNot.A: 0.01% (0.05³) is the probability that all three tests are falsely positive.
whyNot.B: 5% is the false-positive probability of one test, ignoring the other two.
whyNot.D: 15% adds the three probabilities, which double-counts people with more than one false positive.
whyNot.E: 86% (0.95³) is the probability of no false positives.

items.objective: Use the complement rule to find the probability of at least one event.

items.stemHtml: In a fictional population, the ABO blood group distribution is O 45%, A 40%, B 11% and AB 4%. Each person has exactly one blood group. What is the probability that a randomly selected person has group A or group B?
items.explanationHtml:
Blood groups are mutually exclusive (no one can be both A and B), so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.40 + 0.11 = 0.51.

For events that can overlap, subtract the overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

Takeaway: "or" for mutually exclusive events → add.

whyNot.A: 4.4% multiplies the two probabilities, which would apply to two independent events both occurring.
whyNot.B: 40% counts only group A and leaves out the 11% with group B.
whyNot.C: 49% is the probability of having neither A nor B (groups O and AB).
whyNot.E: 89% is 1 − P(B), the probability of not having group B.

items.objective: Apply the addition rule to mutually exclusive events.

items.stemHtml:
A clinic records the smoking status of 500 adult patients.

SmokerNonsmokerTotal
Men60140200
Women40260300
Total100400500

If a patient is selected at random from the smokers, what is the probability that the patient is a woman?
items.explanationHtml:
Conditional probability restricts the denominator to the condition: P(woman | smoker) = women smokers ÷ all smokers = 40 ÷ 100 = 40%.

P(smoker | woman) = 40 ÷ 300 ≈ 13% is a different quantity. Confusing P(A | B) with P(B | A) is the same error as confusing sensitivity with positive predictive value.

Takeaway: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B); the condition sets the denominator.

whyNot.A: 8% is the joint probability of being a woman and a smoker, 40 ÷ 500.
whyNot.B: 13% is the probability that a woman smokes, 40 ÷ 300, which conditions on the wrong variable.
whyNot.C: 20% is the overall probability of smoking, 100 ÷ 500.
whyNot.E: 60% is the overall proportion of women, 300 ÷ 500, ignoring the condition.

items.objective: Calculate a conditional probability from a contingency table.

items.stemHtml: A patient's pre-test probability of a disease is 20%. A test with a positive likelihood ratio of 6.0 is positive. What is the post-test probability of the disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Likelihood ratios multiply odds, not probabilities. Pre-test odds = 0.20 ÷ 0.80 = 0.25. Post-test odds = 0.25 × 6 = 1.5. Post-test probability = 1.5 ÷ (1 + 1.5) = 0.60.

This is Bayes' theorem in odds form: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR. A Fagan nomogram does the same conversion graphically.

Takeaway: probability → odds, multiply by LR, odds → probability.

whyNot.A: 20% is the pre-test probability; a positive result with LR+ of 6 must raise it.
whyNot.B: 25% (0.25) is the pre-test odds, which is not yet a probability.
whyNot.C: 50% comes from converting with p ÷ (1 + p) instead of p ÷ (1 − p) to get the pre-test odds.
whyNot.E: 86% is LR ÷ (LR + 1), which ignores the pre-test probability.

items.objective: Use a likelihood ratio to convert pre-test to post-test probability.

items.stemHtml: Each child of a particular couple independently has a 1 in 4 probability of inheriting an autosomal recessive condition. The couple plans to have 4 children. What is the probability that exactly 2 of the 4 children are affected?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a binomial probability: P(exactly k of n) = C(n, k) × pk × (1 − p)n − k.

C(4, 2) = 6 orders. Each order has probability (¼)² × (¾)² = 1/16 × 9/16 = 9/256. Total = 6 × 9/256 = 54/256 ≈ 0.21.

Each child's probability is independent of the others: having one affected child does not change the next child's 1 in 4 chance.

Takeaway: exactly k of n independent trials = (number of orders) × probability of one order.

whyNot.A: 3.5% is the probability of one specific order (for example, affected, affected, unaffected, unaffected) without counting the other orders.
whyNot.B: 6.3% (1/16) counts only the two affected children and ignores the probability that the other two are unaffected.
whyNot.D: 25% is the probability for a single child, not for exactly 2 of 4.
whyNot.E: 50% treats 2 of 4 as the expected proportion, but the expected number affected is 1 (4 × ¼).

items.objective: Calculate a simple binomial probability for independent events.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, what is the negative predictive value of assay L at the cut-off of 20 units in the study population?
items.explanationHtml:
NPV = true negatives ÷ all negative results = 315 ÷ (315 + 12) = 315 ÷ 327 ≈ 96%.

In this population (prevalence 25%), about 1 in 27 children with a negative result at this cut-off still had appendicitis. Predictive values belong to the population studied; they change with prevalence.

Takeaway: NPV is read across the negative-result row: TN ÷ (TN + FN).

whyNot.A: 51% is the positive predictive value, 138 ÷ 273.
whyNot.B: 70% is the specificity, 315 ÷ 450, read down the column rather than across the row.
whyNot.C: 76% is the overall accuracy, (138 + 315) ÷ 600.
whyNot.D: 92% is the sensitivity, 138 ÷ 150.

items.objective: Calculate the negative predictive value from a diagnostic accuracy study.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy is seen at an urgent care clinic with 1 day of mild periumbilical pain. After history and examination, the physician estimates his probability of appendicitis at 10%. Assay L is negative at the 20-unit cut-off. Based on the study summary, which of the following is closest to his probability of appendicitis after this result?
items.explanationHtml:
Use the negative likelihood ratio, which can be carried to a new pre-test probability. LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity = 0.08 ÷ 0.70 ≈ 0.11.

Pre-test odds = 0.10 ÷ 0.90 ≈ 0.111. Post-test odds = 0.111 × 0.114 ≈ 0.0127. Post-test probability = 0.0127 ÷ 1.0127 ≈ 1.3%.

The study's NPV (96%) applies only at 25% prevalence; for a patient with a different pre-test probability, use the likelihood ratio.

Takeaway: carry test results to a new patient with likelihood ratios, not with the study's predictive values.

whyNot.B: 3.7% is 1 − NPV in the study population, where the prevalence was 25%, not 10%.
whyNot.C: 8% is 1 − sensitivity, the proportion of children with appendicitis who test negative.
whyNot.D: 10% is the pre-test probability; a negative result from a sensitive test should lower it.
whyNot.E: 25% is the prevalence in the study population, not this patient's probability.

items.objective: Apply a negative likelihood ratio to a patient's pre-test probability.

items.stemHtml: The emergency department wants to use assay L to identify children who can safely be observed without imaging. Based on the study summary, which of the following is the most appropriate choice?

options.label: A
options.html: Use the 20-unit cut-off, because few children with appendicitis test negative at it

options.label: B
options.html: Use the 40-unit cut-off, because its higher specificity makes a negative result more reassuring

options.label: C
options.html: Use the 40-unit cut-off, because it has the higher positive likelihood ratio

options.label: D
options.html: Use either cut-off, because the area under the curve is the same at both

options.label: E
options.html: Use neither cut-off, because an area under the curve of 0.86 is too low for any use

items.explanationHtml:
A rule-out strategy needs a cut-off on the high-sensitivity end of the ROC curve, so that a negative result leaves few missed cases. At 20 units, sensitivity is 92% and LR− ≈ 0.11; at 40 units, sensitivity is 70% and LR− ≈ 0.32 (0.30 ÷ 0.94).

The 40-unit cut-off (specificity 94%, LR+ ≈ 11.7) would suit the opposite purpose: identifying children likely enough to have appendicitis to go straight to surgical review.

Takeaway: choose the ROC operating point for its job: high sensitivity to rule out, high specificity to rule in.

whyNot.B: Specificity governs false positives; reassurance from a negative result depends on high sensitivity.
whyNot.C: A high LR+ helps rule disease in, not out; LR− at 40 units is about 0.32, far weaker than 0.11 at 20 units.
whyNot.D: The AUC summarises the whole curve; sensitivity and specificity differ a great deal between the two cut-offs.
whyNot.E: An AUC of 0.86 indicates good discrimination; usefulness depends on the operating point chosen.

items.objective: Choose an ROC operating point that matches a rule-out purpose.

items.stemHtml: A rural urgent care network plans to use assay L at the 20-unit cut-off in children with abdominal pain, of whom about 5% have appendicitis. Assuming a similar spectrum of illness, which of the following changes, compared with the study, is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Higher positive and lower negative predictive value

options.label: B
options.html: Lower positive and higher negative predictive value

options.label: C
options.html: Lower sensitivity and lower specificity

options.label: D
options.html: Higher sensitivity and lower specificity

options.label: E
options.html: No change in any measure of test performance

items.explanationHtml:
Predictive values depend on prevalence. At 5% prevalence, with sensitivity 92% and specificity 70%: PPV = (0.05 × 0.92) ÷ [(0.05 × 0.92) + (0.95 × 0.30)] ≈ 14% (51% in the study), and NPV ≈ 99.4% (96% in the study).

In a low-prevalence setting most positive results at this cut-off will be false positives, so a positive result should prompt further assessment, not surgery.

Takeaway: lower prevalence → PPV falls, NPV rises; sensitivity and specificity stay the same.

whyNot.A: Lower prevalence lowers PPV and raises NPV, the reverse of this option.
whyNot.C: Sensitivity and specificity do not depend on prevalence when the spectrum of illness is similar.
whyNot.D: The cut-off is unchanged, so its operating point on the ROC curve is unchanged.
whyNot.E: Predictive values change with prevalence even though sensitivity and specificity do not.

items.objective: Predict how predictive values change when a test moves to a lower-prevalence setting.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, which of the following is the crude odds ratio, calculated from the exposure counts?
items.explanationHtml:
Cases: 80 exposed, 320 unexposed. Controls: 80 exposed, 720 unexposed. OR = (80 × 720) ÷ (320 × 80) = 57,600 ÷ 25,600 = 2.25.

Equivalently, odds of exposure among cases = 80 ÷ 320 = 0.25 and among controls = 80 ÷ 720 ≈ 0.111; 0.25 ÷ 0.111 = 2.25.

Takeaway: OR = ad ÷ bc; the ratio of exposure percentages is not an odds ratio.

whyNot.A: 0.44 is the reciprocal, the odds for controls over cases.
whyNot.B: 1.60 is the adjusted odds ratio, not the crude value.
whyNot.C: 2.00 is the ratio of exposure proportions (20% ÷ 10%), not a ratio of odds.
whyNot.E: 2.40 is the adjusted odds ratio for the high-dose group only.

items.objective: Calculate a crude odds ratio from a case-control abstract.

items.stemHtml: Which of the following conclusions about the change from the crude to the adjusted odds ratio is best supported by the study summary?

options.label: A
options.html: Adjustment shows that drug V does not affect fracture risk

options.label: B
options.html: The adjusted estimate is less valid because it is closer to 1

options.label: C
options.html: The difference proves that frailty modifies the effect of drug V

options.label: D
options.html: The difference is fully explained by random error

options.label: E
options.html: Part of the crude association reflected confounding, but an association remains after adjustment

items.explanationHtml:
Frailer people with more falls are both more likely to be prescribed a sleep medicine and more likely to break a hip. These factors confound the crude association, inflating it from 1.6 to 2.25. After adjustment the association persists (95% CI 1.10–2.30 excludes 1), and the dose gradient adds some support to a causal link.

Residual confounding by unmeasured factors remains possible in any observational study, so the adjusted estimate is still not proof of causation.

Takeaway: an estimate that moves toward 1 after adjustment but stays significant means confounding explained part, not all, of the association.

whyNot.A: The adjusted OR is still 1.6 with a 95% CI that excludes 1.
whyNot.B: Moving toward 1 after adjustment suggests the crude estimate was inflated by confounders, not that the adjusted one is wrong.
whyNot.C: Effect modification would need stratum-specific estimates that differ; the summary does not report them.
whyNot.D: The crude and adjusted estimates come from the same participants; the change reflects adjustment for measured factors.

items.objective: Interpret the change between crude and adjusted odds ratios.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman who takes drug V asks how much the medicine raises her risk of breaking a hip. Which of the following statements about the adjusted odds ratio of 1.60 is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.html: It cannot be read as a relative risk in a case-control study under any conditions

options.label: B
options.html: It means that 60% of hip fractures in drug V users are caused by the drug

options.label: C
options.html: It means that her absolute risk of hip fracture rises by 1.6 percentage points

options.label: D
options.html: It approximates a relative risk of about 1.6, because hip fracture is uncommon

options.label: E
options.html: It applies only to the controls, because they were matched to the cases

items.explanationHtml:
With an outcome as uncommon as hip fracture in the source population (about 1% per year), the rare-disease assumption holds and the odds ratio closely approximates the relative risk. A fair summary for her: people like those studied who took drug V had about a 60% higher relative risk of hip fracture.

To give her an absolute figure, apply the relative risk to her own baseline risk (e.g. 1% per year × 1.6 ≈ 1.6% per year, an increase of about 0.6 percentage points).

Takeaway: when the outcome is rare, OR ≈ RR; absolute risk still needs a baseline risk from outside the case-control data.

whyNot.A: When the outcome is rare in the source population, the OR from a case-control study is a good estimate of the RR.
whyNot.B: The attributable fraction among users would be (1.6 − 1) ÷ 1.6 ≈ 38%, and only if the association were causal.
whyNot.C: A ratio cannot be turned into an absolute difference without the baseline risk.
whyNot.E: Matching makes cases and controls comparable on age, sex and practice; the OR compares exposure odds between them.

items.objective: Explain when an odds ratio from a case-control study approximates the relative risk, and communicate it to a patient.

items.stemHtml: Which of the following measures would need information from outside this study to be estimated?

options.label: A
options.html: The adjusted odds ratio for high-dose use

options.label: B
options.html: The crude odds ratio

options.label: C
options.html: The incidence of hip fracture among drug V users

options.label: D
options.html: The proportion of cases who had been dispensed drug V

options.label: E
options.html: The proportion of controls who had been dispensed drug V

items.explanationHtml:
In a case-control study the investigators fix the numbers of cases and controls, so the proportion with the outcome reflects their sampling choice, not the population. Incidence (risk), relative risk and risk difference cannot be calculated directly. Odds ratios and exposure proportions can.

Absolute risk can be estimated only with outside information, such as the baseline incidence in the source population.

Takeaway: case-control studies give odds ratios, not incidence or attributable risk.

whyNot.A: This is calculated within the study and reported in the results table.
whyNot.B: The crude OR comes straight from the exposure counts in cases and controls.
whyNot.D: This is 80 ÷ 400 = 20%, directly from the data.
whyNot.E: This is 80 ÷ 800 = 10%, directly from the data.

items.objective: Identify which measures a case-control design can and cannot provide.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has routine opt-out HIV screening at a primary care visit. She has had one male partner for 4 years and reports no injection drug use. The laboratory antigen/antibody immunoassay is reactive. In this clinic population, the prevalence of undiagnosed HIV infection is 0.2%. Assume the immunoassay has a sensitivity of 99.8% and a specificity of 99.5%. Which of the following is closest to the probability that she has HIV infection?
items.explanationHtml:
This asks for the positive predictive value. Per 100,000 people: 200 have HIV, and 99.8% (≈ 200) test reactive. Of 99,800 without HIV, 0.5% (499) test falsely reactive. PPV = 200 ÷ (200 + 499) ≈ 29%.

Even an excellent test produces mostly false positives when the condition is rare. This is why a reactive screening result is never given as a diagnosis; it goes on to supplemental testing.

Takeaway: at very low prevalence, even a 99.5%-specific test has a modest PPV.

whyNot.A: 0.2% is the prevalence (pre-test probability); a reactive result must raise it.
whyNot.C: 50% is not derived from the data; it treats a reactive test as uninformative between two outcomes.
whyNot.D: 99.5% is the specificity, the probability of a negative test in someone without HIV.
whyNot.E: 99.8% is the sensitivity, the probability of a reactive test in someone with HIV, not the reverse.

items.objective: Estimate the positive predictive value of a highly specific test at very low prevalence.

items.stemHtml: The patient's reactive antigen/antibody immunoassay is followed in the laboratory by an HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay, which is negative. She has had no recent fever, rash or sore throat. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Measure the CD4 count

options.label: B
options.html: Repeat the antigen/antibody immunoassay in 6 months

options.label: C
options.html: Start antiretroviral therapy now

options.label: D
options.html: Tell her the reactive result was a false positive

options.label: E
options.html: Perform an HIV-1 nucleic acid test

items.explanationHtml:
The recommended US laboratory sequence is serial testing: a reactive antigen/antibody screen is followed by an antibody differentiation assay. If that is negative or indeterminate, an HIV-1 nucleic acid test (NAT) resolves the discordance. A positive NAT means acute HIV-1 infection; a negative NAT means the original screen was a false positive.

Serial testing raises specificity: a person is called positive only after a second, different test agrees.

Takeaway: reactive screen + negative differentiation assay → HIV-1 NAT before telling the patient either result.

whyNot.A: A CD4 count stages known infection; it does not establish whether she is infected.
whyNot.B: Waiting leaves a possible acute infection undiagnosed and untreated during its most infectious phase.
whyNot.C: Infection has not been confirmed; treatment before diagnosis is not appropriate here.
whyNot.D: A negative antibody differentiation assay does not exclude acute HIV-1 infection, when antibodies are not yet present.

items.objective: Apply serial confirmatory testing after a discordant HIV screening result.

items.stemHtml:
A 79-year-old woman is scheduled for surgical repair of a hip fracture. Her daughter has read about a new drug that is given before surgery to prevent postoperative delirium and asks how well it works. The physician finds a randomized trial in adults aged 70 years or older having hip fracture surgery.

GroupDelirium within 7 daysNo deliriumTotal
Study drug30170200
Placebo50150200

Based on this trial, how many patients like her would need to receive the drug to prevent one case of postoperative delirium?
items.explanationHtml:
Risk with placebo = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%; with the drug = 30 ÷ 200 = 15%. Absolute risk reduction = 25% − 15% = 10 percentage points = 0.10. NNT = 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10.

The relative risk is 0.15 ÷ 0.25 = 0.60, a relative risk reduction of 40%. RRR sounds larger and does not tell the family how many patients benefit; NNT and ARR do. Round NNT up to the next whole number when it is not an integer.

Takeaway: NNT = 1 ÷ ARR, using the absolute difference in event rates over the trial's time frame.

whyNot.A: 3 comes from 1 ÷ relative risk reduction (1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5, rounded up); NNT uses the absolute reduction.
whyNot.B: 4 is 1 ÷ the placebo risk (1 ÷ 0.25), which ignores the treated group.
whyNot.C: 7 is 1 ÷ the treated risk (1 ÷ 0.15, rounded up), which ignores the comparison with placebo.
whyNot.E: 40 is the relative risk reduction expressed as a percentage, not a number of patients.

items.objective: Calculate the number needed to treat from a randomized trial table and use it to answer a family's question.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with chronic insomnia asks about a new prescription sleep medicine. In a 12-week randomized trial in adults aged 65 years or older, a fall occurred in 6% of patients taking the drug and 2% of those taking placebo. Which of the following is the most accurate way to explain this risk to him?

options.label: A
options.html: "About 1 in 6 people who take it fall because of the medicine."

options.label: B
options.html: "For about every 25 people like you who take it for 12 weeks, one extra person would fall."

options.label: C
options.html: "For about every 50 people like you who take it for 12 weeks, one extra person would fall."

options.label: D
options.html: "It triples the risk of falling, so you would probably fall."

options.label: E
options.html: "The difference is too small to matter, so falls are not a concern."

items.explanationHtml:
Absolute risk increase = 6% − 2% = 4 percentage points = 0.04. Number needed to harm = 1 ÷ 0.04 = 25: for every 25 people treated for 12 weeks, one extra person falls.

Absolute measures and natural frequencies ("1 extra in 25") are easier for patients to understand than relative ones ("triples the risk"), which can alarm or mislead without the baseline. Give the time frame with the number.

Takeaway: NNH = 1 ÷ absolute risk increase; explain harms in absolute terms with a time frame.

whyNot.A: 6% is the total fall risk on the drug, and part of it (2%) occurs anyway; the extra risk is 4 percentage points.
whyNot.C: 1 in 50 corresponds to the placebo risk of 2%, not the difference between groups.
whyNot.D: A relative risk of 3 applied to a 2% baseline gives 6%, so a fall is still unlikely.
whyNot.E: An absolute increase of 4 percentage points in 12 weeks is clinically important in an older adult.

items.objective: Calculate the number needed to harm and communicate absolute risk to a patient.

items.stemHtml: A large trial shows that a cholesterol-lowering drug reduces the 10-year risk of a first myocardial infarction by the same relative amount at every level of baseline risk, with a relative risk of 0.75. A 46-year-old woman with no cardiovascular disease has an estimated 10-year risk of 4%. Assuming the trial result applies to her, approximately how many women like her would need to take the drug for 10 years to prevent one myocardial infarction?
items.explanationHtml:
Relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.75 = 25%. Her absolute risk reduction = baseline risk × RRR = 4% × 0.25 = 1 percentage point (4% → 3%). NNT = 1 ÷ 0.01 = 100.

The same relative effect gives very different absolute benefit by baseline risk: a patient with a 20% risk would have an ARR of 5 points and an NNT of 20. This is why treatment decisions weigh absolute risk, and why low-risk patients benefit less from the same drug.

Takeaway: ARR = baseline risk × RRR; NNT = 1 ÷ ARR, so a low baseline risk gives a large NNT.

whyNot.A: 4 is 1 ÷ the relative risk reduction (0.25), which ignores her baseline risk.
whyNot.B: 20 is the NNT for a patient with a 20% baseline risk, not 4%.
whyNot.C: 25 is 1 ÷ her baseline risk (0.04), not 1 ÷ the risk reduction.
whyNot.D: 33 is 1 ÷ her risk on treatment (0.03), which ignores the comparison with no treatment.

items.objective: Apply a constant relative risk reduction to a patient's baseline risk to estimate the NNT.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation asks whether she should stop using a hair dye she uses every 2 months. A prospective cohort study of 5,000 pregnant women found a relative risk of preterm birth with this type of dye of 1.00 (95% CI, 0.85–1.18). Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "The study proves the dye is completely safe in pregnancy."

options.label: B
options.html: "The study shows the dye raises the risk of preterm birth by 18%."

options.label: C
options.html: "The results cannot be interpreted because the interval includes 1."

options.label: D
options.html: "In this large study, women who used the dye did not have more preterm births than women who did not."

options.label: E
options.html: "You should stop using it, because any possible risk is unacceptable in pregnancy."

items.explanationHtml:
A relative risk of 1.00 means the risk was the same in both groups. The narrow interval (0.85–1.18) makes a large effect in either direction unlikely, though it cannot exclude a small one. The honest, accurate summary is that the study found no difference.

Avoid overstating either way: "proves safe" and "raises risk" both misread the result.

Takeaway: RR = 1 means no association in that study; the CI shows how large an effect remains plausible.

whyNot.A: No single observational study proves complete safety; the interval allows a small increase.
whyNot.B: 1.18 is the upper limit of the interval, not the estimate.
whyNot.C: An interval that includes 1 is interpretable: it shows no detectable association and the plausible range.
whyNot.E: This gives advice not supported by the evidence and ignores her preferences.

items.objective: Explain a relative risk of 1 with its confidence interval to a patient.

items.stemHtml: A hospital quality team studies 30-day readmission (yes or no) among 4,000 adults discharged after heart failure admissions. In a multivariable logistic regression model that includes age, ejection fraction, kidney function and number of medicines, living alone has an odds ratio for readmission of 1.8 (95% CI, 1.3–2.5). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: Patients living alone have 80% higher odds of readmission than similar patients who do not

options.label: B
options.html: 80% of patients who live alone are readmitted within 30 days

options.label: C
options.html: Living alone raises the absolute risk of readmission by 1.8 percentage points

options.label: D
options.html: The association is not statistically significant because the interval is wide

options.label: E
options.html: The model proves that living alone causes readmission

items.explanationHtml:
In logistic regression, the exponentiated coefficient for a predictor is an adjusted odds ratio: the odds of the outcome for that predictor, holding the other variables in the model constant. An aOR of 1.8 means 80% higher odds of readmission among patients who live alone than among otherwise similar patients who do not.

Because readmission after heart failure is common, the relative risk would be smaller than 1.8. A reasonable next step for the team is to test an intervention (e.g. early home visits) for patients who live alone.

Takeaway: logistic regression output = adjusted ORs, read as "odds, holding other variables constant".

whyNot.B: The OR compares odds between groups; it gives no readmission proportion.
whyNot.C: An odds ratio is a relative measure and cannot be read as an absolute difference.
whyNot.D: The 95% CI (1.3–2.5) excludes 1, so the association is statistically significant.
whyNot.E: An observational model shows an independent association; unmeasured confounders may remain.

items.objective: Interpret an adjusted odds ratio from multivariable logistic regression.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman with heart failure asks whether a new drug will help her. In a randomized trial of 6,000 patients, the hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalisation with the drug is 0.78 (95% CI, 0.68–0.90). In the prespecified subgroup of women (1,800 patients), the hazard ratio is 0.80 (95% CI, 0.55–1.16); the P value for interaction by sex is 0.85. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The drug benefits men but not women

options.label: B
options.html: The drug harms women, because the upper limit of their interval exceeds 1

options.label: C
options.html: The overall hazard ratio is the best estimate of the effect in women

options.label: D
options.html: The trial should be repeated in women before any woman is treated

options.label: E
options.html: The subgroup result shows the drug is about 20% less effective in women

items.explanationHtml:
The women's subgroup is smaller, so its estimate is less precise and its interval crosses 1. But its point estimate (0.80) is almost the same as the overall one (0.78), and the interaction test (P = 0.85) gives no evidence that the effect differs by sex. The best estimate for her is the overall hazard ratio: about a 22% lower hazard of the composite outcome.

Subgroups are usually underpowered; a non-significant subgroup result alone is not evidence of no effect in that subgroup. Look for a significant interaction and biological plausibility before concluding that effects differ.

Takeaway: judge subgroups by the interaction test, not by whether each subgroup's CI crosses 1.

whyNot.A: The subgroup interval is wide and the interaction test shows no evidence that the effect differs by sex.
whyNot.B: An upper limit above 1 shows imprecision, not harm; the point estimate favours the drug.
whyNot.D: With no sign of a sex difference, withholding an effective treatment from women is not justified by this subgroup result.
whyNot.E: The subgroup point estimate (0.80) is almost identical to the overall estimate (0.78).

items.objective: Interpret a subgroup hazard ratio using the interaction test.

items.stemHtml:
A health department estimates influenza vaccine effectiveness in adults with acute respiratory illness who were tested for influenza at outpatient clinics. Patients testing positive are cases; patients testing negative are controls.

Influenza positiveInfluenza negative
Vaccinated this season60250
Not vaccinated240350
Total300600

Ignoring adjustment for other factors, which of the following is the estimated vaccine effectiveness against medically attended influenza?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a test-negative case-control design, so effectiveness is estimated from the odds ratio: VE = (1 − OR) × 100%.

OR = (60 × 350) ÷ (250 × 240) = 21,000 ÷ 60,000 = 0.35. VE = 1 − 0.35 = 65%: vaccinated patients had 65% lower odds of testing positive.

Real estimates adjust for age, timing in the season and other factors through logistic regression; the adjusted OR is used in the same formula.

Takeaway: vaccine effectiveness from a case-control (test-negative) design = 1 − OR.

whyNot.A: 20% is the proportion of cases who were vaccinated (60 ÷ 300).
whyNot.B: 35% is the odds ratio itself expressed as a percentage, not 1 − OR.
whyNot.C: 52% uses the ratio of vaccination proportions (20% ÷ 41.7%) instead of the odds ratio.
whyNot.E: 80% is 1 − the proportion of cases vaccinated, which ignores the controls.

items.objective: Calculate vaccine effectiveness from an odds ratio in a test-negative case-control design.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman is considering a hormonal medicine. She read that it "triples the risk of blood clots" and is frightened. In the cohort study she read about, venous thromboembolism occurred at a rate of 3 per 10,000 woman-years among nonusers and 9 per 10,000 woman-years among users. Which of the following is the most accurate explanation?

options.label: A
options.html: "If 10,000 women use it for a year, about 3 more would have a clot than among nonusers."

options.label: B
options.html: "If 10,000 women use it for a year, about 6 more would have a clot than among nonusers."

options.label: C
options.html: "Your risk of a clot rises by 6%."

options.label: D
options.html: "Your yearly risk of a clot would be about 9%."

options.label: E
options.html: "Your risk rises by 200%, so a clot is likely."

items.explanationHtml:
The rate ratio is 9 ÷ 3 = 3 ("triples"), but the rate difference (attributable rate) is 9 − 3 = 6 per 10,000 woman-years. Put in natural frequencies, about 6 extra women in 10,000 would have a clot in a year of use.

Patients judge risk better from absolute numbers with a stated denominator and time frame. Relative risks alone exaggerate rare harms and rare benefits.

Takeaway: translate a relative increase into the absolute excess per number of people per unit time.

whyNot.A: 3 per 10,000 is the rate in nonusers, not the extra rate in users.
whyNot.C: The excess is 6 per 10,000 woman-years, which is 0.06%, not 6%.
whyNot.D: The rate in users is 9 per 10,000 woman-years, about 0.09% per year.
whyNot.E: A 200% relative increase on a very small baseline still leaves a low absolute risk.

items.objective: Explain an attributable rate (rate difference) to a patient using natural frequencies.

items.stemHtml: A county health department can fund one prevention programme for a disease. Risk factor X is present in 5% of adults and carries a relative risk of 4.0 for the disease. Risk factor Y is present in 40% of adults and carries a relative risk of 1.5. Each programme would remove its risk factor completely, and both associations are causal. Which of the following is the best-supported choice?

options.label: A
options.html: Factor Y, because it accounts for a larger share of all cases

options.label: B
options.html: Factor X, because its relative risk is higher

options.label: C
options.html: Factor X, because its attributable risk percent among the exposed is higher

options.label: D
options.html: Either factor, because the two would prevent the same number of cases

options.label: E
options.html: Neither factor, because relative risks under 5 are not clinically important

items.explanationHtml:
The population attributable fraction PAF = p(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + p(RR − 1)].

X: 0.05 × 3 = 0.15; 0.15 ÷ 1.15 ≈ 13%. Y: 0.40 × 0.5 = 0.20; 0.20 ÷ 1.20 ≈ 17%. Removing Y would prevent more cases in the county, even though X is the stronger risk factor for an individual.

Clinicians counselling one patient care about relative and absolute individual risk; planners allocating resources care about the population fraction.

Takeaway: population impact depends on exposure prevalence as well as relative risk.

whyNot.B: A high relative risk matters less to the population when few people are exposed; the PAF for X is about 13%.
whyNot.C: The attributable fraction among the exposed (75%) ignores how few people have factor X.
whyNot.D: The population attributable fractions differ (about 13% vs 17%).
whyNot.E: Moderate relative risks can account for many cases when the exposure is common.

items.objective: Use population attributable fractions to prioritise prevention programmes.

items.stemHtml:
An infection prevention team compares central line-associated bloodstream infections in two intensive care units over the same year.

UnitInfectionsCentral line-days
Unit A124,000
Unit B91,500

Which of the following is the infection rate ratio for unit B compared with unit A?
items.explanationHtml:
Rates must use the exposure time at risk. Unit A: 12 ÷ 4,000 = 3.0 per 1,000 line-days. Unit B: 9 ÷ 1,500 = 6.0 per 1,000 line-days. Rate ratio = 6.0 ÷ 3.0 = 2.0.

Unit B had fewer infections but twice the rate, so it is the unit to prioritise for review of insertion and maintenance practices. Comparing raw counts between units with different exposure misleads quality decisions.

Takeaway: compare infection rates per device-day, not counts.

whyNot.A: 0.50 is the ratio for unit A compared with unit B, the inverse of what was asked.
whyNot.B: 0.75 compares the counts (9 ÷ 12) and ignores the much smaller exposure time in unit B.
whyNot.C: 1.33 is the inverse count ratio (12 ÷ 9), again ignoring line-days.
whyNot.E: 3.0 per 1,000 line-days is the rate difference (6.0 − 3.0), not the ratio.

items.objective: Calculate a rate ratio with device-days to compare quality between units.

items.stemHtml:
A study of adults evaluated for a condition reports the accuracy of five clinical findings against a reference standard.

FindingSensitivitySpecificity
190%40%
230%97%
360%85%
480%75%
550%90%

When present in a patient, which of the following findings most increases the probability of the condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Finding 1

options.label: B
options.html: Finding 2

options.label: C
options.html: Finding 3

options.label: D
options.html: Finding 4

options.label: E
options.html: Finding 5

items.explanationHtml:
The effect of a positive finding on probability is set by its positive likelihood ratio, LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity). Finding 2: 0.30 ÷ 0.03 = 10, the largest. Findings 1, 3, 4 and 5 have LR+ of 1.5, 4, 3.2 and 5.

A finding can be uncommon (low sensitivity) yet very informative when present, because it is rarely seen without the condition. Absence of finding 2 helps little (LR− ≈ 0.72); absence of finding 1 helps most (LR− = 0.25).

Takeaway: rank findings for ruling in by LR+, and for ruling out by LR−.

whyNot.A: Finding 1 is sensitive but has LR+ = 0.90 ÷ 0.60 = 1.5, so its presence changes the probability little.
whyNot.C: Finding 3 has LR+ = 0.60 ÷ 0.15 = 4, lower than finding 2.
whyNot.D: Finding 4 has LR+ = 0.80 ÷ 0.25 = 3.2; it is the most balanced, not the most powerful when present.
whyNot.E: Finding 5 has LR+ = 0.50 ÷ 0.10 = 5, half that of finding 2.

items.objective: Use likelihood ratios to rank clinical findings for ruling in a diagnosis.

items.stemHtml: A public health physician compares two workplace exposures. Exposure 1 has a relative risk of 10 for a cancer whose incidence in unexposed adults is 1 per 100,000 per year. Exposure 2 has a relative risk of 1.3 for a cardiovascular disease whose incidence in unexposed adults is 500 per 100,000 per year. Assuming both associations are causal, which of the following is the most accurate comparison among exposed workers?

options.label: A
options.html: Exposure 1 causes about 9 times as many excess cases as exposure 2

options.label: B
options.html: Exposure 1 causes more excess cases because its relative risk is higher

options.label: C
options.html: Both exposures cause about the same number of excess cases

options.label: D
options.html: The comparison cannot be made without odds ratios

options.label: E
options.html: Exposure 2 causes more excess cases per 100,000 exposed workers per year

items.explanationHtml:
The attributable rate (rate difference) among the exposed = baseline rate × (RR − 1).

Exposure 1: 1 × (10 − 1) = 9 excess cases per 100,000 per year. Exposure 2: 500 × (1.3 − 1) = 150 excess cases per 100,000 per year.

Relative risk measures the strength of an association, which helps judge causation; the risk difference measures the burden, which guides prevention and counselling.

Takeaway: a weak relative risk for a common disease can cause far more cases than a strong one for a rare disease.

whyNot.A: Exposure 1 causes 9 excess cases per 100,000 per year, far fewer than exposure 2's 150.
whyNot.B: A high relative risk applied to a very rare disease gives few excess cases.
whyNot.C: The excess rates differ greatly: 9 vs 150 per 100,000 per year.
whyNot.D: Excess risk is calculated from the incidences and relative risks given; odds ratios are not needed.

items.objective: Compare relative and absolute measures of excess risk.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought for a well-child visit. His height plots at a z-score of −2.0 for age and sex on a growth reference whose values are normally distributed. Approximately which percentile does this height represent?

options.label: A
options.html: 0.1st

options.label: B
options.html: 2nd

options.label: C
options.html: 5th

options.label: D
options.html: 16th

options.label: E
options.html: 25th

items.explanationHtml:
In a normal distribution, about 95% of values fall within ±2 SD of the mean, leaving about 2.5% in each tail (more precisely, 2.3% below −2 SD). A z-score of −2.0 is therefore at about the 2nd percentile.

z = (value − mean) ÷ SD. Useful anchors: z = −1 → 16th; z = 0 → 50th; z = +1 → 84th; z = +2 → 98th percentile. A height at about −2 SD or a fall across major percentile lines prompts closer assessment of growth.

Takeaway: z = −2 ≈ 2nd percentile; z = −1 ≈ 16th.

whyNot.A: The 0.1st percentile corresponds to a z-score of about −3.
whyNot.C: The 5th percentile corresponds to a z-score of about −1.6.
whyNot.D: The 16th percentile corresponds to a z-score of −1.
whyNot.E: The 25th percentile corresponds to a z-score of about −0.7.

items.objective: Convert a z-score to an approximate percentile.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman feels well and has a normal examination. A routine chemistry panel shows a serum value just above the upper limit of the laboratory's reference interval; all other results are within their intervals. The laboratory set the interval to include the central 95% of values from a large group of healthy adults. Which of the following statements about this result is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.html: About 1 in 40 healthy people have a value above the upper limit

options.label: B
options.html: About 1 in 20 healthy people have a value above the upper limit

options.label: C
options.html: About 1 in 5 healthy people have a value above the upper limit

options.label: D
options.html: Any value outside the interval indicates disease

options.label: E
options.html: The interval shows that she has a 95% probability of being healthy

items.explanationHtml:
A reference interval built from the central 95% of healthy values leaves 2.5% of healthy people above the upper limit and 2.5% below the lower limit. A slightly high value in a well person is often a normal variant; it is interpreted with her clinical picture and, where appropriate, by repeating the test.

The more tests ordered, the more likely at least one is outside its interval by chance.

Takeaway: "abnormal" lab values occur in 5% of healthy people (2.5% in each tail) by definition.

whyNot.B: 1 in 20 (5%) is the share outside the interval in both tails combined, not above the upper limit alone.
whyNot.C: Only about 2.5% of healthy people lie above the upper limit.
whyNot.D: By definition, 5% of healthy people lie outside a central 95% interval.
whyNot.E: The reference interval describes healthy people; it does not give her probability of disease.

items.objective: Interpret a value just outside a reference interval in a healthy patient.

items.stemHtml: A primary care practice identifies the 50 patients with type 2 diabetes whose most recent hemoglobin A1c values are the highest in the practice (mean 10.8%). Before any new programme starts and without any change in their care, the patients have a routine repeat measurement 3 months later. The patients were not told they had been selected. The mean of the repeat values is 9.7%. Which of the following best explains the fall?

options.label: A
options.html: Confounding by indication

options.label: B
options.html: Hawthorne effect

options.label: C
options.html: Lead-time bias

options.label: D
options.html: Placebo effect

options.label: E
options.html: Regression to the mean

items.explanationHtml:
Patients selected because their measurement is extreme will, on average, have a repeat value closer to the population mean, even with no intervention. Part of any single value is random variation (biological and analytic); selecting the highest values selects those with high random error too. This is regression to the mean.

It is why before-and-after studies of patients enrolled for extreme values overstate benefit. A randomized control group, which regresses equally, is the remedy.

Takeaway: extreme first measurements tend to be followed by less extreme ones; use a control group.

whyNot.A: No treatment was chosen or changed, so there is no indication to confound.
whyNot.B: The patients did not know they were being studied, so changed behaviour due to observation is unlikely.
whyNot.C: Lead-time bias concerns survival measured from an earlier diagnosis, not repeated laboratory values.
whyNot.D: No intervention or inactive treatment was given.

items.objective: Recognise regression to the mean in repeated measurements of patients selected for extreme values.

items.stemHtml: A hospital administrator asks a physician for the typical cost of an elective hip replacement at the hospital. Over the last year, most costs were close to each other, but a few patients with major complications had very high costs. The mean cost is far higher than the median. Which of the following is the best summary to report as the typical cost?

options.label: A
options.html: The mean, because it uses every patient's cost

options.label: B
options.html: The median, because a few very high costs distort the mean

options.label: C
options.html: The mode, because it is the most common exact cost

options.label: D
options.html: The range, because it includes every cost

options.label: E
options.html: The standard deviation, because it shows variation

items.explanationHtml:
A mean far above the median indicates a positively skewed distribution with a long right tail of high costs. The median is resistant to extreme values and better describes the typical patient; the interquartile range is the matching measure of spread.

The mean still matters for budgeting the total cost, so report both when the audience needs both.

Takeaway: for skewed data, report the median (and IQR) as the typical value.

whyNot.A: The mean is pulled upward by the few very costly cases and overstates a typical case.
whyNot.C: Exact costs rarely repeat, so the mode is unstable for continuous data.
whyNot.D: The range describes spread, not a typical value, and depends entirely on the extremes.
whyNot.E: The SD describes spread, not the typical cost, and is inflated by outliers.

items.objective: Choose the median to summarise skewed data.

items.stemHtml: A study of 100 adults with hypertension reports a mean systolic blood pressure of 140 mm Hg, written as 140 ± 1.5 mm Hg (mean ± standard error of the mean). The values are approximately normally distributed. Which of the following ranges contains about 95% of the individual patients' systolic pressures?

options.label: A
options.html: 137 to 143 mm Hg

options.label: C
options.html: 125 to 155 mm Hg

options.label: D
options.html: 110 to 170 mm Hg

options.label: E
options.html: 95 to 185 mm Hg

items.explanationHtml:
Convert the SEM back to the SD: SD = SEM × √n = 1.5 × √100 = 15 mm Hg. About 95% of individuals lie within mean ± 2 SD = 140 ± 30 = 110 to 170 mm Hg.

Papers sometimes report ± SEM because it looks smaller. SEM describes the precision of the mean; SD describes how much patients differ from each other, which is what matters when deciding whether results apply to a patient.

Takeaway: SD = SEM × √n; individuals spread over ±2 SD, the mean's CI over ±2 SEM.

whyNot.A: This is mean ± 2 SEM, an approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean, not the range of individuals.
whyNot.B: This is mean ± 1 SEM, which is narrower still.
whyNot.C: This is mean ± 1 SD, which contains only about 68% of individuals.
whyNot.E: This is mean ± 3 SD, which contains about 99.7% of individuals.

items.objective: Convert a standard error to a standard deviation and describe the spread of individual values.

items.stemHtml: A quality report lists the lengths of stay (days) for 9 patients after a procedure: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12 and 30. A chart review shows that the 30-day value was a data-entry error and the true stay was 13 days. After the correction, which of the following best describes the change in the mean and the median?

options.label: A
options.html: Mean unchanged at about 8.1 days; median falls from 5 to 4 days

options.label: B
options.html: Mean falls from about 8.1 to 6.2 days; median falls from 5 to 4 days

options.label: C
options.html: Mean falls from about 8.1 to 6.2 days; median unchanged at 5 days

options.label: D
options.html: Mean falls from about 8.1 to 7.0 days; median unchanged at 5 days

options.label: E
options.html: Both unchanged, because only one value was corrected

items.explanationHtml:
Before: sum = 73, mean = 73 ÷ 9 ≈ 8.1 days; the median (5th of 9 ordered values) is 5. After: sum = 56, mean = 56 ÷ 9 ≈ 6.2 days; the ordered values are 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 13, and the median is still 5.

The median is resistant to outliers; the mean is not. Before excluding an outlier, check whether it is an error (correct it) or a true value (keep it and use robust summaries).

Takeaway: outliers move the mean, not the median.

whyNot.A: Changing the largest value changes the sum and therefore the mean; the middle value does not move.
whyNot.B: The 5th of 9 ordered values is still 5, so the median does not change.
whyNot.D: The new sum is 56, and 56 ÷ 9 ≈ 6.2, not 7.0.
whyNot.E: One extreme value has a large effect on the mean of a small sample.

items.objective: Show how an outlier affects the mean but not the median.

items.stemHtml: A hospital wants to identify which patient factors predict a fall during admission (fall or no fall), while adjusting for age, sedative use, delirium and mobility score at the same time. Which of the following analyses is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Linear regression

options.label: B
options.html: Multiple logistic regression

options.label: C
options.html: Pearson correlation

options.label: D
options.html: Paired t-test

options.label: E
options.html: Analysis of variance

items.explanationHtml:
A binary outcome with several predictors analysed together calls for multiple logistic regression. Each predictor's exponentiated coefficient is an odds ratio adjusted for the others.

Outcome type chooses the model: continuous → linear regression; binary → logistic regression; time to event with censoring → Cox proportional hazards regression; counts per person-time → Poisson regression.

Takeaway: yes/no outcome with several adjusted predictors → logistic regression.

whyNot.A: Linear regression models a continuous outcome, not a yes/no event.
whyNot.C: Correlation measures the linear relation between two continuous variables and cannot adjust for several predictors.
whyNot.D: A paired t-test compares two related means, such as before and after values in the same patients.
whyNot.E: ANOVA compares a continuous outcome across groups; this outcome is binary.

items.objective: Choose logistic regression for a binary outcome with several predictors.

items.stemHtml: Investigators follow adults after a first episode of major depression treated in primary care. They record the time from remission to first relapse; some patients are lost to follow-up or reach the end of the study without relapse. They want to compare two treatment strategies while adjusting for age and baseline severity. Which of the following analyses is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Cox proportional hazards regression

options.label: B
options.html: Chi-square test

options.label: C
options.html: Two-sample t-test of mean time to relapse

options.label: D
options.html: Linear regression of time to relapse

options.label: E
options.html: Logistic regression for relapse at any time

items.explanationHtml:
Time-to-event data with censoring need survival methods. Kaplan-Meier curves with a log-rank test compare groups without adjustment; Cox proportional hazards regression compares them while adjusting for covariates, giving adjusted hazard ratios.

Censored patients contribute their follow-up time until they leave the study, which simpler methods cannot use.

Takeaway: time to event + censoring + adjustment → Cox regression (hazard ratios).

whyNot.B: Chi-square compares proportions and ignores both timing and censoring.
whyNot.C: A t-test cannot handle patients who had not relapsed when follow-up ended.
whyNot.D: Linear regression treats censored times as if they were relapse times and underestimates time to relapse.
whyNot.E: Logistic regression discards timing and handles unequal follow-up poorly.

items.objective: Choose Cox regression for adjusted time-to-event comparisons.

items.stemHtml: A rehabilitation clinic uses a regression equation from a study of older adults to predict 6-minute walk distance: predicted distance (m) = 620 − 3.0 × age (years) − 2.5 × body mass index (kg/m²). A 70-year-old woman has a body mass index of 30 kg/m². Which of the following is her predicted 6-minute walk distance?
items.explanationHtml:
Substitute each value: 620 − (3.0 × 70) − (2.5 × 30) = 620 − 210 − 75 = 335 m.

In multiple linear regression, each coefficient is the change in the outcome per unit change in that predictor with the others held constant. Predictions are trustworthy only within the range of the data the equation came from.

Takeaway: predicted value = intercept + Σ (coefficient × value), keeping each sign.

whyNot.B: 410 m includes age but leaves out the body mass index term (2.5 × 30 = 75 m).
whyNot.C: 485 m adds the body mass index term instead of subtracting it.
whyNot.D: 545 m leaves out the age term (3.0 × 70 = 210 m).
whyNot.E: 620 m is the intercept, which would apply only at age 0 and BMI 0.

items.objective: Calculate a predicted value from a multiple linear regression equation.

items.stemHtml: An analysis of 60 counties finds a correlation of r = 0.72 between the number of fast-food outlets per 10,000 residents and the county prevalence of diagnosed type 2 diabetes. A county council member says this proves that people who eat fast food develop diabetes. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Eating fast food causes about 72% of diabetes in these counties

options.label: B
options.html: About 72% of the variation in diabetes between counties is due to fast food

options.label: C
options.html: Counties with more outlets tend to have more diabetes, but individual-level effects cannot be inferred

options.label: D
options.html: The association is too weak to be meaningful

options.label: E
options.html: Individuals who eat fast food are 72% more likely to develop diabetes

items.explanationHtml:
This is an ecological correlation: the units are counties, not people. It shows that counties with more outlets tend to have higher diabetes prevalence, but concluding that the individuals who eat fast food are the ones who develop diabetes is the ecological fallacy. County-level confounders (income, age structure, rurality, access to care) may explain both.

Testing the individual-level hypothesis needs individual data, such as a cohort study measuring each person's diet and incident diabetes.

Takeaway: group-level correlation is not causation and does not apply to individuals.

whyNot.A: r is not a measure of attributable cases, and correlation does not establish causation.
whyNot.B: Variance explained is r² ≈ 52%, and even that is statistical, not causal.
whyNot.D: An r of 0.72 indicates a fairly strong linear association.
whyNot.E: r is not a relative risk, and county data say nothing about individual risk.

items.objective: Recognise the limits of an ecological correlation.

items.stemHtml: In a cross-sectional study of 3,000 adults, unadjusted linear regression shows that each additional daily cup of coffee is associated with a 2.0 mm Hg higher systolic blood pressure (95% CI, 1.2–2.8). Coffee drinkers are more likely to smoke. After smoking status is added to the model, the coefficient for coffee is 0.2 mm Hg per cup (95% CI, −0.5 to 0.9). Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Coffee raises systolic pressure by 2.0 mm Hg per cup

options.label: B
options.html: Smoking modifies the effect of coffee on blood pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Coffee lowers systolic pressure once smoking is accounted for

options.label: D
options.html: The association between coffee and blood pressure was largely explained by smoking

options.label: E
options.html: Adjustment introduced bias, so the unadjusted estimate should be used

items.explanationHtml:
When adding a variable to a regression model moves the coefficient of interest substantially (2.0 → 0.2) and the variable is linked to both the exposure (coffee drinkers smoke more) and the outcome, that variable is a confounder. Here smoking accounts for most of the crude association, and the adjusted interval includes 0, the null value for a regression coefficient.

Multiple regression estimates each predictor's association with the outcome while holding the others constant; it adjusts only for variables that were measured and included.

Takeaway: a large change in a coefficient after adding a variable signals confounding by that variable.

whyNot.A: The unadjusted estimate is distorted by smoking; after adjustment there is no clear association.
whyNot.B: Effect modification would need different coffee coefficients in smokers and nonsmokers, which are not reported.
whyNot.C: The adjusted coefficient is slightly positive and its interval includes 0.
whyNot.E: Adjusting for a common cause of the exposure and outcome removes confounding rather than adding bias.

items.objective: Interpret confounding from the change in a regression coefficient after adjustment.

items.stemHtml: A hospital evaluates a new bedside glucose meter against the central laboratory method in 200 paired blood samples. The Pearson correlation between the two methods is 0.98. Regression of meter values on laboratory values gives a slope of 1.15 and an intercept close to 0. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.label: A
options.html: The meter agrees closely with the laboratory and can replace it for patient care

options.label: B
options.html: The meter reads systematically higher than the laboratory, and agreement needs a difference analysis

options.label: C
options.html: The meter is too imprecise for use, because the correlation is not exactly 1.0

options.label: D
options.html: The meter underestimates glucose values at the high end of the measured range

options.label: E
options.html: The two methods cannot be compared, because each sample was measured by both

items.explanationHtml:
Correlation measures how well points fit a straight line, not the line of identity. A slope of 1.15 with an intercept near 0 means the meter reads about 15% higher than the laboratory across the range, so a laboratory glucose of 200 mg/dL would read about 230 mg/dL. Two methods can correlate almost perfectly and still disagree in a clinically important way.

Method comparison uses a difference (Bland-Altman) analysis: plot each pair's difference against its mean, then look at the mean bias and the limits of agreement.

Takeaway: high correlation ≠ agreement; check the bias with a difference analysis.

whyNot.A: A high correlation shows a tight linear relation, not that the two methods give the same values.
whyNot.C: An r of 0.98 indicates very little scatter; the problem is a proportional offset.
whyNot.D: A slope above 1 means meter values rise faster than laboratory values, so high values are overestimated.
whyNot.E: Paired samples are the correct design for comparing two measurement methods.

items.objective: Distinguish correlation from agreement when comparing two measurement methods.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with no symptoms and no significant medical or family history asks his physician to order a whole-body MRI "to catch anything early." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'll order it today, since it's the best way to be sure nothing serious is being missed."

options.label: B
options.html: "Scans like that are useless for healthy people, so there really is nothing to discuss."

options.label: C
options.html: "Can you tell me what has you thinking about this? Then we can talk about what such a scan can and can't do."

options.label: D
options.html: "Your insurance won't cover a scan like that, so I'm not able to order it for you."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll refer you to a radiologist, who can decide whether you need a scan like that."

items.explanationHtml:
A screening test is worthwhile only when finding disease early improves outcomes. Whole-body imaging in people without symptoms has no evidence of benefit and often finds incidental abnormalities that lead to more tests, anxiety, procedures and overdiagnosis.

Before advising, explore why he is asking (a friend's illness, a specific worry). That lets the physician address the concern directly, explain benefits and harms, and offer screening that is recommended for his age and risk.

Takeaway: explore the reason for a screening request, then explain the evidence; don't order or dismiss reflexively.

whyNot.A: Ordering an untested screening test exposes him to incidental findings and follow-up harms without proven benefit.
whyNot.B: Dismissing his request ends the conversation without exploring his concern or explaining the evidence.
whyNot.D: Cost is not the main reason; this avoids the real discussion about benefit and harm.
whyNot.E: Deciding on appropriate screening is the primary physician's job and starts with understanding his concern.

items.objective: Respond to a request for an unproven screening test by exploring concerns and explaining benefits and harms.

items.stemHtml: A health system compares patients whose lung nodules were detected by a new screening programme with patients whose cancers were diagnosed after symptoms. Five-year survival from diagnosis is 70% in screen-detected patients and 45% in symptom-detected patients. Pathology shows similar tumour growth rates in the two groups, and the average age at death from the cancer is the same. Which of the following best explains the difference in survival?

options.label: A
options.html: Earlier diagnosis without later death

options.label: B
options.html: Better treatment of screen-detected tumours

options.label: C
options.html: Detection of slower-growing tumours by screening

options.label: D
options.html: Healthier volunteers in the screened group

options.label: E
options.html: Random variation between the groups

items.explanationHtml:
Screening moved the date of diagnosis earlier while the date of death stayed the same, so survival measured from diagnosis grew longer without any real benefit. This is lead-time bias.

Because survival from diagnosis is distorted by lead time (and by length-time bias and overdiagnosis), screening programmes are judged by mortality rates in randomized comparisons of screened and unscreened populations.

Takeaway: longer survival after screening with unchanged timing of death = lead-time bias.

whyNot.B: If treatment worked better, deaths from the cancer would occur later, but age at death is the same.
whyNot.C: Length-time bias needs screen-detected tumours to grow more slowly, but growth rates were similar.
whyNot.D: Healthier volunteers would tend to die later, not at the same age.
whyNot.E: A 25-point survival difference with identical age at death has a systematic explanation.

items.objective: Recognise lead-time bias in survival comparisons after screening.

items.stemHtml: An emergency department protocol for adults with chest pain classifies a patient as needing admission if either the initial electrocardiogram or the initial cardiac troponin is abnormal. Compared with using either test alone, which of the following best describes this strategy?

options.label: A
options.html: Higher sensitivity and higher specificity

options.label: B
options.html: Higher sensitivity and lower specificity

options.label: C
options.html: Lower sensitivity and higher specificity

options.label: D
options.html: Lower sensitivity and lower specificity

options.label: E
options.html: Unchanged sensitivity and specificity

items.explanationHtml:
Calling a patient positive if either test is positive is parallel testing. A case missed by one test can be caught by the other, so sensitivity rises; but a false positive on either test now counts, so specificity falls.

Parallel testing suits rule-out decisions where missing disease is dangerous (as in chest pain); serial testing (both must be positive) suits confirmation before costly or risky treatment.

Takeaway: "either positive" = parallel → sensitivity ↑, specificity ↓.

whyNot.A: Combining tests in parallel trades specificity for sensitivity; both cannot rise.
whyNot.C: That pattern belongs to serial testing, in which both tests must be abnormal.
whyNot.D: Adding a second route to a positive result cannot lower sensitivity.
whyNot.E: Combining tests changes both measures.

items.objective: Predict the effect of parallel testing on sensitivity and specificity.

items.stemHtml: A hospital audit finds that two pathologists independently grading the same 150 colon polyp biopsies for high-grade dysplasia have a kappa statistic of 0.20. Grading guides whether patients are recalled for earlier colonoscopy. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and response?

options.label: A
options.html: Agreement is excellent, so no change is needed

options.label: B
options.html: One pathologist is inaccurate and should stop grading biopsies

options.label: C
options.html: The biopsies should be cut into more slides before grading

options.label: D
options.html: Agreement is only slightly better than chance, so standardise the criteria and add consensus review

options.label: E
options.html: Agreement is poor because the grading is inaccurate against a reference standard

items.explanationHtml:
Kappa measures inter-rater reliability beyond chance. Common descriptive bands: 0–0.20 slight, 0.21–0.40 fair, 0.41–0.60 moderate, 0.61–0.80 substantial, above 0.80 almost perfect. A kappa of 0.20 means grading is inconsistent enough to change surveillance intervals for patients.

The systems response is to standardise: agreed written criteria, joint training with reference images, consensus or second review of borderline cases, then re-audit. Poor reliability also limits validity, because inconsistent grading cannot be consistently accurate.

Takeaway: low kappa → improve reliability with standard criteria and consensus review.

whyNot.A: A kappa of 0.20 shows only slight agreement beyond chance.
whyNot.B: Kappa measures agreement between raters, not which one is correct.
whyNot.C: More slides do not address inconsistent use of the grading criteria.
whyNot.E: Kappa assesses reliability (consistency), not accuracy against a reference standard.

items.objective: Interpret a low kappa and choose a systems response to improve reliability.

items.stemHtml: An 88-year-old woman with advanced heart failure and frequent hospitalisations has an estimated life expectancy of less than 1 year. She has been having a screening test every few years for a slowly progressing cancer whose screening benefit appears only many years after testing. She asks whether she should continue. Which of the following is the strongest reason to discuss stopping this screening?

options.label: A
options.html: Her age alone makes screening inappropriate

options.label: B
options.html: Screening tests are less accurate in older adults

options.label: C
options.html: Her life expectancy is shorter than the time needed for screening to provide benefit

options.label: D
options.html: The cancer is too rare at her age to be worth screening for

options.label: E
options.html: Earlier screening results were normal, so she cannot develop the cancer

items.explanationHtml:
