Screening carries immediate harms (procedures, false positives, overdiagnosis and treatment) while its benefit, fewer cancer deaths, appears only years later. When life expectancy is shorter than the time to benefit, harms outweigh benefits.

Decisions to stop screening in older adults are individualised by health status, life expectancy and preferences rather than age alone, and should be made with the patient.

Takeaway: screen only when the patient is likely to live long enough to benefit.

whyNot.A: Age alone is not the deciding factor; health status and life expectancy matter more.
whyNot.B: Test accuracy is not the main issue; the problem is whether she can live long enough to benefit.
whyNot.D: The incidence of many cancers rises with age; rarity is not the reason here.
whyNot.E: Past normal results lower but do not remove future risk.

items.objective: Weigh life expectancy against time to benefit when deciding to stop screening.

items.stemHtml:
A blood bank is choosing a cut-off for a new assay that screens donated units for a transfusion-transmitted virus. Units that screen positive are discarded and the donors are sent for confirmatory testing. The ROC study reports:

Cut-off (signal ratio)SensitivitySpecificity
≥ 199.8%88.0%
≥ 299.0%95.0%
≥ 496.0%98.5%
≥ 890.0%99.5%
≥ 1680.0%99.9%

Which of the following cut-offs is most appropriate for screening donated units?
items.explanationHtml:
When a false negative is very harmful (an infected unit transfused) and a false positive is cheap and correctable (a discarded unit, then confirmatory testing of the donor), choose the operating point at the high-sensitivity end of the ROC curve, even at the cost of specificity.

The confirmatory test that follows is chosen for high specificity, a serial strategy that recovers specificity overall.

Takeaway: set the cut-off by the cost of each error: high sensitivity when a miss is disastrous.

whyNot.B: ≥ 2 misses 1 in 100 infected units, five times as many as ≥ 1.
whyNot.C: ≥ 4 balances the errors, but a missed infected unit is far more harmful than a discarded one.
whyNot.D: ≥ 8 would miss 10% of infected units.
whyNot.E: ≥ 16 maximises specificity, which suits confirmation, not donor screening.

items.objective: Select an ROC operating point when false negatives are much more harmful than false positives.

items.stemHtml: Two blood tests for bacterial infection are evaluated in the same 500 febrile adults. The area under the ROC curve is 0.91 (95% CI, 0.88–0.94) for test A and 0.68 (95% CI, 0.63–0.73) for test B. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Test A discriminates better between patients with and without bacterial infection

options.label: B
options.html: Test A has a higher positive predictive value at every cut-off

options.label: C
options.html: Test B is no better than chance

options.label: D
options.html: Test B would perform as well as test A in a population with higher prevalence

options.label: E
options.html: The tests cannot be compared because their cut-offs differ

items.explanationHtml:
The AUC summarises discrimination across all cut-offs: 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect. Test A (0.91) separates infected from non-infected patients much better than test B (0.68), and the confidence intervals do not overlap.

Comparing tests on the same patients avoids differences caused by different populations. The cut-off for clinical use still has to be chosen for the purpose.

Takeaway: higher AUC = better overall discrimination.

whyNot.B: AUC does not give predictive values, which depend on prevalence and the cut-off.
whyNot.C: Test B's interval (0.63–0.73) lies above 0.5, so it discriminates better than chance.
whyNot.D: AUC does not change with prevalence.
whyNot.E: AUC summarises each test across all cut-offs, which is what allows comparison.

items.objective: Compare two tests by their areas under the ROC curve.

items.stemHtml: The figure shows ROC curves for two fictional blood tests, X and Y, for the same disease, measured in the same patients. The areas under the curves are 0.85 for test X and 0.82 for test Y. A positive result will be used to start a treatment with serious toxicity, so the team will accept a false-positive rate of no more than 5%. Which of the following is the best choice?

options.label: A
options.html: Test X, because its area under the curve is higher

options.label: B
options.html: Test X at the cut-off closest to the upper-left corner

options.label: C
options.html: Either test, because their areas under the curve are similar

options.label: D
options.html: Neither test, because curves that cross cannot be compared

options.label: E
options.html: Test Y, because at false-positive rates of 5% or less its sensitivity is higher

items.explanationHtml:
The curves cross at a false-positive rate of about 20%. To the left of that point (high specificity), test Y has the higher sensitivity: at a 5% false-positive rate, test Y detects about 63% of cases and test X about 35%. To the right, test X is better, which is why its overall AUC is slightly higher.

When only part of the curve is clinically acceptable, compare the tests in that part (sometimes called a partial AUC) rather than by the total AUC.

Takeaway: when ROC curves cross, choose the test that performs best in the region of the curve you will actually use.

whyNot.A: The higher AUC reflects test X's better performance at high false-positive rates, which are not acceptable here.
whyNot.B: That point has a false-positive rate of about 25%, well above the 5% limit.
whyNot.C: Similar AUCs can hide large differences in the part of the curve that matters.
whyNot.D: Crossing curves can be compared over a defined range of false-positive rates.

items.objective: Compare crossing ROC curves within the clinically relevant false-positive range.

items.stemHtml: A new serum biomarker for pancreatic cancer had an area under the ROC curve of 0.97 in a study comparing 100 patients with known metastatic pancreatic cancer from an oncology clinic with 100 healthy blood donors. An emergency physician wants to use it in adults presenting with vague abdominal pain and weight loss. Which of the following most likely explains why the reported performance would overstate how well the marker discriminates in her patients?

options.label: A
options.html: The study compared advanced cases with healthy controls, which exaggerates discrimination

options.label: B
options.html: The prevalence of pancreatic cancer among her patients is lower than in the study

options.label: C
options.html: The study included too few patients to calculate an area under the curve reliably

options.label: D
options.html: The area under the curve was calculated without first choosing a single cut-off

options.label: E
options.html: Blood biomarkers always perform less well in emergency departments than in clinics

items.explanationHtml:
Comparing patients with obvious, advanced disease with healthy volunteers places the two groups at the extremes of the marker's range, so they separate easily. In practice the test must distinguish early cancer from other causes of similar symptoms (pancreatitis, biliary disease), where values overlap far more. This spectrum bias inflates sensitivity, specificity and AUC.

A valid diagnostic accuracy study enrols a consecutive series of patients in whom the diagnosis is genuinely in question, as in the intended clinical setting.

Takeaway: "sickest vs healthiest" diagnostic studies overstate the AUC.

whyNot.B: Prevalence affects predictive values, not the ROC curve or AUC.
whyNot.C: 200 participants is adequate to estimate an AUC; the problem is who they were.
whyNot.D: AUC is defined across all cut-offs; not choosing one is correct.
whyNot.E: Performance falls when the patients are harder to distinguish, not because of the setting itself.

items.objective: Recognise spectrum bias as a reason an ROC result may not generalise.

items.stemHtml: A pilot study of 80 adults evaluates a urine biomarker for acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery. The area under the ROC curve is 0.62 (95% CI, 0.48–0.76). Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The biomarker discriminates well and is ready for clinical use

options.label: B
options.html: The biomarker misclassifies 38% of patients

options.label: C
options.html: The study has not shown that the biomarker discriminates better than chance

options.label: D
options.html: The biomarker is proven to have no diagnostic value

options.label: E
options.html: The biomarker would discriminate better at a lower cut-off

items.explanationHtml:
An AUC of 0.5 corresponds to chance. The 95% CI (0.48–0.76) includes 0.5, so the study has not shown discrimination better than chance. The interval is wide because the study is small; a larger study could find the biomarker useless or moderately useful.

For AUC, the null value is 0.5, not 0 or 1.

Takeaway: check whether the AUC confidence interval includes 0.5.

whyNot.A: An AUC of 0.62 is weak even at face value, and the interval includes 0.5.
whyNot.B: 1 − AUC is not a misclassification rate.
whyNot.D: A wide interval reaching 0.76 does not exclude useful discrimination; the study is imprecise.
whyNot.E: Changing the cut-off moves along the same curve; it does not change the AUC.

items.objective: Interpret an AUC whose confidence interval includes 0.5.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has a painful, swollen calf. Using a validated clinical score, the physician estimates a 25% probability of deep venous thrombosis. A bedside test for which the positive likelihood ratio is 4.0 is positive. Which of the following is closest to his post-test probability of deep venous thrombosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Pre-test odds = 0.25 ÷ 0.75 = 0.33. Post-test odds = 0.33 × 4 = 1.33. Post-test probability = 1.33 ÷ 2.33 ≈ 57%.

A moderately positive test in a patient with intermediate pre-test probability leaves real uncertainty; the result is combined with the next diagnostic step rather than read as a definite diagnosis.

Takeaway: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR; convert back to probability.

whyNot.A: 25% is the pre-test probability; a positive result with LR+ of 4 must raise it.
whyNot.B: 44% comes from computing pre-test odds as p ÷ (1 + p) instead of p ÷ (1 − p).
whyNot.D: 80% is LR ÷ (LR + 1), which ignores the pre-test probability.
whyNot.E: 100% multiplies the probability (not the odds) by the LR: 0.25 × 4.

items.objective: Calculate a post-test probability from a pre-test probability and likelihood ratio.

items.stemHtml: A physician estimates that a patient's probability of a treatable bacterial infection is 85%. The treatment is safe and inexpensive, and she would treat at any probability above 50%. A rapid test is available with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.4. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Start treatment without ordering the test

options.label: B
options.html: Order the test and treat only if it is positive

options.label: C
options.html: Order the test and withhold treatment if it is negative

options.label: D
options.html: Order a second, different test before deciding

options.label: E
options.html: Observe without treatment or testing

items.explanationHtml:
A test is worth ordering only if a result could move the probability across a decision threshold. Pre-test odds = 0.85 ÷ 0.15 ≈ 5.67. After a negative result: 5.67 × 0.4 ≈ 2.27 odds, a probability of about 69%, still above the 50% treatment threshold.

Because neither result would change management, the test adds cost and delay but no value. Above the treatment threshold, treat; below the testing threshold, neither test nor treat; between them, test.

Takeaway: order a test only if its result could change the decision.

whyNot.B: Even after a negative result the probability would be about 69%, still above her treatment threshold.
whyNot.C: A negative result would lower the probability only to about 69%, so withholding treatment would be wrong.
whyNot.D: No result could move the probability below the threshold with this test, and more testing only delays treatment.
whyNot.E: With an 85% probability of a treatable infection, observation without treatment is not appropriate.

items.objective: Use a likelihood ratio and a treatment threshold to decide whether a test is worthwhile.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 40-year-old man has a screening panel of 20 laboratory tests. Each test's reference interval includes the central 95% of healthy values, and assume the results are independent. What is the probability that one or more of his results falls outside its reference interval by chance alone?

options.label: A
options.html: Less than 0.001%

items.explanationHtml:
P(all 20 within range) = 0.9520 ≈ 0.36. P(at least one outside) = 1 − 0.36 ≈ 64%.

Broad test panels in healthy people regularly produce abnormal values by chance. Each needs to be judged against the clinical picture, and repeating a mildly abnormal test is often reasonable before further workup.

Takeaway: with n independent tests at 5% each, P(≥ 1 abnormal) = 1 − 0.95n.

whyNot.A: This is the probability that all 20 results are outside their intervals (0.05<sup>20</sup>).
whyNot.B: 5% is the chance of an out-of-range result on a single test.
whyNot.C: 36% (0.95<sup>20</sup>) is the probability that all 20 results are within their intervals.
whyNot.E: 100% adds 5% twenty times, which double-counts overlapping events; a probability cannot be certain here.

items.objective: Apply the complement rule to multiple independent laboratory tests.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman is choosing a contraceptive method. For a method she is considering, the probability of an unintended pregnancy during each year of typical use is 9%. Assuming the probability is the same and independent each year, which of the following is closest to the probability that she has one or more contraceptive failures over 3 years of use?
items.explanationHtml:
P(no failure in a year) = 0.91. P(no failure in 3 years) = 0.91³ ≈ 0.754. P(at least one failure) = 1 − 0.754 ≈ 25%.

Small yearly risks add up over years of use, which matters when counselling about the gap between typical and perfect use, or comparing methods with different failure rates.

Takeaway: cumulative risk over n periods = 1 − (1 − p)n.

whyNot.A: 0.07% (0.09³) is the probability of failure in all three years.
whyNot.B: 9% is the probability for a single year.
whyNot.D: 27% adds the yearly probabilities and double-counts more than one failure.
whyNot.E: 75% (0.91³) is the probability of no failure in 3 years.

items.objective: Calculate cumulative probability over repeated independent periods.

items.stemHtml: An expert panel is reviewing whether long-term occupational exposure to a fictional degreasing solvent causes chronic kidney disease. The panel lists the classic considerations for judging causation and agrees that one of them must be met before any causal conclusion can be drawn, whereas the others only strengthen or weaken the case. Which of the following is the consideration that must be met?

options.label: A
options.html: Strength of association

options.label: B
options.html: Temporality

options.label: C
options.html: Consistency across studies

options.label: D
options.html: Specificity of the association

options.label: E
options.html: Biological plausibility

items.explanationHtml:
Among the considerations usually credited to Bradford Hill (strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy), only temporality is a logical necessity: the exposure must come before the disease. An effect cannot precede its cause.

The other considerations are weighed together. Each one makes causation more or less likely, but a causal relationship can exist when any of them is missing.

Takeaway: temporality (exposure before outcome) is the only consideration a causal claim cannot do without.

whyNot.A: A weak association can still be causal (many real causes carry relative risks below 2), so strength helps but is not required.
whyNot.C: A first study of a new exposure cannot yet be replicated, yet its finding may still be causal; consistency adds support only.
whyNot.D: Most exposures cause several diseases and most diseases have several causes, so lack of specificity does not rule causation out.
whyNot.E: Plausibility depends on what is known today; many causes were accepted before any mechanism was understood.

items.objective: Identify temporality as the only consideration that is required for a causal inference.

items.stemHtml: A cohort study follows 3,000 agricultural workers for 10 years. Workers are grouped by their cumulative days of handling a particular insecticide. The incidence of a tremor disorder is 2 per 1,000 in the lowest third of exposure, 3.6 per 1,000 in the middle third and 6.2 per 1,000 in the highest third. Which consideration for causation do these results most directly illustrate?

options.label: A
options.html: Analogy

options.label: B
options.html: Coherence

options.label: C
options.html: Experimental evidence

options.label: D
options.html: Specificity

options.label: E
options.html: Biological gradient

items.explanationHtml:
Risk rises step by step with the amount of exposure (2.0 → 3.6 → 6.2 per 1,000). A biological gradient (dose-response) makes a causal explanation more convincing, because confounding or chance would rarely produce a smooth increase across exposure levels.

A gradient is supportive but not essential: some causes act only above a threshold, and a confounder that rises with exposure could also create a gradient.

Takeaway: outcome risk that increases with increasing dose or duration of exposure is a biological gradient.

whyNot.A: Analogy is the argument that a similar exposure is already known to cause a similar effect; no comparison agent is described here.
whyNot.B: Coherence means the finding fits with what is known of the disease's natural history and laboratory biology, which the study does not address.
whyNot.C: Experimental evidence comes from changing the exposure (for example, removing it) and seeing the outcome change; these workers were only observed.
whyNot.D: Specificity means one exposure leads to one particular outcome; the study measured a single outcome and says nothing about others.

items.objective: Recognize a dose-response relationship as the biological gradient consideration for causation.

items.stemHtml: A cross-sectional survey of 5,000 adults asks about current hours of weekly exercise and current chronic low back pain. Adults who report chronic back pain exercise much less than those who do not. The authors conclude that physical inactivity causes chronic back pain. Which of the following is the most likely alternative explanation for this association?

options.label: A
options.html: Back pain leads people to reduce how much they exercise

options.label: B
options.html: Inactive adults recall past back pain more fully than active adults

options.label: C
options.html: Back pain is more common in older adults, who also exercise less, so age alone explains the result

options.label: D
options.html: Active adults were less likely than inactive adults to return the survey

options.label: E
options.html: Lifting heavy objects modifies the effect of exercise on back pain

items.explanationHtml:
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at the same moment, so it cannot establish temporality. Here the outcome (pain) very plausibly causes the 'exposure' (less exercise): reverse causation.

Look for reverse causation when the disease or its early symptoms could change the behaviour being studied: people with chest pain stop exercising, people with early dementia change their diet, and people who feel unwell stop drinking alcohol.

Takeaway: when exposure and outcome are measured at the same time, consider that the outcome may have caused the exposure.

whyNot.B: Recall bias needs exposure or outcome to be remembered from the past; both were reported as current states here.
whyNot.C: Age could confound the association, but the authors' error is more basic: a single survey cannot show which came first, and pain itself plainly limits exercise.
whyNot.D: Differential non-response is possible but is not suggested by anything in the study, whereas the direction of the effect is an obvious problem.
whyNot.E: Effect modification describes a different effect size across levels of a third variable; it does not provide an alternative explanation for the association itself.

items.objective: Recognize reverse causation as an alternative explanation for an association in a cross-sectional study.

items.stemHtml: Investigators want to know whether a fictional daily zinc lozenge reduces the number of upper respiratory infections in office workers. Which of the following study designs would provide the strongest evidence that the lozenge itself causes any reduction found?

options.label: A
options.html: Case series

options.label: B
options.html: Cross-sectional survey

options.label: C
options.html: Randomized controlled trial

options.label: D
options.html: Ecological study

options.label: E
options.html: Case-control study

items.explanationHtml:
Random allocation makes the groups similar, on average, in every characteristic, measured or not, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to the intervention. That is why a well-conducted randomized controlled trial gives the strongest evidence of causation when the exposure can ethically be assigned.

Observational designs rank below it, roughly prospective cohort, then case-control, then cross-sectional, ecological and case reports or series. A systematic review of several good trials sits above a single trial.

Takeaway: when an exposure can be assigned, randomization is the best protection against confounding and gives the strongest causal evidence.

whyNot.A: A case series describes people who took the lozenge without any comparison group, so no effect can be estimated.
whyNot.B: A cross-sectional survey measures lozenge use and infections at one time point, so it cannot establish which came first or remove confounding.
whyNot.D: An ecological study compares groups (for example, offices or towns) and cannot link exposure to outcome in individuals, so it risks the ecological fallacy.
whyNot.E: A case-control study can show an association but relies on recalled exposure and cannot balance unmeasured differences between users and non-users.

items.objective: Rank study designs by the strength of the causal evidence they provide.

items.stemHtml: A town's drinking water came from a well contaminated with a fictional industrial chemical. Over several years, physicians noticed a high rate of a particular skin disorder among residents. After the town switched to a clean water source, the incidence of the skin disorder fell to the regional average within 3 years, while it stayed unchanged in neighbouring towns. Which consideration for causation does the fall in incidence most directly support?

options.label: A
options.html: Analogy with similar chemicals

options.label: B
options.html: Coherence with laboratory findings

options.label: C
options.html: Consistency across many studies

options.label: D
options.html: Experimental evidence

options.label: E
options.html: Strength of association

items.explanationHtml:
When removing or reducing an exposure is followed by a fall in the outcome (and the comparison towns show no such change), the observation supports causation in the way an experiment would. This consideration is usually called experiment or reversibility.

It is a natural experiment rather than a randomized one, so other changes at the same time could still explain it; the neighbouring towns act as a control for region-wide trends.

Takeaway: a fall in disease after the exposure is removed is the 'experiment' consideration for causation.

whyNot.A: Analogy draws on knowledge that a similar agent causes a similar disease; no similar agent is mentioned.
whyNot.B: Coherence refers to agreement with known biology and natural history, which this observation does not test.
whyNot.C: Consistency needs repeated findings in different populations or by different investigators; this is a single town.
whyNot.E: Strength is the size of the association (for example, the relative risk), which the stem does not report.

items.objective: Recognize reversibility after removal of an exposure as experimental evidence for causation.

items.stemHtml: Several observational studies report that regular use of a fictional over-the-counter sleep aid is associated with later diagnosis of a progressive neurologic disorder (relative risks 1.4 to 1.7). Which of the following additional findings would most strongly argue against the sleep aid causing the disorder?

options.label: A
options.html: The relative risks are below 2.0

options.label: B
options.html: No biological mechanism linking the sleep aid to the disorder is yet known

options.label: C
options.html: Users of the sleep aid also have higher rates of several other conditions

options.label: D
options.html: Only four studies have examined the question so far

options.label: E
options.html: Disease-related sleep disturbance often began before the first use of the sleep aid

items.explanationHtml:
If the disorder's early symptoms (here, poor sleep) start before the exposure, people may begin the sleep aid because of the developing disease. This is reverse causation (sometimes called protopathic bias) and it breaks the one required consideration, temporality.

The other findings listed make the case weaker or less certain but do not contradict causation; a violated temporal sequence directly undermines it.

Takeaway: evidence that the outcome's early phase preceded the exposure is the strongest argument against causation.

whyNot.A: Modest relative risks are common for real causes; a small effect makes confounding harder to exclude but is not evidence against causation.
whyNot.B: Absence of a known mechanism reflects current knowledge and only weakly counts against causation.
whyNot.C: Lack of specificity is the weakest consideration: a drug can be associated with several outcomes and still cause one of them.
whyNot.D: Four consistent studies are supportive; a small number of studies does not argue against causation.

items.objective: Judge which evidence most undermines a causal interpretation of an observational association.

items.stemHtml: A small randomized trial of 60 adults with chronic rhinosinusitis finds that a new nasal spray does not significantly shorten symptom duration compared with saline (P = .21). Five years later, a well-conducted trial of 2,400 patients clearly shows a moderate benefit of the same spray, and the benefit is confirmed in two further trials. Assuming the later trials are correct, which of the following best describes the result of the first trial?

options.label: A
options.html: Type I error

options.label: B
options.html: Type II error

options.label: C
options.html: Confounding

options.label: D
options.html: Regression to the mean

options.label: E
options.html: Lead-time bias

items.explanationHtml:
A type II error (beta) is failing to reject the null hypothesis when a real effect exists, a false-negative conclusion. Small trials have low power (1 − beta), so they often miss moderate effects.

A non-significant P value from a small study means 'not shown', not 'shown to have no effect'. The confidence interval of such a trial is usually wide and includes clinically important benefit.

Takeaway: missing a real effect, typically because the sample is small, is a type II error.

whyNot.A: A type I error is rejecting a null hypothesis that is true (a false-positive finding); the first trial did not reject the null.
whyNot.C: Randomization balances confounders on average, and nothing suggests an imbalance; the problem is too few participants.
whyNot.D: Regression to the mean is the drift of extreme measurements toward the average on re-measurement; it does not explain failing to detect a real effect.
whyNot.E: Lead-time bias concerns survival measured from an earlier diagnosis in screening studies, not a treatment trial.

items.objective: Recognize a type II error when an underpowered study fails to detect a real effect.

items.stemHtml: Investigators are planning a randomized trial comparing two physiotherapy programmes for knee osteoarthritis, with pain score at 6 months as the outcome. Their draft protocol has 80% power to detect a 1.5-point difference using a two-tailed alpha of 0.05. Which of the following changes to the protocol would increase the trial's power?

options.label: A
options.html: Enrolling more participants in each group

options.label: B
options.html: Lowering alpha from 0.05 to 0.01

options.label: C
options.html: Designing the trial to detect a 0.75-point difference instead

options.label: D
options.html: Widening eligibility so that baseline pain varies much more between participants

options.label: E
options.html: Keeping alpha at 0.05 but planning more pairwise comparisons of secondary outcomes

items.explanationHtml:
Power (1 − beta) is the probability of detecting a true effect of a given size. It rises with a larger sample size, a larger true effect, less variability in the outcome and a higher (less strict) alpha.

Of the levers available to investigators, sample size is the one usually adjusted, which is why sample-size calculations start from the expected effect, its variability, alpha and the desired power.

Takeaway: more participants, a bigger effect, less variability or a higher alpha each increase power.

whyNot.B: A smaller alpha makes it harder to reject the null hypothesis, which lowers power for the same sample size.
whyNot.C: A smaller target difference is harder to detect, so power falls unless the sample size rises.
whyNot.D: More variable outcomes widen the standard error and reduce power to detect the same difference.
whyNot.E: Adding comparisons does not increase power for the primary outcome; it raises the chance of false-positive secondary findings.

items.objective: Identify the factors that increase the statistical power of a study.

items.stemHtml: A hospital-based case-control study of 300 cases of acute pancreatitis and 600 controls finds an odds ratio of 1.6 (95% confidence interval, 0.9 to 2.8) for current use of a fictional lipid-lowering drug. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: The association is statistically significant at the 0.05 level

options.label: B
options.html: The drug increases pancreatitis risk by 60% with 95% certainty

options.label: C
options.html: The drug has been shown to have no effect on pancreatitis risk

options.label: D
options.html: The association is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level

options.label: E
options.html: The P value for the association must be below 0.01

items.explanationHtml:
For a ratio (odds ratio, relative risk, hazard ratio), the null value is 1. A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 corresponds to a two-sided P value greater than 0.05, so the association is not statistically significant at that level.

For a difference (in means or in proportions), the null value is 0. Mixing up the two null values is a frequent exam trap.

Takeaway: a 95% CI for a ratio that crosses 1 means P > 0.05; the result is inconclusive, not negative.

whyNot.A: Significance at 0.05 requires the 95% interval to exclude the null value of 1, and this interval includes 1.
whyNot.B: 1.6 is the point estimate; the interval shows that values from a 10% decrease to a 180% increase are compatible with the data.
whyNot.C: A non-significant result is not proof of no effect; the interval also includes a near-tripling of the odds.
whyNot.E: An interval that includes 1 corresponds to a two-sided P value above 0.05, not below 0.01.

items.objective: Interpret a 95% confidence interval for a ratio measure in relation to statistical significance.

items.stemHtml: Twenty-five adults with hypertension have their systolic blood pressure measured before and after an 8-week slow-breathing programme. The investigators want to know whether the mean systolic pressure changed. Which of the following statistical tests is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Two-sample (independent) t-test

options.label: B
options.html: One-way analysis of variance

options.label: C
options.html: Paired t-test

options.label: D
options.html: Chi-square test

options.label: E
options.html: Fisher exact test

items.explanationHtml:
Each participant contributes a 'before' and an 'after' value, so the data are paired. The paired t-test analyses the mean of the within-person differences, which removes between-person variation and gives more power than treating the measurements as independent.

Choose by outcome type and grouping: two independent means, two-sample t-test; paired means, paired t-test; three or more means, ANOVA; proportions, chi-square (Fisher exact when expected counts are small).

Takeaway: before-and-after measurements in the same people call for a paired t-test.

whyNot.A: An independent t-test compares means of two separate groups and ignores the pairing of two measurements in the same person.
whyNot.B: Analysis of variance compares means of three or more groups; here there are two measurements in one group.
whyNot.D: The chi-square test compares proportions of categorical outcomes, whereas blood pressure is a continuous variable.
whyNot.E: The Fisher exact test compares proportions in small samples of categorical data and does not apply to means.

items.objective: Choose the paired t-test for comparing a continuous outcome measured twice in the same individuals.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial compares a fictional oral glucose-lowering drug with placebo in adults with type 2 diabetes. After 24 weeks, mean hemoglobin A1c is 0.4 percentage points lower with the drug (P = .02, two-tailed). Which of the following statements about this P value is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: There is a 2% probability that the drug has no effect

options.label: B
options.html: If the drug truly had no effect, a difference at least this large would arise by chance in about 2% of similar trials

options.label: C
options.html: There is a 98% probability that the drug truly lowers hemoglobin A<sub>1c</sub>

options.label: D
options.html: A repeat trial of the same size would have a 98% chance of a significant result

options.label: E
options.html: The difference of 0.4 percentage points is clinically important

items.explanationHtml:
A P value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true. Here, a 0.4-point difference or larger would be expected in about 2 in 100 trials if the drug did nothing.

Common misreadings treat P as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, or 1 − P as the probability that the treatment works. Neither is correct, and neither says anything about the size or importance of the effect.

Takeaway: P is the probability of data this extreme given no true effect, not the probability that there is no effect.

whyNot.A: The P value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true, so it cannot be the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
whyNot.C: The P value says nothing directly about the probability that the drug works; that would need prior probabilities as well.
whyNot.D: The chance a repeat trial is significant depends on the true effect and the power, not on 1 minus this P value.
whyNot.E: Statistical significance does not establish clinical importance, which depends on the size of the effect relative to what matters to patients.

items.objective: State the correct meaning of a P value and recognize common misinterpretations.

items.stemHtml: A meta-analysis pools five fictional placebo-controlled trials of a drug intended to prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation. The forest plot is shown. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the figure?

options.label: A
options.html: Trial D shows that the drug increases the odds of the outcome

options.label: B
options.html: Trial A contributed the most weight to the pooled estimate

options.label: C
options.html: Most of the individual trials found a statistically significant benefit

options.label: D
options.html: The pooled estimate is not significant because most trials cross 1

options.label: E
options.html: The pooled estimate shows statistically significantly lower odds of the outcome with the drug

items.explanationHtml:
In a forest plot, each square is a study's point estimate (its size reflects the study's weight), each horizontal line its 95% confidence interval, and the diamond the pooled estimate with its interval as the diamond's width. The vertical line marks no effect (1 for a ratio).

The pooled odds ratio is 0.73 (0.60 to 0.90). Its interval does not cross 1, so the combined evidence shows a statistically significant reduction, even though four of the five trials were individually inconclusive. This is the main reason to pool small trials.

Takeaway: read the diamond for the overall answer; a pooled interval that excludes 1 is significant even when most individual trials are not.

whyNot.A: Trial D's interval runs from 0.50 to 2.42 and includes 1, so it shows neither benefit nor harm with any confidence.
whyNot.B: Weight is shown by square size and depends mainly on precision; Trial C has the largest square and narrowest interval, Trial A one of the smallest.
whyNot.C: Only Trial C's interval lies wholly below 1; the other four intervals cross 1.
whyNot.D: Pooling combines the information from all trials, so the pooled interval is narrower than the individual ones; here it lies wholly below 1.

items.objective: Interpret the individual and pooled estimates in a meta-analysis forest plot.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial of 400 adults with an advanced solid tumour compares a fictional drug with standard therapy. The Kaplan-Meier curves for overall survival are shown. Based on the figure, what is the median overall survival in the drug group?

options.label: A
options.html: 9 months

options.label: B
options.html: 12 months

options.label: C
options.html: 13 months

options.label: D
options.html: 15 months

options.label: E
options.html: 18 months

items.explanationHtml:
The median survival on a Kaplan-Meier curve is the time at which the curve first falls to 0.50 or below. Following the 0.50 gridline across to the solid curve, the drug group drops from 0.54 to 0.47 at 15 months.

The control curve crosses 0.50 at 9 months, so median survival is about 6 months longer with the drug. Each step down is a death; the falling numbers at risk show that later estimates rest on fewer patients and are less precise.

Takeaway: median survival is read where the Kaplan-Meier curve first reaches a survival proportion of 0.50.

whyNot.A: 9 months is the median in the control (dashed) group, where survival first drops below 0.50.
whyNot.B: At 12 months the drug-group curve is at 0.58, so more than half of that group is still alive.
whyNot.C: At 13 months the drug-group curve is at 0.54, still above one half.
whyNot.E: At 18 months the drug-group curve has fallen to 0.40, well past the point where half had died.

items.objective: Read median survival from a Kaplan-Meier curve.

items.stemHtml: A quality report presents hospital length of stay after hip replacement as box plots. For one hospital, the box extends from 3 to 6 days, the line inside the box is at 4 days, the whiskers reach 2 and 9 days, and three separate points are plotted at 15, 18 and 23 days. Which of the following statements about this hospital's patients is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: About half of the patients stayed between 3 and 6 days

options.label: B
options.html: The mean length of stay is 4 days

options.label: C
options.html: About 95% of patients stayed between 2 and 9 days

options.label: D
options.html: The three separate points should be removed as errors

options.label: E
options.html: The distribution of stays is skewed to the left

items.explanationHtml:
A box plot shows the median (line in the box) and the interquartile range (the box, from the 25th to the 75th percentile), so the middle 50% of patients stayed 3 to 6 days. Whiskers commonly extend to the furthest points within 1.5 × IQR of the box, and values beyond that are drawn as individual outliers.

Here the outliers lie far to the right, so the data are right-skewed and the mean exceeds the median. For skewed data like length of stay, the median and IQR describe the typical patient better than the mean and SD.

Takeaway: the box of a box plot holds the middle half of the data; the line is the median.

whyNot.B: The line inside the box is the median, not the mean; with long outliers to the right, the mean will be higher than 4 days.
whyNot.C: Whiskers do not mark a 95% range; they usually extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 interquartile ranges of the box.
whyNot.D: Points beyond the whiskers are plotted as outliers but are often real patients (for example, complications) and should not be discarded without a reason.
whyNot.E: Long values on the high side (15–23 days) with a median near the lower edge of the box indicate a right (positive) skew.

items.objective: Interpret the median, interquartile range, whiskers and outliers in a box plot.

items.stemHtml:
An advertisement for a fictional antiplatelet drug states that it 'cuts strokes by 25%'. The trial on which the claim is based reports the following results over 5 years:

GroupParticipantsStrokes
Drug4,00060 (1.5%)
Placebo4,00080 (2.0%)

What is the absolute risk reduction in stroke with the drug over 5 years?
items.explanationHtml:
Absolute risk reduction = control risk − treated risk = 2.0% − 1.5% = 0.5 percentage points over 5 years (number needed to treat = 1 / 0.005 = 200).

The relative risk reduction is 0.5 / 2.0 = 25%. Relative measures look impressive when the baseline risk is low; the absolute measure tells a patient how much their own risk changes.

Takeaway: ARR is the simple difference in event rates; a large relative reduction can hide a small absolute one.

whyNot.B: 1.5% is the stroke risk in the drug group, not the difference between groups.
whyNot.C: 2.0% is the stroke risk in the placebo group.
whyNot.D: 25% is the relative risk reduction (0.5 / 2.0), the figure the advertisement chose.
whyNot.E: 75% is the relative risk (1.5 / 2.0), not a reduction.

items.objective: Calculate the absolute risk reduction from a results table and distinguish it from the relative risk reduction.

items.stemHtml: A laboratory study reports mean fasting insulin in 36 participants as a bar graph with error bars labelled 'mean ± SEM'. The error bar extends 2 µU/mL above and below the mean. What is the standard deviation of fasting insulin in this sample?

options.label: A
options.html: 0.33 µU/mL

options.label: B
options.html: 2 µU/mL

options.label: C
options.html: 6 µU/mL

options.label: D
options.html: 12 µU/mL

options.label: E
options.html: 72 µU/mL

items.explanationHtml:
SEM = SD / √n, so SD = SEM × √n = 2 × √36 = 2 × 6 = 12 µU/mL.

The SD describes how spread out individual values are; the SEM describes how precisely the mean is estimated and shrinks as n grows. Graphs that show ± SEM make the data look much less variable than ± SD would. Always check which one an error bar shows.

Takeaway: SD = SEM × √n; SEM error bars are much narrower than SD bars.

whyNot.A: 0.33 comes from dividing the SEM by the square root of n (2 / 6) instead of multiplying.
whyNot.B: 2 µU/mL is the standard error of the mean itself, not the standard deviation.
whyNot.C: 6 is the square root of the sample size, not a measure of spread.
whyNot.E: 72 comes from multiplying the SEM by n (2 × 36) instead of by the square root of n.

items.objective: Convert a standard error of the mean to a standard deviation and recognize which an error bar shows.

items.stemHtml: A researcher has measured daily sodium intake and systolic blood pressure in 300 adults and wants a single graph that shows how the two continuous measurements relate to each other across individuals. Which type of graph is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Bar graph of mean blood pressure

options.label: B
options.html: Box plot of sodium intake

options.label: C
options.html: Scatter plot

options.label: D
options.html: Histogram of blood pressure

options.label: E
options.html: Kaplan-Meier curve

items.explanationHtml:
A scatter plot places each participant as a point with one variable on each axis, showing the direction, form and strength of a relationship; a correlation coefficient or regression line can be added.

Match the graph to the question: one continuous variable, histogram or box plot; groups compared on a summary, bar graph or box plots; time to an event, Kaplan-Meier curve; two continuous variables, scatter plot.

Takeaway: use a scatter plot to show the relationship between two continuous variables.

whyNot.A: A bar graph of means shows a summary for categories and hides how the two variables vary together.
whyNot.B: A box plot shows the distribution of one variable, not the relationship between two.
whyNot.D: A histogram shows the frequency distribution of a single continuous variable.
whyNot.E: A Kaplan-Meier curve shows the proportion free of an event over time, which is not what was measured.

items.objective: Choose an appropriate graph type for the data being displayed.

items.stemHtml: A case-control study is done entirely among inpatients at a tertiary hospital. Cases are patients admitted with a fictional autoimmune lung disease, and controls are patients admitted for other conditions. The study finds a strong association between the lung disease and chronic kidney disease. Both conditions independently increase the chance that a person is admitted to this hospital. Which of the following biases most likely explains the association?

options.label: A
options.html: Healthy worker effect

options.label: B
options.html: Recall bias

options.label: C
options.html: Lead-time bias

options.label: D
options.html: Berkson bias

options.label: E
options.html: Hawthorne effect

items.explanationHtml:
Berkson bias is a selection bias in hospital-based studies. When both the exposure and the disease raise the probability of hospital admission, inpatients show an association (or a distorted one) that does not exist in the general population.

Using population-based controls, or controls from the same population that gave rise to the cases, avoids it.

Takeaway: hospital-based cases and controls can create a spurious association when exposure and disease both drive admission.

whyNot.A: The healthy worker effect arises when an employed population is compared with the general population, which includes people too ill to work.
whyNot.B: Recall bias comes from cases remembering past exposures differently; kidney disease is a recorded diagnosis, not a recalled exposure.
whyNot.C: Lead-time bias inflates survival when diagnosis is made earlier by screening, which has nothing to do with this design.
whyNot.E: The Hawthorne effect is a change in behaviour because people know they are being studied.

items.objective: Recognize Berkson bias in a hospital-based case-control study.

items.stemHtml: A prospective cohort study asks 20,000 adults a single, imprecise question about how often they eat processed meat and follows them for colorectal cancer. Because the question is vague, many participants are placed in the wrong exposure category, and the error is equally likely among those who later develop cancer and those who do not. How will this misclassification most likely affect the estimated relative risk?

options.label: A
options.html: It will tend to bias the relative risk away from 1.0

options.label: B
options.html: It will reverse the direction of the association

options.label: C
options.html: It will widen the confidence interval but leave the estimate unbiased

options.label: D
options.html: It will bias the estimate in a direction that cannot be predicted

options.label: E
options.html: It will tend to bias the relative risk toward 1.0

items.explanationHtml:
Exposure was assessed before the outcome occurred, and the errors are the same in people who do and do not get cancer: non-differential misclassification. Mixing truly exposed and unexposed people makes the groups more alike, so the relative risk is pulled toward 1.0 and a real association may be missed.

Differential misclassification (errors that differ by outcome or exposure status, such as recall bias in a case-control study) can bias the estimate in either direction.

Takeaway: non-differential misclassification of a binary exposure usually biases toward the null.

whyNot.A: Bias away from the null is typical of differential misclassification, for example recall bias, not of errors that are equal in both outcome groups.
whyNot.B: Non-differential error of a two-category exposure dilutes the contrast between groups; it does not ordinarily flip the direction.
whyNot.C: Misclassification is a systematic error, so it shifts the estimate itself, not only its precision.
whyNot.D: When the error is non-differential and the exposure has two categories, the expected direction is predictable: toward the null.

items.objective: Predict the effect of non-differential exposure misclassification on a measure of association.

items.stemHtml: A cohort study examines liver injury in adults taking a fictional antifungal drug. Among carriers of a particular drug-metabolizing enzyme variant, the relative risk of liver injury with the drug is 4.0; among non-carriers, it is 1.1. The crude relative risk in all participants is 1.6. The variant is equally common in drug users and non-users. Which of the following best describes the enzyme variant in this analysis?

options.label: A
options.html: A confounder

options.label: B
options.html: An effect modifier

options.label: C
options.html: An intermediate step on the causal pathway

options.label: D
options.html: A source of recall bias

options.label: E
options.html: A source of selection bias

items.explanationHtml:
When the association between exposure and outcome differs in size across levels of a third variable (RR 4.0 versus 1.1), the third variable is an effect modifier: the drug has a different effect in carriers. The stratum-specific estimates should be reported separately, not averaged.

Confounding is different: the stratum estimates are similar to each other but differ from the crude estimate, because the third variable is associated with both exposure and outcome. Here the variant is equally common in users and non-users, so it cannot confound.

Takeaway: different stratum results mean effect modification (report each); similar stratum results that differ from the crude mean confounding (adjust).

whyNot.A: A confounder makes the crude estimate differ from stratum estimates that agree with each other; here the strata differ widely, and the variant is not linked to drug use.
whyNot.C: An intermediate (mediator) is caused by the exposure and in turn causes the outcome; a person's inherited variant is not caused by taking the drug.
whyNot.D: Recall bias concerns remembering past exposures and does not apply to a genotype or to recorded drug use.
whyNot.E: Selection bias arises from how participants enter or leave a study, which is not described here.

items.objective: Distinguish effect modification from confounding using stratum-specific estimates.

items.stemHtml: A randomized, double-blind trial with concealed allocation and complete follow-up reports that a fictional drug lowers migraine frequency. Reviewers agree that, for the people who were enrolled, the result is very unlikely to be explained by bias or confounding. Which property of the study are the reviewers describing?

options.label: A
options.html: Internal validity

options.label: B
options.html: External validity

options.label: C
options.html: Reliability

options.label: D
options.html: Statistical power

options.label: E
options.html: Generalizability to other populations

items.explanationHtml:
Internal validity is the degree to which a study's result is correct for its own participants, that is, free of selection bias, information bias and confounding. Randomization, allocation concealment, blinding and complete follow-up protect it.

External validity (generalizability) asks whether the result applies to other patients, settings or times. Internal validity comes first: a biased result is not worth generalizing.

Takeaway: internal validity = right answer for the people studied; external validity = right answer for my patient.

whyNot.B: External validity is whether the result applies to people and settings beyond those studied, which the reviewers did not comment on.
whyNot.C: Reliability is the reproducibility of a measurement on repeated testing, not freedom from bias in a study's result.
whyNot.D: Power is the probability of detecting a true effect; a trial can be well powered and still biased, or unbiased and underpowered.
whyNot.E: Generalizability is another name for external validity, not the property described.

items.objective: Define internal validity and distinguish it from external validity.

items.stemHtml: A well-conducted randomized trial shows that a fictional inhaled drug reduces asthma exacerbations. It enrolled non-smokers aged 18 to 50 years with no other lung or heart disease. A physician considers prescribing the drug to a 68-year-old woman who has smoked for 40 years and has features of both asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Which of the following is the main limitation of applying the trial to her?

options.label: A
options.html: Poor internal validity due to confounding

options.label: B
options.html: Measurement bias in counting exacerbations

options.label: C
options.html: A likely type I error in the trial

options.label: D
options.html: Limited external validity for patients like her

options.label: E
options.html: Lack of blinding of the outcome assessors

items.explanationHtml:
The trial's eligibility criteria excluded older adults, smokers and people with overlapping lung disease. Its result may be internally valid yet have limited external validity for this patient, whose response and side effects could differ.

Ask whether the patient would have been eligible for the trial and, if not, whether there is a biologically plausible reason the effect would differ. Exclusion criteria are the usual place to look.

Takeaway: strict exclusion criteria protect internal validity but can limit generalizability to older or sicker patients.

whyNot.A: Randomization in a well-conducted trial protects against confounding, so the problem is not the trial's internal validity.
whyNot.B: Nothing suggests exacerbations were counted differently between groups.
whyNot.C: There is no reason to suspect a false-positive result in a well-conducted trial; her problem is that she was not represented.
whyNot.E: The trial is described as well conducted; blinding is not the issue raised by her age and smoking history.

items.objective: Recognize how a trial's eligibility criteria limit its external validity for a particular patient.

items.stemHtml: In a tightly monitored trial with weekly visits and pill counts, a fictional preventive migraine drug reduces migraine days by 4.1 per month compared with placebo. A later study in routine primary care, where patients take the drug as they normally would, finds a reduction of 1.6 days per month. Which of the following best explains the difference between the two results?

options.label: A
options.html: The second study had a type I error

options.label: B
options.html: The first trial was affected by lead-time bias

options.label: C
options.html: The first trial measured efficacy and the second measured effectiveness

options.label: D
options.html: Regression to the mean affected only the second study

options.label: E
options.html: The second study had higher internal validity

items.explanationHtml:
Efficacy is the effect under ideal, controlled conditions (selected patients, close follow-up, good adherence). Effectiveness is the effect in everyday practice, where adherence is lower, patients are more varied and follow-up is looser. Effectiveness is usually smaller.

Explanatory trials estimate efficacy; pragmatic trials, which enrol typical patients in usual settings, estimate effectiveness and have greater external validity.

Takeaway: efficacy = works under ideal conditions; effectiveness = works in real practice, usually less.

whyNot.A: A type I error is a false-positive finding; both studies found a benefit, and the issue is the size of the benefit in different settings.
whyNot.B: Lead-time bias applies to survival after earlier diagnosis by screening, not to a treatment's effect on migraine days.
whyNot.D: Regression to the mean would affect both studies' baseline measurements and is not the systematic explanation here.
whyNot.E: Routine-care studies usually have less control (more confounding or missing data), not higher internal validity than a tightly monitored trial.

items.objective: Distinguish efficacy from effectiveness.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial compares a 12-month supervised exercise programme with usual care for weight loss in adults with obesity. By 12 months, 30% of the exercise group and 5% of the usual-care group have dropped out, and those who dropped out of the exercise group mostly reported that they were not losing weight. The analysis includes only participants who completed the study. Which of the following is most threatened by this pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: External validity, because the participants were adults with obesity

options.label: B
options.html: Internal validity, because losses differ between groups and are related to the outcome

options.label: C
options.html: Statistical power only, because fewer participants were analysed

options.label: D
options.html: Reliability of the weight measurements

options.label: E
options.html: Allocation concealment at the time of randomization

items.explanationHtml:
Unequal dropout that is related to the outcome (attrition bias, a form of selection bias) leaves an exercise group made up mostly of people who were succeeding. Comparing completers then exaggerates the benefit, damaging internal validity.

Intention-to-treat analysis of all randomized participants, with sensible handling of missing data, and efforts to keep follow-up complete limit this problem.

Takeaway: differential, outcome-related loss to follow-up biases a trial's own result, a threat to internal validity.

whyNot.A: Being adults with obesity is the intended study population; the issue is a bias within the trial, not its applicability.
whyNot.C: Fewer participants would reduce power, but the greater problem is that the remaining exercise group is selected for success.
whyNot.D: Nothing suggests that scales or measurement methods were faulty.
whyNot.E: Allocation concealment concerns the assignment process at entry; the bias here arose afterwards, during follow-up.

items.objective: Recognize differential loss to follow-up as a threat to internal validity.

items.stemHtml: Investigators are designing a randomized trial of a fictional antihypertensive drug. They want the results to apply as widely as possible to adults treated in ordinary practice while keeping the comparison between groups unbiased. Which of the following design choices best achieves both aims?

options.label: A
options.html: Excluding patients who miss doses during a placebo run-in before randomization

options.label: B
options.html: Restricting enrolment to patients aged 40 to 55 years without comorbidity

options.label: C
options.html: Running the trial at a single academic centre with specialist staff

options.label: D
options.html: Replacing randomization with a matched cohort drawn from health records

options.label: E
options.html: Randomizing patients with broad eligibility criteria at many community practices

items.explanationHtml:
Randomization keeps the comparison unbiased (internal validity). Broad eligibility criteria and typical community settings make the participants resemble the patients who will use the drug (external validity). This is the logic of a pragmatic trial.

Many design choices trade one form of validity for the other: restriction, run-in periods and expert single-centre care improve control at the cost of generalizability.

Takeaway: randomize for internal validity; enrol broadly in usual settings for external validity.

whyNot.A: A run-in that excludes non-adherent patients makes the enrolled group unrepresentative of ordinary practice and so narrows external validity.
whyNot.B: Restriction reduces variability and possible confounding but limits the people to whom results apply.
whyNot.C: A single academic centre with specialist staff is unlike most practices, which limits external validity.
whyNot.D: A matched cohort gives up randomization, so unmeasured confounding threatens internal validity.

items.objective: Identify trial design features that balance internal and external validity.

items.stemHtml: A state health department wants to estimate the proportion of its adult residents who have untreated hypertension. Which of the following study procedures would most directly improve the external validity of the estimate?

options.label: A
options.html: Selecting participants by random sampling from all adult residents

options.label: B
options.html: Randomly allocating participants to receive blood pressure measurement by a nurse or by a machine

options.label: C
options.html: Blinding the staff who measure blood pressure to participants' medical history

options.label: D
options.html: Recruiting a larger number of volunteers at shopping centres

options.label: E
options.html: Matching participants with and without hypertension on age and sex

items.explanationHtml:
Random sampling gives every member of the target population a known chance of selection, so the sample resembles the population and the estimate can be generalized to it (external validity).

Do not confuse it with random allocation (randomization) in a trial, which assigns participants to groups and protects internal validity. A study can have one without the other.

Takeaway: random sampling supports external validity; random allocation supports internal validity.

whyNot.B: Random allocation to measurement methods compares methods; it does not make the sample represent the state.
whyNot.C: Blinding reduces measurement bias (internal validity) but does not make the sample representative.
whyNot.D: A larger convenience sample is more precise but still unrepresentative, because shoppers who volunteer differ from the general population.
whyNot.E: Matching is used to control confounding in comparative studies and does not help estimate a population prevalence.

items.objective: Distinguish random sampling from random allocation and link each to the validity it protects.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial of 40,000 adults compares a fictional fortified table salt with ordinary salt. After 2 years, mean systolic blood pressure is 0.8 mm Hg lower in the fortified-salt group (95% confidence interval, 0.5 to 1.1 mm Hg; P < .001). Which of the following best describes this result?

options.label: A
options.html: Clinically important but not statistically significant

options.label: B
options.html: Neither statistically significant nor clinically important

options.label: C
options.html: Statistically significant but unlikely to be clinically important for an individual

options.label: D
options.html: Statistically significant and therefore clinically important

options.label: E
options.html: Not interpretable without a larger sample

items.explanationHtml:
Very large studies can detect very small differences. A blood-pressure reduction of under 1 mm Hg (the whole interval lies between 0.5 and 1.1) is statistically significant but too small to matter much for one person, so it is not clinically significant.

Judge clinical importance from the size of the effect and its confidence interval compared with what matters to patients, not from the P value. A small effect may still matter at the population level, which is a separate public health question.

Takeaway: large samples make trivial effects significant; look at the effect size and interval, not just P.

whyNot.A: The P value is below .001 and the interval excludes 0, so the result is statistically significant.
whyNot.B: The interval excludes 0, so the result is statistically significant.
whyNot.D: A small P value shows that chance is an unlikely explanation, not that the effect is large enough to matter to patients.
whyNot.E: With 40,000 participants the estimate is already very precise; a larger sample would only narrow an interval that is already small.

items.objective: Distinguish statistical significance from clinical significance in a very large trial.

items.stemHtml: Before starting a trial of a new pain treatment, investigators review studies of what change on a 0-to-10 pain scale patients notice and value. They decide that a difference of 1.5 points is the smallest change that patients would regard as worthwhile and that would justify a change in treatment. Which of the following terms best describes this value?

options.label: A
options.html: Standard error of the mean

options.label: B
options.html: Effect modifier

options.label: C
options.html: Number needed to treat

options.label: D
options.html: Minimal clinically important difference

options.label: E
options.html: Type I error rate

items.explanationHtml:
The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change in an outcome that patients perceive as beneficial and that would lead to a change in care. Investigators use it to set the target difference in a sample-size calculation and to judge whether a result is clinically meaningful.

A result can be statistically significant yet smaller than the MCID, or larger than the MCID yet not significant because the study was small.

Takeaway: the MCID is the threshold for clinical, not statistical, importance.

whyNot.A: The standard error of the mean measures the precision of an estimated mean, not the importance of a difference.
whyNot.B: An effect modifier is a variable that changes the size of an effect across its levels.
whyNot.C: The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of an absolute risk reduction for a binary outcome.
whyNot.E: The type I error rate (alpha) is the chosen probability of a false-positive result.

items.objective: Define the minimal clinically important difference.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial of a fictional drug in adults with chronic heart failure records the following outcomes. Which of the following is a surrogate end point?

options.label: A
options.html: All-cause death

options.label: B
options.html: Hospitalization for heart failure

options.label: C
options.html: Score on a quality-of-life questionnaire

options.label: D
options.html: Ability to walk one block without stopping

options.label: E
options.html: Change in plasma B-type natriuretic peptide concentration

items.explanationHtml:
A surrogate end point is a laboratory value, imaging finding or physiological measurement used in place of an outcome that matters to patients, on the assumption that changing it will change that outcome. A blood biomarker such as B-type natriuretic peptide is a typical example.

Surrogates allow smaller, shorter trials, but a drug can improve a surrogate without improving, or while worsening, patient-important outcomes such as death, hospitalization and function.

Takeaway: lab values and physiological measures are surrogates; how patients feel, function or survive are patient-important outcomes.

whyNot.A: Death is the most patient-important outcome there is, not a substitute for one.
whyNot.B: Hospitalization is an event that patients experience directly.
whyNot.C: A quality-of-life score measures how patients feel and function, a patient-important outcome.
whyNot.D: Walking ability is a measure of function that patients directly care about.

items.objective: Distinguish a surrogate end point from patient-important outcomes.

items.stemHtml: Investigators planning a cardiovascular prevention trial combine cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke into a single primary outcome. Which of the following is the main advantage of using this composite end point?

options.label: A
options.html: It shows that the treatment affects each component equally

options.label: B
options.html: It increases the number of outcome events, so fewer participants are needed for the same power

options.label: C
options.html: It removes the need to blind outcome assessors

options.label: D
options.html: It makes the results applicable to a wider population

options.label: E
options.html: It allows each component to be tested separately without any adjustment for multiple comparisons

items.explanationHtml:
Combining several outcomes into a composite end point raises the event rate, which increases power and reduces the sample size or follow-up needed.

The cost is interpretation: the components may differ in importance and in how much the treatment affects them. Always look at the components, especially when a less serious one (such as a procedure or hospital visit) accounts for most of the events.

Takeaway: composite end points buy power with more events; check which component drives the result.

whyNot.A: A significant composite does not show that each component was affected; the effect may come mainly from one component.
whyNot.C: Composite outcomes still need blinded, standardized adjudication, especially for less objective components.
whyNot.D: Generalizability depends on who was enrolled and the setting, not on how the outcome is defined.
whyNot.E: Separate testing of components is a secondary analysis and raises the same multiple-comparison concerns as other secondary outcomes.

items.objective: Explain why trials use composite end points and the main caution in interpreting them.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial of a fictional anti-inflammatory drug in adults with rheumatoid arthritis finds no significant difference in its prespecified primary outcome, disease activity score at 6 months (P = .34). Of 15 secondary outcomes, one (morning stiffness duration) is significantly better with the drug (P = .03). The press release states that the drug 'improves morning stiffness'. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: The trial did not show benefit, and the stiffness finding should be treated as hypothesis-generating

options.label: B
options.html: The drug is effective because one outcome reached significance

options.label: C
options.html: The primary outcome should be replaced with morning stiffness in the final report

options.label: D
options.html: The stiffness finding is more reliable than the primary outcome because its P value is smaller

options.label: E
options.html: The stiffness result shows the trial was underpowered for the primary outcome

items.explanationHtml:
A trial's conclusion rests on its prespecified primary end point. With 15 secondary outcomes tested at alpha 0.05, the chance of at least one false-positive result is high (1 − 0.9515 ≈ 54%), so a single significant secondary outcome in a negative trial is best seen as hypothesis-generating.

Watch for 'spin': abstracts and press releases that emphasize a secondary or subgroup finding when the primary outcome was negative.

Takeaway: a negative primary outcome is not rescued by one significant secondary outcome.

whyNot.B: Finding one significant result among 15 secondary tests is roughly what chance alone would produce, so it does not show efficacy.
whyNot.C: Switching the primary outcome after seeing the results is outcome switching and invalidates the trial's main test.
whyNot.D: A smaller P value in a secondary test does not outweigh the prespecified primary analysis, especially with many tests.
whyNot.E: Power for the primary outcome cannot be inferred from a secondary finding; the secondary result says nothing about it.

items.objective: Interpret a significant secondary outcome in a trial with a negative primary end point.

items.stemHtml: A pilot randomized trial of 40 adults with chronic neck pain compares a fictional manual therapy with sham treatment. The prespecified minimal clinically important difference on the pain scale used is 5 points. The mean improvement is 9 points greater with the active therapy (95% confidence interval, −1 to 19 points; P = .08). Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: The therapy has been shown to be ineffective

options.label: B
options.html: The result is statistically significant and clinically important

options.label: C
options.html: The result is clinically trivial because it is not statistically significant

options.label: D
options.html: The best estimate exceeds the clinically important difference, but the result is too imprecise to be conclusive

options.label: E
options.html: The trial shows that the therapy is harmful in some patients

items.explanationHtml:
The point estimate (9 points) is well above the MCID (5 points), so the effect may be clinically important, but the interval (−1 to 19) includes no effect. The study is inconclusive: too small to rule out either no benefit or a large benefit.

Clinical and statistical significance are separate questions. Here the effect may be clinically meaningful yet is not statistically significant, the reverse of the large-trial, trivial-effect pattern. A larger trial is the logical next step.

Takeaway: a wide interval spanning both no effect and important benefit means 'not yet known', not 'no effect'.

whyNot.A: A non-significant result does not show ineffectiveness; most of the interval lies above the clinically important difference.
whyNot.B: The interval includes 0 and P is above .05, so the result is not statistically significant.
whyNot.C: Clinical importance depends on the size of the effect, and the point estimate is nearly twice the clinically important difference.
whyNot.E: The interval's lower limit of −1 point is compatible with a very small worsening on average, but it does not show harm in anyone.

items.objective: Interpret a result that is possibly clinically important but not statistically significant.

items.stemHtml: In a large randomized trial, a fictional cholesterol-lowering drug reduced the 10-year risk of major cardiovascular events from 10% with placebo to 7% with the drug, a relative risk reduction of 30% that was similar across baseline-risk groups. A patient's estimated 10-year risk without treatment is 20%. Assuming the same relative risk reduction applies to him, and rounding up to the next whole number, how many patients with his risk would need to be treated for 10 years to prevent one event?
items.explanationHtml:
For this patient: ARR = baseline risk × RRR = 0.20 × 0.30 = 0.06. NNT = 1 / 0.06 = 16.7, rounded up to 17.

Relative risk reductions are often fairly constant across baseline risk, but absolute benefit is not. The trial's average patient (10% risk) had an ARR of 3% and an NNT of about 34; a patient at twice the risk gains twice as much in absolute terms.

Takeaway: patient-specific NNT = 1 / (patient's baseline risk × RRR); higher baseline risk means smaller NNT.

whyNot.A: 4 is 1 divided by the relative risk reduction (1 / 0.30 = 3.3, rounded up), which is not an absolute difference.
whyNot.B: 5 is 1 divided by his baseline risk (1 / 0.20), ignoring how much the drug lowers it.
whyNot.C: 8 is 1 divided by his expected risk on treatment (1 / 0.14 = 7.1, rounded up), not by the risk reduction.
whyNot.E: 34 is the trial's own number needed to treat (1 / 0.03, rounded up), which applies to patients with a 10% baseline risk, not to him.

items.objective: Calculate a patient-specific number needed to treat from baseline risk and relative risk reduction.

items.stemHtml: Over 2 years, a fictional anticoagulant reduces the risk of ischaemic stroke from 4.0% to 2.0% and increases the risk of major bleeding from 1.0% to 1.5% in a trial of adults with atrial fibrillation. Which of the following best summarizes the expected results for every 200 patients treated for 2 years?

options.label: A
options.html: 2 strokes prevented and 1 major bleed caused

options.label: B
options.html: 4 strokes prevented and 1 major bleed caused

options.label: C
options.html: 4 strokes prevented and 3 major bleeds caused

options.label: D
options.html: 50 strokes prevented and 1 major bleed caused

options.label: E
options.html: 100 strokes prevented and 50 major bleeds caused

items.explanationHtml:
ARR for stroke = 4.0% − 2.0% = 2.0%, so 0.02 × 200 = 4 strokes prevented (NNT = 50). Absolute risk increase for bleeding = 1.5% − 1.0% = 0.5%, so 0.005 × 200 = 1 extra major bleed (NNH = 200).

Expressing benefit and harm as natural frequencies in the same group of patients ('out of 200 people like you…') is the clearest way to weigh them and to discuss them with a patient.

Takeaway: convert ARR and absolute risk increase into events per fixed number of patients to compare benefit and harm.

whyNot.A: 2 strokes prevented would correspond to an absolute risk reduction of 1%, half the true 2%.
whyNot.C: 3 extra bleeds per 200 would need an absolute increase of 1.5%, which is the treated group's total bleeding risk, not the increase.
whyNot.D: 50 is the number needed to treat, not the number of strokes prevented per 200.
whyNot.E: These figures use the relative changes (50% fewer strokes, 50% more bleeds) as if they were counts.

items.objective: Compare benefit and harm using absolute risk differences expressed as natural frequencies.

items.stemHtml: A preventive drug lowers the risk of an outcome by the same relative amount (40%) in all patients. Patient X has a baseline 5-year risk of 2%, and patient Y has a baseline 5-year risk of 20%. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: Both patients gain the same absolute risk reduction

options.label: B
options.html: Patient X gains a larger absolute risk reduction because her risk is lower

options.label: C
options.html: Patient Y gains a larger absolute risk reduction and has a smaller number needed to treat

options.label: D
options.html: Both patients have the same number needed to treat because the relative effect is equal

options.label: E
options.html: The relative risk reduction is larger for patient Y

items.explanationHtml:
ARR = baseline risk × RRR. Patient X: 0.02 × 0.40 = 0.008 (NNT 125). Patient Y: 0.20 × 0.40 = 0.08 (NNT 12.5, about 13).

Because relative effects are often similar across risk groups, absolute benefit is largest in high-risk patients. This is why treatment thresholds in guidelines are commonly based on estimated absolute risk.

Takeaway: same relative effect, higher baseline risk → larger absolute benefit and smaller NNT.

whyNot.A: The absolute reductions differ tenfold: 0.8 versus 8 percentage points.
