She believes that research decisions (here, the treatment assignment) will be individualized for her benefit as in ordinary care. That is therapeutic misconception. In a randomized, blinded trial, assignment is by chance and neither she nor her cardiologist chooses.

It matters because it undermines comprehension, one of the conditions of valid consent. The fix is to explain randomization and blinding plainly and recheck understanding, which is exactly what the coordinator's teach-back question uncovered.

Takeaway: a participant who thinks randomization or protocol rules serve their personal care has a therapeutic misconception.

whyNot.A: The placebo effect is improvement from receiving an inert treatment; she is describing a belief about how treatment is chosen.
whyNot.B: The Hawthorne effect is a change in behaviour because people know they are being observed.
whyNot.C: Undue influence arises from an excessive inducement such as a large payment; no offer is described.
whyNot.E: Recall bias is differential memory of past exposures in retrospective studies.

items.objective: Recognize therapeutic misconception during the research consent process.

items.stemHtml: Researchers plan a minimal-risk study of oral bacteria in healthy 9-year-old children that involves a saliva sample and a short questionnaire. The IRB has approved the protocol. Which of the following is required before a child is enrolled?

options.label: A
options.html: The child's own consent, without parental involvement

options.label: B
options.html: Parental permission only, without informing the child

options.label: C
options.html: Parental permission and the child's assent

options.label: D
options.html: Approval of the child's school principal

options.label: E
options.html: A court order authorizing participation

items.explanationHtml:
Children cannot give legal consent, so research needs the permission of a parent or guardian plus the child's assent, an affirmative agreement appropriate to age, when the child is capable of it. For minimal-risk research, the IRB may find that one parent's permission is enough.

Assent must be active: a child who simply does not object has not assented. A school-age child can understand a saliva test and a questionnaire, so assent should be sought.

Takeaway: pediatric research needs parental permission and, when the child is able, the child's assent.

whyNot.A: A 9-year-old cannot give legally effective consent to research; parental permission is needed.
whyNot.B: Children able to understand should be asked for assent; leaving the child out ignores respect for persons.
whyNot.D: School officials have no authority to give permission for a child's research participation.
whyNot.E: Courts are not involved in routine pediatric research; parental permission and assent suffice for minimal-risk studies.

items.objective: State the consent requirements for minimal-risk research in children.

items.stemHtml: An IRB-approved trial tests a new drug for severe agitation in people with advanced Alzheimer disease. An 81-year-old woman in a nursing home meets the eligibility criteria. Her geriatrician documents that she cannot understand or reason about the study. Her son holds a durable power of attorney for health care, which under state law allows him to make research decisions for her. Which of the following is the most appropriate basis for enrolling her?

options.label: A
options.html: The geriatrician's judgment that the study is in her interest

options.label: B
options.html: The nursing home administrator's signature

options.label: C
options.html: A waiver of consent from the IRB chair

options.label: D
options.html: Her signature, obtained on a day when she seems calm

options.label: E
options.html: Her son's consent, with her own objections respected

items.explanationHtml:
When an adult lacks capacity for a research decision, consent comes from a legally authorized representative (LAR) as defined by applicable law, here her son. The LAR should decide on the basis of her known wishes or, if unknown, her best interests. Researchers should still explain the study to her as far as possible, seek her assent and respect any objection or distress during the study.

The study also needs the IRB to have approved enrolment of adults who lack capacity, which is usually justified when the research is about the condition that causes the incapacity, as here.

Takeaway: adults who lack capacity enter research through LAR consent, with their own dissent respected.

whyNot.A: A physician cannot substitute their own judgment for consent; a legally authorized representative must decide.
whyNot.B: The administrator is not her legally authorized representative and has potential conflicts of interest.
whyNot.C: A greater-than-minimal-risk drug trial does not meet the criteria for a waiver of consent.
whyNot.D: She lacks capacity for this decision; a signature without understanding is not valid consent.

items.objective: Apply surrogate consent and respect for dissent when enrolling adults who lack capacity.

items.stemHtml: A hospital prepares a dataset for public release using the HIPAA safe harbor method. It concerns 600 adults treated for pancreatitis. Which of the following data elements may remain in the released dataset?

options.label: A
options.html: Year of diagnosis

options.label: B
options.html: Exact date of hospital admission

options.label: C
options.html: Five-digit ZIP code of residence

options.label: D
options.html: Exact age of a 93-year-old patient

options.label: E
options.html: Medical record number

items.explanationHtml:
Safe harbor removes 18 types of identifiers. For dates, every element except the year goes: admission, discharge, birth and death dates become years. Geographic units smaller than a state are removed except, in some cases, the first three digits of the ZIP code. Ages above 89 are collapsed into one category. Record numbers, names, contact details and other unique codes are removed.

The year of an event, the diagnosis itself, laboratory values and sex can stay, provided the hospital has no actual knowledge that what remains could identify someone.

Takeaway: under safe harbor, years can stay but full dates, small geography, ages over 89 and record numbers cannot.

whyNot.B: All elements of dates except the year must be removed under safe harbor.
whyNot.C: Safe harbor allows at most the first three ZIP digits, and only when that area holds more than 20,000 people.
whyNot.D: Ages over 89 must be grouped into a single category of 90 or older.
whyNot.E: Medical record numbers are direct identifiers and must be removed.

items.objective: Identify which data elements may remain after safe harbor de-identification.

items.stemHtml: A health services researcher at another university asks a hospital for a dataset of all emergency visits for asthma over 5 years. She needs the exact visit dates and five-digit ZIP codes to link the visits to daily air pollution levels. She does not need names, addresses, phone numbers or record numbers, and she will not contact patients. Which of the following is required for the hospital to release these data without patient authorization?

options.label: A
options.html: Certification that the data meet safe harbor

options.label: B
options.html: Written authorization from each patient

options.label: C
options.html: Notification of HHS before release

options.label: D
options.html: A data use agreement with the researcher

options.label: E
options.html: Nothing, because names are removed

items.explanationHtml:
A dataset that has direct identifiers removed but keeps dates, city, state, ZIP code or ages is a limited data set. It is still PHI, so it cannot be released freely, but it may be disclosed for research, public health or health care operations without individual authorization if the recipient signs a data use agreement. The agreement limits use to the stated purpose and forbids re-identifying or contacting individuals.

Recognize it on the exam by the combination of "no names or record numbers" with "exact dates" or "ZIP codes".

Takeaway: dates plus ZIP codes without direct identifiers is a limited data set, released under a data use agreement.

whyNot.A: Exact dates and five-digit ZIP codes are not permitted under safe harbor, so the dataset is not de-identified.
whyNot.B: A limited data set can be disclosed for research without individual authorization.
whyNot.C: No HHS notification is required for a limited data set; notification applies to breaches.
whyNot.E: Removing names alone does not de-identify data; dates and ZIP codes are still identifiers.

items.objective: Recognize a limited data set and the data use agreement it requires.

items.stemHtml: A hospital trains new staff on the HIPAA minimum necessary standard. The trainer gives several examples of disclosures of a patient's record. Which of the following disclosures is exempt from the minimum necessary standard?

options.label: A
options.html: Claims data sent to the patient's health insurer for payment

options.label: B
options.html: Records reviewed by the hospital's quality committee

options.label: C
options.html: Charts pulled by an internal auditor checking coding accuracy

options.label: D
options.html: The full record sent to a consulting cardiologist treating the patient

options.label: E
options.html: A chart extract given to the billing contractor

items.explanationHtml:
The minimum necessary standard limits uses and disclosures for payment and health care operations, but it does not apply to disclosures to a health care provider for treatment. Clinicians need the freedom to share whatever is relevant for care. It also does not apply to disclosures to the patient, under the patient's authorization, to HHS for enforcement, or when required by law.

On the exam, a stem in which one clinician refuses to share records with another clinician who is treating the same patient is a signal that HIPAA is being misapplied.

Takeaway: minimum necessary applies to payment and operations, not to treatment disclosures between providers.

whyNot.A: Payment disclosures are subject to minimum necessary; only the information needed for the claim should be sent.
whyNot.B: Health care operations such as quality review are subject to minimum necessary.
whyNot.C: Internal auditing is an operations use and must be limited to the information needed.
whyNot.E: A business associate performing billing receives only what billing requires.

items.objective: Identify disclosures that are exempt from the minimum necessary standard.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man's blood pressure readings are recorded in several places: his family physician's office, which bills insurers electronically; a consumer fitness app he downloaded himself; his employer's human resources file; a life insurance application; and his daughter's school nurse log, where he once had his blood pressure checked at a school event. Which of these holders of his information is a HIPAA covered entity?

options.label: A
options.html: The consumer fitness app company

options.label: B
options.html: The family physician's office

options.label: C
options.html: The employer's human resources office

options.label: D
options.html: The life insurance company

options.label: E
options.html: The school nurse's office

items.explanationHtml:
HIPAA covered entities are health plans, health care clearinghouses and health care providers who conduct standard electronic transactions such as electronic billing. The family physician's office qualifies. Business associates working for these entities are also bound.

Many holders of health data are outside HIPAA: consumer apps the person chose, employers (for employment records), life and disability insurers, and schools. Other laws (for example, education privacy law or consumer protection law) may apply, but HIPAA does not.

Takeaway: HIPAA binds plans, clearinghouses and electronically billing providers and their business associates, not everyone who holds health data.

whyNot.A: An app chosen by a consumer and not acting for a provider or plan is outside HIPAA.
whyNot.C: Employment records held by an employer are excluded from protected health information.
whyNot.D: Life insurers are not health plans and are not covered entities under HIPAA.
whyNot.E: Records held by schools are generally governed by education privacy law rather than HIPAA.

items.objective: Identify which organizations are HIPAA covered entities.

items.stemHtml: A psychiatrist keeps her personal session notes on a patient's psychotherapy separately from the medical record, which holds the diagnosis, medications, session dates and treatment plan. The patient's health insurer, processing a claim, asks for copies of the separate session notes. Which of the following best describes the requirement for releasing these notes to the insurer?

options.label: A
options.html: They may be released without authorization because the request concerns payment

options.label: B
options.html: They may be released once the patient's name is removed

options.label: C
options.html: They may be released only with the patient's specific written authorization

options.label: D
options.html: They may be released only if a court orders it

options.label: E
options.html: They may be released if only the minimum necessary pages are sent

items.explanationHtml:
Psychotherapy notes, the clinician's separately kept notes analyzing the content of counselling sessions, receive special protection. Most uses and disclosures of them, including to a health plan for payment, need the patient's specific written authorization. Health plans cannot require that authorization as a condition of enrolment or payment.

The information an insurer usually needs (diagnosis, medications, session start and stop times, treatment plan, results of tests) sits in the medical record, is not psychotherapy notes and can be disclosed for payment under minimum necessary.

Takeaway: separately kept psychotherapy notes need the patient's authorization even for payment.

whyNot.A: Psychotherapy notes are an exception: even for payment they need the patient's specific authorization.
whyNot.B: Removing a name does not de-identify detailed session notes, and the protection is not about names.
whyNot.D: A court order is one route for some disclosures, but the general rule for these notes is the patient's authorization.
whyNot.E: Minimum necessary does not convert a disclosure that needs authorization into one that does not.

items.objective: Apply the special HIPAA protection for psychotherapy notes.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is diagnosed with measles at an urgent care clinic. State law lists measles as a disease that clinicians must report to the health department. The patient asks the physician not to tell anyone. Which of the following best describes the report under HIPAA?

options.label: A
options.html: It requires the patient's written authorization

options.label: B
options.html: It requires the patient's verbal agreement

options.label: C
options.html: It may be made only with the patient's name removed

options.label: D
options.html: It is prohibited unless the patient is a minor

options.label: E
options.html: It is permitted without the patient's authorization

items.explanationHtml:
HIPAA permits covered entities to disclose PHI without authorization to public health authorities legally entitled to receive it, for purposes such as preventing or controlling disease. Reporting a notifiable infection to the health department is the classic example, and when state law requires the report the physician must make it.

The physician should still tell the patient that the report will be made and why, and that the health department keeps the information confidential. Honesty preserves trust even when the patient cannot veto the disclosure.

Takeaway: mandatory disease reporting to public health is a permitted disclosure that needs no authorization.

whyNot.A: Required public health reporting does not need the patient's authorization.
whyNot.B: The patient's agreement is not a condition of mandatory disease reporting.
whyNot.C: Health departments need identifying information to trace contacts; HIPAA permits the identified report.
whyNot.D: Age is irrelevant to public health reporting of infectious diseases.

items.objective: Recognize public health reporting as a permitted disclosure under HIPAA.

items.stemHtml: A community hospital that has started enrolling patients in federally funded trials sets up its own IRB. The six members are four staff physicians, a staff nurse and the hospital's in-house lawyer. All six are employed by the hospital. Which of the following federal requirements does this board fail to meet?

options.label: A
options.html: At least one member not otherwise affiliated with the institution

options.label: B
options.html: At least ten members drawn from different departments

options.label: C
options.html: A majority of members whose main concerns are nonscientific

options.label: D
options.html: A patient advocate serving as the board's chair

options.label: E
options.html: A biostatistician among the voting members

items.explanationHtml:
An IRB must have at least five members with varied backgrounds, including at least one scientist, at least one member whose main concerns are nonscientific, and at least one member who is not otherwise affiliated with the institution and is not in the immediate family of someone who is. The unaffiliated member brings the community's perspective and some independence from institutional interests.

Here the size and the nonscientist requirements are met (the lawyer counts), but everyone is a hospital employee.

Takeaway: an IRB needs five or more members, a scientist, a nonscientist and someone unaffiliated with the institution.

whyNot.B: The minimum is five members, so six is enough.
whyNot.C: Only one member whose main concerns are nonscientific is required; the lawyer satisfies this.
whyNot.D: There is no requirement for the chair to be a patient advocate.
whyNot.E: Statistical expertise can be consulted as needed; it is not a mandatory seat.

items.objective: State the membership requirements for an IRB.

items.stemHtml: An investigator proposes a study in which healthy, nonpregnant adult volunteers give a single small blood sample by venipuncture and complete a 10-minute questionnaire about diet. Results are stored with a study code, and the key linking codes to names is kept separately. No other procedures are involved. Which level of IRB review is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Exempt determination

options.label: B
options.html: Full-board review

options.label: C
options.html: No review, because the data are coded

options.label: D
options.html: Expedited review

options.label: E
options.html: Review by the FDA

items.explanationHtml:
Expedited review applies when research is no more than minimal risk and fits one of the published categories. Collection of small volumes of blood by finger stick, heel stick or venipuncture from healthy nonpregnant adults is one such category, and surveys are another. An experienced IRB member or the chair reviews it instead of the convened board.

Expedited reviewers may approve or require modifications, but they cannot disapprove; a study they would disapprove must go to the full board.

Takeaway: minimal-risk studies in the published categories, such as a single venipuncture, qualify for expedited review.

whyNot.A: Exempt categories do not include blood draws; collecting a specimen by venipuncture needs IRB review.
whyNot.B: Full-board review is for research above minimal risk or outside the expedited categories; this study is minimal risk and fits them.
whyNot.C: Coding does not remove the need for review; the investigator still collects identifiable private information.
whyNot.E: No drug, biologic or device is being tested, so FDA review is not involved.

items.objective: Choose the correct level of IRB review for a minimal-risk study with a blood draw.

items.stemHtml: A medical educator plans an anonymous online survey of adult faculty members about the number of hours they spend teaching each week. The survey collects no names, email addresses or other identifiers, and the questions carry no meaningful risk if answers were disclosed. Which category of IRB review does this study most likely fall into?

options.label: A
options.html: Full-board review

options.label: B
options.html: Exempt

options.label: C
options.html: Expedited review

options.label: D
options.html: Continuing review only

options.label: E
options.html: FDA review

items.explanationHtml:
Surveys of adults that record no identifiers, or whose disclosure would not put participants at risk, fall into an exempt category of the Common Rule. Exempt research is not reviewed by the convened IRB, but it still needs an institutional determination that it qualifies, usually made by the IRB office rather than the investigator, and it should still give participants honest information about the survey.

Other common exempt categories include research on normal educational practices, benign behavioural interventions with adults and some secondary uses of existing information.

Takeaway: an anonymous, low-risk survey of adults is typically exempt, as determined by the institution.

whyNot.A: There is no more than minimal risk, so the convened board is not needed.
whyNot.C: Expedited review is for minimal-risk research that does not fit an exempt category; this survey fits one.
whyNot.D: Continuing review is a stage after approval, not a type of initial review.
whyNot.E: No drug, biologic or device is involved.

items.objective: Recognize research that qualifies for an exempt determination.

items.stemHtml: A federally funded study collects saliva samples and questionnaires from adults. It involves no drug or device and is not regulated by the FDA. The IRB approved it by expedited review under the current Common Rule, and the IRB did not document any special reason for further review. Two years into the study, the coordinator asks whether annual continuing review is required. Which of the following best describes the continuing review requirement for this study?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual continuing review is required for all approved research

options.label: B
options.html: Review is required every 6 months because samples are stored

options.label: C
options.html: Continuing review is generally not required for this study

options.label: D
options.html: The full board must re-approve it every year

options.label: E
options.html: Approval lapses after 1 year and the study must close

items.explanationHtml:
Under the Common Rule as revised (effective 2019), continuing review is generally not required for research eligible for expedited review, or for research that has reached the stage of only analyzing data or collecting follow-up information from routine clinical care, unless the IRB documents why it should occur. Full-board studies are still reviewed at least annually. FDA-regulated research remains subject to annual continuing review under FDA rules.

Removing continuing review does not remove oversight: amendments still need approval before use, unanticipated problems must still be reported, and the institution may require periodic check-ins.

Takeaway: under the revised Common Rule, expedited studies generally no longer need annual continuing review.

whyNot.A: The revised Common Rule removed routine continuing review for studies eligible for expedited review.
whyNot.B: There is no 6-month requirement; storage of samples does not create one.
whyNot.D: Expedited studies never needed annual full-board re-approval, and now generally need no continuing review.
whyNot.E: Approval does not lapse automatically for an expedited study under the revised rule unless the IRB sets an expiry.

items.objective: Apply the revised Common Rule's continuing review requirements.

items.stemHtml: A state prison system receives five research proposals that would use federal funding. An IRB that includes a prisoner representative reviews them under the federal protections for prisoners. Which of the following proposals could be approved?

options.label: A
options.html: A pharmacokinetic study of a new antihypertensive drug in healthy inmates

options.label: B
options.html: A cosmetic sunscreen trial using inmates because they are easy to schedule

options.label: C
options.html: A vaccine trial in which participants earn credit toward early parole

options.label: D
options.html: A study of a weight-loss drug in which wardens choose the participants

options.label: E
options.html: A minimal-risk interview study of how solitary confinement affects sleep

items.explanationHtml:
Subpart C of 45 CFR 46 limits federally funded research involving prisoners to specific categories: minimal-risk studies of the causes, effects and processes of incarceration and of criminal behaviour; minimal-risk studies of prisons as institutions or of prisoners as incarcerated people; research on conditions that particularly affect prisoners as a class (after federal consultation); and research on practices that have the intent and a reasonable probability of improving the participant's health. An interview study of the effects of solitary confinement fits the first category.

The IRB must also find that advantages of joining do not impair judgment, that risks would be acceptable to non-prisoner volunteers, that selection is fair, and that participation will not affect parole decisions.

Takeaway: prisoners may be research participants only in limited categories that relate to incarceration or benefit them, never for convenience.

whyNot.A: A study of a drug in healthy inmates with no link to incarceration and no prospect of benefit falls outside the permitted categories.
whyNot.B: Using prisoners for convenience is exactly what the protections forbid; the research is not about prisoners.
whyNot.C: Parole boards may not take participation into account, and parole credit would be an inducement that impairs free choice.
whyNot.D: Selection must be fair and free of arbitrary intervention by prison authorities.

items.objective: Apply the subpart C categories of permissible research involving prisoners.

items.stemHtml: Investigators propose a study of children aged 8 to 14 years with sickle cell disease. Each child would provide an extra research blood sample and a small skin biopsy. The IRB determines that the procedures present a minor increase over minimal risk, offer no direct benefit to the children and are likely to yield knowledge of vital importance about sickle cell disease. Both parents are available for most children. Under the federal protections for children, which of the following is required for enrolment?

options.label: A
options.html: Permission of both parents and the child's assent

options.label: B
options.html: Permission of one parent, without the child's assent

options.label: C
options.html: The child's assent alone, as the study concerns the child's own disease

options.label: D
options.html: Review by a federal expert panel before any IRB approval

options.label: E
options.html: Nothing further, as the IRB's determination substitutes for permission

items.explanationHtml:
Subpart D defines four categories of research involving children. Research with a minor increase over minimal risk, no prospect of direct benefit, experiences similar to the children's usual care, and likely to yield vitally important knowledge about the children's disorder can be approved by an IRB, but it requires the permission of both parents (unless one is deceased, unknown, incompetent or not reasonably available, or only one has legal responsibility) and the child's assent.

Research that is minimal risk, or that offers a prospect of direct benefit, may proceed with one parent's permission if the IRB agrees. Research that fits none of the three IRB-approvable categories needs federal review.

Takeaway: a minor increase over minimal risk with no direct benefit needs both parents' permission plus child assent.

whyNot.B: Assent should be sought from children capable of giving it; one parent's permission is not enough in this risk category.
whyNot.C: Children cannot enrol on their own assent; parental permission is required.
whyNot.D: Federal panel review is for research that cannot be approved under any of the IRB-approvable categories; this study fits one.
whyNot.E: IRB approval never substitutes for parental permission and child assent.

items.objective: Apply the subpart D permission requirements to research with a minor increase over minimal risk.

items.stemHtml: A double-blind trial is comparing a new antithrombotic drug with standard therapy in 9,000 patients after myocardial infarction, with all-cause mortality as an outcome. The protocol schedules three interim analyses of efficacy and safety. Who should review the comparative results by treatment arm at these interim analyses?

options.label: A
options.html: The sponsor's clinical development team

options.label: B
options.html: The site investigators

options.label: C
options.html: The participants' primary care physicians

options.label: D
options.html: An independent data and safety monitoring board

options.label: E
options.html: The editors of the journal that will publish the trial

items.explanationHtml:
Interim comparative data are reviewed by an independent data and safety monitoring board, a committee of clinicians and a biostatistician with no stake in the trial's success. Keeping everyone else blinded protects participants (a body is watching for harm) and the trial's integrity (people running the trial cannot be influenced by early results).

DSMBs are expected for large trials with mortality or major morbidity outcomes like this one. They recommend continuation, modification or stopping, and the sponsor acts on the recommendation.

Takeaway: only an independent DSMB sees unblinded interim results.

whyNot.A: Sponsor staff have financial and scientific interests in the outcome and should remain blinded.
whyNot.B: Investigators who know interim results may change how they enroll, treat or assess participants.
whyNot.C: Primary care physicians are not part of trial oversight and have no role in reviewing interim data.
whyNot.E: Journal editors review completed manuscripts, not ongoing interim data.

items.objective: Identify the body responsible for reviewing interim comparative data.

items.stemHtml: The statistical plan for a placebo-controlled trial calls for four analyses of the primary outcome: three interim analyses and a final analysis. The protocol requires a much smaller P value than 0.05 to stop the trial for benefit at the interim analyses. Which of the following is the main reason for this requirement?

options.label: A
options.html: Interim analyses use outcome measures that are less accurate

options.label: B
options.html: Repeated testing of accumulating data raises the chance of a false-positive result

options.label: C
options.html: Randomization is not yet balanced at the interim analyses

options.label: D
options.html: A stricter threshold prevents loss to follow-up

options.label: E
options.html: A stricter threshold reduces the type II error at each look

items.explanationHtml:
Each analysis is another chance for random variation to produce P < 0.05. Testing accumulating data several times at 0.05 inflates the overall type I error (the probability of declaring a benefit when there is none) well above 5%. Group sequential designs keep the overall error at 0.05 by requiring stricter thresholds at the interim looks, an approach often described as spending the alpha across the analyses.

The price of a strict threshold is lower power at each interim look, which is acceptable because the aim of an interim look is to stop only for overwhelming evidence.

Takeaway: interim boundaries are stricter than 0.05 to keep the overall false-positive rate at its planned level despite repeated looks.

whyNot.A: The same outcome measures are used at every look; accuracy does not change.
whyNot.C: Randomization balances groups at every stage in expectation; the issue is repeated testing.
whyNot.D: Loss to follow-up depends on retention, not on the significance threshold.
whyNot.E: Making the threshold stricter increases, rather than reduces, the chance of missing a true effect at that look.

items.objective: Explain why interim efficacy boundaries are stricter than the final significance level.

items.stemHtml: A trial plans three interim analyses and one final analysis of its primary outcome. To keep the overall two-sided type I error at 0.05, the statisticians use the simplest conservative approach: they divide the alpha equally among all planned analyses. What significance threshold applies at each analysis?
items.explanationHtml:
There are 3 interim + 1 final = 4 analyses. Dividing the overall alpha equally: 0.05 ÷ 4 = 0.0125 at each analysis.

This equal split (a Bonferroni-type adjustment) is conservative because the analyses use overlapping data. Most trials use boundaries that are very strict early and close to 0.05 at the end, but the principle is the same: the more planned looks, the stricter each one.

Takeaway: with an equal split, the per-analysis threshold is the overall alpha divided by the total number of planned analyses, including the final one.

whyNot.A: 0.0100 divides 0.05 by 5, counting one more analysis than the four planned.
whyNot.C: 0.0167 divides 0.05 by 3, counting only the interim analyses and leaving out the final one.
whyNot.D: 0.0250 divides 0.05 by 2, as if there were one interim and one final analysis.
whyNot.E: 0.0500 applies no correction, which lets the overall false-positive rate rise above 5%.
whyNot.F: 0.2000 multiplies 0.05 by 4 instead of dividing, making each test far too lenient.

items.objective: Calculate an equally divided significance threshold for planned interim analyses.

items.stemHtml: A randomized trial of a new drug for preventing stroke in atrial fibrillation was stopped at its first interim analysis, after 60 strokes, because the drug crossed the efficacy boundary with a relative risk of 0.50. Two later trials of the same drug and dose, each completed as planned with more than 600 strokes, both found a relative risk of about 0.80. Which of the following best explains the larger effect in the first trial?

options.label: A
options.html: Lead-time bias from earlier diagnosis of stroke

options.label: B
options.html: Confounding by indication in the treatment group

options.label: C
options.html: Stopping at a time when chance had exaggerated the benefit

options.label: D
options.html: A higher type II error in the first trial

options.label: E
options.html: Loss to follow-up in the later trials

items.explanationHtml:
Accumulating results fluctuate around the true effect. A trial is most likely to cross a strict efficacy boundary early when random variation happens to make the effect look larger than it is, so trials stopped early for benefit systematically overestimate the effect, especially when they have few events. Completed trials with many events give estimates closer to the truth.

This does not mean the first trial was wrong about the direction of the effect; the drug does reduce stroke. But clinicians should expect the true effect to be smaller than in a truncated trial.

Takeaway: trials stopped early for benefit, particularly with few events, tend to overestimate the effect size.

whyNot.A: Lead-time bias affects survival measured from diagnosis in screening studies, not event rates in a randomized trial.
whyNot.B: Randomization prevents confounding by indication.
whyNot.D: A type II error is missing a real effect; it does not explain an exaggerated one.
whyNot.E: Nothing suggests important losses, and completed trials with many events are the more reliable estimates.

items.objective: Explain why trials stopped early for benefit overestimate treatment effects.

items.stemHtml:
A double-blind trial compares a new oral drug with placebo in adults with chronic kidney disease; the primary outcome is a composite of death and dialysis. An independent monitoring board uses the prespecified boundaries shown in the figure, with the test statistic oriented so that positive values favour the new drug. The figure shows the observed statistic at the first two interim looks.

Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation by the board after the second look?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue unchanged, because the final analysis has not been reached

options.label: B
options.html: Stop the trial and recommend the new drug for approval

options.label: C
options.html: Increase the sample size to gain more statistical power

options.label: D
options.html: Unblind the site investigators and let each site decide

options.label: E
options.html: Recommend stopping because of harm from the new drug

items.explanationHtml:
At the second look the observed statistic (Z = −2.6) lies below the dashed harm boundary. Negative values favour placebo, so participants on the new drug are having more deaths or dialysis. Crossing a prespecified harm boundary is the signal for the monitoring board to recommend stopping, so that no more participants are exposed to the harmful arm.

Note the asymmetry: the efficacy boundary at early looks is far from zero, but the harm boundary is closer, because the evidence needed to stop a harmful treatment is usually less than that needed to declare a new treatment better.

Takeaway: an interim statistic that crosses the harm boundary leads to a recommendation to stop for harm.

whyNot.A: A prespecified boundary exists so that the trial can stop before the final analysis when one is crossed.
whyNot.B: The statistic is negative, which favours placebo; the drug is doing worse, not better.
whyNot.C: More participants would expose more people to an arm already crossing the harm boundary.
whyNot.D: Unblinding investigators breaks the trial's integrity, and the decision belongs with the monitoring board and sponsor.

items.objective: Interpret a group sequential monitoring chart to decide on stopping for harm.

items.stemHtml: A trial of a new drug for preventing hospital admissions in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease reaches 60% of its planned events. The monitoring board calculates that, even if the remaining 40% of the trial showed the benefit originally hypothesized, the probability of a statistically significant result at the end is 4%. The trial stops. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: A worthwhile benefit is unlikely even if the trial continued

options.label: B
options.html: The drug has been shown to be equivalent to placebo

options.label: C
options.html: The drug has been shown to increase admissions

options.label: D
options.html: The overall type I error of the trial was exceeded

options.label: E
options.html: The trial should have continued, as futility can be judged only at the end

items.explanationHtml:
Conditional power is the probability of a significant final result given the data so far and an assumption about the future effect. When it is very low even under optimistic assumptions, a meaningful benefit is unlikely and continuing would expose participants to risk and burden without a realistic chance of answering the question. That is a stop for futility.

A futility stop does not prove that the drug equals placebo, nor that it causes harm. Confidence intervals at the stop show which effects remain compatible with the data.

Takeaway: stopping for futility means a meaningful benefit is unlikely, not that the treatments are proven equivalent.

whyNot.B: Equivalence requires a trial designed and powered to show it; a futility stop does not establish it.
whyNot.C: Low conditional power says a benefit is unlikely; it does not show harm.
whyNot.D: Type I error concerns false-positive conclusions of benefit; no benefit was declared.
whyNot.E: Futility rules exist so that a trial that cannot answer its question stops sparing participants further risk.

items.objective: Interpret a trial stopped for futility.

items.stemHtml: A company gives a new oral anticoagulant to 40 healthy adult volunteers for the first time in humans. Small groups receive increasing single doses while investigators measure plasma concentrations, half-life and adverse effects. No efficacy outcome is measured. Which phase of drug development does this study represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Phase 0

options.label: B
options.html: Phase I

options.label: C
options.html: Phase II

options.label: D
options.html: Phase III

options.label: E
options.html: Phase IV

items.explanationHtml:
Phase I studies are the first full-dose exposures in people. They enroll tens of healthy volunteers (or patients, when the drug is too toxic for healthy people) and establish safety, tolerability, a dose range and pharmacokinetics. Dose escalation in small groups and plasma level measurement are the hallmarks.

Phase II then tests efficacy and dose in patients with the condition; phase III confirms efficacy in large randomized trials; phase IV continues after approval.

Takeaway: first-in-human dose escalation with pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers is phase I.

whyNot.A: Phase 0 studies give tiny, subtherapeutic microdoses to a handful of people to study distribution; this study escalates doses to find a tolerable range.
whyNot.C: Phase II studies are done in patients with the target condition and look for evidence of efficacy.
whyNot.D: Phase III trials are large randomized trials in patients that confirm efficacy.
whyNot.E: Phase IV refers to studies after approval and marketing.

items.objective: Identify a phase I study from its design and participants.

items.stemHtml: A new oral drug for type 2 diabetes was approved on the basis of phase III trials that together enrolled 4,500 patients followed for up to 2 years. Three years after marketing, during which more than a million people have used it, spontaneous reports and a cohort study show that the drug causes acute liver failure in about 1 in 25,000 users. Which of the following best explains why the reaction went unrecognized until after approval?

options.label: A
options.html: Phase I studies were done in healthy volunteers

options.label: B
options.html: The phase III trials were not blinded

options.label: C
options.html: Approval relied on a surrogate end point

options.label: D
options.html: The phase III trials were too small to detect so rare an event

options.label: E
options.html: Liver tests are not done in clinical trials

items.explanationHtml:
With 4,500 participants, the expected number of cases at a rate of 1 in 25,000 is 4,500 ÷ 25,000 = 0.18, so most likely no case at all would occur. A rough rule (the rule of three) says that to have a good chance of seeing at least one event with true frequency 1 in N, you need about 3N people exposed, here about 75,000. Premarketing programs rarely reach that size.

That is why post-marketing surveillance (phase IV studies, MedWatch reports, large databases) exists: rare and delayed harms surface only after wide use.

Takeaway: premarketing trials are too small to detect rare adverse effects; post-marketing surveillance finds them.

whyNot.A: Phase I volunteers are few and briefly exposed; the issue is the limited size of all premarketing trials, not who joined phase I.
whyNot.B: Blinding reduces bias in outcome assessment; it does not determine whether a rare event is observed.
whyNot.C: Even trials with clinical end points of this size would be unlikely to show a 1-in-25,000 event.
whyNot.E: Liver function is routinely monitored in drug trials.

items.objective: Explain why rare adverse drug reactions are typically detected only after approval.

items.stemHtml: A biotechnology company has completed animal toxicology studies of a new monoclonal antibody and wants to start the first clinical trial in people at a US hospital. The hospital's IRB is ready to review the protocol. Which of the following regulatory steps must also occur before the first participant is dosed?

options.label: A
options.html: Approval of a Biologics License Application

options.label: B
options.html: Submission of an IND, with no clinical hold after 30 days

options.label: C
options.html: Publication of the animal data in a peer-reviewed journal

options.label: D
options.html: Approval of a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy

options.label: E
options.html: Designation of the antibody as an orphan drug

items.explanationHtml:
Before an unapproved drug or biologic can be given to people in a US clinical investigation, the sponsor must file an Investigational New Drug (IND) application with the FDA, describing preclinical results, manufacturing and the clinical protocol. The study can start 30 days after the FDA receives it unless the FDA imposes a clinical hold. IRB approval is needed in addition.

The NDA or BLA comes much later, after phase III, when the sponsor seeks permission to market.

Takeaway: human testing of a new drug in the US requires an IND that is in effect (30 days, no clinical hold) plus IRB approval.

whyNot.A: A BLA is the marketing application filed after clinical trials, not before them.
whyNot.C: Publication is not a regulatory requirement for starting human trials.
whyNot.D: A REMS is a post-approval safety program for marketed products.
whyNot.E: Orphan designation is an optional incentive program for rare diseases, not a condition for testing.

items.objective: State the regulatory requirement before first-in-human testing in the United States.

items.stemHtml: When the patent on a brand-name extended-release anticonvulsant expires, a manufacturer applies to market a generic version of the same strength and dosage form. It does not plan any new efficacy trials in patients. Which of the following must the manufacturer demonstrate for approval?

options.label: A
options.html: Superior seizure control compared with the brand-name drug

options.label: B
options.html: Identical tablet colour, shape and inactive ingredients

options.label: C
options.html: Rate and extent of absorption comparable to the brand-name drug

options.label: D
options.html: Efficacy in a new placebo-controlled trial

options.label: E
options.html: Manufacture at the same plant as the brand-name drug

items.explanationHtml:
Generic drugs are approved through an abbreviated application. The manufacturer must show that the generic has the same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route of administration as the reference drug and that it is bioequivalent: its peak concentration and area under the concentration-time curve fall within narrow statistical limits of the reference product, usually in a crossover study in healthy volunteers. Efficacy is inferred from the reference drug's data.

Inactive ingredients, colour and shape may differ, which can matter for patients with excipient allergies or for pill recognition.

Takeaway: generic approval rests on pharmaceutical equivalence and bioequivalence, not new efficacy trials.

whyNot.A: Generic approval does not require superiority, only bioequivalence to the reference product.
whyNot.B: Inactive ingredients and appearance may differ from the brand product.
whyNot.D: Generic applications rely on the reference drug's efficacy data and do not repeat efficacy trials.
whyNot.E: Generics are made by different manufacturers in different facilities, each inspected by the FDA.

items.objective: Describe the bioequivalence requirement for generic drug approval.

items.stemHtml: A new drug for a relapsed, refractory lymphoma with no effective therapy is approved by the FDA on the basis of a single-arm trial showing a high rate of tumour shrinkage. Survival data are not yet available. Which of the following obligations accompanies this type of approval?

options.label: A
options.html: No further studies, because approval has been granted

options.label: B
options.html: Conversion to over-the-counter status after 5 years

options.label: C
options.html: Restriction of use to patients enrolled in research

options.label: D
options.html: Annual re-approval of the label by an advisory committee

options.label: E
options.html: Confirmatory trials to verify clinical benefit

items.explanationHtml:
Accelerated approval allows the FDA to approve a drug for a serious condition with unmet need on the basis of a surrogate end point (here, tumour response) that is reasonably likely to predict real clinical benefit. In return, the sponsor must conduct confirmatory trials to verify benefit on clinical outcomes such as survival. The FDA can require those trials to be under way at approval and can withdraw the indication through an expedited process if they fail or are not done diligently.

Surrogates speed access but carry the risk that a marker improves without patients living longer or better.

Takeaway: accelerated approval on a surrogate end point requires confirmatory trials of clinical benefit.

whyNot.A: Approval based on a surrogate end point carries an obligation to verify clinical benefit.
whyNot.B: There is no such pathway for an oncology drug, and it is unrelated to the approval type.
whyNot.C: The drug is approved for marketing; it is not limited to research use.
whyNot.D: Approvals do not require annual re-approval.

items.objective: Describe the obligations attached to accelerated approval.

items.stemHtml: A pharmacology student searches the FDA's public adverse event reporting database and finds 120 reports of liver injury for drug X and 40 reports for drug Y, two drugs in the same class approved in the same year. Which of the following conclusions about these reports is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: They cannot establish incidence, because exposure and reporting rates are unknown

options.label: B
options.html: Drug X is three times as hepatotoxic as drug Y

options.label: C
options.html: Drug X causes liver injury in 120 of its users per year

options.label: D
options.html: Both drugs are proven causes of liver injury

options.label: E
options.html: Drug Y is safe for the liver

items.explanationHtml:
The FDA Adverse Event Reporting System collects spontaneous reports from clinicians, patients and manufacturers (clinicians usually report through MedWatch). It is a passive surveillance system that is good at generating signals, especially for rare and unexpected events, but it has no denominator (the number of people exposed) and reporting is incomplete and variable (for example, publicity increases reports). So it cannot estimate incidence or compare drugs directly.

Signals are then tested with active methods such as cohort studies in large claims or health record databases.

Takeaway: spontaneous adverse event reports raise signals but cannot measure incidence or compare drug risks.

whyNot.B: Without the number of users and the completeness of reporting for each drug, the report counts cannot be compared as rates.
whyNot.C: The reports are counts of suspected cases, not an annual incidence, and causation is unproven in each.
whyNot.D: Spontaneous reports describe suspected associations; they do not prove causation.
whyNot.E: Fewer reports may reflect fewer users or less reporting, not greater safety.

items.objective: State the limitations of passive post-marketing adverse event reporting.

items.stemHtml: A postdoctoral researcher analyzing a trial of a new antihypertensive drug notices that six participants in the treatment group had rises rather than falls in blood pressure. Without telling anyone or noting it in the methods, he deletes their records from the analysis file, and the drug's effect becomes statistically significant. Which of the following best describes his action?

options.label: A
options.html: Fabrication

options.label: B
options.html: Plagiarism

options.label: C
options.html: Honest error

options.label: D
options.html: Falsification

options.label: E
options.html: Publication bias

items.explanationHtml:
Research misconduct under US federal policy is fabrication, falsification or plagiarism. Falsification is manipulating research materials, equipment or processes, or changing or omitting data, so that the research record misrepresents what happened. Silently deleting real but inconvenient results fits exactly.

Excluding data can be legitimate when the rule is prespecified and reported (for example, a per-protocol analysis); what makes this misconduct is the selective, undisclosed removal to change the result.

Takeaway: omitting or altering real data to change results is falsification; inventing data is fabrication.

whyNot.A: Fabrication is making up data that were never collected; here real data were removed.
whyNot.B: Plagiarism is using another person's words or ideas without credit.
whyNot.C: Deliberately deleting unfavourable results is not an error.
whyNot.E: Publication bias concerns which whole studies are published, not manipulation within a study.

items.objective: Classify a form of research misconduct.

items.stemHtml: A research group prepares a manuscript on a quality improvement study. Five people are being considered for authorship. Which of the following people meets the generally accepted criteria for authorship?

options.label: A
options.html: The department chair, who obtained the funding but did no other work on the study

options.label: B
options.html: The statistician, who designed the analysis, revised the draft, approved it and accepts accountability

options.label: C
options.html: The research nurse, who recruited participants and collected data but did not see the manuscript

options.label: D
options.html: The laboratory director, who provided bench space and equipment

options.label: E
options.html: A senior colleague, who is listed to help the paper get accepted

items.explanationHtml:
The widely used journal-editor criteria require all four of the following: a substantial contribution to conception or design, or to acquisition, analysis or interpretation of data; drafting or critically revising the work for important intellectual content; approval of the final version; and agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work. The statistician meets all four.

Contributors who meet only some criteria are acknowledged. The research nurse could become an author by revising and approving the manuscript and accepting accountability.

Takeaway: authorship requires all four criteria, not funding, supervision or resources alone.

whyNot.A: Obtaining funding alone does not meet the criteria; the chair can be acknowledged.
whyNot.C: Data collection is a substantial contribution, but authors must also revise and approve the manuscript and accept accountability.
whyNot.D: Providing resources is acknowledged, not rewarded with authorship.
whyNot.E: Adding a name for prestige is gift authorship.

items.objective: Apply authorship criteria to contributors to a manuscript.

items.stemHtml: Surgeons propose a randomized trial comparing early operative fixation with casting for a particular wrist fracture in adults over 65 years. Published studies are conflicting, and expert surgeons are genuinely divided about which treatment gives better function. Which of the following concepts provides the ethical justification for randomizing these patients?

options.label: A
options.html: Therapeutic misconception

options.label: B
options.html: Distributive justice

options.label: C
options.html: Clinical equipoise

options.label: D
options.html: Double effect

options.label: E
options.html: Substituted judgment

items.explanationHtml:
Clinical equipoise is genuine uncertainty within the expert medical community about which of the compared treatments is better. When it exists, no participant is knowingly given an inferior treatment, so assigning treatment by chance is ethical. If evidence later shows one arm is clearly better, equipoise is lost, which is one reason trials have interim monitoring.

Equipoise is about the community of experts, not the personal hunch of a single investigator.

Takeaway: randomization is ethical when there is clinical equipoise between the treatments compared.

whyNot.A: Therapeutic misconception is a participant's mistaken belief, not a justification for a design.
whyNot.B: Justice concerns fair selection of participants, not the decision to randomize.
whyNot.D: The doctrine of double effect concerns a single act with good and bad effects, not uncertainty between treatments.
whyNot.E: Substituted judgment is a standard for surrogate decision-making.

items.objective: Define clinical equipoise as the justification for randomized trials.

items.stemHtml: A company proposes a 6-month trial of a new antiseizure drug in adults with frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures that are currently controlled by standard medications. Participants would stop their current medications and be randomized to the new drug or placebo alone. Which of the following designs is most ethically acceptable?

options.label: A
options.html: The trial as proposed, because placebo is the most rigorous comparator

options.label: B
options.html: A nonrandomized comparison with historical controls

options.label: C
options.html: The trial as proposed, if participants are paid more

options.label: D
options.html: Enrolment only of people who prefer placebo

options.label: E
options.html: Randomization of the new drug or placebo added to standard medications

items.explanationHtml:
A placebo control is ethical when no proven treatment exists, or when there are compelling methodological reasons and participants given placebo face no risk of serious or irreversible harm. Uncontrolled generalized tonic-clonic seizures risk injury and death, and proven treatments exist, so a placebo-only arm is not acceptable.

An add-on design, in which everyone continues standard therapy and receives either the new drug or placebo in addition, still allows a placebo comparison of the new drug's added effect without withdrawing proven care. An active-controlled trial against a standard drug is another option.

Takeaway: when proven therapy exists for a serious condition, use add-on or active-control designs rather than placebo alone.

whyNot.A: Withdrawing proven therapy for 6 months in a condition with risk of injury and death exposes the placebo group to serious harm.
whyNot.B: Historical controls avoid the ethical problem but introduce serious bias; a randomized add-on design achieves both rigour and safety.
whyNot.C: Payment does not offset serious, avoidable risk and may become undue influence.
whyNot.D: Preference does not change the risk of stopping effective treatment, and selection would bias results.

items.objective: Judge when placebo control is ethically acceptable.

items.stemHtml: Investigators plan a trial of an invasive new procedure for chronic back pain. They plan to recruit only from a free clinic serving uninsured adults because these patients are easy to enrol and rarely decline. If approved, the procedure is expected to be marketed mainly to insured patients at private hospitals. Which of the following ethical principles is most directly violated by this recruitment plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Justice

options.label: B
options.html: Respect for persons

options.label: C
options.html: Beneficence

options.label: D
options.html: Fidelity

options.label: E
options.html: Veracity

items.explanationHtml:
The Belmont Report's principle of justice requires a fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research. Choosing participants because they are easy to recruit or less likely to refuse, while the benefits go to a different, better-off group, is unfair selection. IRBs must find that selection of participants is equitable.

The other two Belmont principles map onto consent (respect for persons) and risk-benefit assessment (beneficence).

Takeaway: recruiting vulnerable people for convenience while others reap the benefits violates the principle of justice.

whyNot.B: Respect for persons concerns consent and autonomy; the problem here is who carries the burden.
whyNot.C: Beneficence concerns the balance of risk and benefit for participants; the main problem is the unfair distribution.
whyNot.D: Fidelity concerns keeping promises and loyalty, not the selection of research participants.
whyNot.E: Veracity concerns truthfulness; nothing suggests deception.

items.objective: Apply the Belmont principle of justice to participant selection.

items.stemHtml: An NIH-funded study collects identifiable interview data on illicit drug use and related criminal behaviour from adults attending community health centres. Participants worry that police or a court could obtain their answers. Which of the following protections most specifically guards these research records against compelled legal disclosure such as a subpoena?

options.label: A
options.html: A HIPAA research authorization

options.label: B
options.html: A data use agreement

options.label: C
options.html: A waiver of documentation of consent

options.label: D
options.html: A Certificate of Confidentiality

options.label: E
options.html: The education records privacy law

items.explanationHtml:
A Certificate of Confidentiality protects identifiable, sensitive research information from compelled disclosure in civil, criminal, administrative or legislative proceedings. Since the 21st Century Cures Act, NIH-funded research that collects identifiable sensitive information is automatically covered, and investigators must not disclose the information except in limited circumstances such as with the participant's consent or as required for certain reporting.

Investigators should describe the certificate, and its limits, in the consent form.

Takeaway: Certificates of Confidentiality protect sensitive research data from subpoena and other compelled disclosure.

whyNot.A: An authorization permits disclosures; it does not shield records from legal compulsion.
whyNot.B: A data use agreement governs a recipient of a limited data set, not protection from subpoenas.
whyNot.C: Waiving the signature can reduce risk from a linking document but gives no legal protection against compelled disclosure.
whyNot.E: Education privacy law applies to school records, not community health research.

items.objective: Identify the protection against compelled disclosure of sensitive research data.

items.stemHtml: Which of the following conclusions about kelvastan is best supported by this study?

options.label: A
options.html: It reduces the risk of death by 27%, the figure to quote unchanged to families

options.label: B
options.html: It probably reduces mortality, but the true effect is likely smaller than reported

options.label: C
options.html: Its benefit is unreliable because the boundary was crossed at an interim look

options.label: D
options.html: It has been shown to be safe because serious adverse events were similar

options.label: E
options.html: It should now be given to all patients with septic shock off label

items.explanationHtml:
The trial crossed a prespecified, strict efficacy boundary reviewed by an independent board, so a mortality benefit is credible. But trials stopped early for benefit systematically overestimate the effect, because they tend to cross the boundary when random variation has exaggerated it. The true relative reduction is likely smaller than 27% (the confidence interval runs from a 13% to a 38% reduction).

Early stopping also means less safety information and less follow-up. A careful reader accepts the direction of effect, discounts its size, and notes that the drug still needs regulatory approval.

Takeaway: a trial stopped early for benefit supports the direction of effect but probably overstates its size.

whyNot.A: Trials stopped early for benefit tend to overestimate the effect, so the point estimate should be presented with that caution.
whyNot.C: Crossing a prespecified, strict boundary is valid evidence of benefit; the issue is the size of the estimate, not its direction.
whyNot.D: An early stop leaves less information on safety, especially rare or delayed harms; similar totals do not prove safety.
whyNot.E: The drug is investigational, so it cannot be prescribed off label; it has no approved label yet.

items.objective: Draw the best supported conclusion from a trial stopped early for benefit.

items.stemHtml: Before the second interim analysis, an investigator at one of the sites was worried about the high mortality among her participants. She asked the sponsor to send her the current mortality in each arm so that she could decide whether to continue enrolling patients. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to her request?

options.label: A
options.html: Send the arm-specific mortality to her alone, in confidence

options.label: B
options.html: Send the arm-specific mortality to all site investigators

options.label: C
options.html: Decline, and route her safety concern to the monitoring board

options.label: D
options.html: Decline, and suspend her site from the trial

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the IRB to release the interim data to her

items.explanationHtml:
Only the independent data and safety monitoring board sees interim comparative results. Investigators remain blinded so that knowledge of emerging results cannot influence enrolment, treatment or outcome assessment. Her worry is legitimate, so the right step is to report the observed events through the protocol so that the board, which sees all sites and both arms, can judge whether there is a safety signal.

A clinician who fears that a trial is harming patients is not powerless: she can report events, raise concerns with the sponsor, the IRB and the board, and stop enrolling at her site if she believes it unsafe, but she does not obtain the unblinded data herself.

Takeaway: investigators' safety concerns go to the monitoring board; interim comparative data stay with the board.

whyNot.A: Selective unblinding of a site investigator could bias her enrolment and assessments and compromise the trial.
whyNot.B: Unblinding all investigators would destroy the trial's integrity and is not the investigators' role.
whyNot.D: Raising a safety concern is appropriate; there is no reason to penalize the site.
whyNot.E: The IRB does not hold or release interim comparative data; it receives summary reports from the monitoring board.

items.objective: Protect trial blinding while responding to an investigator's safety concern.

items.stemHtml: Two weeks after the results are published, a 63-year-old man is admitted with septic shock to a hospital that did not take part in the trial. No trial of kelvastan is open to new patients. His wife has read about the study and asks the intensivist to give him kelvastan. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Obtain leftover supplies of the drug from a nearby trial site

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe it off label as with any recently studied drug

options.label: C
options.html: Tell her it cannot be given until the FDA approves it

options.label: D
options.html: Enroll him in the closed trial as a late participant

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the manufacturer and the FDA for emergency expanded access

items.explanationHtml:
Expanded access (compassionate use) lets a patient with a serious or immediately life-threatening condition receive an investigational drug outside a trial when there is no comparable or satisfactory alternative and no trial is available. The manufacturer must agree to supply the drug and the FDA must authorize it; in an emergency the FDA can authorize single-patient use quickly, even by telephone, with the IRB informed promptly afterwards. Informed consent is obtained, here from his wife as his representative if he lacks capacity.

The physician should also be honest that the manufacturer may decline and that the trial's estimate of benefit is probably optimistic.

Takeaway: an unapproved drug outside a trial is obtained through FDA expanded access with the manufacturer's agreement, never informally.

whyNot.A: Investigational supplies belong to the trial and may not be diverted informally; doing so bypasses FDA and IRB oversight.
whyNot.B: Off-label prescribing applies only to approved drugs; kelvastan is not approved for any use.
whyNot.C: Expanded access exists for exactly this situation; saying it is impossible is inaccurate.
whyNot.D: The trial has stopped enrolling, and enrolment outside an approved protocol is not possible.

items.objective: Choose the regulatory route for giving an investigational drug to a patient outside a trial.

items.stemHtml: When enrolment stops, 520 survivors are still in the planned 1-year follow-up, and none has been told which drug they received. Which of the following is the most appropriate action regarding these participants?

options.label: A
options.html: Tell them the results promptly and confirm whether they wish to continue follow-up

options.label: B
options.html: Wait until the paper is published before contacting them

options.label: C
options.html: Inform only those who received kelvastan

options.label: D
options.html: End all follow-up without explanation, since treatment is over

options.label: E
options.html: Tell them only if they ask during a follow-up visit

items.explanationHtml:
Consent is an ongoing process. Participants must be told of significant new findings that may affect their willingness to continue, and the early stop is such a finding. Investigators should tell all participants (or their representatives, if they still lack capacity) the results and what they mean for them, offer to tell them which treatment they received if the protocol allows, and ask whether they want to continue the follow-up, with an IRB-approved communication.

Participants who first entered through a representative's consent and have now regained capacity should give their own consent to continue.

Takeaway: after an early stop, participants are told the results promptly and their continued consent is confirmed.

whyNot.B: Significant new findings must be shared promptly, not delayed for publication.
whyNot.C: All participants, including those who received placebo, are entitled to the findings that affect them.
whyNot.D: Stopping enrolment does not end obligations to participants, and abrupt termination without explanation is disrespectful.
whyNot.E: The duty to inform is active; investigators should not rely on participants asking.

items.objective: Apply the duty to inform participants of significant new findings.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has had a partial response to methotrexate. His rheumatologist is the site investigator for a double-blind trial in which a computer randomly assigns participants to a new oral drug or an approved active comparator, both added to methotrexate. During the consent discussion he says, "Since you're my doctor, I know you'll put me on whichever one is better for me." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "That's right, and I'll keep a close eye on how you're doing."

options.label: B
options.html: "Don't worry, both drugs work well, so you can't lose."

options.label: C
options.html: "Let's sign the form now and go through the details at your first visit."

options.label: D
options.html: "Neither of us will choose. A computer assigns the drug by chance, and I won't know which one you get."

options.label: E
options.html: "If you're unsure, it might be best to let your wife decide."

items.explanationHtml:
His statement reveals a therapeutic misconception: he believes the protocol's assignment will be individualized to his benefit. The investigator must correct it plainly, explaining randomization and blinding, and then check his understanding again. Only then is consent informed.

Because his own rheumatologist is the investigator, she should also make clear that his care will be the same whether or not he joins.

Takeaway: correct therapeutic misconception by explaining randomization and blinding in plain words before consent.

whyNot.A: Agreeing reinforces his therapeutic misconception; she will not choose his treatment.
whyNot.B: This is premature reassurance and does not correct his misunderstanding; the new drug's effect is not yet known.
whyNot.C: Consent must come before enrolment and must be based on understanding, not obtained first and explained later.
whyNot.E: He has capacity and the decision is his; deferring to a spouse is inappropriate.

items.objective: Respond to therapeutic misconception during research consent.

items.stemHtml: The man enrolls after a full discussion. Four months later he tells the rheumatologist that the monthly study visits are interfering with his work and he wants to stop. He asks whether he can still come to her clinic. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "You agreed to 12 months, so it would really help us if you finished."

options.label: B
options.html: "Of course you can stop, and your care here won't change. Would you be willing to have us check in by phone?"

options.label: C
options.html: "I'd have to refer you to another rheumatologist if you leave the study."

options.label: D
options.html: "I can increase your study payment if you stay until the end."

options.label: E
options.html: "You can stop, and we'll keep pulling data from your clinic chart for the study."

items.explanationHtml:
Participants may withdraw at any time, for any reason, without penalty or loss of the care they are otherwise entitled to. The best response accepts his decision, reassures him that his clinical care continues, and then, without pressure, clarifies what he wants to stop: the study drug, the visits, or all study contact. Many participants are happy to allow brief follow-up by phone, which helps the trial, but that is his choice.

The study drug should be stopped safely and his rheumatoid arthritis treatment planned in the clinic.

Takeaway: accept withdrawal without penalty, keep clinical care unchanged, and ask what continued contact, if any, the participant agrees to.

whyNot.A: Pressuring him to stay disregards the right to withdraw at any time without penalty.
whyNot.C: Making clinical care conditional on research participation is a penalty and is prohibited.
whyNot.D: Offering more money to prevent withdrawal is an inducement that undermines voluntariness.
whyNot.E: He has not agreed to continued data collection; she should ask, not assume.

items.objective: Handle a participant's request to withdraw from a trial.

items.stemHtml: The man decides to end all study participation, including phone follow-up. He then asks that "everything you collected about me be deleted". His consent form stated that information collected before withdrawal would remain part of the study. Four months of his data are in the trial database. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about his data?

options.label: A
options.html: All of his data must be removed from the database at once

options.label: B
options.html: His missing future visits may be filled in with invented values

options.label: C
options.html: His existing data may be kept, but no new data may be collected

options.label: D
options.html: His data may be kept, and his clinic chart may still be abstracted

options.label: E
options.html: His withdrawal must be hidden from the sponsor

items.explanationHtml:
Data gathered before withdrawal can normally be retained and analyzed as described in the consent form. Deleting them would bias the results (participants who withdraw often differ from those who stay), and for FDA-regulated trials the data already collected must remain in the study record. What withdrawal does stop is any further collection of information for the study, including from his medical record, unless he agrees.

The investigator should explain this respectfully, document the withdrawal and its scope, and handle any stored specimens according to the consent terms.

Takeaway: withdrawal stops new data collection; data already collected stay in the study as the consent described.

whyNot.A: Removing data already collected would bias the trial; the consent form told him these data would be kept.
whyNot.B: Inventing values is fabrication; missing data are handled by prespecified statistical methods.
whyNot.D: He has withdrawn from all participation, so no further information may be collected for the study.
whyNot.E: Withdrawals are documented and reported; concealing them would misrepresent the trial.

items.objective: Explain how data collected before withdrawal are handled.

items.stemHtml: A second-year internal medicine resident is planning a study of outcomes after hospital admission for diabetic ketoacidosis. Before writing the protocol, she wants to know how many such admissions occurred in her hospital over the past 3 years. She plans to run an EHR query that returns only the count, and she will not record or remove any patient information. Which of the following best describes what HIPAA requires for this preliminary step?

options.label: A
options.html: Written authorization from each patient admitted with ketoacidosis

options.label: B
options.html: A data use agreement with the hospital

options.label: C
options.html: Full IRB approval of the finished protocol

options.label: D
options.html: Notification of HHS before the query is run

options.label: E
options.html: A review preparatory to research, with no PHI removed

items.explanationHtml:
HIPAA allows a covered entity to let researchers review PHI preparatory to research, for example to design a protocol or estimate how many patients would be eligible, if the researcher represents that the review is only for that purpose, that no PHI will be removed from the covered entity, and that the PHI is necessary. Counting admissions without recording identifiers is a clear example. Institutions usually have a short process for this.

Once she wants to collect identifiable data for the study itself, she needs IRB approval and either patient authorization or a waiver.

Takeaway: counting eligible patients to plan a study is a review preparatory to research; no PHI leaves the institution.

whyNot.A: Authorization is not needed to count eligible patients when no PHI leaves the covered entity.
whyNot.B: A data use agreement governs disclosure of a limited data set; she is receiving no dataset.
whyNot.C: A review preparatory to research can happen before the protocol is written; IRB approval comes before the research itself.
whyNot.D: There is no requirement to notify HHS of such queries.

items.objective: Recognize a review preparatory to research under HIPAA.

items.stemHtml: The IRB approves her study. Her mentor, who works at a partner university, wants a dataset with each admission's exact admission and discharge dates, the patient's five-digit ZIP code and age, but no names, record numbers or street addresses, without contacting patients for authorization. Which of the following is required before the hospital sends him this dataset?

options.label: A
options.html: A data use agreement signed by the mentor

options.label: B
options.html: A certification that the dataset meets safe harbor

options.label: C
options.html: Written authorization from each patient

options.label: D
