options.html: Nothing further, as names have been removed

options.label: E
options.html: An expert determination that the data are anonymous

items.explanationHtml:
A dataset stripped of direct identifiers but keeping dates, ZIP codes and ages is a limited data set. It is PHI, but it can be disclosed for research without individual authorization when the recipient signs a data use agreement. The agreement states the permitted uses, names who may use the data, requires safeguards and prohibits re-identifying or contacting individuals.

If the mentor does not need exact dates, generalizing them to years and trimming ZIP codes could produce a de-identified dataset that needs no agreement.

Takeaway: sharing dates and ZIP codes without direct identifiers requires a data use agreement.

whyNot.B: Exact dates and five-digit ZIP codes are not allowed under safe harbor, so the dataset is not de-identified.
whyNot.C: A limited data set can be shared for research without individual authorization.
whyNot.D: The remaining dates and ZIP codes are identifiers; the dataset is still PHI.
whyNot.E: Expert determination is a route to de-identification; this dataset is designed as a limited data set instead.

items.objective: Apply the data use agreement requirement for limited data sets.

items.stemHtml: Three months later, the resident's personal laptop is stolen from her car. It held an unencrypted copy of the limited data set for 1,200 patients. She has no evidence that anyone has opened the file. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Wait to see whether there is any sign that the data have been misused

options.label: B
options.html: Email each patient in the dataset herself to apologize

options.label: C
options.html: Take no action, because the dataset has no names

options.label: D
options.html: Report the theft promptly to the hospital's privacy officer and IRB

options.label: E
options.html: Delete the hospital's master copy to limit further exposure

items.explanationHtml:
Loss of unencrypted PHI is presumed to be a reportable breach unless the covered entity's documented risk assessment shows a low probability that the information was compromised. The resident's job is to report promptly to the hospital's privacy officer, who leads the assessment and any notification (to individuals within 60 days of discovery, to HHS and, for large breaches, to the media). The IRB also needs to know, because loss of research data is an unanticipated problem involving risk to participants.

Encryption would likely have made this a non-event: properly encrypted data are considered secured.

Takeaway: lost unencrypted PHI is reported at once to the privacy officer (and the IRB for research data); the institution decides on notification.

whyNot.A: Breach assessment and notification run on fixed timelines from discovery; waiting delays a required process.
whyNot.B: Notification is the covered entity's responsibility after its risk assessment; she also has no contact details in the dataset.
whyNot.C: Dates, ZIP codes and ages are PHI, and unencrypted loss is presumed to be a breach until assessed.
whyNot.E: Deleting the institution's records does nothing about the stolen copy and destroys research data.

items.objective: Take the correct first step after loss of unencrypted research data.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and is resuscitated by paramedics. He is enrolled in a trial of a new intravenous drug given during resuscitation, which the hospital runs under the FDA's exception from informed consent for emergency research after community consultation and IRB approval. Forty minutes after arrival, his wife reaches the intensive care unit. He remains unconscious. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement by the investigator to his wife?

options.label: A
options.html: "Because this was an emergency, the study doesn't need to be discussed with family."

options.label: B
options.html: "He was enrolled in a study of an emergency drug. I'd like to explain it, and you can decide whether he continues."

options.label: C
options.html: "He received the standard treatment for cardiac arrest, nothing more."

options.label: D
options.html: "We'll explain the study once he wakes up, if he does."

options.label: E
options.html: "You'll need to sign this consent form now, or he'll be removed from the hospital's care."

items.explanationHtml:
The FDA exception from informed consent for emergency research allows enrolment of people with life-threatening conditions who cannot consent, when no representative can be reached within the treatment window and strict conditions (community consultation, public disclosure, IRB approval, independent monitoring) are met. Once a legally authorized representative or family member is available, the investigator must tell them about the enrolment, explain the study and give them the opportunity to stop further participation. When the patient regains capacity, he is told and asked himself.

The investigator should be open, use plain language, and make clear that his clinical care continues either way.

Takeaway: after emergency enrolment without consent, the family is told at the first opportunity and may end participation.

whyNot.A: The exception requires investigators to inform the family or representative as soon as feasible and let them decide about continuing.
whyNot.C: Withholding the fact of enrolment is dishonest and violates the conditions of the exception.
whyNot.D: The family or representative must be told at the earliest feasible opportunity, not only if and when he recovers.
whyNot.E: Linking care to signing is coercive, and his clinical care cannot depend on study participation.

items.objective: Communicate with a family after enrolment under the emergency research exception.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman who speaks Spanish and little English is eligible for a randomized trial comparing two approved chemotherapy schedules for early breast cancer. Her treatment does not need to start for another week. The consent form has not yet been translated, and her 16-year-old daughter offers to interpret. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Let the daughter interpret, and have the patient sign the English form

options.label: B
options.html: Have the investigator, who speaks some Spanish, explain the study

options.label: C
options.html: Arrange a qualified interpreter and an IRB-approved Spanish consent process

options.label: D
options.html: Exclude her because the consent form is available only in English

options.label: E
options.html: Show her a video about clinical trials and then obtain her signature

items.explanationHtml:
Consent must be in language the participant understands. For a person with limited English proficiency, that means a qualified medical interpreter and either a translated consent document approved by the IRB or an IRB-approved short-form process (a short written statement in her language, oral presentation through the interpreter and a witness). Family members, especially children, should not interpret consent discussions: they may omit or soften information and the patient may not ask what she wants.

Her treatment can wait a week, so there is time to do this properly. Excluding her because of language would also be unjust.

Takeaway: research consent with limited English proficiency needs a qualified interpreter and an IRB-approved translated or short-form process.

whyNot.A: A minor family member is not a qualified interpreter, and a form she cannot read does not support informed consent.
whyNot.B: Partial fluency risks errors on complex risks and procedures; a qualified interpreter is needed.
whyNot.D: Excluding people by language without justification is unfair selection; an approved alternative process exists.
whyNot.E: A general video does not explain this study and does not replace an approved consent process in her language.

items.objective: Obtain research consent from a participant with limited English proficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes is eligible for an IRB-approved physiology study that involves an overnight hospital stay, an insulin clamp and frequent blood sampling. The study offers no direct benefit to participants. His parents are keen for him to join. After the study is explained, he says clearly and repeatedly that he does not want to take part. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Enroll him on the basis of his parents' permission

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the IRB to override his refusal

options.label: C
options.html: Enroll him and reassess his willingness after the first night

options.label: D
options.html: Request an ethics consultation to resolve the disagreement

options.label: E
options.html: Respect his refusal and do not enroll him

items.explanationHtml:
Research involving children needs parental permission and the child's assent. When research offers no prospect of direct benefit, a child's clear refusal (dissent) should be respected even if the parents want participation. A 14-year-old can understand an overnight study with repeated blood draws, and his objection is decisive.

The investigator can thank the family, make clear that his diabetes care will not be affected and, if appropriate, leave the door open should he change his mind on his own.

Takeaway: a child's dissent from research with no direct benefit is respected regardless of parental wishes.

whyNot.A: Parental permission is necessary but not sufficient; his dissent should be respected in research with no direct benefit.
whyNot.B: The IRB may waive assent only in narrow circumstances such as a prospect of direct benefit unavailable elsewhere, which does not apply.
whyNot.C: Enrolling a dissenting child and hoping he changes his mind disregards his refusal.
whyNot.D: There is no real ethical dilemma to resolve; a child's dissent from no-benefit research is respected.

items.objective: Respect a child's dissent from research without direct benefit.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who is moving to another state asks his primary care practice for a complete copy of his medical record to take to his new physician. The billing office notes that he has an unpaid balance from two visits and proposes holding the records until he pays. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the practice?

options.label: A
options.html: Provide the copy within the rule's deadline for at most a reasonable fee

options.label: B
options.html: Hold the records until the balance is paid in full

options.label: C
options.html: Send the records only to the new physician, not to the patient

options.label: D
options.html: Provide only a summary, because the full record is too long

options.label: E
options.html: Ask him to sign a waiver of future claims before release

items.explanationHtml:
Under HIPAA, patients have a right to inspect and obtain a copy of their health records, in the form and format they request if readily producible, within the deadline the rule sets. The practice may charge only a reasonable, cost-based fee for copying. It may not withhold the records because the patient owes money for care; the debt is pursued separately.

A practice that delays access is a common source of complaints to the HHS Office for Civil Rights.

Takeaway: patients get copies of their records on request, for at most a reasonable cost-based fee, regardless of unpaid bills.

whyNot.B: Patients' right of access does not depend on payment for past services.
whyNot.C: He has a right to his own copy; sending them only to another provider does not satisfy his request.
whyNot.D: He may have the full record he requests, in the requested format if readily producible.
whyNot.E: Access cannot be made conditional on waiving rights.

items.objective: Apply the HIPAA right of access to medical records.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman is admitted for acute pyelonephritis. She has capacity and, on admission, asks that no information about her be given to her mother, with whom she has a difficult relationship. The next day the mother telephones the nurses' station and asks how her daughter is doing. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the mother?

options.label: A
options.html: "She's improving and should go home in a day or two."

options.label: B
options.html: "I can tell you only that she has a kidney infection."

options.label: C
options.html: "You'll need to come in with identification before I can share anything."

options.label: D
options.html: "I'm not able to share any information, but I can pass on a message."

options.label: E
options.html: "Please ask her doctor; I'm sure he'll explain everything."

items.explanationHtml:
A patient with capacity controls who receives information about her care. HIPAA permits sharing with family involved in care when the patient agrees or does not object, but she has objected. The staff member should give no clinical information, and since she has asked that her mother be told nothing, should avoid confirming details. Offering to pass on a message respects the patient and remains courteous to the caller; the patient can then decide whether to respond.

The reply should be polite and nonjudgmental; there is no need to explain the patient's reasons.

Takeaway: when a capable patient has refused disclosure to a relative, share nothing and offer to pass on a message.

whyNot.A: Sharing any clinical information goes against the patient's explicit, capable request.
whyNot.B: Revealing the diagnosis breaches confidentiality as much as a full update does.
whyNot.C: Verifying identity does not override the patient's wish that her mother receive no information.
whyNot.E: Referring the call implies information will be shared and only moves the breach to the physician.

items.objective: Respect a patient's objection to disclosing information to family.

items.stemHtml: A resident is preparing a regional conference presentation about a 71-year-old fisherman from a small island town who had an unusual facial skin infection. Her slides include his initials, his exact admission and discharge dates, the name of his town, and a full-face photograph showing the lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to prepare the presentation?

options.label: A
options.html: Present it as planned, because the conference is educational

options.label: B
options.html: Drop initials, use relative days, omit the town and get authorization for the photo

options.label: C
options.html: Remove his initials but keep the other details

options.label: D
options.html: Present it only to a physician audience

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the program director to approve the slides as they are

items.explanationHtml:
Information used outside the care team should be de-identified. Names and initials are only the start: exact dates, small geographic areas, a distinctive occupation and a full-face photograph can each identify a person, especially in a small community. Dates can be replaced with relative times ("day 3 of admission"), the location generalized or omitted, and the face either cropped so it is unrecognizable or shown only with the patient's written authorization.

Authorization is the cleanest route whenever a recognizable image is essential to the teaching point.

Takeaway: for case presentations, remove dates, small geography and recognizable images, or obtain written authorization.

whyNot.A: Educational purpose does not permit disclosure of identifiable information outside the care team.
whyNot.C: Dates, a small town and his face together could easily identify him.
whyNot.D: Restricting the audience to physicians does not make the information de-identified.
whyNot.E: A supervisor's approval does not substitute for de-identification or the patient's authorization.

items.objective: De-identify a clinical case for presentation outside the care team.

items.stemHtml: A second-year resident wants to review the identifiable electronic records of 300 patients treated under a new sepsis protocol over the past 2 years and publish the outcomes as a research paper. She has not yet accessed the records. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin collecting data and submit to the IRB before submitting the paper

options.label: B
options.html: Call each patient to ask for verbal permission

options.label: C
options.html: Submit the project to the IRB before collecting any data

options.label: D
options.html: Proceed, because retrospective chart reviews do not need review

options.label: E
options.html: Obtain written permission from the department chair

items.explanationHtml:
A systematic review of identifiable records to produce generalizable knowledge for publication is research. Before accessing records for that purpose, the resident submits the protocol to the IRB, which will usually review it by an expedited or exempt pathway and can grant a waiver of consent and of HIPAA authorization because the study is minimal risk and contacting hundreds of past patients is impracticable.

IRBs cannot approve research retrospectively. Whether something is research, quality improvement or neither is decided by the institution, not by the investigator alone.

Takeaway: submit a chart review to the IRB before touching the data.

whyNot.A: Research cannot be approved after it has been done; data collection must wait for IRB approval or a determination.
whyNot.B: Contacting 300 past patients is unnecessary if the IRB grants a waiver, and verbal permission alone is not documentation the IRB has approved.
whyNot.D: Retrospective review of identifiable records for research needs IRB review, often expedited with a HIPAA waiver.
whyNot.E: A chair's permission is not a substitute for IRB review.

items.objective: Seek IRB review before starting a retrospective chart review.

items.stemHtml: A sub-investigator in an approved study of HIV preexposure prophylaxis adherence is asked by the sponsor to add a new questionnaire on sexual behaviour at the next visit for each participant, starting next week. The questionnaire is not in the approved protocol or consent form. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Start the questionnaire and mention it at the next continuing review

options.label: B
options.html: Use it only with participants who agree verbally

options.label: C
options.html: Rely on the sponsor's approval of the change

options.label: D
options.html: Record the questionnaire as a protocol deviation after it is used

options.label: E
options.html: Submit an amendment and wait for IRB approval before using it

items.explanationHtml:
Any change to approved research (new procedures, new questionnaires, new consent language, new recruitment material) must be reviewed and approved by the IRB before it is implemented. The only exception is a change needed to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard to participants, which is reported promptly afterwards. A sensitive questionnaire on sexual behaviour also likely needs updated consent language about confidentiality.

Minor changes can often be approved by expedited review, so the delay may be short.

Takeaway: protocol changes need IRB approval before use, unless they are needed to remove an immediate hazard.

whyNot.A: Changes must be approved before use; reporting later is not acceptable.
whyNot.B: Participant agreement does not replace IRB approval of a change to the protocol and consent.
whyNot.C: Sponsor approval is needed but is not sufficient; the IRB must approve changes too.
whyNot.D: Deliberately implementing an unapproved change is not a deviation to be logged after the fact.

items.objective: Submit protocol amendments for IRB approval before implementation.

items.stemHtml: In an IRB-approved trial of an approved antihypertensive drug for a new indication, a 49-year-old participant is hospitalized with acute pancreatitis 3 weeks after starting the study drug. Pancreatitis is not listed in the investigator brochure or consent form, and the investigator judges it possibly related to the drug. The participant is being treated and is improving. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the investigator?

options.label: A
options.html: Report it promptly to the IRB and the sponsor as the protocol requires

options.label: B
options.html: Record it and report it at the next annual continuing review

options.label: C
options.html: Wait for proof that the drug caused the pancreatitis before reporting

options.label: D
options.html: Unblind the whole trial to see whether others are affected

options.label: E
options.html: Withdraw all of the site's participants immediately

items.explanationHtml:
An event that is unexpected (not described in the protocol, brochure or consent), related or possibly related to the research and suggests greater risk than previously known is an unanticipated problem. It must be reported promptly to the IRB and, as a serious unexpected adverse event in an FDA-regulated trial, to the sponsor, who reports to the FDA as required. The IRB may require changes to the consent form so that current participants are informed.

Expected adverse events listed in the consent form are recorded and reported through routine channels instead.

Takeaway: serious, unexpected, possibly related events are reported promptly to the IRB and sponsor.

whyNot.B: An unexpected, possibly related serious event must be reported promptly, not at the next annual review.
whyNot.C: Certainty is not required; possibly related unexpected events are reported.
whyNot.D: Investigators do not unblind the trial; the sponsor and monitoring board assess events across participants.
whyNot.E: Stopping the whole site is not justified by a single event before assessment; the sponsor and board evaluate it.

items.objective: Identify and report an unanticipated problem in a clinical trial.

items.stemHtml: A hospital is one of 8 US sites in an NIH-funded randomized trial of two approved blood pressure regimens. A different institution's IRB has been designated as the single IRB of record and has approved the protocol. The local research coordinator says that the hospital's own IRB intends to conduct a full separate review and require several protocol changes for local use. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

options.label: A
options.html: Have the local IRB review and modify the protocol for this site

options.label: B
options.html: Enroll participants without involving the local institution at all

options.label: C
options.html: Submit to both IRBs and follow whichever approves first

options.label: D
options.html: Rely on the single IRB and send local context through the reliance process

options.label: E
options.html: Withdraw the site from the trial

items.explanationHtml:
The revised Common Rule requires US institutions in federally funded cooperative research to use a single IRB of record (with limited exceptions). Each participating site signs a reliance agreement, supplies local context (state law, institutional policies, local population considerations) to the single IRB, and handles its own institutional obligations such as conflict-of-interest review and staff training, but it does not conduct a separate full review or change the protocol for its own site.

This reduces delays and inconsistent consent forms across sites.

Takeaway: in federally funded multisite research, sites rely on one IRB of record and contribute local context.

whyNot.A: For federally funded multisite research, a single IRB of record reviews the protocol; local re-review and changes are what the single-IRB rule avoids.
whyNot.B: Local sites still provide local context and institutional requirements to the single IRB.
whyNot.C: Dual review creates conflicting requirements and is not how reliance works.
whyNot.E: There is no reason to withdraw; a reliance agreement resolves the issue.

items.objective: Apply the single IRB requirement for federally funded multisite research.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman at 23 weeks of gestation is carrying a fetus with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. She is eligible for a federally funded trial of a fetoscopic procedure that may improve the fetus's lung development but offers no prospect of benefit to her. The father of the fetus is her husband, who is present, has capacity and is involved in her care. Under the federal protections for pregnant women and fetuses, whose consent is required?

options.label: A
options.html: Hers alone

options.label: B
options.html: Hers and the father's

options.label: C
options.html: The father's alone

options.label: D
options.html: Hers and that of the IRB chair

options.label: E
options.html: Hers and a court's

items.explanationHtml:
Under subpart B, when research holds out a prospect of direct benefit to the pregnant woman, or to both woman and fetus, or offers no benefit but poses no more than minimal risk to the fetus, the woman's consent is sufficient. When the prospect of benefit is solely to the fetus, the consent of both the pregnant woman and the father is obtained, unless the father is unavailable, incompetent or temporarily incapacitated, or the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest.

Here the father is present and capable, so both consents are needed. Investigators must also take no part in decisions about ending the pregnancy and offer no inducement to end it.

Takeaway: research that may benefit only the fetus needs consent from both the pregnant woman and the father, with defined exceptions.

whyNot.A: When the prospect of benefit is solely for the fetus, the father's consent is also required when he is available and capable.
whyNot.C: The pregnant woman's consent is always required; she bears the risk of the procedure.
whyNot.D: The IRB approves the study but does not give consent for individual participants.
whyNot.E: No court involvement is needed.

items.objective: Apply the subpart B consent requirements for research benefiting only the fetus.

items.stemHtml: A federally funded observational cohort study of adults with type 2 diabetes collects annual questionnaires and blood samples; it has no study treatment. The IRB did not review it under the federal protections for prisoners. A 44-year-old participant's spouse calls to say that he has been jailed awaiting trial and asks whether he can still do his annual study visit next month. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the investigator?

options.label: A
options.html: Hold the visit at the jail as planned

options.label: B
options.html: Withdraw him and delete his data

options.label: C
options.html: Pause his study contact and notify the IRB promptly

options.label: D
options.html: Continue, since he was enrolled before incarceration

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the jail warden for permission to continue

items.explanationHtml:
When a participant becomes a prisoner during a study that was not approved under subpart C, research interactions and interventions with that person, and collection of identifiable information, should stop and the IRB should be notified promptly. The IRB then either reviews the study under the prisoner protections (with a prisoner representative) so that he can continue, or he is withdrawn from further participation. An exception allows continuation of a study intervention when stopping would harm the participant's health, but this observational study has none.

This protects people whose freedom to decline may be limited by their new circumstances.

Takeaway: if a participant is incarcerated, pause research contact and notify the IRB for review under the prisoner protections.

whyNot.A: Research interactions with a participant who has become a prisoner must stop until the IRB reviews the study under the prisoner protections.
whyNot.B: Withdrawal and deletion are not required; past data can generally be kept, and the IRB may approve his continued participation.
whyNot.D: Enrolment before incarceration does not exempt the study from prisoner protections once he is a prisoner.
whyNot.E: Prison authorities cannot approve research; the IRB must review under the prisoner protections.

items.objective: Manage a research participant who becomes incarcerated.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with heart failure has been in a double-blind trial of a new drug for 10 months. At a study visit she asks the investigator whether the new drug is working so far and whether she should stay in the trial. The trial's monitoring board met last month and recommended continuing. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "From what I'm seeing in my own patients here, it really does seem to be helping."

options.label: B
options.html: "Let me look up which pill you're taking so that you can decide for yourself."

options.label: C
options.html: "That's confidential information, and I'm not allowed to discuss the study with you."

options.label: D
options.html: "If you have doubts about it, it might be best for you to drop out of the study now."

options.label: E
options.html: "I honestly don't know. An independent board reviews the results and will tell us of anything important."

items.explanationHtml:
In a blinded trial the investigators do not know the comparative results, which are seen only by the independent data and safety monitoring board. The honest answer is that no one running the trial knows yet, that the board is watching for both benefit and harm and recommended continuing, and that she will be told of any finding that affects her decision. She remains free to leave at any time.

The investigator can then ask what is behind the question (new symptoms, worry, burden) and address it.

Takeaway: tell participants honestly that interim results are hidden from investigators and reviewed by an independent board.

whyNot.A: Site impressions are anecdotal, could unblind participants and are not a valid basis for decisions.
whyNot.B: Unblinding for curiosity rather than clinical need compromises the trial and is not allowed by the protocol.
whyNot.C: This is dismissive; she deserves an honest explanation and is entitled to discuss her participation.
whyNot.D: Encouraging withdrawal without exploring her concerns is unhelpful and not patient-centred.

items.objective: Answer a participant's question about interim results honestly without unblinding.

items.stemHtml: A medical newsletter reports that, at the first interim analysis of a trial of a new drug to prevent recurrent venous thromboembolism, with 40% of the planned events, the primary outcome favoured the drug with P = 0.02. The trial's prespecified efficacy boundary for that look was P < 0.001, and the monitoring board recommended continuing. A patient asks her physician whether this means the drug works. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Efficacy has not been established, and the trial should continue as planned

options.label: B
options.html: The drug has been shown to be effective, since P is below 0.05

options.label: C
options.html: The drug has been shown to be ineffective, since the boundary was not crossed

options.label: D
options.html: The trial should have been stopped, since P = 0.02 is significant

options.label: E
options.html: The interim result should be added to the final result to reach significance

items.explanationHtml:
Group sequential trials compare each interim result with a stricter boundary, because repeated looks at accumulating data inflate the false-positive rate. A P value of 0.02 at a look whose boundary was 0.001 has not crossed it, so efficacy has not been established. The correct decision, which the board made, is to continue.

The physician can tell the patient that early results are encouraging but not conclusive, and that early trends often shrink as more data accumulate.

Takeaway: at an interim analysis, compare the P value with the prespecified boundary, not with 0.05.

whyNot.B: At an interim look the prespecified boundary, not 0.05, defines significance; P = 0.02 did not cross it.
whyNot.C: Not crossing an early boundary means the question is unanswered, not that the drug failed.
whyNot.D: Stopping on a nominal P of 0.02 at an early look would inflate the type I error the design was built to control.
whyNot.E: Interim and final analyses use accumulating data; adding P values or results is not a valid method.

items.objective: Interpret an interim P value against a prespecified boundary.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with frequent migraines asks about a drug approved for epilepsy. A randomized trial of the drug for migraine prevention was stopped for futility at its interim analysis, after half of the planned participants had finished, because the probability of showing a meaningful reduction in migraine days was very low. Adverse events were similar in the two groups. A colleague says the trial "proved the drug equals placebo and is safe for migraine". Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: The drug has been proved equivalent to placebo for migraine

options.label: B
options.html: The drug has been proved harmful in migraine

options.label: C
options.html: The drug should be preferred because the trial was stopped early

options.label: D
options.html: A meaningful benefit is unlikely, and safety for this use is uncertain

options.label: E
options.html: The result is invalid because the trial did not finish

items.explanationHtml:
A trial stopped for futility shows that a clinically meaningful benefit is unlikely; continuing would not have changed the answer. It does not prove equivalence to placebo, and a half-completed trial gives limited safety information, especially about uncommon adverse effects. The physician should tell the patient that the evidence does not support the drug for migraine prevention and discuss options with better evidence.

Colleagues often overinterpret negative trials; "no evidence of benefit" is not the same as "evidence of no effect" or "evidence of safety".

Takeaway: a futility stop means benefit is unlikely; it does not prove equivalence or safety.

whyNot.A: Equivalence requires a trial designed to show it; a futility stop does not establish equivalence.
whyNot.B: A futility stop says nothing definite about harm; adverse events were similar.
whyNot.C: Early stopping for futility argues against, not for, using the drug for this purpose.
whyNot.E: Prespecified futility stops are a valid and ethical design feature.

items.objective: Interpret a trial stopped for futility when advising a patient.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man in a double-blind trial comparing a new oral anticoagulant with warfarin for atrial fibrillation arrives in the emergency department with a large gastrointestinal hemorrhage and hypotension. The appropriate reversal agent depends on which drug he is taking, and the trial's double-dummy design means he takes a tablet of each kind. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding the blinding?

options.label: A
options.html: Unblind all participants at this site to guide care

options.label: B
options.html: Unblind his assignment through the protocol's emergency procedure

options.label: C
options.html: Treat without knowing his assignment to protect the blind

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the monitoring board for the interim bleeding results

options.label: E
options.html: Withdraw him from the trial and give no reversal agent

items.explanationHtml:
Blinding protects a trial's validity, but it never outranks a participant's safety. Trials therefore include an emergency unblinding procedure, usually a 24-hour telephone or web system, that reveals one participant's assignment when knowing it would change clinical management. Here the choice of reversal agent depends on it, so his assignment should be revealed, and the event documented and reported as a serious adverse event.

Only the minimum unblinding needed is done: one participant, by the protocol route, and not the interim results of the trial.

Takeaway: unblind a single participant through the emergency procedure when the assignment changes management.

whyNot.A: Only the affected participant's assignment is needed; unblinding others would compromise the trial.
whyNot.C: When management depends on the assignment, a participant's safety takes priority over blinding.
whyNot.D: Interim comparative data do not help this patient and are not released to investigators.
whyNot.E: Withdrawal does not answer the clinical question, and withholding reversal could be fatal.

items.objective: Use emergency unblinding appropriately for participant safety.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman started a recently approved oral drug for type 2 diabetes 3 months ago. She is admitted with acute pancreatitis. She does not drink alcohol, has no gallstones on imaging and her triglyceride level is normal. Pancreatitis is not listed as an adverse effect in the drug's label. The drug is stopped and she recovers. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional step?

options.label: A
options.html: Report it only if a rechallenge reproduces the pancreatitis

options.label: B
options.html: Tell the manufacturer's sales representative at the next visit

options.label: C
options.html: Report the suspected reaction to the FDA through MedWatch

options.label: D
options.html: Write a case report before telling anyone

options.label: E
options.html: Take no action, since one case cannot establish causation

items.explanationHtml:
Clinicians should report suspected serious or unexpected adverse reactions, particularly with newly marketed drugs, to the FDA through MedWatch. Certainty is not required: the FDA pools reports to detect signals that no single clinician could recognize. A serious event not listed in the label, in a patient with no other cause, is exactly the kind of report that matters.

Premarketing trials are too small to reveal uncommon adverse effects, so voluntary reporting by clinicians is an essential safety net.

Takeaway: report suspected serious or unexpected reactions to the FDA via MedWatch without waiting for proof.

whyNot.A: Rechallenge is unnecessary and could be dangerous; reporting does not require proof of causation.
whyNot.B: An informal mention is not a report; the FDA receives reports through MedWatch or the manufacturer's formal process.
whyNot.D: Publication is slow and is not a substitute for prompt reporting to the FDA.
whyNot.E: Post-marketing surveillance depends on reports of suspected, not proven, reactions.

items.objective: Report a suspected adverse drug reaction through MedWatch.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has a chronic condition that has not responded to two approved drugs. Drug L is FDA-approved for a different disease, but several randomized trials and a specialty society guideline support its use for her condition at the approved dose. It has no FDA approval for her indication. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

options.label: A
options.html: Refuse, because prescribing for an unapproved use is illegal

options.label: B
options.html: Apply to the FDA for permission before prescribing

options.label: C
options.html: Enroll her in a research study, since off-label use is research

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain IRB approval before writing the prescription

options.label: E
options.html: Prescribe it after explaining the evidence and its off-label status

items.explanationHtml:
Once a drug is approved, physicians may prescribe it for other uses, doses or populations when sound evidence and clinical judgment support it. Off-label prescribing is legal and common. Good practice is to discuss the evidence and the fact that the use is not on the label, document that discussion and monitor the patient. Insurance coverage may need to be checked.

What is restricted is manufacturer promotion of unapproved uses. A systematic plan to study an off-label use in a group of patients would be research and need IRB review.

Takeaway: evidence-based off-label prescribing is legal; explain it, document it and monitor.

whyNot.A: Physicians may legally prescribe approved drugs for unapproved uses when evidence supports them.
whyNot.B: No FDA permission is needed to prescribe a marketed drug off label.
whyNot.C: Off-label use for an individual patient's care is clinical practice, not research.
whyNot.D: IRB review applies to research, not to off-label treatment of one patient.

items.objective: Apply the rules for off-label prescribing.

items.stemHtml: A dermatologist is covering for a colleague. A 22-year-old woman taking a teratogenic acne medication calls for her monthly prescription. The drug can be dispensed only under a REMS that requires a certified prescriber and a negative pregnancy test each month before dispensing. The covering dermatologist is not certified, and the patient has not had this month's test. She asks for the prescription today so she does not miss doses. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrange the pregnancy test and a prescription from a certified prescriber

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe one month's supply and arrange the test later

options.label: C
options.html: Ask a pharmacist to dispense it without a new prescription

options.label: D
options.html: Prescribe a double dose of another acne drug instead

options.label: E
options.html: Tell her to stop all acne treatment permanently

items.explanationHtml:
A Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy with elements to assure safe use can require prescriber certification, patient enrolment, pharmacy certification and documented tests (here, monthly pregnancy tests) before each dispensing. These rules exist because the drug can cause severe birth defects. A prescriber who is not certified cannot prescribe it within the program, and the test cannot be skipped.

The right step is to arrange the test promptly and have a certified prescriber (the patient's own dermatologist or another certified colleague) issue the prescription. A missed day or two of acne treatment carries little risk compared with fetal exposure.

Takeaway: REMS requirements such as certification and monthly pregnancy tests cannot be bypassed for convenience.

whyNot.B: Prescribing without certification and without the required test breaks the REMS rules that protect against fetal exposure.
whyNot.C: Pharmacies in the program cannot dispense without the required prescriber and test documentation.
whyNot.D: Switching drugs at an improvised dose is not appropriate and does not address her care plan.
whyNot.E: A short interruption may happen, but permanent cessation is not warranted.

items.objective: Follow REMS requirements when prescribing a high-risk drug.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia has taken a brand-name statin for several years. His insurer now covers only the generic version, and he asks whether the generic is weaker, adding that he does not want a cheap copy. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Generics can contain up to 20% less of the drug, so we may need a higher dose."

options.label: B
options.html: "Generics are fine for mild disease, but yours needs the brand."

options.label: C
options.html: "Generics aren't tested in people, but they're usually fine."

options.label: D
options.html: "It has the same medicine at the same dose and was shown to be absorbed the same way."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll write 'brand medically necessary' so you can stay on it."

items.explanationHtml:
A generic drug contains the same active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route as the brand product and must be shown to be bioequivalent, meaning it is absorbed at the same rate and to the same extent within narrow statistical limits. Efficacy and safety can therefore be expected to be the same. The tablet may look different because inactive ingredients, shape and colour can differ.

The idea that generics may contain much less drug comes from misreading the statistical limits used for comparing absorption, which apply to the confidence interval of the ratio, not to the content of the tablets.

Takeaway: generics have the same active ingredient and dose and are bioequivalent to the brand.

whyNot.A: This is a common misunderstanding of bioequivalence limits; generics contain the same amount of active ingredient.
whyNot.B: There is no basis for reserving brand drugs for severe disease.
whyNot.C: Generics are tested in people for bioequivalence, and the FDA reviews them.
whyNot.E: There is no medical reason to require the brand here; this adds cost without benefit.

items.objective: Counsel a patient accurately about generic substitution.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with a relapsed hematologic cancer has taken drug N for 8 months with stable disease and mild fatigue. Drug N received accelerated approval for his cancer on the basis of response rates. The confirmatory randomized trial has now shown no improvement in overall survival, and the indication is being withdrawn. He has read about this and asks what it means for him. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by his oncologist?

options.label: A
options.html: "Nothing changes for you; keep taking it as before."

options.label: B
options.html: "The main trial showed no survival benefit. Let's review how you're doing and your other options."

options.label: C
options.html: "We'll stop it today and not discuss other options until your next scan."

options.label: D
options.html: "The FDA made a mistake, so you can ignore the news."

options.label: E
options.html: "You should have been told it was experimental when you started."

items.explanationHtml:
Accelerated approval rests on a surrogate end point (here, tumour response) that is expected to predict clinical benefit, with confirmatory trials required. When a confirmatory trial fails, the indication may be withdrawn. Patients already on the drug deserve an honest explanation of the new result and a shared review of their own situation and the alternatives, rather than either automatic continuation or abrupt cessation.

Patients who appear to be benefiting may sometimes continue through a manufacturer or regulatory program while alternatives are considered, but that is part of the shared discussion, not a reason to skip it.

Takeaway: when a confirmatory trial fails, explain the result honestly and review options with the patient.

whyNot.A: This dismisses important new evidence without discussing what it means or what alternatives exist.
whyNot.C: An abrupt stop without a plan or discussion fails to involve him in the decision.
whyNot.D: This is inaccurate and undermines trust; the withdrawal reflects new trial evidence.
whyNot.E: Drug N was approved when prescribed; the response also does not address his question or plan.

items.objective: Counsel a patient when an accelerated approval is withdrawn.

items.stemHtml: A second-year resident helping with a faculty member's clinical study notices that a co-resident has entered blood pressure readings for follow-up visits that the clinic schedule shows never took place. When she asks, he says, "Everyone's readings are about the same anyway; I just filled in the gaps." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Correct the entries herself by deleting the invented values

options.label: B
options.html: Email the journal editor to warn about the study

options.label: C
options.html: Report it to the principal investigator or the research integrity office

options.label: D
options.html: Raise it at the next residents' meeting so others learn from it

options.label: E
options.html: Do nothing, because the values are probably close to the real ones

items.explanationHtml:
Entering values for visits that never happened is fabrication, a form of research misconduct, regardless of whether the numbers are plausible. The resident has already raised it with him; the next step is to report it through the proper channel, the principal investigator or the institution's research integrity officer, and to preserve the records. The institution investigates fairly, protects good-faith complainants and decides whether corrections or notifications (IRB, sponsor, journal) are needed.

She should avoid altering the data herself, confronting him publicly or going to outside bodies first.

Takeaway: suspected fabrication is reported to the PI or research integrity office with the evidence preserved.

whyNot.A: Altering the record herself could destroy evidence and does not address the misconduct or the rest of the data.
whyNot.B: Journals are not the first route; the institution must investigate first.
whyNot.D: Public exposure is unfair to the co-resident before investigation and does not secure the data.
whyNot.E: Inventing data is fabrication regardless of how plausible the values are.

items.objective: Report suspected research misconduct through the proper channel.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 45-year-old man volunteers for a brain and abdominal MRI study of body fat distribution. The protocol, which he agreed to in consent, states that findings that may be clinically important will be shared with participants. A research radiologist reviewing his images sees a 3-cm solid mass in the right kidney. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Say nothing, because research scans are not diagnostic studies

options.label: B
options.html: Send the result to the participant's employer for its health program

options.label: C
options.html: Order a full diagnostic work-up as part of the research

options.label: D
options.html: Record the finding in the research database only

options.label: E
options.html: Tell the participant and help arrange clinical evaluation

items.explanationHtml:
Investigators have a responsibility to participants for incidental findings that may be clinically important, especially when the consent form promised to share them. A solid renal mass may be a cancer. The participant should be told what was seen, in plain language and without overstating certainty, and helped to obtain clinical evaluation with his own physician or by referral, because a research scan is not a diagnostic study and the finding needs confirmation.

Planning for incidental findings in the protocol (what will be returned, by whom and how) makes these conversations straightforward.

Takeaway: potentially serious incidental research findings are disclosed to the participant with a route to clinical evaluation.

whyNot.A: The protocol and consent promise to share findings that may matter clinically, and a solid renal mass may be serious.
whyNot.B: Disclosure to an employer breaches confidentiality and has no clinical purpose.
whyNot.C: Diagnostic care belongs in the clinical setting, not as a research procedure added outside the protocol.
whyNot.D: Recording it without telling him fails the duty to share a potentially serious finding.

items.objective: Manage a potentially serious incidental finding in research.

items.stemHtml: A third-year resident designed a study, collected and analyzed the data, and wrote the manuscript with guidance from her faculty mentor, who revised it in detail. Before submission, the division chief, who had no role in the study, asks to be added as senior author "because it's my division". Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the resident and her mentor?

options.label: A
options.html: Explain the authorship criteria and offer him an acknowledgment

options.label: B
options.html: Add him as senior author to avoid conflict

options.label: C
options.html: Add him as an author but in the middle of the list

options.label: D
options.html: Withdraw the manuscript until he agrees to be left off

options.label: E
options.html: Report him to the journal before submitting

items.explanationHtml:
Authorship requires a substantial contribution to the work, drafting or critical revision, approval of the final version and accountability for the whole. Leading a division does not meet these criteria, so adding the chief would be gift (honorary) authorship. The appropriate step is to explain the criteria respectfully and offer an acknowledgment of the division's support. If pressure continues, the mentor can involve the department's research or integrity office.

Discussing authorship early in a project prevents many such disputes.

Takeaway: people who do not meet all authorship criteria are acknowledged, not listed as authors.

whyNot.B: Listing someone who does not meet authorship criteria is gift authorship and misrepresents responsibility for the work.
whyNot.C: Position does not matter; he does not qualify as an author anywhere in the list.
whyNot.D: Withdrawing harms the work and is unnecessary; a respectful explanation should come first.
whyNot.E: Going outside the institution first is disproportionate; the matter can be addressed directly.

items.objective: Handle a request for honorary authorship.

items.stemHtml: A cardiologist is the site principal investigator for an industry-sponsored trial of a new lipid-lowering drug. During the trial she accepts a paid consulting role with the company that makes the drug. The institution's IRB application and conflict-of-interest policy ask investigators to report financial relationships with sponsors. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Keep it private, because the consulting is unrelated to her patients

options.label: B
options.html: Disclose it only if a participant asks

options.label: C
options.html: Disclose it only when the results are published

options.label: D
options.html: Disclose the relationship to the institution and IRB as required

options.label: E
options.html: End the trial at her site to avoid the issue

items.explanationHtml:
A paid consulting relationship with the sponsor creates a financial conflict of interest that could influence how she recruits, assesses outcomes or reports results. She must disclose it to her institution and the IRB as their policies require. The institution then decides how to manage it, for example by telling participants in the consent form, adding independent outcome assessment, or limiting her role.

Disclosure also continues at publication through journal conflict-of-interest forms, and industry payments to physicians are publicly reported through Open Payments.

Takeaway: financial relationships with a trial's sponsor are disclosed to the institution and IRB so that they can be managed.

whyNot.A: A paid role with the sponsor is a financial interest related to the research and must be disclosed.
whyNot.B: Disclosure follows institutional policy and IRB requirements, not participant questions.
whyNot.C: Disclosure is required during the research so that the conflict can be managed.
whyNot.E: Disclosure and management, not abandoning participants, is the usual response.

items.objective: Disclose a financial conflict of interest in research.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with recurrent severe major depressive disorder made a suicide attempt 4 months ago. He has been stable for 3 months on sertraline and weekly psychotherapy. A research coordinator asks his psychiatrist to refer him to a 12-week placebo-controlled trial of a new antidepressant that requires stopping all antidepressants for 2 weeks before randomization. He says he would "try anything to help science". Which of the following is the most appropriate action by his psychiatrist?

options.label: A
options.html: Refer him, as he is enthusiastic and has capacity

options.label: B
options.html: Decide not to refer him to this trial and discuss safer options

options.label: C
options.html: Refer him, but ask the trial to shorten the washout

options.label: D
options.html: Refer him, and see him weekly during the trial

options.label: E
options.html: Leave the decision to the research coordinator

items.explanationHtml:
A placebo-controlled trial that requires stopping proven treatment can be acceptable for some participants, but not for someone at high risk of serious, irreversible harm. A man with a recent suicide attempt who is stable on effective therapy would risk relapse during the washout and on placebo. His psychiatrist's primary duty is to his welfare, so she should not refer him to this trial and can discuss whether he might be eligible for studies that keep current treatment, such as an add-on or active-comparator design.

His willingness to help science is admirable and can be acknowledged; it does not oblige her to propose a risky option.

Takeaway: do not refer high-risk patients to placebo trials that withdraw effective treatment; consider add-on or active-control studies.

whyNot.A: Enthusiasm does not change the serious risk of relapse and suicide from stopping effective treatment.
whyNot.C: Shortening the washout still withdraws effective therapy and exposes him to placebo for 12 weeks.
whyNot.D: Closer monitoring reduces but does not remove the danger of withdrawing effective treatment in a recent attempter.
whyNot.E: The psychiatrist has a duty to her patient and cannot delegate the judgment to the study team.

items.objective: Protect a high-risk patient from referral to a placebo-controlled washout trial.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man comes to the office because he has felt tired for 2 months. After greeting him and sitting down, the physician wants to begin the history of present illness in a way that lets the patient set out his own concerns first. Which of the following questions is the best way to begin?

options.label: A
options.html: "Are you sleeping fewer hours than usual?"

options.label: B
options.html: "Is the tiredness worse in the morning or the evening?"

options.label: C
options.html: "Have you noticed any weight loss?"

options.label: D
options.html: "Tell me about the tiredness and how it has affected you."

options.label: E
options.html: "Would you rate the tiredness as mild, moderate or severe?"

items.explanationHtml:
An open-ended invitation lets the patient describe the problem in his own words and order, which brings out the concerns and context that closed questions miss. Physicians who interrupt early or start with yes/no questions often never hear the patient's main worry.

A good interview moves from open to focused: open invitation, then facilitation ("Go on"), then targeted closed questions to fill gaps such as onset, timing and associated symptoms.

Takeaway: start with an open-ended question; save closed and multiple-choice questions for clarifying details later.

whyNot.A: A yes/no question about sleep narrows the history to one cause before the patient has said what matters to him.
whyNot.B: This is a forced-choice question about timing; useful later, but it steers the patient rather than opening the story.
whyNot.C: Asking about weight loss is an important closed screening question, but it does not let the patient tell his own story first.
whyNot.E: A rating question limits the answer to three choices and skips the patient's own account of the problem.

items.objective: Recognise an open-ended question as the best way to begin a patient-centred history.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation asks how much a new anticoagulant would help her. Based on a large trial, her 10-year risk of stroke is 8% without the drug and 6% with it. She says that she finds percentages confusing. The physician plans to say "Out of 100 women like you treated for 10 years, about ___ would be spared a stroke because of the drug." Which of the following numbers correctly completes the statement?
items.explanationHtml:
Natural frequencies ("x out of 100 people like you") are understood far better than percentages or relative changes, especially by people with limited numeracy. The number spared is the absolute risk reduction expressed per 100 people.

Working: absolute risk reduction = 8% − 6% = 2%, which is 2 per 100 women over 10 years. Relative risk = 6/8 = 0.75; relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.75 = 25%. The number needed to treat is 1/0.02 = 50.

Relative risk reductions sound larger than absolute ones and can mislead. Good risk communication gives both baseline and treated risks with the same denominator and time frame.

Takeaway: spared per 100 = baseline risk − treated risk (here 8 − 6 = 2 of 100).

whyNot.B: Six is the number per 100 who would still have a stroke despite the drug, not the number spared.
whyNot.C: Eight is the number per 100 who would have a stroke without treatment (the baseline risk).
whyNot.D: Twenty-five is the relative risk reduction as a percentage, not a count of women out of 100.
whyNot.E: Seventy-five is the relative risk (0.75) multiplied by 100; it does not describe how many are spared.

items.objective: Convert a treatment effect into an absolute natural frequency for a patient with limited numeracy.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man drinks five or six beers most evenings. At a routine visit he says, "I know I probably drink too much, but it's the only thing that helps me unwind after work." The physician wants to respond in a way that is consistent with motivational interviewing. Which of the following responses is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: "You really need to cut down before this damages your liver."

options.label: B
options.html: "Have you thought about trying exercise or meditation instead?"

options.label: C
options.html: "Why haven't you cut back if you know it's too much?"

options.label: D
options.html: "So drinking helps you relax, and part of you is also worried about how much it has become."

options.label: E
options.html: "Most people your age drink far less than you do."

items.explanationHtml:
Motivational interviewing draws out the patient's own reasons for change. A reflection that holds both sides of the ambivalence (what drinking gives him and his concern about it) invites him to keep talking and to voice reasons to change himself.

The core skills are open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries. Arguing for change, offering unrequested fixes or confronting tends to make the patient defend the status quo.

Takeaway: in motivational interviewing, reflect both sides of ambivalence; avoid lecturing, confronting and quick fixes.

whyNot.A: Telling him he must cut down is a directive warning that usually provokes defence of drinking rather than reflection.
whyNot.B: Jumping to solutions before he has explored his own reasons is the urge to fix things that motivational interviewing avoids.
whyNot.C: "Why" questions about failure sound accusatory and push the patient to justify not changing.
whyNot.E: A comparison with peers can be useful feedback later, but delivered now it sounds like a judgement and ignores what he just shared.

items.objective: Choose a double-sided reflection as a motivational interviewing response to ambivalence.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is starting insulin glargine at bedtime. The physician has explained how to draw up the dose, when to inject and how to recognize low blood glucose. Which of the following is the best way for the physician to confirm that she has understood the instructions?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask, "Do you understand everything I've told you?"

options.label: B
options.html: Ask her to explain in her own words how and when she will take the insulin

options.label: C
options.html: Ask, "Do you have any questions?"

options.label: D
options.html: Ask her what grade of school she completed

options.label: E
options.html: Give her a detailed printed leaflet to read at home

items.explanationHtml:
Teach-back (asking the patient to explain or demonstrate, in her own words, what she will do) checks understanding directly and shows the physician what to re-explain. It works for every patient and should be framed as a check on the physician's explanation, not a test of the patient.

Yes/no checks such as "Do you understand?" are usually answered "yes" even when understanding is poor. Years of schooling are a weak guide to health literacy, and written material does not confirm comprehension.

Takeaway: confirm understanding with teach-back, not with "Do you understand?"

whyNot.A: Most patients say "yes" to this question whether or not they understood, so it confirms nothing.
whyNot.C: Inviting questions is good practice but does not reveal misunderstandings the patient is unaware of.
whyNot.D: Educational level predicts health literacy poorly and can feel shaming; it does not test this explanation.
whyNot.E: Printed material can support teaching, but a detailed leaflet may exceed her reading level and does not check understanding.

items.objective: Use teach-back to confirm patient understanding.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl comes to the office with her father for a sports physical examination. The physician asks the father to step out so that she can speak with the girl alone about home, school, friends, mood, substance use and relationships. Before starting, the physician explains the confidentiality of their conversation. Which of the following statements most accurately describes that confidentiality?

options.label: A
options.html: Everything she says will be shared with her father because she is a minor

options.label: B
options.html: Everything she says will stay private, with no exceptions

options.label: C
options.html: What she says stays private only if her father signs a release

options.label: D
options.html: What she says stays private except anything about sexual activity, which must be reported

options.label: E
options.html: What she says stays private unless it suggests that she or someone else is at serious risk of harm

items.explanationHtml:
Adolescents disclose more about sex, substances, mood and safety when they are seen alone and told that the conversation is confidential. Confidentiality must be explained honestly with its limits: imminent risk of suicide or harm to others and suspected abuse can require disclosure or reporting.

Explain the arrangement to the parent and teen together, then interview the teen alone. Then work from less to more sensitive topics: home and family, school or work, friends and activities, mood and sleep, substances, sexual health, and safety.

Takeaway: adolescent confidentiality is the default, limited by serious risk of harm and suspected abuse.

whyNot.A: Routine sharing with parents would make the teen less likely to disclose risks and is not the standard of care for the confidential interview.
whyNot.B: Promising absolute confidentiality is dishonest, because risk of serious harm and suspected abuse can require disclosure.
whyNot.C: The physician-adolescent confidentiality arrangement does not depend on a parent signing a release.
whyNot.D: Consensual sexual activity is not automatically reportable; only circumstances such as abuse or exploitation trigger reporting.

items.objective: State the limits of confidentiality when interviewing an adolescent alone.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who speaks only Vietnamese comes to the clinic for follow-up of newly diagnosed hepatitis B. He is accompanied by his 12-year-old granddaughter, who is fluent in English and Vietnamese, and his adult son, who speaks some English. A telephone interpreter service is available. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate with the patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Use the telephone medical interpreter

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the son to interpret because he is an adult family member

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the granddaughter to interpret because she is the most fluent

options.label: D
options.html: Use simple English with gestures and diagrams

options.label: E
options.html: Ask a Vietnamese-speaking clerk from the front desk to interpret

items.explanationHtml:
A trained medical interpreter, in person, by telephone or by video, gives accurate, complete and confidential interpretation. Family members and untrained staff omit, add or soften content, and they make more errors of clinical consequence.

Children should not interpret for their relatives: it burdens them, inverts family roles and exposes them to sensitive information. Federal language-access rules expect qualified interpreters at no cost to the patient.

Takeaway: when a qualified interpreter is available, use one; never use a child.

whyNot.B: The son's limited English and family role make errors and filtering likely when a professional interpreter is available.
whyNot.C: A child should not interpret medical information, however fluent; it is inappropriate and unreliable for sensitive topics.
whyNot.D: Simplified English with gestures is inadequate for explaining a chronic infection and its treatment to someone who speaks no English.
whyNot.E: An untrained bilingual clerk lacks medical terminology and interpreter training and is not bound to interpreting standards.

items.objective: Choose a qualified medical interpreter over family members, children and untrained staff.

items.stemHtml: A hospital that receives Medicare and Medicaid payments plans to stop paying for interpreter services to save money and to ask patients with limited English proficiency to bring their own interpreters. Which of the following federal laws most directly establishes the hospital's obligation to provide language assistance?

options.label: A
options.html: Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA)

options.label: B
options.html: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)

options.label: C
options.html: Patient Self-Determination Act

options.label: D
options.html: Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA)

options.label: E
options.html: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964

items.explanationHtml:
Title VI prohibits discrimination on the basis of national origin by any program receiving federal financial assistance. Failing to give people with limited English proficiency meaningful access to services is treated as national-origin discrimination, so federally funded providers must offer language assistance free of charge. Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act reinforces these duties in health programs.

Shifting the cost or the task to patients ("bring your own interpreter") does not meet the obligation.

Takeaway: federally funded providers must give free, qualified language assistance (Title VI, reinforced by ACA Section 1557).

whyNot.A: EMTALA requires screening and stabilisation of emergency conditions; it is not the source of the general duty to provide interpreters.
whyNot.B: HIPAA governs the privacy and security of health information, not language access.
whyNot.C: The Patient Self-Determination Act requires hospitals to inform patients about advance directives.
whyNot.D: CLIA sets quality standards for clinical laboratories and has nothing to do with interpreters.

items.objective: Identify Title VI of the Civil Rights Act as the basis of language-access obligations for federally funded providers.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman who is Deaf and communicates in American Sign Language is scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She can lip-read a few words and write short notes in English. The surgeon needs to explain the procedure, its risks and alternatives. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate with her?

options.label: A
options.html: Speak slowly and clearly so that she can lip-read

options.label: B
options.html: Exchange written notes during the discussion

options.label: C
options.html: Ask her hearing teenage son, who signs, to interpret

options.label: D
options.html: Arrange a qualified sign-language interpreter, in person or by video

options.label: E
options.html: Give her a written consent form to read and sign

items.explanationHtml:
Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, health care providers must ensure effective communication with Deaf patients, which for a complex discussion such as surgical consent usually means a qualified sign-language interpreter (on site or by video remote interpreting), provided at no cost to the patient.

Lip-reading captures only a fraction of spoken English, and English may be a second language for someone whose first language is ASL, so notes and forms are not equivalent access for complex information. Family members, especially children, should not be relied on.

Takeaway: a Deaf patient who signs needs a qualified sign-language interpreter for complex discussions, free of charge.

whyNot.A: Lip-reading conveys only part of speech, so a consent discussion would be incomplete and unreliable.
whyNot.B: Written notes may suffice for simple exchanges but not for a detailed discussion of risks and alternatives, especially if English is her second language.
whyNot.C: A child should not interpret a parent's surgical consent; it is unreliable and places an inappropriate burden on him.
whyNot.E: A form alone does not inform; consent is a discussion, and reading level and language may be barriers.

items.objective: Provide a qualified sign-language interpreter for complex communication with a Deaf patient.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man is unresponsive after a large intracerebral hemorrhage. His daughter, who is his surrogate, tells the team, "Dad told me many times that if he ever couldn't recognize his family, he would not want to be kept alive on machines." She asks that he not be intubated. Which of the following standards is the daughter using?

options.label: A
options.html: Best-interests standard

options.label: B
options.html: Substituted judgment

options.label: C
options.html: Reasonable-person standard

options.label: D
options.html: Therapeutic privilege

options.label: E
options.html: Parens patriae

items.explanationHtml:
Substituted judgment asks the surrogate to decide as the patient would have decided, using what the patient said and valued. The daughter is reporting her father's own stated wishes, which is exactly this standard.

The best-interests standard is used only when the patient's wishes are unknown or the patient never had capacity: the surrogate then weighs benefits and burdens for the patient.

Takeaway: a surrogate who reports what the patient would want is using substituted judgment.

whyNot.A: Best interests applies when the patient's wishes are unknown; here they are known.
whyNot.C: The reasonable-person standard concerns how much information a physician must disclose for informed consent.
whyNot.D: Therapeutic privilege is the rare exception allowing a physician to withhold information that would itself cause serious harm.
whyNot.E: Parens patriae is the state's power to protect people who cannot protect themselves, such as children; it is not a surrogate's decision standard.

items.objective: Recognise substituted judgment as the surrogate decision standard based on the patient's known wishes.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old man has had profound intellectual disability since birth and has never been able to express preferences about medical care. He now has acute cholecystitis, and his sister, who is his court-appointed guardian, must decide whether he should have surgery. Which of the following standards should guide her decision?

options.label: A
options.html: Best interests

options.label: B
options.html: Informed refusal

options.label: C
options.html: Sliding-scale capacity

options.label: D
options.html: Substituted judgment

options.label: E
options.html: Implied consent

items.explanationHtml:
When a person has never had decision-making capacity, there are no prior wishes to reconstruct, so substituted judgment cannot be applied. The surrogate instead uses the best-interests standard: what a reasonable weighing of benefits, burdens, pain and quality of life from the patient's point of view supports.

Substituted judgment comes first whenever the patient's wishes or values are known; best interests is the fallback when they are not.

Takeaway: never-capacitated patient or unknown wishes: the surrogate uses best interests.

whyNot.B: Informed refusal is a capacitated patient's own decision to decline; it is not a surrogate standard.
whyNot.C: The sliding scale describes how much capacity a decision requires; it does not tell a surrogate how to choose.
whyNot.D: Substituted judgment needs the patient's own wishes or values, which a person who never had capacity has not expressed.
whyNot.E: Implied consent covers emergencies when no one can be asked; a guardian is available to decide here.

items.objective: Apply the best-interests standard when a patient has never had capacity.

items.stemHtml: A physician is seeing a 66-year-old Portuguese-speaking woman with heart failure through an in-person medical interpreter. Which of the following statements by the physician reflects the best technique for interpreted communication?

options.label: A
options.html: To the interpreter: "Ask her whether her ankles have been swelling."

options.label: B
options.html: To the interpreter: "Find out what she's been eating and give me the gist."

options.label: C
options.html: To the interpreter: "You can skip the details; just tell her to take the new pills."

options.label: D
options.html: To the interpreter: "Tell her she has fluid overload and that we will start a loop diuretic and an ACE inhibitor today."

options.label: E
options.html: To the patient: "Have your ankles been swelling since your last visit?"

items.explanationHtml:
The physician should face and speak directly to the patient in the first person, in short segments of plain language, and the interpreter interprets everything in the first person. This keeps the relationship between physician and patient and reduces omissions.

Asking the interpreter to summarise ("give me the gist") or to skip details invites omissions, and jargon is hard to interpret accurately.

Takeaway: talk to the patient, not to the interpreter, in short plain-language segments.

whyNot.A: Speaking about the patient in the third person sidelines her and turns the interpreter into the conversation partner.
whyNot.B: Asking for the gist invites summarising and omission instead of complete interpretation.
whyNot.C: Asking the interpreter to drop details undermines accurate, complete communication and informed choice.
whyNot.D: This is third-person and full of jargon, which is difficult to interpret and to understand.

items.objective: Apply first-person, direct, plain-language technique when working with an interpreter.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old Mandarin-speaking man is scheduled for elective hernia repair. A qualified video interpreter is used for the consent discussion with the surgeon. Afterward, a nurse asks who is responsible for making sure that the patient understood the risks and alternatives of the operation. Which of the following is the most accurate answer?

options.label: A
options.html: The interpreter, because she conveyed the information

options.label: B
options.html: The nurse who witnessed the patient's signature

options.label: C
