options.html: The hospital's language-access coordinator

options.label: D
options.html: The surgeon performing the operation

options.label: E
options.html: The patient's family

items.explanationHtml:
The duty to obtain informed consent rests with the physician who will perform the procedure (or a qualified team member acting for that physician). The interpreter's job is to convey meaning accurately and completely; checking understanding, for example with teach-back, remains the physician's job.

A witness's signature confirms only that the patient signed the form, not that the consent discussion was adequate.

Takeaway: the physician doing the procedure owns informed consent; the interpreter is a conduit, not the consenter.

whyNot.A: Interpreters convey meaning; they do not assume the clinician's legal and ethical duty to inform and check understanding.
whyNot.B: Witnessing a signature confirms identity and signing, not comprehension of the risks.
whyNot.C: A coordinator arranges services and has no role in the clinical consent discussion.
whyNot.E: A capacitated adult consents for himself; family members do not carry the responsibility for his understanding.

items.objective: Identify the physician, not the interpreter, as responsible for informed consent in an interpreted encounter.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer is unconscious after a bowel perforation. She named her husband as her health-care agent. He tells the team, "She always said she wanted no more surgery and only comfort care at the end, but I can't bear to lose her yet, so I want everything done." Which of the following should be the basis of the husband's decision as her agent?

options.label: A
options.html: What he believes is best for her overall

options.label: B
options.html: What he would want for himself in her place

options.label: C
options.html: What most patients in her situation choose

options.label: D
options.html: What the surgeons recommend

options.label: E
options.html: What she would choose if she could decide

items.explanationHtml:
An agent or surrogate speaks for the patient, not for himself. When the patient's wishes are known, the agent should apply substituted judgment: decide as she would have decided. Here her stated wishes were for no more surgery and comfort care.

The physician should acknowledge the husband's grief, gently remind him of his role ("What would she say if she could speak to us?"), and support him; an ethics consultation can help if he still insists on care she refused.

Takeaway: an agent must voice the patient's wishes, not his own preferences.

whyNot.A: His own view of her overall good is the best-interests approach, which is used only when her wishes are unknown.
whyNot.B: A surrogate's personal preferences are not the standard; the decision belongs to the patient's values.
whyNot.C: Population choices can inform a best-interests judgment but cannot override her own known wishes.
whyNot.D: Physicians recommend, but the surrogate's decision should follow the patient's wishes, which are known here.

items.objective: Explain that a health-care agent must decide according to the patient's known wishes.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with symptomatic gallstones is scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The surgeon explains his diagnosis, what the operation involves, its likely benefits and its main risks, including bile duct injury and conversion to an open operation. Which of the following must the surgeon also discuss for the patient's consent to be informed?

options.label: A
options.html: The hospital's average charge for the operation

options.label: B
options.html: The alternatives, including not having surgery

options.label: C
options.html: The pharmacology of the anesthetic agents

options.label: D
options.html: The surgeon's annual income from procedures

options.label: E
options.html: The outcomes of every surgeon in the department

items.explanationHtml:
Informed consent requires disclosure of the diagnosis, the nature and purpose of the proposed treatment, its material risks and benefits, and the reasonable alternatives, including no treatment and the consequences of that choice. The patient must have capacity and decide voluntarily.

Material information is what a reasonable patient would want to know to decide. Alternatives are often the element left out, and omitting them makes consent invalid even when risks were described well.

Takeaway: informed consent = diagnosis, nature of the intervention, risks, benefits and alternatives (including doing nothing).

whyNot.A: Cost may matter to a patient and can be discussed, but it is not one of the core elements of informed consent.
whyNot.C: Detailed drug pharmacology is not material to the decision; the anesthesiologist discusses anesthetic risks in plain terms.
whyNot.D: Ordinary professional income is not a required disclosure; a personal financial conflict of interest would be different.
whyNot.E: Department-wide outcome data are not a required element of consent for this operation.

items.objective: List the required elements of informed consent, including alternatives and no treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department unconscious after a motorcycle crash. She is hypotensive, and a CT scan shows a large epidural hematoma with midline shift. No family member or advance directive can be found, and a neurosurgeon recommends immediate craniotomy. Which of the following best justifies operating without her consent?

options.label: A
options.html: Therapeutic privilege

options.label: B
options.html: Waiver of consent

options.label: C
options.html: Presumed consent under organ-donation law

options.label: D
options.html: The best-interests standard applied by a surrogate

options.label: E
options.html: The emergency exception (implied consent)

items.explanationHtml:
When a patient cannot consent, delay would risk death or serious harm, and no surrogate or known refusal is available, physicians may give emergency treatment under the emergency exception. The law presumes that a reasonable person would consent to life-saving care.

The exception ends once the emergency is over or a surrogate becomes available, and it does not apply if the patient's prior refusal of that treatment is known (for example, a valid advance directive).

Takeaway: emergency + no capacity + no surrogate or known refusal = treat under implied consent.

whyNot.A: Therapeutic privilege lets a physician withhold specific information that would itself cause serious harm; it does not authorise treatment without consent.
whyNot.B: Waiver is a capacitated patient's own choice not to hear details; an unconscious patient cannot waive.
whyNot.C: Presumed-consent rules concern organ donation after death and are irrelevant to emergency surgery.
whyNot.D: No surrogate is available, so there is no surrogate decision to rely on.

items.objective: Apply the emergency exception to informed consent.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with a 6-cm abdominal aortic aneurysm agrees to endovascular repair. When the surgeon begins to describe the risks, he says, "Please don't go through all the complications. I trust you. Just tell me what I need to do to get ready." He has full decision-making capacity. Which of the following best describes this situation?

options.label: A
options.html: The emergency exception

options.label: B
options.html: Implied consent

options.label: C
options.html: Informed refusal

options.label: D
options.html: Therapeutic privilege

options.label: E
options.html: Waiver of the right to information

items.explanationHtml:
A capacitated patient may knowingly waive detailed disclosure. The physician should confirm that he understands he is entitled to the information, offer it again later, ask whether he would like someone else (such as a family member) to hear it, and document the waiver. He still consents to the procedure itself.

Therapeutic privilege is different: it is the physician's decision, used rarely, to withhold information whose disclosure would itself cause serious harm. Here the choice not to hear comes from the patient.

Takeaway: waiver is initiated by the patient; therapeutic privilege is initiated by the physician (and is rarely justified).

whyNot.A: An elective aneurysm repair is not an emergency, and he is able to decide.
whyNot.B: Implied consent is inferred from conduct or an emergency; here he is expressly agreeing while declining details.
whyNot.C: He is accepting, not refusing, the procedure; he is declining only the detailed information.
whyNot.D: Therapeutic privilege is a physician's decision to withhold harmful information, not a patient's request.

items.objective: Distinguish a patient's waiver of disclosure from therapeutic privilege.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy comes to a clinic alone. He has had several sexual partners and asks for testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without his parents being told. For which of the following can he consent on his own in every US state?

options.label: A
options.html: Elective tonsillectomy for recurrent pharyngitis

options.label: B
options.html: Arthroscopic repair of a meniscal tear

options.label: C
options.html: Orthodontic braces

options.label: D
options.html: Rhinoplasty for cosmetic reasons

options.label: E
options.html: Treatment of gonococcal urethritis

items.explanationHtml:
Every state allows minors to consent to diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infections, because requiring parental consent would deter care and threaten public health. Other minor-consent rules (contraception, prenatal care, substance-use and mental health treatment) exist in many states but vary in detail.

Elective, non-urgent procedures for a minor generally require a parent's or guardian's consent unless the minor is emancipated or a state mature-minor rule applies.

Takeaway: STI testing and treatment is the minor-consent service available in all states.

whyNot.A: Elective surgery for a minor requires a parent's or guardian's consent.
whyNot.B: Non-emergency orthopedic surgery requires parental consent for an unemancipated minor.
whyNot.C: Orthodontic treatment is elective and requires a parent's or guardian's consent.
whyNot.D: Cosmetic surgery is elective and requires parental consent for a minor.

items.objective: Identify STI care as a service that minors can consent to on their own in all states.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman has chronic tension-type headaches. Her physician is considering prescribing a placebo tablet. Which of the following approaches to placebo use is most consistent with medical ethics?

options.label: A
options.html: Give the placebo and tell her it is a powerful new pain drug

options.label: B
options.html: Give the placebo without comment and observe her response

options.label: C
options.html: Use the placebo to find out whether her headaches are real

options.label: D
options.html: Use a placebo only with her knowledge and agreement

options.label: E
options.html: Give the placebo but record it in the chart as an active drug

items.explanationHtml:
Deceiving a patient violates respect for autonomy and honesty and undermines trust, even when the intent is beneficent. A placebo may be used in clinical practice only if the patient knows and agrees, for example open-label use, or the patient's general agreement that a treatment may include inactive components.

A placebo response does not show that symptoms are "not real"; placebo responses occur in organic disease too. Records must always be accurate.

Takeaway: no deceptive placebos; use a placebo only with the patient's knowledge and agreement.

whyNot.A: Describing a placebo as an active drug is deception, which violates informed consent.
whyNot.B: Giving a placebo without disclosure is still deceptive and bypasses her consent.
whyNot.C: Response to placebo cannot distinguish "real" from psychogenic symptoms, and using it this way is deceptive.
whyNot.E: Falsifying the record is dishonest and dangerous for later care.

items.objective: Explain that placebo use in practice requires the patient's knowledge and agreement.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl with a large Wilms tumor is scheduled for nephrectomy next week, and significant blood loss is expected. Her parents, who are Jehovah's Witnesses, refuse consent for any transfusion. Ethics and legal staff advise the team to seek a court order permitting transfusion if it becomes necessary. Which of the following principles most directly supports this action?

options.label: A
options.html: Respect for parental autonomy

options.label: B
options.html: Substituted judgment for the child

options.label: C
options.html: The mature-minor doctrine

options.label: D
options.html: Therapeutic privilege

options.label: E
options.html: The best interests of the child

items.explanationHtml:
Parents may refuse treatment for their children within limits, but not when refusal exposes the child to serious harm or death. Decisions for a child who has never been able to form settled values are judged by the child's best interests, and the state can protect that interest through the courts. For a planned operation, there is time to seek a court order; in an emergency, physicians transfuse to save the child's life.

An adult Jehovah's Witness with capacity may refuse blood even if death results. The difference is that adults decide for themselves, whereas parents may not make martyrs of their children.

Takeaway: children: best interests can override a parent's refusal of life-saving treatment (court order if time allows; treat if an emergency).

whyNot.A: Parental authority is broad but does not extend to refusing life-saving treatment for a child.
whyNot.B: A 7-year-old has not formed the settled values needed for substituted judgment.
whyNot.C: Mature-minor rules apply to some adolescents deciding for themselves, not to a 7-year-old.
whyNot.D: Therapeutic privilege concerns withholding information, not overriding a refusal.

items.objective: Explain why a parent's refusal of life-saving transfusion for a child can be overridden.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old woman who is serving on active duty in the US Army comes to an off-base clinic with knee pain. She needs arthroscopic surgery for a torn meniscus, and her parents live in another state. Which of the following best describes who may consent to her surgery?

options.label: A
options.html: She may consent herself because she is emancipated

options.label: B
options.html: Only her parents may consent until she turns 18

options.label: C
options.html: Her commanding officer must consent

options.label: D
options.html: A court must appoint a guardian to consent

options.label: E
options.html: Consent is not needed because she is a service member

items.explanationHtml:
Emancipated minors may consent to their own medical care. Active military service and marriage are recognised grounds for emancipation, and many states add living independently and supporting oneself. Emancipation is different from the mature-minor doctrine, which some states use to let a particular adolescent consent to a particular treatment.

Takeaway: an emancipated minor (for example, on active military duty) consents for herself.

whyNot.B: Parental consent is not required once a minor is emancipated.
whyNot.C: Military command has no authority to consent to elective medical care for a service member.
whyNot.D: Guardianship is unnecessary when the patient can legally consent herself.
whyNot.E: Service members, like other patients, must give informed consent for surgery.

items.objective: Recognise active military service as a basis for emancipation and self-consent.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease has a large estate. Her son asks the hospital team to declare her "incompetent" so that he can manage her finances. Which of the following best describes who makes a determination of incompetence?

options.label: A
options.html: The attending physician

options.label: B
options.html: A consulting psychiatrist

options.label: C
options.html: The patient's adult children

options.label: D
options.html: The hospital ethics committee

options.label: E
options.html: A judge

items.explanationHtml:
Competence is a legal status determined by a court. Decision-making capacity is a clinical judgement, made by a physician, about a specific decision at a specific time. A physician's assessment can be evidence in a guardianship or conservatorship hearing, but only a judge can declare someone incompetent and appoint someone to manage her affairs.

Takeaway: capacity is clinical and decision-specific; competence is legal and decided by a court.

whyNot.A: The attending can assess capacity for medical decisions but cannot make the legal finding of incompetence.
whyNot.B: Psychiatrists assess capacity and testify, but the legal finding belongs to the court.
whyNot.C: Family members cannot declare a parent incompetent; they can petition a court.
whyNot.D: Ethics committees advise on conflicts; they have no legal power to declare incompetence.

items.objective: Distinguish legal competence (court) from clinical decision-making capacity (physician).

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with a newly diagnosed lung mass is told that a biopsy is needed to rule out cancer. He states clearly that he refuses the biopsy. He can accurately repeat what the mass is, what the biopsy involves and what could happen if a cancer went untreated. He then says, "That's all true for other people, but those scans are faked. Nothing is wrong with me." He has no history of psychiatric illness. Which of the following abilities required for decision-making capacity is most clearly impaired?

options.label: A
options.html: Appreciating how the information applies to him

options.label: B
options.html: Understanding the relevant information

options.label: C
options.html: Communicating a choice

options.label: D
options.html: Reasoning about the options

options.label: E
options.html: Making a choice voluntarily

items.explanationHtml:
Capacity requires four abilities: to communicate a stable choice, to understand the information, to appreciate that it applies to one's own situation, and to reason by comparing options in light of one's values. This man can state a choice and repeat the facts, but he denies that they apply to him on the basis of a fixed false belief, so appreciation is impaired.

Appreciation failures often look like denial or delusion: the patient can recite risks but insists they do not apply to him.

Takeaway: can repeat the facts but denies they apply to him = impaired appreciation.

whyNot.B: He accurately repeats the information, so understanding is intact.
whyNot.C: He states a clear, consistent refusal, so communicating a choice is intact.
whyNot.D: His problem is not weighing options; he rejects the premise that the facts concern him at all.
whyNot.E: Voluntariness concerns coercion by others, which is not described.

items.objective: Identify impaired appreciation as a failure of decision-making capacity.

items.stemHtml: A 81-year-old woman with mild vascular dementia lives in an assisted-living facility. She cannot reliably manage her finances, but she wants to decline a recommended influenza vaccine. She explains, in her own words, what the vaccine does, its small risks and the risk of influenza, and says she has "never liked shots" and would rather take her chances. Which of the following statements about her decision-making capacity is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.html: She lacks capacity for all decisions because she has dementia

options.label: B
options.html: She lacks capacity because she cannot manage her finances

options.label: C
options.html: She has capacity only if a psychiatrist confirms it

options.label: D
options.html: She may have capacity for this decision even if she lacks it for others

options.label: E
options.html: She has capacity only if her family agrees with her choice

items.explanationHtml:
Capacity is decision-specific. A person can lack capacity for a complex decision such as managing investments and still have it for a simpler one such as declining a vaccine. This woman understands, appreciates and reasons about the choice and expresses it clearly.

A diagnosis such as dementia does not remove capacity on its own. The question is always whether the person can make this decision now.

Takeaway: capacity is judged decision by decision, not by diagnosis.

whyNot.A: A dementia diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity for every decision.
whyNot.B: Inability to manage finances does not mean she cannot make a simple medical decision.
whyNot.C: Any treating physician can assess capacity; psychiatry is consulted when the assessment is difficult.
whyNot.E: Capacity does not depend on whether others agree with the choice.

items.objective: Explain that decision-making capacity is decision-specific.

items.stemHtml: Two hospitalized patients each make a decision. Patient 1 consents to intravenous antibiotics for cellulitis. Patient 2 refuses an appendectomy for uncomplicated acute appendicitis. Their physicians apply a sliding-scale approach to capacity assessment. Which of the following best describes how that approach treats these decisions?

options.label: A
options.html: Patient 2's decision requires more rigorous assessment

options.label: B
options.html: Patient 1's decision requires more rigorous assessment

options.label: C
options.html: Both decisions require the same level of capacity

options.label: D
options.html: Patient 2's refusal shows lack of capacity

options.label: E
options.html: Neither decision requires capacity assessment

items.explanationHtml:
The sliding-scale view holds that the level of certainty needed about capacity rises with the stakes of the decision. Accepting a low-risk, high-benefit treatment requires less scrutiny; refusing a high-benefit treatment that carries a serious risk of harm requires a more careful, documented assessment.

A refusal is not itself evidence of incapacity, but it is a reason to check capacity thoroughly. Capacity can be present and the refusal must then be respected.

Takeaway: the higher the stakes (especially refusing high-benefit care), the more rigorous the capacity assessment.

whyNot.B: Accepting low-risk, high-benefit treatment carries less danger and needs less scrutiny, not more.
whyNot.C: The sliding scale specifically varies the threshold with risk, so these decisions are not treated the same.
whyNot.D: An unusual or risky refusal prompts careful assessment but does not prove incapacity.
whyNot.E: Every decision presumes capacity; the sliding scale concerns how carefully it is checked.

items.objective: Apply the sliding-scale model of capacity to decisions of different risk.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, euthymic on lithium for 3 years, has early-stage hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. After lumpectomy she declines recommended adjuvant chemotherapy but accepts endocrine therapy. She explains the estimated benefit of chemotherapy, the side effects that concern her, and that she values continuing to work and caring for her grandchildren. Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: She lacks capacity because of her psychiatric diagnosis

options.label: B
options.html: She lacks capacity because she declined the recommended plan

options.label: C
options.html: Her decision requires approval by a court

options.label: D
options.html: Her decision requires her family's agreement

options.label: E
options.html: She has capacity to make this decision

items.explanationHtml:
She communicates a stable choice, understands the information, appreciates that it applies to her and reasons with her own values. A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity, and disagreeing with a recommendation is not evidence of incapacity.

Her mood disorder is stable, and nothing suggests mania or depression is driving the decision. Her informed refusal of chemotherapy should be respected and documented, with the option to revisit it.

Takeaway: mental illness does not equal incapacity; assess the four abilities for the decision at hand.

whyNot.A: Bipolar disorder, especially when stable, does not by itself remove decision-making capacity.
whyNot.B: Disagreeing with a recommendation does not show incapacity when the four abilities are intact.
whyNot.C: A capacitated adult's treatment decision does not need court approval.
whyNot.D: An adult with capacity decides for herself; family agreement is not required.

items.objective: Recognise that a stable psychiatric illness does not remove decision-making capacity.

items.stemHtml: A state legislature is revising its civil commitment law. Which of the following is a standard ground for involuntary psychiatric admission across US states?

options.label: A
options.html: Refusing recommended psychiatric medication

options.label: B
options.html: Having a diagnosis of a serious mental illness

options.label: C
options.html: Being dangerous to others because of a mental illness

options.label: D
options.html: Family members requesting admission

options.label: E
options.html: Lacking a permanent home

items.explanationHtml:
Involuntary psychiatric admission requires a mental illness plus a resulting danger: danger to self, danger to others, or (in most states) grave disability, meaning inability to meet basic needs such as food, clothing, shelter or safety. The process is time-limited and subject to court review.

A diagnosis alone, refusal of treatment, family wishes or homelessness does not justify loss of liberty.

Takeaway: commitment = mental illness + danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability.

whyNot.A: Refusing treatment is a right of people with capacity and is not itself a ground for commitment.
whyNot.B: A diagnosis without resulting danger or grave disability does not justify involuntary admission.
whyNot.D: Family wishes cannot by themselves deprive an adult of liberty.
whyNot.E: Homelessness is not a mental illness or a danger and is not a ground for commitment.

items.objective: State the criteria for involuntary psychiatric admission.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by an outreach worker in January. She has been living in a parking garage, believes that all food is contaminated and has eaten little for a week. She has frostbite of two toes and has refused shelter because she believes it is "run by spies." She has no suicidal or homicidal thoughts. Which of the following best describes the criterion for involuntary admission that she meets?

options.label: A
options.html: Danger to others

options.label: B
options.html: Grave disability

options.label: C
options.html: Lack of insight into illness

options.label: D
options.html: Nonadherence to medication

options.label: E
options.html: Suicidal intent

items.explanationHtml:
Grave disability means that, because of a mental illness, a person cannot provide for basic needs such as food, clothing, shelter or medical care, so that serious harm is likely. Her psychotic beliefs stop her from eating and from accepting shelter in freezing weather, and she already has frostbite.

Lack of insight and nonadherence are common in psychosis but are not, by themselves, grounds for commitment.

Takeaway: unable to meet basic needs because of mental illness = grave disability.

whyNot.A: She has no thoughts or behavior that threaten others.
whyNot.C: Poor insight alone does not justify loss of liberty without a resulting danger or disability.
whyNot.D: Not taking medication is not itself a ground for involuntary admission.
whyNot.E: She explicitly has no suicidal thoughts.

items.objective: Recognise grave disability as a criterion for involuntary admission.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with schizophrenia has been involuntarily committed after threatening his landlord. On the psychiatric unit he is calm and causes no danger, but he refuses an antipsychotic medication. Which of the following best describes his right to refuse the medication?

options.label: A
options.html: He lost the right to refuse medication when he was committed

options.label: B
options.html: He may be medicated if his family agrees

options.label: C
options.html: He may be medicated whenever the psychiatrist believes it is needed

options.label: D
options.html: He may be medicated only after he consents in writing, without exception

options.label: E
options.html: He keeps the right to refuse except in an emergency or with a court or legal review

items.explanationHtml:
Involuntary admission and involuntary treatment are separate decisions. A committed patient generally keeps the right to refuse medication. Medication can be given over objection in an emergency (imminent danger) or after a separate legal process, such as a court finding of incapacity or a formal review, depending on the state.

Commitment authorises confinement for evaluation and safety; it is not a finding that the person lacks capacity for every decision.

Takeaway: commitment does not equal consent to treatment; nonemergency forced medication needs a separate legal process.

whyNot.A: Commitment does not by itself remove the right to refuse medication.
whyNot.B: Family agreement does not authorise forced medication of a committed adult.
whyNot.C: The psychiatrist's opinion alone is not enough outside an emergency; due process is required.
whyNot.D: Emergency medication without consent is allowed when there is imminent danger, so this rule is too absolute.

items.objective: Explain the committed patient's right to refuse medication and its exceptions.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with depression tells her psychiatrist that she has had passive thoughts of death but no plan or intent. She has strong family support, no access to firearms, agrees to a safety plan and will return in 3 days. Her psychiatrist decides against hospitalization. Which of the following principles best supports this decision?

options.label: A
options.html: Duty to warn

options.label: B
options.html: Least restrictive alternative

options.label: C
options.html: Parens patriae

options.label: D
options.html: Police power

options.label: E
options.html: Therapeutic privilege

items.explanationHtml:
The least restrictive alternative principle requires that treatment be given in the setting that limits liberty the least while still keeping the patient safe. Involuntary or inpatient care is justified only when less restrictive options, such as intensive outpatient follow-up with a safety plan, are not enough.

Takeaway: use the least restrictive setting that is safe.

whyNot.A: The duty to warn concerns threats to identifiable third parties, which are absent here.
whyNot.C: Parens patriae is the state's protective power used to justify commitment, not a reason to avoid hospitalization.
whyNot.D: Police power justifies confining people who endanger others; she endangers no one.
whyNot.E: Therapeutic privilege concerns withholding information and is unrelated to choosing a treatment setting.

items.objective: Apply the least restrictive alternative principle in psychiatric care.

items.stemHtml: The parents of a 14-year-old boy with severe depression and repeated self-harm want him admitted to a psychiatric hospital. He refuses. Under the framework set by the US Supreme Court for parental admission of minors, which of the following is required?

options.label: A
options.html: An independent medical review that admission is appropriate

options.label: B
options.html: The boy's written agreement to admission

options.label: C
options.html: A full court hearing before any admission

options.label: D
options.html: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt that he is dangerous

options.label: E
options.html: Approval by the hospital ethics committee

items.explanationHtml:
Parents may admit a minor to a psychiatric facility over the minor's objection, but the Supreme Court has held that due process requires a neutral fact-finder, such as an independent physician, to review whether admission is medically appropriate, with periodic re-review. A formal adversarial court hearing is not constitutionally required, although some states give minors more protection.

This differs from adult civil commitment, which requires a judicial hearing for continued involuntary admission.

Takeaway: parental admission of a minor needs an independent medical review, not necessarily a court hearing.

whyNot.B: The minor's agreement is not required when parents admit him with independent review.
whyNot.C: A formal judicial hearing is not constitutionally required for parental admission of a minor, although some states add one.
whyNot.D: Criminal-law proof is not required for any form of civil psychiatric admission.
whyNot.E: Ethics committees advise; they are not the required review for admission.

items.objective: Describe the due-process requirement for parental psychiatric admission of a minor.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man in a hospital psychiatric unit becomes violent, and verbal de-escalation and offered medication fail. Staff place him in physical restraints to prevent imminent injury. Under federal hospital rules for restraint used to manage violent behavior, which of the following is required?

options.label: A
options.html: A standing as-needed restraint order written at admission

options.label: B
options.html: Consent of his family before restraints are applied

options.label: C
options.html: A face-to-face evaluation by a physician or other qualified practitioner within 1 hour

options.label: D
options.html: Renewal of the restraint order once every 24 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Restraint until the end of the order even if he becomes calm

items.explanationHtml:
Federal Medicare hospital rules allow restraint or seclusion only to ensure immediate physical safety when less restrictive measures have failed. The patient must be seen face to face within 1 hour by a physician or another trained, qualified practitioner. Orders are time-limited (for adults, up to 4 hours at a time), may never be written as as-needed (PRN) or standing orders, and restraint must end at the earliest possible time.

Restraint is never for punishment, convenience or staff shortages, and the patient must be monitored throughout.

Takeaway: restraint: last resort, time-limited order, face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour, release as soon as safe.

whyNot.A: PRN or standing orders for restraint are prohibited; each episode needs its own order.
whyNot.B: Restraint in an emergency is based on immediate safety and does not require family consent.
whyNot.D: Adult orders for violent behavior last up to 4 hours at a time, not 24 hours.
whyNot.E: Restraint must be removed as soon as the patient is no longer dangerous, whatever the time on the order.

items.objective: State the federal safeguards for emergency physical restraint.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man with smear-positive cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis repeatedly leaves the hospital's airborne isolation room, stops his medication and returns to a crowded shelter. Education, incentives and directly observed therapy have been offered and refused. Which of the following provides the legal basis for compelling his isolation and treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: The duty to warn identifiable third parties

options.label: B
options.html: Psychiatric civil commitment law

options.label: C
options.html: EMTALA stabilisation requirements

options.label: D
options.html: State public health authority over communicable disease

options.label: E
options.html: The HIPAA Privacy Rule

items.explanationHtml:
States have public health power to protect the community from communicable disease. Health departments can require directly observed therapy and, when less restrictive measures fail, can obtain orders for isolation or detention of a person with infectious tuberculosis who will not adhere, with due-process protections. Tuberculosis is also a reportable disease.

This is not psychiatric commitment: the basis is the risk of transmission, not mental illness.

Takeaway: nonadherent infectious TB: public health law permits escalating measures up to court-ordered isolation.

whyNot.A: The duty to warn concerns specific threats of violence by a patient, not infection control.
whyNot.B: He has no mental illness, so psychiatric commitment criteria do not apply.
whyNot.C: EMTALA governs emergency screening and stabilisation, not long-term public health measures.
whyNot.E: HIPAA permits disclosure to public health authorities but does not give anyone power to detain.

items.objective: Identify public health law as the basis for compelled isolation and treatment of infectious tuberculosis.

items.stemHtml: A county attorney petitions a court for the 90-day involuntary psychiatric commitment of a 31-year-old man with schizophrenia who has threatened a neighbor. Under the US Supreme Court's due-process ruling on civil commitment, which of the following is the minimum standard of proof the state must meet?

options.label: A
options.html: Reasonable suspicion

options.label: B
options.html: Probable cause

options.label: C
options.html: Preponderance of the evidence

options.label: D
options.html: Clear and convincing evidence

options.label: E
options.html: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt

items.explanationHtml:
Because civil commitment is a serious loss of liberty, the Supreme Court held that the state must prove the grounds for commitment by at least clear and convincing evidence. That is more than the preponderance standard of ordinary civil cases but less than the beyond-reasonable-doubt standard of criminal trials. States may set a higher standard.

Short emergency holds are started on a clinician's or officer's judgement, but continued commitment requires a hearing with counsel and this standard of proof.

Takeaway: continued civil commitment requires at least clear and convincing evidence at a hearing.

whyNot.A: Reasonable suspicion is a low criminal-procedure threshold for brief stops, far below what commitment requires.
whyNot.B: Probable cause may support starting an emergency hold but is not enough for a longer commitment.
whyNot.C: Preponderance was held too low for the liberty interest at stake in commitment.
whyNot.E: Beyond a reasonable doubt is not required; it is the criminal standard, although a state may choose it.

items.objective: State the minimum standard of proof for civil commitment.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman comes to the office to discuss the results of a colonoscopy and CT scan done last week for iron-deficiency anemia. The biopsy shows adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon, and the CT shows several liver metastases. She has come alone. The physician has arranged a private room, turned off the pager and sat down facing her. After greeting her, which of the following is the most appropriate thing for the physician to say first?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'm afraid I have bad news: you have stage IV colon cancer."

options.label: B
options.html: "Before we go over the results, what is your understanding of why we did these tests?"

options.label: C
options.html: "The good news is that there are many new treatments for colon cancer."

options.label: D
options.html: "The biopsy shows an adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastases."

options.label: E
options.html: "Would you like to call someone to be with you before we start?"

items.explanationHtml:
After preparing the setting, the next step in breaking bad news is to find out what the patient already knows or suspects. Her answer shows the gap between her understanding and the facts, her vocabulary and her emotional state, and it tells the physician where to start. The physician can then ask how much detail she wants, give a warning that serious news is coming, and share the result in plain words in small pieces.

Leading with the diagnosis skips that step; leading with reassurance or jargon blocks understanding.

Takeaway: set the scene, then ask what the patient understands before you share the news.

whyNot.A: Announcing the diagnosis immediately, before learning what she knows, gives her no preparation; the warning shot comes after assessing her understanding.
whyNot.C: Starting with reassurance before she knows the diagnosis is premature and may make the later news feel dishonest.
whyNot.D: This is medical jargon delivered without preparation, which she may not understand.
whyNot.E: Offering support is kind, but she has already chosen to come alone, and asking her understanding is the essential next step; support can be offered when the plan is discussed.

items.objective: Assess the patient's understanding before delivering bad news.

items.stemHtml: The patient from the previous item says she knew the tests were "to look for a bleed." The physician warns her that the results are serious and then tells her, in plain words, that she has colon cancer that has spread to the liver. She stops talking, looks down and begins to cry. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "There's no need to cry; the treatments today are very effective."

options.label: B
options.html: "Let me explain the chemotherapy options so you can start right away."

options.label: C
options.html: "Many people with this cancer live for years."

options.label: D
options.html: "I know exactly how you feel."

options.label: E
options.html: Pause, offer a tissue and say, "This is a lot to take in. I'm here with you."

items.explanationHtml:
Strong emotion blocks the processing of information. The physician should stop giving facts, allow silence, and respond to the emotion first: name or acknowledge it, express support and stay present. Treatment planning can follow when she is ready, often at a further visit.

Premature reassurance, rushing to logistics and claims to know exactly how she feels all close down the emotion instead of acknowledging it.

Takeaway: respond to emotion with silence and an empathic statement before moving on to the plan.

whyNot.A: Telling her not to cry dismisses her emotion and offers reassurance that may not be accurate for her.
whyNot.B: Moving straight to treatment details ignores her emotional state; she will not absorb the information now.
whyNot.C: This is premature, nonspecific reassurance that may not apply to her and avoids her distress.
whyNot.D: No one knows exactly how another person feels; the statement sounds hollow and centres the physician.

items.objective: Respond empathically to a patient's emotion after delivering bad news.

items.stemHtml: One week later, the patient from the previous items asks the physician to meet with her and her husband to discuss treatment. Her husband speaks mainly Cantonese and has limited English. Their 24-year-old son, who is fluent in both languages, offers to interpret so that the meeting can proceed today. A qualified Cantonese interpreter is available by video, and the patient agrees to use one if the physician recommends it. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to proceed?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask the son to interpret because he is an adult and the family prefers it

options.label: B
options.html: Hold the meeting in English and give the husband written material in Chinese

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the patient to interpret for her husband

options.label: D
options.html: Use the qualified video interpreter for the meeting

options.label: E
options.html: Postpone the meeting until an in-person interpreter can attend

items.explanationHtml:
A treatment-planning meeting about metastatic cancer needs accurate, complete interpretation. A qualified interpreter, whether in person, by telephone or by video, avoids the omissions and softening that family interpreters introduce, and lets the son take part as a family member instead of carrying the burden of interpreting his mother's prognosis. The patient agrees, and video interpretation is available now.

Family members may interpret only when the patient asks for it and the situation allows, and even then a qualified interpreter is preferred for high-stakes discussions.

Takeaway: high-stakes family meetings need a qualified interpreter; video or phone is acceptable when it is available now.

whyNot.A: An adult son is still a family member likely to filter or soften news about his mother, and a qualified interpreter is available.
whyNot.B: Written material cannot replace a conversation in which the husband can ask questions.
whyNot.C: Asking the distressed patient to interpret her own prognosis to her husband is inappropriate and unreliable.
whyNot.E: Delay is unnecessary because qualified video interpretation is available immediately.

items.objective: Use a qualified interpreter, by video if needed, for a high-stakes family meeting.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. He has a temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F), respirations of 24/min and an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air, improving to 94% with 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. Four hours after admission he dresses and tells the nurse that he is leaving because his granddaughter's wedding is tomorrow. He is alert and oriented. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: "You can't leave; I'll have to call security."

options.label: B
options.html: "If you leave, your insurance won't pay for this hospital stay."

options.label: C
options.html: "I'm going to ask a psychiatrist to come and assess you."

options.label: D
options.html: "Sign this against-medical-advice form, and then you're free to go."

options.label: E
options.html: "Tell me what's making it so important to leave today."

items.explanationHtml:
When a patient wants to leave against advice, the first step is to explore the reason. Understanding the concern (here, the wedding) opens the way to solutions: treating the cause of the hurry, negotiating a plan, and checking his understanding of the risks as part of a capacity assessment.

Threats, misinformation and forms do not replace a conversation. Most patients who are heard either stay or accept a safer plan.

Takeaway: a patient asking to leave: first ask why, then assess capacity and negotiate.

whyNot.A: An alert adult cannot be detained simply for wanting to leave; threatening security damages trust.
whyNot.B: This claim is generally untrue and is a coercive scare tactic, not an exploration of his concerns.
whyNot.C: Any physician can assess capacity, and nothing so far suggests a psychiatric problem.
whyNot.D: An AMA form is not a substitute for discussing risks, alternatives and his reasons.

items.objective: Explore the reason first when a patient wants to leave against medical advice.

items.stemHtml: The patient from the previous item explains that he promised to walk his granddaughter down the aisle. The physician explains that leaving could lead to worsening pneumonia, respiratory failure and death. He repeats these risks accurately, says he understands they apply to him, and says that missing the wedding would be worse for him than the risk. He still declines to stay. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Respect his decision, give oral antibiotics and return precautions, and document the discussion

options.label: B
options.html: Place him on an emergency hold until the infection improves

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge him with no prescriptions because he is leaving against advice

options.label: D
options.html: Tell him he must sign the AMA form before he can receive prescriptions

options.label: E
options.html: Ask his family to persuade him to stay before he is allowed to go

items.explanationHtml:
He has capacity: he states a consistent choice, understands and appreciates the risks, and reasons from his own values. A capacitated adult may refuse hospitalization. The physician should still provide the best care he will accept (an oral antibiotic regimen, return precautions, a follow-up appointment, and an invitation to come back at any time) and document the capacity assessment and informed refusal.

Leaving against advice never means forfeiting care: withholding prescriptions or follow-up is punitive and unsafe.

Takeaway: informed refusal by a capacitated patient: respect it, offer the safest alternative plan, document and keep the door open.

whyNot.B: Emergency holds are for danger from mental illness, not for a capacitated adult refusing medical care.
whyNot.C: Withholding treatment because he leaves against advice is punitive and harms him.
whyNot.D: Signing a form is optional; care cannot be made conditional on it.
whyNot.E: He may involve family if he wishes, but his decision does not need their approval.

items.objective: Manage an informed refusal by a capacitated patient with a harm-reduction plan and documentation.

items.stemHtml: Two days later, the patient from the previous items is brought back to the emergency department by his wife. He is febrile and drowsy, does not know where he is, and cannot answer questions or state a preference. His oxygen saturation is 82% on room air. He has no advance directive or named health-care agent. His wife says, "He only left for the wedding. He'd want you to treat him now." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit him and begin treatment with his wife's agreement

options.label: B
options.html: Withhold treatment because he previously refused hospital care

options.label: C
options.html: Wait until he regains capacity before treating

options.label: D
options.html: Ask a court to appoint a guardian before treating

options.label: E
options.html: Request an ethics consultation before treating

items.explanationHtml:
He now lacks capacity, and his earlier refusal was about leaving on a particular day for a particular reason, not a refusal of all pneumonia treatment. His wife is the usual first default surrogate and, using substituted judgment, reports that he would want treatment. The condition is also urgent. The team should treat.

A prior refusal binds only for the decision and circumstances to which it applied. Courts and ethics consultation are for unresolved conflicts or when no surrogate exists, not for situations in which the patient's wishes and the surrogate agree.

Takeaway: a past refusal applies to that decision only; with lost capacity, treat on the surrogate's substituted judgment.

whyNot.B: His previous refusal concerned staying in hospital before the wedding, not all future care.
whyNot.C: Waiting for capacity to return could be fatal; a surrogate can decide now.
whyNot.D: A guardian is unnecessary because his wife can act as surrogate, and delay is dangerous.
whyNot.E: There is no conflict to resolve; delaying urgent care for consultation is inappropriate.

items.objective: Recognise that a prior refusal is decision-specific and use a surrogate when capacity is lost.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after neighbors reported him shouting in the hallway of his apartment building. He says that his neighbors are pumping poison gas through the vents and that he will "take care of them tonight" with a hunting knife he owns. He has not slept for days. He has no medical illness, and a urine drug screen is negative. He demands to leave. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge him with an outpatient psychiatry referral

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the police to arrest him for making threats

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain a court order before keeping him in the emergency department

options.label: D
options.html: Warn the neighbors and then discharge him

options.label: E
options.html: Place him on an emergency involuntary hold for psychiatric evaluation

items.explanationHtml:
He appears to have a psychotic illness and has made a specific threat to harm identifiable people, with access to a weapon. That meets the standard for an emergency involuntary hold, which can be started without first going to court (by a physician, police officer or other person the state authorises) for a time-limited evaluation, followed by court review if longer admission is needed.

Warning potential victims may also become necessary, but it does not replace keeping him and the neighbors safe through evaluation and treatment.

Takeaway: mental illness + imminent danger to others: emergency hold now; court review comes later.

whyNot.A: Discharging a psychotic man who has just threatened to stab his neighbors is unsafe.
whyNot.B: His behaviour seems driven by psychosis, which needs medical evaluation and treatment rather than arrest.
whyNot.C: Emergency holds exist precisely so that dangerous patients can be kept before a court hearing.
whyNot.D: Warning alone and then releasing him leaves the danger in place; the priority is evaluation and treatment.

items.objective: Initiate an emergency involuntary hold for a patient whose mental illness makes him dangerous to others.

items.stemHtml: While on the emergency hold, the patient from the previous item becomes increasingly agitated. He paces, shouts that staff are "working with the neighbors" and punches the wall, but has not yet hit anyone. Staff have tried calm verbal de-escalation in a quiet room for several minutes without success. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Offer him an oral antipsychotic or benzodiazepine

options.label: B
options.html: Place him in four-point restraints with an as-needed order for 24 hours

options.label: C
options.html: Seclude him until morning without further assessment

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain a court order before giving any medication

options.label: E
options.html: Ask security to remove him from the hospital

items.explanationHtml:
Management of agitation moves stepwise from the least restrictive option: verbal de-escalation, then offering medication by mouth, then intramuscular medication or brief restraint or seclusion only if the danger is imminent and less restrictive steps fail. Offering oral medication respects his choice and often avoids coercion.

Emergency medication without consent is permitted when there is imminent danger and does not require a court order, but it follows, not precedes, an offer of voluntary medication when that is safe.

Takeaway: agitation: de-escalate, offer oral medication, and escalate to emergency medication or restraint only if danger is imminent.

whyNot.B: Restraint is a last resort, and as-needed or 24-hour restraint orders are not permitted.
whyNot.C: Seclusion must be time-limited with frequent reassessment and is not the next step while voluntary medication has not been offered.
whyNot.D: A court order is not required for emergency medication when danger is imminent; in any case oral medication should be offered first.
whyNot.E: He is on a legal hold because he is dangerous; releasing him would endanger him and others.

items.objective: Choose the least restrictive next step for an agitated patient on a psychiatric hold.

items.stemHtml: The patient from the previous items accepted oral medication and was admitted to the psychiatric unit on the emergency hold. Three days later the hold is about to expire. He is calmer but still believes his neighbors are poisoning him and says he will "deal with them" when he gets home. He refuses to stay voluntarily. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Petition the court for continued involuntary commitment

options.label: B
options.html: Extend the hold by a physician's order for as long as needed

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge him when the hold expires

options.label: D
options.html: Ask his mother to sign him in voluntarily

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer him to the county jail

items.explanationHtml:
Emergency holds are time-limited. If the patient still meets commitment criteria (here, danger to others from ongoing psychosis) and will not stay voluntarily, the treating team must start the legal process for continued commitment, which gives him a hearing, notice and counsel. A physician cannot extend detention indefinitely on his own authority.

Takeaway: when a hold is ending and the danger persists, petition the court; never extend detention informally.

whyNot.B: Detention beyond the emergency period requires judicial review, not a physician's order alone.
whyNot.C: He remains dangerous to identifiable people, so release without further process is unsafe.
whyNot.D: A parent cannot consent to admission for an adult.
whyNot.E: He has not been charged with a crime and needs treatment for a mental illness, not incarceration.

items.objective: Seek court-ordered commitment when a patient on an expiring hold remains dangerous.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of vomiting and deep, rapid breathing. She is lethargic. Serum glucose is 540 mg/dL (30.0 mmol/L), venous pH is 7.05 and urine ketones are large. Her parents belong to a faith community that relies on prayer, and they refuse insulin and intravenous fluids, saying they will take her home. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge her with the parents after documenting their refusal

options.label: B
options.html: Begin intravenous fluids and insulin now

options.label: C
options.html: Wait for a court order before starting treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the girl whether she wants treatment and follow her choice

options.label: E
options.html: Give oral rehydration only, as a compromise

items.explanationHtml:
Diabetic ketoacidosis is life-threatening. Parents' authority does not extend to refusing emergency life-saving treatment for a child, so the team should start treatment immediately while explaining what they are doing, involving hospital legal staff and child protective services as required, and continuing to work with the parents.

A court order is sought when time allows (nonemergency refusals); it should not delay emergency treatment.

Takeaway: a child in a life-threatening emergency is treated despite parental refusal; seek legal support in parallel, not first.

whyNot.A: Sending a child in severe DKA home would likely be fatal and constitutes medical neglect.
whyNot.C: Delaying emergency treatment for a court order risks her life; the emergency exception applies.
whyNot.D: A 10-year-old's assent matters, but she cannot give binding consent or refusal for life-saving care, and she is lethargic.
whyNot.E: Oral fluids alone cannot treat severe DKA and are unsafe in a vomiting, lethargic child.

items.objective: Treat a child's life-threatening emergency despite parental refusal.

items.stemHtml: The girl from the previous item recovers in the pediatric intensive care unit. Before discharge, her parents say they will stop giving insulin at home because they believe prayer alone will heal her. Several conversations with the diabetes team and the family's own religious leader have not changed their position. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge her home and schedule follow-up in 1 week

options.label: B
options.html: Teach the girl to inject herself secretly

options.label: C
options.html: Report the situation to child protective services

options.label: D
options.html: Keep her in the hospital indefinitely without legal authority

options.label: E
options.html: Switch her to an oral diabetes medication

items.explanationHtml:
Refusing insulin for a child with type 1 diabetes will predictably cause death, so it is medical neglect. Physicians are mandated reporters, and child protective services (with the courts) can ensure that she receives treatment while the family is supported. Respectful engagement with the parents should continue.

Takeaway: planned withholding of life-sustaining treatment for a child is medical neglect: report it to child protective services.

whyNot.A: Discharge with a plan to stop insulin knowingly sends her home to a life-threatening situation.
whyNot.B: Secretly teaching a 10-year-old to defy her parents is unreliable and not a safe or honest plan.
whyNot.D: Holding a child without legal authority is not lawful; protective services and the courts provide that authority.
whyNot.E: Type 1 diabetes requires insulin; oral agents are not a substitute.

items.objective: Report planned withholding of life-sustaining treatment from a child as medical neglect.

items.stemHtml: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the study summary?

options.label: A
options.html: Professional interpretation was associated with better comprehension, and an effect on return visits was not shown

options.label: B
options.html: Professional interpretation caused a reduction in return visits within 14 days

options.label: C
options.html: Professional interpretation was associated with better comprehension only for telephone interpretation

options.label: D
options.html: Ad hoc and professional interpretation produced similar comprehension after adjustment

options.label: E
options.html: Ad hoc interpretation was associated with fewer return visits within 14 days

items.explanationHtml:
Comprehension was higher with professional interpretation (80% vs 55%), and the adjusted odds ratio of 2.9 has a confidence interval that excludes 1. Return visits were lower (8% vs 12%), but the difference was not statistically significant, so the study does not show an effect on that outcome.

Because this is an observational cohort, the findings show association, not causation, and results were not reported by interpretation mode.

Takeaway: read each outcome separately: a significant primary outcome does not make a nonsignificant secondary outcome positive.

whyNot.B: The return-visit difference was not significant, and an observational design cannot establish causation.
whyNot.C: Results were not broken down by interpretation mode, so this subgroup conclusion is unsupported.
whyNot.D: The adjusted odds ratio of 2.9 with a CI excluding 1 shows a difference persisting after adjustment.
whyNot.E: Return visits were numerically fewer with professional, not ad hoc, interpretation, and the difference was not significant.

items.objective: Draw a conclusion from an observational study that separates significant and nonsignificant outcomes.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, approximately how many patients would need to receive professional rather than ad hoc interpretation for one additional patient to give a correct teach-back (to the nearest whole number)?
items.explanationHtml:
Absolute difference in correct teach-back = 80% − 55% = 25 percentage points = 0.25. The number needed = 1/0.25 = 4 patients.

This is the number-needed-to-treat idea applied to a beneficial outcome. It uses the absolute difference, not either group's rate alone.

Takeaway: number needed = 1 / absolute difference in proportions (1/0.25 = 4).

whyNot.A: One comes from 1/0.80 (using only the professional group's rate), which is not a between-group comparison.
whyNot.B: Two comes from 1/0.55 (using only the ad hoc group's rate).
whyNot.D: Eight comes from 1/0.12, the ad hoc group's return-visit rate, which is the wrong outcome and not a difference.
whyNot.E: Twenty-five is the absolute difference expressed as percentage points; the number needed is its reciprocal.

items.objective: Calculate a number needed from the absolute difference in two proportions.

items.stemHtml: Which of the following is the most important threat to the conclusion that professional interpretation improves comprehension?

options.label: A
options.html: Recall bias in how patients reported the outcome

options.label: B
options.html: Lead-time bias in when comprehension was measured

options.label: C
options.html: Observer bias in how teach-back was scored

options.label: D
options.html: Confounding by when and where ad hoc interpreters were used

options.label: E
options.html: Too small a sample to detect a real difference

items.explanationHtml:
Interpretation type was not randomized; ad hoc interpretation clustered on night shifts and in the busiest hours, when discharge teaching may be rushed for any patient. Those circumstances could lower comprehension independently of the interpreter, so they confound the comparison. Adjustment for age, language and triage level cannot remove confounders that were not measured, such as shift, staffing and time spent on teaching.

A randomized design, or at least measuring and adjusting for shift and discharge-teaching time, would strengthen causal inference.

Takeaway: in a nonrandomized comparison, ask what determined who got which exposure; that is where confounding hides.

whyNot.A: Comprehension was measured directly by teach-back, not by patients recalling past exposures.
whyNot.B: Lead-time bias applies to survival measured from earlier diagnosis in screening studies, not to comprehension.
whyNot.C: The assessor was unaware of interpretation type, which limits observer bias.
whyNot.E: With 500 patients and a CI of 1.9–4.4 for the primary outcome, the study had enough power to detect the difference.

items.objective: Identify confounding as the main limitation of an observational comparison of interpreter types.

items.stemHtml: A clinician in one of the intervention practices has just explained drug K to a 68-year-old man. Which of the following statements by the clinician best reflects the intervention tested in this study?

options.label: A
options.html: "Do you understand how to take this medicine?"

options.label: B
options.html: "Here is a leaflet that explains everything about drug K."

options.label: C
options.html: "Your pharmacist will go over the instructions with you."

options.label: D
options.html: "You don't have any questions, do you?"

options.label: E
options.html: "I want to be sure I explained this clearly. How will you take drug K at home?"

items.explanationHtml:
Teach-back asks the patient to explain, in his own words, what he will do, framed as a check on the clinician's explanation rather than a test of the patient. Any gap is then re-explained and checked again.

Yes/no questions, leaflets and handing the task to someone else do not show what the patient actually understood.

Takeaway: teach-back = "Tell me in your own words how you'll…" framed as checking my explanation.

whyNot.A: A yes/no check usually gets "yes" regardless of understanding; it is not teach-back.
whyNot.B: Written information can supplement, but it does not confirm that the patient understood.
whyNot.C: Delegating teaching without checking understanding is not the intervention studied.
whyNot.D: A leading closed question discourages questions and checks nothing.

items.objective: Recognise the wording of teach-back in a clinical encounter.

items.stemHtml: Which of the following is the main reason the investigators randomized practices rather than individual patients?

options.label: A
options.html: To ensure that each practice enrolled the same number of patients

options.label: B
options.html: To prevent trained clinicians from using teach-back with control patients

options.label: C
options.html: To allow blinding of patients to the knowledge check

options.label: D
options.html: To remove the need to account for clustering in the analysis

options.label: E
options.html: To increase statistical power compared with individual randomization

items.explanationHtml:
Once a clinician is trained in teach-back, it is very hard to switch it off for some patients. If patients in the same practice were randomized individually, control patients would receive some of the intervention (contamination), shrinking the measured difference. Randomizing whole practices keeps the groups separate.

Cluster randomization usually reduces statistical power for a given number of patients, because patients in the same practice resemble each other, and the analysis must account for clustering, as this study did.

Takeaway: cluster randomization is chosen to prevent contamination when an intervention acts through clinicians or settings.

whyNot.A: Cluster randomization does not ensure equal enrollment per practice, and that is not its purpose.
whyNot.C: Patients could not easily be blinded either way, and the knowledge check is the same in both arms.
whyNot.D: Cluster randomization creates the need to account for clustering rather than removing it.
whyNot.E: Cluster designs generally lose power compared with individual randomization of the same number of patients.

items.objective: Explain why a communication intervention is tested with cluster randomization.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man has waited 2 hours past his appointment time in a busy clinic because of an emergency earlier in the day. When the physician enters, he says loudly, "This is ridiculous. My time matters too." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "There was an emergency, so the delay couldn't be helped."

options.label: B
options.html: "If you raise your voice, I'll have to ask you to leave."

options.label: C
options.html: "I can see you're frustrated, and I'm sorry you had to wait so long."

options.label: D
options.html: "Let's not waste more time; what brings you in today?"

options.label: E
options.html: "The front desk should have told you about the delay."

items.explanationHtml:
With an angry patient, acknowledge the emotion and apologise for the inconvenience before moving on. Naming the feeling and validating it usually lowers the temperature and lets the visit proceed. Explanations, if any, come after the acknowledgement, and blame should not be shifted to others.

Setting limits is appropriate only for threatening or abusive behavior, which this is not.

Takeaway: angry patient: acknowledge the feeling and apologise for the wait first; don't argue, deflect or threaten.

whyNot.A: Leading with a justification sounds defensive and dismisses his frustration.
whyNot.B: He is upset but not threatening; a warning escalates the encounter.
whyNot.D: Skipping past his concern ignores the emotion and is likely to make him angrier.
whyNot.E: Blaming colleagues is unprofessional and does not address his feelings.

items.objective: Respond to an angry patient by acknowledging emotion and apologising.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman comes to the office because of low back pain that started 5 days ago after she moved furniture. She has no fever, weight loss, cancer history, numbness, weakness or bowel or bladder symptoms, and her examination is normal apart from paraspinal tenderness. She asks for an MRI of her spine "to make sure nothing is seriously wrong." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Sure, I'll order the MRI so you can feel reassured."

options.label: B
options.html: "Insurance won't pay for an MRI, so it's not an option."

options.label: C
options.html: "An MRI isn't needed; it's just a muscle strain."

options.label: D
options.html: "What worries you most about your back?"

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll refer you to a spine surgeon who can decide about the MRI."

items.explanationHtml:
When a patient requests a test that is not indicated, the physician should first explore the concern behind the request. Here she fears something serious; once that fear is known, the physician can explain why her history and examination are reassuring, what imaging cannot add for acute nonspecific back pain, what warning signs would change the plan, and how the pain will be treated.

Ordering an unneeded test is not patient-centred care: it exposes her to incidental findings and cost. Flatly refusing without exploring the worry tends to leave the patient dissatisfied and still anxious.

Takeaway: request for an unnecessary test: explore the underlying concern first, then explain and agree on a plan.

whyNot.A: Ordering an unindicated MRI to placate her exposes her to incidental findings without benefit.
whyNot.B: Citing insurance avoids the real conversation and may not even be accurate.
whyNot.C: Dismissive reassurance before understanding her concern often fails to reassure.
whyNot.E: Referral for uncomplicated acute back pain is unnecessary and avoids the physician's own responsibility.

items.objective: Explore the concern behind a request for an unnecessary test.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy comes to the office with his mother for an annual examination. His mother answers most of the physician's questions for him. The physician wants to take a psychosocial history covering home, school, activities, substance use, sexuality, mood and safety. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask the questions with his mother present so that she can add details

options.label: B
options.html: Give him a written questionnaire and review it with his mother

options.label: C
options.html: Postpone the psychosocial history until he is 18

options.label: D
options.html: Ask his mother to complete the psychosocial history on his behalf

options.label: E
options.html: Explain the plan to both, then ask the mother to step out for part of the visit

items.explanationHtml:
Adolescents should have time alone with the clinician at every routine visit from early adolescence. Explaining to both parent and teen that this is routine, and explaining confidentiality and its limits, makes the request feel ordinary and preserves the parent's trust. Teens disclose far more about substances, sex, mood and safety when alone.

Takeaway: routine adolescent visits include time alone with the teen, introduced to parent and teen together as standard practice.

whyNot.A: With his mother present he is unlikely to disclose sensitive information.
whyNot.B: Reviewing a sensitive questionnaire with his mother removes the confidentiality that makes it useful.
whyNot.C: Risk behaviours often start in early and mid adolescence; waiting until 18 misses the chance to help.
whyNot.D: A parent cannot report a teen's private behaviours reliably, and this bypasses the patient.

items.objective: Arrange confidential time alone with an adolescent for the psychosocial history.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old widow has seen the same physician for 15 years. At a visit shortly after her husband's death, she gives the physician a box containing her late husband's luxury gold watch and says, "He would have wanted you to have it." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Thank you; I'll keep it in his memory."

options.label: B
options.html: "Thank you so much. This means a lot, but I can't accept something this valuable."

options.label: C
options.html: "I'll accept it if you put the gift in writing."

options.label: D
options.html: "Gifts from patients are against the rules, so please take it back."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll accept it, and you can have extra appointment time in return."

items.explanationHtml:
Small, modest gifts given in gratitude (homemade food, a card) can be accepted graciously. A valuable gift should be declined because it can change the relationship, create expectations, and take advantage of a grieving or vulnerable patient. Declining with warmth and acknowledging what the gesture means preserves the relationship.

Gifts must never be linked to better or preferential care.

Takeaway: accept small gifts graciously; decline valuable ones kindly, especially from vulnerable patients.

whyNot.A: Accepting a valuable heirloom from a grieving patient risks exploiting her vulnerability and compromising the relationship.
whyNot.C: Documentation does not make a valuable gift from a vulnerable patient appropriate.
whyNot.D: This is curt and inaccurate: modest gifts are not forbidden, and the response ignores her grief and gratitude.
whyNot.E: Linking a gift to preferential treatment is a clear ethical breach.

items.objective: Decline a valuable gift from a patient while respecting the gesture.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman who recently immigrated from rural Afghanistan has newly diagnosed breast cancer. Through a professional interpreter, she says that in her family important decisions are made together with her husband and eldest son, and she would like them present when treatment is discussed. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Treatment decisions are yours alone; your family can't be involved."

options.label: B
options.html: "Would you like us to plan the next visit so that your husband and son can join us?"

options.label: C
options.html: "I'll explain everything to your son, and he can decide for you."

options.label: D
options.html: "In this country, patients make their own medical decisions."

options.label: E
options.html: "We should decide today; waiting for your family will delay treatment."

items.explanationHtml:
Respect for autonomy includes respecting a capacitated patient's choice about how decisions are made, including making them together with family or delegating them. Cultural humility means asking the patient about her preferences rather than assuming them from her background or imposing the physician's own model.

The physician should confirm with her, privately, what she wants to know and who should be told what, and keep speaking to her directly.

Takeaway: a capacitated patient may choose to decide with her family; ask and respect her preference.

whyNot.A: Excluding family she wants involved disregards her own choice about how to decide.
whyNot.C: She asked for her family to be present, not to hand the decision entirely to her son; that would assume rather than ask.
whyNot.D: This lectures her and imposes one decision-making model instead of respecting her stated preference.
whyNot.E: A short delay to include her family is usually reasonable for planning cancer treatment, and pressuring her undermines trust.

items.objective: Respect a patient's preference to involve family in decisions (cultural humility).

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with hypertension is deciding whether to start a statin. The physician estimates his 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke as 12% without treatment and 9% with treatment. He says, "Numbers confuse me; just tell me what it means for me." Which of the following statements best communicates this information?

options.label: A
options.html: "The statin lowers your risk of a heart attack or stroke by about a quarter."

options.label: B
options.html: "If you take the statin every day, it will prevent you from having a heart attack."

options.label: C
options.html: "Your risk is fairly low for a man your age, so the statin doesn't matter much."

options.label: D
options.html: "Of 100 men like you, about 12 would have a heart attack or stroke in 10 years without it and 9 with it."

options.label: E
options.html: "The statin cuts your risk from 12 to 9, which is a 25% relative risk reduction."

items.explanationHtml:
