Absolute risks expressed as natural frequencies, with the same denominator and time frame for both choices, are the clearest way to convey benefit, particularly for people with low numeracy. Here, of 100 similar men, 3 fewer would have an event over 10 years (12 − 9 = 3), so about 97 would have the same outcome whether or not they took the drug.

Relative risk reductions ("a quarter", "25%") sound impressive but do not convey the size of the benefit, and absolute promises are inaccurate. A pictograph of 100 figures can help further.

Takeaway: present benefit as absolute natural frequencies (x of 100 with vs without), same denominator and time frame.

whyNot.A: A relative reduction alone exaggerates the perceived benefit and gives him no sense of his absolute risk.
whyNot.B: This promise is false: most treated men would not have had an event anyway, and some still will.
whyNot.C: This judgement replaces information with the physician's opinion and understates a meaningful risk.
whyNot.E: This mixes absolute numbers without a denominator with a relative percentage, which is exactly what he finds confusing.

items.objective: Communicate treatment benefit as absolute natural frequencies to a patient with low numeracy.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1c of 8.9% says, "I've tried every diet. Nothing ever works for me, so I've given up on it." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "You just need more willpower this time."

options.label: B
options.html: "If you don't lose weight, you'll end up on insulin."

options.label: C
options.html: "Why do you think the diets didn't work?"

options.label: D
options.html: "Let me give you a strict 1,200-calorie meal plan to follow."

options.label: E
options.html: "It sounds like you've worked hard and it's been discouraging."

items.explanationHtml:
A reflective, empathic statement acknowledges her effort and discouragement and invites her to say more. Rolling with her resistance instead of arguing keeps her engaged and lets her own reasons and ideas for change emerge, which is the basis of motivational interviewing. Affirming past effort also supports self-efficacy.

Takeaway: meet discouragement with reflection and affirmation, not with pressure, threats or a prescription.

whyNot.A: Attributing failure to willpower is judgmental and likely to increase her hopelessness.
whyNot.B: A fear-based warning provokes resistance and does not build motivation.
whyNot.C: A "why" question about failure can sound blaming and push her to defend herself.
whyNot.D: Imposing a strict plan ignores her experience and repeats approaches that have failed for her.

items.objective: Use reflective listening and affirmation to address discouragement (motivational interviewing).

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man is admitted for evaluation of jaundice. Imaging and biopsy show an unresectable cholangiocarcinoma. Before the physician meets with him, his daughter says, "In our family, we don't tell elders bad news. Please don't tell him it's cancer." The patient has full decision-making capacity. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the daughter?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'm required to tell him everything, whatever he wants."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'll respect your wishes and tell him it's an infection."

options.label: C
options.html: "Tell me more about your concerns. I'd also like to ask him how much he wants to know."

options.label: D
options.html: "Let's ask the ethics committee to decide what he should be told."

options.label: E
options.html: "You can tell him yourself whenever you think he's ready."

items.explanationHtml:
The information belongs to the patient. Exploring the daughter's fears shows respect and often reveals a wish to protect him. The physician then asks the patient himself how much he wants to know and who should receive information. Some patients choose to let family hear the details; that is their right. Lying to the patient, or withholding information he wants, is not acceptable.

Forcing full disclosure on a patient who does not want it is also not patient-centred, so the key step is asking him.

Takeaway: when family asks you to withhold news, explore their concern and ask the patient how much he wants to know.

whyNot.A: Disclosure should follow the patient's own preferences; pushing every detail on him regardless is not required and is not patient-centred.
whyNot.B: Lying to a capacitated patient violates honesty and his right to make informed decisions.
whyNot.D: An ethics consultation is unnecessary until the physician has simply asked the patient his preference.
whyNot.E: Handing disclosure to the family abandons the physician's duty and may mean he is never told.

items.objective: Handle a family request to withhold a diagnosis by exploring concerns and asking the patient's preference.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man sees a new physician after a diagnosis of stage III colon cancer. He says angrily, "My last doctor told me my bleeding was hemorrhoids for a year. If he'd done his job, I wouldn't be in this mess. I'm thinking of suing him." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "It sounds like you feel let down, and that's understandable. Tell me more about what happened."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'm sure your previous doctor did his best with the information he had."

options.label: C
options.html: "You're right; he should have ordered a colonoscopy much sooner."

options.label: D
options.html: "I can't discuss other physicians' care, so let's focus on your treatment."

options.label: E
options.html: "You should talk to a lawyer about that before we go any further."

items.explanationHtml:
The physician should acknowledge the patient's anger and loss, then listen. Without the full record, the physician cannot judge the earlier care, so neither defending nor condemning the other doctor is appropriate. Once the emotion is acknowledged, the visit can turn to treatment planning; if the physician later identifies a possible error, the professional response is honest discussion and appropriate reporting, not speculation.

Takeaway: patient angry about prior care: acknowledge and listen; don't defend or blame a colleague without the facts.

whyNot.B: Reflexively defending the colleague dismisses the patient's experience and may be wrong.
whyNot.C: Condemning the previous physician without the records is speculation and unprofessional.
whyNot.D: Refusing to engage shuts down his emotion; acknowledgement is needed before moving on.
whyNot.E: Steering him to legal action before acknowledging his feelings abandons the therapeutic relationship.

items.objective: Respond to anger about previous care without defending or blaming a colleague.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man who speaks only Haitian Creole comes to the emergency department with 3 hours of intermittent chest discomfort. He is hemodynamically stable, and an initial ECG shows no acute changes. His 10-year-old son, who speaks English and Haitian Creole, has come with him. A telephone interpreter service can connect within 2 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to obtain his history?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask his son to interpret

options.label: B
options.html: Use the telephone interpreter

options.label: C
options.html: Wait for an in-person interpreter tomorrow

options.label: D
options.html: Use a translation app on a smartphone

options.label: E
options.html: Rely on the ECG and troponin results alone

items.explanationHtml:
A qualified telephone interpreter, available within minutes, gives accurate interpretation for a stable patient. Children should not be used as interpreters, both because they are unreliable for medical content and because it places an inappropriate burden on them.

Delay for an in-person interpreter is unnecessary when remote interpretation is immediately available, and the history is essential to evaluating chest pain.

Takeaway: stable patient + qualified remote interpreter available = use it; never use a child.

whyNot.A: A 10-year-old should not interpret medical information for a parent, especially with a qualified interpreter available within minutes.
whyNot.C: Waiting until tomorrow delays the evaluation of chest pain when a remote interpreter is available now.
whyNot.D: Machine translation is unreliable for medical histories and is not a qualified interpreter.
whyNot.E: The history is a key part of evaluating chest pain and cannot be replaced by tests.

items.objective: Use a qualified remote interpreter rather than a child for a stable patient.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man who speaks only Polish develops hives, wheezing and lip swelling minutes after a wasp sting at a family picnic and is rushed to the emergency department by his wife, who is fluent in English. His blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. The telephone interpreter line is not connecting. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Wait for the interpreter line before treating

options.label: B
options.html: Ask his wife to interpret a full history before treating

options.label: C
options.html: Give intramuscular epinephrine now, using his wife for urgent questions

options.label: D
options.html: Give oral antihistamines while waiting for the interpreter

options.label: E
options.html: Ask his wife to sign a consent form for epinephrine

items.explanationHtml:
Anaphylaxis with hypotension is a life-threatening emergency, and epinephrine must not be delayed. In an emergency when no qualified interpreter is immediately available, an accompanying adult may interpret the urgent essentials (allergies, medications). A qualified interpreter should be brought in as soon as the patient is stable, for the full history and discussion.

Emergency treatment proceeds under implied consent; a signed form is not needed.

Takeaway: in a true emergency without a qualified interpreter, treat now and use an adult companion only for urgent essentials.

whyNot.A: Delaying epinephrine in anaphylactic shock could be fatal.
whyNot.B: A full history is not needed before giving epinephrine and would dangerously delay treatment.
whyNot.D: Antihistamines do not treat hypotension or airway swelling and are not a substitute for epinephrine.
whyNot.E: Emergency treatment does not require written consent, and his wife's signature is not what authorises it.

items.objective: Use an ad hoc interpreter only for urgent essentials in a true emergency while treating immediately.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman who speaks Korean comes for a routine 3-month follow-up of well-controlled hypertension with her 40-year-old daughter, who is fluent in Korean and English. The physician offers a professional interpreter. The patient says, through her daughter, that she prefers her daughter to interpret, as she always does for her. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Insist on the professional interpreter because family may never interpret

options.label: B
options.html: Use the daughter without offering any further information

options.label: C
options.html: Explain the interpreter is free and, if she still prefers, use her daughter and document it

options.label: D
options.html: Reschedule the visit until she accepts a professional interpreter

options.label: E
options.html: Conduct the visit in English with the daughter present

items.explanationHtml:
Federal language-access rules let an accompanying adult interpret when the patient specifically asks for it, the adult agrees, and relying on the adult is appropriate in the circumstances. A routine visit for stable hypertension with an adult daughter qualifies. The physician should first make sure the patient knows that a qualified interpreter is available at no cost, then respect her choice and document it.

The physician should reconsider if the conversation becomes complex or sensitive (a new serious diagnosis, consent for a procedure, possible abuse), when a professional interpreter is more appropriate.

Takeaway: an adult companion may interpret if the informed patient requests it and the situation is routine; children never.

whyNot.A: This rule is too absolute; a capacitated patient may choose an adult companion for a routine visit after being offered a qualified interpreter.
whyNot.B: She should be told that professional interpretation is free before her choice can be informed.
whyNot.D: Refusing to see her until she accepts a professional interpreter denies care and disregards her informed preference.
whyNot.E: The patient does not speak English, so an English-only visit fails to communicate with her.

items.objective: Respect a patient's informed request for an adult family member to interpret in a routine visit.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman who is Deaf and communicates in American Sign Language is admitted with newly diagnosed lupus nephritis. The nephrologist plans to discuss a kidney biopsy with her using the hospital's video remote interpreting (VRI) tablet. The video repeatedly freezes, and the patient writes on a pad, "I can't follow this. Please get a real interpreter." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue with VRI and repeat each point several times

options.label: B
options.html: Arrange an in-person qualified sign-language interpreter

options.label: C
options.html: Communicate by exchanging written notes

options.label: D
options.html: Ask her hearing sister, who signs a little, to interpret

options.label: E
options.html: Proceed with the biopsy consent because VRI was offered

items.explanationHtml:
Hospitals must provide effective communication to Deaf patients under the Americans with Disabilities Act. VRI is acceptable only when it works: a clear, real-time, high-quality video picture and a user who can see the interpreter. When VRI fails, the hospital must supply another effective aid, typically an in-person qualified interpreter, especially for a consent discussion.

Takeaway: VRI counts only when it works; if it fails, get a qualified in-person interpreter.

whyNot.A: Repeating points over a failing video link does not provide effective communication.
whyNot.C: Written notes are not effective for a complex consent discussion, and English may be her second language.
whyNot.D: A relative with limited signing skill is not a qualified interpreter and may not convey the information accurately.
whyNot.E: Offering a service that does not work does not satisfy the duty to communicate effectively; consent would not be informed.

items.objective: Replace failing video remote interpreting with an in-person qualified interpreter for a Deaf patient.

items.stemHtml: A physician is about to explain a new diagnosis of heart failure to a 72-year-old Tagalog-speaking man through a telephone interpreter on a speakerphone. Which of the following is the best technique?

options.label: A
options.html: Speak in short segments, addressing the patient directly and pausing for interpretation

options.label: B
options.html: Give the full explanation at once, then let the interpreter summarise it

options.label: C
options.html: Speak to the interpreter in the third person about the patient

options.label: D
options.html: Use medical terms so that the interpreter can translate precisely

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the interpreter to leave out details that might upset him

items.explanationHtml:
Good interpreted communication means speaking directly to the patient in the first person, using plain language in short segments, and pausing so the interpreter can render everything accurately. Teach-back through the interpreter then confirms understanding.

Long monologues invite omissions; jargon is hard to interpret; and asking the interpreter to edit content makes the interpreter a filter.

Takeaway: short, plain, first-person segments spoken to the patient; then teach-back.

whyNot.B: Long monologues are hard to interpret completely, and summaries lose content.
whyNot.C: Third-person speech excludes the patient and weakens the relationship.
whyNot.D: Jargon is more likely to be misinterpreted and misunderstood; plain language is better.
whyNot.E: Interpreters should convey everything; deciding what to omit is not their role and undermines informed decisions.

items.objective: Apply correct technique for interpreted communication.

items.stemHtml: During an interpreted visit, a physician asks a 57-year-old Russian-speaking woman how she has been feeling since starting a new antihypertensive. The patient and the professional interpreter speak to each other for nearly a minute. The interpreter then says, "She says she's fine." Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Accept the summary and move on

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the interpreter whether the patient seems truthful

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the interpreter to interpret everything she said, in full

options.label: D
options.html: Ask a family member to listen in and check the interpreter

options.label: E
options.html: End the visit and schedule a new interpreter

items.explanationHtml:
A minute-long exchange reduced to "she's fine" means content has been lost. The physician should politely ask the interpreter to render everything that was said, including side conversations, and remind the interpreter that the patient's own words matter. Symptoms such as dizziness or side effects are often buried in such summaries.

Takeaway: if an interpreter summarises, ask for complete interpretation of everything said.

whyNot.A: Accepting a summary risks missing side effects or symptoms she described.
whyNot.B: Asking the interpreter to judge truthfulness moves her out of her role and does not recover the missing content.
whyNot.D: Using a family member to check a professional reverses the hierarchy of reliability and breaches privacy.
whyNot.E: A simple request for complete interpretation solves the problem without ending the visit.

items.objective: Request complete interpretation when an interpreter summarises the patient's words.

items.stemHtml: An 83-year-old man has had a large left middle cerebral artery stroke and is aphasic and unable to make decisions. He has no advance directive. His daughter, his surrogate, is asked whether he should have a percutaneous feeding tube. She says, "I don't know what to do. Please just tell me what to choose." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: "It's your decision; let me know when you've decided."

options.label: B
options.html: "If he were my father, I'd want everything done."

options.label: C
options.html: "Tell me about your father. What would he say about this if he could join us?"

options.label: D
options.html: "Let's ask your brothers and take a vote."

options.label: E
options.html: "Until you decide, the law requires us to place the tube."

items.explanationHtml:
A surrogate's task is to decide as the patient would (substituted judgment). Many surrogates feel they are being asked what they themselves want; reframing the question around the patient's values, past statements and way of living relieves some of that burden and leads to a decision grounded in his wishes. The physician can then offer a recommendation that fits those values.

Takeaway: guide a surrogate by asking what the patient would say, not what the surrogate wants.

whyNot.A: This abandons the surrogate when she has asked for help; physicians should guide and recommend.
whyNot.B: This imposes the physician's own values before learning anything about the patient's.
whyNot.D: A family vote replaces the patient's values with a majority opinion and bypasses the surrogate.
whyNot.E: This is false and coercive; there is no legal requirement to place a feeding tube while a surrogate decides.

items.objective: Guide a surrogate toward substituted judgment by asking about the patient's values.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has a living will, written after long discussions with his wife, that declines intubation and mechanical ventilation. He names his wife as his health-care agent. He is now unresponsive with hypercapnic respiratory failure. His wife says, "I know what he wrote, but I'm not ready. Please put him on the ventilator." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "You're his agent, so we'll intubate him now."

options.label: B
options.html: "This is so hard. Can we talk about what he told you he'd want if this happened?"

options.label: C
options.html: "Your opinion doesn't matter; the living will decides."

options.label: D
options.html: "We'll let the ethics committee decide whether to intubate."

options.label: E
options.html: "We'll intubate him for now and discuss his wishes later."

items.explanationHtml:
An agent must speak for the patient's wishes. Here those wishes are clear and specific to this exact situation. The physician should acknowledge the wife's grief, then gently help her return to what he wanted, offering full comfort care for his breathlessness. Most agents, supported this way, come to honour the patient's choice. Ethics consultation is reasonable if she continues to insist.

Intubating against a clear, applicable refusal violates the patient's autonomy even if requested by his agent.

Takeaway: when an agent's request conflicts with the patient's clear wishes, empathise and refocus on what the patient wanted.

whyNot.A: An agent's authority is to carry out the patient's wishes, not to override a clear refusal of this exact treatment.
whyNot.C: Although the living will applies, dismissing the grieving wife is harsh and damages the partnership needed for his care.
whyNot.D: Ethics consultation may help if conflict persists, but the first step is a supportive conversation with her.
whyNot.E: Intubating now imposes the very treatment he refused; "for now" does not respect his wishes.

items.objective: Support an agent to follow the patient's known wishes when grief pulls the other way.

items.stemHtml: A neurologist who studied Spanish in college and can hold a basic conversation is about to tell a 35-year-old Spanish-speaking woman that her MRI and spinal fluid findings indicate multiple sclerosis and to discuss disease-modifying treatment. Her language proficiency has never been formally assessed. A Spanish interpreter is available by video. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

options.label: A
options.html: Use the video interpreter for the discussion

options.label: B
options.html: Conduct the discussion in her own basic Spanish

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the patient's 16-year-old son to help with difficult words

options.label: D
options.html: Give the diagnosis in English and a Spanish pamphlet

options.label: E
options.html: Use her basic Spanish and ask the patient to say if she is confused

items.explanationHtml:
Clinicians with partial fluency often overestimate their skill. A complex conversation about a new chronic diagnosis and treatment options needs either an interpreter or a clinician whose proficiency in that language has been assessed. Basic Spanish can build rapport, but the substantive discussion should go through the qualified interpreter.

Takeaway: partial fluency is not enough for complex discussions; use a qualified interpreter unless your proficiency has been assessed.

whyNot.B: Basic conversational Spanish is likely to produce errors in explaining a complex diagnosis and treatment.
whyNot.C: Using a minor as an interpreter is inappropriate and unreliable.
whyNot.D: Giving the diagnosis in a language she does not speak, with a pamphlet, does not allow discussion or questions.
whyNot.E: Patients often do not realise or say they are confused; this places the burden on her.

items.objective: Use a qualified interpreter rather than limited personal language skills for complex discussions.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman is scheduled for total thyroidectomy for a large multinodular goiter. The attending surgeon, running late, asks the surgical intern to have the circulating nurse "get the consent signed." When the nurse brings the form, the patient asks how likely it is that the operation will change her voice. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: The nurse explains the risk from the form and obtains the signature

options.label: B
options.html: The patient signs now, and the surgeon answers her questions after surgery

options.label: C
options.html: The surgeon or a qualified surgical team member discusses the risks before she signs

options.label: D
options.html: The nurse gives her a leaflet on thyroid surgery and obtains the signature

options.label: E
options.html: The anesthesiologist answers her question during the anesthesia consent

items.explanationHtml:
Informed consent is a conversation, not a signature. The duty to inform belongs to the physician performing the procedure, who may involve a qualified member of the surgical team who knows the operation and its risks. A nurse may witness the signature but should not be the one explaining surgical risks. Her question about voice change (recurrent laryngeal nerve injury) must be answered before she signs.

Takeaway: the operating surgeon (or a qualified team member) obtains consent; nurses can witness signatures but do not substitute for the discussion.

whyNot.A: Explaining surgical risks is the surgeon's responsibility; a nurse reading a form is not an informed-consent discussion.
whyNot.B: Consent must be informed before the operation; answering questions afterwards makes the signature meaningless.
whyNot.D: A leaflet can supplement but cannot replace the surgeon's discussion and answers to her questions.
whyNot.E: The anesthesiologist consents for anesthesia; the surgical risks belong to the surgeon's discussion.

items.objective: Identify who must obtain informed consent and when.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman who is a Jehovah's Witness is scheduled for elective total hip arthroplasty. She has full decision-making capacity and states that she will not accept transfusion of red cells, plasma or platelets under any circumstances, even if she would die without them. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Cancel the surgery because it cannot be done safely

options.label: B
options.html: Agree, then transfuse if a life-threatening hemorrhage occurs

options.label: C
options.html: Ask a court for permission to transfuse during surgery

options.label: D
options.html: Ask her family to persuade her to accept blood

options.label: E
options.html: Discuss which blood-conserving measures she accepts and document her refusal

items.explanationHtml:
A capacitated adult may refuse blood products, even if refusal could lead to death. The team should honour that decision and plan accordingly: correct anemia before surgery (for example, iron and, if appropriate, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents), minimise blood loss (tranexamic acid, meticulous hemostasis), and ask about each option individually, because acceptance of measures such as cell salvage or certain fractions varies between individuals. Her decisions should be clearly documented and communicated to the whole team.

Promising to respect her wishes and then transfusing anyway is a battery and a betrayal of trust.

Takeaway: capacitated adult Jehovah's Witness: respect the refusal, plan bloodless strategies, ask about each product, document.

whyNot.A: Bloodless surgical techniques make many operations feasible; cancelling denies her care she wants.
whyNot.B: Transfusing against a capacitated adult's explicit refusal is battery, even in an emergency.
whyNot.C: Courts do not override a capacitated adult's informed refusal of blood for herself.
whyNot.D: Recruiting family to pressure her undermines voluntariness; her decision stands on its own.

items.objective: Respect a capacitated adult's refusal of blood products and plan blood-conserving care.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed 1.5-cm hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer and no nodal involvement tells her surgeon that she wants to treat it with a herbal regimen from a website instead of surgery. She has full decision-making capacity and seems anxious. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "If you won't have surgery, I can't continue as your physician."

options.label: B
options.html: "Herbs don't work, and you'll die without surgery."

options.label: C
options.html: "That's your choice; we can stop discussing surgery."

options.label: D
options.html: "I'd like to understand what draws you to the herbal approach."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'm going to ask psychiatry to assess your capacity."

items.explanationHtml:
Before giving information, the physician should explore why the patient prefers the alternative: fear of surgery, side effects, past experiences or values. Understanding her reasons lets the physician address misconceptions, explain the expected benefit of standard treatment and the lack of evidence for the herbal regimen, discuss which complementary approaches can be used safely alongside standard care, and leave room for her to decide.

A capacitated patient may decline standard treatment, but informed refusal requires that she understand the alternatives and consequences; the relationship should continue either way.

Takeaway: patient prefers an alternative therapy: explore reasons nonjudgmentally, inform honestly, and stay involved.

whyNot.A: Threatening to end the relationship is coercive and abandons her.
whyNot.B: Blunt confrontation is likely to drive her away and overstates certainty.
whyNot.C: Accepting without exploration leaves her uninformed, so any refusal would not be truly informed.
whyNot.E: Choosing an unconventional option does not by itself suggest impaired capacity.

items.objective: Explore a patient's interest in alternative therapy before informing her about standard treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with anxiety disorder is scheduled for elective coronary angiography for stable angina and an abnormal stress test. The cardiologist considers not mentioning the small risk of stroke because the patient is anxious and might decline the procedure. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

options.label: A
options.html: Omit the stroke risk because disclosure could cause anxiety

options.label: B
options.html: Ask his wife whether he should be told about the stroke risk

options.label: C
options.html: Disclose the stroke risk only if the patient asks directly

options.label: D
options.html: Disclose the risk honestly, with context and support

options.label: E
options.html: Postpone consent until his anxiety has been treated

items.explanationHtml:
A material risk such as stroke must be disclosed even if the patient might choose to decline; that possibility is the reason disclosure matters. Therapeutic privilege is a narrow exception for rare situations in which disclosure itself would cause serious, immediate harm to the patient; ordinary anxiety, or the wish to avoid a refusal, does not qualify.

The physician can present the risk honestly with its size in context, address fears and offer support, which most anxious patients can manage.

Takeaway: concern that a patient might refuse never justifies withholding a material risk; therapeutic privilege is rare.

whyNot.A: Withholding a material risk to avoid refusal is a misuse of therapeutic privilege.
whyNot.B: A capacitated patient's right to information does not depend on his wife's permission.
whyNot.C: Material risks must be disclosed proactively, not only if the patient knows to ask.
whyNot.E: Anxiety does not remove capacity; delaying indicated care is unnecessary when he can be informed supportively.

items.objective: Recognise misuse of therapeutic privilege and disclose material risks supportively.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy comes to the clinic alone because of 3 days of dysuria and a urethral discharge. He has had two female sexual partners in the past month. He asks that his parents not be told. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Call his parents for consent before testing

options.label: B
options.html: Test and treat him confidentially for sexually transmitted infections

options.label: C
options.html: Defer testing until he returns with a parent

options.label: D
options.html: Treat him but tell his parents at the next visit

options.label: E
options.html: Refer him to a public health clinic because he is a minor

items.explanationHtml:
Every US state allows minors to consent to testing and treatment of sexually transmitted infections, and confidentiality encourages adolescents to seek care. The physician should test (for gonorrhea and chlamydia, and offer HIV and syphilis testing), treat, counsel about condoms and partner notification, and encourage, but not require, involvement of a trusted adult.

Takeaway: minors can consent to confidential STI care in all states; treat now.

whyNot.A: Parental consent is not required for STI care, and requiring it may stop him from being treated.
whyNot.C: Delay risks complications and transmission and is unnecessary because he can consent himself.
whyNot.D: Promising later disclosure to his parents breaches the confidentiality he is entitled to for STI care.
whyNot.E: He can be treated where he is; referral away is unnecessary and may lose him to follow-up.

items.objective: Provide confidential STI care to a minor without parental consent.

items.stemHtml: An orthopedic surgeon owns stock in, and receives consulting fees from, the company that makes one of the two knee implants she commonly uses. Both implants have similar published outcomes. A 66-year-old man scheduled for total knee arthroplasty asks which implant she recommends. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Recommend the company's implant without comment

options.label: B
options.html: Recommend the other implant without explaining why

options.label: C
options.html: Disclose her financial relationship and explain the evidence for both implants

options.label: D
options.html: Tell him that implant choice is a technical matter he need not consider

options.label: E
options.html: Refer him to another surgeon to avoid the topic

items.explanationHtml:
A financial interest that could influence a recommendation is material information. The surgeon should disclose it and give a balanced account of the options, so the patient can weigh her advice. Institutional conflict-of-interest policies may add further requirements. Federal transparency rules also publish industry payments to physicians, but public reporting does not replace disclosure to the patient.

Takeaway: disclose financial conflicts of interest that bear on your recommendation, and present the options fairly.

whyNot.A: Recommending her company's implant without disclosure hides a conflict that could bias the recommendation.
whyNot.B: Avoiding the conflict silently still deprives him of a reasoned explanation of his options.
whyNot.D: He asked directly, and implant choice is part of the information a patient may want.
whyNot.E: Referring him away is unnecessary; disclosure and a balanced discussion manage the conflict.

items.objective: Disclose a financial conflict of interest when making a treatment recommendation.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with septic shock from a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. She is intubated for airway protection and cannot communicate. Her wallet contains no advance directive or contact details, and the police cannot locate any relatives. The surgeon recommends emergency laparotomy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Proceed with emergency laparotomy

options.label: B
options.html: Wait until a relative can be located

options.label: C
options.html: Request an emergency court order

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the hospital ethics committee to approve surgery

options.label: E
options.html: Treat with antibiotics alone until she can consent

items.explanationHtml:
When delay would threaten life, the patient cannot consent, and no surrogate or known refusal is available, physicians proceed with emergency treatment under implied consent. The team should keep trying to reach family and document the emergency and the reasons for proceeding.

Takeaway: life-threatening emergency, no capacity, no surrogate, no known refusal: treat now.

whyNot.B: Waiting for relatives would allow her to die of a surgically correctable condition.
whyNot.C: A court order is not required for emergency treatment and would cause dangerous delay.
whyNot.D: Ethics committees advise on conflicts; they do not need to approve emergency care.
whyNot.E: Antibiotics alone are inadequate for a perforation with septic shock, and she may never regain capacity without source control.

items.objective: Apply implied consent to an emergency operation when no surrogate can be found.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man who is incarcerated is brought from prison for a colonoscopy to evaluate iron-deficiency anemia. He has full decision-making capacity. After hearing the reasons, risks and alternatives, he declines the procedure. The accompanying corrections officer says, "He's a state prisoner. The prison orders the test, so do it anyway." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Perform the colonoscopy because the prison has authority over his care

options.label: B
options.html: Sedate him and perform the colonoscopy because it is low risk

options.label: C
options.html: Respect his refusal, discuss alternatives and document the discussion

options.label: D
options.html: Ask a court to order the colonoscopy

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the officer to sign the consent form

items.explanationHtml:
People who are incarcerated keep the right to give or refuse informed consent to medical care. Corrections staff cannot consent for a capacitated adult. The physician should respect the refusal, explore his concerns (including whether he feels coerced or unsafe), offer alternatives such as stool testing or imaging if appropriate, and document the discussion.

Prisoners are a vulnerable population; extra care is needed to make sure their choices are voluntary in both directions.

Takeaway: prisoners keep the right to consent and refuse; officers cannot consent for them.

whyNot.A: Prison authority does not extend to overriding a capacitated adult's refusal of a nonemergency procedure.
whyNot.B: Sedating a patient to perform a procedure he refused is battery.
whyNot.D: Courts do not compel a capacitated adult to undergo a diagnostic procedure for his own benefit.
whyNot.E: A corrections officer is not a surrogate and cannot consent for a capacitated patient.

items.objective: Respect a capacitated prisoner's informed refusal of a procedure.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin is recovering from a hernia repair. On the evening after surgery he becomes sweaty and confused, pulls off his gown and insists on leaving the hospital. He cannot say where he is. Fingerstick glucose is 42 mg/dL (2.3 mmol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Allow him to leave because he is an adult

options.label: B
options.html: Ask him to sign an against-medical-advice form

options.label: C
options.html: Request an urgent psychiatry consultation for capacity

options.label: D
options.html: Give intravenous dextrose and reassess him

options.label: E
options.html: Place him in restraints until morning

items.explanationHtml:
Hypoglycemia is a reversible cause of confusion and lost capacity, and it is an emergency. He cannot currently make decisions, so the team treats the emergency, then reassesses his mental status and capacity once glucose is corrected. If he still wants to leave after recovering, his capacity can be assessed at that point.

Takeaway: treat reversible causes of incapacity first (hypoglycemia, hypoxia, intoxication), then reassess.

whyNot.A: He is disoriented and lacks capacity because of hypoglycemia; letting him leave would endanger him.
whyNot.B: He lacks capacity, so any form he signs is meaningless, and the emergency still needs treatment.
whyNot.C: A reversible metabolic cause needs immediate correction; psychiatry is not needed first.
whyNot.E: Restraint is a last resort and would leave the hypoglycemia untreated.

items.objective: Correct a reversible cause of incapacity before reassessing a patient's decision.

items.stemHtml: An 82-year-old woman with a displaced femoral neck fracture refuses surgery. The orthopedic surgeon is unsure whether she has decision-making capacity and asks whether he must go to court. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask a judge to rule on her competence

options.label: B
options.html: Assess her decision-making capacity himself

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the hospital ethics committee to decide

options.label: D
options.html: Ask her daughter to decide for her

options.label: E
options.html: Postpone the decision until she is discharged

items.explanationHtml:
Any treating physician can, and should, assess decision-making capacity for decisions in his area of care. The surgeon should explain the options and test whether she can communicate a choice, understand, appreciate and reason, then document his findings. Psychiatry or geriatrics can help when the assessment is difficult (for example, with psychiatric illness or fluctuating cognition), but a court is involved only for legal competence or unresolved disputes.

Takeaway: capacity is assessed at the bedside by the treating physician; courts decide competence.

whyNot.A: A court determination of competence is not needed for a clinical decision and would delay care.
whyNot.C: Ethics committees advise on conflicts; they do not perform the capacity assessment.
whyNot.D: Her daughter decides only if she is found to lack capacity.
whyNot.E: A fracture needs a decision now; postponing is not a plan.

items.objective: Recognise that the treating physician assesses decision-making capacity.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman remains unresponsive after cardiac arrest and resuscitation. Decisions about further treatment are needed. She has no advance directive and has not named a health-care agent. Present are her husband of 45 years, with whom she lives, her adult daughter and her sister. Under the default surrogate order used in most states, who should make decisions for her?

options.label: A
options.html: Her husband

options.label: B
options.html: Her adult daughter

options.label: C
options.html: Her sister

options.label: D
options.html: The three relatives by majority vote

options.label: E
options.html: The attending physician

items.explanationHtml:
When there is no named agent, state laws set a default order of surrogates. In nearly all states the spouse comes first, followed by adult children, parents, adult siblings and then others. The surrogate should apply substituted judgment, and good practice involves the whole family in discussions, but the spouse holds decision-making authority.

Takeaway: no advance directive or agent: the default surrogate is usually the spouse, then adult children, parents and siblings.

whyNot.B: Adult children follow the spouse in the default order.
whyNot.C: Siblings come after the spouse, adult children and parents.
whyNot.D: Surrogate decisions are not made by family vote; there is a priority order.
whyNot.E: The physician recommends but is not the surrogate when a family member is available.

items.objective: Apply the usual default surrogate order when there is no advance directive.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man with end-stage chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is intubated and sedated. Several years ago he signed a durable power of attorney for health care naming his close friend of 40 years as his agent. The friend reports that the patient often said he never wanted to live long-term on a ventilator, and asks that the team move to comfort care if he cannot be weaned. His two adult sons disagree and want long-term ventilation. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: A
options.html: Follow the sons' wishes because they are his closest relatives

options.label: B
options.html: Follow the friend's decision as his designated agent

options.label: C
options.html: Continue ventilation until the friend and sons agree

options.label: D
options.html: Ask a court to choose between the friend and the sons

options.label: E
options.html: Have the attending physician make the decision

items.explanationHtml:
A health-care agent named by the patient in a durable power of attorney outranks relatives in the default order. The friend is reporting the patient's own expressed wishes, which is the correct standard. The team should still meet with the sons, listen to their concerns, and explain the agent's role and the patient's wishes.

Takeaway: a named health-care agent outranks relatives; support the family, but follow the agent who reflects the patient's wishes.

whyNot.A: Relatives rank below a health-care agent whom the patient chose.
whyNot.C: Requiring consensus gives the sons a veto the law does not give them and prolongs treatment he did not want.
whyNot.D: A court is unnecessary when a valid agent is acting on the patient's known wishes.
whyNot.E: The physician does not replace a valid agent as decision-maker.

items.objective: Follow the designated health-care agent over relatives who disagree.

items.stemHtml: An 86-year-old widower with advanced dementia has recurrent aspiration pneumonia. He has no advance directive. His three adult children are his surrogates with equal standing. Two want a feeding tube; one says their father would have hated it. After two family meetings focusing on their father's values, they still disagree. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Follow the majority view of the children

options.label: B
options.html: Follow the eldest child's view

options.label: C
options.html: Request an ethics consultation

options.label: D
options.html: Petition the court for a guardian immediately

options.label: E
options.html: Place the feeding tube until they agree

items.explanationHtml:
When surrogates of equal priority remain in conflict after good-faith family meetings, an ethics consultation is the next step. Ethics consultants can mediate, clarify the patient's values and the standards for surrogate decisions, and help the family reach a decision. Court involvement is a last resort when mediation fails.

Takeaway: persistent conflict among surrogates after family meetings: ethics consultation before court.

whyNot.A: Equal-priority surrogates are not governed by majority vote as a default rule; the aim is the patient's wishes.
whyNot.B: Birth order gives no priority among adult children.
whyNot.D: Courts are a last resort after mediation and ethics consultation fail.
whyNot.E: Placing the tube by default imposes one side's choice without resolving what the patient would want.

items.objective: Request an ethics consultation when equal-priority surrogates remain in conflict.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman with severe asthma is brought to the emergency department with a life-threatening exacerbation. She is drowsy and exhausted, with rising PaCO2 despite maximal therapy, and needs intubation. Her living will states: "If I have a terminal illness or am permanently unconscious, I do not want mechanical ventilation." Her husband, her named health-care agent, says she has recovered fully from previous severe attacks and asks the team to do everything. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Withhold intubation in accordance with her living will

options.label: B
options.html: Request an ethics consultation before intubating

options.label: C
options.html: Intubate her

options.label: D
options.html: Give noninvasive ventilation only, in accordance with her living will

options.label: E
options.html: Seek a court order to intubate

items.explanationHtml:
A living will applies only to the circumstances it describes. Her directive covers terminal illness or permanent unconsciousness; an acute asthma attack with an expected full recovery meets neither condition. Her agent, applying what he knows of her wishes, supports intubation, and the situation is an emergency. Intubation is appropriate.

Reading an advance directive too broadly can deny patients treatment they would have wanted.

Takeaway: check the directive's trigger conditions; if they are not met, it does not apply.

whyNot.A: Her directive's trigger conditions (terminal illness, permanent unconsciousness) are not present.
whyNot.B: There is no conflict between the directive, the agent and the clinical situation, and delay is dangerous.
whyNot.D: Her directive does not apply, so there is no reason to limit her to noninvasive support when she needs intubation.
whyNot.E: No court involvement is needed when the agent and the directive's terms point the same way.

items.objective: Interpret an advance directive according to its stated trigger conditions.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man at average risk of colorectal cancer declines a screening colonoscopy after the physician explains its benefits and risks. He says he "can't face the bowel prep" and the sedation. He has full decision-making capacity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Refer him to a gastroenterologist to change his mind

options.label: B
options.html: Accept the refusal and drop screening from his care plan

options.label: C
options.html: Tell him the colonoscopy is mandatory at his age

options.label: D
options.html: Offer stool-based screening and document the informed refusal

options.label: E
options.html: Ask him to sign a waiver before he can leave

items.explanationHtml:
A capacitated adult may decline a recommended test. Informed refusal means he understands the consequences, and the physician offers reasonable alternatives that fit his values, such as an annual fecal immunochemical test or a stool DNA test, with colonoscopy if positive. The discussion and his decision should be documented, and screening can be revisited at future visits.

Takeaway: informed refusal: respect it, offer acceptable alternatives, document and revisit.

whyNot.A: Referral to pressure him disrespects his informed choice.
whyNot.B: Dropping screening entirely ignores alternatives he might accept.
whyNot.C: Screening is never mandatory; this is false and coercive.
whyNot.E: A signature is not required, and making his departure conditional on it is coercive.

items.objective: Manage informed refusal of screening by offering alternatives and documenting.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman is hospitalized with a urinary tract infection and has delirium: her attention fluctuates, she is disoriented in the evenings, and she is clearer in the mornings. She is scheduled for an elective inguinal hernia repair later this month. On the evening rounds she says she wants to cancel the operation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Cancel the operation as she has requested

options.label: B
options.html: Ask her son to decide about the operation tonight

options.label: C
options.html: Treat the delirium and revisit the decision when she is clearer

options.label: D
options.html: Ask a court to appoint a guardian

options.label: E
options.html: Proceed with the operation as scheduled

items.explanationHtml:
Delirium causes fluctuating capacity. For a nonurgent decision, the right step is to treat the underlying cause and reassess when she is at her best, often in the morning or after recovery. There is no need to transfer the decision to a surrogate while she may regain capacity, and no reason to proceed with or cancel surgery on the basis of a statement made while confused.

Takeaway: fluctuating capacity and a nonurgent decision: treat the cause and reassess at her best before deciding.

whyNot.A: A wish expressed during an episode of delirium may not reflect a capacitated decision; nothing is lost by waiting.
whyNot.B: Surrogates decide only when the patient lacks capacity and the decision cannot wait; this one can.
whyNot.D: Guardianship is unnecessary for a temporary, treatable condition.
whyNot.E: Proceeding with elective surgery while her capacity is uncertain ignores her objection and the need for informed consent.

items.objective: Defer a nonurgent decision while treating delirium that causes fluctuating capacity.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman with major depressive disorder tells her psychiatrist that she sometimes wishes she would not wake up but has no plan or intention to harm herself. She has never attempted suicide, does not own firearms, lives with a supportive partner and is engaged in therapy. She agrees to a safety plan and to start an antidepressant. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Initiate an emergency involuntary hold

options.label: B
options.html: Admit her voluntarily to an inpatient unit

options.label: C
options.html: Arrange close outpatient follow-up with the safety plan

options.label: D
options.html: Ask her partner to monitor her around the clock

options.label: E
options.html: Refer her to the emergency department for evaluation

items.explanationHtml:
Passive death wishes without plan or intent, with protective factors and engagement in care, are managed in the least restrictive safe setting: outpatient treatment, a written safety plan, means-restriction counselling and close follow-up. Hospitalization is reserved for those whose risk cannot be managed safely as outpatients.

Takeaway: use the least restrictive safe setting; passive ideation without plan or intent and with good support is usually outpatient care.

whyNot.A: She does not meet criteria for involuntary admission: there is no plan, intent or imminent danger.
whyNot.B: Inpatient admission is more restrictive than her risk requires.
whyNot.D: Around-the-clock monitoring by a partner is unnecessary and burdensome for this level of risk.
whyNot.E: An emergency evaluation adds nothing to the psychiatrist's assessment and would delay her care plan.

items.objective: Choose outpatient care for low-risk passive suicidal ideation (least restrictive alternative).

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by friends after drinking heavily at a party. His blood alcohol concentration is 260 mg/dL. He is slurring and says, "I'll just kill myself, nobody cares." He wants to go home. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Keep him under observation until sober, then assess suicide risk

options.label: B
options.html: Begin a petition for 90-day civil commitment

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge him to his friends because his statement was made while drunk

options.label: D
options.html: Accept his statement as a firm plan and admit him to psychiatry

options.label: E
options.html: Give him a list of crisis telephone numbers and discharge him

items.explanationHtml:
A patient who is intoxicated and voicing suicidal thoughts cannot be safely discharged, nor can his risk be properly judged while he is intoxicated. He should be kept safely in the emergency department (with a hold if needed) until clinically sober, and then receive a full suicide risk assessment. Alcohol intoxication raises the risk of impulsive self-harm.

Intoxication alone is not a mental illness that justifies longer commitment; the decision about admission follows the sober assessment.

Takeaway: intoxicated and suicidal: keep safe until sober, then do a full risk assessment.

whyNot.B: Longer commitment requires a sober assessment showing a mental illness with ongoing danger, not an intoxicated statement.
whyNot.C: Suicidal statements while intoxicated must be taken seriously; discharging him now is unsafe.
whyNot.D: Psychiatric admission should follow a sober assessment, not his statement while intoxicated alone.
whyNot.E: Crisis numbers are not adequate for an intoxicated patient who has just said he will kill himself.

items.objective: Hold an intoxicated suicidal patient until sober and then assess risk.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with major depressive disorder was admitted voluntarily to a psychiatric unit 2 days ago after cutting his wrists. He now demands to be discharged immediately and says, "As soon as I'm out, I'm going to the bridge, and this time I'll finish it." He refuses to stay. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge him because he is a voluntary patient

options.label: B
options.html: Begin the state's process to hold him involuntarily

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge him with an outpatient appointment tomorrow

options.label: D
options.html: Ask his family to persuade him to stay

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer him to a medical ward

items.explanationHtml:
Voluntary status does not oblige the team to release a patient who is in imminent danger. When a voluntary patient asks to leave and meets criteria for involuntary admission (here, a specific plan and intent to kill himself after a recent attempt), the team should begin the state's procedure for involuntary hold or commitment, with its due-process protections.

Takeaway: a voluntary patient who asks to leave but is imminently dangerous: convert to involuntary status by the legal process.

whyNot.A: Voluntary status does not require release of a patient who has stated a plan to kill himself.
whyNot.C: Outpatient follow-up cannot manage an imminent, specific suicide plan.
whyNot.D: Family persuasion may help but cannot be relied on to keep him safe from an imminent plan.
whyNot.E: He needs psychiatric care with legal safeguards, not transfer to a less secure medical setting.

items.objective: Convert a dangerous voluntary psychiatric patient to involuntary status.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been involuntarily committed by a court because of danger to others. On the unit she remains psychotic and refuses antipsychotic medication, but she is calm and not presenting an imminent danger. Repeated discussions about the medication have not changed her mind. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give intramuscular antipsychotic medication now

options.label: B
options.html: Hide the medication in her food

options.label: C
options.html: Ask her mother to consent to the medication

options.label: D
options.html: Seek court or formal legal authorization for treatment over objection

options.label: E
options.html: Discharge her because she refuses treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Commitment authorises confinement, not forced treatment. Outside an emergency, a committed patient's refusal of medication can be overridden only through the state's legal process, such as a court or administrative hearing that considers her capacity and the need for treatment. Meanwhile, the team keeps engaging her and offering medication.

Emergency medication without consent is allowed only for imminent danger.

Takeaway: committed but not imminently dangerous and refusing medication: seek legal authorization for treatment over objection.

whyNot.A: Forced injection is permitted only in an emergency with imminent danger, which is not present.
whyNot.B: Covert medication is deceptive and bypasses her legal rights.
whyNot.C: A parent cannot consent to treatment for a committed adult.
whyNot.E: She still meets commitment criteria; refusing medication is not a reason to discharge a dangerous patient.

items.objective: Seek legal authorization to medicate a committed patient over objection outside an emergency.

items.stemHtml:
A 36-year-old man with bipolar I disorder on a psychiatric unit is placed in four-point restraints after he punches a nurse. The restraint flowsheet is shown.

TimeObservation
14:00Restraints applied after assault; 4-hour order written
14:40Face-to-face evaluation by psychiatrist completed; oral medication accepted
15:00Shouting, pulling at restraints
15:30Quieter; circulation and skin checked, normal
16:00Calm, cooperative, asks to use the toilet; denies intent to harm anyone

Which of the following is the most appropriate action at 16:00?

options.label: A
options.html: Keep the restraints on until the order expires at 18:00

options.label: B
options.html: Remove the restraints now and continue close observation

options.label: C
options.html: Renew the order for another 4 hours to be safe

options.label: D
options.html: Change to two-point restraints for the rest of the day

options.label: E
options.html: Obtain a court order before removing the restraints

items.explanationHtml:
Restraint may be used only as long as needed to prevent imminent harm. Once the patient is calm and no longer dangerous, restraints must be removed at the earliest possible time, even if the order has not expired. Observation and support continue, and the episode is reviewed with the patient and staff.

Orders set a maximum duration, not a required one, and renewal requires a continuing need.

Takeaway: remove restraints as soon as the danger has passed; the order time is a limit, not a target.

whyNot.A: Keeping a calm patient restrained until the order expires is not justified by any ongoing danger.
whyNot.C: Renewal requires a continuing need, which no longer exists.
whyNot.D: Partial restraint is still restraint and is unjustified when he is calm and cooperative.
whyNot.E: No court order is needed to end restraint; removal is the default once safety allows.

items.objective: Discontinue restraints as soon as the patient is no longer dangerous.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with smear-positive cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis repeatedly removes his mask, leaves his airborne isolation room to smoke outside and says he will leave the hospital and stop treatment. He has full decision-making capacity and no psychiatric illness. Education, a translated explanation, incentives and an offer of directly observed therapy at home have not changed his plans. The case has already been reported. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge him against medical advice with a supply of medication

options.label: B
options.html: Place him on an emergency psychiatric hold

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the local health department to pursue a legal order for isolation and treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Restrain him in his room until he agrees to treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Respect his refusal because he has decision-making capacity

items.explanationHtml:
A capacitated patient's refusal is usually decisive, but infectious tuberculosis threatens others. Public health law lets health departments escalate, after less restrictive measures fail, to legal orders for isolation, treatment completion or detention, with due-process protections. The physician works with the health department, which holds that authority.

Psychiatric holds do not apply; he has no mental illness. Clinicians should not improvise detention.

Takeaway: nonadherent infectious TB: involve the health department, which can obtain orders for isolation and treatment.

whyNot.A: Discharging a patient with infectious tuberculosis who will stop treatment endangers the public.
whyNot.B: Psychiatric holds require a mental illness, which he does not have.
whyNot.D: Clinical staff cannot detain or restrain him to compel treatment without legal authority.
whyNot.E: His autonomy is limited by the risk of transmitting infection to others, which public health law addresses.

items.objective: Involve public health authorities to compel isolation of a nonadherent patient with infectious tuberculosis.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy is medically cleared after an intentional overdose of acetaminophen. He tells the psychiatrist that he still wants to die and will try again. His parents say the overdose was "a cry for attention" and want to take him home now. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge him with his parents and an outpatient referral

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge him after his parents sign an against-medical-advice form

options.label: C
options.html: Arrange a court hearing before keeping him

options.label: D
options.html: Ask him whether he agrees to go home and follow his choice

options.label: E
options.html: Keep him in the hospital on an emergency psychiatric hold

items.explanationHtml:
He has made a serious attempt and states ongoing intent, so he is in imminent danger. Parents' authority over a minor's care does not extend to refusing emergency care that protects his life. The physician should keep him safe on an emergency psychiatric hold while continuing to work with the parents, explaining the risk, and involving child protective services if they still refuse needed care.

Takeaway: an adolescent with ongoing suicidal intent is kept safe despite parental objection; emergency holds apply to minors.

whyNot.A: Releasing a teen who says he will try again would be unsafe.
whyNot.B: Parents' signatures do not make an unsafe discharge of a minor in imminent danger acceptable.
whyNot.C: Emergency holds come before any court hearing; delay would leave him unprotected.
whyNot.D: His stated choice reflects suicidal intent; he is in danger and is not the decision-maker here.

items.objective: Keep an adolescent with ongoing suicidal intent safe despite his parents' wish to remove him.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man has lived outdoors in a city park for several years. He has paranoid ideas about government surveillance but no hallucinations, and he does not threaten anyone. He eats at a soup kitchen daily, uses a shelter on freezing nights, keeps his belongings organized and comes to a street-medicine clinic for blood pressure checks. A neighbor of the park asks the clinic physician to "get him committed." He declines psychiatric treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Initiate an emergency involuntary hold for grave disability

options.label: B
options.html: Petition for civil commitment because he is homeless

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the police to remove him from the park

options.label: D
options.html: Respect his choice and continue outreach and medical care

options.label: E
options.html: Require psychiatric treatment as a condition of his blood pressure care

items.explanationHtml:
Involuntary admission requires danger to self or others, or grave disability, resulting from mental illness. This man meets his basic needs: he gets food daily, uses shelter in dangerous weather and engages with medical care. Living outdoors and holding unusual beliefs do not on their own make someone gravely disabled. His choice should be respected while outreach, trust and offers of treatment continue.

Compare the patient who, because of illness, refuses food and shelter in freezing weather; that patient may meet the grave-disability standard.

Takeaway: homelessness and unusual beliefs are not grounds for commitment if the person can meet basic needs and is not dangerous.

whyNot.A: He is meeting his basic needs for food, shelter and medical care, so he is not gravely disabled.
whyNot.B: Homelessness itself is not a legal ground for commitment.
whyNot.C: His presence in the park is not a medical matter, and involving police would damage the trust needed for his care.
whyNot.E: Making medical care conditional on psychiatric treatment is coercive and could harm him.

items.objective: Distinguish a person who meets basic needs while homeless from grave disability.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a scheduled visit. Examination shows several curved, loop-shaped bruises on his back and buttocks in different stages of healing. His mother says he fell off his tricycle yesterday. The physician is unsure whether the injuries were inflicted. Which of the following is the standard that triggers the physician's legal obligation to report?

options.label: A
options.html: Confirmation of abuse by a child protection specialist

options.label: B
options.html: A disclosure of abuse by the child or a caregiver

options.label: C
options.html: Reasonable suspicion based on the clinical findings

options.label: D
options.html: Radiographic evidence of an inflicted fracture

options.label: E
options.html: Agreement of a second physician who examines the child

items.explanationHtml:
Every US state makes physicians mandated reporters of suspected child maltreatment. The threshold is reasonable suspicion (wording varies, e.g. "reasonable cause to believe"), not proof. Loop-shaped bruises in several stages of healing on protected areas, with an explanation that does not fit, meet that threshold.

Reporters who act in good faith are immune from civil and criminal liability, even if the investigation finds no abuse. Failure to report can itself be a misdemeanour and a licensing matter. The physician's job is to recognise and report; child protective services (CPS) investigates.

Takeaway: suspicion, not certainty, triggers the duty to report child maltreatment.

whyNot.A: Reporters do not need expert confirmation; deciding whether abuse occurred is the job of child protective services.
whyNot.B: Most abused children never disclose; waiting for a disclosure would miss most cases and is not the legal standard.
whyNot.D: Imaging may strengthen a concern, but the duty to report arises before any test confirms injury.
whyNot.E: No state requires a second opinion before a mandated reporter files; delay for consensus is not required.

items.objective: Identify reasonable suspicion as the threshold for mandated reporting of child maltreatment.

items.stemHtml: A pediatric radiologist teaches residents to distinguish accidental from inflicted fractures in children. Which of the following findings is most specific for physical abuse?

options.label: A
options.html: Healing posterior rib fractures in a 2-month-old with no reported trauma

options.label: B
options.html: Midshaft clavicle fracture in a 2-day-old after a difficult vaginal delivery

options.label: C
options.html: Nondisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibia in a newly walking 20-month-old

options.label: D
options.html: Supracondylar humerus fracture in a 6-year-old who fell from playground bars

options.label: E
options.html: Buckle fracture of the distal radius in an 8-year-old who fell onto an outstretched hand

items.explanationHtml:
Posterior rib fractures in a young infant are produced by squeezing of the chest (anteroposterior compression with the ribs levered over the transverse processes) and almost never result from ordinary handling or falls. Together with classic metaphyseal lesions of the long bones, they are among the fractures with the highest specificity for abuse.

Specificity depends on context: the child's developmental stage, the mechanism offered and whether the injury fits it. Fractures in non-ambulatory infants, multiple fractures of different ages and fractures with no history are the red flags.

Takeaway: posterior rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions in infants are highly specific for abuse.

whyNot.B: Clavicle fracture is the most common birth injury, especially after shoulder dystocia, and fits the history.
whyNot.C: A toddler's fracture after a twisting fall is a typical accidental injury in a child who has started walking.
whyNot.D: Falls on an outstretched arm from a height commonly cause supracondylar fractures in school-age children.
whyNot.E: A torus (buckle) fracture is the classic low-energy accidental injury of the forearm.

items.objective: Recognise fracture patterns that are highly specific for inflicted injury in infants.

items.stemHtml: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of lethargy and vomiting. She received intramuscular vitamin K at birth, and platelet count and coagulation studies are normal. There are no external marks. CT of the head shows thin bilateral crescentic subdural collections of different densities, and a funduscopic examination shows extensive multilayered retinal hemorrhages. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the intracranial bleeding?

options.label: A
options.html: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery after a skull fracture

options.label: B
options.html: Tearing of bridging veins by repeated acceleration and deceleration

options.label: C
options.html: Rupture of a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis

options.label: D
options.html: Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus from dehydration

options.label: E
options.html: Bleeding from vitamin K deficiency

items.explanationHtml:
Violent shaking, with or without impact, makes the infant brain move relative to the skull. Bridging veins that cross the subdural space from the cortex to the dural venous sinuses are stretched and torn, giving subdural hemorrhage. The same rotational forces cause extensive, multilayered retinal hemorrhages extending to the periphery.

Subdural collections of different ages suggest repeated injury. Abusive head trauma often has no external bruise, so the absence of marks does not reassure. A coagulation screen and vitamin K history are part of the workup to exclude medical mimics.

Takeaway: infant subdural hemorrhage with extensive retinal hemorrhages points to abusive head trauma from torn bridging veins.

whyNot.A: That produces an epidural, lens-shaped hematoma, usually with a fracture; neither is present here.
whyNot.C: Aneurysmal rupture gives subarachnoid hemorrhage and is very rare in infants.
whyNot.D: Sinus thrombosis causes venous infarction and edema, not bilateral subdural collections with retinal hemorrhages.
whyNot.E: She received vitamin K and her coagulation studies are normal, which excludes this mimic.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of subdural hemorrhage in abusive head trauma.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a yellow vaginal discharge for 5 days. Nucleic acid amplification testing of the discharge is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Her mother has no history of sexually transmitted infections. Which of the following is the most likely route of acquisition?

options.label: A
options.html: Sexual contact

options.label: B
options.html: Perinatal exposure during vaginal delivery

options.label: C
options.html: Shared towels or bath water at home

options.label: D
options.html: Autoinoculation from a prior conjunctival infection

options.label: E
options.html: Contact with a contaminated toilet seat

items.explanationHtml:
Outside the neonatal period, gonorrhea in a prepubertal child is diagnostic of sexual contact and therefore of sexual abuse, which must be reported to child protective services. Syphilis (when not congenital) and HIV (when not perinatal or transfusion related) carry the same implication; Chlamydia and Trichomonas are also strongly suggestive, with perinatal persistence considered in the youngest children.

Confirmatory testing should use methods accepted for forensic purposes, and the physician should also test for other STIs, offer treatment and report. The physician does not need to identify the perpetrator.

Takeaway: gonorrhea in a prepubertal child beyond infancy means sexual abuse until proven otherwise; report it.

whyNot.B: Perinatally acquired gonococcal infection presents in the first weeks of life (ophthalmia, vaginitis), not at 6 years.
whyNot.C: Gonococci do not survive well on fomites; nonsexual household spread to a school-age child is not a credible explanation.
whyNot.D: Autoinoculation is not an accepted route for genital gonorrhea in a prepubertal child.
whyNot.E: Toilet seats are not a recognised route of gonococcal transmission.

items.objective: Recognise sexually transmitted infections in prepubertal children as indicators of sexual abuse.

items.stemHtml: A public health student reviews national child-protective-services data on substantiated cases of child maltreatment in the United States. Which of the following types of maltreatment accounts for the largest share of victims?

options.label: A
options.html: Physical abuse

options.label: B
options.html: Sexual abuse

options.label: C
options.html: Psychological maltreatment

options.label: D
options.html: Medical child abuse

options.label: E
options.html: Neglect

items.explanationHtml:
Neglect, a failure to provide food, shelter, supervision, medical care or education, is by far the most common form of substantiated child maltreatment in US national data, accounting for roughly three quarters of victims. Parents are the perpetrators in most cases, and children under 1 year have the highest victimisation rate.

Neglect is easy to miss because it shows as poor growth, missed visits, untreated dental caries or repeated preventable injuries rather than dramatic findings.

Takeaway: neglect is the most common type of child maltreatment.

whyNot.A: Physical abuse is the second most common category, well behind neglect.
whyNot.B: Sexual abuse accounts for a much smaller share of substantiated cases than neglect.
whyNot.C: Psychological maltreatment is substantiated far less often, partly because it is hard to document.
whyNot.D: Factitious disorder imposed on another is rare and makes up a tiny fraction of cases.

items.objective: Identify neglect as the most common form of child maltreatment.

items.stemHtml: A 14-month-old boy has been admitted four times in 6 months for episodes of apnea and cyanosis. Every episode began when he was alone with his mother, and extensive cardiac, neurologic and metabolic evaluations have been normal. During the current admission a nurse walks in and sees the mother holding a folded blanket firmly over the child's nose and mouth. The mother is calm and asks many detailed questions about tests. Which of the following best describes this situation?

options.label: A
options.html: Malingering by the mother to obtain disability payments

options.label: B
options.html: Illness anxiety disorder in the mother

options.label: C
options.html: Factitious disorder imposed on another

options.label: D
options.html: Somatic symptom disorder in the mother

options.label: E
options.html: Breath-holding spells in the child

items.explanationHtml:
