Before the clinical examination and apnea test, confounders must be excluded: significant hypothermia, sedative or paralytic drug effects, severe metabolic or endocrine disturbances and hypotension. Current US guidance asks for a core temperature of at least 36 °C.

Spinal reflexes (triple flexion, deep tendon reflexes, some movements on stimulation) may persist and are compatible with brain death. A person who meets the criteria is legally dead in every state.

Takeaway: exclude confounders such as hypothermia before declaring death by neurologic criteria; spinal reflexes may persist.

whyNot.A: Spinal reflexes such as triple flexion can persist after brain death and do not preclude the determination.
whyNot.B: Absent pupillary responses are expected in brain death.
whyNot.C: Diabetes insipidus is common after brain death and is managed, but it does not by itself prevent the evaluation.
whyNot.D: An absent cough is one of the brainstem reflexes expected to be lost.

items.objective: Identify prerequisites and compatible findings in the determination of brain death.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician 14 months after her adult son died suddenly in a car crash. Since then she has felt an intense longing for him nearly every day, spends hours looking at his photos, feels that part of her died with him and avoids places that remind her of him. She has been unable to return to work. She eats and sleeps adequately, does not feel worthless and has no thoughts of suicide. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Normal bereavement

options.label: B
options.html: Major depressive disorder

options.label: C
options.html: Prolonged grief disorder

options.label: D
options.html: Posttraumatic stress disorder

options.label: E
options.html: Adjustment disorder

items.explanationHtml:
Prolonged grief disorder (DSM-5-TR) is diagnosed in adults at least 12 months after a death (6 months in children and adolescents) when intense yearning for or preoccupation with the deceased persists most days, with features such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, numbness or a sense that life is meaningless, causing significant impairment.

Normal grief comes in waves triggered by reminders and gradually eases; brief experiences of seeing or hearing the deceased are common and normal. Depression features pervasive low mood, worthlessness and loss of pleasure in everything, and can coexist with grief.

Takeaway: persistent, disabling yearning ≥ 12 months after a death in an adult = prolonged grief disorder.

whyNot.A: Normal grief gradually eases and allows return to function; intense yearning disabling her after more than a year is beyond the usual course.
whyNot.B: Pervasive low mood, worthlessness and neurovegetative symptoms dominate depression; her distress centres on the loss itself.
whyNot.D: She did not experience or witness the crash, and she has no intrusive re-experiencing or hyperarousal.
whyNot.E: Adjustment disorder is not used when the symptoms meet criteria for a specific disorder such as prolonged grief disorder.

items.objective: Distinguish prolonged grief disorder from normal grief and depression.

items.stemHtml: In a lecture on end-of-life law, a professor lists several actions that clinicians may take near the end of a patient's life. Which of the following actions is illegal in every US state?

options.label: A
options.html: Discontinuing mechanical ventilation at a capacitated patient's request

options.label: B
options.html: Titrating opioids to relieve dyspnea in a dying patient

options.label: C
options.html: A physician injecting a lethal drug at a terminally ill patient's request

options.label: D
options.html: Proportionate palliative sedation for refractory delirium at the end of life

options.label: E
options.html: Prescribing a lethal medication that a terminally ill patient takes himself, where the state authorises it

items.explanationHtml:
Euthanasia, in which the physician administers a drug intended to end the patient's life, is illegal in all US states, even when the patient requests it. Medical aid in dying, in which the physician prescribes a medication that a capacitated, terminally ill adult takes himself, is lawful in a minority of states, each with strict safeguards (adult, terminal illness with a prognosis of 6 months or less, capacity, self-administration, repeated requests).

Withdrawing treatment, symptom-directed opioids and proportionate palliative sedation are legal and ethical everywhere because their intent is to respect refusal or relieve suffering.

Takeaway: euthanasia is illegal throughout the US; medical aid in dying is legal only in some states.

whyNot.A: A capacitated patient may refuse or stop any treatment, including ventilation.
whyNot.B: Symptom-directed opioid dosing is standard palliative care.
whyNot.D: Palliative sedation for refractory symptoms, titrated to relief, is an accepted practice.
whyNot.E: Medical aid in dying is legal in a minority of states under strict conditions, so it is not illegal everywhere.

items.objective: Distinguish euthanasia from medical aid in dying and other legal end-of-life practices.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer has been in the ICU for 6 days with septic shock from cholangitis. She is intubated and sedated and needs two vasopressors; her kidneys and liver are failing despite maximal treatment. She has no advance directive. Her husband and adult daughter come to a family meeting. The physician has to tell them that she is very unlikely to survive. Which of the following is the best way to open the conversation?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'm afraid there is nothing more we can do for her."

options.label: B
options.html: "Would you like us to do everything possible, including CPR if her heart stops?"

options.label: C
options.html: "Before I share the latest results, could you tell me what you understand about how she is doing?"

options.label: D
options.html: "Her lactate is 7, her creatinine has tripled and she needs two vasopressors."

options.label: E
options.html: "Let's wait until she can tell us what she wants."

items.explanationHtml:
Serious-illness conversations start by finding out what the family already knows and how much they want to know (ask before telling). This shows where to begin, reveals misunderstandings and signals that their view matters. The physician then gives a short headline in plain language, pauses for emotion and responds to it with empathy before discussing goals.

Avoid jargon, avoid offering a menu of procedures, and avoid phrases such as "nothing more we can do"; the team can always do more for comfort and dignity.

Takeaway: in a family meeting, ask what they understand before you tell.

whyNot.A: Opening with bad news before checking their understanding is abrupt, and "nothing more we can do" is untrue: comfort care is still possible.
whyNot.B: Asking families to choose interventions before sharing the medical picture places an unfair burden on them.
whyNot.D: Leading with jargon and numbers does not convey meaning and blocks emotional processing.
whyNot.E: She is sedated and critically ill; waiting avoids a necessary conversation with her surrogates.

items.objective: Open a serious-illness family meeting by eliciting the family's understanding.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer and refractory septic shock is intubated in the ICU and lacks capacity. The team believes she is dying. She left no advance directive. Under the law of her state her husband is her surrogate. He says, "She told me many times she never wanted to be kept alive on machines." Their daughter says, "I want everything done. I can't let her go yet." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue full treatment because one family member wants it

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the court to appoint a guardian

options.label: C
options.html: Tell the daughter that her opinion does not matter legally

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the family what she would choose and recommend a plan based on her values

options.label: E
options.html: Request an ethics consultation before talking further with the family

items.explanationHtml:
Surrogates use substituted judgment: they decide as the patient would have decided, based on her known values and statements. The best interest standard applies only when her wishes are unknown. The physician reframes the question from "What do you want?" to "What would she say if she could speak to us?", and then offers a clear recommendation consistent with her values, which lifts some of the burden from the family.

Most such conflicts resolve with time, repeated meetings and support for the grieving relative. Ethics consultation is the next step when disagreement persists.

Takeaway: surrogates decide by what the patient would want; physicians should recommend a plan, not hand over a menu.

whyNot.A: A single relative's distress does not determine treatment; the standard is what the patient would want.
whyNot.B: Guardianship is slow and unnecessary when there is a legal surrogate and evidence of the patient's wishes.
whyNot.C: Dismissing the daughter is unkind and needless; good practice includes her while the surrogate decides.
whyNot.E: An ethics consult can help if conflict persists, but the first step is to guide the family through substituted judgment.

items.objective: Guide surrogates through substituted judgment when family members disagree.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer and refractory septic shock is intubated in the ICU. Her husband and daughter agree that she would not want to continue life support, and the team plans withdrawal of mechanical ventilation with a focus on comfort. Her vasopressors have been stopped. Which of the following is the most appropriate management at the time of extubation?

options.label: A
options.html: Give a neuromuscular blocking agent before extubation so she appears calm

options.label: B
options.html: Withhold opioids to avoid hastening death

options.label: C
options.html: Switch to noninvasive ventilation after extubation

options.label: D
options.html: Give opioids and a sedative titrated to signs of respiratory distress

options.label: E
options.html: Restart vasopressors until all relatives have arrived

items.explanationHtml:
During withdrawal of ventilation, the goal is comfort. Opioids (with a benzodiazepine for anxiety if needed) are given before and after extubation and titrated to signs of distress such as tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, grimacing and agitation. The family is prepared for what they may see, including irregular breathing and noisy respirations.

Neuromuscular blockers must be stopped and not given during withdrawal. Monitors and alarms are usually turned off, and nonessential tests and treatments are discontinued.

Takeaway: during ventilator withdrawal, titrate opioids to distress; never use paralytics.

whyNot.A: Paralysis hides distress without treating it and can cause suffocation while awake; it has no role in withdrawal.
whyNot.B: Undertreating dyspnea causes suffering; opioids titrated to symptoms are ethical under double effect.
whyNot.C: Noninvasive ventilation is life-sustaining treatment that conflicts with the agreed comfort-focused goal.
whyNot.E: Restarting life support contradicts the plan; a short wait for family can be arranged without it.

items.objective: Manage symptoms during compassionate withdrawal of mechanical ventilation.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman has heart failure with severe symptoms at rest despite maximal tolerated medical therapy. She has been admitted four times in 6 months. Her cardiologist and primary care physician agree that her prognosis is less than 6 months and recommend hospice at home. She says, "If I choose hospice, I'm afraid I can never change my mind." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Yes, hospice is a permanent decision, so take your time."

options.label: B
options.html: "Hospice is only for the final days of life, so it's too early to decide."

options.label: C
options.html: "You can leave hospice at any time and go back to your other treatment."

options.label: D
options.html: "In hospice, all your heart medicines will be stopped."

options.label: E
options.html: "Hospice is available only in a nursing home."

items.explanationHtml:
A patient can revoke the hospice election at any time and resume standard Medicare coverage for curative or life-prolonging care, and she can re-elect hospice later. Hospice is provided mainly at home (also in nursing homes and inpatient units) by an interdisciplinary team, and it covers symptom-related medications and equipment.

Correcting misconceptions about hospice (that it is permanent, only for the last days, or means stopping all treatment) is often what allows patients to choose it.

Takeaway: patients can leave hospice at any time and return to other treatment.

whyNot.A: Hospice enrollment is not permanent; this would wrongly discourage her.
whyNot.B: Hospice serves patients with a prognosis of up to 6 months; most benefit from earlier, not last-minute, enrollment.
whyNot.D: Medicines that control symptoms, including many heart failure drugs, are often continued in hospice.
whyNot.E: Hospice is usually provided where the patient lives, including at home.

items.objective: Correct a patient's misconception about the permanence of hospice enrollment.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man has newly diagnosed metastatic non-small cell lung cancer. He has started first-line systemic therapy and his oncologist expects him to respond. He has bone pain from a rib metastasis, poor sleep and anxiety about his family's future. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Referral to hospice

options.label: B
options.html: Delay of palliative care until systemic therapy fails

options.label: C
options.html: Pause systemic therapy until his pain is controlled

options.label: D
options.html: Referral to palliative care while continuing cancer treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Referral to psychiatry alone for his anxiety

items.explanationHtml:
Palliative care is specialised care for people with serious illness at any stage, focused on symptoms, stress and quality of life, and it is given alongside disease-directed treatment. Early palliative care in advanced cancer improves quality of life and mood and is recommended soon after diagnosis of metastatic disease.

Hospice is a form of palliative care for patients with a limited prognosis who choose to forgo curative treatment of the terminal illness.

Takeaway: palliative care can start at diagnosis and run alongside curative or life-prolonging treatment.

whyNot.A: Hospice is for a prognosis of 6 months or less with a comfort focus; he is receiving disease-directed treatment that his oncologist expects to work.
whyNot.B: Waiting deprives him of benefit; palliative care is best started early in serious illness.
whyNot.C: Pain can be treated alongside cancer therapy; stopping effective treatment is unnecessary.
whyNot.E: His needs span pain, sleep, coping and family concerns, which an interdisciplinary palliative team addresses together.

items.objective: Distinguish palliative care from hospice and refer early.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has a do-not-resuscitate order. She is scheduled for surgical fixation of a pathologic femoral fracture to relieve pain. The anesthesiologist notes that general anesthesia commonly causes hypotension and may require airway management and vasopressors. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding her code status?

options.label: A
options.html: Suspend the DNR order automatically for the operation

options.label: B
options.html: Cancel the surgery because a DNR order rules out anesthesia

options.label: C
options.html: Keep the DNR order without discussing it with her

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the surgeon to make the decision in the operating room

options.label: E
options.html: Review with her which resuscitative measures she accepts

items.explanationHtml:
Professional guidance in anesthesiology and surgery calls for required reconsideration of DNR orders before procedures: neither automatic suspension nor automatic continuation. The team discusses with the patient (or surrogate) the specific interventions that may be needed, such as intubation, vasopressors, defibrillation or chest compressions, and records her choices, which may be full resuscitation, a limited plan or a goal-directed plan.

A DNR order means no cardiopulmonary resuscitation in arrest; it does not mean "do not treat", and it does not rule out palliative surgery.

Takeaway: before surgery, revisit a DNR order with the patient; don't suspend or ignore it automatically.

whyNot.A: Automatic suspension ignores her wishes; policies require a discussion instead.
whyNot.B: A DNR order does not preclude surgery or anesthesia that serves her goals.
whyNot.C: Leaving it undiscussed creates confusion about which anesthetic interventions she accepts.
whyNot.D: Code-status decisions belong to the patient, made before surgery.

items.objective: Apply required reconsideration of DNR orders in the perioperative setting.

items.stemHtml: An 88-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease lives in a nursing home. She is brought to the emergency department because of fever, cough and an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air. She has a signed POLST form indicating "Do not attempt resuscitation," "Selective treatment" (antibiotics and IV fluids, avoid intubation and ICU care) and "No artificial nutrition by tube." Chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Intubate her because pneumonia is reversible

options.label: B
options.html: Give antibiotics, oxygen and IV fluids without intubation

options.label: C
options.html: Disregard the POLST because she cannot confirm it now

options.label: D
options.html: Provide comfort measures only and withhold antibiotics

options.label: E
options.html: Place a nasogastric tube for nutrition during the illness

items.explanationHtml:
A POLST (portable medical orders) translates a seriously ill patient's goals into actionable medical orders that travel with her across settings. It is signed by a clinician and the patient or surrogate and is followed by EMS, emergency departments and hospitals. "Selective" or limited treatment allows antibiotics, IV fluids and noninvasive oxygen but avoids intubation and ICU care.

An advance directive states wishes and names a proxy; a POLST is a set of current orders. The two complement each other.

Takeaway: follow a POLST's orders; 'selective treatment' means antibiotics and fluids but no intubation.

whyNot.A: Her POLST explicitly declines intubation; reversibility of the illness does not override her documented choices.
whyNot.C: A POLST is a medical order created for exactly this situation and remains valid when she cannot speak.
whyNot.D: Her POLST selects limited treatment, which includes antibiotics; comfort-only care would not follow her choices.
whyNot.E: She declined artificial nutrition by tube.

items.objective: Interpret and apply a POLST form in an acute illness.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man has been in the ICU for 3 days after a motor vehicle collision with severe traumatic brain injury. Today two physicians complete an examination and apnea test according to hospital policy and declare him dead by neurologic criteria. His parents ask that the ventilator be kept on for several weeks because they are sure he will wake up. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "We will keep the ventilator on for as long as you want."

options.label: B
options.html: "We need your consent to withdraw life support."

options.label: C
options.html: "We will repeat the apnea test each day until you are ready to accept the result."

options.label: D
options.html: "I'm very sorry. His brain has stopped working completely and permanently, which means he has died."

options.label: E
options.html: "We will obtain a court order to stop the ventilator today."

items.explanationHtml:
A person who meets criteria for death by neurologic criteria is legally dead in every state. The physician communicates this clearly and compassionately, using the word "died" and avoiding phrases such as "brain dead but on life support" that suggest he is still alive. The family can be offered time to gather and say goodbye, chaplaincy and social work support.

A few states require reasonable accommodation of religious or moral objections to the neurologic standard, and hospitals may offer a short period of continued support, but the family cannot require indefinite ventilation. The organ procurement organisation is also contacted as required.

Takeaway: after brain death is declared, tell the family clearly and kindly that the patient has died.

whyNot.A: After death by neurologic criteria, ventilation cannot help him; open-ended support is not owed in most states.
whyNot.B: Framing removal of the ventilator as a treatment decision implies he is alive; death has already been declared.
whyNot.C: Repeating a completed, valid determination is not medically justified and prolongs false hope.
whyNot.E: A court order is not needed after death is declared and would escalate a grieving family's distress.

items.objective: Communicate a determination of death by neurologic criteria to a family.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman is intubated in the ICU after a massive subarachnoid hemorrhage. She has lost most brainstem reflexes, and the team expects either death by neurologic criteria or a family decision to withdraw support within the next day. Her family has not yet discussed organ donation with anyone. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the ICU physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask the family whether they would consider donating her organs

options.label: B
options.html: Notify the organ procurement organization

options.label: C
options.html: Wait until death is declared before considering donation

options.label: D
options.html: Start donor-management protocols before the family is approached

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the transplant surgeon to examine her

items.explanationHtml:
Hospitals participating in Medicare must notify their organ procurement organization (OPO) in a timely manner about every death and every imminent death. The OPO determines medical suitability, checks the donor registry and, together with the team, plans a separate approach to the family by trained requesters. Authorization recorded by the patient herself (first-person authorization) is legally valid.

The treating team's duty is to care for the patient and to refer; it does not seek consent. Transplant clinicians are kept apart from the declaration of death (the dead donor rule).

Takeaway: imminent death in the ICU: notify the OPO; don't ask the family about donation yourself.

whyNot.A: Requests by the treating team have lower consent rates and blur roles; trained OPO staff should make the approach.
whyNot.C: Hospitals must refer imminent deaths promptly so the OPO can assess eligibility; waiting can lose the opportunity.
whyNot.D: Interventions for donation require authorization; the first step is referral to the OPO.
whyNot.E: The transplant team must stay separate from the care and death determination of a potential donor.

items.objective: Describe the treating team's role in referral for organ donation.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has progressive weakness and now needs help with eating and bathing. At a clinic visit he says, "I want you to help me die before I become completely trapped." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response?

options.label: A
options.html: "That is illegal, so I can't discuss it."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'll refer you to a psychiatrist for your depression."

options.label: C
options.html: "You still have a lot to live for."

options.label: D
options.html: "I can prescribe something you could take when you are ready."

options.label: E
options.html: "Can you tell me more about what is making you feel this way?"

items.explanationHtml:
A request for help in dying is first a signal to explore: fear of losing control or of being a burden, uncontrolled symptoms, depression, existential distress, financial or family pressures. Many of these can be addressed with palliative care, symptom control, mental health support and advance care planning (for example, decisions about ventilation and feeding tubes).

Medical aid in dying is legal in some states under strict criteria; euthanasia is illegal everywhere. Regardless of the law where he lives, the first response is the same: listen and explore.

Takeaway: a request to hasten death: explore reasons and suffering first.

whyNot.A: Shutting down the conversation misses suffering that can be treated and may not even be accurate in his state.
whyNot.B: Assuming depression without asking is premature; he may have other reasons, though depression should be screened for.
whyNot.C: Reassurance dismisses his concerns and does not explore them.
whyNot.D: Prescribing without exploration, assessment or the legal safeguards of any jurisdiction is inappropriate.

items.objective: Respond to a patient's request for help in dying by exploring its causes.

items.stemHtml: An 86-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease lives in a nursing home. She no longer recognises her family, speaks only a few words and is dependent for all care. Over the past 6 months she has lost 8% of her body weight, eats slowly and coughs occasionally with meals. Her son, who is her health care proxy, asks whether a feeding tube would help her live longer and prevent pneumonia. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Percutaneous gastrostomy tube placement

options.label: B
options.html: Careful hand feeding with food she enjoys

options.label: C
options.html: Nasogastric tube feeding for 2 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Parenteral nutrition through a central line

options.label: E
options.html: Appetite stimulant medication

items.explanationHtml:
Eating difficulty and weight loss are part of the natural course of advanced dementia. Evidence shows that tube feeding does not prolong life, prevent aspiration pneumonia, heal pressure injuries or improve comfort in this setting, and it brings restraints, tube complications and hospital transfers. Geriatric guidance recommends careful hand feeding (comfort feeding) instead.

The physician explains this to the proxy with compassion, focuses on her comfort and prior values, and documents the plan.

Takeaway: advanced dementia with poor intake: recommend careful hand feeding, not a feeding tube.

whyNot.A: In advanced dementia, tube feeding does not prolong survival, prevent aspiration or improve comfort, and it has complications.
whyNot.C: Short-term nasogastric feeding has the same lack of benefit and is uncomfortable and often pulled out.
whyNot.D: Parenteral nutrition is burdensome and risky and does not help in advanced dementia.
whyNot.E: Appetite stimulants have little benefit in advanced dementia and have adverse effects.

items.objective: Counsel a surrogate about tube feeding in advanced dementia.

items.stemHtml: During a regional shortage of a monoclonal antibody, a hospital committee decides that doses will go to patients at the highest risk of severe disease according to published clinical criteria, regardless of insurance status, celebrity or ability to pay. Which of the following ethical principles does this policy most directly apply?

options.label: A
options.html: Justice

options.label: B
options.html: Autonomy

options.label: C
options.html: Beneficence

options.label: D
options.html: Nonmaleficence

options.label: E
options.html: Fidelity

items.explanationHtml:
Justice in medical ethics includes the fair distribution of benefits and burdens. Allocating a scarce resource by medical need and likely benefit, using transparent criteria and excluding social worth, wealth or fame, is an application of distributive justice.

The four principles are respect for autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice. On the exam, scarce resources and equal treatment point to justice; honouring a patient's choice points to autonomy.

Takeaway: fair allocation of scarce resources by need = justice.

whyNot.B: Autonomy concerns an individual's right to make his own decisions, not how a scarce supply is shared.
whyNot.C: Beneficence concerns acting in a patient's best interest; it does not by itself resolve who receives a scarce drug.
whyNot.D: Nonmaleficence is the duty to avoid harm; it does not address fair allocation.
whyNot.E: Fidelity concerns keeping promises and loyalty to the patient, not allocation among patients.

items.objective: Identify the principle of justice in resource allocation.

items.stemHtml: A psychiatrist treated a 34-year-old woman for generalized anxiety disorder for 2 years. Treatment ended 3 years ago by mutual agreement. They meet by chance at a community event, and he would like to ask her out on a date. Which of the following best reflects the professional standard that applies to him?

options.label: A
options.html: A relationship is acceptable because more than 1 year has passed since treatment ended

options.label: B
options.html: A relationship is acceptable if she initiates it

options.label: C
options.html: A relationship is acceptable if another psychiatrist approves it

options.label: D
options.html: A relationship is acceptable if she gives written informed consent

options.label: E
options.html: A relationship with a former patient is unethical for a psychiatrist regardless of the time elapsed

items.explanationHtml:
Sexual or romantic contact with a current patient is unethical for every physician. For physicians in general, a relationship with a former patient is unethical if it exploits trust, knowledge or emotions from the professional relationship, and the professional relationship must be ended before any romantic relationship is considered.

Psychiatry sets a stricter rule: its ethical code states that sexual activity with a current or former patient is unethical, because transference and the intimate knowledge gained in therapy persist after treatment ends.

Takeaway: psychiatrists: no romantic or sexual relationships with former patients, ever.

whyNot.A: No waiting period makes a romantic relationship with a former patient acceptable for a psychiatrist.
whyNot.B: Who initiates does not matter; the duty lies with the physician.
whyNot.C: No peer approval can make such a relationship ethical.
whyNot.D: Consent does not cure the imbalance of power and transference that make the relationship exploitative.

items.objective: State the boundary standard for relationships with former patients in psychiatry.

items.stemHtml: A primary care physician refers a 61-year-old man to a cardiologist for evaluation of exertional chest pain. The cardiologist's office asks for his recent ECGs, lipid results and medication list. The patient has not signed any release form. Under HIPAA, which of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: The records may be shared only after the patient signs a written authorization

options.label: B
options.html: Only a summary may be shared because the minimum necessary standard applies

options.label: C
options.html: The records may be shared only by mail, not electronically

options.label: D
options.html: The records may be shared because disclosure for treatment does not need patient authorization

options.label: E
options.html: The records may be shared only if the patient is incapacitated

items.explanationHtml:
HIPAA permits covered entities to use and disclose protected health information for treatment, payment and health care operations without the patient's authorization. Sending records to a consulting cardiologist is a treatment disclosure.

The minimum necessary standard (share only what is needed) applies to payment and operations and to most other disclosures, but not to disclosures to a provider for treatment, to the patient himself or under a signed authorization.

Takeaway: HIPAA: treatment, payment and operations need no authorization; minimum necessary does not apply to treatment disclosures.

whyNot.A: HIPAA does not require authorization for disclosures between providers for treatment.
whyNot.B: The minimum necessary standard does not apply to disclosures to a provider for treatment.
whyNot.C: HIPAA does not restrict the method in this way; secure electronic exchange is allowed.
whyNot.E: Incapacity is irrelevant; treatment disclosures are permitted for any patient.

items.objective: Apply HIPAA's permitted disclosures for treatment.

items.stemHtml: A psychologist keeps detailed personal notes of the content of her therapy sessions with a 40-year-old man, stored separately from his medical record. The man's health insurer asks for these notes to review a claim. The patient has signed only the standard consent forms for treatment and billing. Under HIPAA, which of the following is required before the notes can be released to the insurer?

options.label: A
options.html: A request from the insurer on its letterhead

options.label: B
options.html: A specific written authorization from the patient for the psychotherapy notes

options.label: C
options.html: No additional step, because the disclosure is for payment

options.label: D
options.html: Approval by the hospital privacy officer

options.label: E
options.html: A court subpoena

items.explanationHtml:
HIPAA gives psychotherapy notes (a clinician's separately kept notes analysing the content of counselling sessions) special protection: nearly every use or disclosure, including for payment, requires a specific authorization from the patient, and health plans may not make treatment or payment conditional on obtaining it.

This protection does not cover the ordinary mental health record (diagnoses, medications, session times, test results, treatment plans), which follows the usual treatment, payment and operations rules.

Takeaway: psychotherapy notes need specific patient authorization even for payment.

whyNot.A: An insurer's request alone does not authorise release of psychotherapy notes.
whyNot.C: Payment disclosures generally do not need authorization, but psychotherapy notes are an exception.
whyNot.D: Internal approval cannot substitute for the patient's specific authorization.
whyNot.E: A subpoena is not the HIPAA requirement here, and insurers cannot obtain the notes this way for claims review.

items.objective: Recognise the special HIPAA protection of psychotherapy notes.

items.stemHtml: A physician diagnoses primary syphilis in a 27-year-old man. The patient asks that his diagnosis not be shared with anyone. The physician tells him that the case will be reported to the state health department. Which of the following best justifies reporting without his consent?

options.label: A
options.html: Public health law requiring reporting of specified communicable diseases

options.label: B
options.html: The physician's duty to protect the patient's own health

options.label: C
options.html: The patient's implied consent by agreeing to be tested

options.label: D
options.html: Therapeutic privilege

options.label: E
options.html: The physician's discretion to inform anyone at risk

items.explanationHtml:
All states require clinicians and laboratories to report specified diseases (for example syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV, tuberculosis, measles) to public health authorities. HIPAA explicitly permits disclosures required by law and disclosures to public health authorities, so no patient authorization is needed.

The health department, not the physician, usually undertakes contact tracing and partner notification, which protects the patient's identity. The physician should tell the patient that the report will be made.

Takeaway: reportable diseases are reported to public health without the patient's consent; HIPAA permits it.

whyNot.B: Treatment protects his health; reporting is justified by protection of the public.
whyNot.C: Agreeing to testing is not consent to disclosure; reporting is lawful regardless of consent.
whyNot.D: Therapeutic privilege concerns withholding information from a patient, not disclosure to public health.
whyNot.E: Reporting is a legal duty to the health department, not a discretionary disclosure to individuals.

items.objective: Explain the legal basis for reporting communicable diseases.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man is found to have HIV infection at a routine visit. He is married and has sex only with his wife, who is not his patient. He refuses to tell her, saying it would end the marriage, and asks the physician to keep the result secret. He agrees to start antiretroviral therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Report the case to the health department and explain partner notification services

options.label: B
options.html: Call his wife today and tell her the diagnosis

options.label: C
options.html: Keep the diagnosis confidential and take no further action

options.label: D
options.html: Refuse to continue his care until he tells his wife

options.label: E
options.html: Ask his wife to come in for a routine visit without telling her why

items.explanationHtml:
HIV is reportable in every state. The physician reports the case, keeps encouraging the patient to tell his wife (offering help with disclosure) and explains that the health department's partner services can notify partners confidentially without naming him. Starting antiretroviral therapy also protects her: sustained viral suppression prevents sexual transmission.

Some states permit physicians themselves to notify an identified partner at risk if the patient refuses, but laws differ, and health department partner notification is the standard route.

Takeaway: new HIV with a partner at risk: report, urge disclosure and use health department partner services.

whyNot.B: Direct notification by the physician is not the first step; encouraging disclosure and using health department partner services come first.
whyNot.C: His wife is at ongoing risk; confidentiality has limits, and HIV is a reportable disease.
whyNot.D: Withholding treatment harms him and does not protect her.
whyNot.E: Arranging a deceptive visit is dishonest and not an accepted notification method.

items.objective: Manage partner notification for a patient with HIV who refuses to disclose.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman undergoes biopsy of a pancreatic mass. Before the physician enters the room to discuss the result, which shows adenocarcinoma, the patient's daughter stops him in the hallway: "In our culture we don't tell elders bad news. Please don't tell her she has cancer." The patient has decision-making capacity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Agree to withhold the diagnosis to respect the family's culture

options.label: B
options.html: Tell the daughter that the law requires full disclosure to the patient immediately

options.label: C
options.html: Give the diagnosis only to the daughter and let her decide what to say

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the patient how much she wants to know and whom she wants involved

options.label: E
options.html: Request an ethics consultation before speaking with the patient

items.explanationHtml:
Information belongs to the capacitated patient. The physician acknowledges the daughter's concern and explains that he will ask her mother how she prefers to receive information. Asking, for example, "Some people want all the details about test results, others prefer that their family handle it. What would you prefer?", respects both autonomy and cultural values.

If the patient chooses to waive disclosure and delegate decisions to her daughter, that choice is valid and should be documented.

Takeaway: when family asks to withhold a diagnosis, ask the patient how she wants to receive information.

whyNot.A: The patient, not the family, decides how much to know; agreeing in advance may violate her rights.
whyNot.B: Insisting on immediate full disclosure ignores the possibility that the patient herself prefers otherwise.
whyNot.C: Disclosing to the daughter first breaches the patient's confidentiality.
whyNot.E: The question can be answered by asking the patient; a consult is not needed first.

items.objective: Handle a family's request to withhold a diagnosis by asking the patient's preferences.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy comes to the clinic alone for testing because a former partner told him she has gonorrhea. He is tested and treated. Two days later his mother calls the clinic and asks for the results, saying she pays for his insurance and has a right to know. The boy has not given permission to share any information. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Give the mother the results because he is a minor

options.label: B
options.html: Give the results because the family insurance pays for the visit

options.label: C
options.html: Confirm that he was seen but not the reason

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the mother to bring him back so the results can be given to both

options.label: E
options.html: Tell the mother you cannot share information without his permission

items.explanationHtml:
Every state allows minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections, and the information is confidential: the physician may not disclose it to parents without the adolescent's permission. The physician can politely decline to share information and suggest that the mother talk with her son, while encouraging the boy to involve a parent if he can.

Insurance explanation-of-benefit statements can inadvertently reveal confidential services; clinics should discuss this with adolescents.

Takeaway: a minor's confidential STI care is not disclosed to parents without his permission.

whyNot.A: Minors can consent to their own STI care in every state, and that care is confidential.
whyNot.B: Paying the premium does not entitle a parent to a minor's confidential results.
whyNot.C: Even confirming the visit discloses confidential information without his permission.
whyNot.D: This pressures the patient and effectively discloses that there is something to discuss.

items.objective: Protect the confidentiality of a minor's sexual health care.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is intubated and sedated in the ICU after a motorcycle crash. His wife, who is listed as his emergency contact, arrives and asks about his injuries and his chances of recovery. He has no documented instructions about sharing information. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Decline to share anything until he can give permission

options.label: B
options.html: Ask her to obtain a court order for access to his information

options.label: C
options.html: Give her a full copy of his medical record

options.label: D
options.html: Share information only if she shows a marriage certificate

options.label: E
options.html: Share information relevant to his care and condition with her

items.explanationHtml:
When a patient is incapacitated or absent, HIPAA lets clinicians use professional judgment to share information that is directly relevant to a family member's involvement in his care, if doing so is in his best interest. His wife is also likely to be his surrogate decision-maker and will need the information to decide.

When the patient is present and capacitated, the clinician should first ask whether he agrees, or give him the chance to object.

Takeaway: incapacitated patient: share relevant information with involved family when it is in his interest.

whyNot.A: When a patient is incapacitated, HIPAA allows sharing relevant information with family involved in care if it is in his interest.
whyNot.B: No court order is needed for family involved in an incapacitated patient's care.
whyNot.C: Only information relevant to her involvement in his care is appropriate, not the entire record.
whyNot.D: Reasonable verification of identity is enough; formal documents are not required.

items.objective: Apply HIPAA rules on sharing information with family of an incapacitated patient.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman is admitted with abdominal pain. The CT results are back and show a mass suspicious for ovarian cancer. When the physician enters her room to discuss them, two friends from her church are visiting. The patient is alert and capacitated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discuss the results now since the friends are already present

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the friends to leave without explanation

options.label: C
options.html: Postpone the discussion until her husband can be present

options.label: D
options.html: Tell her the results are normal for now and return later

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the patient whether she would like to talk privately or with her friends present

items.explanationHtml:
Before discussing health information with others present, the physician asks the patient whether she wants them to stay. HIPAA permits disclosure in front of family or friends if the patient agrees or, given the opportunity, does not object.

Serious news is best given in a private setting, seated, with the people the patient chooses.

Takeaway: ask a capacitated patient before discussing results in front of visitors.

whyNot.A: Sharing serious news in front of visitors without her agreement breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.B: Removing visitors without asking the patient overrides her wishes; she may want them there.
whyNot.C: Delaying news to wait for a spouse she has not asked for is paternalistic.
whyNot.D: Lying is unacceptable, even to delay a difficult conversation.

items.objective: Respect patient preferences about who hears health information.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old man has been off work for a week with an exacerbation of Crohn disease. His employer's human resources manager calls the physician's office, asks for his diagnosis and wants to know whether he will be able to return to full duties. The patient has not signed any release. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Give the diagnosis because the employer needs to plan staffing

options.label: B
options.html: Explain that information can be released only with the patient's written authorization

options.label: C
options.html: Give the expected return-to-work date but not the diagnosis

options.label: D
options.html: Tell the manager to request the information from the patient's insurer

options.label: E
options.html: Confirm the diagnosis only if the manager states it first

items.explanationHtml:
Employers are not entitled to an employee's health information. Disclosure requires the patient's written authorization, which can be limited (for example, a work note with dates and restrictions only, without the diagnosis).

The physician can offer to give the patient a work note himself. Exceptions such as workers' compensation claims or required occupational-health surveillance follow their own rules.

Takeaway: employers get health information only with the patient's written authorization.

whyNot.A: An employer's planning needs do not permit disclosure without the patient's authorization.
whyNot.C: Even limited information is protected without authorization.
whyNot.D: The insurer cannot release it either, and redirecting the request is unhelpful.
whyNot.E: Confirming a guessed diagnosis is still a disclosure.

items.objective: Decline to disclose health information to an employer without authorization.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman whom a family physician has treated for several years sends him a friend request on his personal social media account. She also comments publicly on his post about running a marathon, thanking him for helping with her depression. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Decline the request and offer the practice's secure portal for health matters

options.label: B
options.html: Accept the request because she initiated it

options.label: C
options.html: Accept the request but avoid discussing health online

options.label: D
options.html: Reply to her comment publicly to thank her for sharing

options.label: E
options.html: End the physician-patient relationship to avoid problems

items.explanationHtml:
Professional guidance advises physicians to keep personal and professional online lives separate: not to "friend" current patients on personal accounts, never to discuss patients or identifiable details online, and to direct patients to secure, professional channels for health communication. The physician should not confirm the care relationship publicly, even when the patient discloses it herself.

Declining kindly (for example, by explaining his policy at the next visit) preserves the relationship.

Takeaway: do not friend patients on personal accounts; use secure professional channels.

whyNot.B: Who initiates does not change the risk to boundaries and confidentiality.
whyNot.C: Personal social media connections with patients blur boundaries even if health is not discussed.
whyNot.D: A public reply confirms the care relationship and her health condition to others.
whyNot.E: Ending care is not warranted; boundaries can be maintained.

items.objective: Maintain professional boundaries on social media.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old internist receives a call from her 40-year-old brother, who has had low back pain for 3 days after moving furniture. He asks her to prescribe oxycodone because he cannot get an appointment with his own physician until next week. He has no red-flag symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Prescribe a 3-day supply of oxycodone because the course is short

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe oxycodone after examining him at her home

options.label: C
options.html: Prescribe oxycodone if he signs a written consent

options.label: D
options.html: Ask a colleague to prescribe without seeing him

options.label: E
options.html: Decline, suggest over-the-counter analgesics and urge him to see his own clinician

items.explanationHtml:
Physicians should generally not treat themselves or members of their immediate family, because personal feelings compromise objectivity, history and examination may be incomplete and the patient may not feel free to refuse. Exceptions are emergencies, isolated settings and minor, short-term problems. Prescribing controlled substances to family members is inappropriate except in an emergency.

Acute mechanical back pain without red flags is managed with activity as tolerated and nonopioid analgesics; she can point him toward urgent care or a telehealth visit.

Takeaway: don't prescribe controlled substances to family; refer them to their own clinician.

whyNot.A: Prescribing controlled substances to family members is inappropriate outside emergencies.
whyNot.B: An informal home examination does not remove the problems of objectivity and controlled-substance prescribing for family.
whyNot.C: Consent does not cure the ethical problem of treating a relative with a controlled substance.
whyNot.D: Asking a colleague to prescribe without an evaluation is improper and evades the same concerns.

items.objective: Apply the guidance on treating family members.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old widower whom a physician has treated for 15 years tells her that he has changed his will to leave her $50,000 "for all your kindness." At the same visit he gives her a box of homemade cookies. He has mild cognitive impairment. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Accept both gifts because he has decision-making capacity

options.label: B
options.html: Decline both gifts to avoid any appearance of impropriety

options.label: C
options.html: Accept the bequest but donate it to charity

options.label: D
options.html: Accept the cookies and kindly decline the bequest

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer his care to another physician

items.explanationHtml:
Gifts from patients are judged by their value, the patient's circumstances and their effect on the relationship. Small, spontaneous tokens of gratitude are acceptable. Large gifts or bequests are not: they can affect the physician's objectivity, may exploit a vulnerable patient (here with cognitive impairment) and may cause family conflict.

The physician thanks him warmly, declines the bequest and documents the conversation.

Takeaway: accept small token gifts; decline large gifts or bequests, especially from vulnerable patients.

whyNot.A: Even if he had capacity, a large bequest from a patient compromises the relationship; with cognitive impairment, undue influence is a further concern.
whyNot.B: Small, token gifts such as cookies can be accepted graciously; refusing them may hurt the patient.
whyNot.C: Accepting the bequest still creates the conflict, whatever is done with the money afterwards.
whyNot.E: There is no need to end a long relationship; declining the bequest resolves the problem.

items.objective: Distinguish acceptable from unacceptable gifts from patients.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old college student is seen in the student health clinic for insomnia. He says he has been saving his roommate's sleeping pills and plans to take all of them this weekend when his roommate is away. He asks the physician not to tell anyone, especially his parents. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Everything you tell me is confidential, so this stays between us."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'll call your parents to let them know you need support."

options.label: C
options.html: "Let's meet again on Monday to see how the weekend went."

options.label: D
options.html: "Promise me you won't do it, and I'll trust you."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'm worried for your safety, so we need an urgent evaluation today."

items.explanationHtml:
A specific plan, access to means and a time frame indicate high, imminent suicide risk. Confidentiality yields when disclosure is needed to prevent serious harm to the patient. The physician tells him honestly what will happen and arranges an emergency psychiatric evaluation today (with involuntary measures if he refuses), and limits disclosure to what is necessary to keep him safe.

Telling patients at the outset of care that confidentiality has limits makes these moments easier.

Takeaway: imminent suicide risk overrides confidentiality: arrange urgent evaluation and disclose only what is needed.

whyNot.A: Confidentiality does not cover a serious, imminent risk to the patient's life.
whyNot.B: Calling his parents first is not the priority; urgent evaluation and safety are, and parents are contacted only if needed.
whyNot.C: Waiting until after his planned attempt ignores imminent risk.
whyNot.D: A no-suicide promise is not an effective safety measure and ignores a specific plan with means.

items.objective: Break confidentiality appropriately for a patient at imminent risk of suicide.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with a history of panic attacks has a lung biopsy that shows small cell carcinoma. His physician worries that the news will trigger severe anxiety and plans to tell him only that he has "an inflammation that needs treatment" until he "is in a better frame of mind." The patient has decision-making capacity and has asked to be told his results directly. Which of the following is the most appropriate course?

options.label: A
options.html: Withhold the diagnosis using therapeutic privilege

options.label: B
options.html: Disclose the diagnosis honestly with support and a plan for his anxiety

options.label: C
options.html: Tell his wife first and let her decide when to tell him

options.label: D
options.html: Describe the illness as inflammation and start chemotherapy

options.label: E
options.html: Delay disclosure until a psychiatrist confirms he can cope

items.explanationHtml:
A capacitated patient who wants to know his diagnosis has the right to it, and informed consent to treatment depends on it. Therapeutic privilege, withholding information because disclosure itself would cause serious and immediate harm, is narrowly defined and rarely justified; the possibility of distress or anxiety does not qualify.

The physician can lessen distress through how the news is given: a private setting, a warning shot, plain language, pauses, empathy and a concrete plan, with support for his panic disorder.

Takeaway: therapeutic privilege is rarely justified; disclose honestly, kindly and with support.

whyNot.A: Therapeutic privilege is justified only in rare cases where disclosure itself would cause serious, immediate harm; anxiety is not enough.
whyNot.C: This breaches his confidentiality and his explicit request.
whyNot.D: Treating him without disclosing his diagnosis invalidates his consent.
whyNot.E: Delay is unwarranted; he has capacity and asked to know.

items.objective: Recognise the narrow limits of therapeutic privilege.

items.stemHtml:
A clinic manager reviews the information requests that reached a primary care practice on one day. None of the patients involved has signed an authorization for release, and none is incapacitated.

RequestRequester and information sought
1A patient's employer asking why she missed a week of work
2The adult son of a capacitated 70-year-old man asking for his father's biopsy result
3The county health department asking for treatment details of a patient whose active tuberculosis the practice reported
4A life insurance company asking for a 50-year-old applicant's records
5A patient's neighbour asking whether she has been admitted to hospital

Which of the requests may be fulfilled without the patient's authorization?

options.label: A
options.html: Request 1

options.label: B
options.html: Request 2

options.label: C
options.html: Request 3

options.label: D
options.html: Request 4

options.label: E
options.html: Request 5

items.explanationHtml:
HIPAA permits disclosure without authorization to public health authorities for disease control, including follow-up of a reported case of tuberculosis. Other permitted disclosures include those required by law, for treatment, payment and operations, for certain law-enforcement and judicial processes, and to avert a serious threat to health or safety.

Employers, insurers for underwriting, neighbours and family of a capacitated patient who has not agreed all require the patient's permission.

Takeaway: disclosures to public health authorities for disease control need no patient authorization.

whyNot.A: Employers have no right to health information without the patient's authorization.
whyNot.B: A capacitated adult decides whether his family receives his results; his son must wait for his permission.
whyNot.D: Life insurers obtain records only with the applicant's signed authorization.
whyNot.E: A neighbour has no role in her care; confirming an admission is a disclosure.

items.objective: Identify which disclosures HIPAA permits without patient authorization.

items.stemHtml: A new intern asks the program director about the national limits on resident work hours set by the accrediting body for US graduate medical education. Which of the following is the standard maximum average weekly limit, including in-house call and clinical work done from home?

options.label: A
options.html: 60 hours

options.label: B
options.html: 72 hours

options.label: C
options.html: 80 hours

options.label: D
options.html: 88 hours

options.label: E
options.html: 100 hours

items.explanationHtml:
ACGME requirements limit clinical and educational work to 80 hours per week, averaged over 4 weeks, including in-house call, moonlighting and clinical work done from home. Other limits: continuous scheduled work of no more than 24 hours, with up to 4 more hours for transitions of care and education; at least 1 day in 7 free of duties (averaged over 4 weeks); and in-house call no more often than every third night (averaged).

The rules aim to reduce fatigue-related errors and protect resident wellbeing.

Takeaway: residents: ≤ 80 hours per week averaged over 4 weeks.

whyNot.A: 60 hours is below the national limit; some programs schedule fewer hours, but it is not the standard.
whyNot.B: 72 hours is not the accreditation standard.
whyNot.D: An increase to 88 hours can be granted to a few programs only by specific exception; it is not the standard limit.
whyNot.E: 100 hours was common before duty-hour reform and is not allowed.

items.objective: State the resident duty-hour limit.

items.stemHtml:
A surgical resident's logged clinical and educational work hours over a 4-week rotation are shown below. All hours, including in-house call and clinical work done from home, are included. He had at least 1 day in 7 free of duty and never worked more than 24 hours continuously plus 4 hours for handoffs.

WeekHours worked
186
278
384
470

Which of the following conclusions about his compliance with the 80-hour rule is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: He complied because his average was 79.5 hours per week

options.label: B
options.html: He violated the rule in weeks 1 and 3 because each exceeded 80 hours

options.label: C
options.html: He violated the rule because his total exceeded 300 hours

options.label: D
options.html: He complied only because week 4 was a vacation week

options.label: E
options.html: Compliance cannot be judged without his daily hours

items.explanationHtml:
Total hours = 86 + 78 + 84 + 70 = 318. Average = 318 ÷ 4 = 79.5 hours per week, which is within the limit of 80 hours averaged over 4 weeks. Individual weeks above 80 do not by themselves breach the rule.

On the exam, add the weeks, divide by 4 and compare with 80. Also check the other limits (24 + 4 continuous hours, 1 day off in 7, call no more than every third night).

Takeaway: the 80-hour limit is a 4-week average: (86 + 78 + 84 + 70) ÷ 4 = 79.5, compliant.

whyNot.B: The 80-hour limit is averaged over 4 weeks; single weeks above 80 are allowed if the average is within the limit.
whyNot.C: There is no 300-hour cap; 4 × 80 = 320 hours is the effective ceiling, and his total of 318 is within it.
whyNot.D: Week 4 shows 70 hours of work, not vacation; compliance comes from the 4-week average.
whyNot.E: Daily hours matter for the 24 + 4 rule, which he met; the weekly rule is judged on the 4-week average.

items.objective: Calculate average weekly work hours to judge compliance with duty-hour limits.

items.stemHtml: A second-year internal medicine resident tells his advisor that he feels drained before every shift. He has started referring to patients by their diagnoses ("the pancreatitis in 12"), feels indifferent when they are upset and thinks his work makes no difference. Which of the following features of burnout is illustrated by his indifference toward patients and use of diagnoses in place of names?

options.label: A
options.html: Emotional exhaustion

options.label: B
options.html: Reduced sense of personal accomplishment

options.label: C
options.html: Anhedonia

options.label: D
options.html: Depersonalization

options.label: E
options.html: Compassion satisfaction

items.explanationHtml:
Burnout is a work-related syndrome with three classic dimensions: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization (cynicism and detachment from patients, treating them as objects) and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. It is common among residents and is associated with self-reported errors, lower professionalism, depression and leaving medicine.

Burnout overlaps with depression but is tied to work; screening for depression and suicidal thoughts is still important in a burned-out resident.

Takeaway: detached, cynical treatment of patients = depersonalization.

whyNot.A: Exhaustion is his drained feeling before shifts, not his detached attitude toward patients.
whyNot.B: This is his belief that his work makes no difference.
whyNot.C: Anhedonia is a symptom of depression (loss of pleasure in all activities), not a defined dimension of burnout.
whyNot.E: Compassion satisfaction is the positive feeling from helping others, the opposite of what he describes.

items.objective: Identify the dimensions of physician burnout.

items.stemHtml: A third-year medical student on a pediatrics rotation notices that her supervising resident has pinpoint pupils and slurred speech and keeps nodding off while writing orders. He is about to start a lumbar puncture on an infant. The student is worried about her evaluation. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Say nothing because she is a student and he is her supervisor

options.label: B
options.html: Discuss the problem with him privately after the procedure

options.label: C
options.html: Report him anonymously to the state medical board that evening

options.label: D
options.html: Immediately alert the attending physician so that the procedure does not proceed

options.label: E
options.html: Tell the infant's parents that the resident has been drinking

items.explanationHtml:
When a clinician appears impaired at work, the first duty is immediate patient safety: stop him from providing care now by alerting someone with authority to intervene, usually the supervising attending or chief resident. Students and residents are protected from retaliation for good-faith reports under program policies.

After the immediate risk is managed, the institution handles evaluation and referral, often through a physician health program.

Takeaway: colleague impaired at work: stop patient care now through the supervisor; don't wait.

whyNot.A: Silence leaves an infant at risk; every member of the team has a duty to speak up for patient safety.
whyNot.B: Waiting until after the procedure allows an impaired physician to perform it.
whyNot.C: A board report later does nothing to stop the procedure now.
whyNot.E: Telling parents does not stop the procedure through the proper chain and causes needless alarm.

items.objective: Act to protect patients when a supervisor appears impaired.

items.stemHtml: A hospital pharmacy review examines opioid handling by anesthesiologists, a specialty with a recognised risk of opioid misuse among its members. Which of the following patterns is most suggestive that an anesthesiologist is diverting fentanyl for personal use?

options.label: A
options.html: Refusing breaks and frequent discrepancies in opioid waste records

options.label: B
options.html: Frequent requests for help with difficult intubations

options.label: C
options.html: Consistently lower opioid use than colleagues for similar cases

options.label: D
options.html: Preferring regional anesthesia when appropriate

options.label: E
options.html: Leaving the hospital promptly when shifts end

items.explanationHtml:
Signs of drug diversion by clinicians include high or unusual opioid dispensing, missing or unwitnessed waste, discrepancies in records, patients with poorly controlled pain under that clinician's care, refusing relief or breaks, volunteering for extra cases or call, frequent bathroom breaks, coming in on days off and physical signs (pinpoint pupils, weight loss, long sleeves).

Anesthesiology has a higher reported rate of opioid use disorder than many specialties, attributed to easy access to potent opioids. Suspected diversion is reported through the institution's process and leads to removal from duty and evaluation.

Takeaway: refusing breaks + extra cases + waste discrepancies suggest opioid diversion.

whyNot.B: Seeking help with difficult airways is appropriate practice, not a sign of diversion.
whyNot.C: Low documented use is not a typical sign; diversion more often shows as high or unusual dispensing.
whyNot.D: Using regional techniques when indicated is good practice.
whyNot.E: Leaving on time is normal; diverting clinicians often stay late or come in when not scheduled.

items.objective: Recognise warning signs of drug diversion by a clinician.

items.stemHtml: A department chair learns that one of her surgeons has an alcohol use disorder and arranges a referral to the state physician health program. The surgeon asks what the program is. Which of the following best describes the function of a physician health program?

options.label: A
options.html: A confidential program that arranges evaluation and treatment and monitors recovery

options.label: B
options.html: A disciplinary arm of the licensing board that revokes licenses

options.label: C
options.html: An insurance program that pays for malpractice claims arising from impairment

options.label: D
options.html: A hospital committee that decides on clinical privileges

options.label: E
options.html: A federal agency that tracks controlled-substance prescriptions

items.explanationHtml:
State physician health programs (PHPs) are confidential programs, usually independent of the licensing board, that assess physicians with substance use disorders, mental illness or other potentially impairing conditions, refer them to treatment and monitor recovery (for example random drug testing, workplace monitors and support groups), typically for several years.

Physicians who enrol and comply can often return to practice without public discipline. Long-term outcomes for monitored physicians are generally good, with high rates of sustained abstinence.

Takeaway: PHPs: confidential evaluation, treatment referral and monitoring, not discipline.

whyNot.B: PHPs are not disciplinary bodies; boards discipline, while PHPs evaluate, refer and monitor.
whyNot.C: PHPs have no role in malpractice insurance.
whyNot.D: Privileging is done by the hospital's credentials committee, not the PHP.
whyNot.E: Prescription monitoring is done by state prescription drug monitoring programs and the DEA, not PHPs.

items.objective: Describe the role of state physician health programs.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old pediatrician has bipolar I disorder that has been stable on lithium for 8 years, with regular psychiatric follow-up and no episodes. A colleague who learns of the diagnosis tells the department chair that she is an "impaired physician" who should be reported. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.html: Any physician with a serious psychiatric diagnosis is impaired by definition

options.label: B
options.html: Impairment refers to an inability to practise safely, not to a diagnosis

options.label: C
options.html: She must notify all of her patients of her diagnosis

options.label: D
options.html: She must stop practising until a psychiatrist certifies her yearly

options.label: E
options.html: She must self-report the diagnosis to the licensing board immediately

items.explanationHtml:
Impairment is the inability to practise medicine with reasonable skill and safety because of an illness or condition (for example substance use, mental or physical illness, cognitive decline or fatigue). Having a condition is not the same as being impaired: a physician whose illness is well treated and who practises safely is not impaired.

Physicians have a duty to seek treatment and to limit their practice when a condition does impair them. Stigma about mental illness deters physicians from seeking care; treating diagnosis and impairment as the same thing worsens this.

Takeaway: impairment = cannot practise safely; a treated diagnosis is not impairment.

whyNot.A: A diagnosis alone does not establish impairment.
whyNot.C: There is no duty to disclose a well-controlled condition to patients.
whyNot.D: No such requirement exists for a well-treated condition without impairment.
whyNot.E: Self-reporting obligations depend on current impairment, not on having a treated diagnosis.

items.objective: Distinguish having a medical condition from being an impaired physician.

items.stemHtml: A family physician learns from a pharmacist that a former residency classmate, now in solo private practice in the same state, has been writing prescriptions for hydrocodone in the names of his relatives and filling them for himself. When she calls him, he admits it, refuses treatment and says he will keep seeing patients. He has no hospital privileges or supervisor. To which of the following should she report her concern?

options.label: A
options.html: The local police department

options.label: B
options.html: His patients, by letter

options.label: C
options.html: The hospital where she works

options.label: D
options.html: The state medical licensing board

options.label: E
options.html: His malpractice insurer

items.explanationHtml:
Physicians have an ethical, and in many states legal, duty to report a colleague whose impairment endangers patients. Reports usually go first to someone with authority over the colleague's practice (a chief of service, department chair or the physician health program). When there is no such supervisor, or the colleague refuses help and continues to practise, the report goes to the state medical licensing board, which can require evaluation and restrict practice.

Fraudulent prescribing for his own use and refusal of treatment while seeing patients make this urgent.

Takeaway: impaired colleague with no supervisor who refuses help: report to the state licensing board.

whyNot.A: Police may become involved in drug crimes, but the body responsible for a physician's fitness to practise is the licensing board.
whyNot.B: Contacting his patients breaches confidentiality and does not address his fitness to practise.
whyNot.C: Her hospital has no authority over a physician who does not practise there.
whyNot.E: Insurers do not evaluate or restrict physicians' practice.

items.objective: Choose the reporting route for an impaired colleague outside an institution.

items.stemHtml: A hospitalist arrives for the 7 am handoff. A colleague who is scheduled to take over 18 inpatients this morning has slurred speech, an unsteady gait and smells strongly of alcohol. She insists she is fine to work. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Tell her privately that she cannot see patients today and arrange coverage

options.label: B
options.html: Allow her to round while a nurse watches her closely

options.label: C
options.html: Call the police to remove her from the hospital

options.label: D
options.html: Report her to the state licensing board before taking any other action

options.label: E
options.html: Wait until after rounds to raise the concern with her

items.explanationHtml:
When a colleague is impaired at work, patient safety comes first: she must not provide care now. The physician speaks with her privately and respectfully, makes sure her patients are covered and involves the person in charge (the medical director or chief) to remove her from duty, following hospital policy. Arrange for her to get home safely and not drive.

Formal reporting and referral for evaluation follow, but the first action is to stop the risk to patients.

Takeaway: impaired colleague at work: remove from patient care now and arrange coverage.

whyNot.B: Supervision does not make it safe for an impaired physician to make clinical decisions.
whyNot.C: This escalates unnecessarily; the immediate need is to keep her from patient care and arrange coverage.
whyNot.D: A board report does not protect today's patients; immediate removal from care comes first.
whyNot.E: Waiting lets her care for 18 patients while impaired.

items.objective: Prioritise immediate patient safety when a colleague is impaired at work.

items.stemHtml: A hospitalist has just prevented a visibly intoxicated colleague from starting her shift and has arranged coverage of her patients and a safe ride home. The colleague apologises and says it will not happen again, and asks him to keep it between them. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Keep the episode confidential because she has apologised

options.label: B
options.html: Post a warning about her in the hospitalists' group chat

options.label: C
options.html: Call her spouse to discuss her drinking

options.label: D
options.html: Tell her patients that their physician has an alcohol problem

options.label: E
options.html: Report the episode to the hospital's chief medical officer or department chief

items.explanationHtml:
After the immediate risk is controlled, the physician has an ethical obligation to report impairment through the proper channel, usually the department chief or chief medical officer, who will arrange a fitness-for-duty evaluation and referral to the physician health program. Agreeing to secrecy protects neither patients nor the colleague, who may need treatment.

Reports should be factual, made in good faith and limited to those who need to know.

Takeaway: after protecting patients, report the impaired colleague to institutional leadership.

whyNot.A: A promise not to repeat it does not discharge the duty to report an impaired colleague; patients remain at risk.
whyNot.B: Gossip breaches her privacy and is not a reporting channel.
whyNot.C: Contacting family is not the professional route and breaches her privacy.
whyNot.D: Disclosing her health information to patients is improper and unnecessary.

items.objective: Report an impaired colleague through the appropriate institutional channel.

items.stemHtml: A hospitalist was removed from duty after arriving intoxicated. She completes evaluation and treatment through the state physician health program and returns to work under a monitoring agreement. A nurse asks a colleague at the nurses' station whether she is the doctor who had the drinking problem. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the colleague?

options.label: A
options.html: "Yes, but she's in treatment now, so it's fine."

options.label: B
options.html: "You should ask her yourself."

options.label: C
options.html: "A colleague's health is confidential, so I can't discuss it."

options.label: D
options.html: "I'd prefer to wait until she leaves to discuss it."

options.label: E
options.html: "Yes, and you should keep an eye on her."

items.explanationHtml:
A physician in recovery is entitled to the same confidentiality about her health as any patient. Monitoring is the responsibility of the physician health program and designated workplace monitors, not of the staff at large. Declining politely to discuss it protects her privacy and models professionalism.

Physicians who complete PHP treatment and monitoring generally do well, and a respectful workplace supports recovery.
