Takeaway: a recovering colleague's health information is confidential; don't discuss it with staff.

whyNot.A: Confirming her history discloses confidential health information.
whyNot.B: This invites further intrusion into her private health matters.
whyNot.D: This implies there is something to discuss and continues gossip.
whyNot.E: Disclosure and encouraging surveillance by staff are inappropriate; monitoring is handled by the program.

items.objective: Protect the confidentiality of a colleague in recovery.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.label: A
options.html: Burnout is associated with self-reported major errors, but the direction cannot be determined

options.label: B
options.html: Burnout causes residents to make major medical errors

options.label: C
options.html: Major medical errors cause burnout in residents

options.label: D
options.html: Reducing burnout will halve the rate of major errors

options.label: E
options.html: Burnout has no relationship with actual errors because errors were self-reported

items.explanationHtml:
In a cross-sectional survey, exposure (burnout) and outcome (self-reported errors) are measured at the same time, so temporality cannot be established. Burnout might lead to errors, errors might lead to burnout (guilt and distress after a mistake), or both might share causes such as heavy workload.

Self-reported outcomes and a 61% response rate add risk of reporting and nonresponse bias. Prospective studies with objective error measures would be needed to support a causal claim.

Takeaway: cross-sectional surveys show association, not direction or causation.

whyNot.B: A cross-sectional design measures both at one time and cannot establish which came first.
whyNot.C: Reverse causation is possible, but this design cannot establish it either.
whyNot.D: Predicting the effect of an intervention requires a trial, not a survey.
whyNot.E: Self-report may introduce bias, but it does not show there is no relationship.

items.objective: Interpret the limits of a cross-sectional study of burnout and errors.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, what is the prevalence ratio for self-reported major errors in residents with burnout compared with residents without burnout?
items.explanationHtml:
Prevalence with burnout = 96 ÷ 480 = 0.20 (20%). Prevalence without burnout = 72 ÷ 720 = 0.10 (10%). Prevalence ratio = 0.20 ÷ 0.10 = 2.00.

The odds ratio from the same table is (96 ÷ 384) ÷ (72 ÷ 648) = 0.25 ÷ 0.111 = 2.25; it exceeds the prevalence ratio because the outcome is common (10–20%). Cross-sectional data give prevalence, so the prevalence ratio is the natural measure.

Takeaway: prevalence ratio = prevalence in exposed ÷ prevalence in unexposed = 20% ÷ 10% = 2.0.

whyNot.A: 0.50 is the inverse ratio (no burnout ÷ burnout).
whyNot.B: 1.10 is 1 plus the absolute difference (0.10); it is not a ratio of the two prevalences.
whyNot.D: 2.25 is the odds ratio, (96/384) ÷ (72/648), not the ratio of prevalences.
whyNot.E: 10 is the reciprocal of the 10-percentage-point difference, not a ratio of prevalences.

items.objective: Calculate a prevalence ratio and distinguish it from an odds ratio.

items.stemHtml: A first-year resident finishes a 26-hour in-house shift at 8 am. She has a 50-minute drive home and nearly fell asleep at a red light after her last overnight shift. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Drink a large coffee and drive home with the windows open

options.label: B
options.html: Drive home on back roads to avoid traffic

options.label: C
options.html: Stay at the hospital and pick up an extra shift to finish her notes

options.label: D
options.html: Use the hospital call room to sleep or take a ride service home

options.label: E
options.html: Take a sedating antihistamine so she can sleep as soon as she gets home

items.explanationHtml:
Prolonged wakefulness impairs reaction time and attention much as alcohol does, and residents are at high risk of drowsy-driving crashes after extended shifts. Accreditation standards require programs to provide sleep facilities and safe transportation options for residents too tired to drive.

A nap before driving, or a taxi or ride service, is the safe choice.

Takeaway: too tired after a long shift: nap at the hospital or get a ride; don't drive.

whyNot.A: Caffeine and cold air give only brief alertness and do not make drowsy driving safe.
whyNot.B: Changing route does not reduce the danger of driving while sleep-deprived.
whyNot.C: Working longer while fatigued adds risk to patients and exceeds duty limits.
whyNot.E: A sedative before driving makes the danger worse.

items.objective: Choose a safe option for a fatigued resident after an extended shift.

items.stemHtml: A second-year surgery resident tells a co-resident over coffee that he has been sleeping poorly, has lost interest in things he enjoyed and recently thought "everyone would be better off without me." He asks her not to tell anyone because he fears it will end his career. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Are you having thoughts of ending your life? Let's get you help today."

options.label: B
options.html: "You're just burned out. A weekend off will help."

options.label: C
options.html: "I won't tell anyone, I promise."

options.label: D
options.html: "You should report yourself to the medical board right away."

options.label: E
options.html: "Let's talk about it again at the end of the rotation."

items.explanationHtml:
His statement may signal suicidal ideation. Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and is the necessary first step. The co-resident then helps him get care that day: the program's confidential wellness or mental health service, an emergency evaluation if he has a plan or intent, or a crisis line.

Physicians have a higher suicide rate than the general population, and fear of career consequences is a major barrier. Programs are required to give residents access to confidential mental health care, including urgent care.

Takeaway: a colleague hints at suicide: ask directly and connect him with help today.

whyNot.B: Minimising his symptoms misses depression with possible suicidal ideation.
whyNot.C: Promising secrecy prevents getting help for a colleague who may be at risk of suicide.
whyNot.D: Board reporting is not the priority; he needs assessment and treatment, and seeking care does not equal impairment.
whyNot.E: Delay is dangerous when a colleague has expressed thoughts of being better off dead.

items.objective: Respond to possible suicidal ideation in a fellow resident.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old orthopedic surgeon has practised at a hospital for 40 years. Over the past several months, operating room staff have noticed that he repeats questions, forgot the planned implant size during two cases and became lost walking to the parking garage. A colleague who has seen these events is concerned. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the colleague?

options.label: A
options.html: Report the concern to the chief of surgery so that a fitness-for-duty evaluation can be arranged

options.label: B
options.html: Raise the issue publicly at the department's morbidity and mortality conference

options.label: C
options.html: Wait until a patient is harmed before taking action

options.label: D
options.html: Advise the patients scheduled with him to change surgeons

options.label: E
options.html: Tell him that he must retire immediately

items.explanationHtml:
Possible cognitive decline in a practising physician is a form of potential impairment. The colleague should report factually to the person with authority, here the chief of surgery, who can arrange a confidential fitness-for-duty evaluation (medical, neuropsychological and practice review), temporary changes in privileges if needed and support for the surgeon.

Cognitive change has many causes, some treatable. The process should be respectful and fair, protecting patients while treating the colleague with dignity. Some hospitals use age-based late-career screening policies.

Takeaway: suspected cognitive decline in a colleague: report to the chief for a fitness-for-duty evaluation.

whyNot.B: Public discussion humiliates him and is not a channel for assessing fitness to practise.
whyNot.C: Waiting for harm violates the duty to protect patients.
whyNot.D: Approaching his patients is improper and does not address his fitness.
whyNot.E: The colleague lacks the authority to impose retirement, and the cause has not been evaluated.

items.objective: Respond to suspected cognitive impairment in a senior colleague.

items.stemHtml: At a Saturday barbecue, a 40-year-old pediatrician drinks heavily and becomes loud. He is not on call. His partner, who has worked with him daily for 5 years, has never seen any sign of impairment at work, and his clinical outcomes are good. The partner wonders whether he has a drinking problem. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the partner?

options.label: A
options.html: Report him to the state medical board on Monday

options.label: B
options.html: Notify the hospital chief of pediatrics of an impaired physician

options.label: C
options.html: Take no action, because what he does off duty is never a professional concern

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the office staff to watch him for signs of drinking

options.label: E
options.html: Speak with him privately, express concern and offer help if he wants it

items.explanationHtml:
Duty-to-report obligations concern impairment that affects, or is likely to affect, the ability to practise safely. Heavy drinking at a social event while off duty, with no signs of impairment at work, does not by itself meet that threshold. A caring, private conversation is the right first step, with information about confidential help (including the physician health program, which accepts self-referrals).

If signs of impairment at work appear, if he is drinking before or during clinical duties or call, or if the pattern worsens, the duty to report applies.

Takeaway: off-duty drinking without work impairment: talk privately and offer help; report if practice is affected.

whyNot.A: There is no evidence of impairment in practice, so a board report is out of proportion as a first step.
whyNot.B: A single off-duty episode with no effect on work does not establish impairment requiring a formal report.
whyNot.C: Concern for a colleague's health is appropriate; ignoring a possible problem is not ideal either.
whyNot.D: Recruiting staff to monitor him is a breach of trust and privacy.

items.objective: Distinguish off-duty behaviour from reportable impairment in a colleague.

items.stemHtml: A second-year psychiatry resident meets privately with her program director. She says that for several months she has been drinking most of a bottle of wine every night to cope with stress, has twice called in sick because of hangovers and wants help before it affects her patients. She has not worked while intoxicated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Dismiss her from the program to protect patients

options.label: B
options.html: Advise her to cut down on her own and check in after 6 months

options.label: C
options.html: Refer her to the state physician health program for evaluation and treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Report her to the state medical board

options.label: E
options.html: Inform her co-residents so they can support her

items.explanationHtml:
A physician who recognises a substance use problem and asks for help should be supported. The program director refers her to the physician health program (or the institution's equivalent) for confidential assessment, treatment and monitoring, and arranges leave or schedule changes as needed.

Self-referral to a PHP usually allows treatment without disciplinary action, provided the physician complies with the program. Seeking help early protects both patients and her career.

Takeaway: a physician who seeks help for substance use: refer to the PHP and support her.

whyNot.A: Dismissal punishes a physician who sought help and discourages others from coming forward.
whyNot.B: Unaided reduction is unlikely to succeed and provides no evaluation or monitoring.
whyNot.D: Self-referral to treatment through a PHP is the appropriate route; the board is not the first step for a physician who seeks help.
whyNot.E: Sharing her health information with peers breaches confidentiality.

items.objective: Respond to a resident's self-disclosure of an alcohol problem.

items.stemHtml: A third-year emergency medicine resident is 22 hours into a scheduled 24-hour shift. A patient needs a central venous catheter. The resident realises he has read the same line of a chart three times and nearly mislabeled a specimen a few minutes ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Drink an energy drink and proceed with the procedure

options.label: B
options.html: Tell the supervising attending that he is too fatigued and hand off the procedure

options.label: C
options.html: Perform the procedure quickly to finish before the shift ends

options.label: D
options.html: Say nothing and ask the nurse to double-check his work

options.label: E
options.html: Leave the hospital immediately without signing out

items.explanationHtml:
Recognising and acting on one's own fatigue is a professional duty. Accreditation standards expect residents to tell supervisors when they are too tired to work safely, and programs must allow a handoff without penalty. A structured handoff of the procedure and of pending tasks to a rested colleague protects the patient.

Fatigue, like alcohol, impairs attention and judgement, and the impaired person tends to underestimate the effect.

Takeaway: self-recognised fatigue: tell the supervisor and hand off; don't push through.

whyNot.A: Caffeine does not reliably reverse the effects of severe fatigue on performance.
whyNot.C: Rushing while fatigued compounds the risk.
whyNot.D: Hiding fatigue and relying on others for checks leaves the risk unaddressed.
whyNot.E: Leaving without handoff abandons patients and creates new safety risks.

items.objective: Act appropriately on one's own fatigue during an extended shift.

items.stemHtml: An internal medicine program director notices that a usually engaged second-year resident has become withdrawn, is late with notes and was described by a nurse as "curt with patients." Evaluations from attendings mention fatigue. There have been no patient safety events. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Place the resident on formal probation for unprofessional behaviour

options.label: B
options.html: Wait for the next semiannual evaluation to discuss the concerns

options.label: C
options.html: Meet privately with the resident to ask about wellbeing and offer confidential support

options.label: D
options.html: Report the resident to the state physician health program without speaking to him

options.label: E
options.html: Ask co-residents to report on his behaviour outside work

items.explanationHtml:
A change in behaviour, performance or professionalism is often the first sign of burnout, depression, substance use or personal difficulties. The program director should meet privately and non-judgmentally, ask about wellbeing (including sleep, mood and suicidal thoughts), and offer confidential counselling, schedule adjustment or time off as needed.

Programs are expected to monitor for burnout and to provide access to confidential mental health services. Early supportive action protects both the resident and patients.

Takeaway: a struggling resident: start with a private, supportive conversation and confidential resources.

whyNot.A: Starting with discipline overlooks possible burnout or illness and discourages help-seeking.
whyNot.B: Waiting months allows a treatable problem to worsen.
whyNot.D: Referral may be appropriate later, but the first step is a supportive conversation to understand the problem.
whyNot.E: Surveillance by peers is inappropriate and erodes trust.

items.objective: Respond early and supportively to signs of burnout in a resident.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man sues his primary care physician after a delayed diagnosis. During a law school seminar on health care litigation, students are asked which elements a plaintiff must establish to win a claim of medical negligence. Which of the following lists the required elements?

options.label: A
options.html: Duty, intent to harm, causation and damages

options.label: B
options.html: Consent, breach, causation and damages

options.label: C
options.html: Duty, breach of the standard of care, causation and damages

options.label: D
options.html: Duty, breach of the standard of care, causation and punishment

options.label: E
options.html: Relationship, bad outcome, expert disapproval and damages

items.explanationHtml:
A negligence claim requires four elements: a duty owed to the patient (usually a physician–patient relationship), a breach of that duty by care below the standard of care, causation (the breach more likely than not caused the harm), and damages (an actual, compensable injury). Each must be shown by a preponderance of the evidence.

Negligence does not require intent; it is a failure of reasonable care. A bad outcome alone does not establish any element.

Takeaway: malpractice is duty, breach, causation and damages, and a missing link defeats the claim.

whyNot.A: Negligence requires no intent to harm; intentional harm is a different kind of tort and possibly a crime.
whyNot.B: Consent matters in battery and informed-consent claims, but the first element of negligence is a duty of care.
whyNot.D: The fourth element is damages to the patient; punishment (punitive damages) is rare and is not a required element.
whyNot.E: A bad outcome is not an element; the court asks whether care fell below the standard and caused the harm.

items.objective: List the four elements a plaintiff must prove in a medical negligence claim.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman sues a general surgeon after a bile duct injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. At trial, each side calls a board-certified general surgeon as an expert witness. The jury is told that the experts will address the standard of care. Which of the following questions is the experts' testimony primarily meant to answer?

options.label: A
options.html: Whether a reasonably prudent general surgeon in similar circumstances would have acted as this surgeon did

options.label: B
options.html: Whether the best surgeon at a national referral center would have avoided the injury

options.label: C
options.html: Whether the outcome matched what the patient had been told to expect

options.label: D
options.html: Whether the surgeon followed the technique he personally uses in most cases

options.label: E
options.html: Whether most surgeons at the same hospital have lower complication rates

items.explanationHtml:
The standard of care is what a reasonably careful and prudent physician of the same specialty would do under similar circumstances. Because jurors are not physicians, the standard and whether it was breached are usually established through expert testimony from physicians in the same field.

The standard is not perfection or the best care anywhere, and it is not defined by the outcome or by the defendant's own habits. Complications can occur despite care that meets the standard.

Takeaway: the standard of care is the reasonable, prudent peer in the same specialty and similar circumstances.

whyNot.B: The law asks about reasonable care, not the best care a top expert might give.
whyNot.C: A mismatch between outcome and expectation may matter for informed consent, but it does not define the standard of care.
whyNot.D: A physician's personal routine is not the yardstick; it may itself fall below the standard.
whyNot.E: Comparative complication rates do not show what a reasonable surgeon would have done in this operation.

items.objective: Define the standard of care and explain how it is established in malpractice litigation.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man's primary care physician agrees during a visit that he is due for screening colonoscopy but forgets to place the referral, a lapse that experts agree fell below the standard of care. Two months later, the patient dies of an acute myocardial infarction. Autopsy shows no colorectal lesion. His family files a negligence claim against the physician based on the missed referral. Which of the following is the strongest defense to this claim?

options.label: A
options.html: No physician–patient relationship existed at the time of the visit

options.label: B
options.html: Forgetting a referral meets the usual standard of care

options.label: C
options.html: The family suffered no loss after the patient's death

options.label: D
options.html: The missed referral did not cause the patient's death

options.label: E
options.html: The claim should have been brought against the hospital

items.explanationHtml:
All four elements must be present. A duty existed (an established patient), the breach is conceded, and there are real damages (a death). But the death came from a myocardial infarction, and no colon lesion was found, so the missed colonoscopy referral did not cause the harm. Causation fails.

Exam items often pair an obvious lapse with an unrelated bad outcome to test whether you check causation separately from breach.

Takeaway: breach plus harm is not enough; the breach must have caused the harm.

whyNot.A: He was the physician's established patient seen at a visit, so a duty clearly existed.
whyNot.B: The stem states that experts agree the lapse fell below the standard, so breach is established.
whyNot.C: A death is a serious, compensable loss to the family, so damages exist; they were simply not caused by the lapse.
whyNot.E: Naming another defendant does not answer the claim; the physician's own care is at issue, and the problem is causation.

items.objective: Recognize when a negligence claim fails on causation despite a breach and damages.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has persistent abdominal pain after an open hysterectomy. A CT scan 3 months later shows a retained surgical sponge, which is removed at reoperation. Her attorney argues that she does not need an expert witness to show that the surgical team was negligent, because sponges are not left in patients unless someone was careless. Which of the following legal doctrines is the attorney invoking?

options.label: A
options.html: Respondeat superior

options.label: B
options.html: Res ipsa loquitur

options.label: C
options.html: Contributory negligence

options.label: D
options.html: Battery

options.label: E
options.html: Informed consent

items.explanationHtml:
Res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself") lets a jury infer negligence when the injury would not ordinarily happen without negligence and the cause was under the defendant's exclusive control. A retained sponge or instrument is the classic example; the plaintiff may not need an expert to explain the standard of care.

It is still a negligence claim: damages (here, pain and a second operation) must exist.

Takeaway: an injury that speaks for itself, such as a retained foreign body, allows negligence to be inferred.

whyNot.A: Respondeat superior makes an employer liable for an employee's negligence; it does not remove the need to prove negligence.
whyNot.C: Contributory negligence is a defense claiming the patient's own carelessness contributed; the patient did nothing here.
whyNot.D: Battery is touching without consent; she consented to the hysterectomy.
whyNot.E: An informed-consent claim concerns undisclosed risks, not an obvious technical error inside the operation.

items.objective: Recognize res ipsa loquitur as the doctrine that allows negligence to be inferred from certain injuries.

items.stemHtml: A registered nurse employed by a community hospital gives a 70-year-old man a full dose of a medication that had been discontinued an hour earlier, and the patient has a serious adverse reaction. The patient sues both the nurse and the hospital. The hospital argues that it did nothing wrong because the nurse made the error alone. Which of the following principles best explains why the hospital can still be held liable?

options.label: A
options.html: Res ipsa loquitur

options.label: B
options.html: Good Samaritan protection

options.label: C
options.html: Assumption of risk

options.label: D
options.html: Contributory negligence

options.label: E
options.html: Respondeat superior

items.explanationHtml:
Respondeat superior ("let the master answer") is vicarious liability: an employer is liable for negligent acts of employees done within the scope of their employment. The hospital employs the nurse, and giving medications is part of the job, so the hospital can be held liable even if no hospital manager acted carelessly.

The nurse also remains personally liable. Hospitals may additionally face direct liability for their own failures, such as poor systems for discontinuing orders.

Takeaway: employers answer for employees' negligence within the scope of employment.

whyNot.A: Res ipsa loquitur lets negligence be inferred; it does not explain why an employer is liable for someone else's act.
whyNot.B: Good Samaritan laws protect unpaid volunteers in emergencies, not hospital employees on duty.
whyNot.C: Assumption of risk is a defense when a person knowingly accepts a danger; patients do not accept medication errors.
whyNot.D: Contributory negligence concerns the patient's own fault, which is absent here.

items.objective: Explain vicarious liability (respondeat superior) for employees' negligence.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man arrives at the emergency department of a private hospital that participates in Medicare. He reports 40 minutes of chest pressure. The registration clerk learns that he is uninsured and, before he is examined, tells him that the public hospital across town would be a better place for him. He leaves. Which of the following federal laws did the hospital most likely violate?

options.label: A
options.html: Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act

options.label: B
options.html: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

options.label: C
options.html: Stark Law

options.label: D
options.html: False Claims Act

options.label: E
options.html: Patient Self-Determination Act

items.explanationHtml:
The Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) requires Medicare-participating hospitals with emergency departments to give anyone who comes requesting care a medical screening examination and, if an emergency condition is present, to stabilize it or arrange an appropriate transfer. Screening may not be delayed or denied because of insurance or ability to pay.

Steering an uninsured patient with chest pain away before examination is a textbook violation ("patient dumping").

Takeaway: in the emergency department, screen and stabilize first; payment questions come later.

whyNot.B: HIPAA governs privacy and security of health information; no information was disclosed improperly here.
whyNot.C: The Stark Law concerns physician self-referral to entities in which they have a financial interest.
whyNot.D: The False Claims Act concerns fraudulent billing of federal programs; no claim was submitted.
whyNot.E: The Patient Self-Determination Act requires hospitals to tell patients about advance directives.

items.objective: Identify EMTALA's screening obligation regardless of ability to pay.

items.stemHtml: An off-duty pediatrician watching a community road race sees a runner collapse. She finds him pulseless, starts chest compressions and uses a public defibrillator until paramedics arrive. She is not paid and has no prior relationship with the runner. He survives with a rib fracture from compressions. Under the Good Samaritan laws in effect throughout the United States, which of the following best describes her legal protection?

options.label: A
options.html: She is protected from any claim, including one for reckless or wilful misconduct

options.label: B
options.html: She is protected only if she first obtained the runner's verbal consent

options.label: C
options.html: She is protected only if she later bills for the emergency care she gave

options.label: D
options.html: She is protected from claims of ordinary negligence for care given in good faith

options.label: E
options.html: She is not protected, because a pediatrician acting on an adult exceeds her specialty

items.explanationHtml:
Every state has a Good Samaritan law. Their common core protects a person who gives emergency help in good faith, without compensation and outside a usual care setting, from liability for ordinary negligence. They do not protect gross negligence or wilful misconduct. A rib fracture from properly done CPR is an expected complication, not negligence at all.

Details (who is covered, whether training must be current) differ by state, but the protection for good-faith, unpaid emergency aid is shared.

Takeaway: Good Samaritan laws cover good-faith, unpaid emergency help against ordinary negligence claims, not gross negligence.

whyNot.A: Good Samaritan protection does not extend to gross negligence, recklessness or wilful misconduct.
whyNot.B: An unresponsive person cannot consent; implied consent covers emergency care, and protection does not depend on verbal consent.
whyNot.C: Billing for the care generally removes the protection, which is aimed at unpaid volunteers.
whyNot.E: Emergency help within a physician's general competence, such as CPR, is covered regardless of specialty.

items.objective: Describe the scope and limits of Good Samaritan protection.

items.stemHtml: A jury in a civil medical malpractice trial asks the judge how sure they must be before finding that the defendant physician breached the standard of care. Which of the following standards of proof should the judge describe?

options.label: A
options.html: Reasonable suspicion

options.label: B
options.html: Preponderance of the evidence

options.label: C
options.html: Clear and convincing evidence

options.label: D
options.html: Beyond a reasonable doubt

options.label: E
options.html: Unanimous agreement among the expert witnesses

items.explanationHtml:
Civil cases, including malpractice, are decided on the preponderance of the evidence: each element must be more likely true than not (greater than 50%). This is lower than the criminal standard (beyond a reasonable doubt) and lower than clear and convincing evidence, which applies to certain civil matters such as some decisions about withdrawing life support for incapacitated patients in particular states.

Takeaway: malpractice is proved "more likely than not".

whyNot.A: Reasonable suspicion is a low threshold used for police stops, not for deciding civil liability.
whyNot.C: Clear and convincing evidence is a higher civil standard used in a few special matters, not ordinary malpractice claims.
whyNot.D: Beyond a reasonable doubt is the criminal standard; malpractice is a civil claim.
whyNot.E: Experts often disagree; the jury weighs their testimony and decides by the applicable standard of proof.

items.objective: State the standard of proof in a civil malpractice claim.

items.stemHtml: An orthopedic surgeon in private practice is a 20% owner of a freestanding physical therapy center across the street. He routinely refers his Medicare patients there after knee surgery. He has no written agreement about referrals and says he chooses the center only because it is convenient for patients. No exception applies to this ownership arrangement. Which of the following federal laws is most directly implicated?

options.label: A
options.html: Anti-Kickback Statute

options.label: B
options.html: Sunshine Act

options.label: C
options.html: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

options.label: D
options.html: Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act

options.label: E
options.html: Stark Law

items.explanationHtml:
The Stark Law (physician self-referral law) prohibits a physician from referring Medicare patients for designated health services, which include physical therapy, to an entity with which the physician or an immediate family member has a financial relationship, unless an exception applies. It is a strict-liability civil statute: good intentions or convenience do not matter.

The physician's denial of any intent to profit is a clue: intent is irrelevant under Stark.

Takeaway: physician + financial interest + Medicare referral for designated health services = Stark, regardless of intent.

whyNot.A: The Anti-Kickback Statute requires knowing and wilful payment to induce referrals; the stem emphasizes ownership without proof of such intent.
whyNot.B: The Sunshine Act requires manufacturers to report payments to physicians; it does not govern ownership-based referrals.
whyNot.C: HIPAA concerns privacy of health information, not financial relationships.
whyNot.D: EMTALA concerns emergency screening and stabilization.

items.objective: Recognize a Stark Law self-referral problem.

items.stemHtml: A compliance officer is teaching new faculty about two federal laws that address referrals in programs paid by Medicare and Medicaid: the Anti-Kickback Statute and the physician self-referral (Stark) law. Which of the following statements correctly describes a feature of the Anti-Kickback Statute that distinguishes it from the Stark Law?

options.label: A
options.html: It requires knowing and wilful intent to induce or reward referrals

options.label: B
options.html: It applies only to referrals made by physicians, not companies

options.label: C
options.html: It is limited to a defined list of designated health services

options.label: D
options.html: It imposes liability even when no one intended to influence referrals

options.label: E
options.html: It applies only to services billed under Medicare Part D

items.explanationHtml:
The Anti-Kickback Statute is a criminal law that forbids knowingly and wilfully offering, paying, soliciting or receiving anything of value to induce or reward referrals of items or services paid by federal health care programs. It applies to anyone (physicians, companies, hospitals, laboratories) and to any federally reimbursed item. Safe harbors protect certain arrangements.

The Stark Law is civil and strict liability: no intent is needed, it applies to physicians' referrals, and it covers only designated health services.

Takeaway: anti-kickback = intent, anyone, any federal program item; Stark = no intent needed, physicians, designated health services.

whyNot.B: Limiting coverage to physicians' referrals describes the Stark Law; the Anti-Kickback Statute applies to anyone.
whyNot.C: The list of designated health services belongs to the Stark Law.
whyNot.D: Liability without intent is the hallmark of the Stark Law, not the Anti-Kickback Statute.
whyNot.E: The Anti-Kickback Statute covers all federal health care programs, not one part of Medicare.

items.objective: Distinguish the Anti-Kickback Statute from the Stark Law by intent, scope and coverage.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman searches a federal website before an appointment and finds that her endocrinologist received consulting fees and meals from the manufacturer of the insulin pump he recommended to her. Which of the following programs most likely made this information public?

options.label: A
options.html: National Practitioner Data Bank

options.label: B
options.html: Merit-based Incentive Payment System

options.label: C
options.html: Open Payments

options.label: D
options.html: Prescription drug monitoring program

options.label: E
options.html: Medicare hospital quality star ratings

items.explanationHtml:
The Physician Payments Sunshine Act created Open Payments. Manufacturers of drugs, devices and biologics covered by federal health programs must report payments and other transfers of value (consulting fees, meals, travel, research funding) to physicians and teaching hospitals, and CMS publishes the data in a searchable database.

The program requires transparency; it does not forbid such payments. Physicians should be ready to explain any relationship honestly.

Takeaway: industry payments to physicians are public through Open Payments.

whyNot.A: The National Practitioner Data Bank records malpractice payments and disciplinary actions and is not open to public searching.
whyNot.B: The Merit-based Incentive Payment System adjusts Medicare payments by quality measures; it does not list industry payments.
whyNot.D: A prescription drug monitoring program tracks controlled-substance prescriptions dispensed to patients.
whyNot.E: Hospital star ratings summarize quality measures for hospitals, not payments to individual physicians.

items.objective: Identify Open Payments as the public database of industry payments to physicians.

items.stemHtml: An internal audit of a family medicine practice finds that one physician bills almost every return visit at the highest office-visit level. His notes for many of these visits describe a single stable problem, a brief examination and a medication refill. Which of the following terms best describes this billing pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Unbundling

options.label: B
options.html: Upcoding

options.label: C
options.html: Fee splitting

options.label: D
options.html: Self-referral

options.label: E
options.html: Balance billing

items.explanationHtml:
Upcoding is billing a higher level or more expensive service than was provided or documented. Repeatedly billing simple refill visits at the top level is a classic pattern found on audit. Knowingly submitting such claims to federal programs can violate the False Claims Act.

Unbundling is the related but distinct practice of billing the components of a single package separately.

Takeaway: bill the level the documentation supports; billing higher is upcoding.

whyNot.A: Unbundling means billing parts of a bundled service separately, not inflating the level of a single visit.
whyNot.C: Fee splitting means paying or receiving a share of fees for referrals.
whyNot.D: Self-referral means referring patients to an entity in which the physician has a financial interest.
whyNot.E: Balance billing means billing the patient for the difference between the charge and the insurer's payment.

items.objective: Recognize upcoding as a form of billing fraud.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has been treated by his internist for asthma for 2 years. At the end of a routine visit, he says he has enjoyed getting to know her and invites her to dinner. She is also single and finds him likable. Which of the following best describes the ethics of starting a romantic relationship in this situation?

options.label: A
options.html: It is acceptable because the patient initiated it

options.label: B
options.html: It is acceptable if a chaperone is present at future visits

options.label: C
options.html: It is acceptable if no intimate examinations are involved

options.label: D
options.html: It is unacceptable while he remains her patient

options.label: E
options.html: It is unacceptable only for psychiatrists and their patients

items.explanationHtml:
A romantic or sexual relationship with a current patient is unethical in every specialty, whoever initiates it. The physician's power, the patient's dependence and access to private information make the relationship exploitative regardless of mutual interest. The boundary is the physician's responsibility.

If a physician believes genuine feelings have arisen, the professional relationship must end first, and even then a relationship with a former patient is unethical if it trades on trust or knowledge gained in care.

Takeaway: never with a current patient, regardless of who asks.

whyNot.A: Who initiates the relationship does not change the power imbalance; the physician holds the duty to maintain boundaries.
whyNot.B: A chaperone protects during examinations but cannot make a romantic relationship with a patient acceptable.
whyNot.C: The prohibition does not depend on the type of examination; it rests on the professional relationship itself.
whyNot.E: Psychiatry is stricter about former patients, but a relationship with a current patient is prohibited in every specialty.

items.objective: State the prohibition on romantic relationships with current patients.

items.stemHtml: A university research-integrity office reviews five complaints about faculty manuscripts. Under the federal definition of research misconduct, which of the following complaints, if confirmed, would constitute research misconduct?

options.label: A
options.html: A statistician makes an honest arithmetic error that is corrected after publication

options.label: B
options.html: Two coauthors disagree about whether the results support a causal interpretation

options.label: C
options.html: An investigator copies several paragraphs from another group's grant without attribution

options.label: D
options.html: A team submits a well-conducted negative trial to a journal with a low impact factor

options.label: E
options.html: A senior author lists the middle authors in alphabetical rather than contribution order

items.explanationHtml:
Federal research misconduct is fabrication, falsification or plagiarism in proposing, performing, reviewing or reporting research. Copying another person's text or ideas without credit is plagiarism.

The definition explicitly excludes honest error and differences of opinion. Authorship order conventions and choice of journal are not misconduct.

Takeaway: research misconduct = fabrication, falsification, plagiarism; honest error and disagreement are not.

whyNot.A: Honest error is excluded from the definition of research misconduct, and correcting it is good practice.
whyNot.B: Differences of opinion about interpretation are excluded from the definition.
whyNot.D: Publishing a negative trial anywhere is honest reporting and supports the literature.
whyNot.E: Author-order conventions vary and are not fabrication, falsification or plagiarism.

items.objective: Define research misconduct as fabrication, falsification or plagiarism.

items.stemHtml: A third-year medical student on an internal medicine rotation runs out of time before rounds. In her progress note she records a normal fundoscopic examination and normal reflexes for a patient, copying them from the previous day's note, although she did not perform those examinations today. Which of the following best describes what she has done?

options.label: A
options.html: An acceptable use of the copy-forward function for stable findings

options.label: B
options.html: A documentation shortcut that is acceptable if the resident cosigns the note

options.label: C
options.html: A minor error that matters only if the findings have changed

options.label: D
options.html: A billing problem that does not affect the clinical record

options.label: E
options.html: Falsification of the medical record

items.explanationHtml:
Recording an examination that was not performed is falsification of the medical record, even if the findings are probably unchanged. Others rely on the note to make decisions, and a false normal finding can hide a new problem. It also misrepresents the work done for billing.

Copy-forward tools are allowed only if every copied element is verified and updated; anything not done today must not be documented as done.

Takeaway: document only what you actually did and found.

whyNot.A: Copy-forward is acceptable only when copied findings are re-verified; these examinations were not done today.
whyNot.B: A cosignature does not make a false entry true; it spreads responsibility for it.
whyNot.C: The record is false whether or not the findings changed, and others cannot know what was really checked.
whyNot.D: A false clinical entry corrupts the medical record itself, beyond any billing consequence.

items.objective: Recognize documenting an examination not performed as falsification.

items.stemHtml: A dermatologist licensed only in State A conducts video visits with established patients. One patient, who lives in State A, joins a visit for a new rash while she is spending several months working in State B. The dermatologist plans to diagnose and prescribe. In general, which of the following determines whether the dermatologist may lawfully provide this care?

options.label: A
options.html: Whether the dermatologist is licensed in State B

options.label: B
options.html: Whether the patient's permanent address is in State A

options.label: C
options.html: Whether the dermatologist's own office is in State A

options.label: D
options.html: Whether the patient's health insurer is based in State A

options.label: E
options.html: Whether the visit is billed as a telehealth service

items.explanationHtml:
Medical practice is regulated by states, and practice is generally considered to occur where the patient is located at the time of care. A physician therefore usually needs a license (or a specific legal exception) in the patient's location state, including for telehealth. Interstate compacts make additional licenses easier to obtain but do not remove the requirement.

Some states allow narrow exceptions (for example, brief continuity follow-up), so the safe general rule is licensure where the patient sits.

Takeaway: for telehealth, licensure follows the patient's physical location.

whyNot.B: Licensure generally follows where the patient is during the visit, not her permanent address.
whyNot.C: The location of the physician's office does not settle which state's law governs the practice of medicine on that patient.
whyNot.D: An insurer's location affects coverage, not the physician's authority to practice medicine.
whyNot.E: Billing codes do not grant a license; practicing without one is misconduct regardless of billing.

items.objective: Apply the principle that licensure follows the patient's location in telehealth.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with HIV infection, well controlled on antiretroviral therapy, calls a private dental practice for a routine cleaning. When he mentions his diagnosis, the receptionist says the dentist does not treat patients with HIV and offers the number of a public clinic. Which of the following federal laws most directly prohibits this refusal?

options.label: A
options.html: Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act

options.label: B
options.html: Americans with Disabilities Act

options.label: C
options.html: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

options.label: D
options.html: Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act

options.label: E
options.html: Patient Self-Determination Act

items.explanationHtml:
HIV infection is a disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act, and private health care offices are places of public accommodation. Refusing to treat a person, or referring them elsewhere for routine care, because of HIV status is unlawful discrimination. Standard precautions protect clinicians; HIV status is not a reason to refuse care that the practice provides to others.

A referral is appropriate only when the needed care is beyond the clinician's expertise, not as a way to avoid a patient.

Takeaway: refusing a patient because of HIV violates the ADA.

whyNot.A: GINA forbids genetic discrimination by health insurers and employers; HIV infection is not genetic information.
whyNot.C: HIPAA protects privacy of health information; it does not address refusal of care.
whyNot.D: EMTALA concerns emergency department screening and stabilization, not routine dental care.
whyNot.E: The Patient Self-Determination Act concerns advance-directive information on admission.

items.objective: Recognize that refusing patients with HIV is prohibited by the ADA.

items.stemHtml: A family physician has a sincere religious objection to prescribing hormonal contraception. A 22-year-old new patient asks to start an oral contraceptive. Which of the following best describes the physician's ethical obligations in this situation?

options.label: A
options.html: He must prescribe the contraceptive because objections are not allowed in primary care

options.label: B
options.html: He may decline and has no further obligation once he has declined

options.label: C
options.html: He may decline but should first counsel her on the moral reasons to reconsider

options.label: D
options.html: He may decline but must inform her and arrange a timely referral without obstructing access

options.label: E
options.html: He may decline only if he first obtains approval from the hospital ethics committee

items.explanationHtml:
Ethical guidance allows physicians to decline to provide specific legal services that conflict with deeply held beliefs (conscientious objection). The freedom carries duties: tell patients in advance where possible, give accurate information about options, refer or transfer care in time for the service to remain available, never obstruct or shame, and give emergency care when no one else can.

Objection applies to a service, not to the patient: he continues as her physician for other care.

Takeaway: object, inform, refer promptly, do not obstruct.

whyNot.A: Physicians may decline specific services on grounds of conscience; the duty is to protect access, not necessarily to provide the service personally.
whyNot.B: Declining without information or referral leaves her without access, which violates the limits of conscientious objection.
whyNot.C: Moralizing to persuade the patient is coercive and disrespects her autonomy.
whyNot.E: No committee approval is needed for an individual physician's objection to an outpatient prescription.

items.objective: Describe the obligations attached to conscientious objection.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with heart failure has missed two payments to her cardiologist's practice. The cardiologist's office calls to say he will no longer see her, effective immediately, and cancels her follow-up visit the following week. She has no other cardiologist and her diuretic dose was changed 3 days ago. Which of the following best describes the cardiologist's conduct?

options.label: A
options.html: Abandonment

options.label: B
options.html: Battery

options.label: C
options.html: Conscientious objection

options.label: D
options.html: Fee splitting

options.label: E
options.html: Breach of confidentiality

items.explanationHtml:
Abandonment is the unilateral ending of a physician–patient relationship, without reasonable notice and a chance to find another physician, while the patient still needs care. Ending care immediately for a patient with active heart failure just after a dose change is abandonment.

Unpaid bills can be a valid reason to end a relationship, but only with proper process: written notice, a reasonable interval with continued care, help finding a new physician and transfer of records.

Takeaway: a physician may end the relationship, but not by leaving a patient without care.

whyNot.B: Battery is touching without consent; no procedure was performed.
whyNot.C: Conscientious objection concerns declining a specific service on moral grounds, not ending care over unpaid bills.
whyNot.D: Fee splitting is sharing fees for referrals.
whyNot.E: No information about the patient was disclosed to anyone.

items.objective: Define patient abandonment.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man has repeatedly shouted at and threatened the front-desk staff of a primary care practice despite a written warning. The physician decides to end the professional relationship. The patient takes insulin and has no other physician. Which of the following steps is required to end the relationship properly?

options.label: A
options.html: Obtain the patient's written agreement to the termination

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain a court order before ending the relationship

options.label: C
options.html: Give written notice and provide needed care for a reasonable interval

options.label: D
options.html: Stop all care at once, because the threats override the duty to treat

options.label: E
options.html: Choose a new physician for him and confirm that he attends a first visit

items.explanationHtml:
A physician may end a relationship for good reason, such as threats to staff. To avoid abandonment, the physician gives written notice with an end date, continues to provide needed and emergency care (including refills such as insulin) for a reasonable interval, helps the patient find another physician, and transfers records when authorized.

The patient's agreement is not required, and the physician need not personally secure the next appointment.

Takeaway: notice, interim care, help finding a new physician, records transfer.

whyNot.A: Either party may end the relationship; the patient's consent to termination is not required.
whyNot.B: No court involvement is needed to end an outpatient physician–patient relationship.
whyNot.D: Immediate termination of a patient who needs insulin, without interim care, is abandonment; safety measures can be used instead.
whyNot.E: The physician should help him find a new physician but is not required to choose one or ensure attendance.

items.objective: List the steps for properly ending a physician–patient relationship.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman whose sister has a pathogenic BRCA1 variant is referred for genetic counseling. She works for a large company and is worried that a positive test could be used against her. Under the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, which of the following is protected?

options.label: A
options.html: A life insurer may not consider the result when pricing a new policy

options.label: B
options.html: A disability insurer may not ask whether she has had genetic testing

options.label: C
options.html: A long-term care insurer may not deny coverage based on the result

options.label: D
options.html: Her physician may not record the result in her medical record

options.label: E
options.html: Her health insurer may not use the result to set premiums or eligibility

items.explanationHtml:
The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) prohibits health insurers from using genetic information to determine eligibility or premiums and prohibits employers with 15 or more employees from using it in hiring, firing, pay or promotion. It does not cover life, disability or long-term care insurance.

Genetic counselors explain these limits before testing so patients can make informed choices.

Takeaway: GINA protects health insurance and employment, not life, disability or long-term care insurance.

whyNot.A: Life insurance is outside GINA, so a life insurer may consider genetic results where state law allows.
whyNot.B: Disability insurance is outside GINA's protections.
whyNot.C: Long-term care insurance is outside GINA's protections.
whyNot.D: GINA does not restrict documentation in the medical record; results guide her care and are protected by privacy law.

items.objective: State what GINA does and does not protect.

items.stemHtml: A primary care physician refers a 57-year-old man with a new lung mass to a thoracic surgeon at another health system. Her office sends the surgeon the full chart, including the imaging, pathology and the past 5 years of notes. The patient has not signed an authorization for this disclosure. Which of the following best describes this disclosure under the HIPAA Privacy Rule?

options.label: A
options.html: It is prohibited until the patient signs a written authorization

options.label: B
options.html: It is permitted for treatment and is not subject to the minimum-necessary standard

options.label: C
options.html: It is permitted but must be limited to the minimum information necessary

options.label: D
options.html: It is permitted only if the surgeon belongs to the same health system

options.label: E
options.html: It is permitted only if the patient is told after the records are sent

items.explanationHtml:
The HIPAA Privacy Rule permits a covered entity to disclose protected health information to another health care provider for treatment without the patient's written authorization. The minimum-necessary standard does not apply to disclosures to a provider for treatment, because clinicians need the full picture to care for the patient.

Other permitted uses without authorization include payment and health care operations (to which minimum necessary does apply) and specific public-interest purposes.

Takeaway: provider-to-provider sharing for treatment needs no authorization and is exempt from minimum necessary.

whyNot.A: Treatment disclosures between providers do not require a written authorization.
whyNot.C: Minimum necessary applies to payment and operations, but disclosures to a provider for treatment are exempt.
whyNot.D: The permission for treatment disclosures applies across health systems, not only within one.
whyNot.E: No after-the-fact notice is required for treatment disclosures; they are routine permitted uses.

items.objective: Apply the HIPAA treatment exception and the minimum-necessary exemption to referrals.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman has just been told by her surgeon that she needs a total thyroidectomy for a suspicious nodule. She says, "Please don't take this the wrong way, but I'd like another surgeon to look at this before I decide." Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the surgeon?

options.label: A
options.html: "My recommendation is standard, so a second opinion would only delay your care."

options.label: B
options.html: "If you see someone else, I'll need to transfer your care to that surgeon."

options.label: C
options.html: "You can, but your insurance probably won't pay for that visit."

options.label: D
options.html: "That's a reasonable step. I'll send your records and images to whoever you choose."

options.label: E
options.html: "Let's schedule the surgery now, and you can cancel it if the other surgeon disagrees."

items.explanationHtml:
Seeking a second opinion before major treatment is reasonable and respects patient autonomy. The physician should support it without defensiveness and help by sending records, imaging and pathology. A thyroid nodule workup usually allows time for this.

Patients who feel supported are more likely to trust and return to the original physician.

Takeaway: support second opinions and make them easy.

whyNot.A: Discouraging a second opinion is paternalistic and, for elective surgery, the short delay is usually safe.
whyNot.B: Threatening to end the relationship pressures the patient and is unprofessional.
whyNot.C: Speculating about coverage discourages her and is not the surgeon's role; she can check her plan.
whyNot.E: Booking surgery before she has decided pressures her and undermines the purpose of a second opinion.

items.objective: Respond supportively to a patient's request for a second opinion.

items.stemHtml: A newly hired internist is told by the practice manager that a cardiology group pays the practice a fixed amount for every patient it refers for an outpatient cardiology consultation. The manager says the payment is called a "coordination fee" and requires no additional work. Which of the following best describes this arrangement?

options.label: A
options.html: Acceptable care coordination, because the referrals are clinically indicated

options.label: B
options.html: Acceptable if each patient is told about the payment in advance

options.label: C
options.html: Acceptable if the payment is reported to the Open Payments database

options.label: D
options.html: Acceptable if the fee is less than the cost of a consultation

options.label: E
options.html: Unethical fee splitting that may also violate federal law

items.explanationHtml:
Paying or receiving money for referrals is fee splitting. It is unethical because it puts money into the decision about where to send a patient. When the patients are covered by federal health care programs, payments to induce referrals can also violate the Anti-Kickback Statute.

Telling patients, reporting the payment or keeping it small does not make a payment for referrals acceptable. Referrals must rest on the patient's needs alone.

Takeaway: no payment for referrals, however it is labeled.

whyNot.A: Clinical indication does not justify being paid for the referral; the payment itself is the problem.
whyNot.B: Disclosure does not cure a payment tied to referrals.
whyNot.C: Open Payments covers manufacturer payments and its reporting would not make a referral fee legitimate.
whyNot.D: The size of the payment does not matter; any payment for referrals is improper.

items.objective: Recognize fee splitting as an improper payment for referrals.

items.stemHtml: A residency program replaces a lecture listing the health beliefs of various ethnic groups with a workshop that asks residents to reflect on their own assumptions, to approach each patient as the expert on their own life and values, and to recognize the power imbalance between physician and patient as a lifelong practice. Which of the following concepts does the new workshop best represent?

options.label: A
options.html: Acculturation

options.label: B
options.html: Cultural relativism

options.label: C
options.html: Cultural humility

options.label: D
options.html: Ethnocentrism

options.label: E
options.html: Health literacy

items.explanationHtml:
Cultural humility is a lifelong commitment to self-reflection and self-critique, to learning from each patient, and to redressing power imbalances in the clinical relationship. It replaces the idea that one can become "competent" in a culture by memorizing group traits, an approach that risks stereotyping.

Takeaway: cultural humility = self-reflection, curiosity about each patient, attention to power.

whyNot.A: Acculturation is the process by which a person adopts features of another culture, not a stance for clinicians.
whyNot.B: Cultural relativism holds that practices should be judged only within their own culture; it does not describe reflective clinical practice.
whyNot.D: Ethnocentrism is judging others by the standards of one's own culture, the opposite of the workshop's aim.
whyNot.E: Health literacy is the ability to obtain, understand and use health information.

items.objective: Define cultural humility.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes seems reluctant to start medication. The physician asks him what he thinks caused his blood sugar to go up, what he expects treatment to do, and what worries him about it. Which of the following is the physician mainly trying to elicit?

options.label: A
options.html: The patient's explanatory model of illness

options.label: B
options.html: The patient's level of health literacy

options.label: C
options.html: The patient's decision-making capacity

options.label: D
options.html: The patient's readiness to sign informed consent

options.label: E
options.html: The patient's stage of acculturation

items.explanationHtml:
An explanatory model is the patient's own understanding of an illness: what it is, what caused it, why now, how serious it is, what treatment should do and what they fear. Open questions like these reveal mismatches between the patient's model and the physician's, which often explain reluctance, and allow a negotiated plan.

Takeaway: "What do you think caused it, and what worries you?" elicits the explanatory model.

whyNot.B: Health literacy is assessed by checking understanding of information (for example, teach-back), not by asking about causes and expectations.
whyNot.C: Capacity is assessed when a decision must be made, by testing understanding, appreciation, reasoning and choice.
whyNot.D: Consent comes after information about a specific treatment; these questions explore beliefs first.
whyNot.E: Acculturation describes adoption of another culture, and these questions do not measure it.

items.objective: Recognize questions that elicit a patient's explanatory model.

items.stemHtml: A nephrology department reviews why some Black patients reached kidney failure before being referred for transplant evaluation. For years, the laboratory had reported estimated glomerular filtration rate using an equation that included a race coefficient. Which of the following best describes the effect of that coefficient for Black patients?

options.label: A
options.html: It lowered the estimated GFR at a given creatinine, prompting earlier referral

options.label: B
options.html: It changed the measured serum creatinine rather than the estimated GFR

options.label: C
options.html: It had no effect on eGFR but changed the stage definitions of chronic kidney disease

options.label: D
options.html: It raised the estimated GFR at a given creatinine, which could delay diagnosis and referral

options.label: E
options.html: It applied only to patients receiving dialysis

items.explanationHtml:
Earlier creatinine-based eGFR equations multiplied the result by a coefficient greater than 1 for patients identified as Black, so the same creatinine produced a higher eGFR. Kidney disease could therefore look milder, delaying diagnosis, nephrology referral and accrual of waiting time for transplant. In 2021, race-free equations were recommended to replace it.

The coefficient illustrates structural racism in a clinical tool: harm through an embedded rule rather than an individual's attitude.

Takeaway: the old race coefficient inflated eGFR in Black patients and could delay care.

whyNot.A: The coefficient raised, not lowered, the estimate, which made disease look milder.
whyNot.B: Measured creatinine was unchanged; the coefficient altered only the calculated estimate.
whyNot.C: Stage definitions did not change; the estimate itself was shifted upward.
whyNot.E: The coefficient was applied to everyone identified as Black who had an eGFR reported, not only to dialysis patients.

items.objective: Explain how race-based eGFR adjustment illustrates structural racism in clinical algorithms.

items.stemHtml: A hospital quality team compares paired pulse-oximetry readings and arterial blood gas measurements. Among patients with darker skin pigmentation, they find more cases in which the arterial oxygen saturation was below 88% while the simultaneous pulse oximeter read 92% or higher. Which of the following best describes this finding?

options.label: A
options.html: Pulse oximeters underestimate arterial saturation in darker skin

options.label: B
options.html: Pulse oximeters can overestimate arterial saturation in darker skin

options.label: C
options.html: Arterial blood gas analyzers are inaccurate in darker skin

options.label: D
options.html: The difference reflects a higher rate of carbon monoxide exposure

options.label: E
options.html: The difference is explained by random measurement error alone

items.explanationHtml:
Studies comparing pulse oximetry with arterial blood gases have found that oximeters can overestimate arterial oxygen saturation in people with darker skin pigmentation, so true hypoxemia is missed more often (occult hypoxemia). Device calibration on mostly lighter-skinned volunteers is one explanation. Missed hypoxemia can delay oxygen, treatment and eligibility for therapies.

This is a device-level, structural source of disparity; clinicians should check arterial blood gases when oximetry and the clinical picture disagree.

Takeaway: pulse oximetry can read falsely high in darker skin.

whyNot.A: The readings were higher than the arterial values, which is overestimation, not underestimation.
whyNot.C: Arterial blood gas analysis measures blood directly and is unaffected by skin pigmentation.
whyNot.D: Carbon monoxide falsely raises oximetry in anyone exposed; it does not explain a pattern by skin pigmentation.
whyNot.E: A consistent pattern in one group is a systematic bias, not random error.

items.objective: Recognize pulse-oximetry bias as a source of occult hypoxemia.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old Deaf woman who communicates in American Sign Language makes an appointment at a private primary care practice to discuss a new diagnosis of breast cancer. The office manager suggests that she bring her teenage son to interpret or communicate by writing notes. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, which of the following is the practice's obligation?

options.label: A
options.html: Allow her to bring her son if she agrees

options.label: B
options.html: Use written notes, which are always sufficient

options.label: C
options.html: Provide an interpreter only if she pays the cost

options.label: D
options.html: Refer her to a practice that has signing staff

options.label: E
options.html: Provide a qualified sign language interpreter at no charge to her

items.explanationHtml:
The Americans with Disabilities Act requires health care practices to ensure effective communication with patients who are Deaf or hard of hearing by providing appropriate auxiliary aids, and the practice may not charge the patient for them. For a complex, emotional discussion like a cancer diagnosis, a qualified sign language interpreter (in person or by video) is generally needed. Family members, especially children, should not be relied on except in emergencies.

Takeaway: provide a qualified interpreter, at the practice's cost, for Deaf patients.

whyNot.A: Relying on a minor child to interpret a cancer diagnosis is inappropriate and does not meet the duty to ensure effective communication.
whyNot.B: Written notes may work for simple exchanges but are not effective communication for a complex discussion.
whyNot.C: The ADA forbids charging the patient for auxiliary aids.
whyNot.D: Referring her away to avoid providing an interpreter is discrimination.

items.objective: State ADA requirements for communication with Deaf patients.

items.stemHtml: A health system wants its electronic health record to capture gender identity accurately so that screening reminders and communication fit each patient. Which of the following approaches is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: A single field with the options male or female

options.label: B
options.html: A single field completed by the clerk from the patient's appearance

options.label: C
options.html: Two questions: current gender identity and sex assigned at birth

options.label: D
options.html: A field for gender identity completed only for patients who appear transgender

options.label: E
options.html: Copying the sex recorded on the patient's insurance card

items.explanationHtml:
The recommended two-step approach asks every patient about current gender identity and sex assigned at birth (with options beyond male and female), alongside the name and pronouns the patient uses. It identifies transgender and gender-diverse patients without assumptions and lets screening follow anatomy, such as cervical screening for anyone with a cervix.

Takeaway: ask everyone two questions; never infer gender identity from appearance or documents.

whyNot.A: A binary single field cannot capture transgender or nonbinary identities or the anatomy needed for screening.
whyNot.B: Appearance does not reveal identity; guessing is inaccurate and disrespectful.
whyNot.D: Asking only some patients relies on assumptions; the questions should be asked of everyone.
whyNot.E: Insurance documents may not match a patient's identity or anatomy.

items.objective: Describe the two-step method for recording gender identity.

items.stemHtml: An emergency department reviews 2 years of visits for isolated long-bone fractures. Black patients received opioid analgesia less often than White patients. The gap persisted after adjustment for documented pain score, insurance type, age, fracture site and time of arrival. Clinicians, when surveyed, uniformly endorse treating pain equally. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the remaining difference?

options.label: A
options.html: Implicit bias in clinicians' assessment of pain

options.label: B
options.html: Confounding by insurance type

options.label: C
options.html: Differences in documented pain severity

options.label: D
options.html: Explicit prejudice openly stated by clinicians

options.label: E
options.html: Regression to the mean

items.explanationHtml:
Implicit bias is an automatic, unconscious association that affects judgment without intent, and it can coexist with sincere egalitarian beliefs. A disparity that persists after adjustment for pain scores, insurance and clinical factors, among clinicians who endorse equal treatment, points to implicit bias (and to system factors that allow it to act).

The response is systemic: standardized pain protocols, reassessment and audit with feedback.

Takeaway: an adjusted disparity among well-meaning clinicians suggests implicit bias.

whyNot.B: The analysis adjusted for insurance type, so it cannot explain the residual gap.
whyNot.C: Pain scores were also adjusted for, so documented severity does not explain the gap.
whyNot.D: Clinicians endorsed equal treatment; explicit prejudice is consciously held and openly stated, which is not described.
whyNot.E: Regression to the mean affects repeated measures of extreme values, not group differences in treatment.

items.objective: Recognize implicit bias as an explanation for persistent adjusted disparities in pain treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis tells her physician that she also sees a traditional healer in her community, who leads prayers and massages her knee with a warm oil. She finds it comforting and asks whether she should stop. She takes no other remedies, and the oil causes no skin irritation. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "You should stop, because only proven treatments belong in your care."

options.label: B
options.html: "That's fine, but I'd rather not hear about it during our visits."

options.label: C
options.html: "Let's have the healer speak with me before you continue."

options.label: D
options.html: "If it helps you, I'm glad. Let's keep using it alongside the plan we make here."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll note it, but I can't treat you unless you choose one approach."

items.explanationHtml:
Traditional healing practices that are not harmful should be respected and can run alongside medical care. Supporting them builds trust, respects the patient's values and makes it more likely she will share other practices in future, including any that might interact with treatment.

If a practice carried real risk (a drug interaction, delaying time-sensitive treatment), the physician would discuss it openly and negotiate, without ridicule.

Takeaway: accept harmless traditional practices and integrate them with care.

whyNot.A: Dismissing a harmless, comforting practice damages trust and has no clinical benefit.
whyNot.B: Discouraging discussion makes it less likely she will mention future remedies that could matter.
whyNot.C: Requiring the healer's involvement before she continues places a needless barrier on a harmless practice.
whyNot.E: Forcing a choice between approaches is coercive and unnecessary when the practice is safe.

items.objective: Respond respectfully to a patient's harmless traditional healing practice.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is recovering on the orthopedic ward 2 days after an elective total hip arthroplasty. At 7:30 AM a nurse finds her sweaty and confused. Fingerstick glucose is 38 mg/dL (fasting reference range, 70–99 mg/dL). She is given intravenous dextrose and within 20 minutes is alert and oriented, with a glucose of 142 mg/dL. Review shows that an order for 5 units of insulin lispro was transcribed as 50 units, and that dose was given at 6:00 AM. When the resident returns, the patient asks what happened to her this morning. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Low blood sugar is common after surgery, and we have treated it. You're safe now."

options.label: B
options.html: "You were given far more insulin than was ordered, and that caused the low sugar. I'm very sorry."

options.label: C
options.html: "We're reviewing the morning's events, and the risk manager will speak with you afterward."

options.label: D
options.html: "A nurse gave you the wrong insulin dose, but fortunately there was no real harm done."

options.label: E
options.html: "I can't go into details until the hospital decides who was responsible for this."

items.explanationHtml:
An error that reaches the patient should be disclosed promptly, by the responsible physician, in plain language: what happened, its effects, what is being done, and a sincere apology. The patient is now alert, stable and asking directly, so this is the right moment. The conversation should continue with what will be monitored and how the hospital will find out why the error occurred.

Honest disclosure is an ethical duty and is associated with greater trust and fewer, faster-resolved claims. It is not delayed until an investigation ends, handed to risk management, or framed to blame a colleague.

Takeaway: tell the patient what went wrong, how it affected her, and that you are sorry, as soon as she is stable.

whyNot.A: Describing the episode as a common postoperative event conceals the error and is dishonest.
whyNot.C: Deferring disclosure to risk management after a review delays information the patient has a right to now.
whyNot.D: Blaming an individual before the review is premature, and declaring no harm minimizes a dangerous event.
whyNot.E: Withholding the facts until fault is assigned is evasive; disclosure does not wait for the root cause analysis.

items.objective: Disclose a medication error promptly and honestly to the patient.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman had a hypoglycemic episode on the orthopedic ward after a transcription error led to her receiving 50 units instead of 5 units of insulin lispro. The error was disclosed to her the same morning. She had no seizure, no fall and no further hypoglycemia, and she was discharged on the originally planned day with no lasting effects. Two weeks later she tells her surgeon that she is thinking about suing. If she brought a negligence claim, which of the following would she have the most difficulty establishing?

options.label: A
options.html: That the hospital owed her a duty of care

options.label: B
options.html: That giving 50 units fell below the standard of care

options.label: C
options.html: That the overdose caused her hypoglycemia

options.label: D
options.html: That she suffered a compensable injury

options.label: E
options.html: That the hospital is liable for its employees' acts

items.explanationHtml:
Negligence requires duty, breach, causation and damages. Here, a duty clearly existed (an inpatient), giving ten times the ordered dose is a breach, and the overdose plainly caused the hypoglycemia. But she recovered within minutes, had no further harm, no extra hospital days and no lasting effects, so damages are minimal at most.

An error with no lasting injury usually fails on damages. That does not remove the ethical duty to disclose and to fix the system that allowed the error.
