Takeaway: a clear error that causes no lasting harm is the classic weak link at damages.

whyNot.A: As a hospital inpatient she was clearly owed a duty of care.
whyNot.B: A tenfold dose from a transcription error is plainly below the standard of care.
whyNot.C: The timing and the dose make it clear that the overdose caused the hypoglycemia.
whyNot.E: Hospitals are generally vicariously liable for employees acting within their duties.

items.objective: Identify the negligence element that fails when an error causes no lasting harm.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman experienced hypoglycemia on an orthopedic ward after an insulin transcription error that was disclosed to her the same day. Three weeks after discharge, the hospital's medical records office receives a request signed by the patient, sent through her attorney, for a complete copy of her hospital record. The resident who cared for her notices that his progress note from that morning does not mention the transcription error. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Release the record as it stands through the records office and notify risk management

options.label: B
options.html: Add the error to the original progress note using that morning's date and time

options.label: C
options.html: Decline the request until the hospital's internal review of the event is complete

options.label: D
options.html: Release only the medication administration record related to the event

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the patient to withdraw her attorney's involvement before records are released

items.explanationHtml:
Patients have a right of access to their records, and a signed request is honored through the usual records process; the possibility of a lawsuit does not change that. Risk management should be told so the hospital can respond appropriately.

The record must never be altered or back-dated, least of all after a claim is threatened; doing so destroys credibility and can turn a defensible case into an indefensible one. Incomplete notes are not fixed by rewriting history.

Takeaway: release the record unaltered, and loop in risk management.

whyNot.B: Back-dating an entry falsifies the record, and changes made after a claim is threatened look like tampering.
whyNot.C: An internal review is no reason to deny the patient access to her own record.
whyNot.D: She asked for a complete copy; withholding parts of the record without a valid legal basis is improper.
whyNot.E: Patients may involve attorneys, and access to records cannot be made conditional on dropping one.

items.objective: Handle a records request after an adverse event without altering the record.

items.stemHtml: Using the results table, what is the rate ratio of new claims per patient-day in the period after the program compared with the period before it (rounded to two decimal places)?
items.explanationHtml:
Rates must use the person-time denominators, because the number of patient-days differed between periods.

  • Before: 120 ÷ 1,600,000 = 7.5 per 100,000 patient-days
  • After: 84 ÷ 1,750,000 = 4.8 per 100,000 patient-days
  • Rate ratio (after ÷ before) = 4.8 ÷ 7.5 = 0.64

The claim rate after the program was 64% of the earlier rate, a 36% relative reduction.

Takeaway: compare rates, not counts, when the denominators differ.

whyNot.A: 0.36 is the relative reduction (1 − 0.64), not the rate ratio.
whyNot.C: 0.70 divides the raw claim counts (84 ÷ 120) and ignores the larger number of patient-days after the program.
whyNot.D: 1.43 is the inverse of the raw count ratio (120 ÷ 84), which both ignores the denominators and compares the periods backward.
whyNot.E: 1.56 is the before-to-after rate ratio (7.5 ÷ 4.8), the comparison inverted.

items.objective: Calculate a rate ratio using person-time denominators.

items.stemHtml: Which of the following most weakens the claim that the program itself caused the decline in claims?

options.label: A
options.html: Lead-time bias

options.label: B
options.html: Recall bias among claimants

options.label: C
options.html: Changes over time unrelated to the program

options.label: D
options.html: Loss to follow-up of enrolled patients

options.label: E
options.html: Observer bias in measuring patient-days

items.explanationHtml:
This is an uncontrolled before–after comparison. Anything else that changed between the two periods (state tort law, insurer practices, local attorney behavior, a general trend in claims nationwide, other safety programs) could explain the drop. Without concurrent control hospitals or an interrupted time series showing a break at the start of the program, secular trends (history) cannot be separated from the program's effect.

Takeaway: before–after designs without controls are vulnerable to secular trends.

whyNot.A: Lead-time bias concerns earlier diagnosis making survival look longer, which is not the issue in counting claims.
whyNot.B: Claims were counted from administrative records, not from claimants' memories.
whyNot.D: The outcome was counted across all hospital activity, not in a cohort of enrolled patients who could be lost.
whyNot.E: Patient-days are an administrative count, so observer judgment does not affect them.

items.objective: Identify secular trends as the main threat to validity in an uncontrolled before–after study.

items.stemHtml: A hospitalist in this system asks what the study means for how she should handle errors with her own patients. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the study?

options.label: A
options.html: The program caused a 36% reduction in claims in this system

options.label: B
options.html: Disclosing errors with an apology increases the number of claims

options.label: C
options.html: Compensation should be withheld until a patient files a claim

options.label: D
options.html: The results apply equally to every hospital in the United States

options.label: E
options.html: Prompt disclosure with apology was not followed by more claims here

items.explanationHtml:
The data show that after the system required disclosure and apology, claims did not rise; the rate fell. The design cannot prove the program caused the fall, and one fictional regional system may not represent all hospitals. The safe conclusion is that honest disclosure was not followed by an increase in claims, which removes a common reason clinicians give for avoiding it. Disclosure remains an ethical duty regardless of claims.

Takeaway: state what the design supports: an association, not proof of cause.

whyNot.A: A causal claim overreaches an uncontrolled before–after design.
whyNot.B: Claims fell after disclosure became routine, the opposite of this statement.
whyNot.C: The program offered compensation before claims; nothing in the study supports withholding it.
whyNot.D: Four hospitals in one region cannot be assumed to represent all US hospitals.

items.objective: Draw a conclusion matched to the strength of a before–after study design.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man who smoked for 30 years has a chest CT for a persistent cough. It shows a 14-mm spiculated nodule in the right upper lobe. His primary care physician finds that a CT 14 months ago showed the same nodule at 7 mm, and the radiology report recommended a follow-up CT in 3 months. Her office never arranged it. She has the new result in hand when she meets the patient. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement to the patient?

options.label: A
options.html: "The nodule is larger now, and we need a biopsy. Let's focus on next steps."

options.label: B
options.html: "The radiologist should have called me about this, so the delay wasn't on our end."

options.label: C
options.html: "Last year a follow-up scan was recommended, and we didn't arrange it. I'm sorry."

options.label: D
options.html: "Nodules usually grow slowly, so the timing probably made no difference to you."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll explain what happened once the clinic's review decides who was at fault."

items.explanationHtml:
A missed follow-up that may have delayed diagnosis is an error that reached the patient. The physician should disclose it honestly, take responsibility for her office's role, apologize, and then move quickly to the next diagnostic steps and explain how the office will prevent a repeat (a tracking system for recommended follow-up). She should also report the event through the practice's safety system.

Focusing only on the plan, speculating that the delay did not matter, or shifting blame are the usual wrong answers.

Takeaway: disclose a missed follow-up, apologize, and act quickly on the next steps.

whyNot.A: Moving straight to the biopsy without mentioning the missed follow-up withholds information the patient needs.
whyNot.B: Blaming the radiologist is inaccurate (the report gave the recommendation) and evades responsibility.
whyNot.D: Speculating that the delay did not matter is premature reassurance and minimizes the error.
whyNot.E: Postponing disclosure until fault is assigned delays information he has a right to now.

items.objective: Disclose a diagnostic delay caused by a missed follow-up.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman at high risk for falls is found on the floor of her hospital room at night. Her bed alarm, ordered on admission, is found switched off. Radiographs show a distal radius fracture. The next morning the attending tells the intern, "Just write that she fell. Don't mention the alarm, and don't bother filing a report." Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the intern?

options.label: A
options.html: Follow the instruction, because the attending is responsible for the record

options.label: B
options.html: Document that the nursing staff caused the fall by switching off the alarm

options.label: C
options.html: Record what happened in a personal notebook rather than in the chart

options.label: D
options.html: Wait to write any note until risk management says what to include

options.label: E
options.html: Document the objective facts in the chart and file a patient safety report

items.explanationHtml:
The medical record must be accurate and objective: when and where she was found, her injuries, the finding that the alarm was off, what was done and what she and her family were told, without assigning blame. Adverse events are reported through the hospital's patient safety (incident) reporting system, which is a quality tool kept separate from the chart. An attending cannot instruct a trainee to omit material facts.

The fall should also be disclosed to the patient and family.

Takeaway: chart the facts without blame, and report the event through the safety system.

whyNot.A: Omitting a material fact at a supervisor's request makes the record misleading; the intern is responsible for what he signs.
whyNot.B: The chart should state facts, not assign blame; the cause will be determined by review.
whyNot.C: Private notes are not part of the record and do not meet the duty to document.
whyNot.D: Documentation of clinical events should be timely; risk management does not dictate the clinical facts.

items.objective: Document an adverse event objectively and report it through the safety system.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 39 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department of a private hospital that has a labor and delivery unit. She has contractions every 3 minutes, and the cervix is 7 cm dilated. The fetal heart rate tracing is reassuring. She has no insurance. A hospital administrator asks whether she can be transferred by ambulance to the county hospital 45 minutes away. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit her to labor and delivery and manage the delivery at this hospital

options.label: B
options.html: Transfer her by ambulance after she signs a financial-responsibility form

options.label: C
options.html: Transfer her once the county hospital agrees to accept her

options.label: D
options.html: Discharge her with directions to go to the county hospital

options.label: E
options.html: Delay the decision until her Medicaid eligibility is confirmed

items.explanationHtml:
Under EMTALA, a woman having contractions is considered to have an emergency medical condition until she has delivered (including the placenta), unless an appropriate transfer is made. A transfer of an unstabilized patient is allowed only if she requests it in writing after being informed, or a physician certifies that the medical benefits of transfer outweigh the risks. Neither applies: she is in active labor at 7 cm in a hospital that can deliver her, and the reason for the transfer is financial.

Takeaway: a laboring woman is stabilized by delivery; financial transfer is never allowed.

whyNot.B: A financial form does not justify transfer, and asking about payment must not delay care.
whyNot.C: Acceptance by the receiving hospital is necessary but not sufficient; there is no medical benefit to justify moving a woman in active labor.
whyNot.D: Discharging a woman in active labor is an EMTALA violation and dangerous.
whyNot.E: Delaying care to confirm coverage violates EMTALA's rule that payment questions must not delay screening or stabilization.

items.objective: Apply EMTALA to a woman in active labor.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a small rural hospital after falling from a ladder. He briefly lost consciousness. Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13. Pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 150/86 mm Hg. CT of the head shows an acute epidural hematoma with mild midline shift. The hospital has no neurosurgeon. The nearest trauma center, 50 minutes away by ground, has a neurosurgeon available. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit him to the intensive care unit for hourly neurologic checks

options.label: B
options.html: Have his wife drive him directly to the trauma center

options.label: C
options.html: Hold the transfer until the trauma center confirms his insurance

options.label: D
options.html: Transfer him once the trauma center accepts, with records and critical care transport

options.label: E
options.html: Keep him in the emergency department until a neurosurgeon can travel here

items.explanationHtml:
An epidural hematoma with midline shift needs urgent neurosurgical evacuation, which this hospital cannot provide. Under EMTALA, the hospital stabilizes within its capability and arranges an appropriate transfer: the receiving hospital accepts, copies of records and imaging go with the patient, transport has qualified personnel and equipment, and the transferring physician certifies that the benefits outweigh the risks. A specialized hospital with capacity may not refuse.

Takeaway: when the needed service is not available, stabilize and make an appropriate transfer.

whyNot.A: Observation without a neurosurgeon delays definitive treatment of a lesion that can deteriorate rapidly.
whyNot.B: A private car lacks monitoring and personnel; an unstable patient must travel with appropriate medical transport.
whyNot.C: Holding a transfer for insurance verification violates EMTALA and delays urgent care.
whyNot.E: Waiting for a surgeon to travel delays treatment when the trauma center can treat him sooner.

items.objective: Arrange an EMTALA-compliant transfer for a condition beyond the hospital's capability.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old internist is a passenger on a domestic commercial flight. A flight attendant asks whether there is a doctor on board because a 70-year-old passenger has become pale and sweaty. The internist is not licensed in the state where the airline is based and worries about being sued if something goes wrong. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Stay seated, because she is not licensed in the airline's home state

options.label: B
options.html: Identify herself, assess the passenger, and coordinate with the crew and ground support

options.label: C
options.html: Help only after the passenger signs a written waiver of liability

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the crew to divert the flight before she examines the passenger

options.label: E
options.html: Help only if the airline agrees to pay her for the service

items.explanationHtml:
Physicians are encouraged to help in an in-flight emergency within their competence. A federal law (the Aviation Medical Assistance Act) protects individuals who assist in good faith on flights of US airlines from liability except for gross negligence or wilful misconduct, and state licensure is not a barrier. The physician should identify herself, assess the passenger, use the onboard kit, and work with the crew, who can reach the airline's ground-based medical consultants; diversion is the captain's decision, informed by her assessment.

Takeaway: in-flight, help in good faith, within your skills, and coordinate with the crew.

whyNot.A: Licensure is not a barrier to good-faith emergency help, and good-faith helpers are protected from ordinary negligence claims.
whyNot.C: Requiring a waiver delays care and is not needed for liability protection.
whyNot.D: Diversion should be guided by an assessment, not requested before the passenger is examined.
whyNot.E: Bargaining for payment before helping delays care for a passenger who needs assessment now.

items.objective: Respond appropriately to an in-flight medical emergency, recognizing good-faith liability protection.

items.stemHtml: A general surgeon performed an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy on a 33-year-old man 2 days ago. Before the operation, she explained the risks, including possible conversion to an open operation, and the patient signed the consent form. While reviewing the chart before discharge, she notices that her preoperative note does not mention the discussion of conversion. The patient is doing well. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Edit the original preoperative note so that it includes the discussion

options.label: B
options.html: Write a new note dated on the day of the original discussion

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the patient to sign a new consent form describing the discussion

options.label: D
options.html: Leave the record as it is, because the patient is doing well

options.label: E
options.html: Write an addendum, dated and timed today, describing the earlier discussion

items.explanationHtml:
Omissions are corrected with a late entry or addendum that carries the current date and time, refers to the earlier event and states what happened. The original note stays as written. Editing or back-dating an entry is falsification, even when the added facts are true.

Writing the addendum now, while memory is fresh and before any dispute, keeps the record complete and credible.

Takeaway: correct the chart by dated addendum, never by altering the original.

whyNot.A: Changing an existing note after the fact alters the record and is improper, even if the content is true.
whyNot.B: Dating a new note to an earlier day is back-dating, a form of falsification.
whyNot.C: A new consent form after the operation is meaningless as consent and misrepresents when consent occurred.
whyNot.D: The outcome does not make an incomplete record acceptable; a simple addendum makes it accurate.

items.objective: Correct an omission in the medical record with a properly dated addendum.

items.stemHtml: A fourth-year surgical resident has noticed over 3 months that one attending surgeon closes abdominal incisions before the sponge and instrument counts are reconciled, saying "the count is always fine." Last week a patient needed an abdominal radiograph for a possible retained sponge; none was found. When the resident raised the issue privately, the attending dismissed it. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue reminding the attending privately before each operation

options.label: B
options.html: Report the attending directly to the state medical board

options.label: C
options.html: Report the concern to the department chair or the patient safety office

options.label: D
options.html: Tell the attending's patients that he does not follow safety rules

options.label: E
options.html: Post an anonymous warning in the residents' group chat

items.explanationHtml:
A repeated practice that puts patients at risk, which continues after the colleague has been approached directly, should be reported through institutional channels: the department chair, the chief of surgery, or the patient safety or quality office. Institutions are responsible for oversight and must protect trainees who report in good faith.

The state medical board is appropriate if the institution does not act or the conduct is egregious; it is not the first step for an unsafe practice inside a hospital with working oversight.

Takeaway: after a direct conversation fails, report unsafe practice to institutional leadership or the safety office.

whyNot.A: Repeating private reminders that have already failed leaves patients at continued risk.
whyNot.B: The board is the next step if the institution fails to act; institutional channels come first here.
whyNot.D: Telling patients is unprofessional and does not fix the practice; the institution must address it.
whyNot.E: Informal anonymous posts spread rumor without starting any process that protects patients.

items.objective: Report a colleague's unsafe practice through institutional channels.

items.stemHtml: A third-year medical student spends the morning with an intern on the general medicine service. That afternoon she reads the intern's progress note for a 72-year-old man admitted with pneumonia. It documents a complete neurologic examination with normal findings, copied from the previous day's note, although the student knows the patient was not examined today. The patient is clinically stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the student?

options.label: A
options.html: Say nothing, because students should not question an intern's notes

options.label: B
options.html: Correct the intern's note herself in the electronic record

options.label: C
options.html: Report the intern directly to the state medical board

options.label: D
options.html: Tell the intern privately that the examination was not done and ask that it be corrected

options.label: E
options.html: Tell the patient that part of his chart is not accurate

items.explanationHtml:
Documenting an examination that was not performed makes the record false, and others may rely on it. A proportionate first step for a single episode is to raise it directly and privately with the person who wrote it and ask that the note be corrected (by addendum or by actually doing and recording the examination). If the intern refuses, or the pattern repeats, the student should take it to the resident or attending.

Students have a professional duty to speak up about patient safety and honesty; good programs protect them when they do.

Takeaway: for a first, correctable lapse, speak to the person directly and ask that it be fixed; escalate if it is not.

whyNot.A: Staying silent leaves a false record in place; students share the duty of honesty.
whyNot.B: A student may not alter another clinician's note; changes must come from the author.
whyNot.C: Going to the board skips proportionate first steps for a single, correctable documentation lapse.
whyNot.E: Telling the patient bypasses the team and does not correct the record.

items.objective: Respond proportionately to a colleague's false documentation.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old rheumatologist is invited by a pharmaceutical representative to join an "advisory board" at a beach resort. The company will pay for airfare, 3 nights' lodging and meals for her and a guest, plus an honorarium. The only scheduled activity is a 1-hour presentation about the company's new biologic, which she already prescribes. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Decline the invitation

options.label: B
options.html: Accept, because advisory meetings are educational

options.label: C
options.html: Accept, and report the trip to Open Payments herself

options.label: D
options.html: Accept, after promising herself not to change prescribing

options.label: E
options.html: Accept, and donate the honorarium to a charity

items.explanationHtml:
A paid leisure trip with a guest and an honorarium, for little or no real work, is a gift intended to build loyalty, not a legitimate consulting arrangement. She should decline. Payments to influence the use of federally reimbursed drugs can also implicate the Anti-Kickback Statute.

Legitimate consulting involves real, needed work at fair market value, under a written agreement, and is disclosed. Even then, manufacturers report the payments to Open Payments.

Takeaway: decline paid leisure travel and honoraria for simply attending.

whyNot.B: Calling the event an advisory board does not make a resort trip with a guest and one short talk educational.
whyNot.C: Manufacturers, not physicians, report to Open Payments, and reporting would not make the gift appropriate.
whyNot.D: Gifts influence prescribing even when recipients believe they are unaffected.
whyNot.E: Donating the honorarium does not fix accepting the trip itself, which is the main problem.

items.objective: Decline inappropriate gifts from industry.

items.stemHtml: A second-year internal medicine resident sees a 45-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension for a 10-minute visit to refill one medication. Her note documents a brief history, a focused examination and the refill. Before signing, the attending tells her to bill the highest office-visit level, saying, "We always code at the top; the payers expect it." Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Bill the highest level, because the attending is responsible for billing

options.label: B
options.html: Bill the highest level and add examination findings to support it

options.label: C
options.html: Bill the level the documentation supports and explain this to the attending

options.label: D
options.html: Report the attending to the state medical board before billing

options.label: E
options.html: Ask to be reassigned so that she no longer works with this attending

items.explanationHtml:
Claims must reflect the service actually provided and documented. Coding a brief refill visit at the top level is upcoding, which is fraud when done knowingly, and the person who submits the claim shares responsibility. The resident should bill the level her note supports and explain her reasoning to the attending. If the pressure continues, the practice's compliance office is the right next step.

Adding findings that were not obtained would turn a billing problem into falsification of the record.

Takeaway: bill what was done and documented, and say so plainly.

whyNot.A: Following an instruction to upcode does not shield her; she submits and signs the claim.
whyNot.B: Adding unperformed examination findings falsifies the record to support fraud.
whyNot.D: The board is not the first step; a direct correction and, if needed, the compliance office come first.
whyNot.E: Avoiding the attending does not fix the improper claim in front of her.

items.objective: Refuse to upcode and bill according to documentation.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has seen his family physician several times over the past year for a sports injury and anxiety. At the end of today's visit he says, "I really like talking with you. I'd love to get coffee sometime, just the two of us." Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'd like that, as long as we wait until your treatment is finished next month."

options.label: B
options.html: "Thank you, but I keep things professional with patients. I'm glad to keep being your doctor."

options.label: C
options.html: "That's kind. Let's talk about it once I've transferred you to another physician."

options.label: D
options.html: "You shouldn't have asked me that. You'll need to find another doctor now."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll have to report this request to the medical board, I'm afraid."

items.explanationHtml:
A personal or romantic relationship with a current patient is never acceptable. The physician should decline kindly and clearly, restate the professional boundary, avoid shaming the patient, and continue care if that remains workable. If the physician thinks the boundary cannot be kept, transferring care is the next step, but transferring care in order to date the patient is not acceptable.

Takeaway: decline warmly, hold the boundary, and keep caring for the patient.

whyNot.A: Planning a relationship after a short delay still trades on the trust and knowledge gained in care.
whyNot.C: Transferring care so that a relationship can begin is an attempt to evade the boundary.
whyNot.D: Shaming and dismissing the patient is unkind and abandons care for an honest, if inappropriate, request.
whyNot.E: A patient's request is not misconduct; the duty to hold the boundary lies with the physician.

items.objective: Respond to a patient's romantic interest by maintaining boundaries without shaming.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman establishes care with a new gynecologist after moving from another city. While taking her history, the gynecologist learns that the patient's previous gynecologist made sexual comments during examinations and began a sexual relationship with her while he was still treating her. She says she feels ashamed and has not told anyone. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Since this happened in another city, there's nothing we can do about it now."

options.label: B
options.html: "Are you sure you didn't misunderstand part of the examination?"

options.label: C
options.html: "I'd like to call him to hear his side before we decide anything."

options.label: D
options.html: "Let's focus on your health today rather than dwell on what happened."

options.label: E
options.html: "What he did was wrong and not your fault. I can help you report it if you wish."

items.explanationHtml:
A sexual relationship with a current patient is serious misconduct. The physician should believe and support the patient, say clearly that the conduct was wrong and not her fault, and offer to help her report it to the state medical board in the state where it occurred, which can act regardless of where she now lives. She should also be offered mental health support. Her wishes about reporting should be respected while explaining why reporting protects others.

Takeaway: validate, name the misconduct, and offer help reporting to the medical board.

whyNot.A: State medical boards can act on misconduct whenever it is reported; distance does not end the physician's duty to help.
whyNot.B: Questioning her account is retraumatizing and implies blame.
whyNot.C: Contacting the accused physician breaches the patient's confidentiality and could expose her to pressure.
whyNot.D: Changing the subject dismisses a serious disclosure and misses the chance to support and help her.

items.objective: Respond to a patient's disclosure of sexual misconduct by another physician.

items.stemHtml: A third-year medical student on a surgery rotation tells her resident that the attending has repeatedly commented on her body in the operating room and last week put his hand on her lower back while saying she should "wear something nicer" to get a good evaluation. She is worried about her grade and asks the resident not to make a fuss. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the resident?

options.label: A
options.html: "Try to keep your distance from him until the rotation is over."

options.label: B
options.html: "He jokes like that with everyone, so try not to take it personally."

options.label: C
options.html: "I'll confront him about this in front of the team tomorrow."

options.label: D
options.html: "That's not okay. Let me go over the ways to report it, including confidential ones."

options.label: E
options.html: "You should report it yourself, but only after your grade is submitted."

items.explanationHtml:
Repeated sexual comments, unwanted touching and linking appearance to evaluation are sexual harassment, and in medical education they fall under institutional mistreatment policies and federal civil rights law (Title IX). The resident should listen, validate, explain the reporting options (the school's mistreatment office, the Title IX coordinator, confidential resources), offer to help, and respect the student's choices as far as safety allows. Retaliation for reporting is prohibited.

Takeaway: validate, explain reporting routes, support the learner.

whyNot.A: Advising avoidance leaves the harassment unaddressed and puts the burden on the victim.
whyNot.B: Minimizing the conduct normalizes harassment and discourages reporting.
whyNot.C: A public confrontation ignores her wishes and may expose her to retaliation.
whyNot.E: Delaying until after grading lets harassment continue and implies that retaliation is expected.

items.objective: Support a learner who discloses sexual harassment and explain reporting options.

items.stemHtml:
An internist who owns a small practice reviews an internal audit of claims submitted to Medicare by her practice manager for "telephone follow-up" services over the first quarter of the year.

MonthTelephone follow-up claims submittedCalls documented in the chart or phone log
January4612
February5110
March4911

The manager says that the extra claims were for calls "that probably happened." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Stop these claims, involve compliance counsel and repay the improper payments

options.label: B
options.html: Keep the payments received but stop billing these services in the future

options.label: C
options.html: Have staff write notes for the calls so that the records match the claims

options.label: D
options.html: Wait to see whether Medicare's auditors identify the claims

options.label: E
options.html: Repay only the improper claims submitted in March

items.explanationHtml:
Most of these claims (113 of 146) have no documentation, which amounts to billing for services not rendered. Once a practice identifies an overpayment from Medicare or Medicaid, it must report and return it promptly; keeping it can create liability under the False Claims Act. The right sequence is to stop the improper billing, involve a compliance officer or health care attorney, investigate the full extent, and repay all affected claims.

Creating notes after the fact would add falsified records to fraud.

Takeaway: stop, investigate with compliance help, and repay every improper claim.

whyNot.B: Keeping identified overpayments is itself unlawful; the past claims must be corrected.
whyNot.C: Writing notes for calls that may not have happened falsifies records.
whyNot.D: Waiting for auditors knowingly retains overpayments and worsens liability.
whyNot.E: All improper claims must be repaid, not only the most recent month's.

items.objective: Respond to discovery of billing for services not rendered.

items.stemHtml: A pediatrics resident is a coauthor on a quality-improvement study of blood pressure screening in clinic. Reviewing the dataset the night before an abstract deadline, he finds that a co-resident entered values for 40 visits in which no blood pressure was recorded. When asked, the co-resident says the missing readings "were probably normal anyway" and that he will submit the abstract tonight. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Replace the invented values with chart data himself and submit on time

options.label: B
options.html: Inform the faculty mentor who leads the project before anything is submitted

options.label: C
options.html: Allow the submission, because a conference abstract is not a full publication

options.label: D
options.html: Report the co-resident directly to the state medical board

options.label: E
options.html: Remove his own name from the abstract and say nothing further

items.explanationHtml:
Entering values that were never measured is fabrication, one of the three forms of research misconduct (with falsification and plagiarism). The co-resident has already been asked and intends to submit, so the resident should promptly inform the faculty mentor or principal investigator, who is responsible for the integrity of the work and can stop the submission and involve the institution's research-integrity process if needed.

Takeaway: fabricated data must not be reported; tell the person responsible for the project before submission.

whyNot.A: Quietly editing the data without telling the project lead hides the misconduct and leaves the analysis unverified.
whyNot.C: Fabricated data are misconduct in any format, including an abstract.
whyNot.D: Research integrity is first handled by the project lead and institution; the board is not the first step.
whyNot.E: Withdrawing silently allows fabricated data to be presented.

items.objective: Respond to data fabrication in a research or quality-improvement project.

items.stemHtml: During a proctored end-of-clerkship examination, a medical student sees the classmate next to her repeatedly reading notes on a phone held under the desk. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the student?

options.label: A
options.html: Ignore it, because it does not affect her own score

options.label: B
options.html: Confront the classmate quietly during the examination

options.label: C
options.html: Post a description of the incident on the class social media page

options.label: D
options.html: Tell the classmate afterward that she will not report it this time

options.label: E
options.html: Report what she saw to the proctor or the course director

items.explanationHtml:
Cheating is academic dishonesty and a breach of professionalism that predicts later unprofessional behavior. The student should report what she observed to the proctor or course director, who will handle it under the school's honor code. Reporting is about the integrity of an assessment that certifies readiness to care for patients.

Takeaway: report cheating through the official channel.

whyNot.A: Ignoring it undermines an assessment meant to protect patients, regardless of her own score.
whyNot.B: Confronting the classmate mid-exam disrupts the exam and is the proctor's job.
whyNot.C: Public posting shames without due process and does not trigger the honor-code process.
whyNot.D: Promising silence condones dishonesty.

items.objective: Report academic dishonesty through official channels.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman with frequent migraine has not improved with two preventive medications. Her neurologist recommends a newer injectable preventive. The neurologist is paid by the manufacturer of this drug to give educational talks to other physicians. The patient says, "I saw something online about doctors getting money from drug companies. I'd like to know whether you get paid by the company that makes this one." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "That's not something patients need to worry about when choosing a drug."

options.label: B
options.html: "No, my recommendations are completely independent of any company."

options.label: C
options.html: "Yes, I give paid talks for them. Here is why I suggest it, and the alternatives."

options.label: D
options.html: "I'd rather not discuss my finances, but this drug is excellent."

options.label: E
options.html: "You can search for that online yourself if you're concerned about it."

items.explanationHtml:
The patient is entitled to an honest answer. The neurologist should confirm the relationship, explain the clinical reasons for the recommendation, and offer alternatives so that the patient can decide with full information. Such payments are publicly reported through Open Payments, so evasion also damages trust when she finds the record.

Takeaway: disclose financial ties honestly, explain the reasoning, and offer alternatives.

whyNot.A: Dismissing her question is paternalistic; financial ties are relevant to her decision.
whyNot.B: Denying a real payment relationship is a lie.
whyNot.D: Refusing to answer while praising the drug looks evasive and undermines trust.
whyNot.E: Sending her to search online deflects a direct question the physician should answer.

items.objective: Disclose an industry relationship honestly when a patient asks.

items.stemHtml: A second-year medical student is taking a history from a 68-year-old man in the emergency department before the resident sees him. The patient says, "Thanks, Doctor. So tell me what you think is wrong with me." Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the student?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'm actually a medical student. The doctor will see you soon."

options.label: B
options.html: "It's probably nothing serious, but let's wait and see what the tests show."

options.label: C
options.html: "I'm almost a doctor, so I can give you my best guess."

options.label: D
options.html: "I work with the doctor, so I'll pass along what you told me."

options.label: E
options.html: "Students on this team are called doctors, so you can call me that too."

items.explanationHtml:
Patients have a right to know who is caring for them. A student must correct the misunderstanding about their role, even if it is awkward, and should not offer diagnoses beyond their role. Allowing a patient to believe a student is a physician is a misrepresentation of credentials.

Takeaway: always introduce yourself, and correct others, with your real role.

whyNot.B: Offering reassurance before any assessment is premature and leaves the misunderstanding about her role uncorrected.
whyNot.C: Being close to graduation is not being a physician, and guessing a diagnosis exceeds the student's role.
whyNot.D: This sidesteps the patient's assumption that he is speaking with a physician.
whyNot.E: Accepting the title misrepresents the student's credentials.

items.objective: Correct a patient's misunderstanding of a student's role.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old emergency physician's longtime friend asks her to write a note saying he was too ill to work for the next 3 days. He is healthy and plans to attend a family event out of state. He says the note will be seen only by his manager. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Write the note, because no patient will be harmed

options.label: B
options.html: Write the note but leave out any diagnosis

options.label: C
options.html: Write the note after a brief examination at her home

options.label: D
options.html: Decline to write the note

options.label: E
options.html: Write the note on the condition that he not ask again

items.explanationHtml:
A medical note certifying illness in someone who is not ill is a false document. Physicians may not use their professional authority to deceive employers, insurers or others, whatever the stakes or the relationship. She should decline kindly and suggest he ask for leave honestly.

Writing medical notes for friends and family also blurs the boundary between personal and professional roles.

Takeaway: never sign a false medical certificate.

whyNot.A: Deceiving an employer with a physician's signature is dishonest whether or not anyone is harmed.
whyNot.B: Omitting a diagnosis does not make a false certification of illness true.
whyNot.C: A sham examination does not change the fact that he is not ill.
whyNot.E: Limiting it to once does not make the falsification acceptable.

items.objective: Refuse to issue a false medical certificate.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with severe hip osteoarthritis is scheduled for total hip arthroplasty. His orthopedic surgeon receives consulting fees from the manufacturer of the hip implant he plans to use, which he considers the best choice for this patient based on published outcomes. The hospital's conflict-of-interest policy requires disclosure. The patient has not asked about the implant. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the surgeon?

options.label: A
options.html: Use the implant without mentioning the relationship, because it is the best choice

options.label: B
options.html: Tell the patient about the relationship and base the choice on clinical evidence

options.label: C
options.html: Use a competitor's implant to avoid any appearance of bias

options.label: D
options.html: Stop consulting for the manufacturer before performing this operation

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the manufacturer's representative to explain the implant to the patient

items.explanationHtml:
Financial relationships with manufacturers are not forbidden, but they are a conflict of interest that patients and institutions should know about. The surgeon should disclose the relationship to the patient (and to the institution under its policy), explain why he recommends this implant, and keep the choice grounded in evidence and the patient's needs.

Switching to a different implant only to avoid appearances could disadvantage the patient; ending the consulting relationship is not required for this operation.

Takeaway: disclose financial interests and let clinical evidence drive the choice.

whyNot.A: Even a well-founded choice should be disclosed when the surgeon has a financial interest in it.
whyNot.C: Choosing a different implant for appearances rather than clinical reasons may not serve the patient.
whyNot.D: Disclosure and management of the conflict are expected; ending the relationship is not required.
whyNot.E: Patient counseling is the surgeon's responsibility, and a sales representative is not a neutral source.

items.objective: Disclose and manage a surgeon's financial relationship with a device manufacturer.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 0, comes to her gynecologist to request permanent sterilization. She has thought about it for several years, understands that it is intended to be permanent, and knows about long-acting reversible methods, which she does not want. The gynecologist has a sincere moral objection to performing sterilization. Other gynecologists in the same city perform the procedure. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "You're young, so I'd encourage you to wait a few years and think it over."

options.label: B
options.html: "I don't perform sterilization, so you'll need to find another doctor for that."

options.label: C
options.html: "I don't do this procedure, but I'll refer you today to a colleague who does."

options.label: D
options.html: "I'd consider it once a psychiatrist confirms you won't regret the decision."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'd like you to bring your partner to the next visit to discuss it first."

items.explanationHtml:
An informed adult with capacity may choose sterilization; age and parity alone are not reasons to refuse. A physician with a conscientious objection may decline to perform it, but must not obstruct access: she should say so openly, avoid moralizing, make a timely referral to a clinician who provides the procedure, send records, and continue to provide the patient's other care, including interim contraception if wanted.

Takeaway: object without obstructing: disclose, refer promptly, keep caring for the patient.

whyNot.A: Urging delay substitutes the physician's values for an informed adult's considered decision.
whyNot.B: Declining without a referral leaves her to navigate alone and falls short of the duties attached to objection.
whyNot.D: Requiring psychiatric clearance imposes a barrier not justified by any sign of incapacity.
whyNot.E: Requiring a partner's involvement disregards her autonomy; the decision is hers.

items.objective: Exercise conscientious objection with a timely referral and without obstruction.

items.stemHtml: A gynecologist who does not perform sterilization because of a moral objection referred a 27-year-old woman to a colleague for the procedure. The patient later tells the practice manager that she took unpaid time off work for the visit and was upset to learn only in the examination room that the gynecologist does not offer sterilization. The gynecologist wants to prevent this from happening to other patients. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in practice?

options.label: A
options.html: Stop accepting new patients of reproductive age

options.label: B
options.html: Ask front-desk staff to explain his moral reasons to callers

options.label: C
options.html: Have staff avoid mentioning sterilization unless the patient asks

options.label: D
options.html: Require new patients to sign a form agreeing not to request sterilization

options.label: E
options.html: Tell prospective and new patients in advance which services he does not provide

items.explanationHtml:
One of the duties attached to conscientious objection is to inform patients in advance, ideally when they schedule or establish care, which services the physician does not provide and how to obtain them. This prevents wasted visits and delays and respects patients' time and choices.

Objection must never become a reason to exclude groups of patients or to pressure them.

Takeaway: tell patients up front what you do not provide, and how to get it.

whyNot.A: Refusing a whole group of patients is discrimination and goes far beyond objecting to one procedure.
whyNot.B: Staff explaining his moral reasons moralizes to patients instead of informing them.
whyNot.C: Staying silent unless asked repeats the very problem that caused the wasted visit.
whyNot.D: A form restricting what patients may request is coercive and inappropriate.

items.objective: Inform patients in advance about services a physician does not provide.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old family physician plans to close his solo practice and retire in 4 months. Many of his patients have chronic conditions, including diabetes, heart failure and depression. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to end his relationships with his patients?

options.label: A
options.html: Notify patients in writing well ahead, help them find new physicians, and arrange records transfer

options.label: B
options.html: Post a notice in the waiting room during the final week of practice

options.label: C
options.html: Destroy the records of patients who have not been seen in the past year

options.label: D
options.html: Keep seeing patients until the closing date without telling them

options.label: E
options.html: Ask patients to find new physicians on their own after the practice closes

items.explanationHtml:
Ending relationships because of retirement is legitimate, but patients must have a realistic chance to arrange new care. The physician should give advance written notice (several months is reasonable here), continue care until the closing date, help patients find new physicians, and arrange how records will be kept and transferred at patients' request. Records must be retained according to legal requirements, not destroyed.

Takeaway: early written notice, help finding new physicians, continued care and secure records.

whyNot.B: A notice in the final week gives patients with chronic illness too little time to arrange care.
whyNot.C: Records must be retained as law requires and remain available to patients; destroying them is improper.
whyNot.D: Closing without warning leaves patients without care, which is abandonment.
whyNot.E: Leaving patients to search without help or records creates a gap in care.

items.objective: Close a practice without abandoning patients.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man is seen in a general surgery clinic for a symptomatic inguinal hernia. He has HIV infection with an undetectable viral load and a normal CD4 count on antiretroviral therapy. After the visit, the scheduler asks the surgeon whether the patient should be sent to the academic medical center "because of the HIV." Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the surgeon?

options.label: A
options.html: Refer him to the academic medical center for the repair

options.label: B
options.html: Schedule him as the last case of the day so the room can be cleaned

options.label: C
options.html: Ask him to obtain clearance from his infectious disease physician first

options.label: D
options.html: Schedule the repair as usual, using standard precautions

options.label: E
options.html: Require repeat viral load testing before scheduling the operation

items.explanationHtml:
A well-controlled HIV infection does not change the indications for or the conduct of an inguinal hernia repair. Refusing or deflecting a patient because of HIV status is discrimination prohibited by the Americans with Disabilities Act. Standard precautions, used for every patient, protect the team; no special scheduling or cleaning is required.

Takeaway: treat patients with HIV like everyone else, with standard precautions.

whyNot.A: Referring away a routine operation the surgeon performs, because of HIV, is discriminatory.
whyNot.B: Standard cleaning after every case suffices; last-case scheduling for HIV is unnecessary and stigmatizing.
whyNot.C: Specialist clearance is not required for a routine operation in a patient with controlled HIV.
whyNot.E: He already has documented viral suppression; an extra test only delays care without changing management.

items.objective: Provide routine surgical care to a patient with HIV without discrimination.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman who is moving to another state asks her family physician's office to send her medical records to her new primary care physician. The office manager tells her that the practice's policy is to hold records until her past-due balance for previous visits is paid. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Hold the records until the balance is paid, as the policy states

options.label: B
options.html: Send the records promptly and handle the balance separately

options.label: C
options.html: Send a brief summary letter now and the full record after payment

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the new physician to request the records after the balance is paid

options.label: E
options.html: Add the unpaid balance to the fee for copying the records

items.explanationHtml:
Under HIPAA, patients have a right to access their records and to have copies sent to a person they designate, and a practice may not withhold records because of unpaid bills for earlier care. Only a reasonable, cost-based fee for copying may be charged. Prompt transfer also supports continuity, since the new physician needs the history.

The balance is a separate business matter handled through normal billing.

Takeaway: never hold records hostage to unpaid bills.

whyNot.A: A policy that conditions access on payment for past care conflicts with the patient's right of access.
whyNot.C: Withholding the full record until payment still conditions access on the debt.
whyNot.D: Shifting the request to the new physician still delays records because of the debt.
whyNot.E: Copying fees must be reasonable and cost-based; adding an old debt is not allowed.

items.objective: Transfer records promptly regardless of unpaid bills.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman comes for a routine examination. Her mother was diagnosed with ovarian cancer at age 52, and her maternal aunt with breast cancer at age 44. No relative has had genetic testing. Her breast examination is normal. She asks whether she should be tested for one of those cancer genes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Reassure her that no evaluation is needed until age 40

options.label: B
options.html: Order BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing and call her with the results

options.label: C
options.html: Begin annual breast MRI screening now

options.label: D
options.html: Recommend risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy

options.label: E
options.html: Refer her for genetic counseling

items.explanationHtml:
A family history of ovarian cancer in a first-degree relative and early-onset breast cancer in another relative suggests a possible hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome. Women with a family history that screens positive on a familial risk assessment should be referred for genetic counseling, and testing is offered when counseling indicates it. Counseling builds the pedigree, decides whom to test first (ideally an affected relative), explains possible results, and covers the protections and limits of GINA.

Management such as MRI screening or risk-reducing surgery depends on the results.

Takeaway: suggestive family history → genetic counseling, then testing.

whyNot.A: Her family history already warrants risk assessment; waiting until 40 delays it without reason.
whyNot.B: Testing without counseling risks choosing the wrong test and misinterpreting a negative or uncertain result.
whyNot.C: High-risk MRI screening depends on her assessed risk or a confirmed variant, which are not yet known.
whyNot.D: Risk-reducing surgery is considered only after a pathogenic variant is confirmed and childbearing plans are discussed.

items.objective: Refer a patient with a suggestive family history for genetic counseling.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man has been treated by his psychiatrist for bipolar I disorder for 3 years and has been stable on an atypical antipsychotic. He has gained weight, and laboratory studies ordered by the psychiatrist show a hemoglobin A1c of 7.4% (reference range, <5.7%). He has no primary care physician and asks the psychiatrist to "just handle the diabetes too." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Start basal insulin and manage his diabetes in the psychiatry clinic

options.label: B
options.html: Tell him that diabetes is outside psychiatry and he should see someone

options.label: C
options.html: Help him establish primary care and coordinate care, including a review of his antipsychotic

options.label: D
options.html: Stop the antipsychotic at once because it caused the diabetes

options.label: E
options.html: Ask him to return to psychiatry clinic only after he has found a primary care physician

items.explanationHtml:
New diabetes needs comprehensive management (medication choice, monitoring, eye, kidney and foot care, cardiovascular risk) that is best delivered in primary care. The psychiatrist should help him establish care with a primary care physician, share the results, and coordinate, including whether a change to an antipsychotic with lower metabolic risk is appropriate. Psychiatrists remain responsible for metabolic monitoring of the drugs they prescribe.

Takeaway: refer what is beyond your role, but stay engaged and coordinate.

whyNot.A: Starting insulin in a psychiatry clinic without the broader diabetes care he needs is beyond the usual scope.
whyNot.B: Telling him to find someone without helping leaves a gap; a patient with serious mental illness may struggle to arrange care alone.
whyNot.D: Abruptly stopping a stabilizing antipsychotic risks relapse; changes should be planned.
whyNot.E: Withholding psychiatric care until he finds a primary care physician abandons his ongoing treatment.

items.objective: Coordinate referral for a condition outside one's scope while remaining involved.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman with Medicare has knee pain, and her orthopedic surgeon recommends an MRI of the knee. The surgeon owns 15% of a privately held, freestanding imaging center in another building, which is not part of his group practice. The center is accredited and its MRI quality is excellent. No exception under federal self-referral law applies to this ownership. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Refer her to an imaging facility in which he has no financial interest

options.label: B
options.html: Refer her to his center after disclosing his ownership in writing

options.label: C
options.html: Refer her to his center if she prefers its location

options.label: D
options.html: Refer her to his center and bill the MRI through his practice

options.label: E
options.html: Refer her to his center if it charges Medicare less than nearby centers

items.explanationHtml:
The Stark Law prohibits a physician from referring a Medicare patient for a designated health service (MRI is one) to an entity in which the physician has an ownership or investment interest, unless an exception applies. It is a strict-liability law: disclosure, patient preference, quality and lower prices do not create an exception. The surgeon should refer her to a facility in which he has no financial interest.

Takeaway: disclosure does not cure a prohibited self-referral.

whyNot.B: Disclosure is good ethics but does not satisfy any Stark exception.
whyNot.C: Patient preference does not create an exception to the self-referral prohibition.
whyNot.D: Billing through his practice for a service performed elsewhere misrepresents the claim and does not cure the self-referral.
whyNot.E: Lower prices do not create an exception; the prohibition rests on the financial relationship.

items.objective: Apply the Stark Law to a physician's ownership interest in an imaging center.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman is ready for discharge after 5 days in the hospital for a heart failure exacerbation. Her diuretic dose was doubled, a new medication was started, and one of her previous medications was stopped. A thyroid-stimulating hormone result is still pending. She lives alone and has a primary care physician she has seen for years. Which of the following is the most appropriate step to ensure continuity of care?

options.label: A
options.html: Give her a printed list of her medicines and ask her to call her physician

options.label: B
options.html: Send the discharge summary to her physician within the next month

options.label: C
options.html: Ask her daughter to tell her physician about the medication changes

options.label: D
options.html: Contact her physician directly with the changes and pending result, and book follow-up before she leaves

options.label: E
options.html: Schedule a follow-up visit with the hospital's heart failure clinic in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Transitions of care are high-risk moments, especially for older adults with heart failure and medication changes. The discharging physician should communicate directly with the primary care physician (summary, medication reconciliation, pending results and who will follow them up) and schedule early follow-up before discharge, ideally within 1–2 weeks for heart failure.

Takeaway: a safe handoff names the changes, the pending results and the person responsible, and books the visit.

whyNot.A: Leaving her to arrange follow-up and relay changes risks errors and missed pending results.
whyNot.B: A summary that arrives weeks later will miss the critical early follow-up window.
whyNot.C: Relaying information through family is unreliable and does not transfer responsibility for pending results.
whyNot.E: Follow-up after a heart failure admission should be early; 3 months is far too late.

items.objective: Ensure continuity of care at hospital discharge.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old man with end-stage heart failure is enrolled in hospice. He has decision-making capacity and asks that the shock function of his implantable cardioverter-defibrillator be turned off because he does not want to be shocked as he dies. The cardiology fellow on call tells the team that she personally believes deactivation is wrong and does not want to do it. Another qualified clinician is available today. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Deny the request because deactivation would hasten his death

options.label: B
options.html: Arrange promptly for another qualified clinician to deactivate the shocks

options.label: C
options.html: Require the fellow to deactivate the device despite her objection

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the ethics committee to review the request before any action

options.label: E
options.html: Wait to act until all of his adult children agree

items.explanationHtml:
A patient with capacity may refuse or ask to withdraw any treatment, including an implanted device's therapy; deactivating shocks at his request is ethically and legally the same as withdrawing other life-sustaining treatment and is not physician-assisted death. A clinician with a conscientious objection may step aside, but must not obstruct: the team should arrange promptly for another qualified clinician to carry out the request.

Takeaway: objectors may withdraw from the task, not from the duty to make sure it is done.

whyNot.A: Honoring a capacitated refusal of device therapy is permissible; the underlying disease causes death.
whyNot.C: Clinicians need not personally act against conscience when a colleague can promptly do it.
whyNot.D: An ethics consultation is unnecessary when the patient has capacity and the request is clear and lawful.
whyNot.E: The decision belongs to the patient; family agreement is not required.

items.objective: Handle a clinician's conscientious objection to device deactivation without obstructing the patient's request.

items.stemHtml: A family medicine practice that is accepting new patients receives a call from a 29-year-old transgender woman who wants to establish primary care for asthma and routine preventive care. The receptionist asks the physician whether to suggest that she "try a specialty clinic instead." Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Suggest a specialty gender clinic because the practice has little experience

options.label: B
options.html: Ask her to bring records of her gender-affirming treatment before scheduling

options.label: C
options.html: Schedule her only after the physician has reviewed her history

options.label: D
options.html: Put her on a waiting list until a clinician volunteers to see her

options.label: E
options.html: Schedule her as the practice would any other new patient

items.explanationHtml:
She is asking for routine primary care that the practice provides to everyone. Deflecting, delaying or imposing extra steps because she is transgender is discrimination. A physician may refer for specific care beyond their expertise, but not decline a patient's routine care because of who the patient is.

Takeaway: same access, same scheduling, same welcome.

whyNot.A: Asthma and preventive care are routine; redirecting her because she is transgender is discriminatory.
whyNot.B: Requiring records of unrelated treatment before scheduling is an extra barrier not imposed on others.
whyNot.C: Screening her history before accepting her is a gatekeeping step other new patients do not face.
whyNot.D: A volunteer-only waiting list treats her differently and delays her care.

items.objective: Avoid discrimination in accepting new patients.

items.stemHtml: During an outpatient visit, a 38-year-old man becomes angry when his physician declines to prescribe more alprazolam. He stands up, moves between the physician and the door, clenches his fists and shouts that she will "regret this." The clinic has a panic button and a security team. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Tell him firmly to sit down or the visit will end

options.label: B
options.html: Try to restrain him with the nurse's help

options.label: C
options.html: Stay calm, keep her distance, and summon security

options.label: D
options.html: Agree to the prescription to calm the situation

options.label: E
options.html: Turn back to the computer and ignore the outburst

items.explanationHtml:
When a patient becomes threatening, safety comes first. The physician should speak calmly, avoid confrontation, keep space between them, and summon help (panic button, security). When a clear path opens she should leave the room. Attempting de-escalation alone, physical restraint or appeasement are less safe.

Afterward, the practice can address the behavior, including warning or ending the relationship with proper notice, and still provide emergency care.

Takeaway: calm voice, distance, call security, exit when possible.

whyNot.A: A confrontational ultimatum can escalate a threatening patient.
whyNot.B: Restraining an agitated person without trained staff endangers everyone.
whyNot.D: Giving in to threats is unsafe prescribing and rewards the behavior.
whyNot.E: Turning away from a threatening person removes situational awareness and invites assault.

items.objective: Prioritize personal and staff safety with a threatening patient.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman has had bilateral, pressing headaches several times a week for 3 months. They are worse on busy workdays and improve with rest. She has no fever, weight loss, neurologic symptoms, change in pattern or history of cancer, and her neurologic examination is normal. She asks for an MRI of the brain and a referral to a neurologist. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Your exam is normal, so there's no reason for an MRI or a neurologist."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'll order the MRI and the referral today so you won't have to worry."

options.label: C
options.html: "Headaches like these are almost always stress; try to relax more."

options.label: D
options.html: "It sounds like you're worried this is serious. Tell me more about that."

options.label: E
options.html: "Insurance won't pay for an MRI without warning signs, so I can't order one."

items.explanationHtml:
Her headaches fit tension-type headache with no red flags, so imaging is not indicated. But a request for a test or a referral often carries an unspoken fear (a tumor, a relative's illness). The best first step is to explore the concern; then the physician can explain the findings, address the specific worry, and agree on a plan. If she still wants a specialist after that discussion, a referral is reasonable.

Takeaway: before granting or refusing a referral, find out what the patient is worried about.

whyNot.A: A flat refusal dismisses her concern before it is understood.
whyNot.B: Ordering unindicated tests to end the conversation skips the discussion and exposes her to incidental findings.
whyNot.C: Attributing headaches to stress without exploring her worry is dismissive.
whyNot.E: Blaming insurance avoids the clinical conversation and may not even be accurate.

items.objective: Explore a patient's concerns before responding to a request for an unindicated referral.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man is admitted with painless jaundice and weight loss. CT and biopsy show metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. He speaks English fluently and is alert and oriented. Before the physician meets with him, his adult son asks to speak privately and requests that his father not be told the diagnosis. He explains that in their family, elders are protected from bad news and the family makes such decisions together. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to the son?

options.label: A
options.html: "I can see you want to protect him. I'll ask him how much he wants to know and who he wants involved."

options.label: B
options.html: "The law requires me to tell him everything today, whatever the family prefers."

options.label: C
options.html: "Of course. We'll talk about the results only with you and the rest of the family."

options.label: D
options.html: "Let's ask the hospital ethics committee to decide what he should be told."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'll tell him he has a tumor, but I won't mention that it has spread."

items.explanationHtml:
The information belongs to the patient, but autonomy includes the right to choose how much to hear and who decides. The physician should acknowledge the son's protective intent and then ask the patient, ideally privately, how much he wants to know and whom he wants involved. This respects both the patient's autonomy and a family-centered culture without imposing either the physician's or the family's assumptions.

Takeaway: when family asks to withhold a diagnosis, ask the patient what he wants.

whyNot.B: Forcing full disclosure immediately ignores that a patient may choose to receive less information or to delegate.
whyNot.C: Agreeing to withhold the diagnosis without asking the patient overrides his autonomy.
whyNot.D: An ethics consultation is premature; the next step is simply to ask the patient.
whyNot.E: Partial, selective disclosure decided without the patient is deceptive and still ignores his wishes.

items.objective: Respond to a family's request to withhold a diagnosis by asking the patient's preferences.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man with newly diagnosed metastatic pancreatic cancer has decision-making capacity. When his physician asks him privately how he would like to receive information, he says, "My son handles these things for our family. Tell him everything and decide with him. I don't want to hear the details, but I trust him." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Insist that he hear the details so that he can make his own decisions

options.label: B
options.html: Have the son sign all consent forms without further input from the patient

options.label: C
options.html: Request a psychiatric consultation to confirm his capacity

options.label: D
options.html: Defer treatment decisions until he agrees to hear his prognosis

options.label: E
options.html: Honor his wish, document it, and offer to name his son as health care agent

items.explanationHtml:
A capacitated patient may waive detailed disclosure and delegate decisions; doing so is an exercise of autonomy, not a loss of it. The physician should follow his choice, document it, and suggest formalizing it by naming his son as health care agent (durable power of attorney for health care). The physician should also tell the patient that he can ask questions or change his mind at any time, and check in periodically.

Takeaway: a patient's choice to delegate is respected, documented and revisited.

whyNot.A: Insisting he hear details he has declined overrides his informed choice about information.
whyNot.B: Delegation does not erase the patient; he should remain involved to the extent he wishes and can change his mind.
whyNot.C: Nothing suggests incapacity; choosing to delegate is not a sign of impaired capacity.
whyNot.D: Withholding treatment decisions until he accepts information he declined is coercive.

items.objective: Honor and formalize a capacitated patient's decision to delegate decision-making to family.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer is receiving comfort-focused care in a private hospital room and is expected to die within days. His family asks whether several relatives may gather at the bedside for prayers and quiet chanting, whether they may place a small religious object in his hand, and whether, after he dies, they may wash his body themselves before it is moved. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Allow only two visitors at a time, according to standard policy

options.label: B
options.html: Accommodate the requests and coordinate with nursing and chaplaincy

options.label: C
options.html: Explain that only hospital staff may wash the body after death

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the family to perform the rituals at the funeral home instead

options.label: E
options.html: Permit the prayers but remove the object for infection control

items.explanationHtml:
End-of-life rituals can matter deeply to patients and families. Requests that do not compromise safety or other patients should be accommodated. Nursing can adapt visitor limits for a dying patient in a private room and help the family take part in after-death care, and the chaplaincy service can support the family and help with arrangements.

Takeaway: accommodate harmless end-of-life rituals and enlist chaplaincy and nursing.

whyNot.A: Rigid visitor limits for a dying patient in a private room serve no safety purpose here.
whyNot.C: Families can usually take part in after-death care; a blanket refusal is unnecessary.
whyNot.D: Moving the rituals elsewhere denies the family's wish to be with him as he dies.
whyNot.E: A small object in a comfort-care patient's hand poses no meaningful infection risk.

items.objective: Accommodate a family's religious practices at the end of life.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman who speaks Vietnamese and limited English returns to discuss the results of a breast biopsy, which shows invasive ductal carcinoma. Her 14-year-old son, who is fluent in both languages, offers to interpret. A telephone and video interpreter service is available. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate with her?

options.label: A
options.html: Let her son interpret because she trusts him

options.label: B
options.html: Ask a bilingual receptionist to interpret

options.label: C
options.html: Use a trained medical interpreter by phone or video

options.label: D
options.html: Speak slowly in English using simple words

options.label: E
options.html: Give her a written translation of the report to read at home

items.explanationHtml:
Serious news, treatment options and consent require a trained medical interpreter. Family members, especially children, may omit or soften information, lack medical vocabulary and carry an inappropriate emotional burden; a child should not deliver a parent's cancer diagnosis. Untrained bilingual staff are also error-prone. Phone or video interpreters are acceptable and quickly available.

Takeaway: professional interpreters for important conversations; never children.

whyNot.A: A child interpreting a parent's cancer diagnosis risks errors and places an unfair burden on him.
whyNot.B: Untrained staff make more interpretation errors and are not trained in confidentiality or medical terms.
whyNot.D: Simplified English does not overcome limited proficiency for a complex, emotional discussion.
whyNot.E: A written report is no substitute for a conversation in which she can ask questions.

items.objective: Use a trained medical interpreter for a patient with limited English proficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin twice daily and glipizide each morning. His hemoglobin A1c is 7.2%. He tells his physician that he plans to fast from dawn to sunset every day for a month as part of his religious observance, eating one meal before dawn and one after sunset. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Tell him that people with diabetes are exempt from fasting in his religion

options.label: B
options.html: Tell him that fasting is unsafe with diabetes and he must not fast

options.label: C
