options.html: Continue his current regimen unchanged and recheck at his next visit

options.label: D
options.html: Discuss his plans and adjust medication timing and doses, with glucose monitoring

options.label: E
options.html: Ask him to obtain permission to fast from his religious leader

items.explanationHtml:
The physician should respect the decision, ask about the plan, and work out a safe regimen together: shifting doses to the pre-dawn and evening meals, reducing or retiming the sulfonylurea (the drug most likely to cause hypoglycemia during a fast), checking glucose more often, and agreeing on clear rules for breaking the fast (symptoms of hypoglycemia or very high glucose).

Telling a patient what his religion permits, or forbidding the fast outright, is presumptuous and likely to end the conversation rather than make him safer.

Takeaway: ask, respect, and adjust the regimen so the fast is as safe as possible.

whyNot.A: Interpreting his religion's rules for him is presumptuous; he decides how to practice his faith.
whyNot.B: A blanket prohibition disregards his autonomy, and many people with stable diabetes can fast with planning.
whyNot.C: A morning sulfonylurea taken before a full day without food risks hypoglycemia; the regimen needs changes.
whyNot.E: Sending him for religious permission sidesteps the physician's job of making his plan medically safer.

items.objective: Support a patient who chooses a religious fast by adapting the treatment plan.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman is scheduled for an elective abdominal hysterectomy for symptomatic uterine fibroids. Her hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL (reference range, 12–16 g/dL). She has decision-making capacity and explains that her religious beliefs forbid her from accepting a transfusion of blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask which blood products and blood-sparing methods she accepts and plan around them

options.label: B
options.html: Cancel the operation because she will not accept a transfusion

options.label: C
options.html: Agree to her request but plan to transfuse if she becomes unstable under anesthesia

options.label: D
options.html: Ask her husband to consent to transfusion in case it becomes necessary

options.label: E
options.html: Proceed as scheduled without discussion, since her refusal is documented

items.explanationHtml:
An adult with capacity may refuse transfusion, and the refusal must be honored, including during an emergency in the operating room. Acceptance of specific products and techniques (some plasma fractions, cell salvage, volume expanders) varies between individuals, so the physician should ask about each and plan: correct the anemia before surgery (for example with iron), minimize blood loss, and document her choices. Planning to transfuse secretly would be battery.

Takeaway: respect the refusal, then ask exactly what she will accept and optimize before surgery.

whyNot.B: Refusing to operate abandons her; with planning, many such operations can be done safely.
whyNot.C: Planning to override her refusal is deceptive and would be battery.
whyNot.D: Her husband cannot override a capacitated adult's own decision.
whyNot.E: Proceeding without discussion misses chances to optimize her hemoglobin and to clarify what she accepts.

items.objective: Plan surgical care for an adult who refuses blood transfusion on religious grounds.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with a mild intellectual disability comes to the clinic with knee pain after a fall. He is accompanied by his support worker. He answers simple questions clearly when asked, but the physician has been directing every question to the support worker, and the patient has stopped speaking. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in approach?

options.label: A
options.html: Keep asking the support worker, because that is quicker

options.label: B
options.html: Ask the support worker to answer while the patient waits outside

options.label: C
options.html: Use precise medical terms so that nothing is misunderstood

options.label: D
options.html: Ask the patient to bring a family member to the next visit

options.label: E
options.html: Talk directly to the patient in plain language, with help from the worker as he wishes

items.explanationHtml:
People with intellectual disabilities should be addressed directly, in plain language with time to respond, and involved in decisions to the extent of their abilities; capacity is decision-specific and is not presumed absent. The support person can help, as the patient wishes, but should not replace him. Talking around a patient is disrespectful and loses important history.

Takeaway: speak to the patient, not about him.

whyNot.A: Speed does not justify excluding a patient who can describe his own symptoms.
whyNot.B: Sending him out removes him from his own care and is disrespectful.
whyNot.C: Medical jargon makes communication harder, not clearer, for most patients.
whyNot.D: He has a support worker with him now; a family member is not needed to communicate with him.

items.objective: Communicate directly with a patient who has an intellectual disability.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to an urgent care clinic with 5 days of vaginal discharge. Vital signs are normal and she has no abdominal pain or fever. She asks that a female clinician perform any pelvic examination because of her religious beliefs about modesty. The physician on duty is a man; a female nurse practitioner will be available in about 45 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Explain that the clinician's gender does not matter and proceed

options.label: B
options.html: Arrange for the female nurse practitioner to perform the examination

options.label: C
options.html: Perform the examination with a female chaperone, which meets her request

options.label: D
options.html: Treat her empirically without any examination

options.label: E
options.html: Tell her she must accept the available clinician or return another day

items.explanationHtml:
Requests for a clinician of the same gender for intimate examinations should be accommodated when possible. She is stable, and a short wait for the female clinician poses no risk. In a true emergency, the physician would explain why care cannot wait and proceed with a chaperone.

Takeaway: accommodate gender-concordant examinations when it is safe to do so.

whyNot.A: Dismissing her request disrespects her values when a simple accommodation is available.
whyNot.C: A chaperone does not meet a request for a female examiner, and the accommodation is available.
whyNot.D: Treating without examination risks missing the diagnosis when an examination can be done shortly.
whyNot.E: Making her choose between care and her beliefs is unnecessary when the accommodation is near at hand.

items.objective: Accommodate a religious request for a same-gender clinician when safe.

items.stemHtml:
An emergency department director reviews 12 months of data for adults with isolated long-bone fractures. Groups are similar in age, triage acuity and initial pain score.

Patient groupVisitsReceived any analgesic in the EDMedian minutes to first analgesic
Black31071%74
Hispanic28074%69
White64086%46

Which of the following is the most effective next step to reduce this disparity?

options.label: A
options.html: Require implicit-bias training for all clinicians as the sole intervention

options.label: B
options.html: Ask patients to describe their pain more precisely at triage

options.label: C
options.html: Start a nurse-initiated analgesia protocol with race-stratified audit and feedback

options.label: D
options.html: Assign patients to clinicians of the same race or ethnicity

options.label: E
options.html: Publish the names of clinicians with the longest delays to analgesia

items.explanationHtml:
The data show a disparity in whether and how quickly analgesia is given, despite similar acuity and pain scores, a pattern consistent with implicit bias and system factors. The most effective responses are system-level: a standardized, triage- or nurse-initiated analgesia protocol reduces discretionary variation, and stratified audit with feedback shows whether the gap closes. Bias training alone has limited, short-lived effects on behavior.

Takeaway: fix disparities with standard protocols and stratified measurement, not with training alone or by blaming patients.

whyNot.A: Implicit-bias training alone has limited, short-lived effects on clinical behavior; it works only alongside system changes.
whyNot.B: Pain scores were already similar; asking patients to describe pain better blames them for a clinician-side gap.
whyNot.D: Racial matching of patients and clinicians is impractical, discriminatory as a policy, and leaves the process unchanged.
whyNot.E: Public shaming damages a safety culture and does not change the process that produces the gap.

items.objective: Choose a system-level intervention to reduce a measured disparity in analgesia.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old transgender man comes for an asthma follow-up visit and asks what preventive care he needs. He has taken testosterone for 4 years and has had no gender-affirming surgery. He has never had cervical cancer screening. He is sexually active with one partner. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding cervical cancer screening?

options.label: A
options.html: It is not needed because testosterone lowers the risk of cervical cancer

options.label: B
options.html: It is needed only if he develops abnormal bleeding or pain

options.label: C
options.html: It is needed only if he has had sexual partners who were assigned male at birth

options.label: D
options.html: It is not needed until age 40 because of his testosterone use

options.label: E
options.html: It is recommended as for anyone with a cervix, with attention to comfort

items.explanationHtml:
Screening follows anatomy, not gender identity: a transgender man who has a cervix should be offered cervical cancer screening on the same schedule as anyone with a cervix (at his age, cytology every 3 years, or HPV testing alone or with cytology every 5 years). Testosterone does not remove the need, though it can cause atrophy that makes the examination uncomfortable and samples harder to interpret; the clinician should explain each step, use a small speculum and offer choices to improve comfort.

Takeaway: screen the organs a person has.

whyNot.A: Testosterone does not lower cervical cancer risk enough to remove the need for screening.
whyNot.B: Screening is for people without symptoms; waiting for symptoms misses the purpose.
whyNot.C: HPV spreads through many kinds of sexual contact, so partners' sex assigned at birth does not decide the need.
whyNot.D: Testosterone does not change the screening start age or schedule for someone with a cervix.

items.objective: Apply organ-based cervical cancer screening to a transgender man.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man comes to a walk-in clinic with 3 days of dysuria and urethral discharge. The physician wants to take a sexual history that is accurate and does not make assumptions. Which of the following is the best opening question?

options.label: A
options.html: "What are the genders of your sexual partners in the past few months?"

options.label: B
options.html: "Do you have a girlfriend at the moment, or more than one?"

options.label: C
options.html: "Are you married or in a long-term relationship right now?"

options.label: D
options.html: "I assume your partners have been women; is that right?"

options.label: E
options.html: "Have you been careless about using protection lately?"

items.explanationHtml:
An inclusive sexual history asks open, nonjudgmental questions that do not presume the genders of partners. Partners' genders, numbers and practices guide which sites to test (urethral, pharyngeal, rectal) and which infections to consider. Questions that assume heterosexuality or marriage, or that sound judgmental, lead to incomplete answers and missed infections.

Takeaway: ask, don't assume, about partners.

whyNot.B: Asking about a girlfriend assumes his partners are women.
whyNot.C: Marital status does not tell the physician who his sexual partners are or what testing he needs.
whyNot.D: Stating an assumption makes it harder for him to correct it.
whyNot.E: A judgmental question discourages honest answers.

items.objective: Take an inclusive, nonjudgmental sexual history.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a community clinic. His hemoglobin A1c is 9.1%, and he has no symptoms of hyperglycemia or ketosis. He sleeps in a shelter at night and spends days outdoors, has a basic cell phone, and eats at meal programs. The resident drafts a plan for basal-bolus insulin with four fingerstick checks a day. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Start the basal-bolus regimen and give him a glucometer

options.label: B
options.html: Defer diabetes treatment until he has stable housing

options.label: C
options.html: Admit him to the hospital to start insulin

options.label: D
options.html: Ask about his routine, food and storage, and choose a simpler regimen with social work help

options.label: E
options.html: Give him written instructions and emphasize that adherence is his responsibility

items.explanationHtml:
A plan must fit the patient's life. The physician should ask about the barriers (where he sleeps, food timing, where medicines can be stored and kept safe, phone access) and design a feasible plan: here, oral therapy such as metformin is an appropriate first step for an asymptomatic patient with this A1c, with simple monitoring, walk-in follow-up and referral to social work for housing, benefits and food resources.

Takeaway: ask what would make the plan hard, then build one he can follow.

whyNot.A: A complex insulin regimen needing meals, storage and frequent checks is unlikely to be feasible, and he does not need insulin first.
whyNot.B: Treatment should not wait for housing; diabetes can be managed now with a realistic plan.
whyNot.C: He has no hyperglycemic emergency, and hospitalization does not solve the barriers he faces after discharge.
whyNot.E: Placing the burden on him ignores structural barriers and sets the plan up to fail.

items.objective: Tailor a treatment plan to the circumstances of a patient experiencing homelessness.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 2 days of fever, dysuria and right flank pain. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). As the physician begins the history, she hesitates to give her address and says quietly that she is in the country without legal permission. She asks whether anyone will report her if she stays. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "We need to verify immigration status before we can treat you."

options.label: B
options.html: "Your medical information is confidential, and your care here doesn't depend on immigration status."

options.label: C
options.html: "You'll need to pay before treatment, since you may not have insurance."

options.label: D
options.html: "I can't promise anything, so you may want to leave if you're worried."

options.label: E
options.html: "We'll treat you, but we are required to notify the authorities."

items.explanationHtml:
She probably has pyelonephritis and needs care now. Under EMTALA, the emergency department must screen and stabilize her regardless of immigration status or ability to pay, and her medical information is protected by confidentiality. Clinicians do not need her immigration status to treat her. Reassuring her honestly about these points keeps her in care; fear of authorities is a common reason immigrants delay care.

Social work can help afterward with follow-up and payment options.

Takeaway: explain confidentiality and that emergency care does not depend on immigration status.

whyNot.A: Immigration status is not required for treatment, and asking for it would delay care she needs.
whyNot.C: EMTALA forbids delaying screening and stabilization to ask about payment.
whyNot.D: Encouraging her to leave with likely pyelonephritis is unsafe and abandons her.
whyNot.E: Clinicians have no general duty to report patients' immigration status, and saying so falsely drives patients away.

items.objective: Reassure an undocumented patient about confidentiality and access to emergency care.

items.stemHtml: A hospital reviews an event in which a patient on a medical ward received an intravenous potassium chloride bolus instead of a saline flush. The review finds that concentrated potassium vials were stocked in the same ward drawer as saline vials of similar size, that the ward had run with one nurse fewer than planned for 3 months, and that the nurse who gave the drug picked the vial while being called to another room. In the terms of the Swiss-cheese model of error, which of the following is a latent condition in this event?

options.label: A
options.html: The nurse's selection of the wrong vial from the drawer

options.label: B
options.html: The nurse being called away while preparing the flush

options.label: C
options.html: Stocking concentrated potassium vials beside saline vials

options.label: D
options.html: Injection of the potassium bolus through the patient's line

options.label: E
options.html: The patient's resulting cardiac arrhythmia

items.explanationHtml:
Latent conditions are weaknesses designed or built into the system, often by people far from the bedside, that lie dormant until they combine with an active failure. Storing a lethal look-alike drug next to a routine one is a classic latent condition (so is the chronic understaffing). The front-line act of picking the wrong vial is the active failure.

In the Swiss-cheese model, harm needs holes in several layers to align. Removing the latent condition (taking concentrated potassium off the ward altogether) closes a hole permanently for every future nurse.

Takeaway: active failures happen at the sharp end and are immediate; latent conditions sit at the blunt end and are where durable fixes lie.

whyNot.A: Selecting the wrong vial is the active failure at the sharp end: the unsafe act whose effect was immediate.
whyNot.B: The interruption is a circumstance at the moment of the act; the persistent staffing and storage choices are the latent conditions.
whyNot.D: Giving the drug is the final step of the active failure, not a pre-existing weakness in the system.
whyNot.E: The arrhythmia is the harm (the outcome), not one of the layers of defence.

items.objective: Distinguish latent conditions from active failures using the Swiss-cheese model.

items.stemHtml: On a surgical unit, bedside barcode scanners often fail to read wristbands, so several nurses have begun scanning a spare copy of each patient's wristband label kept at the nursing station. A nurse who uses this workaround gives a drug to the right patient without harm, but a safety officer notices the practice during an audit. The nurse says that "everyone does it to keep up with the medication pass." Under a just-culture framework, which of the following is the most appropriate response to this nurse's behaviour?

options.label: A
options.html: Consoling the nurse and taking no further action

options.label: B
options.html: Formal disciplinary action against the nurse

options.label: C
options.html: No response, because the patient was not harmed

options.label: D
options.html: Coaching the nurse and removing the reasons for the workaround

options.label: E
options.html: Reporting the nurse to the state board of nursing

items.explanationHtml:
Just culture sorts behaviour into three types. Human error (a slip or lapse) calls for consoling and system redesign. At-risk behaviour is a choice whose risk the person does not recognise or believes is justified, typically a normalised workaround, and calls for coaching plus fixing whatever made the shortcut attractive (here, unreliable scanners). Reckless behaviour, conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk, can justify discipline.

Scanning a spare label is a drift into unsafe practice that the whole unit shares; the system response matters as much as the individual one.

Takeaway: human error → console; at-risk behaviour → coach and fix the incentive; reckless behaviour → discipline, regardless of the outcome.

whyNot.A: Consoling fits an inadvertent human error; this was a deliberate choice to bypass a safety check, which needs coaching.
whyNot.B: Discipline is reserved for reckless behaviour (conscious disregard of a substantial risk); a widespread, normalised shortcut is at-risk behaviour.
whyNot.C: Just culture judges the behaviour, not the outcome; the shortcut defeats the barcode check whether or not harm occurred this time.
whyNot.E: A licensing report is for serious misconduct or impairment, not for a common system-driven workaround.

items.objective: Apply just-culture categories to choose a response to at-risk behaviour.

items.stemHtml: A hospital pharmacy finds that most errors in compounding intravenous infusions occur when technicians are interrupted by telephone calls and questions while measuring doses. Which of the following changes best applies human factors principles to reduce these errors?

options.label: A
options.html: Designating a protected, no-interruption zone for infusion preparation

options.label: B
options.html: Reminding technicians in writing to concentrate harder during compounding

options.label: C
options.html: Adding a compounding accuracy quiz to the annual competency review

options.label: D
options.html: Disciplining technicians whose infusions contain errors

options.label: E
options.html: Increasing the number of infusions each technician prepares per hour

items.explanationHtml:
Interruptions during a multistep task are a well-known cause of omitted or repeated steps. Human factors engineering changes the work environment so that the error is less likely, for example a protected preparation area where phones are diverted and staff are not approached, sometimes marked by a visible signal such as a vest or floor marking.

Education, reminders and discipline depend on people being more careful and are weak interventions.

Takeaway: fix interruptions and cognitive overload by redesigning the environment, not by asking people to try harder.

whyNot.B: Exhortation relies on vigilance, which is exactly what interruptions defeat; it is the weakest type of fix.
whyNot.C: Training does not remove the interruptions that cause the errors in a skilled workforce.
whyNot.D: Punishing people for a system-induced error discourages reporting and leaves the cause in place.
whyNot.E: Higher workload raises cognitive load and would likely increase errors.

items.objective: Apply human factors principles to reduce interruption-related errors.

items.stemHtml: In an intensive care unit, the newest respiratory therapist notices that a ventilated patient's alarms have been silenced and calls a halt to a bedside procedure being led by the unit director. The director pauses, listens, agrees with the concern and thanks the therapist. Afterwards the unit reviews the episode at its daily safety huddle, even though no harm occurred. This unit's behaviour best illustrates which of the following characteristics of a high-reliability organisation?

options.label: A
options.html: Strict hierarchy with decisions reserved for the most senior person

options.label: B
options.html: Deference to expertise and preoccupation with failure

options.label: C
options.html: Simplification of explanations for adverse events

options.label: D
options.html: Focus on outcome measures rather than near misses

options.label: E
options.html: Reliance on individual vigilance rather than team processes

items.explanationHtml:
High-reliability organisations share five habits: preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience and deference to expertise. Here the most junior team member, who held the critical information, was allowed to stop the procedure (deference to expertise, a flattened hierarchy), and the unit studied a near miss rather than ignoring it (preoccupation with failure).

Takeaway: in a high-reliability culture, anyone can stop the line, and near misses are treated as free lessons.

whyNot.A: High-reliability organisations do the opposite: authority shifts to whoever has the relevant knowledge.
whyNot.C: High-reliability organisations are reluctant to simplify; they seek the full set of contributing causes.
whyNot.D: Reviewing a no-harm episode is the preoccupation with failure that treats near misses as warnings.
whyNot.E: The episode shows a team process (anyone may stop the line, followed by a huddle), not reliance on one person.

items.objective: Recognise the characteristics of a high-reliability organisation.

items.stemHtml: During a resuscitation, the team leader says to the room, "Somebody push an amp of bicarb." Two nurses each assume the other will do it, and the drug is not given for several minutes. Which of the following communication techniques would most directly have prevented this delay?

options.label: A
options.html: A written summary of the resuscitation entered after the event

options.label: B
options.html: An end-of-shift structured handoff between nurses

options.label: C
options.html: A debriefing session after the resuscitation

options.label: D
options.html: Using a louder voice for all orders during the code

options.label: E
options.html: Closed-loop communication directed to a named team member

items.explanationHtml:
Closed-loop communication has three parts: the sender gives a clear order to a named person, the receiver repeats it back, and the receiver reports when it is done (the sender confirms). An order to "somebody" invites diffusion of responsibility, as happened here. The leader should also avoid vague terms ("an amp") and state drug, dose and route.

Takeaway: in a crisis, name the person, state the order exactly, and expect a read-back and a "done".

whyNot.A: Documentation after the event does not make sure the order is carried out during it.
whyNot.B: A shift handoff transfers responsibility for patients; it does not govern real-time orders in a code.
whyNot.C: Debriefing helps the team learn afterwards but would not have prevented the delay in real time.
whyNot.D: Volume does not assign responsibility; the problem was that nobody owned the order.

items.objective: Describe closed-loop communication and why it prevents dropped tasks.

items.stemHtml: A public health team studies why adults in one urban neighbourhood have higher rates of poorly controlled hypertension than adults in a neighbouring district, although both groups attend the same clinic and receive the same prescribing. The team finds that the first neighbourhood has no full-service grocery store, few safe places to walk, and many residents working night shifts at two jobs. These findings are best described as which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Errors in clinical decision-making

options.label: B
options.html: Genetic predisposition to hypertension

options.label: C
options.html: Social determinants of health

options.label: D
options.html: Differences in health care quality measures

options.label: E
options.html: Selection bias in the study population

items.explanationHtml:
Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, live, work and age: income, food access, housing, the built environment, education, transport and work schedules. They often outweigh clinical care in explaining differences in outcomes between groups receiving the same treatment.

Responses range from individual (screening for food insecurity and linking to resources) to population level (zoning for grocery stores, safe parks).

Takeaway: when the care is the same and outcomes differ, look at where and how people live.

whyNot.A: Both groups receive the same prescribing at the same clinic, so clinical decisions do not explain the difference.
whyNot.B: The factors found are features of the environment and work, not inherited traits.
whyNot.D: Quality measures describe care delivered; the care is the same and the differences lie outside the clinic.
whyNot.E: Selection bias is a study-design error; the findings describe real conditions in the neighbourhood.

items.objective: Identify social determinants of health as causes of outcome differences.

items.stemHtml: After several patients receive enteral feeding formula through intravenous lines, a hospital safety committee considers ways to prevent recurrence. Which of the following interventions is likely to be most effective?

options.label: A
options.html: Colour-coded labels on all enteral feeding bags

options.label: B
options.html: Enteral tubing connectors that cannot physically attach to intravenous ports

options.label: C
options.html: A mandatory annual education module on tubing misconnections

options.label: D
options.html: A policy requiring two nurses to trace every line before connection

options.label: E
options.html: Suspension of the nurses involved in the misconnections

items.explanationHtml:
The hierarchy of intervention strength runs from forcing functions and hazard removal (strongest), through standardisation, simplification, checklists and double checks (intermediate), to education, policies and warnings (weakest). A connector that physically cannot join an IV port is a forcing function: it makes the wrong action impossible for every future user, regardless of fatigue or distraction.

Takeaway: design out the error when you can; rely on people being careful only when you must.

whyNot.A: Labels help but still rely on the user noticing them under pressure, so they are weaker than a physical barrier.
whyNot.C: Education is among the weakest interventions because it depends on memory and attention.
whyNot.D: A double check adds a layer but is a human process that fails when staff are busy; it cannot make the error impossible.
whyNot.E: Punishment does not remove the design flaw and discourages reporting.

items.objective: Rank safety interventions by strength and recognise a forcing function.

items.stemHtml: A health system compares its hospitals using several indicators. Which of the following indicators is a structure measure in the Donabedian framework?

options.label: A
options.html: The number of registered nurses per occupied bed

options.label: B
options.html: The percentage of patients with stroke who receive a swallow screen before oral intake

options.label: C
options.html: The 30-day mortality rate after admission for heart attack

options.label: D
options.html: The proportion of discharges with a medication list given to the patient

options.label: E
options.html: The rate of pressure injuries acquired in hospital

items.explanationHtml:
Donabedian's triad links structure (the setting and resources: staffing, equipment, buildings, policies) to process (what is done for patients) to outcome (the effect on health). Nurse staffing is a structural attribute of the hospital.

Takeaway: structure = what you have, process = what you do, outcome = what happens to the patient.

whyNot.B: This counts whether a recommended action was done for patients: a process measure.
whyNot.C: Mortality is the end result of care for patients: an outcome measure.
whyNot.D: Giving the medication list is something done for the patient: a process measure.
whyNot.E: Pressure injuries are a health result of care: an outcome measure.

items.objective: Classify quality measures as structure, process or outcome.

items.stemHtml: A hospital launches a project to shorten the average length of stay of patients admitted with pneumonia by starting discharge planning on the first day. Which of the following measures should the team track as a balancing measure?

options.label: A
options.html: The average length of stay for pneumonia

options.label: B
options.html: The percentage of patients with a discharge plan started on day 1

options.label: C
options.html: The number of case managers on staff

options.label: D
options.html: The number of patients with pneumonia admitted per month

options.label: E
options.html: The 30-day readmission rate for pneumonia

items.explanationHtml:
A balancing measure looks for unintended harm elsewhere in the system caused by the improvement. Sending patients home sooner could cause more of them to bounce back, so readmissions are the natural balancing measure for a length-of-stay project.

Takeaway: for each improvement ask, "What could get worse because of this change?" and measure that.

whyNot.A: Length of stay is the measure the project is trying to improve (its main outcome), not a balancing measure.
whyNot.B: This checks whether the change is being carried out: a process measure.
whyNot.C: Staffing is a structure measure.
whyNot.D: Admission volume describes demand; it does not detect harm caused by the change.

items.objective: Identify a balancing measure for a quality improvement project.

items.stemHtml: A hospital plans to replace all of its infusion pumps with a new model next quarter. Before the pumps are used on patients, the safety team wants to identify each way the new process of programming and starting an infusion could fail and to rank those failures by risk. Which of the following methods is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Root-cause analysis

options.label: B
options.html: Pareto analysis of past incident reports

options.label: C
options.html: Failure mode and effects analysis

options.label: D
options.html: Run chart of infusion errors

options.label: E
options.html: Randomised controlled trial of the two pump models

items.explanationHtml:
Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is the prospective tool: map each step of a new process, list the ways each step can fail, and score each failure for severity, occurrence and detectability to set priorities before harm happens. Root-cause analysis is its retrospective counterpart after an event.

Takeaway: before something new goes live → FMEA; after something has gone wrong → RCA.

whyNot.A: Root-cause analysis is retrospective, done after an event; the team wants to look ahead before the pumps are used.
whyNot.B: A Pareto chart ranks categories of past problems, and there are no reports yet for the new pumps.
whyNot.D: A run chart tracks a measure over time; it cannot anticipate failures of a process not yet in use.
whyNot.E: A trial compares outcomes after implementation and is not a method for mapping and ranking potential failures.

items.objective: Distinguish prospective FMEA from retrospective root-cause analysis.

items.stemHtml:
A team performs a failure mode and effects analysis before introducing a new weight-based heparin infusion protocol. Each failure mode is scored from 1 (best) to 10 (worst) for severity, likelihood of occurrence and difficulty of detection.

Failure modeSeverityOccurrenceDetection
Wrong drug concentration chosen from pump library1024
Pump battery fails during transport653
Infusion tubing left clamped565
Weight entered in pounds instead of kilograms946
Alarm volume set too low to hear737

Based on the risk priority number, which failure mode should the team address first?

options.label: A
options.html: Wrong drug concentration chosen from pump library

options.label: B
options.html: Pump battery fails during transport

options.label: C
options.html: Infusion tubing left clamped

options.label: D
options.html: Weight entered in pounds instead of kilograms

options.label: E
options.html: Alarm volume set too low to hear

items.explanationHtml:
The risk priority number (RPN) is severity × occurrence × detection:

  • Wrong concentration: 10 × 2 × 4 = 80
  • Battery failure: 6 × 5 × 3 = 90
  • Tubing clamped: 5 × 6 × 5 = 150
  • Pounds instead of kilograms: 9 × 4 × 6 = 216
  • Alarm volume: 7 × 3 × 7 = 147

The weight-unit error has the highest RPN. (Teams also give attention to any mode with catastrophic severity, but the question asks for the RPN ranking.) A typical fix is a forcing function: the pump or order system accepts weight only in kilograms.

Takeaway: RPN = severity × occurrence × detection; rank by the product, not by any single score.

whyNot.A: This mode has the highest severity score (10) but its RPN is only 10 × 2 × 4 = 80.
whyNot.B: Its RPN is 6 × 5 × 3 = 90, well below the highest.
whyNot.C: This mode has the highest occurrence score (6), but its RPN of 150 is lower than 216.
whyNot.E: This mode is hardest to detect (7), but its RPN is 7 × 3 × 7 = 147.

items.objective: Calculate and use risk priority numbers in an FMEA.

items.stemHtml: A clinic tracks the percentage of patients with diabetes whose glycated haemoglobin is measured on time each month. A control chart of 24 months shows every point within the control limits with no runs or trends, around a mean of 62%, well below the clinic's target of 90%. The medical director proposes reviewing each month in which the value falls below 60% to find out what went wrong that month. Which of the following is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: Each low month reflects special-cause variation that should be investigated

options.label: B
options.html: The process is performing acceptably because it is in statistical control

options.label: C
options.html: The control limits should be narrowed until the low months fall outside them

options.label: D
options.html: The variation is common cause, so the underlying process should be redesigned

options.label: E
options.html: A randomised trial is required before any change is made to the process

items.explanationHtml:
A process whose points all lie within the control limits without non-random patterns is in statistical control: its variation is common cause, the noise built into the way the work is designed. Investigating individual low months will find stories but not causes, and reacting to them ("tampering") tends to make performance more variable.

Because the stable average (62%) is unacceptable, the right approach is to redesign the process itself (for example, standing orders for nurses to order the test, automated reminders) and test the change with PDSA cycles.

Takeaway: stable but bad → change the system for everyone; a point outside the limits → look for the special cause.

whyNot.A: Points within the limits without patterns are not special causes; investigating each low month is tampering with noise.
whyNot.B: A stable process can be stably poor; 62% is far below the 90% target.
whyNot.C: Control limits come from the data's own variation; moving them to create signals is not valid.
whyNot.E: QI tests changes with PDSA cycles and charts; a trial is not needed to improve a local process.

items.objective: Differentiate common-cause from special-cause variation and the response to each.

items.stemHtml: A physician enters an order for oral methotrexate 7.5 mg daily for a patient with rheumatoid arthritis; the intended regimen was 7.5 mg once weekly. The hospital pharmacist notices the frequency during order verification, calls the physician, and the order is corrected before any dose is dispensed. Which of the following best describes this event?

options.label: A
options.html: Adverse drug event

options.label: B
options.html: Near miss

options.label: C
options.html: Sentinel event

options.label: D
options.html: No-harm event

options.label: E
options.html: Never event

items.explanationHtml:
A near miss is an error that is caught before it reaches the patient. A daily rather than weekly methotrexate order is a dangerous error, and the pharmacist's check intercepted it. It should still be reported: near misses reveal the same weaknesses (here, order entry that allows daily methotrexate without a warning) as harmful events, without the harm.

Takeaway: caught before reaching the patient = near miss; reached the patient but no harm = no-harm event; harm = adverse event.

whyNot.A: No dose reached the patient and no harm occurred, so there was no adverse event.
whyNot.C: A sentinel event involves death, permanent harm or severe temporary harm; this error caused none.
whyNot.D: A no-harm event is an error that reaches the patient without causing harm; this one was stopped before dispensing.
whyNot.E: Never events are specific serious events such as wrong-site surgery; an intercepted prescribing error is not one.

items.objective: Classify a patient safety event as a near miss.

items.stemHtml: A first-year resident prescribes a full standard dose of a renally excreted antibiotic to a patient with severely reduced kidney function. The resident entered the order exactly as intended but did not know that the drug's dose must be reduced in kidney failure. The error is classified by type. Which of the following best describes this error?

options.label: A
options.html: A slip

options.label: B
options.html: A lapse

options.label: C
options.html: A violation

options.label: D
options.html: A latent condition

options.label: E
options.html: A mistake

items.explanationHtml:
Errors in carrying out a correct plan are slips (attention failures) and lapses (memory failures). A mistake is an error in the plan itself, arising from a gap in knowledge or a misapplied rule. The resident executed the order perfectly; the plan was wrong because of missing knowledge.

Mistakes are reduced by decision support (renal dose alerts in order entry), pharmacist review and supervision; slips and lapses by design changes such as forcing functions and checklists.

Takeaway: right plan done wrong = slip or lapse; wrong plan done right = mistake.

whyNot.A: A slip is a correct plan carried out wrongly through inattention; here the order was carried out as intended.
whyNot.B: A lapse is a forgotten step in a correct plan; the plan itself was wrong.
whyNot.C: A violation is a deliberate departure from a rule; the resident did not know the rule existed.
whyNot.D: A latent condition is a system weakness built in upstream, not the resident's own prescribing decision.

items.objective: Distinguish slips, lapses and mistakes.

items.stemHtml: An emergency physician cared for two patients with aortic dissection during the previous week. Today a 34-year-old man arrives with burning epigastric discomfort after large meals that is relieved by antacids, normal vital signs and equal blood pressures in both arms. The physician feels strongly that dissection is likely and orders CT angiography. Which cognitive bias best explains the physician's estimate of the probability of dissection?

options.label: A
options.html: Availability bias

options.label: B
options.html: Anchoring

options.label: C
options.html: Premature closure

options.label: D
options.html: Confirmation bias

options.label: E
options.html: Framing effect

items.explanationHtml:
Availability bias is judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Recent, vivid or memorable cases inflate the estimated probability of the same diagnosis in the next patient, even when the clinical picture (typical reflux symptoms, normal findings) makes it unlikely.

Takeaway: "I just saw two of these" is not evidence about this patient; anchor on the base rate and the findings.

whyNot.B: Anchoring is clinging to an initial impression of this patient despite new data; the estimate here is driven by memorable recent cases.
whyNot.C: Premature closure is ending the search after a plausible diagnosis; the physician is widening the search, not ending it.
whyNot.D: Confirmation bias is seeking data that support a favoured diagnosis; the error is the inflated prior probability from recent cases.
whyNot.E: A framing effect arises from how information is presented by others; nothing in the presentation framed the case as dissection.

items.objective: Recognise availability bias in diagnostic reasoning.

items.stemHtml: An intensive care unit audits 50 central venous catheter insertions against a five-element insertion bundle. Each element on its own was performed in at least 90% of insertions (average across elements 94%), but all five elements were performed together in 30 insertions. Using all-or-none measurement, what is the unit's bundle compliance?
items.explanationHtml:
All-or-none (composite) measurement counts an insertion as compliant only when every element of the bundle was done, because bundle elements are expected to work together. Compliance = 30 ÷ 50 = 60%.

Reporting each element separately (90–94%) hides the fact that 2 in 5 patients missed at least one element.

Takeaway: bundle compliance = insertions with every element ÷ all insertions.

whyNot.A: 30 is the number of fully compliant insertions, not the percentage of 50.
whyNot.B: 40% is the proportion of insertions that missed at least one element (20 of 50).
whyNot.D: 90% is the lowest single-element rate, which ignores insertions that missed a different element.
whyNot.E: 94% is the average element compliance, which is not how an all-or-none bundle is scored.

items.objective: Calculate all-or-none bundle compliance.

items.stemHtml: A primary care clinic maps every step of a typical visit and finds that patients spend 70 of the 90 minutes between arrival and departure waiting for a room, a nurse or a form, steps that add nothing for the patient. The team then redesigns the flow to remove these steps. Which improvement approach is the team using?

options.label: A
options.html: Six Sigma

options.label: B
options.html: Failure mode and effects analysis

options.label: C
options.html: Root-cause analysis

options.label: D
options.html: Benchmarking

options.label: E
options.html: Lean

items.explanationHtml:
Lean, derived from manufacturing, maps the value stream of a process and removes waste: waiting, unnecessary steps, transport, rework and excess inventory, so that every remaining step adds value for the patient. Six Sigma instead targets variation and defects.

Takeaway: remove waste → Lean; reduce variation and defects → Six Sigma.

whyNot.A: Six Sigma focuses on reducing variation and defects with statistical tools, not primarily on removing wasteful waits.
whyNot.B: FMEA predicts how a process could fail and ranks risks; it is not a method for removing waiting time.
whyNot.C: Root-cause analysis investigates a specific adverse event after it occurs.
whyNot.D: Benchmarking compares performance with other organisations; it does not itself map and remove steps.

items.objective: Recognise Lean methods for removing waste in a care process.

items.stemHtml: A hospital's electronic order system and pharmacy shelf labels display certain drug names with selected letters in capitals, such as "hydrOXYzine" and "hydrALAZINE". This practice is primarily intended to reduce which type of medication error?

options.label: A
options.html: Giving the correct drug to the wrong patient

options.label: B
options.html: Calculating a weight-based dose incorrectly

options.label: C
options.html: Prescribing two drugs that interact

options.label: D
options.html: Selecting a drug whose name looks like the intended drug

options.label: E
options.html: Giving a drug to which the patient is allergic

items.explanationHtml:
Tall-man lettering uses capital letters to highlight the parts of look-alike/sound-alike drug names that differ, making a wrong selection from a list or shelf less likely. It is a modest, intermediate-strength measure that works alongside barcode scanning and separate storage of confusable drugs.

Takeaway: mixed-case drug names target look-alike name confusion.

whyNot.A: Patient identification errors are addressed by two identifiers and barcode scanning, not by drug-name formatting.
whyNot.B: Dose calculation errors are reduced by order-entry dose checks and smart pumps.
whyNot.C: Interaction checking in order entry and pharmacist review address interactions.
whyNot.E: Allergy errors are caught by documented allergies and order-entry alerts.

items.objective: Identify the purpose of tall-man lettering in medication safety.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is treated in the intensive care unit with an intravenous insulin infusion for diabetic ketoacidosis. When he improves he is moved to a medical ward; the infusion is stopped on transfer, but no subcutaneous basal insulin is ordered, and his glucose rises sharply overnight. Which of the following processes is specifically designed to prevent this type of error?

options.label: A
options.html: Barcode scanning at medication administration

options.label: B
options.html: Medication reconciliation at the time of transfer

options.label: C
options.html: Order-entry dose-range checking

options.label: D
options.html: Tall-man lettering of insulin products

options.label: E
options.html: Independent double check of insulin doses

items.explanationHtml:
Transitions between care settings are where medicines are most often omitted, duplicated or changed by accident. Medication reconciliation compares the patient's current medicines (here, the IV insulin and the home basal insulin) with the new orders at every transition and resolves each difference. Stopping an insulin infusion without starting basal insulin is a classic omission it is designed to catch.

Takeaway: omissions at admission, transfer and discharge are prevented by reconciling the lists at every transition.

whyNot.A: Barcode scanning confirms that a given dose matches an existing order and patient; it cannot detect an order that was never written.
whyNot.C: Dose-range checks flag an order whose dose is out of range, not an omitted order.
whyNot.D: Tall-man lettering reduces look-alike name confusion, which played no part here.
whyNot.E: A double check verifies a dose about to be given; with no order, there was nothing to check.

items.objective: Explain the role of medication reconciliation at care transitions.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who has worked as a warehouse supervisor for 20 years develops end-stage renal disease from diabetic nephropathy and starts maintenance haemodialysis. His household income is too high for Medicaid in his state, and he wants to know whether a public programme will help pay for his dialysis. Which programme is he most likely eligible for?

options.label: A
options.html: Medicaid

options.label: B
options.html: The Children's Health Insurance Program

options.label: C
options.html: Medicare

options.label: D
options.html: TRICARE

options.label: E
options.html: The Indian Health Service

items.explanationHtml:
Medicare covers people aged 65 or older and some younger groups: those who have received Social Security disability benefits for 24 months, people with end-stage renal disease who need dialysis or a transplant (if they or a spouse have enough work history), and people with ALS. Eligibility is not based on income.

Takeaway: under 65 but on dialysis → Medicare, whatever the income.

whyNot.A: Medicaid eligibility depends on income and category, and his income is above his state's limit.
whyNot.B: CHIP covers children in families with modest incomes, not a 46-year-old adult.
whyNot.D: TRICARE covers military service members, retirees and their families; nothing suggests military service.
whyNot.E: The Indian Health Service serves members of federally recognised tribes, which is not described.

items.objective: Identify the groups younger than 65 who qualify for Medicare.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with traditional Medicare (Parts A and B) is started on an oral anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation at an outpatient visit. She has no other coverage, and her income is too high for Medicaid. She asks which type of coverage would help pay for this prescription. Which of the following is the most accurate answer?

options.label: A
options.html: Medicare Part A

options.label: B
options.html: Medicare Part B

options.label: C
options.html: Medicaid

options.label: D
options.html: A supplemental (Medigap) policy

options.label: E
options.html: A Medicare Part D drug plan

items.explanationHtml:
Outpatient prescription drugs are covered by Medicare Part D, which is delivered through private plans approved by Medicare (either a stand-alone drug plan alongside traditional Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage). Part A is hospital insurance; Part B is medical insurance for physician and outpatient care.

Takeaway: outpatient pills for a Medicare beneficiary → Part D.

whyNot.A: Part A covers inpatient hospital, limited skilled nursing, hospice and some home health care, not outpatient prescriptions.
whyNot.B: Part B covers physician and outpatient services and some clinician-administered drugs, but not most self-administered outpatient pills.
whyNot.C: Her income is above the Medicaid limit, so she does not qualify.
whyNot.D: Medigap policies sold today help with Part A and B cost-sharing but do not include outpatient drug coverage.

items.objective: Identify which part of Medicare covers outpatient prescription drugs.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old widow with advanced dementia can no longer be cared for at home and moves permanently to a nursing home for help with bathing, dressing, eating and supervision. She has no skilled medical needs. After her savings are used up on nursing home fees, which of the following is the most likely payer for her ongoing care?

options.label: A
options.html: Medicaid

options.label: B
options.html: Medicare Part A

options.label: C
options.html: Medicare Part B

options.label: D
options.html: Medicare Part D

options.label: E
options.html: Her former employer's retiree health plan

items.explanationHtml:
Medicaid is the largest payer of long-term nursing home care in the US. Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care (help with activities of daily living), only for limited skilled nursing or rehabilitation after a hospital stay. Many older adults pay privately until their assets fall to their state's Medicaid limits ("spend-down") and then qualify.

Takeaway: long-term custodial nursing home care → Medicaid (after spend-down), not Medicare.

whyNot.B: Part A pays only for a limited period of skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying hospital stay, not for long-term custodial care.
whyNot.C: Part B covers physician and outpatient services, not room and board in a nursing home.
whyNot.D: Part D covers outpatient prescription drugs, not nursing home care.
whyNot.E: Retiree health plans generally supplement Medicare and rarely pay for long-term custodial care.

items.objective: Identify Medicaid as the main payer of long-term nursing home care.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl lives with her parents, who both work for small businesses that do not offer family health coverage. Their household income is slightly too high for the girl to qualify for Medicaid, and they cannot afford a private family plan. Which programme was designed for children in this situation?

options.label: A
options.html: Medicare

options.label: B
options.html: The Children's Health Insurance Program

options.label: C
options.html: EMTALA

options.label: D
options.html: The Vaccines for Children program

options.label: E
options.html: Title X family planning grants

items.explanationHtml:
The Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) is jointly funded by the federal government and the states and covers children in families whose income is above Medicaid limits but too low to afford private insurance. States may run it as part of Medicaid, as a separate programme or as a combination.

Takeaway: family income just above Medicaid limits, child uninsured → CHIP.

whyNot.A: Medicare covers older adults and specific disability groups, not healthy children.
whyNot.C: EMTALA requires emergency screening and stabilisation; it is not a coverage programme.
whyNot.D: Vaccines for Children supplies vaccines only, not general health coverage.
whyNot.E: Title X funds family planning services, not comprehensive coverage for children.

items.objective: Describe the population served by CHIP.

items.stemHtml: A manufacturer learns that a batch of implantable insulin pumps can deliver an unintended extra dose because of a software defect. Which federal agency is primarily responsible for overseeing the recall of these devices?

options.label: A
options.html: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

options.label: B
options.html: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

options.label: C
options.html: The state medical board

options.label: D
options.html: The Food and Drug Administration

options.label: E
options.html: The National Institutes of Health

items.explanationHtml:
The FDA approves or clears drugs, biologics and medical devices, monitors them after marketing (including through adverse-event reports) and oversees recalls. The CDC handles disease surveillance and prevention; CMS runs Medicare and oversees Medicaid.

Takeaway: drugs, vaccines and devices → FDA.

whyNot.A: The CDC leads surveillance and outbreak response; it does not regulate medical devices.
whyNot.B: CMS administers payment programmes and hospital conditions of participation, not device safety.
whyNot.C: State medical boards license and discipline physicians; they have no role in device recalls.
whyNot.E: The NIH funds and conducts research; it does not regulate products.

items.objective: Identify the regulatory role of the FDA for medical devices.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman finishes graduate school and loses her student health plan. She is married, lives with her husband in another city, and is not claimed as a dependent on her parents' tax return. Her mother's employer plan offers coverage for children. Which statement about her eligibility to join her mother's plan is correct?

options.label: A
options.html: She may enrol as a dependent until she turns 26

options.label: B
options.html: She is ineligible because she is married

options.label: C
options.html: She is eligible only if she lives with her parents

options.label: D
options.html: She is eligible only if her parents claim her for taxes

options.label: E
options.html: She is ineligible because she is no longer a student

items.explanationHtml:
The Affordable Care Act requires plans that offer dependent coverage to let adult children stay on or join a parent's plan until age 26, regardless of marriage, residence, student status, financial dependence or eligibility for their own employer's plan.

Takeaway: under 26 → can be on a parent's plan, with few strings attached.

whyNot.B: Under the ACA, marriage does not end eligibility for dependent coverage before age 26.
whyNot.C: Residence with the parents is not a condition for coverage up to age 26.
whyNot.D: Tax-dependent status is not required for coverage of an adult child under 26.
whyNot.E: Student status is not required; the rule depends only on age for plans that offer dependent coverage.

items.objective: State the ACA rule on dependent coverage for young adults.

items.stemHtml: A state requires children to receive certain vaccines before entering public school, with exemptions for children who have a documented medical contraindication. A parent challenges the law, arguing that the state has no authority to require vaccination. Which of the following is the main legal basis for the state's requirement?

options.label: A
options.html: Federal Medicaid funding rules

options.label: B
options.html: The state's police power to protect public health

options.label: C
options.html: The Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act

options.label: D
options.html: The HIPAA Privacy Rule

options.label: E
options.html: CDC regulations on interstate quarantine

items.explanationHtml:
Public-health laws such as school vaccine requirements, notifiable-disease reporting and isolation orders rest on the states' police power, their inherent authority to protect the health, safety and welfare of the population. The Supreme Court upheld a compulsory vaccination law on this basis in Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905). States set the vaccines required and the exemptions; all permit medical exemptions.

Takeaway: state public-health mandates come from state police power; federal quarantine authority is limited to interstate and international spread.

whyNot.A: Medicaid rules govern payment for care, not a state's authority to set school-entry requirements.
whyNot.C: EMTALA concerns emergency department screening and stabilisation and has no bearing on vaccination.
whyNot.D: HIPAA protects health information; it does not authorise vaccine mandates.
whyNot.E: CDC quarantine powers cover interstate and international spread, not state school-entry laws.

items.objective: Identify the legal basis of state public-health mandates such as school vaccination.

items.stemHtml: A primary care group agrees to receive a fixed monthly payment for each person enrolled with it, regardless of how many visits, tests or referrals each person uses. Which incentive does this payment arrangement create for the group?

options.label: A
options.html: To increase the number of visits and procedures

options.label: B
options.html: To lengthen hospital stays

options.label: C
options.html: To enrol as many patients with chronic illness as possible

options.label: D
options.html: No financial incentive regarding the amount of care

options.label: E
options.html: To limit services, with a risk of underuse

items.explanationHtml:
Under capitation, a provider is paid a fixed amount per enrolled person per period and bears the financial risk for the care that person uses. The incentive is to keep patients healthy and avoid unnecessary services, but the danger is underuse of needed care and avoidance of high-risk patients (which risk adjustment and quality measures try to counter).

Takeaway: paid per person → fewer services; paid per service → more services.

whyNot.A: Rewarding more services is the incentive of fee-for-service, not of a fixed per-person payment.
whyNot.B: Longer stays add cost without adding revenue under a fixed payment, so there is no such incentive.
whyNot.C: Sicker enrolees use more services for the same payment, so the incentive is to avoid them unless payments are risk-adjusted.
whyNot.D: Unlike salary, capitation makes the group bear the cost of each extra service, so there is a strong incentive.

items.objective: Predict the incentive created by capitation.

items.stemHtml: Under Medicare's inpatient prospective payment system, a hospital receives a set amount for each admission based on the patient's diagnosis-related group, whatever the actual length of stay or services used. Which behaviour does this payment method most directly encourage?

options.label: A
options.html: Ordering additional inpatient tests

options.label: B
options.html: Keeping patients until all follow-up tests are complete

options.label: C
options.html: Shortening hospital length of stay

options.label: D
options.html: Reducing the number of admissions

options.label: E
options.html: Avoiding all outpatient follow-up

items.explanationHtml:
With a fixed payment per admission determined by the diagnosis-related group (DRG), the hospital keeps the difference if the stay costs less than the payment and loses money if it costs more. The incentive is efficient, shorter stays. Risks include premature discharge and coding patients into higher-paying groups (upcoding). Because extra admissions bring extra payments, readmission penalties were added to counter that incentive.

Takeaway: paid per stay → shorter stays.

whyNot.A: Extra inpatient tests add cost without raising the fixed payment, so they are discouraged.
whyNot.B: Longer stays reduce the hospital's margin under a fixed per-admission payment.
whyNot.D: Each admission brings a payment, so the system does not itself discourage admissions.
whyNot.E: Outpatient follow-up is paid separately and is not what the DRG payment targets.

items.objective: Predict the incentive created by DRG-based prospective payment.

items.stemHtml: After a large employer removes all copayments for emergency department visits, the number of visits for minor complaints such as mild colds and small cuts rises sharply among its employees, while the number of serious emergencies is unchanged. Which economic concept best explains this change?

options.label: A
options.html: Moral hazard

options.label: B
options.html: Adverse selection

options.label: C
options.html: Supplier-induced demand

options.label: D
options.html: Risk pooling

options.label: E
options.html: Economies of scale

items.explanationHtml:
Moral hazard is the change in behaviour that follows insurance: when people no longer pay the full price of care, they use more of it, especially discretionary or low-value care. Cost-sharing (copayments, coinsurance, deductibles) is the usual counter, though high cost-sharing can also deter needed care.

Takeaway: insured people using more care because it is cheaper to them = moral hazard.

whyNot.B: Adverse selection concerns who chooses to buy insurance; here the same insured group changed its use of care.
whyNot.C: Supplier-induced demand is created by providers recommending more care; the change came from patients' lower price.
whyNot.D: Risk pooling is the spreading of costs across a group; it does not explain increased use when the price falls.
whyNot.E: Economies of scale are falling costs per unit as output grows; they do not explain patient behaviour.

items.objective: Define moral hazard in health insurance.

items.stemHtml: A new voluntary health plan is offered to the residents of a county at a single price for everyone. In its first year, people with chronic illnesses enrol at much higher rates than healthy people. Claims exceed expectations, the plan raises its price, more healthy enrolees leave, and the price rises again. Which concept best describes this sequence?

options.label: A
options.html: Moral hazard

options.label: B
options.html: Community rating

options.label: C
options.html: Cost-shifting

options.label: D
options.html: Risk adjustment

options.label: E
options.html: Adverse selection

items.explanationHtml:
Adverse selection occurs when people who expect high health care costs are more likely to buy coverage than those who expect low costs. The pool becomes sicker and costlier, premiums rise, healthier members leave, and the cycle can repeat (a "death spiral"). Remedies include requirements or incentives for everyone to enrol, subsidies, group coverage through employers, limited enrolment periods and risk adjustment.

Takeaway: who buys insurance = adverse selection; how insured people behave = moral hazard.

whyNot.A: Moral hazard is increased use of care after insurance; the problem here is who chose to enrol.
whyNot.B: Community rating (one price for all) creates the setting, but the spiral itself is adverse selection.
whyNot.C: Cost-shifting is charging some payers more to cover losses from others, which is not what happened.
whyNot.D: Risk adjustment is a remedy that pays plans more for sicker enrolees, not the problem itself.

items.objective: Explain adverse selection and the insurance premium spiral.

items.stemHtml:
An economic evaluation compares a new drug with standard therapy for chronic heart failure over a patient's lifetime (all values per patient, fictional).

StrategyLifetime costQuality-adjusted life-years (QALYs)
Standard therapy$20,0004.0
New drug$50,0004.6

What is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of the new drug compared with standard therapy (rounded to the nearest dollar)?

options.label: A
options.html: $6,522 per QALY

options.label: B
options.html: $10,870 per QALY

options.label: C
options.html: $30,000 per QALY

options.label: D
options.html: $50,000 per QALY

options.label: E
options.html: $83,333 per QALY

items.explanationHtml:
ICER = (costnew − coststandard) ÷ (QALYnew − QALYstandard) = ($50,000 − $20,000) ÷ (4.6 − 4.0) = $30,000 ÷ 0.6 = $50,000 per QALY gained.

The ICER uses the differences in cost and effect. Dividing a strategy's own cost by its own QALYs gives an average cost-effectiveness ratio, which does not answer whether the extra money buys enough extra health.

Takeaway: ICER = ΔCost ÷ ΔEffect.

whyNot.A: This divides the cost difference by the new drug's total QALYs (4.6) instead of the QALY difference.
whyNot.B: This is the new drug's average ratio ($50,000 ÷ 4.6), not an incremental comparison.
whyNot.C: $30,000 is the cost difference alone; it has not been divided by the 0.6 QALY gained.
whyNot.E: This divides the new drug's total cost ($50,000) by the QALY difference instead of the cost difference.

items.objective: Calculate an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio.

items.stemHtml: Researchers compare two treatments for knee osteoarthritis. Costs are measured in dollars, and health effects are measured in quality-adjusted life-years, combining length of life with health-related quality of life. The result is reported as additional cost per quality-adjusted life-year gained. Which type of economic evaluation is this?

options.label: A
options.html: Cost-minimisation analysis

options.label: B
options.html: Cost-utility analysis

options.label: C
options.html: Cost-benefit analysis

options.label: D
options.html: Budget impact analysis

options.label: E
options.html: Cost-of-illness analysis

items.explanationHtml:
Economic evaluations differ by how outcomes are measured. Cost-utility analysis uses QALYs (or similar utility-weighted measures) and reports cost per QALY gained, allowing comparison across diseases. Cost-effectiveness analysis in the narrow sense uses natural units (life-years, cases detected); cost-benefit analysis converts outcomes to money; cost-minimisation compares costs of options with equivalent outcomes.

Takeaway: outcome in QALYs = cost-utility; outcome in money = cost-benefit.

whyNot.A: Cost-minimisation compares costs only, after showing outcomes are equivalent; here outcomes are measured and differ.
whyNot.C: Cost-benefit analysis values health effects in money; here they are in QALYs.
whyNot.D: Budget impact analysis estimates total spending for a payer, without a health-outcome ratio.
whyNot.E: Cost-of-illness studies describe the economic burden of a disease, not a comparison of treatments.

items.objective: Classify a type of economic evaluation by its outcome measure.

items.stemHtml: A woman's hypothetical health plan has a yearly deductible of $1,500, then 20% coinsurance, and an in-network out-of-pocket maximum of $4,000; all of her deductible and coinsurance payments count toward the maximum. Earlier this year she paid $1,000 toward her deductible for office visits and imaging. She is then hospitalised in network, with an allowed charge of $30,000. How much will she pay for this hospitalisation (excluding premiums)?
items.explanationHtml:
Work through the rules in order:

  • Remaining deductible: $1,500 − $1,000 = $500.
  • Coinsurance: 20% × ($30,000 − $500) = $5,900.
  • Uncapped cost for this stay: $500 + $5,900 = $6,400.
  • But she has already paid $1,000 this year, so the out-of-pocket maximum leaves room for only $4,000 − $1,000 = $3,000.

The plan pays everything above the maximum for the rest of the year.

Takeaway: apply the remaining deductible, then coinsurance, then cap the year's total at the out-of-pocket maximum, counting what was already paid.

whyNot.B: $4,000 is the full yearly maximum; it ignores the $1,000 she had already paid toward it.
whyNot.C: $6,000 is 20% of the whole bill, ignoring the deductible and the out-of-pocket maximum.
whyNot.D: $6,400 applies the remaining deductible and coinsurance correctly but ignores the out-of-pocket maximum.
whyNot.E: $7,200 applies the full $1,500 deductible again and ignores both her earlier payments and the maximum.

items.objective: Calculate patient cost-sharing with a deductible, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward on the first day after repair of a hip fracture. A telephone order for intravenous hydromorphone, intended as 0.5 mg, was transcribed as ".5 mg", and the night nurse gave 5 mg 40 minutes ago. He is now difficult to arouse. Respirations are 6/min and shallow, pulse is 64/min, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Pupils are pinpoint. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Call the patient's daughter to tell her about the error

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain an arterial blood gas before giving any drug

options.label: C
options.html: Support ventilation and give intravenous naloxone

options.label: D
options.html: Complete an incident report while the details are fresh

options.label: E
options.html: Arrange transfer to the intensive care unit before treatment

items.explanationHtml:
The first duty after any error is to the patient: assess and treat the harm it caused. This man has opioid toxicity with hypoventilation and hypoxaemia after a tenfold overdose. Open the airway, give oxygen and bag-mask ventilation as needed, and give naloxone intravenously, titrated to restore adequate breathing. Because hydromorphone may outlast a single naloxone dose, he needs close monitoring and possibly repeat doses or an infusion.

Once he is safe, the attending is informed, the error is disclosed to the patient, an incident report is filed and the system is reviewed.

Takeaway: after an error, treat the patient first; disclosure, reporting and analysis come next.

whyNot.A: Disclosure is required but comes after the patient has been made safe; he is hypoventilating now.
whyNot.B: The diagnosis is clinically clear; waiting for a blood gas delays treatment of life-threatening respiratory depression.
whyNot.D: Reporting matters, but never before treating the patient's immediate harm.
whyNot.E: Treatment should start at the bedside immediately; transfer may follow if he needs ongoing monitoring.

items.objective: Prioritise treatment of harm caused by a medication error before disclosure and reporting.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man on the orthopaedic ward received 5 mg of intravenous hydromorphone instead of the intended 0.5 mg because a telephone order was transcribed without a leading zero. He needed naloxone and close monitoring overnight and is now alert and breathing normally. He knows he "had trouble breathing" but has not been told why. The resident and the attending go to see him. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement?

options.label: A
options.html: "You had a strong reaction to your pain medicine last night, but you are fine now."

options.label: B
options.html: "The night nurse misread the order and gave too much, so she is being retrained."

options.label: C
options.html: "We are still reviewing the event, so we can't say anything until the review ends."

options.label: D
options.html: "We made an error: you got ten times the intended dose of a pain medicine, and I am sorry."

options.label: E
options.html: "Since you recovered completely, there is no need to worry about last night."

items.explanationHtml:
Patients should be told promptly and honestly about errors that reach them. Good disclosure states plainly that an error occurred and what it was, explains its effects and what was done, includes a sincere apology, and commits to explaining how recurrence will be prevented and to sharing the results of the review. It avoids euphemisms, speculation and blaming individuals.

The keyed statement opens the conversation correctly; the physician then explains the effects, what the hospital is changing, and who he can contact with questions.

Takeaway: say what happened, say sorry, say what you are doing about it, and do not wait for the investigation.

whyNot.A: Calling a tenfold overdose a "reaction" is a misleading euphemism that hides the error.
whyNot.B: Blaming an individual is inaccurate (the transcription system failed too) and undermines trust in the team.
whyNot.C: Disclosure should not wait for the investigation; tell him what is known now and promise follow-up.
whyNot.E: This gives false reassurance and avoids telling him what happened.

items.objective: Disclose a medication error honestly with an apology.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man received a tenfold overdose of intravenous hydromorphone because a telephone order for 0.5 mg was transcribed as ".5 mg" and read as 5 mg. He developed severe respiratory depression that required naloxone and overnight monitoring, then recovered. The error has been disclosed to him and reported through the hospital's incident system. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the hospital in analysing this event?

options.label: A
options.html: A disciplinary review of the nurse who gave the dose

options.label: B
options.html: A root-cause analysis by an interdisciplinary team

options.label: C
options.html: A failure mode and effects analysis of the event

options.label: D
options.html: A survey of patient satisfaction on the ward

options.label: E
options.html: A review of the transcribing clerk's training record

items.explanationHtml:
A serious event that caused severe temporary harm warrants a root-cause analysis (RCA): a retrospective, structured review by an interdisciplinary team (physicians, nurses, pharmacy, risk management) that asks what happened, why it happened and what will prevent it, focusing on systems rather than blame. Here likely findings include telephone orders for high-alert drugs without read-back, transcription without a leading zero, and no dose-range check. Strong actions would be order entry with dose limits for opioids and removing telephone orders for high-alert drugs except in emergencies.

Takeaway: after a serious event → interdisciplinary, system-focused RCA with an action plan.

whyNot.A: A disciplinary focus addresses one person, not the transcription and ordering system that allowed the error, and discourages reporting.
whyNot.C: FMEA is a prospective tool for a process not yet in use; this event has already happened.
whyNot.D: Satisfaction surveys do not explain why this error occurred.
whyNot.E: Looking at one person's training stops at the individual and misses the latent causes.

items.objective: Choose root-cause analysis to investigate a serious adverse event.

items.stemHtml: A medical ward has had more catheter-associated urinary tract infections than other wards in the hospital. The nurse manager and a hospitalist form a team to reduce unnecessary indwelling urinary catheters. Which of the following is a process measure for this project?

options.label: A
options.html: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections per 1,000 catheter-days

options.label: B
options.html: Number of bladder scanners available on the ward

options.label: C
options.html: Rate of urinary retention needing re-catheterisation

options.label: D
options.html: Length of stay of patients on the ward

options.label: E
options.html: Percentage of catheterised patients whose catheter indication is reviewed each day

items.explanationHtml:
A process measure tracks whether the planned care steps are actually carried out: here, whether the need for each catheter is reviewed every day. Process measures respond quickly and show whether the change is being used; the CAUTI rate is the outcome; scanners are structure; re-catheterisation for retention is the balancing measure.
