Takeaway: a good QI project tracks a family of measures: outcome, process and balancing.

whyNot.A: Infection rate is the health result the project aims to change: an outcome measure.
whyNot.B: Available equipment is a structure measure.
whyNot.C: This watches for harm caused by removing catheters: a balancing measure.
whyNot.D: Length of stay is an overall outcome, not a measure of whether the catheter process is being followed.

items.objective: Identify a process measure in a quality improvement project.

items.stemHtml:
A medical ward team trying to reduce urinary catheter use introduces a nurse-driven protocol for catheter removal at the start of month 11. They plot the monthly catheter utilisation ratio (catheter-days ÷ patient-days). The median of the 10 baseline months is 0.25.

MonthUtilisation ratio
10.24
20.26
30.23
40.25
50.27
60.24
70.25
80.26
90.23
100.25
110.21
120.20
130.22
140.19
150.21
160.20
170.18

Which conclusion is best supported by these data?

options.label: A
options.html: A shift below the baseline median shows non-random change after the protocol

options.label: B
options.html: No conclusion is possible without a randomised control ward

options.label: C
options.html: The variation after month 10 is consistent with chance alone

options.label: D
options.html: The data show a trend of steadily falling values since month 11

options.label: E
options.html: The protocol has been shown to lower the infection rate

items.explanationHtml:
On a run chart, a shift is six or more consecutive points all above or all below the median. Months 11–17 (0.21, 0.20, 0.22, 0.19, 0.21, 0.20, 0.18) are seven consecutive points below the baseline median of 0.25, a signal of non-random change that coincides with the protocol. This is the expected evidence in QI; a randomised trial is not needed to know that a local process has changed.

It is not a trend (five or more consecutive increases or decreases), and the chart shows catheter use, not infections.

Takeaway: six or more points on one side of the median = shift = non-random change.

whyNot.B: Run-chart rules can detect non-random change in a local process without a randomised comparison.
whyNot.C: Seven consecutive points below the median would be very unlikely by chance; it meets the shift rule.
whyNot.D: The values after month 11 go up and down, so there is no run of five consecutive decreases.
whyNot.E: Catheter use is a process measure; the infection outcome was not shown in these data.

items.objective: Interpret a shift on a run chart.

items.stemHtml: A nurse-driven protocol for removing unneeded urinary catheters has been tested on one medical ward for 2 months. Catheter use has fallen, run-chart data show a shift below the baseline median, and urinary retention needing re-catheterisation is unchanged. Nurses on other wards and on night shifts have not yet used the protocol. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the team?

options.label: A
options.html: Require the protocol on every ward at once and stop collecting data

options.label: B
options.html: Stop the project because its aim has been reached

options.label: C
options.html: Test the protocol on another ward and night shifts while measuring

options.label: D
options.html: Run a randomised trial before using the protocol anywhere else

options.label: E
options.html: Replace the protocol with an education campaign on catheter use

items.explanationHtml:
In the Model for Improvement, a change that works in one small test is next tested under wider conditions (another ward, night shifts, different staff) in further PDSA cycles before it is spread across the organisation. Measurement continues throughout, including the balancing measure (re-catheterisation for retention), so that problems in the new setting are found early. Spreading everywhere at once, or stopping measurement, loses this learning.

Takeaway: after a successful small test, scale up step by step and keep measuring.

whyNot.A: Spreading at once without further testing skips learning about new conditions, and stopping measurement means problems would go unseen.
whyNot.B: Success on one ward is not success for the hospital; the gains also need to be sustained.
whyNot.D: A trial is not needed to improve a local process that has worked under test; further PDSA cycles are the method.
whyNot.E: Education is a weaker change than a protocol built into the work, and the protocol is working.

items.objective: Choose the next PDSA step after a successful small test of change.

items.stemHtml:
An 81-year-old man is ready for discharge home after 4 days in hospital for a heart failure exacerbation. Warfarin for atrial fibrillation was held on admission because his INR was 4.6 (therapeutic range 2.0–3.0); today it is 2.2. The team reviews his medication lists.

Home medicines before admissionDraft discharge list
Furosemide 40 mg dailyFurosemide 40 mg twice daily
Metoprolol succinate 50 mg dailyMetoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
Lisinopril 10 mg dailyLisinopril 10 mg daily
Warfarin 5 mg daily(not listed)

The chart has no note explaining the change in furosemide or the omission of warfarin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before discharge?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge him with the draft list and let his primary care physician decide

options.label: B
options.html: Confirm and document the plan for warfarin and the furosemide change

options.label: C
options.html: Tell him to restart all of his home medicines at their usual doses

options.label: D
options.html: Replace warfarin with aspirin to avoid further INR problems

options.label: E
options.html: Remove warfarin permanently because his INR was too high

items.explanationHtml:
Medication reconciliation compares what the patient took at home with the discharge plan and resolves every difference. Each change must be either intentional and documented (with the reason and the plan explained to the patient and the next clinician) or corrected. Here the furosemide increase may be intentional but is undocumented, and warfarin, held for a high INR that has now corrected, has simply dropped off the list. The team must decide whether and at what dose to restart it, arrange INR follow-up, and document the plan.

Takeaway: at discharge, every difference between the home and discharge lists must be explained or fixed, especially for anticoagulants.

whyNot.A: Passing an unexplained discrepancy to the next clinician is exactly how anticoagulants are lost at discharge.
whyNot.C: This ignores the intended furosemide increase and the reason warfarin was held, and could repeat the high INR.
whyNot.D: Aspirin is not an adequate substitute for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation, and the change has no indication here.
whyNot.E: A single high INR is a reason to adjust the dose and monitoring, not to stop anticoagulation without a decision.

items.objective: Perform medication reconciliation at discharge and resolve unexplained discrepancies.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old man with heart failure is about to be discharged with a reconciled medication list. When asked to explain his plan in his own words, he says he often skips his furosemide and "stretches" his other pills because he cannot afford all of them each month, and that he has no way to get to the pharmacy since he stopped driving. He lives alone; his daughter lives in another state. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Stress to him that skipping furosemide could put him back in hospital

options.label: B
options.html: Delay discharge until his daughter can come to supervise him

options.label: C
options.html: Document non-adherence and give him a written medication schedule

options.label: D
options.html: Add a second diuretic so that missed doses matter less

options.label: E
options.html: Involve the social worker to arrange affordable medicines and transport

items.explanationHtml:
Non-adherence often reflects social determinants (cost, transport, living alone) rather than lack of knowledge. The right response is to address the barrier before discharge: a social worker or case manager can enrol him in drug assistance or a lower-cost plan, switch to cheaper equivalents with the team, arrange mail-order or delivered prescriptions and transport for follow-up visits, and consider home health support. Teach-back is what revealed the problem.

Takeaway: when a social need blocks the plan, connect the patient to resources that remove it, rather than repeating the instructions.

whyNot.A: He already understands; the barrier is cost and access, which education does not solve.
whyNot.B: Holding a medically ready patient does not fix the cost or transport problem and adds hospital risk.
whyNot.C: Documenting the barrier without addressing it leaves him likely to skip doses again.
whyNot.D: Adding a drug raises cost and complexity and could cause harm; it does not address the barrier.

items.objective: Respond to social barriers to adherence identified at discharge.

items.stemHtml: A hospital's quality committee learns that its risk-adjusted 30-day readmission rate for Medicare patients with heart failure is higher than expected for the third consecutive year. The committee asks how Medicare's Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program affects the hospital financially. Which of the following is the most accurate answer?

options.label: A
options.html: Its base Medicare payments for inpatient stays are reduced by a capped percentage

options.label: B
options.html: Medicare refuses to pay anything for each heart failure readmission

options.label: C
options.html: The hospital must refund the cost of each readmission to the patient

options.label: D
options.html: The hospital is excluded from Medicare until its rate improves

options.label: E
options.html: Only physicians who discharged the patients have their fees reduced

items.explanationHtml:
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program compares each hospital's risk-adjusted 30-day readmissions for selected conditions (including heart failure, myocardial infarction, pneumonia, COPD, coronary artery bypass grafting and elective hip or knee replacement) with expected rates. Hospitals with excess readmissions have their base payments for all Medicare fee-for-service inpatient stays reduced in the following year, up to a capped percentage. It is a value-based payment adjustment, not a denial of individual claims.

Hospitals respond with better discharge planning, medication reconciliation, early follow-up and transitional care.

Takeaway: excess readmissions → a capped percentage cut to all of the hospital's Medicare inpatient payments.

whyNot.B: The programme does not deny payment for individual readmission stays; it applies a percentage reduction to payments.
whyNot.C: Penalties are applied to the hospital's Medicare payments, not paid to patients.
whyNot.D: Excess readmissions lead to payment reductions, not exclusion from the programme.
whyNot.E: The programme adjusts hospital inpatient payments, not individual physicians' fees.

items.objective: Describe how the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program penalises hospitals.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man comes to the emergency department of a community hospital with 12 hours of worsening right lower abdominal pain, nausea and a temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F). At registration he says he has no insurance. The triage nurse suggests that he go to the county hospital 20 minutes away, which "takes uninsured patients." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct him to the county hospital as the nurse suggests

options.label: B
options.html: Ask him to sign a payment agreement before he is examined

options.label: C
options.html: Call the county hospital to arrange a transfer before examination

options.label: D
options.html: Perform a medical screening examination here without delay

options.label: E
options.html: Give oral analgesia and advise him to return if the pain worsens

items.explanationHtml:
Under EMTALA, a Medicare-participating hospital must give anyone who comes to its emergency department a medical screening examination to determine whether an emergency medical condition exists, regardless of insurance or ability to pay. Registration can continue, but inquiries about payment must not delay the examination. Suggesting that an uninsured patient go elsewhere before screening is a classic violation.

Takeaway: screen first; insurance never decides whether an emergency patient is examined.

whyNot.A: Sending him away before screening because he is uninsured violates EMTALA.
whyNot.B: Payment questions may not delay screening or treatment.
whyNot.C: Transfer arrangements cannot replace the screening examination, and transfer for financial reasons is not allowed.
whyNot.E: Discharging him without a screening examination for possible appendicitis is unsafe and unlawful.

items.objective: Apply EMTALA's screening requirement to an uninsured patient.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old uninsured man in the emergency department has CT findings of acute, uncomplicated appendicitis. The hospital's general surgeon is on call and an operating room is available. A hospital administrator asks whether he can be transferred to the county hospital, which is accepting patients, because he cannot pay. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: He may be transferred because the county hospital has agreed to accept him

options.label: B
options.html: He must receive stabilising treatment here, which includes surgery

options.label: C
options.html: He may be transferred once his pain is controlled with opioids

options.label: D
options.html: He may be discharged with oral antibiotics and an outpatient referral

options.label: E
options.html: He may have surgery only after a payment plan is signed

items.explanationHtml:
When screening finds an emergency medical condition, EMTALA requires the hospital to stabilise it within its capabilities or to arrange an appropriate transfer. An appropriate transfer is one made because the patient needs care the hospital cannot provide (or because the patient requests it after being told the risks), with physician certification, an accepting facility and records. This hospital has a surgeon and an operating room, so transfer because he is uninsured is not permitted, even if another hospital would accept him.

Takeaway: if you can stabilise the emergency, you must; transfer is for capability, not for payment.

whyNot.A: Acceptance by the receiving hospital does not permit a transfer made for financial reasons when this hospital can treat him.
whyNot.C: Pain control does not stabilise appendicitis, and the reason for transfer would still be financial.
whyNot.D: Discharging an uninsured patient instead of offering the indicated operation avoids the duty to stabilise.
whyNot.E: Treatment of an emergency condition may not be conditioned on payment arrangements.

items.objective: Apply EMTALA's stabilisation and transfer rules.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has an uncomplicated recovery after an appendectomy. He works part-time, has no children, has a low income and no health insurance, and lives in a state that expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. It is July. He asks how he can get coverage for his follow-up care and future needs. Which of the following is the most accurate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: He must wait for the autumn open-enrolment period to apply for Medicaid

options.label: B
options.html: He cannot get Medicaid because he is a single adult without children

options.label: C
options.html: He should apply for Medicare because he has had major surgery

options.label: D
options.html: He can buy a marketplace plan now without any qualifying event

options.label: E
options.html: He can apply for Medicaid now; enrolment is open all year

items.explanationHtml:
The ACA expanded Medicaid to most low-income adults, but a Supreme Court decision made expansion optional, so eligibility for childless adults depends on the state. In an expansion state, his low income qualifies him. Medicaid and CHIP accept applications at any time of year; only marketplace plans are limited to open enrolment or special enrolment after a qualifying life event. A hospital financial counsellor or social worker can help him apply.

Takeaway: Medicaid: apply any time (if eligible in that state); marketplace: open enrolment or a qualifying event.

whyNot.A: Open-enrolment periods apply to marketplace plans, not to Medicaid.
whyNot.B: In an expansion state, low-income adults qualify without needing to be parents.
whyNot.C: Medicare depends on age 65, long-term disability, ESRD or ALS, not on recent surgery.
whyNot.D: Outside open enrolment, a marketplace plan requires a qualifying life event.

items.objective: Advise a low-income adult about Medicaid eligibility and enrolment timing.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, what is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of Program R compared with usual care for all participants (rounded to the nearest dollar)?

options.label: A
options.html: $5,935 per QALY

options.label: B
options.html: $6,200 per QALY

options.label: C
options.html: $7,455 per QALY

options.label: D
options.html: $31,000 per QALY

options.label: E
options.html: $123,000 per QALY

items.explanationHtml:
ICER = ΔCost ÷ ΔQALY = ($24,600 − $18,400) ÷ (3.30 − 3.10) = $6,200 ÷ 0.20 = $31,000 per QALY gained.

The ICER compares the two strategies; a strategy's own cost divided by its own QALYs (an average ratio) does not tell a decision-maker what the extra spending buys.

Takeaway: subtract, then divide: ΔCost over ΔEffect.

whyNot.A: This is usual care's average ratio ($18,400 ÷ 3.10), not an incremental comparison.
whyNot.B: $6,200 is the cost difference; it has not been divided by the 0.20 QALY gained.
whyNot.C: This is Program R's average ratio ($24,600 ÷ 3.30), not the incremental ratio.
whyNot.E: This divides Program R's total cost by the QALY difference instead of the cost difference.

items.objective: Calculate an ICER from a cost-utility abstract.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, which type of economic evaluation was performed?

options.label: A
options.html: Cost-minimisation analysis

options.label: B
options.html: Cost-benefit analysis

options.label: C
options.html: Cost-utility analysis

options.label: D
options.html: Budget impact analysis

options.label: E
options.html: Cost-of-illness analysis

items.explanationHtml:
Because health effects are measured in quality-adjusted life-years and the result is a cost per QALY gained, this is a cost-utility analysis, a form of cost-effectiveness analysis that allows comparison across conditions. The health-system perspective means patient time and travel costs are not counted.

Takeaway: QALYs in the denominator = cost-utility.

whyNot.A: Cost-minimisation assumes equal outcomes and compares only costs; here outcomes differ and are measured.
whyNot.B: Cost-benefit analysis values health outcomes in money; here they are in QALYs.
whyNot.D: Budget impact analysis projects a payer's total spending without a cost-per-outcome ratio.
whyNot.E: Cost-of-illness studies measure the economic burden of a disease rather than comparing interventions.

items.objective: Identify a cost-utility analysis in a study abstract.

items.stemHtml: Based on the study summary, which conclusion is best supported for patients with 2 or more admissions in the prior year?

options.label: A
options.html: Program R is dominated by usual care in this subgroup

options.label: B
options.html: Program R dominates usual care in this subgroup

options.label: C
options.html: Program R is not cost-effective because the ratio is negative

options.label: D
options.html: Program R costs more per QALY gained than in all participants

options.label: E
options.html: No conclusion is possible without a willingness-to-pay threshold

items.explanationHtml:
In this subgroup Program R costs less ($21,000 vs $23,500, a saving of $2,500) and yields more QALYs (3.05 vs 2.85, a gain of 0.20). A strategy that is both cheaper and more effective dominates its comparator; it is preferred whatever the decision-maker is willing to pay. Computing an ICER here gives a negative number, which should be reported as dominance rather than interpreted as a ratio.

The likely mechanism is fewer readmissions in patients at highest risk of them.

Takeaway: cheaper and better = dominant; dearer and worse = dominated.

whyNot.A: A dominated strategy costs more and achieves less; Program R costs less and achieves more.
whyNot.C: A negative ratio from lower cost and higher effect is the best case (dominance), not a sign of poor value.
whyNot.D: In this subgroup Program R saves money while adding QALYs, so there is no extra cost per QALY.
whyNot.E: A threshold is needed only when a strategy costs more and does more; a dominant option is preferred at any threshold.

items.objective: Recognise dominance in a cost-effectiveness analysis.

items.stemHtml: At 6 PM a day-team resident is going off duty and handing over 14 inpatients to the night resident. One patient, a 67-year-old woman with pneumonia, has had a rising lactate and borderline blood pressure all afternoon and may need transfer to the intensive care unit overnight. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to hand off this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Discuss her first, face to face, with contingency plans and a read-back

options.label: B
options.html: Send a detailed text message so the night resident can read it later

options.label: C
options.html: Add her to the written sign-out list in the order of her room number

options.label: D
options.html: Tell the night resident to read the progress notes in the record

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the nurse to pass the plan to the night resident later

items.explanationHtml:
Handoffs are a major source of communication failure. Best practice is a verbal, face-to-face handoff in a quiet place, supported by a written summary, using a standard structure: illness severity (here, unstable or "watcher"), a brief summary, a to-do list, contingency plans ("if her mean arterial pressure falls below 65 after fluids, call the ICU"), and a synthesis by the receiver, who restates the key points and asks questions. The sickest patients are discussed first and in most detail.

Takeaway: unstable patient → first, in person, with if-then plans, and with the receiver reading it back.

whyNot.B: A text alone allows no questions or confirmation and is unsafe for an unstable patient.
whyNot.C: Written lists support a handoff but do not replace a verbal exchange, and the sickest patient should go first.
whyNot.D: Expecting the receiver to reconstruct the plan from notes loses the sender's judgement and pending tasks.
whyNot.E: Indirect relay through a third person adds a link where information is lost.

items.objective: Conduct a structured, verbal handoff for an unstable patient.

items.stemHtml: On morning rounds, the attending physician asks an intern to start subcutaneous enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in a 74-year-old man admitted with a COPD exacerbation. The intern has just seen this morning's laboratory results, which the attending has not reviewed: the platelet count has fallen from 210,000/mm³ to 38,000/mm³ (reference 150,000–450,000/mm³) since admission. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the intern?

options.label: A
options.html: "OK, I'll put the order in," and enter the order as asked

options.label: B
options.html: "I'll mention the platelet count at sign-out this evening," and enter the order

options.label: C
options.html: "I'd rather not," and leave the enoxaparin order unentered without explanation

options.label: D
options.html: "I'll ask the pharmacist to decide," and leave the decision to pharmacy

options.label: E
options.html: "I'm concerned: his platelets fell to 38,000 today. Should we hold the enoxaparin?"

items.explanationHtml:
Any team member who sees a risk to a patient should speak up directly and promptly, giving the specific fact and a proposed action, in a respectful way. A sudden fall in platelet count is a reason to stop and reconsider anticoagulation (and to look for causes). If a concern is dismissed while the risk remains, the team member repeats it and escalates up the chain of command.

Takeaway: state the concern, the data and the request clearly, now, to the person making the decision.

whyNot.A: Following an order that may cause harm without raising the new data fails the duty to speak up.
whyNot.B: Waiting until sign-out lets a possibly harmful drug be given in the meantime.
whyNot.C: Silently not carrying out an order leaves the team unaware of the risk and of the plan.
whyNot.D: The pharmacist can help, but the intern holds the key information and should state it to the attending directly now.

items.objective: Speak up about a safety concern to a senior colleague.

items.stemHtml: At 2 AM a nurse telephones the covering resident to report that a 58-year-old man on the cardiology ward has a serum potassium of 6.8 mEq/L (reference 3.5–5.0 mEq/L). The resident asks for an ECG and gives a series of medication orders by phone. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the communication?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask the nurse to enter the orders as she understood them

options.label: B
options.html: Hang up and enter the orders in the record in the morning

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the nurse to write down and read back the orders

options.label: D
options.html: Send the orders again by text message to the nurse

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the charge nurse to confirm the orders later

items.explanationHtml:
Verbal and telephone orders are error-prone (look-alike drug names, misheard numbers). The receiver should write the order down and read it back in full, and the prescriber confirms that it is correct (closed-loop communication). The same read-back applies when a lab calls with a critical result. Numbers are best stated digit by digit ("one-zero units"), and the order is entered or signed in the record as soon as possible.

Takeaway: every verbal or telephone order and every critical result → write down, read back, confirm.

whyNot.A: Without a read-back there is no check that the orders were heard correctly, which is the main risk of phone orders.
whyNot.B: Orders for an emergency must be documented promptly, and the read-back step has been skipped.
whyNot.D: Texted orders are not a safe substitute for a confirmed order and create a second, uncontrolled record.
whyNot.E: Delayed confirmation through a third person does not verify the original order in real time.

items.objective: Use read-back for telephone orders and critical results.

items.stemHtml: A second-year resident is in the 20th hour of a scheduled 24-hour in-house call. She has had no sleep and notices that she has had to recalculate a weight-based vancomycin dose three times and is still unsure of the result. A senior resident is also in the hospital. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Drink more coffee and enter the dose she calculated last

options.label: B
options.html: Tell the senior resident she is too tired and ask for help with the task

options.label: C
options.html: Delay the dose until she has finished her shift and rested

options.label: D
options.html: Enter the dose without telling anyone so she does not appear weak

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the nurse to give whatever dose seems right

items.explanationHtml:
Fatigue impairs attention, memory and calculation, and tired clinicians underestimate their own impairment. Residency programmes must provide back-up and expect residents to recognise fatigue and act on it. The safe action is to tell the supervising or senior physician and get a colleague to do or double-check the critical task (and a pharmacist can verify the dose). Programmes also provide rest or safe transport home after long shifts.

Takeaway: fatigue is a system hazard: say so, get help, and do not hide it.

whyNot.A: Caffeine does not restore the judgement impaired by sleep loss, and entering an uncertain dose risks harm.
whyNot.C: Delaying an antibiotic for hours could harm the patient.
whyNot.D: Hiding fatigue puts the patient at risk and contradicts a culture of safety.
whyNot.E: Shifting the decision to the nurse without an order or check is unsafe and outside the nurse's role.

items.objective: Respond safely to fatigue that is impairing clinical work.

items.stemHtml: An experienced ICU nurse programmes an intravenous infusion pump for a sedative and accidentally selects the drug entry directly above the intended one in the pump's drug library; both entries have nearly identical names. The patient becomes briefly hypotensive and recovers with fluids. The nurse reports the event herself. She had followed every step of the unit's procedure, and the drug library has not been updated in several years. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the nurse manager?

options.label: A
options.html: Support the nurse and have the pump library reviewed and redesigned

options.label: B
options.html: Give the nurse a written warning for the error

options.label: C
options.html: Suspend the nurse until she completes a pump competency test

options.label: D
options.html: Require the nurse to repeat the hospital orientation programme

options.label: E
options.html: Report the nurse to the state board of nursing

items.explanationHtml:
This is human error (a slip): an inadvertent action by a competent person following the correct procedure, made likely by a design flaw (adjacent look-alike entries in an outdated drug library). Under just culture, the response is to console and support the clinician (who may be a second victim) and to fix the system: review the library, separate or rename confusable entries and add confirmation steps. Punishment would discourage reporting and leave the hazard for the next nurse.

Takeaway: a slip by someone doing the right thing → support the person, redesign the system.

whyNot.B: A written warning punishes an inadvertent slip and discourages the self-reporting the hospital needs.
whyNot.C: Suspension treats a design-induced slip as misconduct and leaves the confusing library in place.
whyNot.D: Retraining a skilled nurse who followed procedure does not address the cause.
whyNot.E: A licensing report is for misconduct or impairment, not for a self-reported slip.

items.objective: Apply just culture to a human error caused by poor design.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin glargine and glipizide comes for follow-up. She has had three episodes of hypoglycaemia in the past 2 months, all in the last week of the month. Her glycated haemoglobin is 7.4%. On a screening questionnaire she reports that her food often runs out before she has money to buy more, and she skips meals then. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Increase the dose of insulin glargine to improve control

options.label: B
options.html: Advise her to eat three regular meals each day

options.label: C
options.html: Refer her to endocrinology for an insulin pump

options.label: D
options.html: Stop glipizide and refer her to food assistance resources

options.label: E
options.html: Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist to her regimen

items.explanationHtml:
Her hypoglycaemia follows a monthly pattern of food insecurity, a social determinant of health. The response is two-part: make the regimen safer for her real circumstances (a sulfonylurea causes hypoglycaemia when meals are missed, so stopping it is reasonable with glycated haemoglobin near target) and connect her with food resources (food assistance programmes, food banks, a social worker or community health worker).

Takeaway: when a positive social-needs screen explains the clinical problem, adapt the treatment to it and refer to resources that address it.

whyNot.A: Her control is near target, and more insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia during food shortages.
whyNot.B: Advice to eat regularly ignores that she cannot afford food at the end of the month.
whyNot.C: Technology does not address the food insecurity driving her hypoglycaemia.
whyNot.E: Adding a drug increases cost and does not address her missed meals or the sulfonylurea risk.

items.objective: Adapt management and refer to community resources for food insecurity.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy with moderate persistent asthma is seen for follow-up. His mother says he had a severe episode at school last month, and the school nurse would not let him use his albuterol inhaler because there was no paperwork on file. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by his physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Advise his mother to keep him home on days with asthma symptoms

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe an oral corticosteroid for him to take before school each day

options.label: C
options.html: Give the school a written asthma action plan and medication authorisation

options.label: D
options.html: Tell his mother to put the inhaler in his backpack without telling the school

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the school to call an ambulance for every episode of wheezing

items.explanationHtml:
Schools are part of a child's care system. A school nurse needs a written asthma action plan (daily medicines, warning signs, what to give and when to call for help) and a physician-signed medication authorisation to give, or let the child carry, a rescue inhaler.

Takeaway: for children with chronic conditions, the clinician's paperwork (action plan and authorisation) is what lets the school act.

whyNot.A: Keeping him home limits his schooling and does not prepare the school for an attack.
whyNot.B: Daily oral steroids are not appropriate for routine control and do not solve the access problem.
whyNot.D: Bypassing the school's process leaves staff unaware of his needs during an emergency.
whyNot.E: Most episodes can be treated promptly with albuterol at school; calling an ambulance every time delays treatment.

items.objective: Coordinate with the school to support a child with asthma.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes is about to be discharged on once-daily insulin glargine. The nurse has demonstrated the pen, and the patient nods throughout the explanation. She completed school to grade 8 and lives alone. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement by the physician to confirm that she understands her plan?

options.label: A
options.html: "Do you have any questions about your insulin before you go?"

options.label: B
options.html: "You understand how to use the insulin pen, don't you?"

options.label: C
options.html: "Here is a detailed booklet about insulin to read at home."

options.label: D
options.html: "Your primary care doctor will go over the insulin with you next month."

options.label: E
options.html: "So I know I explained it well, show me how you'll take your insulin tonight."

items.explanationHtml:
Teach-back asks patients to explain or demonstrate the plan in their own words or actions, framed as a check on the clinician's explanation rather than a test of the patient. It reveals misunderstandings that nodding and "any questions?" hide, and it works across health-literacy levels. If she makes an error, the clinician re-explains and checks again.

Takeaway: confirm understanding with teach-back, not with "Do you understand?".

whyNot.A: Most patients say no to this question even when they have not understood the plan.
whyNot.B: A leading yes/no question invites agreement without showing understanding.
whyNot.C: Written material alone does not confirm understanding, especially with limited health literacy.
whyNot.D: Deferring education leaves her without a safe plan for the first weeks at home.

items.objective: Use teach-back to confirm understanding at a care transition.

items.stemHtml: An emergency department team is working to give antibiotics sooner to patients with suspected sepsis. Panel A of the figure shows the monthly median time from arrival to first antibiotic dose over 18 months, with the median of the first 10 months drawn as a dashed line. A nurse-led sepsis screen at triage began at the start of month 11. Which conclusion is best supported by panel A?

options.label: A
options.html: The variation after month 10 is consistent with common-cause variation

options.label: B
options.html: The chart shows a trend because each month after month 10 is lower than the last

options.label: C
options.html: Months 11–18 show a shift, a non-random change after the screen began

options.label: D
options.html: A conclusion requires a randomised trial comparing triage with and without the screen

options.label: E
options.html: The screen has been shown to lower sepsis mortality

items.explanationHtml:
Every point from month 11 to month 18 (eight consecutive months) lies below the baseline median of 179 minutes. A run of six or more consecutive points on one side of the median is a shift, a signal of non-random (special-cause) change; here it is the change the team intended, beginning when the screen started.

The pattern is not a trend, and the chart tracks a process measure, so claims about mortality would need outcome data.

Takeaway: on a run chart, six or more consecutive points on one side of the median = shift.

whyNot.A: Eight consecutive points below the median would be very unlikely if the process were unchanged.
whyNot.B: The values after month 10 rise and fall (152 then 158, 149 then 155), so they do not form five consecutive decreases.
whyNot.D: Run-chart rules detect non-random change in a local process; a trial is not needed for this purpose.
whyNot.E: Door-to-antibiotic time is a process measure; mortality is not shown in the chart.

items.objective: Interpret a shift on a run chart presented as a figure.

items.stemHtml: A hospital tracks the weekly number of inpatient falls on its medical wards. Panel B of the figure shows a control chart with the centre line and control limits calculated from weeks 1 to 12. The patient safety officer asks the falls committee how to respond to the data. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Investigate what was different on the wards during week 15

options.label: B
options.html: Redesign the whole falls-prevention programme because of the high week

options.label: C
options.html: Take no action because the fluctuations are common-cause variation

options.label: D
options.html: Recalculate the control limits including week 15 so that it falls within them

options.label: E
options.html: Review each week with more than 4 falls to find out what went wrong

items.explanationHtml:
On a control chart, points inside the limits without a pattern reflect common-cause variation; a point outside a control limit (week 15, 13 falls against an upper limit of 10.3) signals special-cause variation. The right response is to find out what was different that week: a staffing shortage, a cluster of delirious patients, a broken bed alarm system, a change in a sedative order set or a data-entry error, and address that cause.

Takeaway: outside the limits → look for the special cause in that period; inside the limits → judge the process as a whole.

whyNot.B: One point outside the limits points to a specific cause in that week, not a failure of the whole process.
whyNot.C: Week 15 lies above the upper control limit, which is a special-cause signal and should be investigated.
whyNot.D: Altering the limits to absorb an outlier hides a signal rather than explaining it.
whyNot.E: Weeks within the limits reflect common-cause variation; reviewing each one is tampering.

items.objective: Respond to a special-cause signal on a control chart.

items.stemHtml:
A hospital's medication safety committee reviews 200 medication event reports from the past 6 months, sorted by category.

CategoryReports
Dose late or missed because drug not yet delivered from pharmacy96
Documentation error on the administration record42
Wrong dose22
Wrong drug14
Wrong patient6
Allergy not checked4
Other16

The committee wants to reduce the total number of reported events as much as possible with its first project. On which problem should it focus first?

options.label: A
options.html: Errors in documentation on the administration record

options.label: B
options.html: Delays in delivering drugs from the pharmacy

options.label: C
options.html: Doses given to the wrong patient

options.label: D
options.html: Doses given at the wrong strength

options.label: E
options.html: Allergies not checked before administration

items.explanationHtml:
A Pareto analysis ranks categories by frequency to identify the "vital few" that account for most of a problem. Late or missed doses from delivery delays make up 96 of 200 reports (48%); together with documentation errors (42), the top two categories account for 138 of 200 (69%). Targeting the largest category gives the biggest reduction in event numbers. (A committee may also act on rare but severe categories such as wrong-patient events, but the stated goal here is the total number.)

Takeaway: Pareto: fix the few categories that produce most of the events.

whyNot.A: Documentation errors are the second-largest category (21%), less than half the size of the largest.
whyNot.C: Wrong-patient events are serious but are only 3% of reports, so fixing them would reduce the total least.
whyNot.D: Wrong-dose events make up 11% of reports, far fewer than delivery delays.
whyNot.E: Allergy events are the smallest category (2%), so targeting them would barely change the total.

items.objective: Use Pareto analysis to choose an improvement target.

items.stemHtml:
An infection preventionist compares central line–associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) in two intensive care units over one year.

UnitCLABSIsCentral line-daysPatient-days
Unit A (medical ICU)62,4003,000
Unit B (surgical ICU)41,0003,200

What are the CLABSI rates per 1,000 central line-days for Unit A and Unit B, respectively?
items.explanationHtml:
Device-associated infection rates use device-days as the denominator, because risk accrues for each day a line is in place:

  • Unit A: 6 ÷ 2,400 × 1,000 = 2.5 per 1,000 line-days
  • Unit B: 4 ÷ 1,000 × 1,000 = 4.0 per 1,000 line-days

Although Unit A has more infections, Unit B's rate is higher. Using patient-days instead (2.0 and 1.25) would reverse the comparison, because Unit A's patients have lines for more of their stay. Unit B is the place to look at line care and line necessity.

Takeaway: CLABSI rate = infections ÷ central line-days × 1,000.

whyNot.A: These are the rates per 100 line-days, not per 1,000.
whyNot.B: These use patient-days as the denominator, which does not measure exposure to central lines.
whyNot.D: These are the correct rates but assigned to the wrong units.
whyNot.E: These are the raw infection counts without any denominator.

items.objective: Calculate device-associated infection rates with the correct denominator.

items.stemHtml: A primary care clinic wants to reduce missed appointments. A nurse suggests calling patients 2 days before their visit to confirm, and a team agrees to test the idea using the Plan-Do-Study-Act method. Which of the following is the most appropriate first test of this change?

options.label: A
options.html: All clinic sites start calls for every patient next month

options.label: B
options.html: The clinic waits for a published trial of reminder calls

options.label: C
options.html: Staff receive a lecture on the importance of attendance

options.label: D
options.html: One nurse calls her own patients for one week and records the results

options.label: E
options.html: The clinic adds a fee for every missed appointment

items.explanationHtml:
PDSA cycles start with the smallest useful test: one clinician, a few patients, a short time, with a prediction and simple data (how many patients reached, how many attended). Small tests are cheap and safe, reveal practical problems quickly and build confidence before the change is widened.

Takeaway: test small and fast first; scale up after it works.

whyNot.A: A system-wide launch of an untested idea risks wasted effort and gives little chance to learn and adjust.
whyNot.B: Waiting for external evidence delays local improvement; PDSA tests a change locally.
whyNot.C: Education is not the change being tested and is a weak intervention.
whyNot.E: A missed-appointment fee is a different change and may harm access for vulnerable patients.

items.objective: Design a first small-scale PDSA test of change.

items.stemHtml: A hospital medicine group finds that physicians order routine daily blood counts and metabolic panels for clinically stable inpatients at very different rates: some for nearly every patient each day, others rarely, with no difference in outcomes. The group wants to reduce unnecessary daily testing. Which of the following interventions is most likely to help?

options.label: A
options.html: Give each physician regular reports of their own ordering compared with peers

options.label: B
options.html: Penalise the physicians with the highest ordering rates

options.label: C
options.html: Remove the ability to order daily laboratory tests for all patients

options.label: D
options.html: Send one group email asking everyone to order fewer tests

options.label: E
options.html: Take no action because the variation does not affect outcomes

items.explanationHtml:
Audit and feedback, regular summaries of a clinician's own performance, ideally compared with peers or a benchmark and paired with a clear target and suggested actions, reliably produces modest improvements in practice, especially when baseline performance is poor. It can be combined with changes to order sets (removing default daily repeats) for a stronger effect.

Takeaway: show clinicians their own data against peers and a target.

whyNot.B: Punishment tends to damage engagement and does not show physicians where they stand relative to colleagues.
whyNot.C: Blocking all daily tests would harm patients who need them; the aim is to reduce unnecessary tests.
whyNot.D: A single reminder is a weak intervention with little lasting effect.
whyNot.E: Tests without benefit cause cost, anaemia from blood draws and discomfort, so the waste is worth reducing.

items.objective: Use audit and feedback with peer comparison to reduce practice variation.

items.stemHtml: A hospital performs a root-cause analysis after a patient receives a scheduled dose of rapid-acting insulin while hypoglycaemic and becomes unresponsive. The first draft of the report concludes that "the root cause was that the nurse forgot to check the fingerstick glucose before giving insulin." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the analysis team?

options.label: A
options.html: Accept the conclusion and require the nurse to complete retraining

options.label: B
options.html: Close the review, since the patient has since recovered

options.label: C
options.html: Ask the nurse's colleagues whether she is usually careful

options.label: D
options.html: Change the conclusion to "patient factors" because hypoglycaemia was unexpected

options.label: E
options.html: Keep asking why the check was missed until a fixable system cause is found

items.explanationHtml:
"The nurse forgot" describes the active failure, not the root cause. A root-cause analysis keeps asking "why?" (the "5 whys") and uses tools such as a fishbone diagram to reach latent causes: for example, the electronic administration record does not require a recent glucose before insulin can be documented, glucose meters do not transmit results to the record, and glucose checks and insulin are scheduled at different times. Each root cause then gets a strong corrective action, an owner and a measure.

Takeaway: a root cause is something the organisation can redesign, not a person to blame.

whyNot.A: Stopping at the individual's lapse leaves the system weakness that let the lapse cause harm.
whyNot.B: Recovery does not remove the need to fix a hazard that could harm the next patient.
whyNot.C: A judgement of one nurse's character does not identify system causes.
whyNot.D: Relabelling the cause avoids analysis rather than finding what allowed insulin to be given without a glucose check.

items.objective: Apply the 5 whys to reach system-level root causes.

items.stemHtml:
A surgical ward has measured monthly hand-hygiene compliance by direct observation for 12 months; the median is 80.5%. A poster campaign began at the start of month 12.

MonthCompliance (%)
178
282
376
481
579
684
777
880
983
1079
1181
1286

The ward manager says that month 12, the highest value so far, proves that the campaign worked. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?

options.label: A
options.html: The campaign worked because month 12 is the highest value

options.label: B
options.html: No signal of change yet; keep collecting monthly data

options.label: C
options.html: A shift above the median has begun

options.label: D
options.html: An upward trend is present over the last months

options.label: E
options.html: Compliance is worsening and the campaign should stop

items.explanationHtml:
Applying run-chart rules: there is no shift (the longest run on one side of 80.5% is two points), no trend (the longest consecutive rise is three points), and 86% is not far outside the range already seen (76–84%). The variation is consistent with chance, so no conclusion about the campaign can be drawn from one month. The team should keep plotting and, if they want stronger improvement, test changes built into the work rather than posters.

Takeaway: one good month is not a signal; use the run-chart rules.

whyNot.A: One high point within the usual range is not a signal; earlier months reached 84% without any campaign.
whyNot.C: Only months 11 and 12 are consecutive points above the median, far short of the six needed for a shift.
whyNot.D: The last rising run is months 10–12 (three points); a trend needs five consecutive increases.
whyNot.E: There is no downward signal; the data show stable variation around the median.

items.objective: Apply run-chart rules to avoid over-interpreting a single data point.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman develops hives and itching within minutes of receiving intravenous contrast for an abdominal CT. She is treated with an antihistamine and recovers fully. The resident realises that a prior severe reaction to iodinated contrast was documented in the record and that the team did not check it or give premedication. The attending tells the resident, "It was minor. Just tell her she had a reaction; there is no need to mention the chart." Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the resident?

options.label: A
options.html: "All right, I'll tell her she had an unexpected reaction to the contrast."

options.label: B
options.html: "I'll leave that to you, since you are the attending on the case."

options.label: C
options.html: "I think we should tell her the allergy was recorded and we missed it. Can we tell her together?"

options.label: D
options.html: "I'll file an incident report and let risk management decide what to tell her."

options.label: E
options.html: "I'm going to report you to the medical board for asking me to hide this."

items.explanationHtml:
Patients are entitled to honest disclosure of errors that reach them, even when the harm is small, because the information matters for their future care (here, a documented allergy that must be respected next time) and for trust. A senior colleague's request to conceal an error does not change this duty. The best first response is respectful but firm: raise the concern with the attending directly and propose disclosing together. If the attending still refuses, the resident escalates through internal channels (programme director, department chief, patient safety office) while making sure the patient is told.

Takeaway: disclose errors honestly even when harm is minor, and address pressure to conceal directly before escalating.

whyNot.A: Describing a missed documented allergy as "unexpected" is misleading and fails the duty of honest disclosure.
whyNot.B: Stepping back leaves the patient without the truth; the resident shares the duty to see that disclosure happens.
whyNot.D: Reporting is appropriate but does not replace disclosure, and handing the decision away delays it.
whyNot.E: Jumping to an external report skips a direct conversation and internal channels, which are the right first steps.

items.objective: Respond to a supervisor's request not to disclose an error.

items.stemHtml: A laboratory technician notices that the name on a blood sample tube does not match the name on its requisition form. The sample is rejected, the patient's blood is redrawn and correctly labelled, and no result is ever reported. The ward nurse asks whether anything else needs to be done, since no patient was harmed. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Take no further action because the error was caught

options.label: B
options.html: Document the labelling error in the patient's progress note as a nursing error

options.label: C
options.html: Inform the nurse who drew the sample that she will be disciplined

options.label: D
options.html: Notify the patient's insurer about the mislabelled sample

options.label: E
options.html: Submit a report through the hospital's incident reporting system

items.explanationHtml:
This is a near miss: an error (a mislabelled specimen) caught before it reached the patient. Near misses should be entered in the incident reporting system, which is confidential and non-punitive, because they show where the process can fail (here, labelling away from the bedside) without anyone having been harmed. Patterns of reports guide fixes such as printing labels at the bedside after scanning the wristband.

Takeaway: report near misses: they are free lessons.

whyNot.A: Near misses reveal the same system weaknesses as harmful events and should be reported.
whyNot.B: The record should state facts relevant to care, not assign blame; the system learns through incident reporting.
whyNot.C: Discipline for an inadvertent error discourages reporting and does not fix labelling processes.
whyNot.D: Insurers have no role in reviewing near misses.

items.objective: Report near misses through a non-punitive incident system.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department at midnight by police, who found him lying in a car park smelling of alcohol. His fingerstick glucose is 104 mg/dL. He is handed over at 2 AM as "intoxicated, sleeping it off." At 6 AM a new physician finds that he is harder to rouse than before: his Glasgow Coma Scale score has fallen from 14 to 12, and there is a small swelling over the back of his scalp. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Noncontrast CT of the head

options.label: B
options.html: Continued observation until he is sober

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous haloperidol and soft restraints

options.label: D
options.html: Discharge home with a friend once he can walk

options.label: E
options.html: Intravenous thiamine as the only intervention

items.explanationHtml:
The label "intoxicated" passed on at handoff invites diagnostic momentum and anchoring: later clinicians accept the diagnosis without re-examining it. Intoxication should improve with time; a falling Glasgow Coma Scale score and a scalp haematoma point to a possible intracranial haemorrhage (for example, a subdural haematoma), so an urgent noncontrast head CT is needed.

Takeaway: when a patient's course does not fit the label, question the label.

whyNot.B: Worsening consciousness hours later is not expected from alcohol alone; waiting risks a missed intracranial bleed.
whyNot.C: Sedation would obscure his neurological status and does not address the possible cause.
whyNot.D: He is deteriorating and has not been evaluated for head injury.
whyNot.E: Thiamine is reasonable in alcohol use, but it does not evaluate a head injury in a patient whose consciousness is declining.

items.objective: Recognise anchoring and diagnostic momentum and re-evaluate a deteriorating patient.

items.stemHtml: During the time-out before an inguinal hernia repair in a 52-year-old man, the circulating nurse reads the signed consent form, which states "left inguinal hernia repair." The operative site mark and the surgeon's clinic note indicate the right side. The patient is under general anaesthesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Proceed on the right side, because the mark and the note agree

options.label: B
options.html: Proceed on the left side, because the consent form is the legal document

options.label: C
options.html: Repair both sides to make sure the correct side is treated

options.label: D
options.html: Stop and resolve the discrepancy before any incision is made

options.label: E
options.html: Proceed as marked and correct the consent form after surgery

items.explanationHtml:
The time-out, done immediately before incision with the whole team, is the last check of the Universal Protocol against wrong-site, wrong-procedure and wrong-patient surgery. Any discrepancy means the procedure stops until it is resolved, by reviewing the clinic record, imaging and the history and, if needed, postponing until the patient can confirm and a correct consent is signed. Anyone on the team may call a stop.

Takeaway: a time-out discrepancy is a hard stop until it is resolved.

whyNot.A: Two sources agreeing does not resolve a conflict with the consent; the team must stop and verify.
whyNot.B: The consent may itself contain the error; operating without resolving the conflict risks wrong-site surgery.
whyNot.C: Operating on a side without consent or indication is not acceptable.
whyNot.E: Changing the paperwork afterwards does not make an unverified operation safe.

items.objective: Respond to a discrepancy found during the surgical time-out.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman is scheduled for arthroscopy of the right knee. The surgical team is reviewing its preoperative process. According to the Universal Protocol for preventing wrong-site surgery, who should mark the operative site, and when?

options.label: A
options.html: The circulating nurse, after the patient is anaesthetised

options.label: B
options.html: The surgeon doing the operation, with the patient awake

options.label: C
options.html: The patient, at home on the morning of surgery

options.label: D
options.html: The anaesthesiologist, during the preoperative interview

options.label: E
options.html: No one, since knee arthroscopy has a low risk of wrong-site error

items.explanationHtml:
The Universal Protocol has three parts: a pre-procedure verification of the patient, procedure and site; site marking by the person who will do the procedure (the accountable practitioner), done before sedation with the patient involved so that they can confirm the site; and a time-out immediately before incision. The mark must be visible after prepping and draping.

Takeaway: the operator marks the site, with the awake patient confirming.

whyNot.A: Marking after anaesthesia removes the patient's ability to confirm the site, and the nurse is not doing the procedure.
whyNot.C: A patient-made mark is not a verified mark by the person accountable for the procedure.
whyNot.D: The mark should be made by the person who will do the procedure.
whyNot.E: Laterality procedures such as knee arthroscopy are exactly where marking is required.

items.objective: State who marks the operative site and when under the Universal Protocol.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman is 2 days past repair of a hip fracture. Since last night she has been intermittently confused and has twice tried to climb out of bed. She is receiving opioids as needed and has had no bowel movement since surgery. The night nurse asks the covering physician to order wrist restraints and a sedative to keep her safe. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Look for and treat causes of delirium and arrange close observation

options.label: B
options.html: Order bilateral wrist restraints for the rest of the night

options.label: C
options.html: Order a benzodiazepine at bedtime to help her sleep

options.label: D
options.html: Raise all four bed rails to keep her in bed

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer her to the intensive care unit for monitoring

items.explanationHtml:
New confusion after surgery in an older adult is delirium until proven otherwise, and it is a major risk factor for falls. Management is to find and treat the causes (here, opioids, constipation and possible urinary retention, infection, pain, dehydration and sleep disruption), and to keep her safe without restraints: frequent observation or a sitter, a low bed, bed alarm, scheduled toileting, glasses and hearing aids, reorientation and family presence. Physical restraints and sedatives increase injury and prolong delirium.

Takeaway: prevent falls in delirious patients by treating the delirium and watching closely, not by restraint or sedation.

whyNot.B: Restraints do not prevent falls, can worsen agitation and cause injury, and leave the delirium untreated.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in older adults and raise the risk of falls.
whyNot.D: Climbing over full bed rails increases the height of a fall and the risk of injury.
whyNot.E: Delirium with stable vital signs does not need intensive care; bedside measures are the appropriate response.

items.objective: Prevent falls in a hospitalised older adult with delirium.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man comes for a routine visit. He has cared for his wife, who has moderate Alzheimer disease, at home for 3 years. He says he sleeps about 4 hours a night because she wanders, has stopped seeing his friends, and feels "worn out" but not hopeless. His blood pressure is higher than at previous visits. He wants to keep his wife at home. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Prescribe a sedative-hypnotic so that he sleeps through the night

options.label: B
options.html: Refer him to caregiver support and respite or adult day services

options.label: C
options.html: Recommend that his wife move to a nursing home immediately

options.label: D
options.html: Reassure him that caregiver fatigue usually resolves with time

options.label: E
options.html: Increase his antihypertensive medicine and review him in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
Caregiver strain harms the caregiver's health and threatens the arrangement he wants to keep. Community resources are part of the health system: respite care, adult day programmes, in-home help, caregiver support groups and local aging-services agencies, often coordinated through a social worker. His wife's physician should also review her night-time wandering and sleep.

Takeaway: screen caregivers for strain and connect them with respite and community services.

whyNot.A: A hypnotic could leave him unable to respond when his wife wanders and does not reduce his burden.
whyNot.C: He wants to keep her at home, and community supports may make that sustainable; placement is his decision to make.
whyNot.D: Caregiver strain tends to grow as dementia progresses, so reassurance alone is inadequate.
whyNot.E: Treating the blood pressure alone ignores the caregiver burden that is driving his decline.

items.objective: Link an overburdened caregiver with community resources.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man was transferred from the intensive care unit to a medical ward yesterday after recovering from septic shock. A right internal jugular central venous catheter placed 6 days ago for vasopressors is still in place. He is now taking oral antibiotics and fluids, and he has good peripheral veins. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to reduce his risk of a catheter-associated bloodstream infection?

options.label: A
options.html: Replace the catheter over a guidewire

options.label: B
options.html: Start prophylactic systemic antibiotics for the line

options.label: C
options.html: Remove the central venous catheter

options.label: D
options.html: Flush the catheter with heparin every 8 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Change the catheter dressing daily

items.explanationHtml:
The risk of CLABSI rises with every day a central line stays in. A core element of prevention is daily review of whether the line is still needed and prompt removal when it is not. This patient no longer needs vasopressors or central access, so the line should come out. Other measures (hand hygiene, chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, full barrier precautions at insertion, careful site selection, good dressing care) matter while a line is needed.

Takeaway: the best way to prevent a line infection is to remove a line that is no longer needed.

whyNot.A: Routine exchange does not lower infection risk and is pointless when the line is no longer needed.
whyNot.B: Prophylactic antibiotics for catheters are not recommended and promote resistance.
whyNot.D: Flushing maintains patency but does not prevent infection in a line that has no purpose.
whyNot.E: Dressing care matters while a line is needed, but the line itself is the main risk and is no longer indicated.

items.objective: Prevent CLABSI by removing unnecessary central lines.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old girl has a confirmed venous blood lead level well above the CDC reference value but below the range at which chelation is recommended. Her family rents an apartment built in the 1940s with peeling paint on the window frames. She has no symptoms, and her development is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate step to identify and remove the source of exposure?

options.label: A
options.html: Start oral chelation therapy to remove the lead

options.label: B
options.html: Advise the parents to sand and repaint the window frames themselves

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat the blood lead test in 1 year

options.label: D
options.html: Notify the local health department for an environmental home investigation

options.label: E
options.html: Prescribe iron supplements and take no further action

items.explanationHtml:
Lead poisoning is a public-health problem: elevated blood lead levels are reported to the health department, which carries out an environmental investigation of the home (and other places the child spends time), identifies hazards such as deteriorating paint and dust, and works with property owners on safe abatement. The clinician also gives the family guidance on nutrition, wet cleaning and hand washing, checks for iron deficiency, arranges repeat testing and monitors development.

Takeaway: the clinician treats the child; the health department finds and removes the source.

whyNot.A: Chelation is reserved for much higher levels and does not remove the source.
whyNot.B: Dry sanding of lead paint releases dust and can sharply increase exposure.
whyNot.C: Waiting a year without action leaves her exposed during a critical developmental period.
whyNot.E: Treating iron deficiency helps if present but does nothing about the lead in the home.

items.objective: Describe the public health department's role in childhood lead exposure.

items.stemHtml: A handwritten order for "regular insulin 10U before meals" on a scanned paper form is read by a nurse as 100 units, and the patient develops severe hypoglycaemia. The hospital reviews documentation practices. Which of the following practices would most directly have prevented this misreading?

options.label: A
options.html: Adding a trailing zero, writing 10.0 units

options.label: B
options.html: Using the abbreviation "IU" for international units

options.label: C
options.html: Writing the dose as a Roman numeral

options.label: D
options.html: Writing the word "units" in full

options.label: E
options.html: Placing the dose after the timing instruction

items.explanationHtml:
The abbreviation "U" can be mistaken for a zero, turning 10 units into 100. Do-not-use lists for medication orders include "U" and "IU", trailing zeros (5.0 mg) and missing leading zeros (.5 mg). The fix is to write "units" and, better still, to use electronic order entry with structured dose fields and dose-range alerts for high-alert drugs such as insulin.

Takeaway: never write U for units; avoid trailing zeros; always use leading zeros.

whyNot.A: A trailing zero causes tenfold errors of its own when the decimal point is missed.
whyNot.B: "IU" is also on do-not-use lists because it can be misread as "IV" or "10".
whyNot.C: Roman numerals are uncommon in dosing and introduce new chances for misreading.
whyNot.E: Moving the dose within the order does not prevent the letter U being read as a zero.

items.objective: Avoid error-prone abbreviations in medication orders.

items.stemHtml: A second-year resident tells a colleague that a patient she sent home from the emergency department last week returned with a perforated appendix after she attributed his pain to gastroenteritis. The error has been disclosed to the patient. She says she cannot sleep, keeps replaying the case and wonders whether she should be a doctor. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the colleague?

options.label: A
options.html: "Everybody misses things. Try to put it out of your mind and move on."

options.label: B
options.html: "That sounds really hard. Would you like help contacting the peer support programme?"

options.label: C
options.html: "You should keep this to yourself so that it doesn't affect your evaluations."

options.label: D
options.html: "You probably should take a break from seeing patients for a few months."

options.label: E
options.html: "Next time, get a CT scan for every patient with abdominal pain."

items.explanationHtml:
Clinicians involved in errors often experience the second-victim response: guilt, anxiety, insomnia, loss of confidence and sometimes thoughts of leaving medicine. The supportive response acknowledges the distress, normalises seeking help and points to timely peer support (many hospitals have formal programmes), while the event itself is reviewed for learning. If she showed signs of depression or suicidal thinking, more urgent help would be needed.

Takeaway: support second victims with acknowledgement and peer support, not silence or blame.

whyNot.A: Telling her to forget it dismisses her distress and the learning that should follow.
whyNot.C: Advising secrecy isolates her and discourages the openness that safety depends on.
whyNot.D: Prolonged removal from work is not warranted by distress alone and may deepen her sense of failure.
whyNot.E: Blanket overtesting is poor practice and ignores her emotional need.

items.objective: Support a colleague experiencing the second-victim response.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with traditional Medicare (Parts A and B) is admitted to hospital for an elective total knee replacement and stays 3 days. He asks which part of Medicare pays the orthopaedic surgeon's professional fee for the operation. Which of the following is the most accurate answer?

options.label: A
options.html: Medicare Part A

options.label: B
options.html: Medicare Part C

options.label: C
options.html: Medicare Part D

options.label: D
options.html: Medicaid

options.label: E
options.html: Medicare Part B

items.explanationHtml:
For an inpatient admission under traditional Medicare, Part A pays the hospital (room, nursing, operating room, inpatient drugs), while Part B pays physicians' professional services wherever they are delivered, including the surgeon's and anaesthesiologist's fees in hospital, as well as outpatient care.

Takeaway: hospital facility = Part A; physician services, inpatient or outpatient = Part B.

whyNot.A: Part A pays the hospital's facility charges for the inpatient stay, not the physician's professional fee.
whyNot.B: Part C is Medicare Advantage, a private-plan alternative he has not chosen.
whyNot.C: Part D covers outpatient prescription drugs, not physician services.
whyNot.D: Medicaid is income-based, and nothing suggests he qualifies; Medicare is his primary coverage.

items.objective: Distinguish Medicare Part A and Part B coverage during a hospital stay.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman with traditional Medicare lives on a small Social Security benefit and has almost no savings. She has been skipping specialist visits because of the Part B premium and coinsurance. Her income and assets fall within her state's Medicaid limits. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about her coverage?

options.label: A
options.html: She may be dually eligible, and Medicaid can help pay Medicare costs

options.label: B
options.html: She cannot have Medicaid because she already has Medicare

options.label: C
options.html: She must give up Medicare to enrol in Medicaid

options.label: D
options.html: Medicaid would replace Medicare as her primary payer

options.label: E
options.html: She qualifies only for help with outpatient drugs, not other costs

items.explanationHtml:
Low-income Medicare beneficiaries can be dual eligible for Medicare and Medicaid. Medicare pays first; Medicaid then helps with Medicare premiums and cost-sharing (through Medicare Savings Programs and full Medicaid benefits) and covers services Medicare does not, such as long-term nursing home care. A social worker or a state health insurance counselling programme can help her apply.

Takeaway: Medicare and Medicaid can stack; Medicare is primary.

whyNot.B: People can have both programmes; those who do are called dual eligible.
whyNot.C: Medicare remains her primary coverage; Medicaid supplements it.
whyNot.D: For dual eligibles, Medicare pays first and Medicaid pays after it.
whyNot.E: Medicaid can cover Medicare premiums, cost-sharing and services Medicare does not cover, such as long-term care.

items.objective: Explain dual eligibility for Medicare and Medicaid.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 4 years ago is in remission. She wants to leave her job, which provides her health insurance, to start her own business, but fears that no insurer will cover her or that she will be charged much more because of her cancer history. Which of the following is the most accurate information for her?

options.label: A
options.html: Insurers may exclude cancer-related care for 12 months after enrolment

options.label: B
options.html: Insurers may charge her a higher premium based on her medical history

options.label: C
options.html: An individual plan cannot refuse her or raise her premium because of her cancer

options.label: D
options.html: She can buy coverage only through a high-risk pool for people with cancer

options.label: E
options.html: She must stay on her employer's plan to keep any coverage for cancer care

items.explanationHtml:
Under the Affordable Care Act, insurers in the individual and group markets must accept applicants regardless of health status (guaranteed issue), may not exclude pre-existing conditions, and may vary individual premiums only by age, tobacco use, geographic area and family size. Losing job-based coverage also opens a special enrolment period for marketplace plans, with income-based premium help where she qualifies.

Takeaway: a history of illness no longer blocks or prices people out of individual coverage.

whyNot.A: Pre-existing condition exclusions were banned by the Affordable Care Act.
whyNot.B: Premiums for individual plans may vary only by age, tobacco use, location and family size, not health status.
whyNot.D: Guaranteed issue in the regular market replaced the need for high-risk pools.
whyNot.E: Her cancer history does not tie her to employer coverage; individual plans must cover her on the same terms.

items.objective: Describe ACA protections for people with pre-existing conditions.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is laid off in March and will lose his employer health coverage at the end of the month. He is worried about paying for insulin and asks whether he must wait until the annual open-enrolment period to buy a marketplace plan. His income is now too high for Medicaid in his state. Which of the following is the most accurate answer?

options.label: A
options.html: He must wait for open enrolment later in the year

options.label: B
options.html: Losing job-based coverage lets him enrol in a marketplace plan now

options.label: C
options.html: He can keep his employer coverage free of charge for 18 months

options.label: D
options.html: He is automatically enrolled in Medicare because he has diabetes

options.label: E
options.html: He can buy coverage only after a 6-month waiting period

items.explanationHtml:
Marketplace plans are bought during annual open enrolment or during a special enrolment period after a qualifying life event: losing job-based coverage, marriage, birth or adoption, or moving. He may also be able to continue his employer plan temporarily under COBRA (for employers above a minimum size), but he usually pays nearly the full premium himself. Comparing the two options with a navigator or counsellor is reasonable.

Takeaway: job loss → special enrolment period; no need to wait for open enrolment.

whyNot.A: Loss of other coverage is a qualifying life event that opens a special enrolment period.
whyNot.C: Continuation coverage after a layoff (COBRA) is usually paid for by the former employee at close to the full premium, not free.
whyNot.D: Diabetes does not confer Medicare eligibility; age, long-term disability, ESRD or ALS does.
whyNot.E: There is no waiting period; coverage can begin soon after the special enrolment application.

items.objective: Explain special enrolment periods after loss of job-based coverage.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is receiving maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. His parents say his school requires proof of measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccination before he can return. He has never received his second doses. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Give the measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines today

options.label: B
options.html: Advise the parents to file a religious exemption instead

options.label: C
options.html: Keep him out of school until chemotherapy is complete

options.label: D
options.html: Complete a medical exemption for the live vaccines during chemotherapy

options.label: E
options.html: Tell the parents the school cannot require vaccines

items.explanationHtml:
States set school-entry vaccine requirements under their public-health powers, and every state accepts medical exemptions for true contraindications. Live vaccines (measles-mumps-rubella, varicella) are contraindicated during chemotherapy, so the physician documents a medical exemption and plans to vaccinate when immune function recovers.
