His household contacts should be fully vaccinated (including against influenza) to protect him, and the school and health department may exclude him during an outbreak.

Takeaway: a real contraindication → a medical exemption, which every state allows; protect the child by vaccinating those around him.

whyNot.A: Live vaccines are contraindicated during chemotherapy because they can cause severe infection.
whyNot.B: A medical reason exists, and steering parents to a non-medical exemption misrepresents the situation.
whyNot.C: A medical exemption allows him to attend; long absence is not needed.
whyNot.E: States can and do require vaccines for school entry, and medical exemptions exist for children like him.

items.objective: Apply medical exemptions to school vaccine requirements.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man with a cough for 2 months has a cavitary upper-lobe lesion and sputum smears positive for acid-fast bacilli. He refuses to remain in airborne isolation or to start treatment and says he plans to go back to his job in a crowded warehouse tomorrow. He has decision-making capacity and understands the risks. After counselling him, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Respect his refusal and discharge him without further action

options.label: B
options.html: Place him on an involuntary psychiatric hold

options.label: C
options.html: Call his employer and tell them not to let him work

options.label: D
options.html: Ask hospital security to keep him in his room indefinitely

options.label: E
options.html: Notify the local health department of the case and his refusal

items.explanationHtml:
Active tuberculosis is a notifiable disease, and reporting it to the health department is required and is a permitted disclosure without consent. Public-health authority rests with the states, exercised by state and local health departments, which can require directly observed therapy and, if a person with infectious disease refuses to isolate, obtain a legal order for isolation as a last resort. The clinician keeps counselling, offers treatment and works with the department.

Takeaway: a competent adult may refuse treatment, but the health department can act to protect others from infectious tuberculosis.

whyNot.A: His autonomy to refuse treatment does not extend to exposing others to infectious tuberculosis.
whyNot.B: He has capacity and no psychiatric emergency; a psychiatric hold is not the legal tool for infectious disease.
whyNot.C: Disclosing his diagnosis to his employer is not the clinician's role; the health department manages contacts and exclusion.
whyNot.D: Detaining him without legal authority is unlawful; legal isolation orders come through the health department.

items.objective: Describe public-health powers for a patient with infectious tuberculosis who refuses isolation.

items.stemHtml: A family physician licensed only in State A has cared for a 19-year-old woman with epilepsy for 10 years. The patient has moved to State B for university and asks to continue her routine follow-up by video while she is at her dormitory. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about licensure for these visits?

options.label: A
options.html: He generally needs a licence in State B, where she is during the visit

options.label: B
options.html: His State A licence is enough because he is in State A

options.label: C
options.html: No licence is needed because the visits are by video

options.label: D
options.html: An interstate compact gives him a single national licence

options.label: E
options.html: She must travel back to State A for each visit by law

items.explanationHtml:
Medical licensure is granted by each state, and for telehealth the practice of medicine is generally considered to occur where the patient is located at the time of the visit. A physician therefore usually needs a licence in the patient's state (some states allow limited exceptions, such as brief continuity-of-care visits). Interstate licensure compacts make it faster to obtain more licences but do not replace them.

Takeaway: telehealth licensure follows the patient's location.

whyNot.B: For telehealth, licensure generally follows the patient's location, not the physician's.
whyNot.C: Telehealth is the practice of medicine and is subject to the same licensure rules.
whyNot.D: Licensure compacts speed up getting additional state licences but do not create a national licence.
whyNot.E: Travel is one option but not a legal requirement if he holds a State B licence.

items.objective: State the licensure rule for telehealth across state lines.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man develops ascending leg weakness and areflexia 2 weeks after receiving an influenza vaccine and is diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome. His physician wants to report this possible vaccine-related adverse event. To which of the following should the report be made?

options.label: A
options.html: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

options.label: B
options.html: The National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System

options.label: C
options.html: The Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System

options.label: D
options.html: The state medical board

options.label: E
options.html: The vaccine manufacturer only

items.explanationHtml:
The Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) is the national early-warning system for vaccine safety, co-managed by the CDC and FDA. Anyone may report, and clinicians should report clinically important events after vaccination even if causation is uncertain; patterns of reports prompt further study. Adverse events from drugs and devices are reported to the FDA's general adverse-event system.

Takeaway: possible vaccine reaction → VAERS (CDC and FDA).

whyNot.A: CMS runs payment programmes and does not collect vaccine safety reports.
whyNot.B: That system collects reports of notifiable infections, not adverse events after vaccination.
whyNot.D: Medical boards license and discipline physicians and have no role in vaccine safety.
whyNot.E: Manufacturers must report events they learn of, but the clinician's report belongs in the national system.

items.objective: Identify where to report adverse events after vaccination.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old electrician with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis can no longer work and has been approved for Social Security disability benefits. He asks when he will be able to get Medicare. Which of the following is the most accurate answer?

options.label: A
options.html: When he turns 65, like other adults

options.label: B
options.html: When his disability benefits begin, without the usual 24-month wait

options.label: C
options.html: After he has received disability benefits for 24 months

options.label: D
options.html: Only if his household income falls below the poverty line

options.label: E
options.html: Only if he also develops end-stage renal disease

items.explanationHtml:
People under 65 generally become eligible for Medicare after receiving Social Security disability benefits for 24 months. Two conditions are exceptions: ALS, for which Medicare begins as soon as disability benefits begin, and end-stage renal disease, which has its own eligibility route. Medicare eligibility is never income-based.

Takeaway: under 65, Medicare comes through disability (usually after 24 months), ESRD, or ALS (no wait).

whyNot.A: People under 65 with ALS qualify through disability without waiting until 65.
whyNot.C: The 24-month waiting period applies to most disabilities but is waived for ALS.
whyNot.D: Medicare eligibility does not depend on income; that describes Medicaid.
whyNot.E: ESRD is a separate route to Medicare and is not needed here.

items.objective: Describe Medicare eligibility for people younger than 65 with ALS.

items.stemHtml: A 65-year-old woman becoming eligible for Medicare spends half of each year in a different state from her home and wants to be able to see any physician who accepts Medicare in either place without referrals. She asks how traditional Medicare compares with a Medicare Advantage plan. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.html: Medicare Advantage plans have no provider networks or prior authorisation

options.label: B
options.html: Traditional Medicare includes outpatient prescription drug coverage

options.label: C
options.html: Medicare Advantage plans have no annual limit on out-of-pocket costs

options.label: D
options.html: Traditional Medicare allows any clinician who accepts Medicare but has no yearly out-of-pocket cap

options.label: E
options.html: A Medigap policy can be added to a Medicare Advantage plan

items.explanationHtml:
Traditional Medicare lets beneficiaries see any clinician or hospital in the country that accepts Medicare, generally without referrals, but Parts A and B have no annual out-of-pocket limit, so many people add a Medigap supplemental policy and a Part D drug plan. Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans are run by private insurers, usually bundle drug coverage and extra benefits, and must have an out-of-pocket maximum, but most use provider networks and prior authorisation. For someone who splits the year between two states, the network question matters a great deal.

Takeaway: traditional Medicare = broad choice, no built-in cap; Medicare Advantage = networks, a cap and often extras.

whyNot.A: Most Advantage plans use networks and prior authorisation, which may limit care in her second state.
whyNot.B: Outpatient drugs require a separate Part D plan alongside traditional Medicare.
whyNot.C: Advantage plans are required to have a yearly out-of-pocket maximum; traditional Medicare is the one without.
whyNot.E: Medigap policies supplement traditional Medicare and cannot be used with an Advantage plan.

items.objective: Compare traditional Medicare with Medicare Advantage.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old woman is choosing among three hypothetical employer health plans for next year. She will have a scheduled knee replacement (allowed cost $28,000) and expects 6 office visits (allowed cost $150 each). All care will be in network.

Plan XPlan YPlan Z
Her yearly premium share$1,200$3,600$5,400
Deductible$3,000 (applies to all care)$500 (surgery only)None
Office visitCounts toward deductible, then 20%$30 copay$20 copay
Coinsurance after deductible20%10%5%
Out-of-pocket maximum$6,000$3,000$2,000

Copays and coinsurance count toward each out-of-pocket maximum; premiums do not. Which plan gives her the lowest expected total yearly cost (premium plus out-of-pocket), and what is that total?

options.label: A
options.html: Plan X, $1,200

options.label: B
options.html: Plan X, $7,200

options.label: C
options.html: Plan Y, $6,600

options.label: D
options.html: Plan Z, $1,520

options.label: E
options.html: Plan Z, $6,920

items.explanationHtml:
Total = premium + out-of-pocket (capped at the maximum).

  • Plan X: all care $28,900; deductible $3,000 + 20% × $25,900 = $8,180 → capped at $6,000. Total $1,200 + $6,000 = $7,200.
  • Plan Y: visits 6 × $30 = $180; surgery $500 + 10% × $27,500 = $3,250; sum $3,430 → capped at $3,000. Total $3,600 + $3,000 = $6,600.
  • Plan Z: visits 6 × $20 = $120; surgery 5% × $28,000 = $1,400; sum $1,520 (below the cap). Total $5,400 + $1,520 = $6,920.

Plan Y is cheapest overall, although it has neither the lowest premium nor the lowest out-of-pocket cost.

Takeaway: compare plans by premium plus capped out-of-pocket cost for the care you expect.

whyNot.A: $1,200 is Plan X's premium alone; it ignores her large out-of-pocket costs.
whyNot.B: This is Plan X's correct total, but it is $600 higher than Plan Y's.
whyNot.D: $1,520 is Plan Z's out-of-pocket cost without its $5,400 premium.
whyNot.E: This is Plan Z's correct total, but it is $320 higher than Plan Y's.

items.objective: Compare insurance plans by total expected yearly cost.

items.stemHtml:
A health department compares four strategies for colorectal cancer screening in a fictional population (values per person, discounted).

StrategyCostQALYs
No screening$1,00010.00
Strategy P$3,00010.05
Strategy Q$4,50010.04
Strategy R$9,00010.10

After excluding any dominated strategy, what is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of Strategy R compared with the next most effective remaining strategy?

options.label: A
options.html: $40,000 per QALY

options.label: B
options.html: $75,000 per QALY

options.label: C
options.html: $80,000 per QALY

options.label: D
options.html: $120,000 per QALY

options.label: E
options.html: $180,000 per QALY

items.explanationHtml:
First remove dominated strategies. Strategy Q costs more than P ($4,500 vs $3,000) and gives fewer QALYs (10.04 vs 10.05), so Q is dominated by P and drops out.

Order the remaining strategies by effectiveness: no screening → P → R. Compare each with the next less effective one:

  • P vs no screening: $2,000 ÷ 0.05 = $40,000 per QALY.
  • R vs P: ($9,000 − $3,000) ÷ (10.10 − 10.05) = $6,000 ÷ 0.05 = $120,000 per QALY.

Comparing R with no screening ($80,000) hides how expensive R's extra benefit over P really is.

Takeaway: drop dominated options, then compare each strategy with the next best one, not with doing nothing.

whyNot.A: $40,000 is the ICER of Strategy P versus no screening, not of R.
whyNot.B: This compares R with Q, which is dominated and should have been excluded.
whyNot.C: This compares R with no screening, skipping the more effective non-dominated strategy P.
whyNot.E: This divides R's total cost by the QALY difference from P instead of the cost difference.

items.objective: Calculate ICERs between non-dominated strategies.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has had a changing mole on his back for 2 months and calls a dermatologist's office directly to book an appointment. He has a health maintenance organisation (HMO) plan, and the dermatologist is in his plan's network. Which of the following is most likely needed for the visit to be covered?

options.label: A
options.html: No requirement, because the dermatologist is in network

options.label: B
options.html: Payment of the full fee, since HMOs do not cover specialists

options.label: C
options.html: A second opinion from another dermatologist first

options.label: D
options.html: Enrolment in a separate dermatology insurance plan

options.label: E
options.html: A referral from his primary care physician

items.explanationHtml:
In an HMO, the primary care physician usually acts as a gatekeeper: specialist care is covered when the primary care physician refers the patient to an in-network specialist, and out-of-network care is not covered except in emergencies. PPOs allow self-referral and some out-of-network coverage at higher cost; EPOs have networks like HMOs, usually without referrals; POS plans combine a gatekeeper with some out-of-network coverage.

Takeaway: HMO: in network and referred by the primary care physician.

whyNot.A: In an HMO, being in network is not enough; specialist visits usually need a primary care referral.
whyNot.B: HMOs cover specialist care when it is referred within the network.
whyNot.C: No second opinion is needed before a first specialist visit.
whyNot.D: Specialist care is part of his HMO benefits; no separate plan is needed.

items.objective: Explain the gatekeeper and referral requirements of an HMO.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with an exclusive provider organisation (EPO) plan wants to see a well-known rheumatologist for a second opinion about lupus. The rheumatologist is not in her plan's network, and her situation is not an emergency. Which of the following best describes her coverage for this visit?

options.label: A
options.html: The plan will generally pay nothing for the visit

options.label: B
options.html: The plan will pay at a lower out-of-network rate

options.label: C
options.html: The plan will pay fully once she obtains a referral

options.label: D
options.html: The plan will pay fully because she has a chronic illness

options.label: E
options.html: The plan will pay fully because it is a second opinion

items.explanationHtml:
An EPO works like an HMO network (care must be in network, except emergencies) but usually without a primary care gatekeeper. Out-of-network, non-emergency care is generally not covered at all, so she would pay the full charge unless the plan grants an exception. She could look for an in-network rheumatologist or ask the plan about a network exception.

Takeaway: HMO and EPO: no out-of-network coverage except emergencies; PPO and POS: some, at higher cost.

whyNot.B: Partial out-of-network payment is a feature of PPO and POS plans, not EPOs.
whyNot.C: A referral does not create out-of-network coverage in an EPO.
whyNot.D: Chronic illness does not change network rules for non-emergency care.
whyNot.E: Second opinions are subject to the same network rules unless the plan says otherwise.

items.objective: Describe out-of-network coverage in an EPO plan.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with an employer health plan has an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at a hospital in his plan's network, performed by an in-network surgeon. Weeks later he receives a large bill from the anaesthesiologist, who is not in his plan's network and whom he did not choose; he signed no waiver. He brings the bill to his primary care physician. Which of the following is the most accurate information?

options.label: A
options.html: He owes the full bill because the anaesthesiologist is out of network

options.label: B
options.html: He owes the bill unless the surgeon agrees to pay it

options.label: C
options.html: He owes the bill because the operation was elective, not an emergency

options.label: D
options.html: He should owe only his in-network cost-sharing for the anaesthesia

options.label: E
options.html: He owes half the bill as a compromise between the parties

items.explanationHtml:
The No Surprises Act protects patients in covered plans from surprise out-of-network bills for emergency care and for out-of-network clinicians who treat them at an in-network facility. For ancillary clinicians the patient does not choose, such as anaesthesiologists, radiologists, pathologists and assistant surgeons, the protection cannot be waived. The patient pays only in-network cost-sharing, and the clinician and plan settle payment between themselves. He should contact his plan, and the bill can be disputed.

Takeaway: out-of-network anaesthesia at an in-network hospital → in-network cost-sharing only.

whyNot.A: Federal surprise-billing protections apply to out-of-network clinicians at in-network facilities.
whyNot.B: The surgeon is not responsible, and the protection does not depend on the surgeon.
whyNot.C: The protection for ancillary clinicians such as anaesthesiologists at in-network facilities covers scheduled care too.
whyNot.E: There is no split rule; the patient's share is limited to in-network cost-sharing.

items.objective: Apply federal surprise-billing protections to a patient's bill.

items.stemHtml: A hospital joins a payment programme in which Medicare pays a single target amount for all care related to an elective hip replacement, from admission through 90 days after discharge, including the surgeon, the hospital stay, rehabilitation and readmissions. If actual spending is below the target and quality standards are met, the hospital keeps part of the difference. Which change in care is this payment most likely to encourage?

options.label: A
options.html: Longer hospital stays to make sure patients are fully recovered

options.label: B
options.html: Fewer complications and discharge home rather than to a facility when safe

options.label: C
options.html: More readmissions, since each is paid separately

options.label: D
options.html: Referral of all patients to inpatient rehabilitation

options.label: E
options.html: Billing each service separately at higher rates

items.explanationHtml:
A bundled (episode-based) payment sets one price for all services in a defined episode of care. Because complications, readmissions and post-acute facility stays add to episode spending, the incentive is to coordinate care across settings, prevent complications, plan discharge early and send patients home with home services when that is safe. Risks include avoiding high-risk patients and doing more episodes, which programmes counter with risk adjustment and quality requirements.

Takeaway: bundled payment rewards a lean, coordinated episode, including what happens after discharge.

whyNot.A: Longer stays raise episode spending, which the target payment discourages.
whyNot.C: Readmissions within 90 days are inside the episode and reduce the hospital's share of savings.
whyNot.D: Facility-based rehabilitation is costly and is discouraged when home recovery is safe.
whyNot.E: A bundled payment replaces separate fees for the episode with one target amount.

items.objective: Predict the incentives of an episode-based bundled payment.

items.stemHtml: A multispecialty physician group and a community hospital form an accountable care organisation for 20,000 Medicare patients attributed to their primary care physicians. They continue to be paid fee-for-service, but a yearly spending benchmark is set for the population, and quality is measured. Which of the following best describes how the organisation can earn additional payment?

options.label: A
options.html: By sharing savings when spending is below the benchmark and quality targets are met

options.label: B
options.html: By billing for more visits and procedures than in previous years

options.label: C
options.html: By receiving a fixed payment per enrolled patient each month

options.label: D
options.html: By receiving a bonus for each patient admitted to the hospital

options.label: E
options.html: By enrolling patients in a separate ACO insurance plan

items.explanationHtml:
An accountable care organisation is a group of clinicians and hospitals that accepts responsibility for the total cost and quality of care for a defined population. In the shared-savings model, fee-for-service payments continue, but if total spending for the attributed population is below a benchmark and quality standards are met, the ACO shares the savings (and in some arrangements shares losses too). ACOs therefore invest in care coordination, management of high-risk patients, preventive care and avoiding duplicate tests and avoidable admissions.

Takeaway: ACO = accountable for total cost and quality of a population; rewarded through shared savings.

whyNot.B: Higher volume raises total spending, which reduces or removes any shared savings.
whyNot.C: A fixed per-person payment describes capitation, not the shared-savings model described.
whyNot.D: Admissions add to total cost of care and work against the benchmark.
whyNot.E: Attributed patients remain in Medicare; the ACO is not an insurance plan they enrol in.

items.objective: Describe how accountable care organisations are paid.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old self-employed woman without health insurance is scheduled for an outpatient colonoscopy in 3 weeks because of a family history of colon cancer. She is worried about the cost and asks how she can find out what she will be charged. Which of the following is the most accurate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: Prices cannot be known until after the bill is sent

options.label: B
options.html: Only insured patients can ask for a cost estimate

options.label: C
options.html: She is entitled to a written good-faith estimate of the charges in advance

options.label: D
options.html: She must agree to pay before learning the price

options.label: E
options.html: She should delay the procedure until she has insurance

items.explanationHtml:
Under the No Surprises Act, people who are uninsured or choose to self-pay are entitled to a good-faith estimate of expected charges for scheduled services, given in advance; if the final bill is substantially higher than the estimate, they can dispute it. Hospitals must also publish prices for common shoppable services. A financial counsellor can review charity care or discount programmes and her options for coverage.

Takeaway: uninsured or self-pay and scheduling care → ask for the good-faith estimate.

whyNot.A: Federal rules require advance estimates for uninsured or self-pay patients scheduling care.
whyNot.B: The good-faith estimate requirement applies specifically to uninsured and self-pay patients.
whyNot.D: Providers must give the estimate before the service; she is not required to agree to an unknown price.
whyNot.E: Delaying indicated screening is not appropriate advice and the estimate addresses her concern.

items.objective: Advise an uninsured patient about price transparency protections.

items.stemHtml:
A policy analyst compares two fictional high-income countries. Indices are scaled so that Country N = 100.

MeasureCountry MCountry N
Health spending per person (index)200100
Physician visits per person per year4.06.5
Hospital days per person per year0.60.9
Price of a typical hospital stay (index)250100
Price of common brand-name drugs (index)260100
Administrative costs as share of spending8%3%

Which conclusion is best supported by these data?

options.label: A
options.html: Country M spends more because its residents use more physician visits

options.label: B
options.html: Country M spends more because its residents spend more days in hospital

options.label: C
options.html: Country M's spending gap is explained entirely by its administrative costs

options.label: D
options.html: Country M's higher spending shows that its residents receive better care

options.label: E
options.html: Country M's higher spending is driven mainly by higher prices, not more care

items.explanationHtml:
Spending is price × quantity. Country M uses less care (fewer visits and hospital days) yet spends twice as much, while its prices for hospital stays and drugs are 2.5–2.6 times higher. The gap is therefore driven mainly by prices, with higher administrative costs adding to it. This mirrors the usual finding when the US is compared with other high-income countries.

Takeaway: similar or lower use but much higher prices → prices drive the spending gap.

whyNot.A: Country M has fewer physician visits per person than Country N.
whyNot.B: Country M has fewer hospital days per person than Country N.
whyNot.C: A 5-point difference in administrative share cannot explain spending that is twice as high.
whyNot.D: The table contains no quality or outcome data, so no conclusion about quality is possible.

items.objective: Interpret international spending data to identify prices as the main driver.
